cradles.p:
For most of human history, people lived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants, moving with the seasons.

About 11,500 years ago, around 9500 BC, people in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East began planting wheat and barley and herding sheep and goats. Farming was invented separately in several other places too, including China, New Guinea and the Americas.

pins: One of the oldest towns on Earth

steps: One field of grain could feed far more people than the same land left wild.
Farmers grew more than they ate. Stored grain could feed people who did not farm.
Priests, soldiers, potters, metalworkers and rulers appeared.
Thousands of people lived together under kings, with laws, temples and taxes.

cradles.q: Why did farming let some people stop growing food?
a: Farmers produced a surplus that could feed others
Hunting became illegal
Kings banned farming in cities
Wild plants ran out everywhere
cradles.why: A surplus of grain could feed priests, craftsmen, soldiers and rulers.

cradles.p:
The first civilisations all grew up along great rivers: the Tigris and Euphrates in Iraq, the Nile in Egypt, the Indus in Pakistan and the Yellow River in China.

Rivers gave water and fertile silt for crops. But irrigation canals needed planning and labour, and whoever organised the water and the grain stores gained power.

cradles.s: The first civilisations grew up in deserts far from rivers.
cradles.why: They grew along great rivers, which supplied water and fertile soil.

cradles.p:
By about 3500 BC, Sumer in southern Iraq had true cities, such as Uruk, with tens of thousands of people, giant temples called ziggurats, and kings.

Around 3200 BC the Sumerians invented writing. It began as bookkeeping: marks pressed into clay to count grain and animals. Over time it grew into cuneiform, used to write laws, letters and the first great story, the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Around 3100 BC Egypt was united under one king, the pharaoh, who was treated as a god. Every summer the Nile flooded and left rich black soil behind, so Egypt was famously fertile.

The Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs and built huge tombs: the Great Pyramid of Giza rose around 2560 BC, and was the tallest building on Earth for almost 4,000 years.

In what is now Pakistan and north-west India, cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro peaked around 2600 to 1900 BC. They had straight grid streets, brick houses, and drains and toilets far ahead of their time.

Their writing has never been deciphered, so we still know little about their rulers or beliefs. After about 1900 BC the cities declined, probably partly because of drought and shifting rivers.

From about 1600 BC the Shang dynasty ruled the Yellow River valley. Shang kings asked their ancestors questions by cracking animal bones with heat and reading the cracks.

The questions and answers were carved on these 'oracle bones'. They are the oldest Chinese writing, and the script is the direct ancestor of the characters used in China today.

items: King Hammurabi carved 282 laws in stone: 'an eye for an eye'.
To track seasons, floods and festivals.

a: Sumer, in what is now Iraq
Ancient Greece
Rome
Shang China
cradles.why: Writing appeared in Sumer around 3200 BC, and in Egypt at about the same time.

a: Bones carved with the oldest Chinese writing
Egyptian mummies
Tools used to build the pyramids
Sumerian clay tablets
cradles.why: Shang kings used them to ask their ancestors questions; the carvings are the oldest Chinese script.

items: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent

cradles.p:
The Americas were cut off from Africa, Europe and Asia, yet people there invented farming, cities and states on their own, with crops such as maize, potatoes, beans and squash.

That civilisation appeared independently in several places suggests it follows naturally once people farm and live close together.

In Peru, Caral, of the Norte Chico culture, had pyramids and plazas by about 2600 BC, around the time Egypt's pyramids were being built.

In Mexico, the Olmecs, from about 1200 BC, carved colossal stone heads up to 3 metres tall. They are often called the 'mother culture' of later peoples such as the Maya.

cradles.s: Civilisation in the Americas was brought by travellers from Egypt.
cradles.why: It developed independently, with its own crops, cities and writing.

cradles.p:
Around 1200 BC many kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed in the 'Late Bronze Age collapse', amid drought, invasions and war. Cities burned and trade broke down.

Out of the ruins came new peoples and new ideas, including the alphabet, spread by the Phoenicians, which is the ancestor of the Greek and Latin letters you are reading now.

religions.p:
Hinduism has no single founder. In northern India, hymns called the Rigveda were composed from about 1500 BC, and over many centuries this Vedic religion grew into Hinduism.

Hindus worship many gods, often seen as forms of one ultimate reality. Key ideas include karma, that actions have consequences, and rebirth, the cycle of life, death and life again.

Around 500 BC a prince named Siddhartha Gautama left his palace to understand suffering. After years of searching he reached 'enlightenment' and became the Buddha, 'the awakened one'.

He taught that suffering comes from craving, and that a path of right living and meditation can end it.

About 250 BC the Indian emperor Ashoka, sickened by the slaughter of his own wars, embraced Buddhism and sent missionaries abroad.

Buddhism later faded in India itself, but it became central across Sri Lanka, South-East Asia, China, Korea and Japan.

religions.q: According to the Buddha, what causes suffering?
a: Craving
The gods
Bad luck
Poverty
religions.why: He taught that suffering comes from craving, and that it can be ended.

religions.p:
The Israelites of the land of Canaan came to worship a single God. After the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 586 BC, many were taken into exile, and in that time the Hebrew Bible took much of its final shape.

Judaism was one of the first religions to worship only one God, an idea called monotheism.

Around AD 30 the Romans crucified Jesus, a Jewish teacher, in Jerusalem. His followers believed he had risen from the dead and was the Son of God.

Missionaries such as Paul spread the faith across the Roman Empire. It was often persecuted, but in 380 Rome made Christianity its official religion.

pins: Christianity became the empire’s religion in 380

religions.p:
From 610 Muhammad, a merchant in Mecca in Arabia, preached that he received revelations from God, later written down as the Quran. Persecuted, he moved to Medina in 622, the first year of the Islamic calendar.

By his death in 632, most of Arabia followed Islam.

r: Christians: Jesus is the Son of God
Muslims: Muhammad is the final prophet

religions.p:
On the map, Christianity dominates the Americas, Europe, southern Africa and Oceania; Islam runs from North Africa through the Middle East to Indonesia; Hinduism is centred on India and Nepal; Buddhism on South-East and East Asia.

Many Chinese people follow no organised religion.

religions.q: Which religion has the most followers today?
a: Christianity
Islam
Hinduism
Buddhism
religions.why: About 2.3 billion Christians, ahead of about 2 billion Muslims.

religions.s: Buddhism is most widely followed today in India, where it began.
religions.why: It faded in India; today it is strongest in South-East and East Asia.

ancient.p:
In the 550s BC Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire. Under Darius I it ran from Egypt and Turkey to the Indus River: the largest empire the world had yet seen.

Persia ruled with a light touch. Conquered peoples kept their gods and customs, and Cyrus even let the exiled Jews return home. A Royal Road and a postal system tied the provinces together.

Greece's mountains and islands split it into hundreds of independent city-states, such as Athens and Sparta. They shared a language, gods and the Olympic Games, but often fought each other.

In 508 BC Athens began the world's first democracy: male citizens voted directly on laws in an assembly.

When Persia invaded Greece, the Greeks won against the odds: on land at Marathon in 490 BC, and at sea at Salamis in 480 BC.

Victory began Athens's golden age of theatre, philosophy and building, including the Parthenon. But Athens and Sparta then fought each other in the long Peloponnesian War, which Athens lost in 404 BC.

ancient.q: What did Athens begin in 508 BC?
a: Democracy
The Olympic Games
The Persian Empire
Christianity
ancient.why: Citizens voted on laws directly: the first democracy.

ancient.p: Athens produced thinkers who still shape how we reason. Socrates questioned everything and was executed in 399 BC. His student Plato imagined an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings; Plato's student Aristotle wrote on logic, science, ethics and politics, and tutored the young Alexander.

r: Ruled by two kings and elders
Every man trained as a soldier from age 7

ancient.p:
Philip II of Macedon, north of Greece, built a professional army and conquered the Greek cities. His son Alexander became king at 20.

In 334 BC Alexander invaded Persia. In eleven years he never lost a battle, took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, destroyed the Persian Empire and reached India. His soldiers refused to go further, and he died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

ancient.h: to conquer an empire from Greece to India
ancient.p: Alexander set out in 334 BC and reached the Indus by 326 BC. He spread Greek language and culture across all of it.

After his death his generals split the empire into rival kingdoms, such as the Ptolemies in Egypt, ending with Cleopatra.

But Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean for centuries, and Greek learning, from Plato and Aristotle to geometry and medicine, became a foundation of Western thought.

ancient.s: Alexander the Great lived to old age and died in Greece.
ancient.why: He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

ancient.p:
For centuries China was split into warring states. In 221 BC the state of Qin conquered all the others, and its king named himself the First Emperor.

He standardised writing, coins, weights and even cart axles, and linked walls in the north into an early Great Wall. He was buried with an army of about 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers.

pins: The capital, near the Terracotta Army

ancient.p:
The harsh Qin collapsed soon after the First Emperor died. The Han dynasty ruled from 202 BC to AD 220 and made Confucian scholars its officials.

Han China invented paper, opened the Silk Road and was as large and rich as Rome at the same time. To this day most Chinese call themselves the Han people.

ancient.q: Who first united China, in 221 BC?
a: The First Emperor of Qin
Confucius
Kublai Khan
Alexander the Great
ancient.why: He ended the Warring States period and standardised writing, coins and weights.

ancient.p: In 322 BC Chandragupta Maurya founded India's first great empire, which under his grandson Ashoka covered almost the whole subcontinent. After a bloody war in Kalinga, Ashoka turned to Buddhism and carved edicts on pillars urging non-violence and tolerance.

Under the Gupta dynasty, about AD 320–550, northern India had a golden age of science, art and literature. Indian mathematicians developed the decimal place-value system and the concept of zero as a number; through Arab scholars these became the numbers used worldwide.

ancient.q: Where does our system of numbers, with zero, come from?
a: Ancient India, via Arab scholars
Ancient Rome
Ancient Egypt
Medieval England
ancient.why: Indian mathematicians developed decimal place value and zero.

silk.p:
In 138 BC the Han emperor sent the envoy Zhang Qian west to find allies. He brought back news of rich kingdoms, and of strong horses China wanted for its cavalry.

Soon caravans of camels were linking China, through Central Asian oasis cities such as Kashgar, Samarkand and Bukhara, to Persia and the Mediterranean.

It was not one road but a web of routes, and few merchants travelled the whole way. Goods passed from trader to trader, city to city, with Sogdian and Persian merchants as key middlemen. Each sale added to the price.

silk.s: Most merchants carried their goods all the way from China to Rome.
silk.why: Goods were passed along by many middlemen; few people made the whole journey.

silk.p:
At sea, ships rode the monsoon winds: they blow from the south-west in summer and from the north-east in winter. Sailors could cross the Indian Ocean one way and return months later.

Ships linked China, South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, and sea transport was cheaper than camels.

From 1405 to 1433 the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean, as far as Arabia and East Africa. His treasure ships were among the largest wooden ships ever built.

Then China stopped the voyages and turned inward, decades before Europeans arrived by sea.

silk.q: What made long sea voyages across the Indian Ocean predictable?
a: The monsoon winds
Steam engines
Ocean currents from the Arctic
Roman roads
silk.why: The monsoon blows one way in summer and the other in winter.

silk.p:
The routes carried ideas as well as goods. Buddhism spread from India into China, Korea and Japan. Islam spread into Central Asia and, by sea, to Indonesia and Malaysia.

Paper reached the Islamic world in the 700s and Europe centuries later.

silk.h: The Mongols and the Black Death
silk.p:
In the 1200s the Mongol Empire controlled almost the whole land route, making it safer than ever: the age of Marco Polo.

But in the 1340s the routes also carried the Black Death, a plague that killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people.

Venice and Muslim traders controlled the spice trade into Europe, and prices were high. So the Portuguese looked for their own sea route to Asia.

In 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India. The age of the Silk Road was giving way to the age of European ships.
Long before European rule, Africa had powerful kingdoms, great cities and long-distance trade. Africa's history is often told as if it began with colonisation; it did not.

In what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, the kingdom of Aksum traded across the Red Sea from about AD 100, minted its own coins and became Christian in the 300s. Ethiopia's Christian kingdom lasted into modern times.

In West Africa, empires grew rich on gold traded across the Sahara: Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai. Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning.

In 1324 Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca with so much gold that he lowered its price in Cairo for years. He may have been one of the richest people in history.

silk.h: The Swahili coast and Great Zimbabwe
silk.p:
On the east coast, Swahili city-states such as Kilwa and Mombasa traded gold, ivory and slaves with Arabia, India and China across the Indian Ocean.

Inland, Great Zimbabwe, built of fitted stone without mortar, controlled the gold trade from about 1100 to 1450.

In West Africa's forests, the kingdom of Benin, in today's Nigeria, was famous for its bronze sculptures. In central Africa, the Kongo kingdom's king converted to Christianity and exchanged ambassadors with Portugal and the Pope in the 1500s.

a: A ruler of Mali famed for his gold
An Ethiopian emperor
A Portuguese explorer
The builder of Great Zimbabwe
silk.why: His 1324 pilgrimage spread Mali’s fame to Europe and the Middle East.

items: Great Zimbabwe at its height ends

rome.p:
Rome began as a small town on the River Tiber in central Italy. According to legend, it was founded in 753 BC by Romulus.

Around 509 BC the Romans threw out their king and set up a republic: elected officials called consuls, advised by the Senate. No one man was supposed to rule.

Rome conquered Italy, then fought three wars against Carthage, a trading power in North Africa. The Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants, but in 146 BC Rome destroyed Carthage.

Rome then took Greece and the east. The Mediterranean became 'our sea'.

Victories brought slaves and wealth, but also civil wars between generals. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul (France), seized power and was murdered by senators in 44 BC.

His adopted heir Octavian won the next civil war. In 27 BC he became Augustus, the first emperor. The forms of the republic remained, but one man ruled.

rome.q: Who became the first Roman emperor, in 27 BC?
a: Augustus
Julius Caesar
Hannibal
Constantine
rome.why: Julius Caesar was murdered in 44 BC; his heir Octavian became Augustus.

rome.s: Julius Caesar was the first Roman emperor.
rome.why: Caesar was a dictator who was killed in 44 BC; Augustus was the first emperor.

rome.p:
Augustus began two centuries of relative peace, the Pax Romana. Trade flowed along 80,000 km of paved roads and across the sea.

Under the emperor Trajan, in AD 117, the empire reached its largest: from northern Britain to Egypt and Mesopotamia, with perhaps 60 million people.
Built for the legions, they carried trade and ideas too. Some are still used as routes today.

items: Disciplined, well-trained soldiers guarding long frontiers.
Conquered peoples could become Romans; in 212 almost all free men were.
Cities with baths, arenas and running water.

rome.q: What were Roman roads mainly built for?
a: Moving the army quickly
Racing chariots
Pilgrims to Jerusalem
Marking the empire’s border
rome.why: They moved the legions, and with them trade and ideas.

rome.p:
In the 200s the empire nearly collapsed amid civil wars, invasions and plague. Later emperors split it into eastern and western halves to rule it better.

The emperor Constantine backed Christianity and in 330 founded a new capital, Constantinople. In 380 Christianity became the official religion.

From 395 the empire was split for good. Germanic peoples, pushed west by the Huns, settled inside the western half. The Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, and in 476 the last western emperor was deposed.

The richer East, with its walled capital, survived as the Byzantine Empire until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

rome.h: Why the West fell and the East survived

rome.p: Latin grew into Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian, and the Latin alphabet is now the most used in the world. Roman law shapes the legal systems of much of Europe and Latin America, and the Catholic Church kept Rome's language and organisation.

items: The last western emperor is deposed

americas.p:
In the jungles of southern Mexico and Guatemala, Maya city-states flourished from about AD 250 to 900, the Classic period. Cities such as Tikal had stone pyramids, ball courts and tens of thousands of people.

The Maya had the Americas' most complete writing system, a calendar of remarkable accuracy and the concept of zero. Many southern cities were abandoned around 900, probably after drought and war, but Maya people still live there today.

In about 1325 the Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake, where Mexico City stands now. By 1500 it was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 200,000 people, causeways, canals and floating gardens.

The Aztec Empire was a network of conquered city-states that paid tribute. Its religion demanded human sacrifice, which made it many enemies.

In the Andes, the Inca ruler Pachacuti began a rapid expansion around 1438. By 1530 the Inca Empire ran 4,000 km along the mountains, from Ecuador to Chile: the largest empire in the Americas.

With no wheels or writing, it was held together by 40,000 km of roads, relay runners, rope bridges, storehouses and knotted cords called quipu for record-keeping.

items: Roads, terraces and a vast empire.

americas.q: How did the Inca keep records without writing?
a: With knotted cords called quipu
On clay tablets
With oracle bones
On papyrus scrolls
americas.why: Coloured, knotted strings recorded numbers such as taxes and census counts.

americas.p: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean, believing he had found Asia. Spanish settlers soon took the islands, and the native Taíno people were almost wiped out by forced labour and disease.
In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with about 500 men. He won thousands of allies among peoples who hated the Aztecs, above all the Tlaxcalans. After a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell in 1521.

In 1532 Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than 200 men, captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa, who had just won a civil war against his brother. Pizarro took a room full of gold as ransom, then executed him anyway and took Cusco.

americas.h: Why so few could conquer so many
steps: Smallpox and other European diseases killed most native people, who had no immunity.
Many native peoples joined the Spanish against their Aztec or Inca rulers.
The Inca had just fought a civil war; the Aztecs were already hated by subjects.
Steel swords, armour, horses and guns gave an edge in battle.

americas.h: of native people died in the century after 1492
americas.p: Mostly from diseases such as smallpox and measles. Estimates vary widely, but it was among the worst population collapses in history.

americas.s: Disease killed more native Americans than Spanish weapons did.
americas.why: Smallpox and other diseases spread ahead of the conquerors and devastated populations.

islam.p:
Around 610, Muhammad, a merchant in the trading town of Mecca in Arabia, began to preach that there is one God, Allah, and that he was God's messenger. His revelations were later written down as the Quran.

Mecca's leaders, who profited from pilgrims to its many idols, persecuted his followers.

In 622 Muhammad and his followers moved to Medina. This migration, the Hijra, is year one of the Islamic calendar.

In Medina he led a community, fought Mecca and won it over in 630. By his death in 632 most of Arabia was Muslim.

items: There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger.
Five times a day, facing Mecca.
From dawn to dusk in the month of Ramadan.
To Mecca, once in a lifetime if possible.

islam.q: Why is 622 year one of the Islamic calendar?
a: Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina
Muhammad was born
The Quran was completed
Muslims conquered Jerusalem
islam.why: The Hijra, the move to Medina, began the Muslim community.

islam.p:
After Muhammad died, his successors, the caliphs, led the Muslim community. Arab armies burst out of Arabia, into two great empires exhausted by fighting each other: the Byzantines and the Persians.

Between 636 and 651 they took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and all of Persia.

Muslims disagreed over who should lead them. Those who became the Shia believed leadership belonged to Muhammad's family, through his cousin and son-in-law Ali. The majority, the Sunni, accepted the elected caliphs.

The split hardened after Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680. Today about 85 to 90% of Muslims are Sunni; Iran and Iraq have Shia majorities.

Under the Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus, the conquests reached Spain in 711 and Sindh in India in 711–712. By 732, a century after Muhammad's death, the caliphate stretched from the Atlantic to Central Asia.

In 750 a rival family, the Abbasids, overthrew the Umayyads and built a new capital, Baghdad.

islam.h: from Arabia to Spain and India
islam.p: One of the fastest expansions in history: the caliphate became larger than the Roman Empire at its height.

islam.why: About 85 to 90% are Sunni; Shia majorities are in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Bahrain.

islam.p:
The Abbasid capital, Baghdad, became perhaps the largest city in the world. In its House of Wisdom, scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and went beyond them.

Paper, learned from China, made books cheap.

items: The word comes from his book's title; 'algorithm' from his name.
His Canon was taught in European universities for 500 years.

islam.q: Where does the word 'algorithm' come from?
a: The name of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi
A Greek god
Latin for counting
A Chinese emperor
islam.why: Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad in the 800s; his book also gave us the word algebra.

crusades.p:
When the Western Roman Empire fell in 476, Europe broke into Germanic kingdoms. Towns shrank, trade fell and most people became farmers on great estates. This thousand-year period, from about 500 to 1500, is called the Middle Ages.

The Church survived Rome's fall and became the one institution shared across western Europe.

Charlemagne, king of the Franks, conquered most of western Europe. On Christmas Day 800 the Pope crowned him emperor, reviving the idea of a Roman Empire in the West.

His empire was split among his grandsons in 843; its western part grew into France and its eastern part into Germany.

steps: Granted land to great lords in return for loyalty and soldiers.
Held land, ran courts, and fought on horseback for their lord.
Most people. Farmed the lord's land; serfs could not leave it.
Owned vast lands, ran monasteries and schools, and took a tenth of everyone's produce.
crusades.p: Land was wealth and power. Everyone owed service to someone above them.

From 793 Vikings from Scandinavia raided Europe's coasts, then settled in England, Ireland, Normandy, Iceland and Russia. Their descendants, the Normans, conquered England in 1066 under William the Conqueror at the Battle of Hastings.

In 1215 English barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta, the 'Great Charter'. It said even the king had to obey the law and could not jail free men without a lawful judgement.

It was soon broken, but it became a symbol of limited government that later inspired parliaments and the US Constitution.

a: That even the king must obey the law
That England would become a republic
That the Pope ruled England
That serfs were free
crusades.why: It was a landmark for the idea of limited government.

crusades.s: Most people in medieval Europe were knights.
crusades.why: Most were peasants who farmed the land; knights were a small elite.

crusades.p:
In 1071 the Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantine army and overran Anatolia. The Byzantine emperor asked the West for help.

In 1095 Pope Urban II, at Clermont in France, called on Christians to free Jerusalem from Muslim rule, promising forgiveness of their sins. Tens of thousands of knights and peasants took the cross.

In 1099, after a long and brutal march, the crusaders took Jerusalem and massacred much of its population, Muslim and Jewish.

They set up four crusader states along the eastern Mediterranean: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Tripoli, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Edessa.

crusades.q: Who called the First Crusade in 1095?
a: Pope Urban II
Saladin
Richard the Lionheart
The Byzantine emperor
crusades.why: He called it at Clermont in France.

steps: Freeing the holy places and earning forgiveness for sins.
Younger sons of nobles hoped for land of their own.
Knights answered the call of their lords and church.

crusades.p: Muslim rulers slowly united against the crusaders. Edessa fell in 1144. Then Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, crushed the crusader army at Hattin in 1187 and retook Jerusalem, this time without a massacre.

Europe's kings, including England's Richard the Lionheart, launched the Third Crusade (1189–1192). They won back part of the coast, but never Jerusalem. Richard and Saladin made a truce letting Christian pilgrims visit.

The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land. In 1204, deep in debt to Venice, the crusaders attacked and sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city, and split the Byzantine Empire.

The wound between Catholic and Orthodox Christians never fully healed.

crusades.s: The Fourth Crusade sacked the Christian city of Constantinople.
crusades.why: In 1204 it attacked the Byzantine capital instead of reaching the Holy Land.

crusades.p: In 1291 the Mamluks of Egypt took Acre, the last crusader stronghold. The crusades had failed in their aim, but they deepened hostility between Christians, Muslims and Jews, and boosted trade between Europe and the East.

In 1347 a plague, carried by fleas on rats along trade routes from Central Asia, reached Europe through the Black Sea port of Kaffa and Italian ships. In five years it killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people.

Whole villages vanished. Some blamed the Jews, and massacred Jewish communities.

crusades.h: Europeans killed by the Black Death, 1347–51
crusades.p: Perhaps 25 to 50 million people. It took Europe 200 years to recover its population.

steps: With so many dead, labour was scarce.
Peasants could demand more pay or leave for better lords.
Rulers tried to freeze wages; peasants rose up, as in England's revolt of 1381.
In western Europe the old feudal bonds weakened.

crusades.p:
England and France fought on and off from 1337 to 1453 over the French throne. English longbowmen won famous victories such as Agincourt (1415), but a peasant girl, Joan of Arc, inspired a French revival before she was burned in 1431. France won.

That same year, 1453, the Ottomans took Constantinople. Many historians mark the end of the Middle Ages around then.

pins: Joan of Arc lifts the siege, 1429

mongol.p:
On the steppes of Mongolia, a boy named Temüjin survived poverty and enemies to unite the warring Mongol tribes. In 1206 he was proclaimed Genghis Khan, 'universal ruler'.

He organised his people into an army of units of ten, a hundred and a thousand, promoted men for loyalty and skill, and punished disobedience with death.

Every Mongol warrior was a horseman from childhood, with several horses each. They could ride 100 km a day, fire arrows at the gallop, fake retreats and encircle their enemies.

Cities that surrendered were usually spared. Cities that resisted were often destroyed and their people killed, a reputation that made many surrender.
When the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia killed his envoys, Genghis Khan destroyed it (1219–21). Great cities such as Samarkand, Bukhara and Merv were sacked and huge numbers killed.

mongol.q: How did the Mongols usually treat a city that surrendered without a fight?
a: They usually spared it
They always destroyed it
They made it the capital
They converted it to Buddhism
mongol.why: Surrender usually meant survival; resistance often meant destruction.

mongol.p:
Genghis Khan's sons and grandsons kept conquering. Batu took the Russian principalities and Kyiv (1237–40). Hülegü sacked Baghdad in 1258 and ended the Abbasid caliphate. Kublai Khan conquered Song China by 1279.

The empire split into four khanates: the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde in Russia, the Chagatai in Central Asia and the Ilkhanate in Persia.

mongol.h: the largest land empire in history
mongol.p: At its height the Mongol Empire ran from Korea to Hungary, about a sixth of the world’s land.

Kublai Khan ruled China as the Yuan dynasty from Beijing, where Marco Polo claimed to have served him. His invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281, were wrecked by storms the Japanese called kamikaze, 'divine winds'.

Under Mongol rule, trade along the Silk Road was safer than ever, and ideas, goods and people moved across Eurasia. But the same routes spread the Black Death in the 1340s.

In 1368 the Ming drove the Mongols out of China. In Russia, the Golden Horde's power faded over the next century.

mongol.q: Which city did Hülegü sack in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate?
a: Baghdad
Beijing
Kyiv
Constantinople
mongol.why: The sack of Baghdad was one of the great catastrophes of the medieval Islamic world.

items: The Ming drive out the Yuan

ottoman.p:
Around 1300 a Turkish leader named Osman founded a small state in north-west Anatolia, on the edge of the weakening Byzantine Empire. His dynasty, the Ottomans, would rule for over 600 years.

They crossed into Europe in the 1350s and conquered much of the Balkans.

In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople with huge cannon and broke its ancient walls. The last Byzantine emperor died fighting, ending the Roman Empire in the East.

The city, later called Istanbul, became the Ottoman capital, and the great church of Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

Selim I conquered Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia (1516–17). His son Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–66) took Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529 and made the empire a great naval power.

At its height the empire ruled south-east Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.

a: Mehmed II
Suleiman the Magnificent
Saladin
Osman
ottoman.why: His cannon broke the city’s walls, ending the Byzantine Empire.

ottoman.p:
In 1683 the Ottomans besieged Vienna a second time and failed. A long retreat began: Hungary was lost by 1699.

Europe's armies, economies and technology were pulling ahead, and Russia pushed south towards the Black Sea.

In the 1800s nations broke away one by one: Greece, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria. Egypt went its own way. European powers lent money and meddled.

Reformers tried to modernise the army, law and schools, and in 1908 the Young Turks forced the sultan to restore a constitution.

The Ottomans joined World War I on Germany's side and lost. Britain and France divided its Arab lands, and an Allied army occupied Istanbul.

Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk, led a war of independence. The sultanate was abolished in 1922, and in 1923 the Republic of Turkey was founded.

l: Egypt, much of North Africa, the Hejaz

ottoman.s: The Ottoman Empire fought on the winning side in World War I.
ottoman.why: It fought with Germany and lost; it was broken up afterwards.

items: The second siege of Vienna fails
The Republic of Turkey is founded

old.p: Europe still has five microstates left over from older times. San Marino claims to date from 301, the oldest surviving republic. Andorra has been shared since 1278 between a French ruler (today France's president) and a Catalan bishop. The Grimaldi family has ruled Monaco since 1297. Liechtenstein became a principality in 1719, and Vatican City was created in 1929.

In the age of European empires, a few countries kept their independence. Japan and Thailand modernised fast and played rivals off against each other. Iran and Nepal survived between empires.

Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896, a victory celebrated across Africa.

Some others were never formally colonies but came close: Afghanistan's foreign policy was run by Britain for decades; Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, lost land to its neighbours; Bhutan was guided by Britain and then India; Ethiopia was occupied by Italy from 1936 to 1941.

old.q: Which African country defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896?
a: Ethiopia
Egypt
Liberia
Morocco
old.why: Victory at Adwa kept Ethiopia independent when almost all of Africa was colonised.

old.s: Thailand was never colonised by a European power.
old.why: Thailand stayed independent, a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina.

explore.p:
In the 1400s Venice and Muslim traders controlled the overland spice trade, and pepper, cloves and nutmeg were worth a fortune in Europe. Portugal and Spain, on the Atlantic edge, wanted their own route to Asia.

New ships called caravels, the compass and better maps made long ocean voyages possible.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, an Italian sailing for Spain, crossed the Atlantic, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west. He landed in the Caribbean, and believed until he died that he had reached the Indies.

In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas split the newly found lands between Spain and Portugal along a line in the Atlantic.

In 1498 the Portuguese Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India, opening the sea route to the spice trade.

In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan, sailing for Spain, set out west. He was killed in the Philippines, but in 1522 one of his five ships returned to Spain: the first voyage around the world.

explore.q: What was the first voyage around the world?
a: Magellan's expedition, 1519–1522
Columbus's first voyage
Vasco da Gama's voyage to India
Zheng He's voyages
explore.why: Magellan died on the way, but one ship made it home in 1522.

explore.p:
Spain conquered the Aztecs and Inca and built an empire from Mexico to Chile. In 1545 a mountain of silver was found at Potosí in Bolivia; Spanish silver flowed to Europe and to China, creating the first truly global trade.

Portugal took Brazil and a chain of trading forts from Africa to India, Malacca and Macau.

Crops, animals and diseases crossed the ocean both ways. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chillies spread around the world; horses, cattle, wheat and sugar came to the Americas.

Smallpox and other diseases killed most of the native peoples of the Americas.

explore.s: Potatoes and tomatoes came to Europe from the Americas.
explore.why: Both were unknown outside the Americas before 1492.

explore.p:
Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean needed huge numbers of workers. Europeans bought captives from African rulers and traders along the coast and shipped them across the Atlantic.

Ships carried goods to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco and cotton back to Europe.
About 1.8 million died on the crossing, the Middle Passage. Most of the rest were taken to Brazil and the Caribbean; about 400,000 to North America.

explore.note: Arrivals, from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (rounded).

explore.p:
Enslaved people resisted, from revolts to the Haitian Revolution. Campaigners, many of them Quakers and former slaves, built movements against the trade.

Britain banned the trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire in 1833; the US ended slavery in 1865 after the Civil War, and Brazil, the last in the Americas, in 1888.

explore.q: Which country received the most enslaved Africans?
a: Brazil
The United States
Britain
Spain
explore.why: Almost 5 million were taken to Brazil, the last country in the Americas to end slavery, in 1888.

reformation.p:
From about 1400, in the rich trading cities of Italy, scholars and artists rediscovered the learning of ancient Greece and Rome. The French word Renaissance means 'rebirth'.

They called their outlook humanism: a belief in human potential and in studying this world, not only the next.

Florence, grown rich on banking and wool, was the centre. Its leading banking family, the Medici, paid artists and scholars.

Artists studied anatomy and used perspective to make paintings look three-dimensional. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with inventions; Michelangelo carved David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, in Mainz, Germany, built a printing press with movable metal type. A book that took a scribe months could now be printed in days.

By 1500 European presses had printed millions of books. Ideas spread faster than ever, making the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution possible.

items: Painter, engineer and anatomist: the Mona Lisa, the Last Supper.
Sculptor of David; painter of the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
The Prince: politics as it is, not as it should be.

reformation.q: What did Gutenberg’s printing press do?
a: Made books cheap and fast to produce
Invented paper
Translated the Bible into Latin
Built the first library
reformation.why: It spread ideas faster than ever before.

reformation.s: The Renaissance began in the trading cities of Italy.
reformation.why: Rich cities such as Florence and Venice paid for artists and scholars.

reformation.p: In 1500 Western Europe was united in one Catholic Church, led by the Pope in Rome. But many complained of corruption: church offices were bought and sold, and the church sold 'indulgences', promising less time in purgatory for a payment.

In 1517 Martin Luther, a German monk and professor, published 95 theses attacking indulgences, in Wittenberg.

Luther taught that people are saved by faith alone, not by good works or payments, and that the Bible, not the Pope, is the final authority. He translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it.

Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, from about 1450, made Luther's pamphlets spread across Germany within weeks. Hundreds of thousands of copies were printed.

The Church excommunicated Luther, but German princes protected him. His followers became known as Protestants.

reformation.q: What did Luther attack in his 95 theses?
a: The sale of indulgences
The printing press
The Ottoman Empire
The English king
reformation.why: Indulgences promised less punishment after death in return for money.

reformation.s: The printing press helped Luther’s ideas spread quickly.
reformation.why: Cheap printed pamphlets spread his ideas across Germany within weeks.

items: Luther's followers; princes chose their land's faith.
Followers of John Calvin of Geneva.
Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 to end his marriage.

reformation.p: The Catholic Church fought back. The Council of Trent (1545–63) reformed abuses but restated Catholic beliefs. New orders such as the Jesuits ran schools and sent missionaries worldwide, and Catholic rulers suppressed Protestants.

Religious wars tore Europe apart. In 1618 a Protestant revolt in Bohemia began the Thirty Years' War, which pulled in most of Europe. Parts of Germany lost a third or more of their people.

The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended the wars of religion and recognised states as sovereign: rulers, not the Pope, decided their own affairs.

By 1600 the map was set much as it still is: Catholic in the south and in Ireland and Poland; Lutheran in north Germany and Scandinavia; Reformed in the Netherlands, Scotland and parts of Switzerland; Anglican in England; Orthodox in the east.

reformation.q: Why did Henry VIII break with the Pope?
a: The Pope would not end his marriage
He became a Lutheran monk
The Pope invaded England
He wanted to join the Ottomans
reformation.why: Refused an annulment, Henry made himself head of the Church of England in 1534.

items: Henry VIII heads the English church

reformation.p:
For centuries Europeans had trusted ancient authorities such as Aristotle and the Church's teaching. In the 1500s and 1600s scientists began to test ideas by observation, experiment and mathematics.

This new scientific method changed how humans understand the world.

In 1543 Copernicus, a Polish astronomer, argued that the Earth goes around the Sun, not the other way round.

Galileo, in Italy, used a new telescope to see moons circling Jupiter and supported Copernicus. In 1633 the Church put him on trial and forced him to take it back; he spent his last years under house arrest.

In 1687 Isaac Newton, in England, published his laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation: the same force that makes an apple fall holds the planets in their orbits.

The universe, it seemed, ran by laws that humans could discover, an idea that powered the Enlightenment.

steps: Test it in a way others can repeat.
Keep, change or reject the idea based on the evidence.

a: The Earth goes around the Sun
The Earth is flat
Gravity holds the planets
Jupiter has moons
reformation.why: This heliocentric idea overturned 1,400 years of belief.

items: Copernicus says the Earth circles the Sun

asiaemp.p:
In 1526 Babur, a descendant of both Genghis Khan and Timur, rode from Afghanistan into India, won at Panipat with cannon and founded the Mughal Empire.

At its height the Mughals ruled almost all of the Indian subcontinent and were among the richest rulers on Earth.

Akbar (1556–1605) won over his many Hindu subjects by ending a tax on non-Muslims and inviting scholars of all faiths to debate.

His grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife. But Aurangzeb (1658–1707) fought endless wars and imposed stricter Islamic rule; after his death the empire broke up.
The English East India Company came to trade. As the Mughals weakened, it used its own army to win Bengal at Plassey in 1757, and over the next century it took most of India.

asiaemp.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal?
a: Shah Jahan
Akbar
Babur
Aurangzeb
asiaemp.why: He built it in Agra as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

asiaemp.p:
In 1644 rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. The Manchus, from north-east of the Great Wall, swept in and founded the Qing dynasty, the last to rule China.

They made Han Chinese men wear the Manchu queue hairstyle as a sign of loyalty.

Under the Qing emperors Kangxi and Qianlong, China doubled in size, adding Taiwan, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet. Its population rose to about 300 million by 1800, and China made perhaps a third of the world's goods.

asiaemp.s: The Qing were the last dynasty to rule China.
asiaemp.why: They ruled from 1644 until the revolution of 1911–12.

asiaemp.p:
From the 1580s Russian Cossacks and fur traders pushed east across Siberia, river by river. In 1647 they founded Okhotsk on the Pacific coast.

In about 60 years Russia had crossed Asia, making it the largest country on Earth.

Peter the Great (1682–1725) modernised Russia on western lines and built a new capital, St Petersburg. Catherine the Great (1762–96) took Crimea and much of Poland.

In the 1800s Russia conquered the Caucasus and Central Asia.

items: The East India Company wins at Plassey

asiaemp.p:
In the 1500s Japan was torn by wars between rival lords, the daimyo, and their samurai warriors. In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara, and in 1603 he became shogun, military ruler in the emperor's name.

His family ruled Japan for over 250 years of peace from Edo, today's Tokyo.

Fearing Christian missionaries and foreign influence, the shoguns banned Christianity and in the 1630s closed Japan to almost all foreigners. Only Dutch and Chinese traders could visit, at Nagasaki.

Inside, Japan prospered: cities grew, and kabuki theatre, woodblock prints and haiku poetry flourished.

pins: The only door for Dutch traders

asiaemp.p: In 1853 US warships under Commodore Perry sailed into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open to trade. The shogunate gave way, which discredited it. In 1868 reformers overthrew it and restored the emperor: the Meiji Restoration launched Japan's race to modernise.

asiaemp.q: Who held real power in Tokugawa Japan?
a: The shogun
The emperor
The Dutch
The Pope
asiaemp.why: The emperor reigned; the shogun ruled.

industry.p: Around 1760, in Britain, people began making goods with machines and steam power instead of by hand. It was the biggest change in how people lived since farming.

steps: Plenty of it, near the surface, to fuel engines and smelt iron.
Banks, investors and an empire to buy goods and supply cotton.
It paid to replace expensive workers with machines.
A culture of tinkering, patents and practical science.

industry.p:
The first factories spun cotton. Richard Arkwright's water-powered mill at Cromford opened in 1771.

James Watt improved the steam engine, and from 1776 his engines went into commercial use. Steam could power factories anywhere, not just by rivers, and later drove trains and ships.

In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first to run entirely on steam with timetabled trains. Within 20 years Britain had 10,000 km of track.

Food, goods and people could cross the country in hours instead of days.

industry.q: What did Watt's steam engine make possible?
a: Factories that did not need to be beside rivers
The first printing press
Electric light
Flight
industry.why: Steam power freed factories from waterwheels; later it drove trains and ships.

industry.p:
Industry spread from Britain in waves: to Belgium, France, the north-eastern US and Germany by about 1870; then to Russia, Japan, Italy and others by 1914.

Around 1900 the United States became the world's largest industrial economy.

Japan was closed to the world until US warships arrived in 1853. In 1868 the Meiji Restoration put reformers in power, who set out to industrialise as fast as possible. Its first railway opened in 1872, and by 1905 Japan could defeat Russia in war.

items: Cheap steel for rails, ships and skyscrapers.
Light bulbs, motors and power grids.

industry.s: The Industrial Revolution began in the United States.
industry.why: It began in Britain around 1760; the US overtook it as the largest industrial economy around 1900.

industry.p:
Millions left farms for factory towns. In 1801 about 1 in 3 people in England and Wales lived in towns; by 1901, about 3 in 4.

The new cities were crowded, smoky and unhealthy: children worked long shifts in mills and mines, and cholera spread through dirty water.

industry.h: Share of people living in towns, Britain
industry.note: Rounded census figures for England and Wales.

industry.p:
Workers formed trade unions and new ideas spread, from liberal reform to Karl Marx's communism. Laws limited child labour, cities built sewers, and over time wages and life expectancy rose.

Industry also made the West rich and powerful enough to dominate much of the world.

Industrial society also changed women's lives: more worked outside the home, and campaigners called suffragists and suffragettes demanded the vote.

New Zealand was the first country to let women vote, in 1893. Australia followed, then Finland and Norway; Britain in 1918 (fully in 1928), the US in 1920. Switzerland held out until 1971.

industry.q: Which was the first country to give women the vote?
a: New Zealand
Britain
The United States
France

industry.q: About how many people in England and Wales lived in towns by 1901?
a: About three in four
About one in ten
About one in five
Almost none
industry.why: Britain became the first mainly urban nation.

revolutions.p:
Inspired by the Scientific Revolution, 18th-century thinkers argued that reason, not tradition or religious authority, should guide how people live and are governed. They called their age the Enlightenment.

Paris salons, coffee houses and cheap printed pamphlets spread these ideas across Europe and to the American colonies.

items: People have natural rights to life, liberty and property; government rests on their consent.
Separate the powers of government so none becomes a tyrant.
Freedom of speech and religion; mocked intolerance.
The Social Contract: legitimate power comes from 'the general will' of the people.

steps: Everyone has rights simply by being human.
Rulers govern only with the agreement of the governed.
If government violates rights, the people may replace it.
Americans and French used these ideas to justify revolution.

revolutions.q: Which idea did John Locke argue for?
a: Government rests on the consent of the people
Kings rule by divine right
The Earth circles the Sun
Workers should own the factories
revolutions.why: Jefferson echoed him in the Declaration of Independence.

revolutions.s: Montesquieu argued for separating the powers of government.
revolutions.why: Legislative, executive and judicial powers, as in the US Constitution.

revolutions.p:
Britain's thirteen colonies in North America had their own assemblies. After an expensive war with France, Britain taxed them directly, and the colonists protested that they had no say in Parliament.

Protest turned to war in 1775. On 4 July 1776 the colonies declared independence, saying 'all men are created equal' with rights to 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness'.

With French help, George Washington's army won. Britain recognised American independence in 1783. The US Constitution of 1787 created a federal republic with checks and balances, which still governs the country.

revolutions.q: What did the American colonists object to?
a: Being taxed without a say in Parliament
French rule
The Catholic Church
The slave trade

revolutions.p:
France was nearly bankrupt, bread was expensive, and nobles and clergy paid little tax. In 1789 the king called an assembly to raise money; instead it declared itself the National Assembly.

On 14 July a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille prison. The Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed liberty and equality.

steps: Bastille stormed; rights of man declared.
France becomes a republic; King Louis XVI is executed.
The Terror: about 17,000 people officially executed.

revolutions.p:
Napoleon won brilliant victories and by 1810 dominated Europe from Spain to Poland. His law code, the Code Napoléon, spread equality before the law.

But in 1812 he invaded Russia with about 600,000 men; most never returned. He was finally beaten at Waterloo in 1815.

revolutions.q: Where was Napoleon finally defeated in 1815?
a: Waterloo
Moscow
Austerlitz
Trafalgar
revolutions.why: British, Dutch and Prussian armies beat him in what is now Belgium.

revolutions.s: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was a great success.
revolutions.why: His army was destroyed by battle, disease and the Russian winter.

revolutions.p:
In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up. Led by Toussaint Louverture and later Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, Spanish and British armies.

In 1804 Haiti became independent: the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people, and the first to abolish slavery for good.

When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808, Spain's American colonies began to govern themselves. Simón Bolívar in the north and José de San Martín in the south led wars of independence.

Victory at Ayacucho in Peru in 1824 sealed Spanish America's independence. Brazil broke from Portugal peacefully in 1822.

In about 50 years, revolutions turned most of the Americas from colonies into independent republics. They spread the ideas of citizenship, constitutions and national self-rule, ideas that would transform Europe too.

revolutions.q: What was the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people?
a: Haiti
Brazil
Liberia
Mexico
revolutions.why: Haiti won independence from France in 1804.

nations.p:
After Napoleon, a powerful new idea spread: that people who share a language, culture and history form a nation, and that each nation should rule itself in its own state.

It broke up empires and united divided peoples.
Greece won independence from the Ottomans in 1830 after a long war, and Belgium broke from the Netherlands the same year. Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria followed later in the century.

Italy was split into many states, some ruled by Austria. Led by the statesman Cavour of Piedmont and the soldier Garibaldi, whose volunteer 'Red Shirts' took Sicily and Naples in 1860, Italy was united as a kingdom in 1861. Rome was added in 1870.

Prussia's chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, united Germany through 'blood and iron': three short wars against Denmark, Austria and France. In 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the King of Prussia was proclaimed German emperor.

A powerful new empire now sat in the middle of Europe.

nations.q: Who united Germany through "blood and iron"?
a: Otto von Bismarck
Garibaldi
Napoleon
Cavour
nations.why: Bismarck’s wars against Denmark, Austria and France created the German Empire in 1871.

nations.p:
The US pushed west across North America, taking land from Native Americans. In the war with Mexico (1846–48) it took California and the south-west.

Then in 1861–65 the Civil War tested whether the nation would survive. The North won, the Union held, and slavery was ended.
Britain's settler colonies became self-governing dominions: Canada in 1867, Australia in 1901, New Zealand in 1907 and South Africa in 1910. They ran their own affairs but kept the British monarch.
In South America new states fought over borders and resources. In the War of the Pacific (1879–84) Chile took Bolivia's coast, leaving Bolivia landlocked to this day.

nations.s: Bolivia lost its coastline in a war with Chile.
nations.why: In the War of the Pacific, 1879–84.

scramble.h: An empire on which the sun never set
scramble.p:
By 1914 Britain ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people: Canada, Australia, India, much of Africa and islands across every ocean. It was the largest empire in history.

The Royal Navy ruled the seas, and London was the centre of world finance.

After a great rebellion in 1857, the British government took India from the East India Company, and in 1877 Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India. Indian soldiers, taxes and markets underpinned British power.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, and cut the voyage from London to India by thousands of kilometres. Britain bought a stake and in 1882 occupied Egypt to protect it.

scramble.h: of the world’s people were ruled by Britain in 1914
scramble.p: About 400 million people, most of them in India.

scramble.q: What did the Suez Canal link?
a: The Mediterranean and the Red Sea
The Atlantic and the Pacific
The Black Sea and the Baltic
The Indian Ocean and the Pacific
scramble.why: It opened in 1869 and greatly shortened the route to India.

scramble.p:
In 1870 Europeans held only about a tenth of Africa, mostly along the coasts. By 1914 they held about nine-tenths.

New medicine against malaria, steamboats and machine guns let them push inland. Rivalry drove them on: each power rushed to grab land before the others.

In 1884–85 European powers met in Berlin to set rules for claiming Africa. No Africans were invited.

Borders were drawn with rulers on maps, often cutting across peoples and kingdoms. Most of Africa's borders today still follow them.

Africans resisted, often fiercely. But conquest was brutal. In the Congo, run as the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium, millions died through forced labour for rubber. In Namibia, Germany killed most of the Herero and Nama peoples in 1904–08, now recognised as a genocide.

Only Ethiopia, which beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia stayed independent.

scramble.q: Which two African countries stayed independent in 1914?
a: Ethiopia and Liberia
Egypt and Morocco
Nigeria and Kenya
South Africa and Ghana
scramble.why: Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa; Liberia survived, though it lost land to its neighbours.

scramble.s: Africans were represented at the Berlin Conference that divided Africa.

scramble.p: Elsewhere, France took Indochina, the US took the Philippines in 1898, and Japan, now an industrial power, annexed Korea in 1910. By 1914 almost the whole world was ruled by a handful of empires.

ww1.p: In 1914 Europe was at the height of its power, but its great empires were rivals. Germany, united only in 1871, was building a navy to challenge Britain. France wanted back the land it lost to Germany in 1871. Austria-Hungary and Russia competed for the Balkans, where the Ottoman Empire was retreating.

steps: An arms race: huge armies, war plans ready, a naval race between Britain and Germany.
Europe split into two blocs, so a local war could pull everyone in.
Proud nations, and peoples such as the Serbs wanting their own states.

ww1.p:
On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was shot in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist.

Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, backed by Germany, declared war. Russia backed Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia and France, and invaded Belgium to reach France. Britain declared war on Germany. Within six weeks Europe was at war.

ww1.q: Where was Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated?
a: Sarajevo
Vienna
Berlin
Belgrade
ww1.why: He was shot there on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip.

ww1.p:
Germany's plan was to knock out France quickly, then turn east. It failed at the Marne in September 1914.

Both sides dug in. By the end of 1914 a line of trenches ran about 700 km from the Channel to Switzerland, and it barely moved for over three years.

Soldiers lived in mud, among rats, lice and the dead. Between the lines lay 'no man's land', crossed by barbed wire.

Machine guns, artillery and later poison gas made attacking across open ground suicidal. Generals kept trying to break through, at terrible cost.

In 1916 came the deadliest battles. At Verdun, Germany tried to 'bleed France white': the battle lasted ten months and cost around 700,000 casualties.

On 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, the British army suffered almost 60,000 casualties, about 19,000 of them killed. After five months the Allies had advanced about 10 km.

ww1.h: British casualties on the first day of the Somme
ww1.p: The worst day in the British army’s history: about 19,000 killed.

The war spread far beyond the Western Front: on the Eastern Front against Russia, in Italy, at Gallipoli in Turkey, in the Middle East and in Africa. Soldiers came from India, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Africa and beyond.

ww1.s: The trench lines on the Western Front moved hundreds of kilometres each year.
ww1.why: They barely moved between late 1914 and 1918.

ww1.p:
Two events changed everything in 1917. German submarines sinking American ships, and a German offer to help Mexico win back land from the US, brought the United States into the war in April.

In Russia, revolution overthrew the Tsar, and in November the Bolsheviks seized power. In March 1918 they made peace with Germany.

Freed from fighting Russia, Germany threw everything into a spring offensive in 1918 and came close to Paris. Then the Allies, with fresh American troops and new tanks, pushed back.

Germany's allies collapsed, its people were starving under a British naval blockade, and revolution broke out. The Kaiser fled.
At 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918, the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, the guns fell silent. It is still marked each year as Armistice or Remembrance Day.

ww1.note: Rounded estimates. In all about 9 to 10 million soldiers and millions of civilians died.

ww1.q: When did the fighting in World War I end?
a: 11 November 1918
28 June 1914
1 July 1916
ww1.why: The armistice came into force at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

ww1.p: The war destroyed four empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. Their emperors and sultans were gone within a few years.

In 1919 the winners met in Paris. The Treaty of Versailles made Germany accept guilt for the war, pay reparations, give up land and colonies, and limit its army to 100,000 men.

Many Germans felt humiliated, a resentment Hitler would exploit.

On the ruins came new nation-states: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states, Austria and Hungary. In the Middle East, Britain and France took the Ottoman Arab lands as League of Nations 'mandates'.

The new League of Nations was meant to keep the peace, but the US never joined.

ww1.q: Which of these countries was created after World War I?
a: Poland
Germany
Italy
France
ww1.why: Poland was reborn in 1918 after more than a century of partition.

ww1.s: The United States joined the League of Nations.
ww1.why: The US Senate rejected it, weakening the League from the start.

interwar.p:
War, hunger and defeat brought down the Tsar in March 1917. In November Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power, promising 'peace, land and bread'.

They won a brutal civil war and in 1922 founded the Soviet Union, the world's first communist state.

After Lenin died in 1924, Joseph Stalin won power. He forced peasants into collective farms and drove rapid industrialisation through five-year plans.

The cost was enormous: a famine in 1932–33 killed millions, especially in Ukraine, and in the Great Terror of 1936–38 hundreds of thousands were shot and many more sent to Gulag labour camps.

interwar.q: Who led the Bolshevik revolution in 1917?
a: Lenin
Stalin
The Tsar
Mussolini
interwar.why: Lenin led the Bolsheviks; Stalin took over after his death in 1924.

interwar.p: In Italy, Benito Mussolini's Fascists promised order and national glory. In 1922 they marched on Rome and the king made Mussolini prime minister. He soon became a dictator, the first fascist ruler.

In October 1929 the Wall Street stock market crashed. Banks failed, trade collapsed and unemployment soared around the world: a quarter of American workers lost their jobs.

In desperate times, many people turned to extremists who promised strong leadership.

interwar.note: Rough peak rates of the workforce, 1932–33.

interwar.p: In Germany, the Depression hit hard. The Nazi Party became the largest in parliament, and in January 1933 Adolf Hitler became chancellor. Within months he had banned other parties and made himself dictator.
Both were one-party dictatorships that crushed opponents, controlled the press and used terror.

interwar.s: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 began the Great Depression.
interwar.why: It set off a worldwide economic collapse.

interwar.p:
Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937. Italy conquered Ethiopia in 1935–36. Germany rearmed, sent troops into the Rhineland in 1936, and helped Franco's nationalists win the Spanish Civil War.

The League of Nations protested but did nothing effective.

Britain and France hoped to avoid another world war by giving way. Germany took Austria in March 1938, and at Munich in September they agreed it could take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia.

In March 1939 Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia. Then, in August, he and Stalin signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland.

interwar.q: What was the Munich Agreement of 1938?
a: Britain and France let Germany take the Sudetenland
Germany and the Soviet Union agreed to split Poland
The treaty that ended World War I
An alliance between Germany and Japan
interwar.why: It was the high point of appeasement.

ww2.p:
World War I ended in 1918. Just twenty-one years later the world was at war again, and this time it was bigger, deadlier and truly global.

To understand why, start with the peace that ended the first war.

ww2.h: From one war to the next
steps: Germany loses land and colonies, its army is capped at 100,000 men, it must pay huge reparations and accept the blame for the war. Most Germans feel humiliated.
A world economic crash. By 1932 about six million Germans are out of work, and many lose faith in democracy.
The Nazi Party promises to tear up Versailles, make Germany great again and blame its troubles on Jews and communists.
Germany rearms, marches into the Rhineland (1936), joins with Austria and takes the Sudetenland (1938).

ww2.p:
Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born World War I veteran who led the Nazi Party. Within months of becoming chancellor in 1933 he had made himself a dictator: other parties were banned, opponents were jailed and the press was controlled.

Nazi ideas were built on race. Hitler taught that Germans were a superior 'Aryan' race, that Jews were an enemy to be removed, and that Germany needed Lebensraum, 'living space', to be conquered in the east from Poland and the Soviet Union.

ww2.q: What did Hitler mean by Lebensraum, or 'living space'?
a: Land to be conquered in eastern Europe for Germans
Colonies in Africa and Asia
New housing for German workers
A neutral zone between Germany and France
ww2.why: Hitler planned to seize land in Poland and the Soviet Union, and to remove or enslave the people living there.

ww2.p: In the 1930s three states set out to build empires by force. Later they would be called the Axis.
items: Wanted to undo Versailles and conquer living space in the east.
Dreamed of a new Roman empire; invaded Ethiopia in 1935.
Seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded the rest of China in 1937.

ww2.p:
Britain and France remembered the slaughter of World War I and badly wanted to avoid another. So they appeased Hitler: they gave in to his demands, hoping each one would be the last.

At the Munich Agreement in September 1938 they let Germany take the Sudetenland, the German-speaking edge of Czechoslovakia. Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, promised 'peace for our time'.

In March 1939 Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia anyway. Appeasement had failed, and Britain and France promised to defend Poland if it was attacked.

ww2.s: At Munich in 1938, Britain and France went to war to stop Hitler taking the Sudetenland.
ww2.why: They did the opposite: they agreed to let him take it, hoping that would satisfy him.

ww2.p:
In August 1939 the world was stunned. Hitler and Stalin, the communist ruler of the Soviet Union and Hitler's sworn enemy, signed a pact promising not to attack each other.

Secretly, they also agreed to split Poland and eastern Europe between them. Now Hitler could attack Poland without fearing a war on two fronts. Nine days later, he did.

ww2.h: Put the road to war in order

ww2.p:
On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. Two days later Britain and France declared war on Germany. World War II had begun.

On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east, as the secret pact allowed. Within five weeks Poland was gone, divided between Germany and the Soviet Union.

Germany won with a new way of fighting called blitzkrieg, 'lightning war'. Tanks and dive-bombers punched a hole in the enemy line, fast troops poured through it and circled round behind, and the defenders were cut off before they could react.

The idea was speed: win short wars quickly, before a stronger alliance could gather.

pts: April
Germany invades Denmark and Norway
May
Germany attacks the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Its tanks race through the Ardennes forest, which the French thought too thick for tanks, going around France's Maginot Line forts
Late May
British and French troops are trapped at Dunkirk; 338,000 are rescued by sea
June
France surrenders. Germany occupies the north; a collaborating French government rules the south from Vichy

lines: The tanks' route to the sea

ww2.q: How did the German army get around France's main defences in 1940?
a: Through the Ardennes forest
By sea across the English Channel
Through Switzerland
By parachute into Paris
ww2.why: France's Maginot Line forts guarded the border, but German tanks went through the Ardennes, which the French thought impassable.

ww2.p: Warships, ferries and hundreds of small civilian boats carried them across the Channel to Britain. The army had lost its equipment, but it survived to fight again.

By the summer of 1940 Britain, with its empire and the Commonwealth, stood alone against Germany. Its new prime minister, Winston Churchill, refused to make peace.

Hitler needed control of the skies before he could invade. In the Battle of Britain, from July to October 1940, the Royal Air Force fought off the German air force, helped by radar that warned of each attack. Germany failed, and the invasion was called off.

Germany switched to the Blitz: night bombing of British cities that killed about 43,000 civilians.

hl: Germany and the lands it held
pins: Bombed for 57 nights in a row in the Blitz
Its centre was destroyed in one raid in November 1940

ww2.s: The Battle of Britain was fought mainly in the air.
ww2.why: It was a struggle between the RAF and the Luftwaffe for control of the skies over southern England.

ww2.p:
Italy joined the war in June 1940, as France was falling. In September 1940 Germany, Italy and Japan signed the Tripartite Pact, an alliance known as the Axis.

Italy's attacks on Egypt and Greece went badly, and Germany had to send help. By the spring of 1941 Germany controlled the Balkans, and Erwin Rommel's Afrika Korps was fighting the British in the North African desert.

The United States was neutral, and most Americans wanted to stay out of the war. But President Franklin D. Roosevelt believed Britain had to survive.

In March 1941 the Lend-Lease Act let the US send Britain, and later the Soviet Union and China, weapons, food and fuel without immediate payment. America became, in Roosevelt's words, 'the arsenal of democracy'.

On 22 June 1941 Hitler broke his pact with Stalin. More than three million German and allied soldiers invaded the Soviet Union along a front of almost 3,000 km: the largest invasion in history.

Hitler wanted the living space he had always talked about, the grain of Ukraine and the oil of the Caucasus, and the destruction of communism.

At first the Germans swept forward. Whole Soviet armies were surrounded and millions of soldiers taken prisoner; most of them would die in German captivity.

Leningrad was besieged for almost 900 days, and about a million of its people starved or froze. By December 1941 German troops could see the outskirts of Moscow. Then the Russian winter, fresh Soviet troops from Siberia and a counter-attack drove them back. Germany would not win a quick war after all.

pins: Germans reached its outskirts in December 1941

ww2.q: Why was invading the Soviet Union such a gamble for Germany?
a: Britain was still undefeated, so Germany now fought on two fronts
The Soviet Union was a German ally with a huge army
Germany had no tanks left after France
The US had already joined the war
ww2.why: With Britain still fighting in the west, Germany now faced the two-front war it had tried to avoid in 1939.

hl: Britain, still fighting in the west

ww2.p:
Japan had been at war in China since 1937, and was bogged down. It wanted an empire across East Asia, but it had almost no oil, rubber or metals of its own.

When Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941, the US, Britain and the Netherlands cut off its oil. Japan's leaders decided to seize the oil fields of the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia), and first to knock out the one force that could stop them: the US Pacific Fleet.

On the morning of 7 December 1941, Japanese aircraft from six carriers attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. They sank or damaged eight battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans.

But America's aircraft carriers were out at sea, and they survived. The next day the US declared war on Japan. On 11 December Hitler declared war on the United States. Now the war spanned the whole world.

ww2.s: The United States declared war on Germany first, and Germany responded.
ww2.why: Hitler declared war on the US on 11 December 1941, four days after Pearl Harbor. It was one of his biggest mistakes.

ww2.p:
In a few months Japan took Hong Kong, the Philippines, Malaya, Burma and the Dutch East Indies. In February 1942 the British base at Singapore fell, and some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops were taken prisoner: Britain's worst defeat.

Japan called its empire the 'Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere'. In practice its rule was brutal, with forced labour, massacres and millions of deaths.

l: Allies such as Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria
r: China, the Free French, Poland and many more
ww2.p: Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States were the 'Big Three'. They disagreed on almost everything except beating Hitler.

The Holocaust was the deliberate, organised murder of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators: two of every three Jews in Europe.

It was not a side effect of the war. For the Nazis, destroying the Jewish people was a central aim.

ww2.h: Jewish men, women and children murdered
ww2.p: About 1.5 million of them were children. The Nazis also murdered Roma, disabled people, Polish civilians and millions of Soviet prisoners of war.

pts: Nazis take power; Jews are pushed out of jobs and boycotted
The Nuremberg Laws strip German Jews of citizenship
Kristallnacht: synagogues burned and Jewish shops smashed across Germany
In occupied Poland, Jews are forced into sealed, starving ghettos, such as Warsaw's
Behind the invasion of the Soviet Union, killing squads shoot Jews in mass graves
The Wannsee Conference coordinates the 'Final Solution': deportation to death camps
Allied soldiers liberate the camps and find the survivors

ww2.p:
About a third of the victims were never deported. In the lands taken from the Soviet Union, mobile killing units shot Jews near their homes, often helped by local collaborators.

At Babi Yar, a ravine outside Kyiv, more than 33,000 Jews were shot in two days in September 1941.

From 1942 Jews from all over Europe were packed into freight trains and taken to death camps in occupied Poland: Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibor and Chełmno. Most were murdered in gas chambers within hours of arriving.

At Auschwitz alone about 1.1 million people were killed, about a million of them Jews.

ww2.q: Where did the Nazis build the main death camps?
a: In occupied Poland
In Germany's cities
In France
In the Soviet Union's far east
ww2.why: Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibor and Chełmno were all in occupied Poland.

ww2.note: Rounded estimates, using pre-war borders. Poland had Europe's largest Jewish community: about 90% of it was destroyed.

ww2.p:
Some fought back. In April 1943 the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto rose up against the Germans and held out for almost a month.

Some were saved. In October 1943 the Danes smuggled almost all of Denmark's 7,000 Jews across the sea to neutral Sweden. Bulgaria refused to hand over its own Jews, and in Albania families hid Jewish refugees.

ww2.s: Most Holocaust victims were killed inside Germany.
ww2.why: Most were killed in occupied Poland and in the occupied Soviet lands, far from German cities.

ww2.p:
After the war, Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg for crimes against humanity. A Polish-Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, coined a new word for the crime of destroying a people: genocide. In 1948 the United Nations made genocide a crime under international law.

The Holocaust also strengthened the case for a Jewish state, created in 1948 as Israel.

By late 1942 the Axis ruled from France to the edge of the Caspian Sea, and from Manchuria to the jungles of New Guinea.

Then, within a few months, three battles on three continents turned the war.

items: US code-breakers learned Japan's plan. Japan lost four aircraft carriers and never attacked on this scale again.
Britain's Eighth Army under Montgomery beat Rommel and saved the Suez Canal. By May 1943 the Axis was out of Africa.
The Red Army trapped a whole German army in the ruined city. About 91,000 Germans surrendered.

ww2.p:
In the summer of 1942 Hitler sent his armies south towards the oil of the Caucasus, and to take the city on the Volga that bore Stalin's name.

The fighting was street by street and house by house. In November the Red Army struck the weaker Romanian troops guarding the flanks and encircled the Germans inside the city. Hitler forbade a retreat. In February 1943 the survivors of the Sixth Army surrendered.

About two million soldiers and civilians were killed, wounded or captured. After Stalingrad, Germany was retreating in the east.

ww2.q: Which battle ended with an entire German army surrendering?
a: Stalingrad
Midway
The Battle of Britain
Pearl Harbor
ww2.why: The German Sixth Army was trapped in Stalingrad and surrendered in February 1943.

ww2.p: In July 1943 Germany made one last great attack in the east, at Kursk. The Soviets knew it was coming and had dug in deep. It became one of the largest tank battles in history, and Germany lost. From then on the Red Army only moved forward.

pins: July 1943: one of the largest tank battles in history

ww2.p:
In July 1943 British, American and Canadian troops landed in Sicily. The Italian king had Mussolini arrested, and in September Italy surrendered.

Germany seized the north of Italy and put Mussolini back in charge there. The Allies had to fight their way up the mountainous peninsula until the spring of 1945.

Britain depended on ships bringing food, fuel and weapons from America. German submarines, the U-boats, hunted them in 'wolf packs' and sank thousands.

By mid-1943 the Allies were winning: convoys had escorts and air cover, radar found U-boats on the surface, and code-breakers at Bletchley Park could read Germany's Enigma messages.

ww2.h: The war of factories: aircraft built, 1939–45
ww2.note: The Allies could simply make more of everything. Women took millions of factory jobs, and food and fuel were rationed at home.
