ww2.p:
On 6 June 1944 the Allies opened a second front in the west. About 156,000 American, British, Canadian and other troops landed on five beaches in Normandy, codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword. It was the largest invasion by sea in history.

After weeks of hard fighting they broke out, and Paris was liberated in August.

Two weeks after D-Day the Red Army launched Operation Bagration and destroyed a whole German army group in Belarus. By the end of 1944 the Soviets had reached Warsaw and the Balkans.

Most German soldiers who died in the war died fighting the Soviet Union.

l: December 1944 · Germany's last attack, the Battle of the Bulge, fails
r: 25 April 1945 · US and Soviet troops meet on the Elbe

ww2.p:
In February 1945 Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met at Yalta, in Crimea, to plan the peace. They agreed to split Germany into zones, to create the United Nations, and that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan.

With the Red Army already in eastern Europe, Stalin got his way there.

By late April 1945 Soviet troops were fighting in the streets of Berlin. On 30 April Hitler killed himself in his bunker beneath the city.

Germany surrendered unconditionally, and 8 May 1945 was celebrated as Victory in Europe Day, VE Day.

pins: Where the surrender was first signed

ww2.q: When did World War II end in Europe?
a: May 1945
June 1944
August 1945
November 1918
ww2.why: Germany surrendered in early May 1945, a week after Hitler's suicide; 8 May is VE Day.

ww2.p:
In the Pacific the Americans and their allies 'island-hopped' towards Japan, capturing some islands and bypassing others: Guadalcanal, the Philippines, Iwo Jima, Okinawa.

The fighting was ferocious. Japanese soldiers rarely surrendered, and kamikaze pilots crashed their planes into Allied ships. On Okinawa alone, in 1945, more than 200,000 people died, about half of them civilians.

In secret, the US had built a new weapon: the atomic bomb. On 6 August 1945 one destroyed Hiroshima. On 8 August the Soviet Union declared war on Japan, and within hours its armies poured into Manchuria. On 9 August a second bomb hit Nagasaki.

By the end of 1945 the two bombs had killed an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 people. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed it on 2 September 1945. World War II was over.

ww2.why: Germany surrendered in May 1945; Japan in August, after the atomic bombs and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria.

ww2.h: Put the end of the war in order
people died in World War II
ww2.p: The deadliest war in history. Most of the dead were civilians: killed by bombing, massacres, starvation, disease and genocide.

ww2.h: Deaths by country, soldiers and civilians
ww2.note: Estimates vary, especially for China. Poland lost about one in six of its people, the highest share of any country.

ww2.q: Which country suffered the most deaths in World War II?
a: The Soviet Union
Germany
The United States
Britain
ww2.why: About 27 million Soviet soldiers and civilians died, more than any other country.

ww2.p:
Germany and Austria were each split into four zones, run by the US, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, was split four ways too.

As the winners fell out, the zones hardened. In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone became communist East Germany. Germany stayed divided until 1990.

hl: Germany and Austria, in four zones
pins: Split four ways, inside the Soviet zone

ww2.p:
Stalin kept the eastern half of pre-war Poland. In return Poland was given German land in the west, up to the Oder and Neisse rivers. The whole country shifted about 200 km west.

About 12 million Germans fled or were expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia and elsewhere in eastern Europe: one of the largest forced migrations in history.

In 1945 fifty nations met in San Francisco to found the United Nations, meant to stop another world war.

The five main winners, the US, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, became permanent members of its Security Council, each with a veto. They still are today.

pins: The UN Charter was signed here in June 1945

ww2.q: Which of these was NOT one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council?
a: Germany
China
France
The Soviet Union
ww2.why: The five permanent members were the main winners: the US, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China.

steps: Japan's colony is divided at the 38th parallel: Soviet troops in the north, Americans in the south.
A weakened Britain leaves India, which is partitioned. About a million die in the violence and 15 million flee.
The state of Israel is founded; war with its Arab neighbours follows, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee or are driven out.
Mao Zedong's communists win China's civil war. The Nationalists flee to Taiwan.

ww2.p:
Only two superpowers were left standing: the United States and the Soviet Union. As Churchill put it in 1946, an 'iron curtain' had come down across Europe, with Soviet-controlled communist states to the east.

The US paid to rebuild western Europe through the Marshall Plan, and in 1949 founded the NATO alliance. The same year the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb. The Cold War had begun.

r: Soviet troops stay in eastern Europe

asia.p:
Mohandas Gandhi led India's independence movement with non-violent protest: boycotts of British goods, strikes and marches, such as the 1930 Salt March to the sea.

Millions joined, and the cost of holding India rose. After World War II a weakened Britain agreed to leave.

In August 1947 British India was split into two states: mostly Hindu India and mostly Muslim Pakistan, in two parts, west and east.

As millions fled across the new borders, communal violence killed perhaps a million people, and about 15 million were uprooted: one of the largest migrations in history.
East Pakistan, over 1,500 km from the west and with a different language, broke away in a bloody war in 1971, with Indian help, and became Bangladesh.

asia.q: How did Gandhi oppose British rule?
a: With non-violent protest
With a guerrilla army
By allying with Japan
By asking the Soviet Union to invade
asia.why: Boycotts, strikes and marches such as the Salt March.

asia.p:
Japan's wartime conquests had shown that European rulers could be beaten. When it surrendered in 1945, independence movements were ready.

The Philippines became independent from the US in 1946; Burma and Ceylon (Sri Lanka) from Britain in 1948; Indonesia from the Netherlands in 1949, after four years of war.

In Vietnam, Ho Chi Minh's communist-led Viet Minh fought France. At Dien Bien Phu in 1954 they won a decisive victory, and France left Indochina.

Vietnam was split in two, and the war with the US that followed lasted until 1975.

Britain fought a long communist insurgency in Malaya before granting independence in 1957. Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled in 1965, and became one of the world's richest city-states.

asia.why: It won independence from the Netherlands in 1949.

coldwar.p:
The US and the Soviet Union beat Hitler together, but they were opposites: a capitalist democracy and a communist dictatorship. Each feared the other wanted to dominate the world.

They never fought each other directly, which is why it is called a 'cold' war. Instead they competed through alliances, arms, spies, propaganda and wars fought by others.

Soviet troops stayed in eastern Europe after 1945 and installed communist governments in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and East Germany.

In 1946 Churchill warned that an 'iron curtain' had come down across Europe.

In 1947 the US pledged to 'contain' communism. The Marshall Plan poured billions of dollars into rebuilding western Europe.

When the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948, the West flew in food and coal for almost a year: the Berlin Airlift.

coldwar.q: Why was it called a "cold" war?
a: The superpowers never fought each other directly
It was fought mainly in the Arctic
It happened in winter
No one died in it
coldwar.why: They competed through arms, alliances and proxy wars instead.

coldwar.p: In 1950 communist North Korea invaded the South. A UN force led by the US pushed it back almost to China, then China sent hundreds of thousands of troops. The war ended in 1953 near where it began, at the 38th parallel. Korea is still divided.

In October 1962 US spy planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 150 km from Florida. For thirteen days the world was on the brink of nuclear war.

President Kennedy blockaded Cuba; Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and the quiet removal of US missiles from Turkey.

coldwar.h: when the world came closest to nuclear war
coldwar.p: The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962. Afterwards a hotline linked Washington and Moscow.

The US sent troops to stop communist North Vietnam taking the South. At its peak over 500,000 Americans were there. The war killed perhaps two million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans and divided American society.

The US withdrew in 1973, and in 1975 Saigon fell to the North.
Elsewhere the superpowers backed rival sides in wars in Angola, Ethiopia, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and beyond. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 became the Soviets' own Vietnam.

coldwar.q: Where did the Soviet Union place nuclear missiles in 1962?
a: Cuba
Turkey
Vietnam
East Berlin
coldwar.why: The discovery set off the Cuban Missile Crisis.

coldwar.p:
The US dropped the first atomic bombs in 1945; the Soviets tested their own in 1949. Both then built hydrogen bombs, far more powerful, and missiles that could cross the world in 30 minutes.

By the 1980s they had about 60,000 nuclear weapons between them. The logic was 'mutually assured destruction': neither side could attack without being destroyed too.

In 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite, and in 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. The US answered with the Apollo programme: in July 1969 Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon.

coldwar.s: The first person in space was an American.
coldwar.why: It was the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, in 1961.

coldwar.p: From 1910 a revolution against the long dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz tore Mexico apart for a decade; perhaps a million died. Leaders such as Emiliano Zapata fought for land for poor peasants. The 1917 constitution promised land reform and workers' rights.

In 1959 Fidel Castro and Che Guevara's guerrillas overthrew Cuba's US-backed dictator. Castro nationalised US-owned businesses and allied with the Soviet Union, bringing the Cold War 150 km from Florida. The US imposed an embargo that still largely stands.

Fearing more Cubas, the US backed anti-communist governments. Military coups took power in Brazil (1964), Chile (1973), where General Pinochet overthrew the elected socialist Salvador Allende, and Argentina (1976). Tens of thousands were tortured, killed or 'disappeared'.

Through the 1980s the dictatorships fell one by one, weakened by debt crises and protest. Argentina's junta collapsed after losing the Falklands War to Britain in 1982; Chile voted Pinochet out in a 1988 referendum. By 1990 almost all of Latin America was democratic.

coldwar.q: Who led the Cuban Revolution of 1959?
a: Fidel Castro
Augusto Pinochet
Emiliano Zapata
Simón Bolívar
coldwar.why: Castro allied Cuba with the Soviet Union.

coldwar.p: By the 1980s the Soviet economy was failing and the war in Afghanistan dragged on. In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev came to power and tried to reform: glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring. He cut nuclear arms with US President Reagan.

In 1989 Gorbachev let eastern Europe go. Poland held free elections, Hungary opened its border, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall, built in 1961, was opened. Crowds tore it down.

Communist governments fell across eastern Europe within weeks, and Germany reunited in 1990.
In 1991 the Soviet republics declared independence one after another. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet Union ceased to exist. The Cold War was over.

coldwar.q: When did the Berlin Wall open?
a: November 1989
August 1961
December 1991
June 1948
coldwar.why: It opened on 9 November 1989; Germany reunited in 1990.

mideast.p:
Two national movements claimed the same small land: Zionism, the movement for a Jewish homeland, and Palestinian Arab nationalism. In World War I Britain made promises to both Arabs and Zionists, then ruled Palestine from 1920.

After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew. In 1947 the UN proposed splitting Palestine in two; Jewish leaders accepted, Arab leaders rejected the plan.

In May 1948, as British rule ended, Israel declared independence and its Arab neighbours attacked. Israel won. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, an event Palestinians call the Nakba, 'catastrophe'. Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt held Gaza.

In the years after, most Jews of the Arab world left or were driven out, many to Israel.

In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel took the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, the Golan Heights and Sinai. Egypt made peace in 1979 and got Sinai back.

The 1993 Oslo Accords brought limited Palestinian self-rule but no state. Israeli settlements in the West Bank have grown. After Hamas's attack on 7 October 2023, war followed in Gaza.

mideast.q: What did Israel take in the 1967 Six-Day War?
a: The West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, Golan and Sinai
All of Egypt
Lebanon and Syria
Nothing; it lost the war
mideast.why: Sinai was later returned to Egypt after the 1979 peace.

mideast.p: In 1952 army officers overthrew Egypt's king, and Gamal Abdel Nasser became the hero of Arab nationalism. In 1956 he nationalised the Suez Canal. Britain, France and Israel invaded, but US pressure forced them out: a humiliation that showed the old empires' day was over.

The Middle East holds nearly half the world's proven oil. In 1960 producers founded OPEC to control prices.

After the 1973 war, Arab producers cut oil to the US and others, and prices quadrupled. Oil made the Gulf states rich and central to world politics.

In 1979 a revolution overthrew Iran's shah, and Ayatollah Khomeini created an Islamic republic, hostile to the US. Iraq's Saddam Hussein attacked Iran in 1980, starting an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands.

Iran's shah ruled with US backing and a feared secret police. In 1979 mass protests drove him out and Ayatollah Khomeini set up an Islamic republic, ruled by clerics. Students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait; a US-led coalition drove it out in 1991. In 2003 the US invaded Iraq and toppled Saddam, but years of insurgency and civil war followed.

mideast.s: The Middle East holds nearly half the world’s proven oil.
mideast.why: That is why outside powers have competed for influence there.

china.p: After decades of civil war and Japanese invasion, Mao Zedong's communists won. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. The Nationalist government fled to Taiwan, which has governed itself ever since.

In 1958 Mao tried to industrialise overnight, forcing peasants into giant communes and backyard steel furnaces. Harvests collapsed while officials reported record crops.

The famine of 1959–61 killed tens of millions of people: the deadliest famine in history.

In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution against 'enemies' of communism. Young Red Guards attacked teachers, officials and old traditions; schools closed and millions were persecuted. It ended only with Mao's death in 1976.

china.q: What happened in the Great Leap Forward?
a: A famine that killed tens of millions
China landed on the Moon
China joined the WTO
Mao fled to Taiwan
china.why: Forced communes and false reports led to the deadliest famine in history.

china.p:
From 1978 Deng Xiaoping opened China to markets and foreign investment, starting with special economic zones such as Shenzhen. Farmers could sell their own crops, and private business returned.

China grew about 10% a year for three decades. Hundreds of millions escaped poverty.

pins: A fishing town in 1978, a city of millions today

china.p: To slow population growth, from 1980 most urban couples were allowed only one child, enforced with fines and sometimes forced abortions. It ended in 2015, but China's population is now ageing and shrinking.

china.h: China’s share of world output (at market prices)

china.p: Economic freedom did not bring political freedom. In 1989 students and workers protested for reform in Tiananmen Square in Beijing; in June the army crushed them, killing hundreds or more. The Communist Party still rules alone.

China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became 'the world's factory'. In 2010 it passed Japan as the second-largest economy.

Its power brings rivalry with the US and disputes over Taiwan and the South China Sea, where its claims overlap with its neighbours'.

china.s: Taiwan is ruled by the People’s Republic of China.
china.why: Taiwan has governed itself since 1949, though Beijing claims it.

europe.p:
In 1945 Europe lay in ruins: cities bombed flat, economies wrecked, millions homeless. Twice in thirty years, wars between European nations, above all France and Germany, had pulled in the world.

The US Marshall Plan poured in money to rebuild western Europe and keep it from communism.

In 1950 the French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling French and German coal and steel, the raw materials of war, under a shared authority. War between them would become 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'.

In 1951 six countries signed up: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
In 1957 the six signed the Treaty of Rome, creating the European Economic Community: a common market with no tariffs between members and shared rules for trade and farming.

a: To make war between France and Germany impossible
To sell coal to the US
To fight the Soviet Union directly
To fund the Olympics
europe.why: Shared control of the raw materials of war bound former enemies together.

europe.p:
The community kept growing: Britain, Ireland and Denmark in 1973; Greece, Spain and Portugal in the 1980s, after their dictatorships ended; Austria, Finland and Sweden in 1995.

In 2004, fifteen years after the fall of the Berlin Wall, ten countries joined, most of them former communist states, followed by Romania, Bulgaria and Croatia.

The 1992 Maastricht Treaty founded the European Union, with EU citizenship and plans for a single currency. The euro arrived in 1999 and its coins and notes in 2002. Most EU members use it; Denmark, Sweden and Poland, among others, do not.

The single market lets goods, services, money and people move freely, and the Schengen area removed most border checks.

items: Proposes laws and enforces the rules.
Votes on laws with the member governments.

europe.p: After the 2008 financial crisis, Greece and others could not pay their debts. Rescue loans came with harsh spending cuts, and for a time it seemed the euro might break apart. It held.
In 2016 British voters chose by 52% to 48% to leave the EU, worried about sovereignty and immigration. Britain left in 2020, the first country ever to do so.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 pulled the EU together: sanctions on Russia, aid to Ukraine and a push to cut dependence on Russian gas. Ukraine, Moldova and several Balkan countries want to join.

europe.q: Which country was the first to leave the EU?
a: Britain
Greece
Norway
Switzerland
europe.why: Norway and Switzerland never joined; Britain left in 2020.

africa.p:
After World War II, Africans who had fought for the empires demanded freedom, and weakened European powers could no longer hold on.

In 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence.
In 1960 alone, 17 countries became independent, most of them former French colonies, plus Nigeria and the Congo.

Where many white settlers lived, independence came through war. Algeria fought France for eight years before winning in 1962. Kenya's Mau Mau uprising was crushed brutally, though Kenya became independent in 1963.

Portugal held on until its own revolution in 1974, which freed Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau. Rhodesia became Zimbabwe in 1980.

Borders drawn by Europeans held, but many new states struggled with poverty, coups, civil wars and Cold War rivalry. In South Africa, white minority rule under apartheid lasted until 1994, when Nelson Mandela became president.

africa.q: Which was the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, in 1957?
a: Ghana
Nigeria
Kenya
South Africa
africa.why: Kwame Nkrumah led it to independence.

africa.p:
In 1948 South Africa's white minority government began apartheid, 'apartness': laws that classified everyone by race, banned mixed marriages, segregated schools, hospitals and beaches, and pushed Black South Africans into poor 'homelands'.

Black South Africans, about three-quarters of the population, had no vote.

The African National Congress resisted. After police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, the ANC was banned and turned to sabotage. Its leader Nelson Mandela was jailed in 1962 and spent 27 years in prison.

International sanctions, boycotts and resistance at home made apartheid unworkable. In 1990 President de Klerk freed Mandela.
In April 1994 South Africa held its first election in which all races could vote. Mandela became president and chose reconciliation over revenge, setting up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
He was released in 1990 and elected president in 1994.

a: Laws separating people by race in South Africa
A South African independence war
A trade union movement
A peace treaty with Britain
africa.why: It lasted from 1948 until the early 1990s.

africa.p: Many new states struggled. Colonial borders lumped rival groups together, economies depended on a few exports, and Cold War rivals armed both sides. Coups were common, and civil wars hit Nigeria (Biafra, 1967–70), Angola, Mozambique, Ethiopia and Sudan.

In 1994, in Rwanda, Hutu extremists murdered about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days, while the world failed to intervene. The aftermath spilled into the Democratic Republic of Congo, where wars from 1996 killed millions.

Since 2000 many African economies have grown fast, mobile phones and mobile money have spread, and democracy has taken root in countries such as Ghana and Botswana. Africa's young, growing population is expected to be about a quarter of humanity by 2050.

africa.s: About 800,000 people were murdered in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

islands.p:
From the 1960s Britain, France, Australia and others let their island colonies go. Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago became independent in 1962, Barbados in 1966, Papua New Guinea in 1975.

Some have fewer than 100,000 people, but each has a seat at the United Nations.

items: Including some of the smallest states on Earth.

islands.p: For low-lying states such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives, rising seas are an existential threat: much of their land is only a metre or two above sea level.

islands.s: Small island states have a vote at the United Nations, just like large countries.
islands.why: Every member state has one vote in the General Assembly.

collapse.p: Eastern Europeans rose against Soviet control more than once. Hungary revolted in 1956 and Czechoslovakia tried 'socialism with a human face' in the Prague Spring of 1968; both times Soviet tanks crushed them.

In 1980 Polish shipyard workers led by Lech Wałęsa formed Solidarity, the first free trade union in the bloc, with ten million members. It was banned under martial law in 1981 but survived underground, backed by the Polish Pope, John Paul II.

By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating, shops had empty shelves, and the war in Afghanistan was costly. Gorbachev, leader from 1985, tried to reform with glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), and told eastern Europe it could choose its own path.

a: A free trade union in communist Poland
A Soviet army
A West German party
A NATO treaty
collapse.why: Founded in 1980 at the Gdańsk shipyard.

collapse.p:
In 1989, one by one, the communist governments of eastern Europe fell, mostly peacefully. Poland held free elections, Hungary opened its border, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened. In Romania, the dictator Ceaușescu was overthrown and shot.

Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.

Inside the Soviet Union, nationalism surged. The Baltic states led the way. In August 1991 hard-liners tried a coup against Gorbachev and failed. By December all fifteen republics had declared independence, and the Soviet Union was gone.

items: Now in the EU and NATO.
The core of the old union.
Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and four more

collapse.p: Not every split was violent. On 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia divided peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

collapse.q: How many countries did the Soviet Union break into?
collapse.why: Each of its fifteen republics became independent in 1991.

collapse.s: The Soviet Union broke up in 1989.
collapse.why: 1989 was the fall of communism in eastern Europe; the Soviet Union itself ended in December 1991.

collapse.p: Under Boris Yeltsin, Russia's first elected president, prices were freed overnight and state companies sold off. Inflation wiped out savings, life expectancy fell, and a few well-connected 'oligarchs' grabbed huge fortunes.

Vladimir Putin, a former KGB officer, became president in 2000. Rising oil prices brought a boom, but he steadily took control of television, crushed opponents and rebuilt Russian power, fighting wars in Chechnya and in Georgia in 2008.

collapse.s: Boris Yeltsin was the first elected president of Russia.
collapse.why: He was elected in 1991 and resigned at the end of 1999.

balkans.p: Yugoslavia united Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Bosnians, Macedonians, Montenegrins and others. Its communist leader Tito held it together; after he died in 1980, nationalism and economic crisis pulled it apart.

Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, and war began. The worst fighting was in Bosnia (1992–95), where all sides committed atrocities and 'ethnic cleansing' drove people from their homes.

In July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since World War II. The Dayton agreement ended the war that year.

In 1999 NATO bombed Yugoslavia to stop attacks on Kosovo's Albanians. Montenegro left its union with Serbia peacefully in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia and some other countries do not recognise.

a: About 8,000 Muslim men and boys were murdered
A peace treaty was signed
Tito was born
NATO was founded
balkans.why: It was ruled a genocide by international courts.

recent.p:
The world map is still changing. Namibia won independence from South Africa in 1990, and Palau from US trusteeship in 1994. Eritrea broke from Ethiopia after a long war and a referendum in 1993. Timor-Leste became independent from Indonesia in 2002.

The newest country is South Sudan, which split from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war.
Some countries joined up: East and West Germany in 1990, and North and South Yemen the same year. Others split peacefully: Czechoslovakia in 1993, and Serbia and Montenegro in 2006.

recent.q: What is the world's newest country?
a: South Sudan
Timor-Leste
Eritrea
Kosovo
recent.why: It became independent from Sudan in 2011.

recent.s: Germany and Yemen were both reunified in 1990.
recent.why: East and West Germany, and North and South Yemen.

today.p:
On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes and killed nearly 3,000 people in the United States. The US invaded Afghanistan, and in 2003 Iraq.

The wars lasted years; the Taliban retook Kabul in 2021.
In 2011 protests swept the Arab world. Rulers fell in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen, but Libya, Yemen and Syria slid into civil wars.

Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Hamas's attack on Israel in October 2023 began a war in Gaza. In February 2026 US and Israeli strikes on Iran killed its supreme leader, and the war since has disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

today.q: When did Russia launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine?

today.p:
The 2008 financial crisis began in the US and hit the West hard, while China kept growing. Covid-19 killed millions from 2020 and shut down much of the world.

Inequality and migration fed populist politics in many countries.

US banks had lent heavily to home buyers who could not repay, and bundled those loans into complex investments sold worldwide. When house prices fell, banks failed: Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008. Governments spent trillions on rescues, and the worst recession since the 1930s followed.

Covid-19 emerged in Wuhan, China, at the end of 2019 and spread worldwide in weeks. Lockdowns shut much of the world in 2020. Vaccines were developed in under a year, but the pandemic killed millions.

The age of one superpower and ever-freer trade has given way to rivalry between the US, China and Russia, higher tariffs and rising military spending. NATO has grown to 32 members and Europe is rearming.

Smartphones, social media and now artificial intelligence keep changing daily life and politics.

today.h: people driven from their homes by war and persecution
today.p: A UN count; the highest ever recorded.

now.p:
More than 8.2 billion people live on Earth, over a third of them in India and China. India passed China as the most populous country in 2023.

As countries get richer, birth rates fall: populations age and shrink in rich countries and China, while Africa's grow fast.

The United States is still the largest economy, with about a quarter of world output; China is second. Countries that industrialised first, and East Asian economies that joined world trade later, are richest.

now.q: Which is the world’s most populous country?
a: India
China
The United States
Indonesia

now.s: Africa’s population is expected to grow to about a quarter of humanity by 2050.
now.why: Its populations are young and growing while much of the world ages.

now.p: Burning coal, oil and gas released a record of about 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, roughly a third of it from China. In 2024 the world was more than 1.5°C warmer than before industrialisation for a whole year, for the first time.
Nine countries hold about 12,200 nuclear warheads, nearly 86% of them Russian or American. In 2026 the last US–Russian treaty limiting them, New START, expired.
NATO has 32 members, and the EU 27. Rivalry between the US and China and Russia's confrontation with the West are the central story of world politics.

now.q: Which country emits the most CO2 today?
a: China
The United States
India
Russia
now.why: Roughly a third of the world’s fossil-fuel CO2.

us-colonies.p:
People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago, probably across a land bridge where the Bering Strait is now, and along the Pacific coast. Over thousands of years they spread across both continents.

By 1492 perhaps several million people lived in what is now the United States, in hundreds of nations with their own languages, beliefs and ways of life.

us-colonies.h: Many nations, many ways of life
items: Farming villages; a confederacy of six nations with a council.
Farmers; earlier, Mississippian cities like Cahokia.

us-colonies.p: Near today's St Louis, the city of Cahokia had perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100, more than London at the time, with huge earthen mounds. It was the centre of the Mississippian culture, which had faded by the time Europeans arrived.

European diseases such as smallpox often spread ahead of the colonists, along native trade routes. Many communities were devastated before they ever saw a European, which made it easier for settlers to take the land.

us-colonies.q: How did the first people reach the Americas?
a: From Asia, across a land bridge and along the coast
By sea from Africa
From Europe by Viking ship
From Australia across the Pacific

us-colonies.p: Spain came first, looking for gold: it explored Florida and the south-west and founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest lasting European town in the US. France claimed the Mississippi valley and Canada, trading furs with Native peoples. England's colonies hugged the Atlantic coast.

England's first lasting colony, Jamestown in Virginia, nearly starved. It survived by growing tobacco for export, which needed huge amounts of labour.

In 1619 Virginia held the first elected assembly in English America, and the first enslaved Africans arrived. Freedom and slavery grew up together from the start.

In 1620 the Pilgrims, religious separatists, landed at Plymouth after signing the Mayflower Compact to govern themselves. Thousands of Puritans followed to Massachusetts from 1630, hoping to build a godly 'city upon a hill'.

The idea that America has a special mission, and the habit of town meetings and self-government, began here.

items: Small farms, fishing, trade, schools and town meetings.
Mixed peoples and faiths; Quaker Pennsylvania offered religious freedom.
Tobacco, rice and indigo plantations worked by enslaved Africans.

us-colonies.p:
Britain and France fought for the continent from 1754 to 1763, with Native nations on both sides. A young Virginian officer, George Washington, fired some of the first shots. Britain won and took Canada and the land to the Mississippi.

But the war doubled Britain's debt, and London decided the colonists should help pay.

us-colonies.q: Which crop saved Jamestown and shaped the South?
a: Tobacco
Cotton
Wheat
Sugar
us-colonies.why: Tobacco exports made Virginia rich, and fuelled demand for enslaved labour.

items: The first enslaved Africans arrive in Virginia
The French and Indian War ends

us-independence.p:
To pay its war debts, Britain taxed the colonies directly for the first time: the Stamp Act (1765) taxed every newspaper and legal document. Colonists, used to their own assemblies, protested: 'No taxation without representation'.

Boycotts forced repeal, but Britain kept insisting on its right to tax. In 1770 British soldiers killed five people in the Boston Massacre.

In 1773 protesters dressed as Mohawks dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston harbour. Britain punished Massachusetts by closing the port. The colonies formed a Continental Congress to coordinate resistance.

In April 1775 British troops marching to seize weapons met militia at Lexington and Concord. The war had begun.

On 4 July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson. Drawing on Enlightenment thinkers such as Locke, it declared that 'all men are created equal' with rights to 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness', and that governments get their power from the consent of the governed.

Its words were not true for enslaved people, women or Native Americans, but later movements would hold the country to them.

us-independence.q: What did 'no taxation without representation' mean?
a: Colonists should not be taxed by a Parliament they could not vote for
No one should pay any taxes
Only the king could tax
Taxes should go to Native nations
us-independence.why: They had their own assemblies but no seats in Parliament.

us-independence.p:
Britain had the world's strongest navy and a professional army. George Washington's Continental Army lost many battles, and nearly fell apart at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777–78.

But it survived. The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 convinced France to join the war, and later Spain and the Netherlands. France's navy and money were decisive.

In 1781 Washington's army and a French army and fleet trapped the British at Yorktown, Virginia, and forced their surrender. In the 1783 Treaty of Paris Britain recognised the United States, with land stretching to the Mississippi.

Perhaps a fifth of colonists stayed loyal to Britain; about 60,000 to 80,000 left, many to Canada. Most Native nations sided with Britain, fearing settlers, and lost land as the new country grew. Thousands of enslaved people escaped to the British, who had promised them freedom.

us-independence.s: France helped the Americans win independence.
us-independence.why: France's navy and money were decisive, especially at Yorktown.

us-independence.p: The first national government, under the Articles of Confederation, was too weak: it could not tax, raise an army or settle quarrels between states. In 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia to fix it, and wrote a whole new Constitution instead.

items: Makes the laws. The Senate gives each state two votes; the House is by population.
Carries out the laws, commands the military, can veto laws.
Decides what the laws and the Constitution mean.
us-independence.p: Each branch can block the others, so no one can become a tyrant: Montesquieu's idea put into practice.

Big and small states compromised on Congress. The South got the 'three-fifths' clause, counting enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for seats in Congress, which gave slave states extra power.

In 1791 the Bill of Rights added ten amendments protecting freedom of speech, religion and the press, the right to bear arms, and fair trials. Washington became the first president in 1789.
It is the oldest written national constitution still in use, amended only 27 times.

us-independence.q: Why did the Constitution split power into three branches?
a: So no single person or group could become a tyrant
Because there were three original states
To copy the British monarchy
To give the president total power
us-independence.why: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.

us-expansion.p:
In 1803 President Jefferson bought the vast Louisiana territory from Napoleon's France for $15 million, about three cents an acre. It doubled the size of the country and gave it the Mississippi and the port of New Orleans.

Napoleon sold because he had lost Haiti to a slave revolt and needed money for war in Europe.

Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the new land. From 1804 to 1806 they travelled up the Missouri, over the Rockies and down to the Pacific and back, guided in part by Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman.

Angry at British seizures of American sailors and British support for Native resistance in the west, the US went to war with Britain in 1812. The British burned Washington, DC, and American invasions of Canada failed; the war ended in a draw in 1815.

It broke Native resistance east of the Mississippi and gave Americans a new patriotic song, the Star-Spangled Banner.

a: He had lost Haiti and needed money for war in Europe
The US won it in a war
Spain forced him to
It was worthless swamp
us-expansion.why: The Haitian Revolution ended his dream of an American empire.

us-expansion.p:
Many Americans came to believe it was their 'manifest destiny', given by God, to spread across the continent. Settlers poured west on trails such as the Oregon Trail.

The idea justified taking land from Native nations and from Mexico.

American settlers in Mexican Texas, many with enslaved workers, revolted in 1836. After the defeat at the Alamo, they won independence at San Jacinto. Texas was an independent republic until it joined the US in 1845.

In 1846 the US went to war with Mexico over the Texas border. American troops took Mexico City, and in 1848 Mexico gave up California and the south-west, about half its territory.

The same year gold was found in California, and the Gold Rush brought 300,000 people west. California became a state in 1850.
Every new territory raised one explosive question: would it allow slavery? The land won from Mexico made the quarrel between North and South far worse, and set the country on the road to civil war.

a: That Americans were destined by God to spread across the continent
That slavery should end
That the US should stay small
That Mexico should rule Texas

us-civilwar.p:
In 1793 Eli Whitney's cotton gin made it easy to clean cotton, and cotton became the South's great crop, feeding the mills of Britain and New England. Slavery, which some had expected to fade, boomed.

By 1860 about 4 million people were enslaved, almost a third of the South's population. Families were split by sale, and the law treated enslaved people as property.

Enslaved people resisted: by working slowly, running away on the 'Underground Railroad' with helpers like Harriet Tubman, and sometimes by revolt, as in Nat Turner's rebellion of 1831.

In the North an abolitionist movement grew, led by people such as Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery. Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) turned millions against slavery.

The Missouri Compromise (1820) drew a line across the West: slavery north of it was banned. But new territories reopened the fight. In 'Bleeding Kansas' in the 1850s settlers killed each other over the question.

In 1857 the Supreme Court's Dred Scott ruling said Black people could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

In 1860 Abraham Lincoln, of the new Republican Party, which opposed the spread of slavery, won the presidency without a single Southern state. Believing slavery was doomed in the Union, seven Southern states seceded and formed the Confederate States of America.

In April 1861 Confederates fired on Fort Sumter in South Carolina, and four more states joined them.

us-civilwar.q: What was the main cause of the Civil War?
a: Slavery, and whether it would spread west
A dispute over taxes with Britain
A border war with Mexico
Religious differences between Catholics and Protestants
us-civilwar.why: The seceding states said so themselves in their declarations.

l: A navy to blockade the South
r: About 9 million, 3.5 million of them enslaved

us-civilwar.p:
At first Lincoln fought to save the Union, not to end slavery. But from 1 January 1863 his Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in Confederate areas free, and about 180,000 Black soldiers joined the Union army.

The war became a war to end slavery.

In July 1863 the Union won at Gettysburg, the war's largest battle, and took Vicksburg, splitting the Confederacy along the Mississippi. At Gettysburg Lincoln gave his famous address, calling for 'a new birth of freedom' and 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

General Sherman's army burned a path through Georgia in 1864. In April 1865 General Lee surrendered at Appomattox. Five days later Lincoln was assassinated at a theatre in Washington.

The 13th Amendment abolished slavery throughout the US.

us-civilwar.h: soldiers died in the Civil War
us-civilwar.p: More than in any other American war, about 2% of the whole population.

us-west.p:
In 1830, under President Andrew Jackson, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. The 'Five Tribes' of the south-east (Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole), many of whom farmed, ran schools and had written constitutions, were forced to leave their homelands for 'Indian Territory', now Oklahoma.

White settlers wanted their land, especially after gold was found in Cherokee Georgia.
The Cherokee won a Supreme Court case in 1832, but Jackson ignored it. In 1838–39 the army forced about 16,000 Cherokee west; about 4,000 died on the march, the 'Trail of Tears'.

us-west.q: Where were the south-eastern nations forced to move?
a: Indian Territory, now Oklahoma
Canada
California
Mexico

us-west.p: The 1862 Homestead Act offered 160 acres free to settlers who farmed the land for five years. In 1869 the first transcontinental railroad was completed, built largely by Chinese and Irish workers, and the journey across the country fell from months to a week.

The Plains nations depended on the bison. Commercial hunters, encouraged by the army, slaughtered them: from tens of millions to a few hundred by the 1880s.

The Lakota and Cheyenne fought back and destroyed Custer's force at the Little Bighorn in 1876. But by 1890, when soldiers massacred about 250 Lakota at Wounded Knee, most Native Americans had been forced onto reservations.

Statehood followed settlement: by 1912 all 48 contiguous states had joined. In 1890 the census declared the frontier closed. Native nations survived on a fraction of their land, and today there are 574 federally recognised tribes, with their own governments.

us-west.n: Tens of millions to a few hundred
us-west.h: bison left on the Plains by the late 1880s
us-west.p: Their destruction broke the economy of the Plains nations.

us-reconstruction.p: After the war about 4 million people were free. Many searched for family members sold away, founded churches and schools, and sought land of their own: 'forty acres and a mule', which most never got.

items: Citizenship and equal protection of the laws for everyone born in the US.
The vote cannot be denied because of race.
us-reconstruction.p: These 'Reconstruction amendments' are sometimes called the second founding of the United States.

For a few years Black men voted in large numbers and held office: Hiram Revels became the first Black senator in 1870, and hundreds served in Southern legislatures.

White terror groups such as the Ku Klux Klan fought back with violence. In 1877, in a deal to settle a disputed election, federal troops left the South and Reconstruction ended.

a: Citizenship and equal protection for all born in the US
Votes for women
The end of the income tax
Prohibition of alcohol
us-reconstruction.why: It is central to many later civil rights rulings.

us-reconstruction.p:
White Southern governments stripped Black citizens of the vote with poll taxes, literacy tests and violence, and passed segregation laws, nicknamed 'Jim Crow': separate schools, trains, restaurants and drinking fountains.

In 1896 the Supreme Court approved 'separate but equal' in Plessy v. Ferguson. In practice it was separate and unequal.
Thousands of Black Americans were lynched, murdered by mobs, often in public, from the 1880s to the 1950s. Journalists such as Ida B. Wells campaigned against it at great risk.

From 1910 to 1970 about 6 million Black Southerners moved to cities of the North and West, such as Chicago, Detroit, New York and Los Angeles, for factory jobs and to escape Jim Crow. They transformed American cities, politics and music, from jazz and the blues to the Harlem Renaissance.

us-reconstruction.s: 'Separate but equal' was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1896.
us-reconstruction.why: Plessy v. Ferguson; it was overturned for schools in 1954.

us-industry.p:
Between the Civil War and 1900 the US became the world's largest industrial economy. Railroads linked the country; steel, oil, electricity and the telephone created new industries.

Tycoons built enormous fortunes: Carnegie in steel, Rockefeller in oil, J.P. Morgan in banking. Critics called them 'robber barons'; the era, glittering on top and grim below, the 'Gilded Age'.

Factory workers, many of them children, worked 60-hour weeks in dangerous conditions. Strikes were often crushed violently. Reformers called Progressives pushed back: breaking up monopolies, food safety laws, limits on child labour, and in 1913 a federal income tax.

In 1913 Henry Ford's moving assembly line made cars cheap enough for ordinary families.

us-industry.q: Why was the late 1800s called the 'Gilded Age'?
a: It glittered with wealth on top but hid poverty and corruption below
Gold was discovered everywhere
Everyone became rich
The dollar was backed by gold for the first time

us-industry.p: About 25 million immigrants arrived between 1870 and 1920. Earlier most came from Britain, Ireland and Germany; later from Italy, Poland, Russia and eastern Europe, including millions of Jews fleeing persecution. Many passed through Ellis Island in New York harbour, opened in 1892, under the Statue of Liberty.

Nativists resented newcomers. The 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act barred Chinese labourers, the first law to ban a group by nationality, and in 1924 strict quotas sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe and banned it from Asia.

us-industry.s: The Chinese Exclusion Act barred Chinese labourers from entering the US.

us-industry.p:
The US bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. In 1893 American planters overthrew Hawaii's queen, and the US annexed the islands in 1898.

That year the US fought Spain and took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where it then fought a brutal war against Filipino independence fighters until 1902.

The US helped Panama break away from Colombia in 1903 and built the Panama Canal, opened in 1914, linking the Atlantic and the Pacific. The US was now a world power, though most Americans still wanted to stay out of Europe's wars.

us-depression.p: The US joined World War I in 1917, after German submarines sank American ships. Over 2 million Americans went to France, and President Wilson tried to shape the peace with his Fourteen Points and a League of Nations, which the Senate refused to join.

The 1920s boomed: cars, radios, the movies and jazz. In 1920 the 19th Amendment gave women the vote. Prohibition banned alcohol from 1920 to 1933, which fed organised crime under gangsters such as Al Capone.

The Harlem Renaissance brought Black writers and musicians to national fame.

Easy credit fuelled a stock market bubble. In October 1929 it burst. Banks failed and wiped out savings, factories closed, and by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job. Families lost homes and farms, and lived in shanty towns called 'Hoovervilles'.

On the southern Plains, years of drought and ploughing up the grassland turned the soil to dust. Huge 'black blizzards' buried farms. Hundreds of thousands of 'Okies' fled west to California, as told in Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath.

Franklin D. Roosevelt, elected in 1932, promised a 'New Deal'. The government hired millions to build roads, dams, schools and parks, regulated banks and the stock market, protected unions, and in 1935 created Social Security pensions.

It changed Americans' idea of what government should do, and still divides them.

a: Roosevelt's programmes of jobs, relief and reform in the Depression
A peace treaty after World War I
A trade deal with Britain
A plan to buy Alaska
us-depression.why: Social Security is its most lasting legacy.

items: The US joins World War I

us-superpower.p:
On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the US fleet at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The US declared war on Japan, and Germany declared war on the US.

American factories out-produced every other country, women took millions of factory jobs ('Rosie the Riveter'), and 16 million Americans served.

Over 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were forced into incarceration camps. Black soldiers fought in a segregated army, a contradiction that fed the civil rights movement after the war.
In the secret Manhattan Project, scientists at Los Alamos built the atomic bomb. In August 1945 the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan surrendered.

a: The secret programme that built the atomic bomb
A plan to rebuild New York
The Moon landing programme
A New Deal jobs scheme
us-superpower.why: It was based at Los Alamos, New Mexico.

us-superpower.p: The US came out of the war as the richest country on Earth. It helped found the United Nations, rebuilt western Europe with the Marshall Plan and led NATO against the Soviet Union for 45 years.

us-superpower.h: Fear at home and wars abroad
us-superpower.p:
Fear of communism led to the 'Red Scare' of Senator McCarthy in the 1950s. The US fought in Korea (1950–53) and Vietnam, where 58,000 Americans died and the war split the country before the US withdrew in 1973.

In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war.

The 1950s brought suburbs, cars, television and a 'baby boom'. In July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on it. In 1991 the Soviet Union collapsed, leaving the US the only superpower.

us-civilrights.p: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional, overturning 'separate but equal'. In 1957 President Eisenhower sent troops to escort nine Black students into Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas.

In 1955 Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. Black residents boycotted the buses for 381 days, led by a young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., until the buses were desegregated.

King preached non-violent resistance, inspired by Jesus and Gandhi.

In 1960 students sat in at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and sit-ins spread across the South. Freedom Riders rode buses to challenge segregation and were beaten by mobs. In Birmingham in 1963 police turned fire hoses and dogs on children, and the images shocked the nation.

In August 1963, at the March on Washington, King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech to 250,000 people. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation and discrimination, and after police attacked marchers at Selma, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 protected Black voters.

King was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

The civil rights movement inspired others: the women's movement, Mexican American farmworkers led by César Chávez, Native American activists, and the gay rights movement after the Stonewall riots in New York in 1969.

us-civilrights.q: What did Martin Luther King Jr. use to fight segregation?
a: Non-violent protest
Armed revolution
Lawsuits only
Moving to Canada

us-today.p: Watergate forced President Nixon to resign in 1974. The 1980s under Ronald Reagan brought tax cuts and a renewed Cold War, then victory in it. The 1990s were a boom, driven by computers and the internet, with Silicon Valley at its heart.

The 11 September 2001 attacks killed nearly 3,000 people and led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. The 2008 financial crisis caused the worst recession since the 1930s, and that year Barack Obama was elected the first Black president.

COVID-19 killed over a million Americans from 2020.

Politics have grown sharply polarised between Republicans and Democrats, often along lines of city and countryside, religion and education. Donald Trump was president from 2017 to 2021, and won a second, non-consecutive term in 2024.
Americans keep moving to the Sun Belt, to states such as Texas, Florida and Arizona, and after each census House seats move with them.

items: Argued over constantly, but shared by all sides.
Still central to politics and inequality.
About 1 in 7 Americans was born abroad.
More religious than most rich countries; wary of big government.

us-today.s: Barack Obama was the first Black president of the United States.

cn-origins.p:
China's heartland is two great river valleys: the Yellow River in the north, where millet and wheat grew, and the Yangtze in the south, where rice was farmed from about 7000 BC. To the west lie the Himalayas, Tibetan plateau and deserts; to the north, the steppe of the nomads. Those barriers made China a world of its own.

The Yellow River's floods were so deadly it was called 'China's Sorrow'. Controlling water was one of the first jobs of government.

The Shang dynasty ruled the North China Plain from about 1600 BC. Oracle bones from their capital at Anyang carry the earliest known Chinese writing, ancestor of today's characters.

Around 1046 BC the Zhou overthrew the Shang. They claimed the 'Mandate of Heaven': Heaven gives a just ruler the right to rule and withdraws it from a cruel one, shown by floods, famine and revolt. Every later dynasty used the idea, and rebels used it too.

As Zhou power faded, China split into warring states. In this age of chaos Confucius (551–479 BC) taught that order comes from virtue: rulers should set a moral example, children should honour parents, and everyone should know their role and behave with propriety.

His ideas shaped Chinese government, education and family life for over 2,000 years, and still do in East Asia.

items: Family, respect, education, rule by moral example.
Simplicity and going with nature; Laozi.
Strict laws and harsh punishments; used by Qin.

a: The idea that Heaven grants a just ruler the right to rule and can take it away
A Shang law code
The Great Wall
A Buddhist scripture
cn-origins.why: It explained why dynasties rose and fell.

cn-qin.p:
From 356 BC the minister Shang Yang reformed the state of Qin, in the far west, into a machine for farming and war: rewards for soldiers, harsh punishments, and whole families punished for one member's crime. This was Legalism.

Between 230 and 221 BC Qin conquered its six rivals. King Zheng named himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. The name 'China' probably comes from Qin.

items: People speaking different dialects could read the same texts: still true today.
Trade across the empire got easier.
Roads, canals and an early Great Wall
Built by forced labour that killed many.

cn-qin.p:
The First Emperor was obsessed with immortality. He died in 210 BC and was buried near Xi'an with an army of about 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, horses and chariots, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

His rule was so harsh that revolts brought the Qin down in 206 BC. But the idea that China should be one country under one ruler outlived him, and has guided Chinese politics ever since.

cn-qin.s: The Qin dynasty ruled China for centuries.
cn-qin.why: Only 15 years after unification, but the idea of one China lasted.

cn-hantang.p:
The Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220) kept the Qin's unified state but softened it. Officials were chosen for their Confucian learning, a system that later became the imperial exams.

The Han invented paper, fought the nomadic Xiongnu, and sent the envoy Zhang Qian west, opening the Silk Road. A census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people, as many as the Roman Empire. Most Chinese still call themselves the Han people.

Along the Silk Road, Buddhism reached China from India in the first century AD. After the Han collapsed in 220, nearly four centuries of division followed, and in those troubled times Buddhism spread widely, blending with Chinese traditions.

cn-hantang.q: Which invention came from Han China?
a: Paper
The printing press
Gunpowder
The compass
cn-hantang.why: Paper is traditionally dated to about AD 105.

cn-hantang.p:
The Sui reunified China in 589 and dug the Grand Canal, linking the rice-growing south with the political north. It is still the longest canal in the world.

The Sui exhausted the people and fell quickly, but the Tang dynasty that followed, from 618, made China the richest and most open empire on Earth.

The Tang capital Chang'an, today's Xi'an, may have had a million people, with merchants from Persia, Arabia and Central Asia. Buddhism flourished, poetry reached its peak with Li Bai and Du Fu, and woodblock printing was invented. Wu Zetian became China's only woman emperor.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 broke Tang power, and the dynasty fell in 907.

cn-songming.p:
The Song dynasty (960–1279) was one of history's great ages of invention and trade: movable-type printing, gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass at sea and the world's first government paper money. Its cities, such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou, were the largest on Earth, and the imperial exams opened government to talent.

But it was militarily weak. In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took the north, and the Song fled south.

items: Navigation out of sight of land.
cn-songming.p: Chinese schoolchildren learn these as China's gifts to the world.

In 1279 Kublai Khan's Mongols finished the Song. For the first time all of China was ruled by foreigners, as the Yuan dynasty, from Beijing (Dadu). Marco Polo described its wealth. Mongol rule was resented, and plague, floods and famine fed rebellion.

cn-songming.q: Which of these did NOT come from China?
a: The steam engine
Paper
Gunpowder
The compass
cn-songming.why: The steam engine came from Britain in the 1700s.

cn-songming.p:
In 1368 a former peasant and monk, Zhu Yuanzhang, drove out the Mongols and founded the Ming. In 1421 the capital moved to Beijing, with its new Forbidden City, the emperor's palace.

The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in the stone and brick that visitors see today.

From 1405 to 1433 Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed as far as Arabia and East Africa. Then the voyages stopped and the records were reportedly destroyed; the Ming focused on the northern frontier and limited foreign trade.

Silver from Spanish America flowed in to pay for Chinese silk and porcelain, but the dynasty weakened and fell to rebels in 1644.

cn-songming.q: Which dynasty built most of the Great Wall that stands today?
a: The Ming
The Qin
The Han
The Tang
cn-songming.why: Earlier walls were mostly packed earth.

cn-qing.p: In 1644 rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. The Manchus, from beyond the Great Wall, swept in and founded the Qing dynasty, the last to rule China. Han Chinese men had to wear the Manchu queue hairstyle as a sign of loyalty.

The great Qing emperors Kangxi and Qianlong ruled for 120 years between them. They took Taiwan (1683), set the border with Russia at Nerchinsk (1689), brought Tibet under Qing control and conquered Xinjiang (1755–59), destroying the Dzungar people.

China reached the borders it largely claims today, and its population tripled to about 300 million by 1800.

In 1793 Britain's Macartney mission asked for more trade. The Qianlong emperor replied that China had 'all things' and no need of British goods.

Within 50 years, Britain would force the door open with gunboats.

a: The Manchus
The Mongols
The Han Chinese
The Japanese

cn-humiliation.p:
Britain bought huge amounts of Chinese tea but China wanted little in return. So British merchants sold opium grown in India, and millions of Chinese became addicted. When official Lin Zexu destroyed the opium stocks at Canton in 1839, Britain went to war.

Britain won (1839–42), took Hong Kong Island and forced open five ports. A second war (1856–60) ended with British and French troops burning the emperor's Summer Palace.

From 1850 Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, led the Taiping Rebellion, which conquered much of southern China. Perhaps 20 to 30 million people died before it was crushed in 1864, making it one of the deadliest wars in history.

cn-humiliation.q: What did Britain take after the First Opium War?
a: Hong Kong Island
Taiwan
Shanghai
Macao

cn-humiliation.p:
In 1894–95 Japan, which had modernised far faster, crushed China and took Taiwan. European powers and Japan carved China into 'spheres of influence'.

In 1900 the anti-foreign Boxer uprising besieged the foreign embassies in Beijing; an army of eight nations crushed it and forced China to pay a huge indemnity.

Reforms came too late. In 1911 an army uprising in Wuchang set off a revolution, and in 1912 the last emperor, the six-year-old Puyi, abdicated. More than 2,000 years of imperial rule were over.

Chinese call 1839–1949 the 'century of humiliation'. Its memory still shapes how China sees the West and Japan.

cn-republic.p:
Sun Yat-sen's Republic of China was founded in 1912, but warlords soon carved up the country. In 1919 students protested against the Versailles treaty giving Germany's rights in China to Japan: the May Fourth Movement, which demanded science, democracy and a new China.

In 1921 the Chinese Communist Party held its first congress in Shanghai.

Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists (Kuomintang) united most of China by 1928, then turned on their Communist allies, massacring them in Shanghai in 1927. Surrounded in Jiangxi, the Communists escaped on the Long March (1934–35), about 10,000 km to Shaanxi. Most did not survive, but Mao Zedong emerged as leader.

cn-republic.q: Who led the Communists after the Long March?
a: Mao Zedong
Chiang Kai-shek
Sun Yat-sen
Puyi
cn-republic.why: He led them to victory in 1949.

cn-republic.p:
Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded the rest of China in 1937. At Nanjing its troops massacred huge numbers of civilians. Japan occupied the east and the coast; the Nationalist government retreated inland to Chongqing.

Perhaps 15 to 20 million Chinese died in the war with Japan.

After Japan's surrender in 1945, the civil war resumed. The Communists, popular with peasants for land reform and disciplined, defeated the corrupt and exhausted Nationalists. In 1949 Chiang's government fled to Taiwan, where the Republic of China still governs.

cn-mao.p: On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic in Beijing. Land was seized from landlords, many of whom were killed, and industry was taken over by the state. China fought the US in Korea (1950–53) and the army entered Tibet in 1950; after a failed uprising in 1959 the Dalai Lama fled to India.

In 1958 Mao tried to overtake Britain's industry in 15 years. Peasants were forced into giant communes and backyard steel furnaces; officials, afraid to report failure, claimed record harvests while grain was taken away.

The famine of 1959–61 killed tens of millions of people: the deadliest famine in history.

In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution to purge 'enemies' and revive revolutionary zeal. Teenage Red Guards attacked teachers, officials and 'old ideas', destroyed temples and books, and waved Mao's Little Red Book. Schools closed and millions were persecuted or sent to the countryside.

It ended only with Mao's death in 1976.
In 1971 Beijing took China's seat at the UN from Taiwan, and in 1972 US President Nixon visited Mao: the two rivals of the Soviet Union came together.

cn-mao.q: What was the Great Leap Forward?
a: A crash industrial and farming campaign that caused a huge famine
The market reforms of the 1980s
A Tang poetry movement
The Long March

cn-reform.p:
After Mao's death Deng Xiaoping took charge. From 1978 farmers could sell surplus crops, and special economic zones such as Shenzhen welcomed foreign investment. 'It doesn't matter if a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice,' Deng said: what works matters more than ideology.

China grew about 10% a year for three decades, and hundreds of millions escaped poverty: the fastest rise in living standards in history.

To slow population growth, from 1980 most urban couples were allowed one child, enforced with fines and sometimes forced abortions. It ended in 2015, but left China ageing fast, with more men than women.

In 1989 students and workers filled Tiananmen Square calling for reform and an end to corruption. On 3–4 June the army crushed the protests, killing hundreds, perhaps thousands. The event cannot be discussed in China today.

The message was clear: economic freedom, yes; political freedom, no.
Britain returned Hong Kong in 1997 and Portugal returned Macao in 1999, as special administrative regions promised 'one country, two systems' for 50 years.

cn-reform.q: What did Deng's 'reform and opening' do?
a: Opened China to markets and foreign investment while the Party kept power
Restarted the Cultural Revolution
Held free elections
Gave Taiwan independence

cn-today.p: China joined the WTO in 2001 and became 'the world's factory'. It hosted the Olympics in 2008 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. It now leads the world in manufacturing, high-speed rail, solar panels and electric cars.

Xi Jinping became leader in 2012 and has concentrated power more than anyone since Mao, removing term limits in 2018. He launched a vast anti-corruption campaign and a global Belt and Road building programme.

Control has tightened: mass detention of Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang, and a national security law in 2020 that ended Hong Kong's protest movement.

Beijing claims Taiwan, a democracy of 23 million, and has not ruled out force. Rivalry with the US over trade, technology and Taiwan is the central tension in world politics.

China's population is now shrinking and ageing; India passed it in 2023.

items: Rooted in 2,000 years of empire and the fear of breakup.
Drives nationalism and the claim to Taiwan.
Still strong beneath the communist label.
Its legitimacy rests on growth and stability.

cn-today.q: When did China pass Japan as the world’s second-largest economy?
cn-today.why: Only the US economy is larger.

ca-first.p: Most of Canada lay under ice sheets until about 13,000 years ago. As the ice melted, people moved in, following animals north. Some sites are far older than the pyramids: Plains peoples drove bison over the cliffs at Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump for over 5,000 years.

items: Seals, whales and caribou; igloos and kayaks.
Hunting moose and caribou across the forests.
Corn, beans and squash; longhouse villages.
Salmon, cedar, totem poles and potlatches.

ca-first.p: South of the St Lawrence, five, later six, nations formed the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, perhaps in the 1400s or earlier, under a 'Great Law of Peace' with a council of chiefs chosen by clan mothers. Some historians think it influenced American founders.

Around 1000, Norse from Greenland camped at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, the first known Europeans in the Americas, nearly 500 years before Columbus. Around 1200 the ancestors of the Inuit spread east across the Arctic. In 1497 John Cabot reached Newfoundland for England, and European fishermen soon came for its rich cod banks.

ca-first.s: Vikings reached Canada about 500 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic.
ca-first.why: Norse camped at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000.

ca-newfrance.p:
In 1534 Jacques Cartier claimed the Gulf of St Lawrence for France; the name 'Canada' comes from an Iroquoian word, kanata, 'village'. In 1608 Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City, and Montreal followed in 1642.

New France grew slowly: by 1760 only about 70,000 settlers, the habitants, farmed along the St Lawrence.

New France lived on fur. Beaver pelts, made into felt hats in Europe, were traded by First Nations for metal tools, cloth and guns. French coureurs des bois and voyageurs paddled deep into the interior, often marrying into First Nations; their descendants include the Métis.

In 1670 England chartered the Hudson's Bay Company, which claimed all the land draining into Hudson Bay: Rupert's Land, a third of today's Canada.

France allied with the Huron-Wendat and Algonquin; the Haudenosaunee, allied with the Dutch and English, nearly destroyed the Huron in the 1640s. In 1701 the Great Peace of Montreal brought peace with about 40 First Nations.

In 1713 France gave Britain Acadia (Nova Scotia), Newfoundland and Hudson Bay. From 1755 Britain deported about 10,000 French-speaking Acadians, the 'Great Upheaval'; some ended up in Louisiana as the Cajuns.

ca-newfrance.q: What was New France's main trade?
a: Fur, especially beaver
Gold
Sugar
Tobacco
ca-newfrance.why: Beaver felt hats were the fashion in Europe.

ca-british.p:
In 1759, in the Seven Years' War, British troops under General Wolfe climbed the cliffs to the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec and won a battle in which both Wolfe and the French general Montcalm died. In 1763 France handed New France to Britain.

The Royal Proclamation of 1763 recognised First Nations' rights to land not yet ceded, the basis of treaty-making ever since.

To keep 70,000 French Catholics loyal, the 1774 Quebec Act protected French civil law and the Catholic Church. When the American Revolution broke out, Quebec did not join it, and an American invasion of Quebec in 1775 failed.

After the Revolution about 40,000 Loyalists, Americans who had sided with Britain, moved north, including Black Loyalists and Haudenosaunee led by Joseph Brant. They made English-speaking settlement grow fast, and in 1791 Britain split the colony into English Upper Canada (Ontario) and French Lower Canada (Quebec).

When the US declared war on Britain in 1812, American armies invaded the Canadas. They were driven back by British troops, Canadian militia and First Nations allies led by Tecumseh, and by Laura Secord's famous warning. The war helped forge a sense of being different from the Americans.

ca-confed.p:
In 1837 rebels in both Canadas rose against rule by small elites; they were crushed. Britain united the two in 1841, and by 1848 the colonies had won 'responsible government': cabinets answerable to elected assemblies, not to the governor.

Canada would gain independence step by step, by negotiation, not revolution.

In the 1860s the colonies had reasons to unite: fear of the huge US army after its Civil War, the need for railways, and political deadlock in the Province of Canada. Leaders such as John A. Macdonald and George-Étienne Cartier planned a union at Charlottetown and Quebec in 1864.

On 1 July 1867 Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick formed the Dominion of Canada, a federation with a parliament in Ottawa and the British monarch as head of state. Macdonald was the first prime minister. 1 July is Canada Day.

ca-confed.q: How did Canada gain independence from Britain?
a: Gradually, by negotiation
Through a war of independence
By a single referendum in 1867
It was given to the US
ca-confed.why: From responsible government in 1848 to full control of its constitution in 1982.

ca-confed.p:
Canada bought Rupert's Land in 1869; Manitoba (1870), British Columbia (1871, promised a railway) and PEI (1873) joined; Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905; Newfoundland joined only in 1949, after a close referendum.

In 1999 Nunavut was carved out of the Northwest Territories, an Inuit-majority territory.

Canada fought in the world wars as a dominion but signed its own treaties. The Statute of Westminster (1931) made it fully self-governing; it got its own flag, the maple leaf, in 1965; and in 1982 the constitution was 'patriated' from Britain with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The British monarch remains Canada's head of state.

ca-west.p: When Canada bought Rupert's Land in 1869 without asking its people, the Métis of Red River, led by Louis Riel, set up their own government. The result was a new province, Manitoba, in 1870, with protections for French and Catholics; Riel fled into exile.

From 1871 to 1877 Canada signed treaties 1–7 with Plains and woodland nations, which ceded vast lands in return for reserves, payments and promises of help. First Nations understood them as agreements to share the land; the government treated them as land surrenders.

The 1876 Indian Act put First Nations under tight federal control, and still exists.

In 1885 the Canadian Pacific Railway's last spike was driven at Craigellachie, BC, linking the country from sea to sea, built partly by about 15,000 Chinese workers, who then faced a head tax.

That year Métis and some Cree rose in the North-West Resistance; it was crushed and Riel was hanged, deeply dividing English and French Canada. Settlers, many from Ukraine and eastern Europe, soon poured onto the Prairies.

a: He led Métis resistance and helped found Manitoba
He was the first prime minister
He built the railway
He led Canada in World War I
ca-west.why: He was hanged in 1885 and is now seen by many as a founder of Manitoba.

ca-wars.p:
Canada went to war in 1914 as part of the British Empire. Canadians held the line against the first gas attack at Ypres in 1915, and in April 1917 all four Canadian divisions together took Vimy Ridge, a victory many saw as Canada's coming of age.

About 61,000 Canadians died, from a population of 8 million.

In 1917 the government brought in conscription. English Canada largely supported it; Quebec, which felt little loyalty to Britain, strongly opposed it, and riots broke out. The split between English and French Canada deepened.

In 1939 Canada declared war on Germany on its own, on 10 September, a week after Britain. Over a million Canadians served. They landed on Juno Beach on D-Day and freed much of the Netherlands in 1945, which still sends Ottawa tulips every year.

At home, about 22,000 Japanese Canadians were removed from the coast, interned and their property sold.

ca-wars.q: Which 1917 battle is seen as Canada’s coming of age?
a: Vimy Ridge
Juno Beach
Dieppe
Ypres
ca-wars.why: All four Canadian divisions fought together for the first time.

items: Canada declares war on its own

ca-wars.p:
After 1945 Canada built a welfare state, with public health care (medicare) starting in Saskatchewan under Tommy Douglas and spreading nationwide by 1972. Lester Pearson won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957 for inventing UN peacekeeping during the Suez crisis.

The maple leaf flag arrived in 1965, and Expo 67 in Montreal celebrated the centennial.

Immigration rules stopped favouring Europeans in 1967. In 1971 Pierre Trudeau made Canada the first country with an official policy of multiculturalism, and in 1969 French and English became official languages across the federal government.

ca-wars.s: Public health care in Canada began in Saskatchewan.
ca-wars.why: Tommy Douglas’s government introduced it; it went national by 1972.

ca-quebec.p:
Until 1960 Quebec was rural, Catholic and dominated by English-speaking business. Jean Lesage's Liberals then modernised it fast: the Church lost control of schools and hospitals, hydro power was nationalised, and French speakers took charge of the economy: 'Maîtres chez nous', masters in our own house.

A movement for Quebec independence, sovereignty, grew.

In 1970 the FLQ, a violent separatist group, kidnapped a British diplomat and murdered Quebec minister Pierre Laporte. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act and sent troops. In 1977 the sovereigntist Parti Québécois passed Bill 101, making French Quebec's common public language.

In 1980 about 60% of Quebecers voted No to sovereignty. In 1982 Trudeau patriated the constitution with a Charter of Rights, but Quebec's government refused to sign. Attempts to win Quebec's agreement (Meech Lake, 1990) failed.

In 1995 No won a second referendum by just 50.6% to 49.4%.

ca-quebec.note: No to sovereignty won both times.

ca-quebec.s: Quebec voted to leave Canada in 1995.

ca-rights.p:
From the 1880s to 1996, about 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were taken from their families to residential schools run for the government by churches, to 'kill the Indian in the child'. Languages were forbidden, abuse was common and thousands died.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later called it cultural genocide.

First Nations pushed back: they defeated a 1969 plan to abolish Indian status. Courts accepted in 1973 that Aboriginal title existed, and the 1975 James Bay agreement with the Cree and Inuit was the first modern treaty. The 1982 Constitution recognised and affirmed Aboriginal and treaty rights.

In 2008 Prime Minister Harper apologised for the residential schools. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued 94 Calls to Action. In 2021 searches found possible unmarked graves at former schools, and 30 September became a national day for truth and reconciliation.

ca-rights.q: About how many Indigenous children attended residential schools?
a: About 150,000
About 1,500
About 15,000
About 1.5 million

ca-today.p: Canada has about 41.8 million people, most within a few hundred kilometres of the US border. In 2021 a record 23% were immigrants, and Toronto and Vancouver are among the world's most diverse cities.
