dd-vikings.p: On 8 June 793 raiders from Scandinavia sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, and for two centuries Vikings raided coasts and rivers across Europe. Raiding grew into conquest: a Danish Great Army landed in England in 865 and settled the north and east, the Danelaw, and in 911 the Frankish king granted the lower Seine to the chief Rollo, founding Normandy. Norse settlers founded Dublin, settled Iceland from about 870 and Greenland around 985, and briefly reached Newfoundland around 1000.

steps: Fast, shallow boats that could cross oceans and row up rivers.
Little farmland in Norway and a growing population.
Rich, undefended monasteries and trading towns.
Raiding brought silver, status and stories.

items: Scotland, Ireland, Iceland, Greenland, North America.
Russian rivers to Constantinople and Baghdad.

a: Leif Erikson
Harald Hardrada
Ragnar Lothbrok
Cnut

dd-vikings.p: In the east, Swedes called the Rus traded down the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and the Caspian, and their princes ruled Kyiv. The age is often said to end in 1066, when the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada was killed at Stamford Bridge.

dd-vikings.q: How did Viking activity change between the sack of Lindisfarne in 793 and about 1000?
a: Raiding grew into conquest and settlement across Europe and the Atlantic
Vikings stopped raiding and turned only to farming at home
Vikings were driven out of every land they had raided
Raids stayed small and never went beyond Britain
dd-vikings.why: Raids grew into conquest: the Danelaw in England, Normandy in France, Dublin, Iceland, Greenland and, briefly, Newfoundland.

dd-vikings.p: Historians still debate the causes. Ambitious chiefs needed silver and land to reward their followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare. Fast, shallow ships let them cross open sea and row far up rivers, and rich, poorly defended monasteries and trading towns made easy targets. Booming trade with the Islamic world, and quarrels among the Frankish and English kingdoms, drew them further in.

dd-vikings.h: Raids and settlements in the west, 793–c. 1000
dd-vikings.p: Viking raids began with the sack of Lindisfarne in 793. Danes later settled the north and east of England, the Danelaw, and in 911 a Frankish king granted Normandy in France to the chief Rollo. Norwegians founded Dublin in Ireland and sailed on to Iceland and Greenland, and around 1000 they reached Newfoundland in Canada, five centuries before Columbus.

dd-vikings.q: What gave the Vikings their great advantage in reaching so many places?
a: Horse archers who could ride across the steppe
Heavy warships armed with catapults
Light, shallow longships that crossed open sea and rowed up rivers
Maps bought from Arab merchants
dd-vikings.why: Longships drew only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach, cross open sea and row far up rivers like the Seine.

dd-vikings.p:
Norway, Denmark and Sweden

Norwegians raided Scotland and Ireland and settled the Atlantic islands, Iceland and Greenland. Norway became one kingdom under Harald Fairhair and his successors in the late 800s and 900s.

Danes led the great armies that raided the Frankish lands and conquered much of England. Danish king Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the 1020s.

Lands where Norse settlers took over or founded towns

Settlers arrived from about 870, many from Norway and the British Isles. In 930 they founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest assemblies.

Norse farmers settled the Faroe Islands in the 800s, and their language became today's Faroese.

dd-vikings.q: Why does Kyivan Rus still matter to several countries today?
a: It is a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
It was the first kingdom of Sweden
It founded the city of Constantinople
It is where the English language began
dd-vikings.why: Rus princes of Norse origin ruled Kyiv, and after Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988 it became a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

dd-vikings.p:
A small base used for a few years around 1000

Leif Erikson's voyages reached a land the sagas called Vinland. The base at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, was used only briefly.

The longship was the Vikings' great advantage. Built of overlapping oak planks, it was light, flexible and shallow, drawing only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach and row far up rivers like the Seine. A big square woollen sail drove it at sea, and oars took over in calm water or on rivers. The warship Skuldelev 2, built near Dublin around 1042 and sunk in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark, was about 30 metres long and carried around 60–70 men; a replica sailed from Roskilde to Dublin in 2007. Grand ships were also buried with the dead, as at Oseberg in Norway in 834. Sailors navigated by coastlines, sun, stars, birds and whales.

'Viking' meant going raiding, not a people: most Norse were farmers, fishers and craftspeople who never went 'a-viking'. They wore no horned helmets. The only fairly complete Viking helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway, is a plain iron cap; the horns come from 19th-century painters and the costumes for Wagner's operas in 1876. Combs are among the commonest finds, and free women could own property and divorce. Communities settled disputes at assemblies called things, the root of Iceland's Althing. But the raids were brutal, and slaving was central to the economy: captives from Ireland, Britain and eastern Europe were sold in markets from Dublin to the Volga.

dd-vikings.h: The Rus and the river roads, c. 860–1000
dd-vikings.p: Swedish Vikings, called the Rus, rowed and dragged their boats along the rivers of eastern Europe. On the Dnieper they reached Kyiv and the Black Sea, then Constantinople, the 'great city' they called Miklagard. On the Volga they traded furs and slaves for Arab silver. Their leaders founded Kyivan Rus, a state spanning today's Ukraine, Belarus and western Russia.

Sweden, home of most eastern Vikings

Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins have been found on the Swedish island of Gotland alone, brought back by trade along the eastern rivers.

dd-vikings.q: What drove ambitious Scandinavian chiefs to go raiding, according to the chapter?
a: They were fleeing a Christian invasion of Scandinavia
They needed silver and land to reward their followers
Their kings ordered them to spread the Norse religion
The Frankish king paid them to attack England
dd-vikings.why: Chiefs needed silver and land to reward followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare, though historians still debate the causes.

dd-vikings.p:
Ruled by Norse-descended princes who soon spoke Slavic

Polotsk, in today's Belarus, was one of the oldest towns of the Rus, ruled by its own princes.

Kyiv became the Rus capital around 882. The state's princes made treaties with the Byzantine Empire in 911 and 944.

dd-vikings.h: The Rus: Vikings in the east
dd-vikings.p: Swedish traders, known to their neighbours as the Rus, rowed across the Baltic and up the rivers of eastern Europe, dragging their boats overland between rivers. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII recorded the names of the Dnieper rapids in both Norse and Slavic. According to the Primary Chronicle, written around 1113, the Varangian Rurik was invited to rule Novgorod in 862; how much of this is legend is debated. The Rus raided Constantinople in 860, and Rurik's successors ruled from Kyiv and made trade treaties with the Byzantines. Norsemen served the emperor in the Varangian Guard, and one carved runes into a balustrade in Hagia Sophia. Within a few generations the Rus princes spoke Slavic and, from 988, worshipped as Orthodox Christians.

dd-vikings.q: What did Rollo's settlers in Normandy go on to do?
a: They founded Dublin and the first Irish towns
They settled Iceland and founded the Althing
They ruled Kyiv and traded with Constantinople
Their Norman descendants conquered England, southern Italy and Sicily
dd-vikings.why: Normandy grew from lands granted to Rollo in 911, and the Normans descended from his settlers conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily.

dd-vikings.p: Denmark, Norway and Sweden became Christian kingdoms, taking shape around 1000. Norse settlers peopled Iceland and the Faroes, founded Dublin, and left English with words such as 'sky', 'egg' and 'they'. The Normans, descended from Rollo's settlers, conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily. In the east, Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988, a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.
Vikings founded Dublin, settled Iceland and Normandy, and helped found the first Russian state. English took hundreds of Norse words such as 'sky', 'egg', 'knife' and 'Thursday' (Thor’s day).

The Danish Great Army lands in England
Rollo is granted the land that becomes Normandy
Iceland's settlers found the Althing assembly
Norse reach Newfoundland, at L'Anse aux Meadows
Harald Hardrada is killed at Stamford Bridge

dd-russia.p: In the 800s Scandinavian-led princes built a state, Rus', along the rivers from Novgorod to Kyiv, and in 988 it adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium. Mongol armies conquered it in 1237–40. Moscow's princes rose as the Mongols' tax collectors, threw off their rule in 1480, and under Ivan IV took the title of tsar.

steps: Ivan the Terrible crowns himself tsar in 1547.
Siberia conquered by 1640; Russia spans 11 time zones.

l: Peter the Great’s new capital, St Petersburg
dd-russia.p: This tension runs through Russian history to today.

Cossacks crossed Siberia to the Pacific by 1639. Peter the Great made Russia a European great power and an empire in 1721, and Catherine the Great pushed it to the Black Sea. By 1914 the tsars ruled a sixth of the world's land, until war and revolution brought them down in 1917.

dd-russia.q: What is the broad story of Russia from Kyivan Rus to 1914?
a: A small principality that stayed confined to the area around Moscow
Growth from river princedoms into an empire covering a sixth of the world's land
A Mongol state that ruled China and Europe until 1917
A republic that became a monarchy under Peter the Great
dd-russia.why: From Rus' along the rivers, Moscow rose, expanded across Siberia, the Black Sea and Central Asia, and by 1914 ruled a sixth of the world's land.

dd-russia.p: Russia grew across open plains with few natural barriers, where expansion meant security and new lands to tax, and Siberia's furs drew traders east. Its rulers concentrated power in an autocratic tsar, backed by the Orthodox Church and a service nobility rewarded with land and serfs. Rivals were weakened in turn: the Mongol khanates, Sweden, Poland-Lithuania and the Ottomans. The empire's weaknesses were rigid autocracy, peasant poverty and late industrialisation, which defeat in war exposed.

According to the Primary Chronicle, a Scandinavian named Rurik began to rule at Novgorod in 862, and his successors made Kyiv their capital. Their state, Rus', grew along the river route from the Baltic to the Byzantine Empire. In 988 Prince Volodymyr (Vladimir) was baptised, bringing Orthodox Christianity from Constantinople. Today's Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all trace their history to this state.

dd-russia.q: What finally brought down the tsars in 1917?
a: A Swedish invasion of St Petersburg
The sale of Alaska to the United States
A peaceful vote in the Duma to become a republic
A disastrous world war that exposed autocracy, poverty and late industrialisation
dd-russia.why: The First World War brought huge losses and bread shortages; strikes and mutinies forced Nicholas II to abdicate, and the Bolsheviks then seized power.

dd-russia.p:
A federation of principalities under the princes of Kyiv

The principalities of Polotsk and Turov, in today's Belarus, were part of Rus'. Belarusians also count it as part of their history.

Kyiv was the capital of Rus' and its greatest city. Ukrainians see Rus' as the foundation of their own history.

Rus' trading partner and source of its faith

Greek clergy, icon painters and architects brought Byzantine religion and art to Rus'; its first metropolitans of Kyiv were mostly Greeks.

Church books reached Rus' in Old Church Slavonic, written in the Cyrillic script that grew up in Bulgaria around 900.

Scandinavian traders and warriors came from here

Scandinavian traders, called Varangians, travelled the rivers to trade furs and slaves for silver; they merged into the local Slavic population within a few generations.

Peter I, who ruled from 1682 to 1725, stood about two metres tall and was determined to modernise Russia on European lines. In 1697–98 he toured Western Europe with a large embassy, working for a time in a Dutch shipyard. Back home he ordered nobles to shave their beards or pay a tax, built a navy, and forced the nobility to serve the state. In 1703, on land taken from Sweden, he founded St Petersburg, built by tens of thousands of conscripted labourers, many of whom died. Victory over Sweden at Poltava in 1709 made Russia the leading power in the Baltic, and in 1721 he took the title of emperor.

Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240, and for two centuries the Rus' principalities paid tribute to the Golden Horde. Moscow rose by collecting that tribute. Ivan III ended Mongol overlordship in 1480, and Ivan IV, the Terrible, crowned himself tsar in 1547 and took Kazan and Astrakhan. Cossacks then pushed into Siberia. To the west, Poland-Lithuania ruled much of today's Ukraine and Belarus, and Sweden contested the Baltic coast.

Muscovy, expanding east into Siberia

Russia doubled in size in the 1500s, taking the Volga khanates and western Siberia. The Time of Troubles followed in 1598–1613, ending with the first Romanov tsar.

dd-russia.q: Why did Russia keep expanding across Eurasia?
a: Mountains and seas forced it to look only eastward
Open plains with few barriers made expansion mean security and new lands to tax
The Ottomans gave it Siberia in exchange for peace
It needed colonies to settle a shrinking population
dd-russia.why: Russia grew across open plains with few natural barriers, where expansion meant security and new lands to tax, and Siberia's furs drew traders east.

dd-russia.p:
Commonwealth of Poland and Lithuania, from 1569

The Grand Duchy of Lithuania had absorbed most of the old Rus' lands in the west during the 1300s, including Kyiv.

Belarus was part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania for about four centuries, until the partitions of Poland in 1772–95.

Rival for the Baltic coast

Sweden, which then lacked its far south, still Danish, fought Russia for the Baltic coast. In 1617 it shut Russia out of the Baltic until Peter the Great's victory in the Great Northern War, 1700–21.

Northern Estonia came under Swedish rule in 1561, after Ivan IV's Livonian War broke up the old Livonian Order.

dd-russia.q: How does the empire's history still shape the region today?
a: Rival readings of Kyivan Rus' have featured in Russia's war on Ukraine
Russia is now smaller than any of its former republics
Ukraine and Belarus rejoined the Russian Empire in 1991
No country today claims Kyivan Rus' as its history
dd-russia.why: Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all claim Kyivan Rus', and rival readings of that shared past have featured in the full-scale war Russia launched in 2022.

dd-russia.p: For centuries most Russians were peasants, and from the law code of 1649 most were serfs, bound to the land and to their lords. Landowners could sell serfs, send them into the army for 25 years or have them flogged. Serfdom held back farming and industry, and peasant revolts, such as Pugachev's uprising in 1773–75, terrified the nobility. After defeat in the Crimean War, Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861; more than 20 million privately owned serfs gained their freedom, two years before slaves were freed in the United States. But they had to pay for their land over 49 years, and rural poverty fuelled the unrest that followed.

Peter the Great named Russia an empire in 1721 and moved the capital to St Petersburg. Catherine the Great took Crimea and much of Ukraine and Poland. In the 1800s Russia added Finland, the Caucasus and Central Asia, such as Kazakhstan. By 1914 it covered about 22 million km², a sixth of the world's land, with over 160 million people. Fewer than half spoke Russian as their first language.

The empire held nearly all of today's Russia, except Kaliningrad, then German, and southern Sakhalin and the Kurils, then Japanese. The 1897 census counted about 44% of its people as native Russian speakers.

Eastern Georgia was annexed in 1801, the west over the following decades. The wider Caucasus took until 1864 to conquer; hundreds of thousands of Circassians, in today's southern Russia, were killed or expelled to the Ottoman Empire.

dd-russia.q: How did Moscow rise to lead the Rus' lands?
a: It was the capital chosen by Rurik in 862
It defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut
It collected tribute for the Mongols, then threw off their rule in 1480
Byzantium made it the seat of its emperor
dd-russia.why: Moscow's princes rose as the Golden Horde's tax collectors, and Ivan III ended Mongol overlordship in 1480.

dd-russia.p:
Part of the empire from 1809, with its own laws

Finland was taken from Sweden in 1809 and kept its own parliament and laws; it declared independence in December 1917.

Nicholas II believed he ruled by God's will and resisted sharing power. Defeat by Japan in 1905 brought strikes and revolution, forcing him to allow an elected parliament, the Duma, though he soon limited its power. The First World War was disastrous: millions of soldiers were killed, wounded or captured, and cities ran short of bread. In March 1917, by the Western calendar, strikes and mutinies in Petrograd forced Nicholas to abdicate, ending three centuries of Romanov rule. A Provisional Government kept fighting the war, and in November the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power. Nicholas and his family were shot at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

The Bolsheviks who seized power in 1917 rebuilt most of the empire as the Soviet Union, and when it broke up in 1991, its 15 republics became independent along borders largely drawn in Soviet times. Russia remains the world's largest country, stretching across 11 time zones. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all claim Kyivan Rus' as part of their history, and rival readings of that shared past have featured in the full-scale war Russia launched against Ukraine in 2022.
Russia is the largest country on Earth. Its history of invasion from the West (Napoleon, Hitler) and its imperial past help explain its sense of insecurity and its war in Ukraine.

Ivan III ends Mongol overlordship after the stand on the Ugra

Nicholas II abdicates; the Bolsheviks take power

dd-mongols.p: Temüjin, born around 1162, survived exile and feuds to unite the Mongol tribes, and in 1206 he was proclaimed Genghis Khan. He attacked the Western Xia and Jin in northern China, took Beijing in 1215, and in 1219–21 destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire of Central Asia and Iran. After his death in 1227 his sons and grandsons conquered the rest of northern China, the Russian principalities and Iraq, raided Poland and Hungary, and sacked Baghdad in 1258.

items: Adopted Chinese and Persian siege engines

steps: The largest connected land empire ever.
Trade along the Silk Road was protected.
Marco Polo travels; gunpowder and printing spread west.
The Black Death spread along the same routes.

a: Genghis Khan
Kublai Khan
Tamerlane
Attila

dd-mongols.p: Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China in 1279. But the empire split into four rival khanates, and the Yuan were driven out of China in 1368.

dd-mongols.q: What did Genghis Khan and his heirs achieve in the 1200s?
a: They united the Mongol tribes and conquered lands from China to Russia and Iraq
They built a navy that ruled the Indian Ocean
They conquered Egypt and Japan after long sieges
They founded the Ottoman Empire in Anatolia
dd-mongols.why: Temüjin united the tribes in 1206; he and his heirs took northern China, Central Asia, the Rus principalities and Iraq, and Kublai completed Song China.

dd-mongols.p: Mongol armies were made up of superb horse archers, each with several horses, who could cover huge distances fast. Genghis Khan broke up old tribal loyalties, organised his men in units of tens, hundreds and thousands, and promoted for loyalty and talent. Spies, feigned retreats, captured engineers and calculated terror made cities surrender. Their enemies were often divided, and some, like the Rus princes, never united against them.

Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin turned the united tribes of Mongolia on their neighbours. He forced the Western Xia to submit, took the Jin capital, today's Beijing, in 1215, and seized Kara Khitai, in Kyrgyzstan. When the Khwarazmian Empire killed his envoys and merchants in 1218, he destroyed it, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand in Uzbekistan. Two of his generals rode on round the Caspian into Russia and back.

dd-mongols.q: Besides great destruction, what did Mongol rule bring across Eurasia?
a: A single empire that lasted unbroken until 1900
The end of all trade between Europe and China
The spread of Islam to China and Japan
Links that let merchants, envoys and ideas travel from Italy to China
dd-mongols.why: The Pax Mongolica protected merchants and travel, spreading paper money, gunpowder, maps and, probably, the Black Death.

dd-mongols.p:
United under Genghis Khan in 1206

Temüjin, born around 1162, rose from poverty after his father was poisoned. By 1206 he had defeated or absorbed every rival tribe on the Mongolian plateau.

Northern China, attacked from 1209

The Western Xia submitted in 1210 and were wiped out in 1227. The Jin lost Beijing in 1215 and fell in 1234, after Genghis Khan's death.
Kara Khitai, a state founded by Khitans fleeing China, was seized by the Naiman prince Kuchlug. Jebe took it in 1218, welcomed by Muslims Kuchlug had persecuted.

Every Mongol man was a cavalryman, trained from childhood to ride and shoot a powerful composite bow from the saddle. On campaign each rider brought several spare horses, so armies could move scores of kilometres a day, living on mare's milk, dried meat and whatever they took. Genghis Khan organised them in a decimal system: units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, the tumen. Their favourite tactic was the feigned retreat, luring enemies into a chase and then surrounding them. Against walled cities they used Chinese and Persian engineers, catapults and captured prisoners pushed in front as shields. Cities that surrendered at once were usually spared; those that resisted were often massacred, and word of it spread ahead of the army.

In 1236 Batu, Genghis Khan's grandson, and the veteran general Subutai led a great army west. They crushed Volga Bulgaria and the principalities of Russia, took Kyiv in Ukraine in 1240, and in April 1241 won two battles in two days, in Poland and Hungary. In 1242 they suddenly withdrew east. Batu settled on the Volga, and his Golden Horde ruled the Rus princes for over two centuries.

Volga Bulgaria, the Rus principalities and the Cuman steppe

Kyiv fell in December 1240, and Galicia-Volhynia in the west was devastated and became tributary. The southern steppe became Golden Horde pasture.

The lands between the Prut and the Dniester, on the western edge of the Cuman steppe, came under the Golden Horde.

dd-mongols.q: What made Mongol armies so effective in the field?
a: Heavy armoured infantry fighting in tight ranks
Fast horse archers, each with several horses, covering huge distances
Gunpowder cannons bought from European traders
Large fleets that landed troops behind enemy lines
dd-mongols.why: Mongol riders were superb horse archers with spare horses, so armies could move scores of kilometres a day and outpace their enemies.

dd-mongols.p:
Hungary suffered worst: after Mohi the Mongols ravaged the country for a year. Estimates of its losses vary widely, often put at 15–25% of the population.

Upper Hungary, today's Slovakia, was plundered in 1241, though some stone castles held out, a lesson Hungary's king took to heart.

To hold their empire together the Mongols built the yam, a relay network of post stations with fresh horses, roughly a day's ride apart or less, where messengers could cover hundreds of kilometres in a day. Officials carried a paiza, a metal tablet that served as a passport and ordered locals to give them horses and food. The khans protected merchants and tolerated every religion, taxing trade rather than blocking it. Travellers crossed Asia as never before: the friar William of Rubruck reached Karakorum in 1254, Marco Polo spent about 17 years in Kublai's China, and the Nestorian monk Rabban Bar Sauma travelled from Beijing to Rome and Paris in 1287–88. Historians call this the Pax Mongolica, the Mongol peace.

dd-mongols.q: How is Genghis Khan remembered today?
a: Mongolia reveres him as its father; Iran, Iraq and Russia, as a destroyer
Everywhere as a peaceful lawgiver
As a minor chief forgotten outside Mongolia
As the founder of modern China's Communist Party
dd-mongols.why: Memory is divided: Mongolia reveres him as the nation's father, while Iran, Iraq and Russia remember him above all as a destroyer.

dd-mongols.p: Mongol armies were not invincible. Egypt's Mamluks beat them at Ain Jalut in 1260 and held Syria and Egypt. Kublai Khan's invasions of Japan failed in 1274 and 1281, his invasions of Đại Việt, in northern Vietnam, failed three times, and a fleet sent to Java, in Indonesia, was driven out in 1293. The Delhi Sultanate in India beat back repeated Mongol raids.

Slave soldiers who ruled Egypt and Syria

The Mamluks, former slave soldiers mostly from the Cuman steppe, seized power in Egypt in 1250. They fought the Ilkhanate for 60 years and never lost Egypt.

Ain Jalut, in the Jezreel Valley, was fought in 1260 after Hülegü had taken most of his army east on news of the Great Khan's death.
Japan's Kamakura shogunate refused Kublai's demands for submission. The storms credited with wrecking his fleets were later called kamikaze, 'divine winds'.

dd-mongols.q: Why did so many cities surrender to the Mongols without a fight?
a: The Mongols promised to make each city independent
The cities were mostly Mongol settlements already
Calculated terror: resisting cities were often massacred, and word spread ahead
Mongol envoys bribed every city governor
dd-mongols.why: Cities that surrendered at once were usually spared, while those that resisted were often massacred, and the news made others give in.

dd-mongols.p:
The Trần dynasty

Đại Việt was invaded in 1258, 1285 and 1287–88. Each time the Trần court left its capital, waged a war of attrition and struck back.

Medieval chroniclers gave staggering death tolls, such as over a million at Merv in 1221, which historians regard as exaggerated. Even so, the destruction was real: whole cities in Central Asia and Iran were depopulated, and Iraq's ancient irrigation took centuries to recover. A popular claim is that one in 200 men alive today descends from Genghis Khan. It comes from a 2003 genetic study that found one male lineage shared by about 8% of men in a large region of Asia; the authors linked it to Genghis Khan's family, but this link is unproven. Another story says Mongols hurled plague corpses into the besieged Crimean port of Caffa in 1346; it comes from one Italian writer and is debated.

The conquests killed huge numbers of people and wrecked cities and irrigation systems from Iran to Hungary. Yet the empire also linked Eurasia: merchants, missionaries and envoys travelled from Italy to China, spreading paper money, gunpowder, maps and, probably, the Black Death. Moscow rose as the Golden Horde's tax collector. In Mongolia Genghis Khan is revered as the father of the nation, while in Iran, Iraq and Russia he is remembered above all as a destroyer.

dd-habsburgs.p: In 1273 the German princes elected Rudolf of Habsburg, a minor Swiss count, as their king, and in 1278 he won Austria. From 1438 Habsburgs held the title of Holy Roman Emperor almost without a break until 1806. Well-planned marriages gave Charles V the Netherlands, Spain and its American empire, and his brother Ferdinand Bohemia and Hungary. After 1556 the family split into Spanish and Austrian lines.

steps: Their son marries the heiress of Spain.
Rules Spain, Austria, the Netherlands, much of Italy and the Americas.
dd-habsburgs.p: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry.'

dd-habsburgs.q: How did the Habsburgs gain much of their land?
a: Through marriages
Through crusades
By buying it
Through colonies only

dd-habsburgs.p: The Spanish line died out in 1700, but the Austrians drove back the Ottomans after 1683 and ruled a vast Danube empire. Defeated by Prussia in 1866, they shared power with Hungary from 1867. Defeat in World War I broke the empire apart in 1918.

dd-habsburgs.q: What did the Habsburg family achieve between 1273 and 1918?
a: They united all of Germany into one nation-state
They rose from minor Swiss counts to rule a vast Central European empire
They conquered the Ottoman Empire and took Constantinople
They ruled France until the Revolution of 1789
dd-habsburgs.why: From Rudolf's election in 1273, the Habsburgs held Austria, the imperial title and, at their height, Spain and its empire, ruling for 640 years.

dd-habsburgs.p: The Habsburgs rose through elections, inheritance and alliances more than conquest. Each marriage was a bet that the other line might die out, and several times it did. Their lands had no common language or nation, so the dynasty itself, the Catholic Church, the army and the civil service held them together. That worked in an age of kings but grew weaker as nationalism spread in the 1800s.

The Habsburgs took their name from a castle in Switzerland and won Austria in 1278. Then came a run of lucky marriages: Burgundy's Netherlands in 1477, Spain and its empire through Charles V, king from 1516, and Bohemia and part of Hungary in 1526. By 1550 Charles ruled Spain, the Netherlands, much of Italy and the Americas, while his brother Ferdinand ruled the Austrian lands.

dd-habsburgs.q: What happened when Austria-Hungary collapsed after defeat in World War I?
a: New or enlarged states such as Czechoslovakia, Poland and Yugoslavia emerged
The empire was absorbed whole into Germany
Spain inherited the Habsburg lands
The Ottomans took back Hungary and Vienna
dd-habsburgs.why: Its collapse in 1918 created or enlarged Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Romania and Italy, with border and minority quarrels for decades.

dd-habsburgs.p:
Habsburg since 1278–82

Rudolf I, elected King of the Germans in 1273, took Austria from Bohemia's king in 1278. The family ruled Austria for the next 640 years.

The Netherlands and Franche-Comté, from 1477

Maximilian I married Mary, heiress of Burgundy, in 1477. Their grandson Charles V united all 17 provinces of the Netherlands by 1543.

Brussels was the capital of the Burgundian Netherlands, then the richest region of northern Europe. Charles V grew up nearby, in Mechelen.

Castile, Aragon and their Italian lands, from 1516

Philip the Handsome, Maximilian's son, married Joanna of Castile, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, in 1496. Deaths in the family made their son Charles heir to all Spain and its American empire.

Through Aragon the Habsburgs held Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, and Charles V took Milan in 1535. Imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527.

A Latin saying summed up the family's method: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry.' Emperor Maximilian I married Mary of Burgundy in 1477 and gained the rich Netherlands. He then married his son Philip to Joanna, heiress of Castile and Aragon, and in 1515, at a double wedding in Vienna, matched two of his grandchildren with the children of King Vladislaus of Bohemia and Hungary. Within 11 years both bets paid off. Spain's other heirs died young, and in 1526 the young King Louis II of Hungary drowned fleeing the battle of Mohács, so his crowns passed to his Habsburg brother-in-law, Ferdinand. The Habsburgs did fight many wars, but marriage made their empire.

Charles V split his lands in 1556: Spain went to his son Philip, Austria to Ferdinand. The Spanish line died out in 1700, and after a long war a French Bourbon kept Spain, while Austria took Belgium and Spain's Italian lands. Meanwhile, after the Ottomans' failed siege of Vienna in 1683, Habsburg armies retook all of Hungary and pushed into Serbia and Romania. The monarchy now centred on the Danube.

The Habsburgs' hereditary lands

Vienna rebuilt in Baroque splendour after 1683. Emperor Charles VI's Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 let a daughter inherit, and Maria Theresa took the throne in 1740.

After Bohemia's Protestant nobles revolted and lost at the White Mountain in 1620, the Habsburgs ruled it as a Catholic hereditary land.

dd-habsburgs.q: How did the Habsburgs mainly gain their lands?
a: By conquering their neighbours in long wars
By buying territory from bankrupt kings
Through elections, inheritance and well-planned marriages
Through colonies founded by Habsburg merchants
dd-habsburgs.why: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry': marriages brought the Netherlands, Spain, Bohemia and Hungary when other lines died out.

dd-habsburgs.p:
Mostly won from the Ottomans, 1683–1718

The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 gave the Habsburgs almost all of Hungary and Transylvania. A Hungarian revolt led by Ferenc Rákóczi II was put down in 1711.

Croatia's Slavonia was won back from the Ottomans in 1699, but Dalmatia was still Venetian. The Military Frontier, settled by Serbs and Croats, guarded the border.

Austrian from 1714

The Spanish Netherlands became the Austrian Netherlands in 1714 and stayed so until French revolutionary armies took them in the 1790s.

Austria gained Milan, Naples and Sardinia in 1714, then swapped Sardinia for Sicily in 1720. It lost Naples and Sicily to a Spanish Bourbon prince in 1735.

dd-habsburgs.q: What visible legacy did the Habsburgs leave across Central Europe?
a: A single currency still used from Brussels to Lviv
Baroque palaces, churches and cafés, and Vienna as a capital of music
The German language as the region's only official tongue
A ruling monarchy still governing Austria today
dd-habsburgs.why: The Habsburgs left Baroque palaces, churches and cafés from Brussels to Lviv, and made Vienna a great capital of music.

dd-habsburgs.p: To keep thrones in the family, Habsburgs often married cousins, and King Philip IV of Spain married his own niece. Portraits across two centuries show a jutting lower jaw and heavy lip, often called the 'Habsburg jaw'. A 2019 study by Spanish geneticists and facial surgeons linked the feature to the family's inbreeding. The extreme case was Charles II of Spain, the last of his line: his parents were uncle and niece, and he was sickly, struggled to chew and had no children. His death in 1700 ended Habsburg rule in Spain and set off the War of the Spanish Succession.

After defeat by Prussia in 1866, Emperor Franz Joseph made a deal with Hungary in 1867: two states under one monarch, sharing only foreign policy, the army and the budget for them. Austria ruled the west and north, from Czechia to Galicia in Poland; Hungary ruled the east, including Croatia. Bosnia, taken from the Ottomans, belonged to both. Its 51 million people spoke about a dozen main languages.

Its 'lands represented in the Reichsrat', ruled from Vienna

German-speaking Austrians were about a quarter of the whole empire's people, the largest single group but far from a majority. Franz Joseph reigned for 68 years, from 1848 to 1916.

Bohemia and Moravia were the empire's industrial heartland. Czechs and Germans fought bitterly over language in schools and offices.

The lands of the Hungarian crown, ruled from Budapest

The 1867 Compromise gave Hungary its own parliament and government. Hungarian speakers were about half its people, and its leaders pressed others to adopt Hungarian.

Slovakia was 'Upper Hungary', ruled from Budapest, where Slovak schools were squeezed in favour of Hungarian.

dd-habsburgs.q: What held the Habsburg lands together, and why did that grow weaker?
a: A shared language, until Latin fell out of use
A common nation, until the family moved to Spain
Protestant churches, until the Catholic revival
The dynasty, Church, army and civil service, until nationalism spread
dd-habsburgs.why: The lands had no common language or nation, so dynasty, Church, army and civil service held them; that weakened as nationalism spread in the 1800s.

dd-habsburgs.p:
Occupied in 1878, annexed in 1908, run jointly

Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908, enraging Serbia. The joint finance ministry ran it.

Emperor Charles VI had no sons, so in 1713 he issued the Pragmatic Sanction to let his daughter inherit. When Maria Theresa took the throne in 1740, aged 23, Prussia's Frederick II invaded rich Silesia at once, and a European war followed. She lost Silesia but kept the rest, and ruled for 40 years. She centralised taxes and the army, and in 1774 brought in compulsory schooling for children aged six to twelve. She also had 16 children; her daughter Marie Antoinette married the future Louis XVI of France. Her son Joseph II pushed further, easing serfdom and granting religious toleration in 1781.

Austria-Hungary's collapse created or enlarged Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Romania and Italy, and its quarrels over borders and minorities shaped Central Europe for decades. The Habsburgs left Baroque palaces, churches and cafés from Brussels to Lviv, and Vienna as a great capital of music. The family still exists: Otto von Habsburg, son of the last emperor, sat in the European Parliament for 20 years.

Maximilian marries Mary of Burgundy, heiress to the Netherlands
Charles V rules Spain, the Netherlands and the Holy Roman Empire
The Ottoman siege of Vienna fails
The Compromise creates Austria-Hungary
Defeat in war ends 640 years of Habsburg rule

dd-ottomans.p: Around 1300 Osman, a Turkish chief on the Byzantine frontier, founded a small state in north-west Anatolia. His heirs took Bursa, crossed into Europe in 1354 and conquered much of the Balkans, survived a crushing defeat by Timur in 1402, and in 1453 Mehmed II captured Constantinople. Selim I conquered Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia in 1516–17, and Suleiman the Magnificent took Hungary and Iraq.

items: Christian boys taken and trained as soldiers.
Christians and Jews ran their own affairs and paid a tax.
A city of mosques, bazaars and many peoples.

steps: Europe industrialises; the empire borrows and loses wars.
Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians and Arabs break away.
Joins Germany, loses, and is partitioned; Turkey is born in 1923.

a: Elite Ottoman soldiers
Ottoman tax collectors
Sultan’s wives
Merchants

dd-ottomans.p: After the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 the empire slowly lost land to Austria, Russia and its own peoples. It joined World War I on Germany's side, lost, and was dissolved in 1922; the Republic of Turkey followed in 1923.

dd-ottomans.q: What was the arc of Ottoman history from about 1300 to 1923?
a: A frontier state became an empire on three continents, then broke up
A Byzantine province that briefly rebelled and was reconquered
An Arab kingdom that ruled only Egypt and Arabia
A Persian dynasty that moved its capital to Vienna
dd-ottomans.why: Osman's small state took Constantinople in 1453, spread from Hungary to Egypt and Iraq, slowly lost land after 1683 and was dissolved in 1922.

dd-ottomans.p: The Ottomans rose on a frontier where Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided. They built a strong centralised state, an elite slave army of Janissaries and early skill with cannon, and they let Christians and Jews keep their faiths in return for taxes and loyalty. Their decline is debated: historians now stress reform and adaptation as much as decay, but Europe's growing economic and military power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism wore the empire down.

dd-ottomans.h: From frontier state to empire, c. 1300–1481
dd-ottomans.p: Osman's small state on the Byzantine frontier in north-west Turkey grew fast. His son Orhan took Bursa, and in 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe at Gallipoli. Bulgaria, Macedonia and much of northern Greece fell by 1400. Timur crushed them at Ankara in 1402, but they recovered, and Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, then Serbia, Bosnia and Albania.

dd-ottomans.q: What wore the empire down after the failed siege of Vienna in 1683?
a: A Mongol invasion led by Timur
The loss of Constantinople to Venice
The conversion of the sultans to Christianity
Europe's rising power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism
dd-ottomans.why: Historians stress reform as well as decay, but Europe's economic and military power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism wore the empire down.

dd-ottomans.p:
Osman's state grew to most of Anatolia by 1481

Osman's emirate was one of many Turkish states in Anatolia. The Ottomans absorbed rivals such as Karaman by the 1470s, but the far east stayed outside until the 1500s.

Conquered under Murad I and Bayezid I

The Bulgarian capital, Tarnovo, fell in 1393, and the last Bulgarian state was gone by 1396.

Thessaly fell in the 1390s, Thessaloniki in 1430 and the Peloponnese in 1460. Venice still held Crete and other islands.

Serbia fought on after Kosovo as an Ottoman vassal, and its last fortress capital, Smederevo, fell in 1459. Belgrade, a Hungarian fortress, held out until 1521.

Kosovo, scene of the battle of 1389, was fully under Ottoman rule by 1455.

The sultan's best soldiers were slaves. Under the devshirme, or 'collection', officials visited Christian villages, mostly in the Balkans, every few years and took a share of the boys, roughly aged 8 to 18. They were converted to Islam, taught Turkish and trained. The strongest became Janissaries, a paid standing infantry armed with guns long before most European armies had one; the brightest went to the palace school and could rise to the top. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, taken from a Serbian Orthodox family in Bosnia, became grand vizier to three sultans. Over time Janissaries married, ran businesses and toppled sultans they disliked, until Mahmud II destroyed the corps in 1826.

dd-ottomans.h: Selim and Suleiman build a world empire, 1512–1566
dd-ottomans.p: Selim I beat Safavid Persia at Chaldiran in 1514, then conquered the Mamluk sultanate in 1516–17, taking Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. His son Suleiman, 'the Magnificent' to Europeans and 'the Lawgiver' to Ottomans, took Belgrade, most of Hungary and Baghdad in Iraq. His navy under Hayreddin Barbarossa dominated the Mediterranean, and North African ports such as Algiers, in Algeria, accepted Ottoman rule.

The Mamluk lands, the holy cities and Algiers

Egypt was the richest province, sending grain and gold to Istanbul. Its conquest made the sultan protector of Mecca and Medina.

Selim took Syria in 1516. Damascus became the gathering point for the great annual pilgrim caravan to Mecca.

dd-ottomans.q: Why could the early Ottomans expand so quickly?
a: They had the help of a large Venetian fleet
Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided
The Mongols handed them Anatolia
Europe's kings invited them in against the Pope
dd-ottomans.why: They rose on a frontier where Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided, and built a strong centralised state.

dd-ottomans.p:
Suleiman took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534 and Basra in 1546, gaining the shrines of Shia Islam and access to the Persian Gulf.

After Mohács in 1526 Hungary fell apart. Suleiman annexed its centre, with Buda, in 1541, while the Habsburgs held the west and north.

From the 1460s sultans lived in Topkapı Palace in Istanbul, which mixed government offices with the harem, the private household of the sultan's mother, wives, concubines, children and servants. The Ottomans had no rule that the eldest son inherited, so princes fought for the throne. Mehmed II's law code allowed a new sultan to execute his brothers for the sake of order, and in 1595 Mehmed III had 19 brothers killed. Later, princes were instead confined in palace apartments. In the 'sultanate of women' from the mid-1500s, mothers and wives such as Hürrem, a captive from today's Ukraine whom Suleiman freed and married, wielded real political power.

dd-ottomans.q: How does the Ottoman Empire still shape the world today?
a: Over 30 countries were once Ottoman, and many borders trace back to it
Turkey still rules most of the Balkans
The sultanate survives as Turkey's head of state
Ottoman rule left no trace outside Istanbul
dd-ottomans.why: Many borders, conflicts and mixed communities, from Bosnia to Iraq and Israel and Palestine, go back to the empire and its breakup.

dd-ottomans.p: In the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 the empire lost almost all its European land, including Albania and Macedonia. In World War I it fought for Germany, deported and killed Armenians in Anatolia, and lost its Arab lands from Iraq to Syria. The 1920 Treaty of Sèvres planned to carve up Anatolia too, but Mustafa Kemal's nationalists fought on, and in 1923 founded the Republic of Turkey.

Albania declared independence in November 1912, as Serbian, Montenegrin and Greek armies overran the Ottoman Balkans.

Ottoman Macedonia was conquered in 1912 and divided between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria in 1913.

dd-ottomans.h: Arab lands lost in World War I
dd-ottomans.p:
Lost to British, French and Arab forces, 1916–19

British and Arab forces took Damascus in October 1918. France then ruled Syria and Lebanon as League of Nations mandates.

British forces took Jerusalem in December 1917, ending 400 years of Ottoman rule in Palestine.

dd-ottomans.q: How did the Ottomans rule their many Christian and Jewish subjects?
a: They forced everyone to convert to Islam at once
They expelled all non-Muslims from their cities
They let them keep their faiths in return for taxes and loyalty
They gave them full equality from the start
dd-ottomans.why: Non-Muslims paid an extra tax and faced limits, but could worship and run their own schools and courts; it was not equality.

dd-ottomans.p: Kemal's nationalists drove out Greek, French and Armenian forces in 1919–22. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne recognised the republic, declared on 29 October; the caliphate was abolished in 1924.

The Ottoman Empire was a Muslim state with huge Christian and Jewish populations, and for centuries Christians were a majority in its European provinces. Non-Muslims paid an extra tax and faced legal limits, but they could worship, run their own schools and courts, and were led by their own religious heads, an arrangement later called the millet system. When Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, Sultan Bayezid II welcomed many to Thessaloniki and Istanbul. This was not equality, and there were forced conversions and violence. In the 1800s, reforms called the Tanzimat promised equal rights, but rising nationalism turned communities against one another, with tragic results in the empire's final decades.

More than 30 countries today were once wholly or partly Ottoman, and many of their borders, conflicts and mixed communities, from Bosnia to Iraq and Israel and Palestine, go back to the empire and its breakup. Its end brought the Armenian genocide, which Turkey disputes, and the Greek–Turkish population exchange. Atatürk's republic turned away from the Ottoman past, but Ottoman food, music, architecture and words live on across the Balkans and the Middle East.

Much of the modern Middle East and Balkans was carved from the Ottoman Empire after 1918, including Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Israel and Palestine. Many of today's borders and conflicts date from that partition.

dd-aztecinca.p: In 1428 the Mexica of Tenochtitlan and two allied cities overthrew their overlords and built an empire across central Mexico, ruled from an island city in a lake. In the Andes, the Inca ruler Pachacuti began conquests around 1438 that created the largest state in the Americas. In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico; with tens of thousands of native allies and the help of a smallpox epidemic, he took Tenochtitlan in August 1521.

l: Human sacrifice to feed the sun
r: 40,000 km of roads; no wheel or writing

dd-aztecinca.h: How a few hundred Spaniards won
steps: Smallpox killed up to 90% of many populations.
Tens of thousands of local enemies of the Aztecs joined Cortés.
The Inca had just fought a civil war between two brothers.
Unknown weapons gave a shock advantage.

dd-aztecinca.q: What was the main cause of the collapse of Native American populations?
a: Disease from Europe
Battles
Famine
Volcanoes

dd-aztecinca.p: In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, collected a vast ransom and executed him. Inca resistance held out in the forests of Vilcabamba until 1572.

dd-aztecinca.q: What happened to the Aztec and Inca empires in the 1500s?
a: They united to drive the Spanish from the Americas
Small Spanish forces, with native allies and disease, conquered both
They traded peacefully with Spain for two centuries
Portugal conquered them both in a single campaign
dd-aztecinca.why: Cortés took Tenochtitlan in 1521 with tens of thousands of native allies, and Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532; Inca resistance lasted until 1572.

dd-aztecinca.p: Both empires were young, built by conquest within a century, and many subject peoples resented paying tribute; Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Aztecs joined the Spaniards in large numbers. European diseases, to which Americans had no immunity, killed rulers and armies, and in Peru an epidemic set off a civil war between two royal brothers just before Pizarro arrived. Steel, horses and guns helped too, but the Spaniards were always vastly outnumbered and could not have won alone.

In 1428 the Mexica of Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan, and this Triple Alliance came to rule much of central and southern Mexico, taking tribute from 38 provinces. Some neighbours, such as Tlaxcala and the Purépecha, were never conquered. In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast with about 600 Spaniards, gathered thousands of Tlaxcalan and other native allies, and marched inland to the island capital.

dd-aztecinca.q: What role did European diseases play in the conquests?
a: They had little effect because Americans were immune
They struck only the Spanish soldiers
They arrived a century after the conquests ended
They killed rulers and armies and set off an Inca civil war
dd-aztecinca.why: Smallpox killed many of Tenochtitlan's defenders and its emperor, and in Peru an epidemic set off a civil war between royal brothers before Pizarro arrived.

dd-aztecinca.p:
The Triple Alliance and its tributary provinces

Aztec rule covered much of central and southern Mexico, from the Gulf coast to the Pacific, but not the north, the Purépecha west or the Maya Yucatán. Mexico City now stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan.

Outside Aztec rule; conquered by Spain only in 1524–1697

Highland Maya kingdoms such as the K'iche' and Kaqchikel were independent of the Aztecs. Pedro de Alvarado conquered much of the highlands from 1524.

Belize was Maya country beyond Aztec rule. The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén in nearby Guatemala, fell to Spain only in 1697.

dd-aztecinca.q: How do these civilisations live on today?
a: Their languages died out by 1600
Millions still speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag recalls Tenochtitlan
Their cities still stand unchanged as capitals
Spain still governs Mexico and Peru
dd-aztecinca.why: Despite a terrible population collapse, Indigenous peoples endured: millions speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag shows Tenochtitlan's eagle and cactus.

dd-aztecinca.p: According to Mexica tradition, their god told them to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus, and they founded Tenochtitlan on a swampy island around 1325. Two centuries later it was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 200,000 people by many estimates. Causeways linked it to the shore, an aqueduct brought fresh water, and farmers grew crops on chinampas, fertile plots built up from the lake bed. A great market at Tlatelolco amazed the Spaniards. At the centre rose the Templo Mayor, a twin pyramid to the rain god Tlaloc and the war god Huitzilopochtli, where captives were sacrificed; the numbers are debated, and some Spanish figures are surely inflated.

dd-aztecinca.h: How so few defeated so many
dd-aztecinca.p: Cortés began with about 600 Spaniards, and Pizarro had 168 at Cajamarca. Their success was not a matter of a few men conquering empires alone. In Mexico, Tlaxcala and other peoples who hated Aztec rule supplied most of the soldiers; the final siege involved tens of thousands of native warriors. Smallpox arrived in 1520 and killed many of the city's defenders and its new emperor, Cuitláhuac. In Peru, epidemic disease and a war of succession between Atahualpa and Huáscar had already shattered the empire. A popular story says Moctezuma took Cortés for the returning god Quetzalcoatl, but many historians think this was invented after the conquest.

From Cusco in Peru, the Inca ruler Pachacuti began a rapid expansion from about 1438. Within a century the empire, Tawantinsuyu or 'the four parts together', ran some 4,000 km along the Andes, from southern Colombia to central Chile, ruling perhaps 10 million people. A road network tied it together. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and 168 Spaniards captured the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca.

Tawantinsuyu, ruled from Cusco

Peru was the empire's heart, from Cusco to the coast. Spain made Lima, founded by Pizarro in 1535, the capital of its South American empire.

The Incas conquered Ecuador's highlands and coast only in the late 1400s. Huayna Capac died there around 1527, probably of an epidemic, setting off a civil war.

dd-aztecinca.q: Why did peoples such as Tlaxcala join the Spaniards against the Aztecs?
a: Spain promised to make them Christian kings of Spain
They mistook the Spaniards for gods
They resented Aztec rule and the tribute they paid
They were Spanish colonists who had settled earlier
dd-aztecinca.why: Both empires were young and built by conquest; many subject peoples resented paying tribute, and Aztec enemies joined the Spaniards in large numbers.

dd-aztecinca.p: The Inca state ran without coins, markets in the European sense or a known writing system. Instead, households owed labour, called mit'a: farming state fields, building roads, weaving cloth or serving in the army. The state stored the produce in thousands of warehouses and redistributed food and cloth in hard times and at feasts. Officials recorded censuses and tribute on quipus, knotted cords whose numbers can be read but whose full meaning is still debated. Relay runners, the chasquis, carried messages along some 30,000–40,000 km of roads, with rope bridges over gorges. The Spaniards later turned the mit'a into forced labour in the silver mines.

Spain built a new empire on the ruins: Mexico City rose over Tenochtitlan, and Lima became the capital of Spanish South America. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas flowed to Europe and China. Epidemics, war and forced labour caused one of history's worst population collapses. Yet Indigenous peoples endured: millions still speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag shows the eagle and cactus of Tenochtitlan's founding legend.

dd-aztecinca.q: What did Spain build on the ruins of the two empires?
a: A new empire, with Mexico City and Lima as capitals and silver flowing out
A set of independent Indigenous kingdoms under Spanish protection
Nothing, since Spain soon abandoned the Americas
A single Inca-Aztec state ruled from Cusco
dd-aztecinca.why: Mexico City rose over Tenochtitlan, Lima became the capital of Spanish South America, and silver from Potosí and Zacatecas flowed to Europe and China.

dd-spanish.p: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada and sent Columbus west. Spanish settlers seized the Caribbean islands, then Hernán Cortés toppled the Aztecs in 1519–21 and Francisco Pizarro the Incas from 1532, with Indigenous allies and epidemics doing much of the work. Silver strikes at Potosí and Zacatecas in the 1540s paid for a global empire, and from 1565 galleons linked Mexico with Manila.

steps: Granada falls and Columbus sails west for Castile.
Potosí and Mexican mines fill Spain’s treasure fleets.
Manila galleons link the Americas and Asia.

dd-spanish.h: of New World silver flowed through Asia
dd-spanish.p: Spanish silver became the first global currency, used from China to Europe.

dd-spanish.q: Where was the great silver mountain of the Spanish Empire?
a: Potosí, Bolivia
Mexico City
Havana
Lima

dd-spanish.p: Under Philip II Spain also ruled much of Italy, the Netherlands and, from 1580, Portugal. Wars, debt and the Dutch revolt wore it down, Napoleon's invasion in 1808 set off the independence wars, and in 1898 the United States took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines.

dd-spanish.q: What did Spain build in the century after 1492?
a: A small trading network of forts on the African coast
The first empire that spanned the globe, from the Americas to the Philippines
A Mediterranean kingdom with no lands outside Europe
A colony limited to the Caribbean islands
dd-spanish.why: From Granada and Columbus in 1492, Spain came to rule Mexico, Peru, the Philippines, much of Italy, the Netherlands and, from 1580, Portugal.

dd-spanish.p: Spain's crowns emerged from the Reconquista united, militant and Catholic, with nobles hungry for land and glory. Columbus's voyage opened a hemisphere whose peoples had no immunity to Old World diseases. Royal law made conquerors' gains the Crown's, and American silver let Spain's Habsburg kings fight wars across Europe. But it also brought inflation and debt, and Spain's rivals, the Dutch, English and French, grew stronger on trade.

dd-spanish.h: The empire on which the sun never set, 1598
dd-spanish.p: In a century Spain went from finishing the conquest of Granada to ruling the first empire that spanned the globe. Conquistadors took Mexico and Peru, Manila made the Philippines its Asian outpost, and Habsburg inheritance added Italian lands and the Netherlands. In 1580 Philip II also became king of Portugal and its empire. But the northern Dutch provinces, in today's Netherlands, were in open revolt.

dd-spanish.q: What set off the wars that freed Spanish America?
a: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808
The loss of the Spanish Armada
The discovery of silver at Potosí
The United States' victory in 1898
dd-spanish.why: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 set off the independence wars, and by 1825 Spain had lost the American mainland.

dd-spanish.p:
Castile and Aragon, the southern Netherlands, Milan, Naples, Sicily, Sardinia

Castile ran the American empire, through the Council of the Indies, while Aragon looked to the Mediterranean. From 1561 the court was based in Madrid.

The southern Netherlands, today's Belgium and Luxembourg, stayed under Spain and Catholic. Antwerp, sacked by unpaid Spanish troops in 1576, later lost much of its trade to Amsterdam.

Lighter where large areas were still beyond Spanish control

All of Hispaniola was Spanish. The western third, today's Haiti, was later settled by French buccaneers and ceded to France in 1697.

Jamaica was Spanish until England captured it in 1655.

Ruled by Spain's kings from 1580 to 1640

When Portugal's king died without an heir in 1580, his nephew Philip II claimed the throne. Portugal kept its own laws and empire, and broke away again in 1640.

Brazil was Portuguese, so it came under Philip's crown in 1580. The Dutch, at war with Spain, attacked and for a time held its sugar-growing north-east.

In 1545 silver was found in the Cerro Rico, a mountain over 4,000 metres up in the Andes. Within decades Potosí was one of the largest cities in the Americas, with churches, gambling houses and a royal mint. In the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo adapted an Inca labour draft, the mita, forcing thousands of Indigenous men each year to work the mines, where accidents, cold and mercury poisoning killed many. Coins struck there, the famous 'pieces of eight', circulated from Europe to China. 'Vale un Potosí', it is worth a Potosí, entered Spanish as a phrase for great riches, and in Don Quixote even 'the mines of Potosí' are too little to repay Sancho.

dd-spanish.h: The silver that paid for an empire, c. 1600
dd-spanish.p: Silver from Potosí, in Bolivia, and from the mines of Mexico became the empire's lifeblood. Twice a year armed fleets carried it from the Caribbean to Seville in Spain, and from 1565 the Manila galleons carried more across the Pacific to the Philippines, to buy silk and porcelain from China. By some estimates Spanish America produced about 80% of the world's silver between the 1500s and 1800.

Potosí in Upper Peru; Zacatecas and Guanajuato in New Spain

Potosí's silver was mined by Indigenous workers drafted under the mita, a forced labour system adapted from the Incas. Many died from accidents and mercury poisoning.

Mexico's mines, at Zacatecas and later Guanajuato, overtook Potosí in the 1700s. Silver was refined with mercury, by a process introduced in New Spain in the 1550s.

dd-spanish.q: What paid for Spain's global empire and its wars across Europe?
a: Spices grown in the Philippines
Taxes on the Dutch provinces alone
Silver from mines such as Potosí and Zacatecas
Loans from the Aztec and Inca rulers
dd-spanish.why: Silver strikes in the 1540s paid for the empire; the Crown took a fifth as tax and used it to fight wars across Europe.

dd-spanish.p:
Seville held the monopoly of American trade

The Crown took a fifth of all silver as tax and used it to fight wars across Europe. Even so Philip II defaulted on his debts four times, and much of the silver flowed on to bankers in Genoa and Antwerp.

Where silver met Chinese trade

Manila lived off the galleon trade. Each year one or two great ships sailed to Acapulco with Chinese goods and returned with silver.

dd-spanish.q: Which is a lasting legacy of the Spanish Empire?
a: Most people in the Philippines speak Spanish at home
Spanish is the native language of about 500 million people
Latin America has few Catholics today
Spain still governs Cuba and Puerto Rico
dd-spanish.why: Spanish is now the native language of about 500 million people, and Latin America is home to roughly 40% of the world's Catholics.

dd-spanish.p: Spaniards argued fiercely about whether conquest was just. Bartolomé de las Casas, a settler who became a Dominican friar, spent 50 years denouncing the abuse of Indigenous people, and his 'Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' was published in 1552. Pressure from him and others helped produce the New Laws of 1542, which banned enslaving Indigenous people and limited the encomienda labour grants, though settlers resisted them. In 1550–51 Las Casas debated the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda at Valladolid on whether Native peoples could be conquered for their own good. Neither was declared the winner. Spain's enemies later used Las Casas's writings to build the 'Black Legend' of unique Spanish cruelty.

The empire's deepest legacy is language and faith. Spanish is official and spoken by most people in Spain and 18 American countries plus Puerto Rico, and the Instituto Cervantes counted about 519 million native speakers in 2025. Mexico has the most. The United States has tens of millions of speakers, while in the Philippines, ruled from Madrid for over 300 years, Spanish has almost vanished.

Spanish, or Castilian, is spoken across Spain, alongside Catalan, Galician and Basque, which are co-official in their regions.

Mexico has the largest number of Spanish speakers in the world, well over 100 million. Its government also recognises 68 Indigenous languages, such as Nahuatl and Maya.

dd-spanish.h: Official, not the main home language
dd-spanish.p: Equatorial Guinea, a Spanish colony until 1968, is the only African country with Spanish as an official language, though most people speak Fang, Bubi and other African languages at home.

dd-spanish.q: Why did American silver not make Spain lastingly strong?
a: It was all sunk at sea before reaching Seville
Spain was forbidden from spending it by the Pope
The mines ran dry within ten years
It brought inflation and debt while rivals grew stronger on trade
dd-spanish.why: Silver also brought inflation and debt; Philip II defaulted four times, and the Dutch, English and French grew stronger on trade.

dd-spanish.p: Spain once held Florida, Texas and the Southwest, and many place names are Spanish. Most of today's speakers come from later migration from Latin America; the Instituto Cervantes counts over 40 million native speakers.

By 1825 Spain had lost the American mainland, but Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish, kept rich by sugar and by slavery, abolished only in 1873 in Puerto Rico and 1886 in Cuba. Cubans rose in 1868 and again in 1895, when the poet José Martí helped launch the revolt and was killed in battle. In February 1898 the US warship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, and the United States declared war that April. It destroyed one Spanish fleet at Manila Bay and another off Santiago de Cuba. In the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last for 20 million dollars. Spaniards called it simply 'the Disaster', and a generation of writers set out to rethink their country.

Spanish is now the native language of about 500 million people, and Latin America is home to roughly 40% of the world's Catholics, by Pew Research estimates. The empire also left mixed societies, cities on a grid around a central plaza, and deep inequality rooted in colonial land and labour systems. Its silver dollar, the 'piece of eight', became the first global currency and the model for the US dollar.
Spanish is the native language of nearly 500 million people, and Catholicism shapes most of Latin America. Mixed Indigenous, European and African ancestry defines much of the region.

dd-mughals.p: In 1526 Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded from Kabul and defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat. His son Humayun was driven out by the Afghan Sher Shah Suri but returned in 1555. Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, built a vast, well-run empire across northern India.

items: From Central Asia; wins at Panipat with cannons.
Tolerant; abolished the tax on Hindus.
Built the Taj Mahal for his wife.
Largest extent, but strict rule caused revolts.

dd-mughals.q: Why was the Taj Mahal built?
a: As a tomb for Shah Jahan’s wife
As a palace
As a fort
As a mosque for Akbar

dd-mughals.p: Jahangir and Shah Jahan presided over a golden age of painting and architecture, including the Taj Mahal. Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its greatest size, but after his death in 1707 it fragmented. Persians, Afghans, Marathas and finally the British took its lands, and in 1858 Britain exiled the last emperor.

a: A Persian kingdom that never ruled in India
A British trading company based in Bengal
An empire founded by Babur in 1526 that came to rule most of India
A Maratha state founded by Shivaji
dd-mughals.why: Babur, from Central Asia, beat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526; Akbar and his heirs built a vast empire across India.

dd-mughals.p: The Mughals won with cavalry, gunpowder and skilled generals, and held power by bringing local elites into the system: Hindu Rajput princes became generals and in-laws, and nobles held ranked offices paid from land revenue. Decline came from long, costly wars in the Deccan, succession struggles, nobles turning governorships into hereditary states, and Maratha, Sikh and Afghan challengers. Historians still debate how much Aurangzeb's religious policies also played a part.

Babur, born in 1483 in the Ferghana Valley of today's Uzbekistan, ruled Kabul in Afghanistan before invading India. In 1526 his guns and cavalry beat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat. His son Humayun lost the throne and regained it in 1555 with help from Persia. Babur's grandson Akbar, who reigned 1556–1605, conquered northern India, Pakistan and Bengal, and won over Hindu Rajput princes.

dd-mughals.q: Who gained most from the Mughal collapse in the long run?
a: The Ottoman Empire
The British East India Company, using Bengal's wealth
The Portuguese at Goa
The Dutch, who conquered Delhi
dd-mughals.why: The Company won at Plassey in 1757, took Bengal's revenues in 1765 and used them to conquer India; Britain exiled the last emperor in 1858.

dd-mughals.p:
At the death of Akbar

Akbar ruled northern and central India, from Gujarat to Bengal and south into the Deccan. Most of his subjects were Hindu.

Lahore was one of the Mughal capitals, and Akbar added Kashmir in 1586 and Sindh in 1591.

The Ferghana Valley, where he was born in 1483

Babur descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's. Driven out of Ferghana and Samarkand by the Uzbeks, he turned south.

Neighbour, ally and rival

Shah Tahmasp of Persia sheltered the exiled Humayun and lent him troops to regain his throne. Persian was the language of the Mughal court.

Akbar came to the throne at 13 and ruled for almost 50 years. He married Rajput princesses, made Hindu nobles generals and ministers, and in 1564 abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims. At his new city of Fatehpur Sikri he built a House of Worship where Sunni and Shia scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests debated before him. He promoted sulh-i kul, 'peace with all', and late in life founded a small devotional circle around himself, the Din-i Ilahi, which did not outlast him. Though he probably could not read, he built a huge library and had Hindu epics translated into Persian. His finance minister, Todar Mal, surveyed lands to set fair taxes.

dd-mughals.h: Mughal India and the world, c. 1650
dd-mughals.p: Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, Mughal India was one of the richest states on earth, with perhaps 150 million people. Its cotton and silk cloth sold from Japan to Europe, and Europeans paid in silver. Trading companies from England and the Netherlands set up posts on the coasts by the emperor's leave, joining the Portuguese; France followed in the 1660s. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal and a new walled city at Delhi.

Under Shah Jahan

The empire drew most of its revenue from land tax on farmers, much of it assigned to ranked officers called mansabdars, whose rank set how many cavalry they had to keep.

Lahore, Multan and Thatta were major cities, and the Mughal road from Kabul through Lahore to Delhi and Agra carried trade and armies.

dd-mughals.q: How did the Mughals hold power over so many people?
a: They brought local elites, such as Hindu Rajput princes, into the system
They forced all subjects to convert to Islam
They ruled only through Persian governors sent from Iran
They relied on British troops to keep order
dd-mughals.why: Rajput princes became generals and in-laws, and nobles held ranked offices paid from land revenue; Akbar also promoted 'peace with all'.

dd-mughals.p:
Took Kandahar from the Mughals in 1649

Safavid Persia was the Mughals' main rival in the west and a model for their court culture, art and language.

Trading posts and forts on India's coasts

England's East India Company, founded in 1600, sent Sir Thomas Roe to Jahangir's court in 1615 to seek trading rights.

The Dutch East India Company traded in Bengal and Gujarat, buying cloth to swap for spices in Indonesia.

dd-mughals.q: How is the Mughal past still present in South Asia?
a: Mughal rulers still govern part of India
Persian is India's national language
Its buildings are national symbols, and Urdu, food and music carry its influence
Its legacy is forgotten and plays no part in politics
dd-mughals.why: The Taj Mahal and Red Fort are national symbols, Urdu grew from the empire's speech, and the Mughal past is argued over in Indian politics.

dd-mughals.h: The Taj Mahal: facts and legends
dd-mughals.p: When his wife Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to their 14th child in 1631, Shah Jahan ordered a tomb for her at Agra. Building went on for about 20 years, with some 20,000 workers according to traditional accounts, and craftsmen inlaid the white marble with semi-precious stones. Some well-known stories are legends. There is no evidence that the emperor cut off the builders' hands so they could never build anything as fine. Nor is there evidence that he planned a black twin across the river. What is recorded is that his son Aurangzeb deposed him in 1658, and he spent his last years confined in Agra Fort, within sight of the tomb, where he was buried beside his wife.

After Aurangzeb died in 1707, governors and rivals broke away. In 1739 Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi, and Afghan armies from Afghanistan raided repeatedly. The Marathas came to dominate much of India. In Bengal, now Bangladesh and eastern India, the British East India Company won at Plassey in 1757 and took over tax collection in 1765. By 1803 the emperor lived under British protection.

Tax rights granted by the emperor after Buxar

The 1765 grant of Bengal's revenues gave the Company the wealth of India's richest province to pay for armies and further conquests.

The Marathas, rising since Shivaji in the 1600s, became the strongest Indian power; they dominated Delhi and the emperor from the 1770s until the British took the city in 1803.

Founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747

Ahmad Shah Durrani, a former officer of Nadir Shah, founded the state that became modern Afghanistan and raided India several times.

Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh fell under Afghan rule or overlordship after 1747. Punjab later became the core of Ranjit Singh's Sikh kingdom.

dd-mughals.q: What weakened the empire after Aurangzeb?
a: A sudden Mongol invasion from the north
The loss of the Taj Mahal to Persia
A ban on trade with Europe
Costly Deccan wars, succession struggles and rising Maratha, Sikh and Afghan challengers
dd-mughals.why: Long wars in the Deccan drained the treasury; succession fights, breakaway governors and rival powers followed, and historians debate Aurangzeb's religious policies' role.

dd-mughals.p:
Invaded India in 1739

Nadir Shah's loot from Delhi was so vast that he suspended taxes in Persia for three years.

Aurangzeb seized the throne in 1658 and defeated his three brothers, two of whom he had executed. A devout Sunni, he ruled by Islamic law, banned some court music and in 1679 reimposed the jizya; he also destroyed some major temples, though he funded others and still employed many Hindu nobles. Historians argue over how far his religious policies turned subjects against him. Certain is that from 1681 he spent his last 26 years campaigning in the Deccan. He conquered Bijapur and Golconda, but the Marathas, built up by Shivaji, fought on. The wars drained the treasury, and when he died in 1707 aged 88, a rapid break-up followed.

The Mughal collapse opened the way for the British East India Company, which used Bengal's wealth to conquer India. Mughal buildings such as the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and Lahore's Badshahi Mosque are national symbols; India's prime minister speaks from the Red Fort each Independence Day. Urdu grew from the empire's mix of Persian and local speech, and Mughal food, painting and music still shape South Asian culture. The Mughal past is also argued over in today's Indian politics.
Mughal architecture, food (biryani, kebabs), painting and the Urdu language still shape India and Pakistan. As Mughal power faded after 1707, the British East India Company stepped in.
