dd-capitalism.p: Capitalism is an economic system in which private owners, not the state, run most businesses and markets set prices. Its modern form began in the 1600s, when Dutch and English trading companies sold shares to investors. In 1776 Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations argued that free markets and competition make nations rich.

items: Prices set by supply and demand
Self-interest can serve the common good.

dd-capitalism.p: Most rich countries combine both.

dd-capitalism.q: Who wrote The Wealth of Nations?
a: Adam Smith
Karl Marx
John Maynard Keynes
David Ricardo

dd-capitalism.p: The Industrial Revolution turned capitalism into a world system of factories, railways, banks and global trade, creating huge wealth and harsh inequality. Crashes such as the Great Depression led governments to regulate markets, and after the Cold War most of the world, including China, embraced markets in some form.

Markets rewarded people who invented, invested and took risks, and joint-stock companies let many investors share the costs and dangers of big ventures. Secure property rights, banks and stock exchanges made it easier to raise money. In the 20th century, the failures of planned economies persuaded many countries that markets delivered growth more reliably.

dd-capitalism.q: What made the Dutch East India Company a milestone in capitalism?
a: It was run by the king
It sold shares that investors could buy and resell
It banned foreign trade
It printed the first paper money
dd-capitalism.why: From 1602 the VOC raised money from many investors by selling shares, traded on Amsterdam's exchange, often called the first modern stock market.

dd-capitalism.p: Modern capitalism grew up in Europe's richest trading nations. In the Netherlands, the Dutch East India Company sold shares from 1602, and its trading posts stretched from South Africa to Indonesia and Japan. Britain followed with its own East India Company and the Bank of England. In 1776 the Scot Adam Smith argued that free markets, not monopolies, were the true source of the wealth of nations.

Home of the VOC and the Amsterdam exchange

In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic was Europe's richest trading nation, with the biggest merchant fleet and the first modern stock exchange.

East India Company, Bank of England

The East India Company, chartered in 1600, grew from a trading firm into a private army and government ruling much of India.

dd-capitalism.q: Which country began market reforms under Deng Xiaoping in 1978?
a: Japan
Vietnam
China
India
dd-capitalism.why: Deng's reforms let farmers sell surplus crops and opened China to foreign investment, starting decades of rapid growth.

dd-capitalism.p:
Parts of Java and the Spice Islands, the Cape and coastal Ceylon

The VOC made Batavia, today's Jakarta, its Asian headquarters in 1619 and fought wars to control the trade in nutmeg, cloves and pepper.

The VOC founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station for ships sailing between Europe and Asia.

In 1602 the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, raised money by selling shares that anyone could buy and later resell, and Amsterdam's exchange became the first modern stock market. Investors shared both the profits and the risks of long voyages to Asia. England's East India Company, chartered in 1600, and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, showed how private money could fund trade and even wars. These companies were also tools of empire: the VOC fought wars in Indonesia, and the English company eventually ruled much of India.

Adam Smith, a Scottish professor, argued in 1776 that people pursuing their own interest in free markets are led 'as if by an invisible hand' to benefit society: a baker sells good bread not out of kindness but to earn a living. Smith attacked mercantilism, the policy of hoarding gold and protecting home industries with tariffs and monopolies, and praised the division of labour, using a pin factory as his example. He also warned that business owners often conspire against the public, and said the state must provide defence, justice and public works.

Factories, steam power and railways began in Britain around 1760 and made it the 'workshop of the world'. Belgium was the first to follow on the continent, then France, Germany and the United States, which by 1900 had the world's largest economy. Japan industrialised after 1868 and Russia from the 1890s. Industrial capitalism created vast fortunes, big cities and a new working class, and with it trade unions and socialism.
Coal, cotton, steam engines and a global empire gave Britain a head start; by 1850 it made about half the world's iron and cotton cloth.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Adam Smith argue in The Wealth of Nations?
a: Free markets and competition make nations rich
Governments should own all factories
Countries should hoard gold
Trade between countries is harmful
dd-capitalism.why: Smith argued that self-interest in free markets benefits society 'as if by an invisible hand', and attacked mercantilist tariffs and monopolies.

dd-capitalism.p: Railways, steel, oil and mass immigration made the United States the world's largest economy, and men like Carnegie and Rockefeller among the richest people in history.

After 1868 Meiji Japan built railways, shipyards and textile mills, often starting them as state firms and then selling them to private companies.

Finance minister Sergei Witte drove a rush of railway building and foreign investment in the 1890s, including the Trans-Siberian Railway.

dd-capitalism.q: What started the 2008 global financial crisis?
a: Risky mortgage lending in the United States
A war in the Middle East
The collapse of the euro
A pandemic
dd-capitalism.why: Banks made and traded huge numbers of risky American home loans; when house prices fell, the losses spread through the global financial system.

dd-capitalism.p: Capitalism grew in booms and busts. After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, banks failed and by 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed. The British economist John Maynard Keynes argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump, and after World War II most Western countries built mixed economies, with welfare states, regulated banks and some state-owned industries. In the 1970s high inflation and slow growth turned many against this model, and economists such as Milton Friedman argued for freer markets, lower taxes and less regulation.

From the late 1970s, governments across the world turned to markets. Chile began in 1975 and China in 1978. Margaret Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States cut taxes and regulation. Vietnam opened up in 1986 and India in 1991. When communism fell, Eastern Europe and Russia switched to markets in a rush known as 'shock therapy'.

Economists trained in Chicago, the 'Chicago Boys', freed prices and trade under General Pinochet's dictatorship from 1975.

Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops and opened special economic zones to foreign investors.

The Doi Moi ('renovation') reforms of 1986 brought markets to communist Vietnam.

In 1991, facing a currency crisis, finance minister Manmohan Singh scrapped licences and cut tariffs and controls.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Keynes say governments should do in an economic slump?
a: Cut all spending
Abolish the banks
Ban imports
Spend to revive demand
dd-capitalism.why: After the Great Depression, Keynes argued that government spending could revive demand and jobs, shaping the mixed economies built after World War II.

dd-capitalism.p:
Poland's 1990 'shock therapy', designed by Leszek Balcerowicz, freed prices and trade almost overnight.

Prices were freed in January 1992, and rushed privatisation created a small class of super-rich 'oligarchs'.

From the late 1970s a wave of market reforms swept the world. Chile's military government opened its economy from 1975, China's Deng Xiaoping began reforms in 1978, and Margaret Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States cut taxes and sold off or deregulated industries. Vietnam followed in 1986, and after communism collapsed, Eastern Europe and Russia switched to markets almost overnight, often painfully. India opened up in 1991. Global trade boomed, but the 2008 financial crisis, which began with risky American mortgage lending, revived old doubts about unregulated markets.

Capitalism has helped lift billions of people out of poverty, especially since China and India opened their economies. But it also brings booms and busts, such as the 2008 financial crisis, and wide gaps between rich and poor. Arguments about how far governments should tax, regulate and spend remain at the heart of politics almost everywhere.

dd-pirates.p: From the mid-1600s buccaneers based at Tortuga and Port Royal raided Spanish towns and ships in the Caribbean, often with licences from England or France. In the 1690s pirates sailed the 'Pirate Round' to the Indian Ocean, where Henry Every seized a Mughal treasure ship in 1695.

items: North African raiders took Europeans as slaves.

dd-pirates.s: Privateers were pirates licensed by a government.
dd-pirates.why: Like Francis Drake, who raided Spain for England.

dd-pirates.p: The busiest years came after 1715, when crews based at Nassau in the Bahamas, led by men such as Benjamin Hornigold, Blackbeard and Charles Vane, attacked merchant shipping, and later crews such as Bartholomew Roberts's raided from Newfoundland to West Africa. Then the tide turned: Woodes Rogers took back Nassau in 1718, Blackbeard was killed that November, and by about 1726 the great pirate crews were gone.

dd-pirates.q: What was the 'pirate republic' at Nassau?
a: A Spanish fort guarding silver fleets
A Royal Navy base for hunting pirates
A pirate haven in the Bahamas from about 1715 to 1718
A French colony on Hispaniola
dd-pirates.why: Hundreds of pirates, including Hornigold, Blackbeard and Vane, used Nassau's harbour in the neglected Bahamas until Woodes Rogers arrived as governor in 1718.

dd-pirates.p: Spanish silver and the booming trade in sugar, slaves and Asian goods offered rich prizes on long, poorly guarded routes. Wars between European powers trained thousands of sailors as privateers, licensed raiders, and when peace came in 1713 many were thrown out of work. Merchant sailors faced low pay and brutal discipline, so some joined pirates willingly. Weak colonial government and merchants happy to buy cheap goods gave pirates safe harbours.

dd-pirates.h: Pirate havens in the Caribbean, c. 1715
dd-pirates.p: Spain's silver fleets sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana, then home through the Florida Straits, past islands held by rival empires. Pirates used havens in the gaps: buccaneers at Tortuga in French Haiti and Port Royal in English Jamaica in the 1600s, then the 'pirate republic' at Nassau in the Bahamas until 1718. Blackbeard sailed from Nassau and died off North Carolina.

dd-pirates.q: Why could pirates find safe harbours in the Americas?
a: The Royal Navy protected them
Weak colonial government and merchants keen on cheap goods
Spain gave them its ports
They were all pardoned each year
dd-pirates.why: Colonies like the Bahamas were neglected, and merchants in places such as New York financed pirates and bought their stolen goods.

dd-pirates.p:
Most of the mainland and the big islands

Havana was where Spain's fleets gathered each year before sailing home with silver from Mexico and Peru.

Spanish Puerto Rico licensed its own privateers, who raided British shipping.

Jamaica, the Bahamas and small islands

England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655 and at first welcomed buccaneers as a defence. Port Royal later turned to hanging pirates.

The Bahamas were a neglected English colony. After 1713 hundreds of pirates used Nassau's harbour, until the first royal governor arrived in 1718.

dd-pirates.q: What does this history suggest about piracy today?
a: It returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia
It ended for good in the 1720s
It exists only in novels and films
It is now legal under licence
dd-pirates.why: Piracy never vanished; it reappeared off Somalia in the 2000s, while novels and films reshaped the golden age into a romantic legend.

dd-pirates.p:
Saint-Domingue, plus Martinique and Guadeloupe

French buccaneers settled western Hispaniola from Tortuga, and Spain recognised it as French Saint-Domingue in 1697.

Edward Teach, or Thatch, was a pirate for only about two years, from 1716 to 1718, but no pirate is more famous. In late 1717 he captured a French slave ship and renamed it Queen Anne's Revenge, armed with dozens of cannon. In May 1718 he blockaded Charleston for about a week and released his hostages for a chest of medicines. Soon after, his flagship ran aground off North Carolina; its wreck was found in 1996. He accepted a royal pardon but returned to piracy, and on 22 November 1718 he died fighting a Royal Navy party at Ocracoke. According to a 1724 book, he lit slow fuses under his hat to frighten victims.

Many pirate crews signed written articles, rules that every man swore to. Captains were usually elected and could be voted out, and a quartermaster shared out the loot, with the captain typically taking only one and a half or two shares. Some articles promised payouts for lost limbs, banned gambling or fighting on board, and set punishments such as marooning. Crews were young, mostly former merchant sailors and navy men, and included many men of African descent, some free crewmen and some still treated as slaves. Life was crowded, often drunk and dangerous, and most pirate careers ended within a few years at the end of a rope or in a fight.

dd-pirates.h: The Pirate Round to the Indian Ocean, 1690s
dd-pirates.p: In the 1690s some pirates sailed from the Americas round Africa to the Indian Ocean, a voyage called the Pirate Round. They sheltered at Île Sainte-Marie off Madagascar and hunted rich Indian ships in the Red Sea and Arabian Sea. In 1695 Henry Every captured the Mughal ship Ganj-i-Sawai, and the anger in Mughal India put the English East India Company in danger.

The richest state in the Indian Ocean

Bengal was one of the Mughal Empire's richest provinces, famous for its cotton cloth.

The Mughal Empire ruled most of India. When its ships were plundered by English pirates, Emperor Aurangzeb's officials briefly shut down English trade and confined English merchants.

dd-pirates.q: Why did so many sailors turn to piracy after 1713?
a: Peace threw thousands of trained privateers out of work
Spain paid them to attack England
The Royal Navy doubled its wages
Pirates were legally licensed by Parliament
dd-pirates.why: Wars had trained thousands as licensed privateers; when peace came in 1713 many lost their work, and harsh merchant life pushed others to join willingly.

dd-pirates.p:
Madagascar's coast was outside European rule

Madagascar had no European colony and lay near the shipping lanes. Pirates settled on its east coast in the 1690s–1720s, some marrying into local families.

Walking the plank is mostly fiction: there is almost no evidence for it in the golden age, and the few recorded cases come from later. Buried treasure was rare, because pirates usually spent or shared loot quickly; the best-known real case is William Kidd's cache on Gardiners Island near New York, dug up by the authorities in 1699. Treasure maps marked with an X, peg legs and parrots owe more to Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island (1883) than to history. The Jolly Roger was real, though flags varied, and a black flag usually offered mercy if a ship surrendered.

dd-pirates.q: How was the golden age of piracy brought to an end?
a: Pirates retired rich on buried treasure
Spain conquered the Bahamas
A great hurricane destroyed their ships
Pardons, naval patrols and colonial courts with mass hangings
dd-pirates.why: The 1717 pardon, Rogers taking Nassau, navy hunts and local trials under a 1700 law broke the havens; by about 1726 the great crews were gone.

dd-pirates.p: In 1717 King George I offered a pardon to pirates who surrendered, and in July 1718 Woodes Rogers, a former privateer, arrived at Nassau as governor with warships. Many pirates accepted the pardon; those who carried on were hunted down. Under a 1700 law, colonial courts could try pirates without sending them to London, and mass hangings followed. The navy killed Bartholomew Roberts, the most successful pirate of the age, off West Africa in 1722, and 52 of his crew were hanged at Cape Coast Castle. By the late 1720s the great Atlantic pirate crews had gone.

Britain's Royal Navy, colonial courts and a 1717 royal pardon broke the pirate havens, and hundreds of pirates were hanged, which helped make the Atlantic safe for the trade of growing empires. Piracy never vanished, and it returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia in the 2000s. The golden age also left a powerful legend, reshaped by novels and films, of free outlaws under the skull and crossbones.

dd-enlightenment.p: The Enlightenment was an 18th-century movement of writers and scientists who believed that reason and evidence, rather than tradition, Church or king, should guide human affairs. Building on Newton's laws of motion of 1687, thinkers such as John Locke, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Adam Smith and Immanuel Kant questioned how societies should be run.

items: The social contract and the general will.

steps: Governments rule by consent of the governed.

dd-enlightenment.q: Whose idea was the separation of powers?
a: Montesquieu
Locke
Hobbes
Voltaire

dd-enlightenment.p: They argued for natural rights to life, liberty and property, freedom of speech and religion, government by consent and the separation of powers. Books, pamphlets, salons and the great French Encyclopédie spread these ideas across Europe and the Americas, where they inspired the American Revolution of 1776, the French Revolution of 1789 and the Haitian Revolution, which ended in 1804.

dd-enlightenment.q: What did Enlightenment thinkers believe should guide how society is run?
a: Reason and evidence
The will of the king
Church tradition alone
Ancient custom
dd-enlightenment.why: They argued that reason and evidence, rather than tradition, Church or king, should decide how people live and are governed.

dd-enlightenment.p: The Scientific Revolution showed that nature followed laws people could discover, which encouraged thinkers to apply reason to society too. Europe's wars of religion had left many weary of intolerance. Growing literacy, cheap printing, coffee houses and a rising middle class created an eager public for new ideas, while censorship was often easy to dodge by printing abroad, especially in the Dutch Republic.

The Enlightenment was a conversation across borders, carried by letters, books and travellers. Britain gave it Newton, Locke, Hume and Adam Smith. France was its heart, with Voltaire, Montesquieu, Diderot and the Paris salons. The Netherlands printed books banned elsewhere. In the German lands Kant asked 'What is Enlightenment?', and in Italy Cesare Beccaria argued against torture and the death penalty.

dd-enlightenment.q: Why did Enlightenment ideas spread so quickly in the 1700s?
a: Governments paid for every book
Cheap printing, rising literacy and coffee houses created eager readers
Universities taught nothing else
Kings ordered everyone to read them
dd-enlightenment.why: Rising literacy, cheap printing, salons and coffee houses gave new ideas a wide public, and banned books were often printed abroad.

dd-enlightenment.p:
Newton, Locke, Hume, Adam Smith

Newton's Principia (1687) showed the universe ran by natural laws. Locke, Hume and Adam Smith applied reason to government, knowledge and economics.

Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Diderot

Paris salons hosted by women such as Madame Geoffrin brought writers, scientists and nobles together. Many French books were banned, and their authors risked prison.

dd-enlightenment.q: What was a major contradiction in the Enlightenment?
a: It rejected all science
Many of its thinkers accepted slavery and excluded women
It banned printing
It defended rule by priests
dd-enlightenment.why: Jefferson owned enslaved people and most thinkers kept women out of politics; critics like Wollstonecraft and Toussaint Louverture used its own ideas against these limits.

dd-enlightenment.p:
The Dutch Republic printed books banned in France

The Dutch Republic's relatively free press made it Europe's publisher. Descartes and Locke both spent years there.

Before the Enlightenment, most Europeans accepted that kings ruled by the will of God and that the Church decided what was true. Enlightenment thinkers asked people to test ideas by reason and evidence instead. Kant summed it up in 1784 with the motto 'Dare to know'. Voltaire mocked religious intolerance and was jailed in the Bastille and later exiled from Paris for his writing. Many thinkers were still believers, but they wanted religion to be a private choice, not something enforced by the state. Scientists, from Newton to the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, were heroes of the age.

John Locke argued that people are born with natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government which breaks its trust may be overthrown. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) proposed splitting power between a legislature, an executive and courts so that no one could become a tyrant. Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) opened with 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' These ideas went straight into the US Constitution of 1787, with its checks and balances, and into France's Declaration of the Rights of Man.

Enlightenment ideas left the salons. Some kings tried reform from above: Catherine the Great in Russia, Joseph II in Austria and Frederick the Great in Prussia. Elsewhere people took power themselves. The United States declared independence in 1776, France proclaimed the Rights of Man in 1789, and in Haiti enslaved people rose up in 1791 and won independence in 1804.

Rights claimed by the people

The Declaration of Independence borrowed Locke's ideas about rights and government by consent, and the 1787 Constitution built in Montesquieu's separation of powers.

The 1789 Declaration said that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. The revolution later turned to terror and war.

dd-enlightenment.q: What did Montesquieu propose to stop any ruler becoming a tyrant?
a: A state religion
Rule by philosophers
Separate legislative, executive and judicial powers
Abolishing all laws
dd-enlightenment.why: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that dividing power between separate branches protects liberty, an idea built into the US Constitution.

dd-enlightenment.p:
Monarchs who reformed from above

Catherine the Great corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, but serfdom grew harsher during her reign.

Joseph II abolished serfdom in his lands and tolerated Protestants and Jews in the 1780s.

Some monarchs liked the new ideas, as long as they kept their own power. Frederick the Great of Prussia corresponded with Voltaire, allowed religious freedom and abolished most torture. Catherine the Great of Russia exchanged letters with Diderot and bought his library, yet serfdom grew harsher in her reign. Joseph II of Austria abolished serfdom in his lands and tolerated Protestants and Jews, but many of his reforms were reversed after his death. Historians call them 'enlightened absolutists': rulers who reformed from above but never shared power with their people.

dd-enlightenment.q: Which revolutions drew directly on Enlightenment ideas?
a: The Russian and Chinese revolutions
The Meiji Restoration and the Glorious Revolution
The Mexican and Iranian revolutions
The American, French and Haitian revolutions
dd-enlightenment.why: The American Declaration of Independence, France's Rights of Man and Haiti's revolt against slavery all used the language of natural rights and equality.

dd-enlightenment.p: The Enlightenment's promises were not meant for everyone. Thomas Jefferson, who wrote that 'all men are created equal', owned more than 600 enslaved people over his life. Most thinkers excluded women from politics, and Rousseau thought girls should be educated to please men. Critics soon turned the movement's logic against these limits. Olympe de Gouges published a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791, and Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman followed in 1792. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people led by Toussaint Louverture claimed the rights of man for themselves.

Enlightenment ideas underpin modern democracies, constitutions, free speech and human rights, and the belief that science can improve lives. Yet many of its thinkers accepted slavery and the exclusion of women. Later campaigners, from abolitionists to Mary Wollstonecraft, attacked these contradictions using the Enlightenment's own arguments about equal rights.

dd-nationalism.p: Nationalism is the idea that people who share a language, culture or history form a nation, and that each nation should govern itself in its own state. It took off with the French Revolution, which declared that sovereignty belonged to the nation rather than the king. In the 1800s it united Italy and Germany and helped Greeks, Serbs and others break away from the Ottoman Empire.

After World War I it broke up the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires, and after 1945 it powered independence movements across Asia and Africa. It also fuelled wars, ethnic cleansing and fascism.

dd-nationalism.q: What is the central idea of nationalism?
a: Each nation should govern itself in its own state
Kings rule by the will of God
All countries should merge into one
Trade should always be free
dd-nationalism.why: Nationalists believe that people sharing a language, culture or history form a nation that should rule itself.

dd-nationalism.p: Before 1800 most people's loyalty went to their village, religion or ruler. Mass schooling, newspapers, railways and conscript armies spread a shared national language and identity. Empires made many peoples feel like second-class subjects, and nationalism offered them dignity, self-rule and a reason to resist foreign domination.

In 1815 Italy and Germany were divided into many states, while the Ottoman Empire ruled the Balkans. Over the next 60 years nationalism remade the map. Greece won independence in 1830, and Belgium broke away from the Netherlands the same year. Italy was united by 1870 and Germany in 1871, and in 1878 Serbia, Montenegro and Romania were recognised as independent.

dd-nationalism.q: What did Woodrow Wilson call for in 1918?
a: A return of the monarchies
A world government
German unification
Self-determination for peoples
dd-nationalism.why: Wilson argued that peoples should choose their own governments, encouraging new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.

dd-nationalism.p:
Italy, 1861–70; Germany, 1871

Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's 'Thousand' volunteers united Italy under Victor Emmanuel II, proclaimed King of Italy in 1861.

Bismarck's wars with Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71) created a German Empire led by Prussia.

From the Ottomans, or Belgium from the Netherlands

French-speaking and Catholic Belgians rose against Dutch rule in 1830 and chose a king of their own.

Greece's war of independence began in 1821 and won the backing of Britain, France and Russia, which recognised a small Greek state in 1830.

In 1789 France's revolutionaries declared that power came from the nation, not the king. The new republic promoted one language, French, in its schools, though many citizens still spoke Breton, Occitan or other tongues, and in 1793 it raised a mass army of citizens. Napoleon's conquests then spread the idea, and stirred nationalism against him in Germany, Spain and Russia. Writers collected folk tales and songs to define their nations: the Brothers Grimm in Germany, and Elias Lönnrot, whose Kalevala epic of 1835 became Finland's national story.

In 1815 Italy and Germany were both patchworks of states. Italy was united between 1859 and 1870 under the King of Piedmont-Sardinia, through the diplomacy of Count Cavour and the volunteer army of Giuseppe Garibaldi, who conquered Sicily and Naples in 1860. German unity came through 'blood and iron'. Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chief minister, fought wars against Denmark, Austria and France, and in January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Both new nations soon sought colonies and great-power status.

World War I destroyed four empires. In their place, nationalists founded new states in the name of self-determination: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the three Baltic states, an Irish Free State and Atatürk's Turkey. But borders never matched peoples neatly, leaving millions of people as minorities on the wrong side and grievances that fed the next war.

From the Russian, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires

Poland reappeared in 1918 after 123 years of being partitioned between Russia, Prussia and Austria.

Czechoslovakia joined Czechs and Slovaks, but also included about three million Germans in the Sudetenland.

a: By a vote of all Germans
Through Bismarck's wars against Denmark, Austria and France
By Napoleon's conquests
Through a treaty with Britain
dd-nationalism.why: Bismarck united Germany by 'blood and iron', and the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles after France's defeat in 1871.

dd-nationalism.p: After a war of independence, 26 Irish counties became the Irish Free State in 1922, while Northern Ireland stayed in the UK.

Nationalism was deadly for empires that ruled many peoples. The Ottoman Empire lost Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria in the 1800s, and in 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist's assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand helped trigger World War I. In 1918 US President Woodrow Wilson called for self-determination, and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia rose from the ruins of the Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. After World War II, nationalist leaders such as Gandhi, Sukarno and Kwame Nkrumah won independence from European empires across Asia and Africa.

dd-nationalism.q: Which event shows the dark side of nationalism?
a: The forced population exchange between Greece and Turkey in 1923
The founding of the Red Cross
The first modern Olympic Games
The invention of the printing press
dd-nationalism.why: Building nation-states often meant expelling minorities: about 1.6 million people were forced to move between Greece and Turkey in 1923.

dd-nationalism.h: Nationalism today: new states and independence votes
dd-nationalism.p: Nationalism still makes and breaks countries. Since 2000, Timor-Leste, Montenegro, Kosovo and South Sudan have become independent. Other movements have voted and lost, or been blocked: Quebec narrowly voted to stay in Canada in 1995, Scotland chose to stay in the United Kingdom in 2014, and 2017 referendums in Catalonia, in Spain, and Iraqi Kurdistan were rejected by their national governments.

Timor-Leste voted for independence from Indonesia in 1999 and became independent in 2002.

Montenegro voted to leave its union with Serbia in 2006, with 55.5% in favour.

dd-nationalism.q: Why was nationalism dangerous for Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire?
a: They had no armies
Their capitals were too small
They ruled many peoples who wanted their own states
They were too democratic
dd-nationalism.why: These empires ruled Serbs, Poles, Czechs, Arabs and many others. As each people demanded self-rule, the empires broke apart, finally after World War I.

dd-nationalism.p:
Quebec, Scotland, Catalonia, Iraqi Kurdistan

Quebec voted to stay in Canada by just over one percentage point in 1995.

Scotland voted by 55% to 45% to stay in the United Kingdom in 2014.

Nationalism could unite people, but it could also turn them against outsiders and minorities. Extreme nationalism fed fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany, which claimed the nation needed racial purity and 'living space'. Creating nation-states often meant moving or expelling minorities. In 1923 Greece and Turkey exchanged about 1.6 million people, and the partition of India in 1947 uprooted about 15 million. In the 1990s the breakup of Yugoslavia brought 'ethnic cleansing' back to Europe, and rival nationalisms still drive conflicts from the Caucasus to the Middle East.

Today almost the whole world is divided into nation-states, and the United Nations has 193 members. Nationalism still shapes politics: independence movements in Scotland, Catalonia and Kurdistan, wars over territory such as Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and populist parties that promise to put the nation first.

dd-women.p: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women were not naturally inferior to men, only less educated. In 1848 American campaigners met at Seneca Falls and demanded equal rights, including the vote. Over the next century movements in dozens of countries won women entry to universities, control of their own property and wages, and the vote, first in New Zealand in 1893.

steps: Equal pay, work, education and reproductive rights.

dd-women.p: After 1945 the fight moved to work, family law and the body: equal pay laws, the contraceptive pill, divorce reform and laws against violence. Today women vote almost everywhere and lead governments, but they still earn less, hold under a third of parliamentary seats, and in Afghanistan are barred from school.

Industrialisation, mass schooling and cities drew women into paid work and public life, and Enlightenment ideas of equal rights were hard to limit to men. Women organised petitions, marches and, in Britain, militant protest. Two world wars, when women filled factories and offices, made the case harder to refuse. Later, safer contraception, higher education and service-sector jobs let women plan careers, and international agreements put pressure on governments.

dd-women.q: What did women's movements win over the century after Seneca Falls?
a: Equal seats in every parliament
University entry, control of property and wages, and the vote
An end to all pay gaps
The right to lead the Church
dd-women.why: Movements in dozens of countries won access to universities, rights to their own property and wages, and the vote, first in New Zealand in 1893.

dd-women.p: The demand for equal rights was argued in Britain in 1792 and organised in the United States from 1848. New Zealand gave women the national vote first, in 1893. Most of Europe and North America followed around World War I, much of Latin America and Asia by 1950, and newly independent nations often from the start. Switzerland waited until 1971, and Saudi Arabia allowed women to vote in local elections in 2015.

The first countries to give women the national vote

In 1893 New Zealand gave women, including Māori women, the vote after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures.

Australian women won the federal vote and the right to stand for parliament in 1902, but most Aboriginal people were shut out until 1962.

Main examples, some at first with age or other limits

Most Canadian women won the federal vote in 1918, but many Asian Canadians and First Nations people were excluded for decades longer.

Mary Wollstonecraft argued for women's equality in 1792. After decades of campaigning by suffragists and suffragettes, women over 30 won the vote in 1918, and on equal terms with men in 1928.

dd-women.q: After 1945, what changes let women plan careers as well as families?
a: Laws banning women from factories
The end of universities for men
Fewer service-sector jobs
The contraceptive pill, higher education and equal pay laws
dd-women.why: The pill, approved in the US in 1960, more education and equal pay laws such as Britain's in 1970 opened paid careers to women.

dd-women.p:
Main examples

Turkey gave women the national vote in 1934, as part of Atatürk's modernising reforms, earlier than France or Italy.

France, home of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man, gave women the vote only in 1944. They first voted in 1945.

In Britain the vote was fought for in two ways. From 1897 Millicent Fawcett's suffragists lobbied politely through petitions and meetings. From 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst's suffragettes chose 'deeds, not words': they chained themselves to railings, smashed shop windows and set fire to empty buildings. Jailed suffragettes went on hunger strike and were force-fed through tubes. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison ran onto the track at the Derby and was fatally struck by the King's horse. Historians still debate whether militancy helped or hurt. War work by millions of women from 1914 shifted opinion, and in 1918 women over 30 won the vote.

For much of history married women had few legal rights of their own: in English common law a wife's property and earnings belonged to her husband until the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882. After 1945 more women took paid work, and campaigners turned to equal pay. The US passed an Equal Pay Act in 1963 and Britain in 1970, after women machinists at Ford's Dagenham factory went on strike in 1968. The contraceptive pill, approved in the US in 1960, let women plan families and careers. In many countries women now outnumber men at university, but they still earn less, partly because they do most unpaid care work.

In 1960 Sri Lanka's Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first woman elected prime minister. India and Israel followed in the 1960s, Britain in 1979, and Iceland elected the first woman president by popular vote in 1980. In 1988 Pakistan's Benazir Bhutto became the first woman to lead a Muslim-majority democracy. Recent firsts include Mexico in 2024 and Japan in 2025.

Prime ministers of Sri Lanka, India and Israel

Sirimavo Bandaranaike led her party after her husband, the prime minister, was assassinated, and won the 1960 election. She served three terms as prime minister.

Indira Gandhi became prime minister in 1966 and led India for about 16 years in all. She was assassinated in 1984.

dd-women.q: Why did Enlightenment ideas help women's rights campaigners?
a: They said only the rich should vote
They praised the old monarchies
Ideas of equal rights were hard to limit to men
They called for women to stay at home
dd-women.why: Wollstonecraft argued women were only less educated, not inferior, and claims of equal rights proved hard to restrict to men alone.

dd-women.p:
Isabel Perón, vice-president, succeeded her husband Juan Perón on his death in 1974, becoming the world's first woman president. She was overthrown by a military coup in 1976.

Elisabeth Domitien became prime minister of the Central African Republic in 1975, the first woman to head a government in Africa.

Iceland elected Vigdís Finnbogadóttir president in 1980. It has ranked first in the World Economic Forum's gender gap index every year since 2009.

Eugenia Charles became prime minister of Dominica in 1980 and served 15 years, the first woman to lead a Caribbean country.

dd-women.q: Which describes women's rights around the world today?
a: Full equality has been reached everywhere
Big gains, but gaps in pay and politics remain
Women still cannot vote in most countries
Girls are barred from school in most of Asia
dd-women.why: Women vote almost everywhere, yet hold about 27.5% of parliamentary seats, earn roughly a fifth less, and Afghanistan alone bars girls from secondary school.

dd-women.p: After 1945 women's rights became an international cause. In 1979 the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), which 189 countries have ratified; the United States has signed but not ratified it. In 1995, at the Beijing conference, 189 governments agreed a plan for action on education, health, work and violence. Movements took local forms: Indian campaigners fought dowry deaths, Latin Americans won quotas for women in parliament, and in 2017 the #MeToo campaign against sexual harassment spread worldwide from the United States. In Iran the 2022 protests after Mahsa Amini's death in police custody took the slogan 'Woman, life, freedom'.

On 1 January 2026 women held 27.5% of seats in the world's parliaments, the Inter-Parliamentary Union counted. Seven countries, including Rwanda, Mexico and Bolivia, had at least as many women as men in their lower or single chamber, while Oman, Tuvalu and Yemen had none. Iceland tops the World Economic Forum's gender gap index, and Afghanistan bars girls from school after the age of about 12.

Half or more of the lower or single chamber, Jan 2026

Women hold 51 of 80 seats in Rwanda's Chamber of Deputies, about 64%, the world's highest share. Its 2003 constitution reserves at least 30% of seats for women.

Women hold over half of the seats in Cuba's National Assembly, though the Communist Party is the only legal party.

Top three in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026

Iceland has topped the gender gap index for 17 years in a row. On 24 October 1975 about 90% of Icelandic women went on strike for a day to show their value to society.

Finland ranked second in the 2026 index. It was the first country in Europe to give women the vote, in 1906.

dd-women.q: How did the two world wars help win the vote in countries like Britain?
a: Women filling factories and offices made the case harder to refuse
Governments needed women as soldiers
Suffragettes stopped campaigning entirely
The wars ended militant protest by law
dd-women.why: War work by millions of women from 1914 shifted opinion, and in 1918 British women over 30 won the vote.

dd-women.p:
Lower or single chamber, Jan 2026

Omani women can vote and stand for the elected Consultative Assembly, but none won a seat in the 2023 election.

No woman won a seat in Tuvalu's 16-member parliament at the 2024 election.

By the World Economic Forum's 2026 measure, the world has closed about 69% of the gap between men and women in health, education, work and politics. Health and education gaps are nearly closed in most countries; the largest gaps are in politics and the economy. Women hold about 27.5% of seats in parliaments, and the International Labour Organization estimates they earn roughly a fifth less than men worldwide. Iceland, Finland and Norway come closest to equality. The widest gaps are in parts of South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and Afghanistan under the Taliban is the only country that bars girls from secondary school.

Women's rights changed daily life more than almost any other movement: in most countries girls now go to school as long as boys, and women make up about four in ten workers. Gaps remain. The World Economic Forum estimated in 2026 that at current rates full equality is about 120 years away. Debates continue over pay, care work, abortion, violence, and religious and cultural rules on dress and family.

The UN adopts CEDAW, the international bill of rights for women

dd-communism.p: In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto, predicting that workers would overthrow capitalism. The first communist revolution came in Russia in 1917, where Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and founded the Soviet Union. Under Stalin it industrialised at enormous human cost, and after World War II the Red Army installed communist governments across Eastern Europe.

steps: History is a struggle between classes.
A classless society with shared property.

dd-communism.q: Which countries are still ruled by communist parties?
a: China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba, North Korea
Russia and Ukraine
Venezuela and Bolivia
None

dd-communism.p: Mao Zedong won China's civil war in 1949, and communists later took power in North Korea, Vietnam, Cuba and parts of Africa. By the 1980s these states held about a third of humanity, but in 1989 Eastern Europe's regimes fell, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself dissolved.

dd-communism.q: Where did the first communist revolution actually happen?
a: Industrial Britain in 1848
Germany after World War I
Russia in 1917
China in 1911
dd-communism.why: Marx expected revolution in industrial countries like Britain and Germany, but Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in war-weary Russia in 1917.

dd-communism.p: Industrialisation brought great wealth alongside harsh poverty, and Marx's promise of a classless society of equals inspired millions. Communists won power mostly where wars had shattered old regimes, as in Russia in 1917 and China in the 1940s, or where they led struggles against colonial rule. The systems later failed because planned economies stagnated, people resented the lack of freedom, and Gorbachev's reforms loosened control.

dd-communism.h: From Marx to the Soviet Union, 1848–1924
dd-communism.p: In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, both from Germany, published The Communist Manifesto, and Marx wrote most of his later work in exile in Britain. They expected revolution in industrial countries, but it came first in war-weary Russia. In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power, won a brutal civil war and in 1922 founded the Soviet Union. Mongolia became the second communist state in 1924.

dd-communism.q: Which describes the five communist-ruled states today?
a: They all run strict planned economies
They have all become democracies
China and Vietnam keep one-party rule but run market economies
They are all allied with Russia
dd-communism.why: China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea are still ruled by communist parties, and China and Vietnam have opened their economies to markets.

dd-communism.p:
Marx and Engels' homeland and place of exile

Marx and Engels were born in the German Rhineland. Germany had Europe's biggest socialist party, but its communist uprisings in 1919 failed.

The Manifesto was first printed in London in February 1848. Marx lived in London from 1849 until his death in 1883 and is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Founded in December 1922

World War I broke Russia's monarchy in early 1917. In November Lenin's Bolsheviks took power, and the civil war of 1918–21 left millions dead.

Kazakhstan's steppe came under Soviet rule after the civil war. Forced collectivisation in the early 1930s caused a famine that killed over a million Kazakhs.

Soviet-backed People's Republic from 1924

With Red Army help, Mongolian revolutionaries took power in 1921, and the Mongolian People's Republic was declared in 1924, closely tied to Moscow.

Marx argued that history is driven by struggle between classes. Under capitalism, he said, factory owners, the bourgeoisie, grew rich by paying workers, the proletariat, less than the value they produced. Competition would squeeze wages and concentrate wealth until workers rose up, took over the means of production and built a classless society in which the state would eventually 'wither away'. He expected this in advanced industrial countries such as Britain and Germany. Instead, revolutions succeeded in largely peasant countries, Russia and China, and the state grew more powerful rather than withering. Marx gave few details of how a communist society would actually work, leaving Lenin and others to invent it.

Communism spread in waves. Lenin's revolution in Russia came first. World War II carried the Red Army into Eastern Europe, where Moscow installed communist governments, while Mao Zedong won China in 1949 and Kim Il Sung ruled North Korea. Wars against colonial rule brought communists to power in Vietnam, and Castro took Cuba in 1959. A last wave in the 1970s reached Angola, Ethiopia, Cambodia and Afghanistan.
The Soviet Union and Mongolia

dd-communism.q: Why did Marx's ideas inspire millions of people?
a: Industrialisation brought great wealth alongside harsh poverty
They promised a return to monarchy
They were imposed by the Church
They guaranteed free travel abroad
dd-communism.why: Amid the harsh poverty of industrial society, Marx's promise of a classless society of equals drew millions of followers.

dd-communism.p:
Annexed by Moscow or ruled by communists it installed; Yugoslavia and Albania by their own partisans

The Red Army drove out the Nazis in 1944–45, and by 1947 Moscow-backed communists controlled Poland through rigged elections.

Tito's partisans freed Yugoslavia largely by themselves, which let him break with Stalin in 1948.

Kim Il Sung's North Korea and Mao's People's Republic

Mao's army of peasants, not factory workers, won China's revolution. China later broke with Moscow and became a rival centre of communism.

Soviet troops occupied the north of Korea in 1945 and put Kim Il Sung in charge. His family still rules.

From 1928 the Soviet Union ran its economy by five-year plans: officials, not markets, decided what to make and at what price. This built steel mills, dams and a huge arms industry quickly, and brought near-universal literacy, free health care and guaranteed jobs. But consumer goods were scarce and often poor. People queued for meat, shoes and toilet paper, and in East Germany buyers could wait more than ten years for a Trabant car. Housing was cheap but cramped, and many families shared flats. Criticism could cost a job or worse, and travel abroad was tightly restricted. Jokes and black markets became part of everyday survival.

dd-communism.h: The communist world at its height, 1985
dd-communism.p: World War II spread communism to Eastern Europe, occupied by the Red Army, and in 1949 Mao Zedong won China's civil war. Revolutions followed in Vietnam, Cuba and parts of Africa. By the 1980s communist parties ruled about a third of humanity. They were rivals as often as allies: China split from the Soviet Union around 1960, and Yugoslavia went its own way from 1948.

15 Soviet republics

The Soviet Union was a superpower with the world's largest territory. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation, famine and purges killed millions, and its Gulag camps held millions more.

dd-communism.q: Where did communists most often win power?
a: In rich, peaceful democracies
Where wars had shattered old regimes or against colonial rule
Only through free elections
Mainly in Western Europe
dd-communism.why: World War I broke Russia's monarchy, war shattered China in the 1940s, and in places like Vietnam communists led struggles against colonial rule.

dd-communism.p:
Soviet allies in the Warsaw Pact

Poland's Solidarity trade union, founded in 1980 with about 10 million members, became the first big challenge to communist rule from below.

Czechoslovakia's 'Prague Spring' reforms were crushed by a Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968.

Yugoslavia and Albania

Tito's Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and ran its own looser system, with workers' councils and open borders for travel.

Communist states caused some of the 20th century's worst disasters, though death tolls are debated. In 1932–33 famine caused by Soviet collectivisation killed millions, including an estimated 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine, where it is known as the Holodomor. In Stalin's Great Terror of 1937–38 about 680,000 people were shot, according to Soviet records, and millions passed through the Gulag labour camps. China's Great Leap Forward caused a famine in 1959–61 with estimates ranging from about 15 million to over 40 million deaths. In Cambodia the Khmer Rouge's rule in 1975–79 left an estimated 1.5 to 2 million dead.

In 1989 revolutions, mostly peaceful, swept away communist rule in Eastern Europe, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union broke into 15 countries. Today only five states are ruled by communist parties: China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea. China and Vietnam keep one-party rule but have opened their economies to markets, foreign investment and private business.

China's Communist Party has ruled since 1949. Market reforms since 1978 made China the world's second-largest economy, while the party keeps firm political control.

Vietnam's 'Doi Moi' reforms of 1986 opened the economy, and it is now a major exporter of electronics and clothing, still under one-party rule.

dd-communism.q: Why did communist rule collapse in Eastern Europe in 1989?
a: NATO invaded the Soviet bloc
China ordered its allies to reform
Mao's death ended Soviet support
Stagnant economies, lack of freedom and Gorbachev's refusal to use force
dd-communism.why: Planned economies stagnated, people resented the lack of freedom, and Gorbachev made clear he would not send tanks, so the regimes fell one after another.

dd-communism.p:
Communist states of the Cold War, as on the 1985 map

The Soviet Union was dissolved in December 1991. Russia's 1990s shift to capitalism brought a deep economic slump before recovery in the 2000s.

Poland's June 1989 elections, the first partly free ones in the bloc, gave Solidarity a landslide. It joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.

By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating and the war in Afghanistan was draining it. Mikhail Gorbachev, leader from 1985, tried to revive it with perestroika, restructuring, and glasnost, openness, and made clear he would not send tanks to save Eastern Europe's regimes. In 1989 they fell one after another: Poland's Solidarity won elections in June, the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November, and Czechoslovakia's 'Velvet Revolution' followed. That same June, China's leaders chose force instead, crushing protests in Tiananmen Square. After a failed hardline coup in August 1991, the Soviet republics declared independence, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned.

Five states, China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, are still ruled by communist parties, though China and Vietnam now run market economies. Former Soviet bloc countries in Central Europe joined NATO and the EU. The era left deep scars: famines, purges and labour camps killed millions, and historians still debate the totals. Many former communist states remain under authoritarian rule.

The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia
Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China
Deng Xiaoping begins China's market reforms
The Berlin Wall falls; communist rule ends across Eastern Europe
The Soviet Union dissolves into 15 countries

dd-climate.p: From the 1800s, burning coal, then oil and gas, powered industry, transport and electricity, first in Europe and North America and later across Asia. Scientists showed as early as the 1850s that carbon dioxide traps heat, and from 1958 measurements in Hawaii tracked its steady rise. By the 1980s many scientists were warning that the planet was warming, and governments set up the IPCC in 1988 to assess the evidence.

steps: CO₂, methane and water vapour keep some heat in.
Burning fossil fuels has raised CO₂ by 50% since 1800.

dd-climate.h: Largest CO₂ emitters, share of world total

dd-climate.q: What did the Paris Agreement (2015) aim for?
a: Keep warming well below 2 °C
Ban all cars
End coal by 2020
Plant a trillion trees

dd-climate.p: Treaties followed in Rio in 1992, Kyoto in 1997 and Paris in 2015, but global emissions kept rising and reached a record in 2025. That year the world was about 1.4°C warmer than before industrialisation.

Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide that has been locked underground for millions of years, and it stays in the air for centuries, so warming builds up as emissions accumulate. Cutting emissions has been hard because fossil fuels were cheap and reliable and underpin modern economies, the benefits of cutting are shared globally while the costs are local, and countries disagree over who should cut first and pay.

dd-climate.q: What happened to global emissions after the climate treaties of 1992, 1997 and 2015?
a: They fell to pre-industrial levels
They kept rising, reaching a record in 2025
They stopped completely after Paris
They halved within a decade
dd-climate.why: Despite Rio, Kyoto and Paris, burning fossil fuels released a record 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, when the world was about 1.4°C warmer.

dd-climate.p: Burning coal powered the Industrial Revolution, first in Britain, then in Belgium, Germany, France and the United States. At the same time scientists found that carbon dioxide traps heat. In 1896 Sweden's Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling it would warm the Earth by several degrees. Few took the warning seriously until 1958, when precise measurements began in Hawaii.

Britain, from the late 1700s

Britain was the first country to run on coal: by 1850 it mined over half the world's coal. In 1859 John Tyndall showed in London that carbon dioxide absorbs heat.

Main industrial economies of the 1800s

Belgium was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, on the coalfields of Wallonia, in the early 1800s.

The Ruhr valley's coal and steel made Germany Europe's leading industrial power by 1900.

dd-climate.q: What does the IPCC conclude about the effects of warming?
a: Warming is entirely natural
It affects only polar regions
It will bring only milder winters
Human activity has warmed the planet, bringing more extremes and rising seas
dd-climate.why: The IPCC finds human influence has unequivocally warmed the planet, bringing heatwaves, heavier rain, melting ice and rising seas, with the poorest often hit hardest.

dd-climate.p:
The first estimate of global warming, 1896

Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist, published the first estimate of how much burning fossil fuels could warm the planet in 1896. He thought it would take thousands of years and might be welcome.

In 1856 the American scientist Eunice Foote put jars of different gases in the sun and found that the one filled with carbon dioxide grew hottest. In 1859 John Tyndall in London measured how carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb heat. In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius estimated that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the world by about 5–6°C, though he expected it to take thousands of years. In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring the air on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, at about 315 parts per million. His 'Keeling Curve' rose every year, passing 425 in 2025, about 50% above pre-industrial levels.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, founded in 1988, reviews thousands of studies and has its summaries approved line by line by governments. Its 2021–2023 assessment concluded that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, by about 1.1°C in 2011–2020 compared with 1850–1900. Warming has since continued: the World Meteorological Organization says 2015–2025 were the eleven warmest years on record. The IPCC finds that each extra fraction of a degree brings more heat extremes, heavier downpours, droughts in some regions and rising seas, and that limiting warming to 1.5°C would require global emissions to fall steeply and reach net zero around 2050.

Burning fossil fuels released a record 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, by the Global Carbon Project's estimate. China emitted about 32%, the United States 13%, India 8% and the European Union 6%. Over history the picture differs: the United States has emitted about a quarter of all fossil CO2 since 1850, the most of any country. Per person, Americans emit about seven times as much as Indians.

About 32% of fossil CO2 in 2025

China became the largest emitter in about 2006 and now emits more than the US and EU combined, mostly from coal. It also installs more solar and wind power than the rest of the world put together, and aims to peak emissions before 2030.

dd-climate.q: Why does warming build up as fossil fuels are burned?
a: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries and traps heat
Coal smoke blocks out the Sun
Burning fuel heats the oceans directly
Factories release heat that cannot escape
dd-climate.why: Fossil fuels release long-buried carbon dioxide that traps heat and lingers for centuries, so warming grows as emissions accumulate.

dd-climate.p:
About 13%

The US has emitted about a quarter of all fossil CO2 since the industrial age began, more than any other country. Its emissions peaked around 2007 but rose again in 2025.

About 8%

India's emissions are growing fast as its economy expands, but each Indian emits only about 2 tonnes a year, under half the world average.

dd-climate.q: Which change in 2025 shows how the energy picture is shifting?
a: Renewables overtook coal as the largest source of electricity
Oil replaced coal for power stations
Every country closed its coal plants
The US rejoined the Paris Agreement
dd-climate.why: Solar and wind became the cheapest new electricity in most places, though debates continue over the speed of change, its costs and who pays.

dd-climate.p: Most governments accept the mainstream science, though the US government under Trump rejects much of it, and countries disagree about what to do and how fast. Developing countries such as India argue that rich nations, which emitted most of the carbon already in the air, should cut first and pay for poorer ones to adapt; rich countries point out that most emissions now come from developing economies, led by China. Some favour carbon taxes or trading schemes, others subsidies, regulation or nuclear power. Critics of rapid change, including the Trump administration, argue that it raises energy prices, threatens jobs and hurts competitiveness; supporters argue that clean energy is now often cheaper and that delay makes the damage costlier.

In 2015 nearly every country signed the Paris Agreement, aiming to hold warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C. Each sets its own target. The United States left it in January 2026. Several countries, such as Britain in 2024, have shut their last coal power station, while low-lying islands such as Tuvalu and the Maldives face rising seas. In 2025, renewables overtook coal as the world's largest source of electricity.

The US left in 2026; Iran, Libya and Yemen never ratified

The US joined the Paris Agreement under President Obama, left under Trump in 2020, rejoined under Biden in 2021 and left again on 27 January 2026. In January 2026 it also announced it would quit the UN climate convention and the IPCC.

Iran signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 but its parliament has not ratified it.

Main examples, 2016–2025

Belgium closed its last coal power station in 2016.

Austria closed its last coal power station, at Mellach, in April 2020.

dd-climate.q: Why has cutting emissions proved so hard for governments?
a: Scientists disagree that CO2 traps heat
Renewables have always cost more than coal
Cheap fuels underpin economies, and countries dispute who cuts first and pays
No country has ever signed a climate treaty
dd-climate.why: Fossil fuels were cheap and reliable, the benefits of cutting are global while costs are local, and rich and developing countries disagree over who should act first.

dd-climate.p:
Countries mostly under 5 metres above sea level

The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country, with an average height of about 1.5 metres above sea level.

Most of Tuvalu is less than 3 metres above sea level. Under a 2023 treaty, Australia offers up to 280 Tuvaluans a year the right to move there.

In the 1970s scientists found that chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, used in spray cans and fridges, were destroying the ozone layer that shields life from ultraviolet light, and in 1985 British researchers reported a 'hole' over Antarctica. In 1987 the Montreal Protocol agreed to phase out these chemicals, and every UN member eventually ratified it. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering, and UN scientists expect it to return to 1980 levels over most of the world by about 2040, and over Antarctica by about 2066. It is often cited as proof that global environmental agreements can work, though cutting CFCs was far easier than replacing fossil fuels.

The IPCC concludes that human activity has unequivocally warmed the planet, bringing more intense heatwaves, heavier rain, melting ice and rising seas, with the poorest countries often hit hardest. At the same time solar and wind power have become the cheapest new electricity in most places, and in 2025 renewables overtook coal worldwide. Debates continue over the speed of change, its costs, and who pays.

Charles David Keeling begins measuring CO2 on Mauna Loa, Hawaii
The UN sets up the IPCC to assess climate science
Nearly 200 countries adopt the Paris Agreement
The first calendar year more than 1.5°C warmer than pre-industrial times
Renewables overtake coal as the world's largest source of electricity

dd-oil.p: In 1859 Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial oil well in Pennsylvania, and kerosene lamps soon lit homes worldwide. Cars, ships and aircraft then made oil the fuel of the 20th century, and both world wars were fought partly over access to it. Huge finds in Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia shifted the centre of the oil world to the Gulf.

items: A fifth of world oil passes through.

dd-oil.p: Producers founded OPEC in 1960, and in 1973 an Arab embargo quadrupled prices and stunned the West. Since then oil has shaped wars from Kuwait in 1990 to the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, while the US shale boom made America the top producer again.

Oil packs a lot of energy into a liquid that is easy to move and store, so it beat coal for transport and became the base of plastics and chemicals. But the cheapest oil lies in a few places, often far from the countries that use the most. That mismatch made oil a source of wealth, power and conflict: governments fought for supplies, and producers fought foreign companies for control of their own resources.

dd-oil.q: How did oil's place in the world change during the 20th century?
a: It was replaced by coal for transport
It became the fuel of cars, ships, aircraft and war
It was used only for lamps
It stayed a minor American industry
dd-oil.why: Kerosene lamps came first, but cars, ships and aircraft made oil the fuel of the 20th century, and world wars were fought partly over access to it.

dd-oil.p: In 1859 Edwin Drake struck oil in Pennsylvania, and kerosene for lamps was the first big market. Cars, ships and planes soon made oil vital. The United States led the world, with Baku in the Russian Empire its great rival around 1900, and Mexico and Venezuela booming in the 1920s. Britain's companies found oil in Persia in 1908, and Americans struck it in Saudi Arabia in 1938.

The world's top producer for most of a century

Oil began here in 1859. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil came to dominate refining until it was broken up in 1911. In 1945 the US produced about two-thirds of the world's oil.

The Russian Empire's oil city

Baku, then in the Russian Empire, was producing about half the world's oil around 1900. In 1942 Hitler's armies drove towards it but never reached it.

dd-oil.q: What did the 1973 Arab oil embargo do to the West?
a: It lowered petrol prices
It ended US support for Israel
It made Western companies take over Gulf oilfields
It quadrupled prices, caused queues and pushed the West into recession
dd-oil.why: Saudi crude rose from about $3 to almost $12 a barrel, petrol ran short, and the shock spurred searches for new oil in the North Sea and Alaska.

dd-oil.p:
Boom years from the 1910s

Mexico's oil boom began in the 1910s, and by 1921 it was the world's second-largest producer. In 1938 it nationalised the foreign oil companies, creating Pemex.

Oil was found around Lake Maracaibo in the 1910s. By 1928 Venezuela was the world's biggest oil exporter, and oil soon dominated its economy.

On 6 October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. When the US rushed weapons to Israel, Arab producers led by Saudi Arabia cut output and banned sales to the United States and the Netherlands. The price of a barrel of Saudi crude went from about $3 to almost $12 within months. Americans waited in long queues for petrol, some stations ran dry, and Congress set a national speed limit of 55 mph. The Netherlands and West Germany banned most Sunday driving, and people cycled and skated on empty motorways. The embargo ended in March 1974, but the shock pushed the West into recession and started the search for new oil in the North Sea and Alaska.

In 1950 Dubai and Doha were small towns of traders, fishermen and pearl divers. Oil changed everything. At first Western companies controlled the fields and paid the rulers royalties. From the 1970s producers took over: Saudi Arabia bought full ownership of Aramco by 1980, and Kuwait, Iraq and others nationalised their oil. The money paid for cities, airports, free health care and education, and generous state jobs for citizens, while millions of foreign workers came to build it all. Today Gulf states use their oil income to diversify into finance, tourism and airlines, and their sovereign wealth funds are among the largest investors in the world.

In 1960 five producers founded OPEC in Baghdad to win back control of prices from the big Western oil companies. In October 1973, during the Arab–Israeli war, Arab producers cut output and banned sales to the United States and the Netherlands for backing Israel. By early 1974 the oil price had roughly quadrupled. Iran's revolution in 1979 caused a second shock.

Iran nationalised its oil in 1951, which led to a 1953 coup backed by the US and Britain. In 1973 it did not join the Arab embargo, but its 1979 revolution sent prices soaring.

Iraq hosted OPEC's founding in 1960 and nationalised its oil industry in 1972. Its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, an oil-rich neighbour, led to the Gulf War.

dd-oil.q: Why did oil beat coal as the fuel for transport?
a: It was found in every country
It produced no carbon dioxide
It packs much energy into an easily moved, stored liquid
Governments banned coal in 1912
dd-oil.why: Oil's energy-rich liquid form made it ideal for vehicles, and it also became the base of plastics and chemicals.

dd-oil.p:
Libya's new leader, Muammar Gaddafi, forced oil companies to pay higher prices in 1970, a first crack in their control.

Abu Dhabi joined OPEC in 1967, and its membership passed to the United Arab Emirates, formed in 1971.

Arab producers banned oil sales to them in 1973–74

The embargo hit a country that now imported a third of its oil. Americans queued for petrol, and Congress set a national 55 mph speed limit in 1974.

Embargoed for its support for Israel, the Netherlands banned Sunday driving on ten Sundays from November 1973 to January 1974, leaving motorways to cyclists and walkers.

dd-oil.q: Why is oil's future now being reshaped?
a: The world's oil has run out
Burning oil drives climate change, and electric cars are spreading
OPEC has banned new drilling
Plastics no longer use oil
dd-oil.why: Oil produces about a third of fossil-fuel carbon dioxide, so the shift to electric cars and clean energy is reshaping the industry, though demand still rose slowly.

dd-oil.p: In 1912 Britain's navy began switching from coal to oil, and two years later the government bought control of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company to secure supplies. In World War II oil shaped strategy: Japan attacked the US and the oil-rich Dutch East Indies after America cut off its oil in 1941, and Germany drove towards the Caucasus oilfields in 1942. In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, and a US-led coalition drove it out in 1991, as retreating troops set over 600 wells on fire. In 2026 war between the US, Israel and Iran choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow outlet for about a fifth of the world's oil.

Thanks to shale drilling, the United States is now the biggest producer, ahead of Russia and Saudi Arabia. OPEC's 11 members and 10 partners, together OPEC+, agree output targets. The UAE quit both on 1 May 2026. From March 2026, war between the US, Israel and Iran choked tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and oil passed $100 a barrel.

11 members since 1 May 2026

Saudi Arabia leads OPEC and holds some of the world's largest reserves. Its state company, Saudi Aramco, is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Iraq was OPEC's second-largest producer before the 2026 Hormuz crisis, and oil pays for most of its government budget.

Outside OPEC but agree output targets with it

Russia is the second- or third-largest producer and co-leads OPEC+ with Saudi Arabia. Western sanctions after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine pushed its exports towards China and India.

Kazakhstan's giant Tengiz and Kashagan fields make it a major OPEC+ partner, though it has often pumped above its targets.

dd-oil.q: Why has oil so often been a source of conflict?
a: The cheapest oil lies in a few places, far from big users
Oil companies refused to sell to anyone
Oil was found only in Europe
OPEC banned all exports after 1960
dd-oil.why: This mismatch made governments fight for supplies and producers fight foreign companies for control, from the 1973 embargo to Kuwait in 1990.

dd-oil.p: The UAE announced on 28 April 2026 that it would leave OPEC and OPEC+ from 1 May, saying it wanted to use its expanded production capacity.

Burning oil releases carbon dioxide, the main gas driving climate change. Oil accounts for roughly a third of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, coming mostly from cars, lorries, ships and planes. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nearly every country promised to cut emissions, and at the 2023 COP28 climate summit in Dubai countries agreed for the first time to 'transition away from fossil fuels'. Electric cars are spreading fast, especially in China and Europe. Producers argue the world will still need oil for decades, while critics say new fields are incompatible with climate goals. World demand was still rising slowly in the mid-2020s.

Oil wealth built the modern Gulf states and funds governments from Norway to Nigeria, though many producers struggle with corruption and dependence on one product. Price shocks still ripple through the world economy, as in 2026. Burning oil also releases about a third of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, so the shift to electric cars and clean energy is now reshaping the industry's future.
