In 1789 a bankrupt France erupted: crowds stormed the Bastille, the monarchy fell, Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793, and the Terror followed. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804. Napoleon seized power in 1799 and conquered much of Europe, but his invasion of Russia in 1812 cost him around half a million men, and he fell at Waterloo in 1815. His occupation of Spain in 1808 set off the wars in which Bolívar, San Martín and others freed Spanish America.
revolutions.why: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent gave rebels a cause. Britain's new taxes after the Seven Years' War angered its colonists. France's debts, partly from aiding the Americans, high bread prices and anger at noble privilege broke the old regime. Haiti's revolt grew from the brutality of slavery and the French Revolution's talk of equality. When Napoleon toppled Spain's king, colonial elites took power themselves.
revolutions.after: The revolutions made popular sovereignty, written constitutions and rights of citizens central to politics, and even gave us 'left' and 'right'. Napoleon's law code and the nationalism he stirred reshaped Europe. Haiti abolished slavery but was forced in 1825 to pay France a huge indemnity. Latin America gained independence but often saw instability and rule by strongmen, while slavery lasted in the US until 1865 and Brazil until 1888.

nations.what: After 1815 nationalism, the idea that each people should have its own state, kept redrawing the map. Greece, Belgium, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away from larger states, most from the shrinking Ottoman Empire. Piedmont united Italy in 1861, helped by Garibaldi's conquest of the south, and Bismarck's Prussia beat Denmark, Austria and France to found the German Empire in 1871. Across the Atlantic the United States bought Louisiana, took the south-west in its war with Mexico in 1846–48 and reached the Pacific. Latin American wars fixed borders that still stand: Chile's victory in the War of the Pacific left Bolivia landlocked. Britain's settler colonies united as Canada in 1867, Australia in 1901 and South Africa in 1910.
nations.why: The French Revolution, newspapers and schools taught people to see themselves as Italians, Germans or Greeks rather than subjects of a dynasty. Railways and industry made bigger states possible and profitable, but armies settled the borders: Bismarck said the great questions would be decided by 'iron and blood'. In the Americas, cheap land, mass immigration and a belief in 'Manifest Destiny' drove settlers west, at the expense of Mexico and Indigenous nations.
nations.after: Europe and the Americas took much of their modern shape. A united Germany became the strongest power in Europe, and France longed to win back Alsace-Lorraine, while rival nationalisms made the Balkans a powder keg; both fed into 1914. The United States, now spanning a continent, became the world's largest economy by about 1890. Indigenous peoples in North America and Australia lost most of their land.

scramble.what: In 1870 Europeans held only about a tenth of Africa, mostly on the coasts. Then the race began. At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, hosted by Bismarck, European powers agreed rules for claiming land, with no Africans present. By 1914 they ruled about nine-tenths of the continent, often with straight-line borders. Conquest was often brutal: forced labour for rubber in King Leopold's Congo caused an international outcry, and Germany crushed the Herero and Nama in Namibia. Only Ethiopia, which beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia stayed independent. In Asia France took Indochina, the US took the Philippines and Japan took Taiwan and Korea, while Britain's empire grew to rule nearly a quarter of the world's people.
scramble.why: Industrial Europe wanted raw materials such as rubber, cotton and copper, new markets, and safe sea routes, above all Britain's route to India through the Suez Canal. Rivalry fed on itself: each power grabbed land to keep others out, and colonies became a badge of national prestige. Machine guns, steamships and quinine against malaria made conquest cheap, and racist ideas of a 'civilising mission' were used to justify it.
scramble.after: Colonial lines became the borders of most African states at independence, often splitting peoples or joining rivals. Colonial economies were built to export raw materials, a pattern many countries still struggle to escape. Imperial rivalry added to the tensions behind World War I, and resentment of foreign rule fed the independence movements that brought these empires down after 1945.

ww1.what: In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, declared war on Serbia. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and its march through neutral Belgium brought in Britain. In the west the armies dug trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland, and battles such as Verdun and the Somme killed hundreds of thousands for a few miles of mud. The war spread to the Ottoman Empire, Italy and the colonies. Russia collapsed into revolution in 1917, but the United States joined the Allies, and an exhausted Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918.
ww1.why: Europe's great powers were locked into rival alliances: Germany and Austria-Hungary against France and Russia, with Britain tied to both. Decades of imperial rivalry, an arms race and nationalism, above all in the Balkans, turned a local crisis into a general war. Military plans built for speed, like Germany's scheme to defeat France first by going through Belgium, left little room for diplomacy in July 1914. Historians still debate how much of the blame lies with Germany.
ww1.after: About 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Four empires fell, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, and new countries such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared, while Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East between them. The Russian Revolution produced the Soviet Union, and the harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter, helping set the stage for World War II. The United States emerged as a world power.

interwar.what: In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia, won a civil war and founded the Soviet Union in 1922. Under Stalin, forced collective farming brought a famine that killed millions, above all in Ukraine, and the Great Terror of 1937–38 shot about 700,000 people. In Italy Mussolini's Fascists took power in 1922. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 began the Great Depression: world trade collapsed, and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs. With six million Germans unemployed, Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and built a dictatorship. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937, Italy conquered Ethiopia, and Hitler took Austria and the Czech lands. After a pact with Stalin, he invaded Poland in 1939.
interwar.why: World War I toppled empires, left millions of bitter veterans and spread fear of communist revolution, which fascists exploited by promising order and national glory. Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles, and the Depression's mass unemployment drove voters to extremes. The League of Nations had no army, the US stayed out, and Britain and France, dreading another war, chose appeasement. Historians still debate whether standing firm earlier, say over the Rhineland in 1936, would have stopped Hitler.
interwar.after: The decade ended in the deadliest war in history. Its lessons shaped the world after 1945: the belief that appeasing aggressors invites war, welfare states and government economic management meant to prevent another depression, and institutions such as the UN and the IMF built to protect peace and trade. The Soviet one-party state built in these years lasted until 1991.

ww2.what: Germany invaded Poland in September 1939 and by mid-1940 had overrun western Europe, leaving Britain fighting alone. In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, and in December Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and overran South-East Asia. In occupied Europe the Nazis carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews in mass shootings and in death camps such as Auschwitz. The tide turned in 1942–43 at Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad. The Red Army drove west, the Allies landed in Normandy in 1944, and Germany surrendered in May 1945. In the Pacific, US forces fought island by island towards Japan; after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, killing an estimated 150,000–200,000 by the end of 1945, Japan surrendered.
ww2.why: The war grew out of the failures of the 1919 peace: German resentment of Versailles, the Depression, and regimes that glorified conquest. Hitler wanted 'living space' in the east and a Europe without Jews; Japan wanted an Asian empire and the oil it lacked, which the US cut off in 1941. Appeasement, and then the Nazi–Soviet Pact, let Hitler attack Poland without fearing a war on two fronts.
ww2.after: Over 60 million people died, most of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens. Europe was split between US and Soviet camps, Germany and Korea were divided, and Poland was moved west as millions were expelled. The United Nations was founded, and the Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention and strengthened the case for a Jewish state. Weakened Britain and France began losing their empires, and nuclear weapons changed war for ever.

asia.what: Japan's defeat in 1945 left Europe's Asian empires shaken, and nationalists moved fast. The US granted the Philippines independence in 1946. In 1947 Britain left India, splitting it into India and Muslim-majority Pakistan; over 10 million people fled across the new borders, and estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to 2 million. Burma and Ceylon followed in 1948. Indonesia fought the Dutch until 1949, and Vietnam defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. In the Middle East, Britain and France gave up their mandates: Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Palestine, where Israel was founded in 1948. Malaya became independent in 1957, and Britain's withdrawal from the Gulf in 1971 created the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain.
asia.why: The war shattered the myth of European invincibility: Japan took Singapore and the Dutch East Indies within three months. Nationalist movements, some decades old like Gandhi's Indian National Congress, were ready to take over, and Britain, nearly bankrupted by the war, could no longer afford to hold India by force. The US and the new United Nations opposed old-style empires, while France and the Netherlands, which fought to stay, lost costly wars.
asia.after: The new states, from India to Indonesia, held a large share of humanity, and several grew into major powers. Hasty borders left lasting conflicts: India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir and have fought over it repeatedly, and both now have nuclear weapons, while Bangladesh broke from Pakistan in 1971. Vietnam's struggle merged into the Cold War. Many new states joined the Non-Aligned Movement, refusing to take sides between the superpowers.

coldwar.what: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union, allies against Hitler, became rivals. Soviet-backed communists took over Eastern Europe, an 'Iron Curtain' fell across the continent, and the US answered with Marshall Plan aid and the NATO alliance. Germany and Korea were split; the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948–49, and in 1961 East Germany built the Berlin Wall. Both sides raced to build nuclear weapons, and in 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the world close to nuclear war. Instead the superpowers fought through others, in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola and Central America. Under Gorbachev the Soviet grip loosened: the Berlin Wall opened in 1989, and the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
coldwar.why: The two powers had opposite systems, one-party communism with a planned economy against democracy and markets, and each believed the other wanted to spread its own. Stalin wanted friendly governments as a buffer after two German invasions; the US, resolved not to repeat the appeasement of the 1930s, set out to 'contain' communism. Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal, so the rivalry ran through arms races, spies, aid and proxy wars. Historians still argue over which side bore more blame.
coldwar.after: The United States was left as the only superpower, and NATO and the European Union expanded east, which Russia's leaders came to oppose. Fifteen countries emerged from the Soviet Union. Korea remains divided, communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and thousands of nuclear warheads built in these years still exist. Proxy wars left long civil conflicts, as in Afghanistan and Angola.

mideast.what: In 1948, as British rule ended, Israel declared independence and neighbouring Arab states attacked. Israel won, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, and Jordan and Egypt held the West Bank and Gaza. In 1967 Israel took those lands, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai. After Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973, Arab producers cut off oil to the US and others and prices quadrupled. Egypt made peace in 1979 and regained Sinai. That year Iran's revolution created an Islamic republic; Iraq attacked it in 1980, starting an eight-year war, then invaded Kuwait in 1990. The 1993 Oslo Accords brought limited Palestinian self-rule but no state, and wars followed, including in Gaza after Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023.
mideast.why: Two national movements, Zionism and Palestinian Arab nationalism, claimed the same land, and in World War I Britain made promises to both Arabs and Zionists that were hard to reconcile. After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew; the UN's 1947 partition plan was accepted by Jewish leaders and rejected by Arab leaders, and war followed. Meanwhile the region holds nearly half the world's proven oil, so outside powers competed for influence there.
mideast.after: The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is unresolved: Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and settlements there have grown, while Jerusalem and the refugees' future remain disputed. Most UN members recognise a State of Palestine; Israel and the US do not. Most Jews of the Arab world left or were driven out after 1948, many to Israel. Oil made the Gulf states rich and central to US strategy, and the US fought repeated wars there, from Kuwait in 1991 to Iraq in 2003.

china.what: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the defeated Nationalists withdrew to Taiwan. Mao's Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 forced peasants into communes and caused a famine that killed tens of millions; scholars' estimates range from 15 to over 40 million. His Cultural Revolution of 1966–76 brought a decade of purges and chaos. After Mao died, Deng Xiaoping from 1978 let farmers sell their crops, opened special economic zones such as Shenzhen and welcomed foreign investment. Growth near 10% a year followed for three decades. The party crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989, joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
china.why: The Communists won the civil war because the Nationalist government was weakened by corruption, runaway inflation and eight years of war with Japan, while Mao's party won over the peasants. Mao's disasters came from forcing utopian plans on the country with no one able to object. Deng's reforms worked because China had a vast, cheap, disciplined workforce, and it opened just as world trade boomed and Western firms looked for low-cost factories.
china.after: About 800 million people left extreme poverty, the largest fall in poverty in history, and China became the world's biggest manufacturer and goods exporter. One-party rule stayed and tightened under Xi Jinping from 2012: after the 2019 protests Beijing imposed a security law on Hong Kong that critics say ended many freedoms, and Western governments and UN experts condemned mass detention in Xinjiang, which Beijing calls counter-terrorism. Rivalry with the US over trade, technology, Taiwan and the South China Sea now shapes world politics.

europe.what: In 1950 France proposed pooling its coal and steel, the industries of war, with West Germany's, and in 1951 six countries signed up. The Treaty of Rome created a common market from 1958. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, then Greece, Spain and Portugal after their dictatorships ended. The 1992 Maastricht Treaty founded the European Union, and the euro was launched in 1999, with notes and coins in 2002. In 2004 ten countries joined, most of them former communist states. The euro crisis from 2010 nearly forced Greece out, and in 2016 Britain voted to leave, departing in 2020.
europe.why: Two world wars had wrecked Europe, and its leaders wanted to bind France and Germany so tightly that another war between them would be impossible. A bigger shared market promised prosperity, and unity, encouraged by the United States, gave strength against the Soviet threat. Later, joining became the way for former dictatorships and communist states to lock in democracy and catch up economically.
europe.after: The old rivals of Western Europe have not fought each other since 1945, their longest peace in centuries. The EU is a single market of about 450 million people, 21 of its 27 members use the euro, and its rules on trade, competition and data are followed far beyond its borders. Arguments over national sovereignty, migration and debt continue. Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed the EU towards closer defence ties and a new wave of candidates, Ukraine among them.

africa.what: In March 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first black African colony south of the Sahara to win independence. In 1960, the "Year of Africa", 17 countries followed, most of them French colonies freed by negotiation. Elsewhere freedom came through war: Algeria fought France from 1954 to 1962, and Portugal fought guerrillas in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau until its own army overthrew the dictatorship in Lisbon in 1974. The Congo fell into crisis within days of its sudden independence from Belgium in 1960. White-minority Rhodesia broke from Britain in 1965 to avoid majority rule and held out until 1980, when it became Zimbabwe.
africa.why: The Second World War weakened Britain and France, and Africans who had fought for them came home demanding rights. Nationalist leaders built mass parties, the new United Nations backed self-determination, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires, while colonies grew costly to hold. Where many white settlers lived, as in Algeria, Kenya and Rhodesia, or where the colonial power was a dictatorship, as in Portugal, the end came through war.
africa.after: Almost every new state kept the colonial borders, which African leaders agreed in 1964 to respect, so many countries joined rival peoples and divided others. Many fell to one-party rule or military coups, and Cold War rivals armed opposing sides in wars such as Angola's. Economies built to export raw materials stayed dependent on them. Today Africa has 54 countries in the UN and the world's youngest and fastest-growing population.

islands.what: In 1962 Western Samoa, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago became independent, and over the next two decades dozens of small territories followed. Malta left British rule in 1964 and the Maldives in 1965. Britain's other Caribbean colonies followed, from Barbados and Guyana in 1966 to St Kitts and Nevis in 1983. In the Pacific, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu and Kiribati followed, and Vanuatu, ruled jointly by Britain and France, became independent in 1980. In the Indian Ocean, Mauritius, the Seychelles and the Comoros won independence, though the island of Mayotte voted to stay French. Some, such as Nauru and Tuvalu, had fewer than 10,000 people at independence.
islands.why: Once the big colonies had gone, keeping small ones made little sense to a Britain that was cutting overseas costs and turning towards Europe. A UN declaration of 1960 called for a swift end to colonialism in all its forms. A British-led West Indies Federation collapsed in 1962 after Jamaica voted to leave, so each island went its own way. Many territories were thought too small to stand alone, but local leaders pressed for statehood anyway.
islands.after: Dozens of microstates now each hold a vote in the UN General Assembly equal to that of China or the United States. Many use it to press on climate change, since rising seas threaten low-lying nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives. Most joined the Commonwealth, and several still have the British monarch as head of state. Many depend on tourism, offshore finance or fishing licences, while places such as Bermuda and New Caledonia remain attached to Britain or France.

collapse.what: In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev took charge of a stagnating Soviet Union and began reforms: glasnost, or openness, and perestroika, or restructuring. In 1989 he let Eastern Europe go. Poland elected a Solidarity-led government, Hungary opened its border, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened; by Christmas communist rule had fallen across the bloc, peacefully everywhere except Romania. Germany reunited in October 1990. Inside the Soviet Union the Baltic republics led a push for independence. A failed hard-line coup in Moscow in August 1991 broke central power, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned as the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries.
collapse.why: The Soviet economy had stagnated: it could not match Western technology, spent heavily on arms and a war in Afghanistan, and lost income when oil prices fell in the 1980s. Gorbachev hoped openness would revive the system, but it let people voice decades of grievances, and nationalism surged in the republics. Above all, he refused to use mass force to hold Eastern Europe, and that unravelled the whole empire.
collapse.after: The Cold War ended, leaving the United States the only superpower. Most of the former Eastern Bloc and the Baltic states became democracies and joined NATO and the EU. Russia suffered an economic collapse in the 1990s; under Vladimir Putin, in power since 1999, it rebuilt central control, and its leaders came to cite NATO's eastward expansion as a grievance in their wars with Georgia and Ukraine. The end of superpower rivalry also helped end apartheid and freed Namibia and Eritrea.

balkans.what: Tito held Yugoslavia's six republics and many peoples together until his death in 1980. As communism collapsed, Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia on Serb nationalism, and in June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Slovenia left after a ten-day war, but Croatia fought Serb rebels and the Yugoslav army until 1995. The worst war was in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992–95: Sarajevo was besieged, about 100,000 people died, and at Srebrenica Bosnian Serb forces killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys. NATO air strikes and the Dayton agreement ended it. NATO bombed Yugoslavia in 1999 over Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008.
balkans.why: Memories of mass killing between Yugoslavia's peoples in the Second World War had been held down by Tito's one-party rule and his slogan of "brotherhood and unity". When communism and the economy failed in the 1980s, leaders in each republic, above all Milošević in Serbia and Franjo Tuđman in Croatia, turned to nationalism. The republics' borders left large Serb and Croat minorities outside their home states, and armed forces tried to redraw the map through "ethnic cleansing".
balkans.after: About 140,000 people died in the wars and millions were driven from their homes. A UN tribunal in The Hague convicted the Bosnian Serb leaders Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić of genocide; Milošević died in 2006 before his trial ended. Bosnia remains split into a Serb republic and a Bosniak-Croat federation. Slovenia and Croatia joined the EU and others are candidates, while about half of UN members recognise Kosovo and Serbia does not.

recent.what: The map kept changing after the Cold War. Namibia won independence from South Africa in 1990, and Eritrea broke away from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war. In 1999 Canada carved Nunavut, a territory with an Inuit majority, out of the Northwest Territories, a new internal border rather than a new country. In East Timor, a former Portuguese colony that Indonesia had invaded in 1975, people voted for independence in 1999; pro-Indonesian militias then destroyed much of the territory until UN-backed peacekeepers arrived, and Timor-Leste became independent in 2002. In 2011 South Sudan split from Sudan after decades of civil war, becoming the world's newest country.
recent.why: Most of these changes undid arrangements left over from colonial rule, when borders and rulers were imposed without the consent of the people living there. The end of the Cold War removed superpower backing that had kept such disputes frozen, and the UN and outside powers became readier to support referendums. Nunavut was different: it grew out of an Inuit land claim settled by negotiation with Canada's government.
recent.after: The world now has 193 UN member states, and new ones are rare because governments fear secession and international law strongly protects existing borders. Independence has not guaranteed peace: South Sudan fell into civil war in 2013, and Eritrea became one of the world's most closed states, while Timor-Leste built a working democracy. Unresolved cases remain: Western Sahara, Kosovo, recognised by about half of UN members, and Somaliland, which only Israel recognises.

today.what: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in the United States, which then invaded Afghanistan and, in 2003, Iraq; the Taliban retook Kabul in 2021. The 2008 financial crisis hit the West hard while China kept growing. Arab Spring uprisings in 2011 toppled four rulers but led to civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen. Covid-19 killed millions from 2020. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Hamas's attack on Israel in October 2023 began a war in Gaza. In February 2026 US and Israeli strikes on Iran killed its supreme leader, and the war since has disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
today.why: The United States left the Cold War as the only superpower, and its response to 9/11 drew it into long wars. Globalisation spread wealth but also shocks, and widening inequality and migration fed populist politics in many countries. China's rise and a resurgent Russia challenged American leadership. In the Middle East, authoritarian rule, jobless young people and rivalry between Iran and its opponents fuelled uprisings and wars.
today.after: The age of a single dominant power and ever-freer trade has given way to rivalry between great powers, higher tariffs and rising military spending; NATO has grown to 32 members and Europe is rearming. Wars and persecution have driven more than 100 million people from their homes, by UN count. Smartphones and social media changed politics and daily life, and artificial intelligence is spreading fast. In October 2026 talks had brought no general ceasefire in Ukraine, and a truce with Iran agreed in April had collapsed in July.

now.what: More than 8.2 billion people live on Earth, over a third of them in India and China, and India has been the most populous country since 2023. The United States is still the largest economy, producing about a quarter of world output at market exchange rates, with China second; together they make over two-fifths. Nine countries hold about 12,200 nuclear warheads, nearly 86% of them Russian or American, and China's arsenal is growing fastest. Burning fossil fuels released a record of about 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, roughly a third of it from China. NATO has 32 members, and wars in Ukraine, Sudan and around Iran go on.
now.why: A few big forces explain the picture. Countries that industrialised first, in Europe, North America and Japan, grew rich, and those that later joined world trade, above all in East Asia, are catching up. As countries get richer, birth rates fall, so populations age and shrink in the rich world and China while Africa's grow. Cheap coal, oil and gas powered that growth, which is why emissions follow industry. Fear of rivals drives nuclear arsenals and alliances.
now.after: These forces set the agenda for the coming decades. Africa is expected to hold about a quarter of humanity by 2050, while ageing societies struggle to pay for pensions and care. In 2024 the world was more than 1.5°C warmer than before industrialisation for a whole year for the first time, raising the costs of heat, drought and floods. Rivalry between the US and China, Russia's confrontation with the West and the end of US–Russian nuclear treaty limits make great-power competition the central story of world politics.

us-colonies.what: For thousands of years hundreds of Native nations farmed, hunted, traded and built towns across the land, from the mound city of Cahokia to the Pueblos of the Southwest. Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565 and Santa Fe around 1610. England planted Jamestown in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620, while France built Quebec and a chain of forts down the Mississippi to New Orleans. Britain's colonies grew fast on tobacco, rice, trade and farming, with enslaved Africans forced to work the Southern plantations. By 1750 they held over a million people. The French and Indian War, from 1754, ended in 1763 with France driven from the mainland.
us-colonies.why: Europeans came for land, trade, gold and religious freedom, and rival empires raced to claim the continent. Diseases such as smallpox, to which Native people had no immunity, killed huge numbers, often ahead of the settlers themselves, and made conquest easier. Britain outgrew its rivals because it sent families, not just soldiers and traders: its colonies had about fifteen times as many settlers as New France. Cheap land and demand for labour also drove the growth of slavery.
us-colonies.after: Native nations lost most of their eastern lands, though many, like the Haudenosaunee and Cherokee, remained powerful for decades. Slavery took root, and by 1750 roughly one colonist in five was enslaved, above all in Virginia and the Carolinas. The colonies built their own elected assemblies and habits of self-government. Britain's victory in 1763 removed the French threat, which made the colonists less dependent on Britain.

us-independence.what: After 1763 Britain taxed the colonies to pay its war debts, through the Stamp Act of 1765 and duties on tea. Colonists protested 'no taxation without representation', and Boston threw British tea into its harbour in 1773. Fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, and on 4 July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. George Washington's army survived near defeat, the victory at Saratoga in 1777 brought France in, and a French and American force trapped the British at Yorktown in 1781. In 1787 delegates in Philadelphia wrote a new Constitution, and Washington became the first president in 1789.
us-independence.why: The colonists had long run their own affairs through elected assemblies, so taxes voted by a Parliament where they had no seats felt like tyranny. Britain saw them as subjects who should share the cost of their defence, and each crackdown hardened opinion on both sides. Enlightenment ideas of natural rights gave the rebels a cause. With France gone, they no longer needed British protection, and French money, troops and ships proved decisive.
us-independence.after: The United States became the first modern republic of its size, and its Declaration's claim that 'all men are created equal' inspired revolutions elsewhere. The Constitution of 1787 and the Bill of Rights still govern the country. But it left slavery in place, counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for seats in Congress, and Native nations west of the Appalachians faced a new, expanding nation. Tens of thousands of Loyalists moved to Canada.

us-expansion.what: In 1803 President Thomas Jefferson bought Louisiana from Napoleon for $15 million, doubling the country overnight, and Lewis and Clark crossed it to the Pacific. Spain gave up Florida in 1819 after Andrew Jackson's troops invaded it. American settlers in Mexican Texas rebelled in 1836 and joined the US in 1845. In 1846 Britain and the US split the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel, and the same year war with Mexico began. US troops took Mexico City in 1847, and in 1848 Mexico ceded California and the Southwest. Gold found in California set off the rush of 1849.
us-expansion.why: Americans wanted land: the population doubled roughly every 25 years, and farmers pushed constantly west. Many believed in 'Manifest Destiny', the idea, named in 1845, that the country was meant to spread across the continent. Rivals were weak at the right moment: Napoleon needed cash for war with Britain, Spain was losing its empire, and Mexico was newly independent and divided. Southern leaders also wanted new land where slavery could spread.
us-expansion.after: The United States became a continental power with ports on two oceans, and Mexico lost about half its territory, a memory that still shapes relations between them. The Native nations of the West now lay inside US borders, and millions of Spanish-speaking people's homeland became part of the country. Above all, the new land reopened the fight over whether slavery could spread west, which led directly to the Civil War.

us-civilwar.what: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 split the Louisiana lands between slave and free, but the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers vote on slavery, and Kansas fell into violence. In 1857 the Supreme Court's Dred Scott ruling declared that Black people could not be citizens. When Abraham Lincoln won the presidency in 1860 on a promise to stop slavery spreading, South Carolina seceded. Six more states followed before war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861, and four more after, forming the Confederacy. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 made freedom a war aim, and about 180,000 Black men served in the Union army. Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865, and days later Lincoln was assassinated.
us-civilwar.why: Slavery was the central cause, and the seceding states said so in their own declarations. By 1860 about 4 million enslaved people were, by historians' estimates, worth more than all the country's railroads and factories combined, and cotton they grew was its largest export. As the country grew west, each new state threatened the balance between North and South in Congress. When a party pledged to stop slavery's spread won the White House without a single Southern state, Southern leaders chose to leave.
us-civilwar.after: The Union survived, and the idea that a state could leave it died. The 13th Amendment abolished slavery everywhere in 1865, freeing about 4 million people. An estimated 620,000–750,000 soldiers died, more than in any other American war, and much of the South lay in ruins. The federal government emerged far stronger, and the struggle over what freedom and equal citizenship would mean for Black Americans began.

us-west.what: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 let the government trade western land for Native homelands in the East. Over two decades about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people were forced to Indian Territory, and on the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838–39 about 4,000 died. After the Civil War, the Homestead Act and the transcontinental railroad of 1869 drew settlers onto the Plains. Lakota, Cheyenne and other nations fought back, defeating Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876, but the army and the slaughter of the bison forced them onto reservations. The killing of at least 250 Lakota at Wounded Knee in 1890 ended armed resistance.
us-west.why: Settlers, miners and railroads wanted Native land, and governments from Georgia to Washington backed them, often breaking treaties they had signed. Gold strikes, in Georgia in 1829 and the Black Hills in 1874, brought sudden waves of intruders. Many white Americans held that Native peoples must give way or be 'civilised'. Railroads, repeating rifles and a far larger population gave the United States overwhelming power, and the destruction of the bison herds took away the Plains nations' food.
us-west.after: Native Americans fell to fewer than 250,000 by 1900, and the 1887 Dawes Act broke up reservations so that Native landholdings shrank from about 138 million acres to 48 million by 1934. Boarding schools tried to erase Native languages and cultures. Yet the nations survived: today there are 575 federally recognised tribes with their own governments. Out of the conquered West came new states, completing the 48 contiguous states by 1912.

us-reconstruction.what: After the war Congress passed three amendments: the 13th ended slavery, the 14th made everyone born in the US a citizen with equal protection of the laws, and the 15th barred denying the vote on grounds of race. Under federal troops, Black men voted, and about 2,000 held office, from sheriffs to US senators. Freed people built churches and schools and searched for lost family. White terror groups such as the Ku Klux Klan fought back. After a disputed election, the last troops left in 1877, and Southern states imposed 'Jim Crow' segregation, upheld by the Supreme Court in 1896. From 1910 about 6 million Black Southerners moved north and west.
us-reconstruction.why: Reconstruction collapsed because most white Southerners refused to accept Black political equality and used violence, fraud and economic pressure to regain power. Northern voters grew tired of the cost of occupying the South, and economic depression after 1873 turned their attention elsewhere. Freed people had won rights but little land, so most became poor sharecroppers dependent on white landowners. Without federal protection, their votes could be taken away.
us-reconstruction.after: Jim Crow ruled the South for about 80 years: segregated schools and public places, poll taxes and literacy tests that barred most Black voters, and lynching, which killed over 4,000 Black people between 1877 and 1950. The Great Migration moved Black Americans to Northern and Western cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, reshaping their politics and culture. The 14th Amendment, long ignored, later became the legal basis of the civil rights movement.

us-industry.what: After the Civil War railroads tied the continent together, and steel, oil and electricity built vast new industries. Men such as Andrew Carnegie in steel and John D. Rockefeller in oil made giant fortunes, while factory workers often laboured twelve-hour days and fought bloody strikes. More than 20 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920, now mostly from southern and eastern Europe, and cities such as Chicago and New York grew enormously. In 1898 the US annexed Hawaii and, after a short war with Spain, took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where it then fought Filipino independence fighters until 1902.
us-industry.why: The United States had huge natural resources, a large market without internal tariffs, and railroads that linked it up. Immigrants supplied cheap labour, and high tariffs, cheap land and few rules on business helped companies grow. By the 1890s many leaders believed a great industrial nation needed overseas markets, naval bases and coaling stations, as European empires had. Sympathy for Cuba's revolt against Spain and the sinking of the battleship Maine in 1898 set off the war.
us-industry.after: By about 1900 the US was the world's largest industrial producer, a lead it held for over a century. The excesses of the age brought a Progressive reaction: antitrust laws, food safety rules, a federal income tax and, in 1920, votes for women. Immigrants reshaped American cities and culture, though laws barred Chinese workers from 1882 and sharply cut immigration in 1924. Puerto Rico and Guam remain US territories, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

us-depression.what: The US joined the First World War in 1917, and about 116,000 Americans died before the armistice. The 1920s brought cars, radio, film and a soaring stock market, along with Prohibition of alcohol and votes for women. In October 1929 the market crashed. Banks failed by the thousand, output fell by about a quarter, and by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job, while drought turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl. President Franklin Roosevelt, elected in 1932, launched the New Deal: bank reform, relief, public works such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, rights for unions and, in 1935, Social Security.
us-depression.why: The boom of the 1920s rested on borrowed money and stock speculation, and much of the wealth went to the few. When the market crashed, panicked savers pulled money from banks, and the Federal Reserve let the money supply shrink, turning a downturn into a collapse. High tariffs and the gold standard spread the slump worldwide. Economists still debate how much weight each cause deserves.
us-depression.after: The New Deal made the federal government responsible for the economy and for a basic safety net, a role it has kept. Social Security, insured bank deposits and the right to join a union still shape American life. Many Black Americans and urban workers moved to Roosevelt's Democratic Party, which won most elections for decades. Unemployment stayed high through the 1930s, and only the vast spending of the Second World War restored full employment.

us-superpower.what: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the US into the Second World War. Its factories outproduced every other country, about 16 million Americans served. Japan surrendered in August 1945 after two atomic bombs and a Soviet declaration of war. Meanwhile about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were held in camps. After the war the US rebuilt Western Europe through the Marshall Plan and in 1949 formed NATO against the Soviet Union. The Cold War brought an arms race, wars in Korea and Vietnam, and near-disaster over Soviet missiles in Cuba in 1962. In 1969 Americans landed on the Moon. The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
us-superpower.why: The war left the US the only great power with its homeland untouched and its economy booming, producing about half the world's manufactured goods. Leaders blamed the 1930s retreat into isolation for letting fascism grow, and resolved to stay engaged. The Soviet Union's grip on Eastern Europe and its spread of communism convinced Washington to 'contain' it everywhere. Nuclear weapons on both sides kept the rivalry a cold war, fought through arms races and proxy wars.
us-superpower.after: The US built the world order that still largely stands: the United Nations, NATO, the dollar at the centre of world finance, and alliances with Japan and South Korea. At home, the GI Bill, highways and suburbs created a huge middle class. Vietnam, where about 58,000 Americans died, divided the country and shook trust in government. With the Soviet collapse in 1991, the United States was left as the only superpower.

us-civilrights.what: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional. A year later Rosa Parks' arrest began the Montgomery bus boycott, which made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Southern officials resisted, and in 1957 army troops had to escort nine Black students into Little Rock's Central High. Students launched sit-ins in 1960, Freedom Riders rode buses across the South, and in 1963 about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington. Televised violence against marchers, from Birmingham to Selma, pushed Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. King was assassinated in 1968.
us-civilrights.why: Black Americans had fought segregation for decades, through the NAACP's long court strategy and through churches, colleges and local groups that organised the protests. Black veterans of the Second World War, who had fought fascism abroad, refused to accept second-class citizenship at home. The Great Migration gave Black voters weight in Northern elections. The Cold War made Southern racism an embarrassment abroad, and television brought the brutality of its defenders into living rooms.
us-civilrights.after: Legal segregation ended, and Black voter registration in the South soared: in Mississippi it rose from about 7% to about 60% within two years. Thousands of Black officials were elected, and in 2008 Barack Obama became the first Black president. The movement inspired campaigns for the rights of women, Latinos, Native Americans and others. Gaps in wealth, housing and schooling persisted, and debates over race, policing and voting rules continue.

us-today.what: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. The US invaded Afghanistan that year and Iraq in 2003, and stayed in both for years, leaving Afghanistan only in 2021. In 2008 a housing crash set off the worst financial crisis since the 1930s. Barack Obama was elected the first Black president that year, and Donald Trump won in 2016. The COVID-19 pandemic killed over a million Americans. After the 2020 election, which Joe Biden won, a crowd of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol on 6 January 2021 as Congress met to certify the result. Trump won the presidency again in 2024.
us-today.why: As the only superpower, the US took on a global role that drew it into long wars after 9/11. Risky mortgage lending and loosely regulated finance caused the 2008 crash. Political scientists link growing division to differences between cities and rural areas, education levels and regions, and to partisan media and the internet. Immigration, trade, the loss of factory jobs and cultural questions became sharply contested, and surveys showed growing numbers of voters viewing the other party very unfavourably.
us-today.after: The US remains the largest economy, with about a quarter of world output, and the strongest military, but faces a rising China. Shale drilling made it the world's top oil producer. Population, now about 340 million, keeps shifting to the South and West, moving House seats with it. The country has become more diverse, while its politics remain closely and sharply divided between the two main parties.

cn-origins.what: Farming villages grew millet on the Yellow River's loess soils and rice along the Yangtze thousands of years before the first kings. By about 1600 BC the Shang ruled the North China Plain, casting fine bronzes and, at their last capital, Anyang, carving questions to their ancestors on oracle bones: the earliest known Chinese writing. Around 1046 BC the Zhou, from the Wei valley in the west, overthrew them and handed out land to relatives and allies. In 771 BC raiders sacked the Zhou capital, and the court moved east to Luoyang with little real power. Its former vassals became rival states and fought for five centuries, until 221 BC.
cn-origins.why: The soft, fertile loess was easy to farm with simple tools, so dense populations and strong rulers appeared early on the North China Plain. The Zhou justified their conquest with the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven gave power to a virtuous ruler and took it away from a corrupt one. As Zhou kings weakened, nothing held back the great lords, who built their own states, armies and bureaucracies.
cn-origins.after: The Shang script is the direct ancestor of the characters used today, making Chinese one of the world's oldest continuously written languages. The Mandate of Heaven became the standard explanation for the rise and fall of every later dynasty. The chaos of the Warring States produced China's great schools of thought: Confucius taught duty, ritual and rule by moral example, Daoists sought harmony with nature, and Legalists argued for strict laws and harsh punishments, the creed Qin would use to unify China.

cn-qin.what: Qin was a frontier state in the Wei valley that had reorganised itself for war. Between 230 and 221 BC its armies destroyed the six rival states one by one, and King Zheng declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He abolished the old noble domains and split the land into commanderies run by officials he could appoint and dismiss. He standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even axle widths, built roads and canals, and joined existing walls along the northern frontier against the Xiongnu. By tradition, scholars who praised the past were persecuted. After he died in 210 BC, revolts broke out, and the dynasty fell in 206 BC.
cn-qin.why: From the 350s BC the minister Shang Yang reformed Qin along Legalist lines: farmers and soldiers were rewarded for results, not birth, and harsh laws made families answer for one another's crimes. That gave Qin a disciplined state able to field huge armies. Mountain passes protected its base, and the conquest of rich Sichuan added grain and manpower. The same severity, with forced labour on vast projects, turned people against the dynasty once the First Emperor was gone.
cn-qin.after: Qin lasted only 15 years, but it set the pattern for the next two thousand: one emperor ruling through a salaried bureaucracy rather than hereditary lords. Its common script let people who spoke very different languages read the same texts, which helped hold China together. The name 'China' itself probably comes from Qin. Later dynasties condemned Qin's cruelty yet kept its system, and unity became the norm against which every later period of division was judged.

cn-hantang.what: Liu Bang, a rebel of humble birth, won the wars that followed Qin's fall and founded the Han. Emperor Wu (141–87 BC) promoted Confucian learning, fought the Xiongnu nomads and pushed into Korea, northern Vietnam and the Hexi corridor, opening the Silk Road. Han craftsmen made the first paper, and a census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people. After the Han fell in 220, China stayed divided for nearly four centuries. The Sui reunited it in 589 and dug the Grand Canal. The Tang (618–907) ruled into Central Asia from Chang'an, until defeat at Talas in 751 and the An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 broke their power.
cn-hantang.why: The Han kept Qin's centralised machinery but softened it with Confucian ideals of benevolent rule, and trained officials in the classics, which gave the state legitimacy and continuity. Expansion west was driven by the Xiongnu threat and the search for allies and horses. Both empires broke down in similar ways: great families and generals gathered land and armies, peasants rebelled, and the court lost control of the provinces.
cn-hantang.after: The Han gave the Chinese majority its name and the Confucian bureaucracy its lasting form. From the Sui and Tang, civil service exams began choosing officials partly by merit, a system that lasted until 1905. Buddhism, arriving from India along the Silk Road, became one of China's great religions. Tang script, law and culture spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, creating an East Asian world that shared Chinese characters and Confucian ideas for over a thousand years.

cn-songming.what: The Song (960–1279) built a rich, urban society run by scholar-officials chosen by exam. They printed books, issued paper money, and used gunpowder weapons and the compass. In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng, and the Song kept only the south. The Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234 and the Song in 1279, and Kublai Khan ruled all China as the Yuan dynasty from today's Beijing. Famine, floods and revolts ended Mongol rule, and in 1368 the rebel Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming. Zheng He's fleets reached East Africa in 1405–33, but then the voyages stopped, and the Ming built most of the brick Great Wall seen today.
cn-songming.why: Fast-ripening rice and the draining of the Yangtze delta let the Song population pass 100 million, feeding trade and cities. But the Song kept generals on a short leash after the Tang disaster and could not hold off the cavalry states of the north. The Mongols combined steppe horsemen with Chinese and Muslim siege engineers. The Ming ended the costly voyages partly because the real danger, the Mongols, lay on the northern frontier.
cn-songming.after: The south, with its rice and ports, became China's economic centre for good, and Beijing became its usual capital. Song inventions such as gunpowder and the compass spread west and later helped transform Europe. Mongol rule linked China to the whole of Eurasia, and Marco Polo's account fed European dreams of Asian wealth. The Ming retreat from the oceans left the seas to European ships, a contrast many historians use to ask why Europe, not China, built global empires.

cn-qing.what: In 1644 rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. A Ming general opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who seized the capital and founded the Qing. It took decades to crush Ming loyalists in the south and on Taiwan, which fell in 1683. Under the long reigns of the Kangxi (1661–1722) and Qianlong (1735–96) emperors, the Qing absorbed Mongolia, sent troops to Lhasa in 1720 and then stationed residents there, and conquered Xinjiang in 1755–59, destroying the Dzungar state. By the late 1700s China had, by most estimates, the world's largest economy, and its population roughly doubled in the 1700s, to about 300 million.
cn-qing.why: The Ming had been ruined by factional politics, bankruptcy, famine and peasant revolts, and its collapse opened the way for a small, well-organised Manchu army allied with Mongols and Han defectors. The Qing ruled the old provinces through Chinese officials and the exams, while governing Inner Asia as khans and patrons of Tibetan Buddhism. Long wars against the Dzungar Mongols drew them deep into Central Asia. New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes helped feed the booming population.
cn-qing.after: Today's China inherits most of the Qing's borders, including Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan, though Outer Mongolia broke away in 1911. Beijing cites this inheritance in support of its claims; Tibetan and Uyghur exile groups argue the Qing tie was imperial overlordship, not union with China. Confidence ran high: when Britain's Macartney mission sought freer trade in 1793, Qianlong replied that China needed nothing from it. By 1800 rising population, land hunger and corruption were straining the empire.

cn-humiliation.what: When the Qing seized and destroyed British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain went to war. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave it Hong Kong Island and opened five ports, the first of many 'unequal treaties'. A second war ended in 1860 with British and French troops burning the Summer Palace, and Russia took land in the north. The Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) cost an estimated 20–30 million lives. Japan defeated China in 1894–95 and took Taiwan, and the powers carved out spheres of influence. An eight-nation army crushed the Boxer uprising of 1900, and in 1911 a revolution toppled the Qing.
cn-humiliation.why: Britain bought vast amounts of Chinese tea but had little China wanted, so its merchants smuggled in Indian opium, and the Qing ban became a war over trade and diplomatic equality. Industrial navies and guns far outclassed Qing forces. Inside China, population pressure, poverty and corruption fed huge rebellions. The Self-Strengthening reforms bought arsenals and ships but left the old system intact, and conservatives around the Empress Dowager Cixi crushed deeper reform in 1898.
cn-humiliation.after: The Qing fell in 1911–12, ending more than 2,000 years of imperial rule. The memory of invasion and lost territory became central to Chinese nationalism, and both Nationalists and Communists promised to end the 'century of humiliation'. Beijing still invokes it when it speaks of Taiwan, foreign criticism and national 'rejuvenation'. Britain's 99-year lease of Hong Kong's New Territories in 1898 later set 1997 as the date of its return.

cn-republic.what: The 1911 revolution made Sun Yat-sen provisional president, but power passed to the general Yuan Shikai, and after his death in 1916 China split among warlords. In 1919 the May Fourth protests against the Versailles treaty spread nationalist and radical ideas, and the Communist Party was founded in 1921. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, then allied with the Communists, reunified most of China in 1926–28 and turned on their allies. The Communists survived the Long March of 1934–35. Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded in 1937, occupying the east. After Japan's surrender in 1945 the civil war resumed, and the Communists won in 1949.
cn-republic.why: The republic inherited a bankrupt state, no national army and provinces run by military strongmen. Foreign powers kept their privileges, and at Versailles Germany's rights in Shandong went to Japan, outraging students. Chiang's government was worn down by corruption, inflation and eight years of war, while the Communists built a disciplined army and won peasant support with land reform where they ruled. Japan's invasion grew from its hunger for resources and its army's ambitions in China.
cn-republic.after: War with Japan killed, by historians' estimates, about 14 to 20 million Chinese and exhausted the Nationalists, while Communist forces grew from tens of thousands to around a million. The Republic of China, which had taken over Taiwan from Japan in 1945, survived only there, creating the cross-Strait division that persists today. The war also made China one of the Allied 'Big Four' and a permanent member of the UN Security Council in 1945.

cn-mao.what: On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic, and the Nationalist government moved to Taiwan. The People's Liberation Army defeated Tibet's army in 1950, and a 1951 agreement, signed under military pressure, placed Tibet under Chinese rule. Chinese troops fought US-led UN forces in Korea from 1950 to 1953. Land reform seized landlords' fields, and campaigns killed landlords and 'counter-revolutionaries': historians' estimates run from several hundred thousand to a few million. The Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 caused a famine that, by scholars' estimates, killed 15 to over 40 million. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution, turning Red Guards against teachers, officials and his rivals in the Party.
cn-mao.why: Mao and the Party set out to make China strong, equal and socialist fast, first copying the Soviet model and then trying to outrun it. The Great Leap's targets were impossible, but officials who doubted them were purged, so inflated harvest reports led the state to take grain from starving villages. The Cultural Revolution grew from Mao's fear that the Party was turning bureaucratic and 'revisionist', and his wish to crush rivals after the Leap's failure.
cn-mao.after: The Party built a unified state, raised literacy and life expectancy, and tested an atomic bomb in 1964. But the famine and the Cultural Revolution, whose violence killed, by estimates, hundreds of thousands to millions, left deep scars. China split from the Soviet Union around 1960 and turned to the US: Beijing took China's UN seat in 1971, and Nixon visited in 1972. In Tibet an uprising was crushed in 1959 and the Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile that continues today.

cn-reform.what: Mao died in 1976, and the radical 'Gang of Four' around his widow were arrested. By 1978 Deng Xiaoping led China. Farm families got their own plots and could sell crops beyond a quota, and output soared. From 1980 special economic zones such as Shenzhen drew foreign investment, and fourteen coastal cities opened in 1984. The one-child policy began in 1980. In spring 1989 students and workers filled Tiananmen Square calling for reform; on 3–4 June the army cleared central Beijing, killing protesters and bystanders. Deng's 1992 southern tour relaunched reform, and Hong Kong returned to China in 1997 and Macao in 1999.
cn-reform.why: Mao's campaigns had left China poor and exhausted, while neighbours such as Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong grew rich. Deng judged that the Party's survival depended on raising living standards and was willing to try markets and foreign capital, 'crossing the river by feeling for the stones'. Reform also brought inflation and corruption, which helped fuel the 1989 protests. Party leaders saw the protests as a threat to their rule and declared martial law.
cn-reform.after: China's economy grew by roughly 10% a year for three decades, and hundreds of millions of people left poverty. Political control stayed firm. The government put the June 1989 dead at about 240, including soldiers; other estimates range from several hundred to the low thousands, and the subject remains censored in China. Hong Kong and Macao kept their own systems for a promised 50 years under 'one country, two systems'. Taiwan, meanwhile, became a multiparty democracy.

cn-today.what: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became the world's factory, building vast cities, motorways and high-speed railways. It hosted the Olympics in 2008 and passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010. Xi Jinping became Party leader in 2012, launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, and had presidential term limits removed in 2018. China built artificial islands in the South China Sea. After mass protests in 2019, Beijing imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020. Covid-19 was first identified in Wuhan in late 2019, and China kept strict 'zero-Covid' controls until December 2022.
cn-today.why: Cheap labour, huge infrastructure spending, foreign investment and open world markets after 2001 drove growth. Xi argued that corruption, factions and Western ideas threatened the Party, and centralised power to restore its authority and pursue 'national rejuvenation'. Beijing treats Taiwan and the South China Sea as matters of sovereignty; Taiwan, neighbours and the United States see growing military pressure. Decades of the one-child policy, replaced by a two-child limit only in 2016, left a shrinking workforce.
cn-today.after: Rivalry with the United States over trade, technology and Taiwan now shapes world politics. Since about 2017 large numbers of Uyghurs and other Muslims in Xinjiang have been held in camps China calls vocational training centres; a 2022 UN report said abuses may amount to crimes against humanity, which China rejects. Critics say Hong Kong's new law ended many freedoms; Beijing says it restored stability. China's population began to fall in 2022, and by UN estimates India passed it in 2023.

ca-first.what: People reached what is now Canada at least 12,000 years ago, following game as the great ice sheets melted. Over thousands of years they built hundreds of distinct nations. On the Pacific coast, salmon fed large towns of cedar plank houses, totem poles and potlatch feasts. On the Plains, peoples such as the Blackfoot hunted bison on foot, driving herds over cliffs. Iroquoian farmers around the Great Lakes grew corn, beans and squash in palisaded villages, while Cree, Dene and Innu hunted and fished across the northern forests. In the Arctic, the Thule ancestors of the Inuit spread east from Alaska about 800 years ago. Around 1000, Norse from Greenland camped briefly in Newfoundland.
ca-first.why: The land itself shaped each way of life: where crops could grow, people farmed and settled; where they could not, people moved with the seasons, following caribou, bison, fish and seals. Nations traded copper, shells and food over long distances, made alliances and fought wars. Some built lasting political unions, such as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy south of Lake Ontario, whose founding date is still debated.
ca-first.after: When Europeans arrived from the 1500s, they met peoples whose knowledge made survival possible: canoe routes, snowshoes, toboggans and the fur trade itself. Diseases brought by newcomers killed many, and the population, estimated at roughly 500,000 or more, fell sharply. Yet these nations endured. Their treaties and land rights still shape Canada, about 1.8 million people identified as Indigenous in 2021, and names such as Canada, Ottawa and Saskatchewan come from their languages.

ca-newfrance.what: In 1534 Jacques Cartier planted a cross at Gaspé and claimed the land for France. Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608 and allied with the Wendat, Algonquin and Innu, joining their wars against the Haudenosaunee. European diseases devastated the Wendat, and in 1649 Haudenosaunee attacks scattered them. From 1663 Louis XIV ran New France as a royal colony and sent settlers, including about 800 young women, the filles du roi. In 1670 England chartered the Hudson's Bay Company to trade on the rivers draining into Hudson Bay. In 1701 about 1,300 delegates from nearly 40 nations made the Great Peace of Montreal. Then Britain and France fought for the continent.
ca-newfrance.why: Europe's craze for beaver-felt hats made furs valuable, and First Nations controlled the animals, the routes and the know-how, so trade depended on alliances with them. France sent few settlers, which kept New France small: by 1760 about 60,000–70,000 Canadiens faced more than a million people in the British colonies to the south. The rivalry of the two empires, fought in Europe and America alike, made every peace temporary.
ca-newfrance.after: France lost Acadia and Newfoundland in 1713, and in 1755 Britain began deporting about 10,000 Acadians, scattering them as far as Louisiana. The Seven Years' War then ended New France. But it left a French-speaking, Catholic society on the St Lawrence that survives as today's Quebec, Acadian communities in the Maritimes, the Métis peoples born of the fur trade, and a pattern of alliances and treaties with First Nations.

ca-british.what: On 13 September 1759 British troops under James Wolfe defeated Montcalm's army on the Plains of Abraham, and Quebec fell. Montreal surrendered in 1760, and in 1763 France gave up Canada. The 1774 Quebec Act let the Canadiens keep their Catholic faith and French civil law. When the American Revolution broke out, the Canadiens mostly stayed out, and an American attack on Quebec failed. After the war about 40,000 Loyalists fled north, among them Black Loyalists and Haudenosaunee allies led by Joseph Brant. In 1791 Britain split the colony into Upper and Lower Canada. In the War of 1812 British soldiers, Canadian militia and First Nations warriors under Tecumseh threw back American invasions.
ca-british.why: Britain won the Seven Years' War with more troops, more ships and colonies far larger than New France. To rule some 70,000 French Catholics, and to keep them loyal as the thirteen colonies grew restless, it chose tolerance over assimilation. Loyalist arrivals then created an English-speaking colony that wanted its own laws. The War of 1812 grew out of disputes over British naval seizures and over Indigenous resistance to American expansion.
ca-british.after: The 1763 Royal Proclamation said only the Crown could buy Indigenous land, by agreement, the basis of later treaties. Quebec's French civil law and language survived and still shape the province. The Loyalists founded English Canada and New Brunswick, and beating back the Americans in 1812–14 gave the colonies a sense of identity apart from the United States. First Nations allies, though, gained little: the peace left the border unchanged and their lands open to settlers.

ca-confed.what: In 1864 leaders of the Province of Canada and the Maritime colonies met at Charlottetown and Quebec City to plan a union. On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act joined Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as the Dominion of Canada, with John A. Macdonald as prime minister. In 1870 Canada took over the Hudson's Bay Company's vast lands, and British Columbia and Prince Edward Island joined in 1871 and 1873. Britain handed over the Arctic islands in 1880, Yukon split off during the Klondike gold rush in 1898, and Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905. Newfoundland narrowly voted to join in 1948, and Nunavut became a territory in 1999.
ca-confed.why: The Province of Canada, joining English- and French-speaking halves, was stuck in political deadlock, and federation offered a way out: Quebec could run its own schools, language and civil law while Ontario got seats by population. The US Civil War, Fenian raids and American talk of expansion frightened the colonies, and Britain wanted them to pay for their own defence. Union also promised railways, trade and the West.
ca-confed.after: Canada became a federation with strong provinces, a balance between Ottawa and Quebec that is still argued over. It grew to span three oceans, largely on lands where First Nations, Métis and Inuit lived and had not been consulted. It won full control of its foreign policy with the 1931 Statute of Westminster, but only in 1982 could it amend its own constitution.

ca-west.what: When Canada bought Rupert's Land in 1869, nobody asked the people living there. The Métis of Red River, led by Louis Riel, set up a provisional government, and their deal with Ottawa created Manitoba in 1870. From 1871 to 1877 the Crown signed seven numbered treaties with the First Nations of the Plains and the woodlands, promising reserves, payments and help with farming. The bison vanished, hunger spread, and settlers began arriving. In 1885 the Métis, with some Cree, rose again in the North-West Resistance. Troops rushed west on the unfinished Canadian Pacific Railway defeated them at Batoche. Riel was hanged for treason that November, days after the line's last spike was driven at Craigellachie.
ca-west.why: Ottawa wanted the West farmed by settlers and tied to Canada before Americans moved in, and it had promised British Columbia a railway. The Métis feared for their land and rights, and their petitions were ignored. As the bison collapsed, starving Plains nations signed treaties for survival, and, as historians such as James Daschuk have shown, officials withheld food rations to push them onto reserves. Many First Nations understood the treaties as agreements to share the land, not to sell it.
ca-west.after: The railway opened the Prairies to a flood of settlers from about 1896 and bound the country from sea to sea. For First Nations it brought reserves, the 1876 Indian Act, a pass system and residential schools. Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged at Battleford in 1885, Canada's largest mass execution. Riel's hanging set French Quebec against English Ontario for generations; today many honour him as a founder of Manitoba.

ca-wars.what: In 1914 Canada, as part of the British Empire, went to war automatically. About 620,000 Canadians enlisted from a population under 8 million. They held the line against poison gas at Ypres in 1915, took Vimy Ridge in April 1917 and Passchendaele that autumn, and spearheaded the Allied advance in the last Hundred Days of 1918. About 61,000 died. In 1939 Canada declared war on its own, a week after Britain. Over a million served. Canadians were captured and killed in large numbers at Hong Kong and Dieppe, escorted convoys across the Atlantic, trained Allied airmen and fought up Italy. On D-Day they landed on Juno Beach, then freed much of the Netherlands. More than 45,000 died.
ca-wars.why: Canada fought in 1914 because Britain did, and many Canadians, most of them of British descent, felt loyal to the Empire. In 1939 it chose to fight Nazi Germany alongside Britain. Conscription split the country both times: most English Canadians wanted everyone to share the burden, while most French Canadians, with fewer ties to Britain, saw these as Britain's wars. In 1917 and again in 1944 Ottawa imposed conscription for overseas service, over Quebec's opposition.
ca-wars.after: Canada's wartime role won it a separate signature on the Treaty of Versailles, and the 1931 Statute of Westminster made it fully self-governing. After 1945 it was a founding member of NATO and the UN, with a booming economy and its own citizenship from 1947. Both wars also left scars: internment of 'enemy aliens', the uprooting of more than 20,000 Japanese Canadians in 1942, and lasting distrust between English and French Canada.

ca-quebec.what: In 1960 Jean Lesage's Liberals won power in Quebec and launched the Quiet Revolution: the province took schools, hospitals and welfare from the Catholic Church and nationalised electricity under the slogan 'Maîtres chez nous'. In October 1970 a small armed group, the FLQ, kidnapped a British diplomat and killed a Quebec minister, and Ottawa invoked the War Measures Act. In 1976 René Lévesque's Parti Québécois took office and in 1977 passed Bill 101, making French the language of work and public life. In 1980 about 60% of Quebecers voted against sovereignty. Pierre Trudeau then brought the constitution home in 1982, with a Charter of Rights, but Quebec's government refused to sign. In 1995 sovereignty lost by 50.6% to 49.4%.
ca-quebec.why: For generations French-speaking Quebecers had been a majority at home but often poorer than the English-speaking minority who ran much of business, and the Church shaped schools and social life. Rising education and a new middle class wanted a modern state that worked in French. Many came to see Quebec as a nation that needed more powers, or a country of its own; others, Quebecers among them, saw a bilingual Canada as the answer.
ca-quebec.after: Quebec today is a confident, mostly French-speaking society, and federal institutions became officially bilingual from 1969. The constitutional question was never settled: Quebec has not formally endorsed the 1982 constitution, and the Meech Lake and Charlottetown accords failed. In 1998 the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec could not leave on its own, but that a clear majority on a clear question would oblige negotiations. Support for sovereignty has risen and fallen since.

ca-rights.what: In 1969 the federal government proposed abolishing Indian status and the Indian Act. First Nations leaders rejected it as assimilation and it was withdrawn, and their organisations grew stronger. In 1973 the Supreme Court's Calder decision accepted that Aboriginal title to land had existed before colonisation, and in 1975 the James Bay agreement with the Cree and Inuit became the first modern treaty. The 1982 Constitution recognised and affirmed Aboriginal and treaty rights. Courts gave those words force, and a 1990 armed standoff at Oka, Quebec, drew national attention. Former residential school students won a settlement in 2006, an apology in 2008, and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported in 2015.
ca-rights.why: For over a century Ottawa had aimed to assimilate Indigenous peoples. The Indian Act controlled their lives, and from the 1880s residential schools run with the churches took more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children from their families to strip away their languages and cultures. Thousands died. Survivors' testimony, Indigenous political organising and courts that took treaty promises seriously forced governments to change course.
ca-rights.after: Modern land claims now cover much of the North, including the 1993 agreement that created Nunavut, and self-government agreements are spreading. The TRC called the policy behind the schools cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action. In 2021 a First Nation reported potential unmarked graves at the former Kamloops school, and Canada adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into law; Pope Francis apologised in 2022. Land rights, especially in British Columbia, and gaps in living conditions remain unresolved.

ca-today.what: Canada entered the 21st century as a wealthy, peaceful country whose population grew faster than any other in the G7. Canadian troops fought in Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014, and 158 of them died. In 2005 Canada became one of the first countries to legalise same-sex marriage nationwide. Immigration rose steeply, and by 2021 almost one in four Canadians had been born abroad, more and more of them in Asia. In 2023 the population grew by more than a million, but housing costs soared, and from 2024 Ottawa cut immigration and temporary residents. In 2025 US tariffs and President Trump's talk of annexation set off a wave of Canadian patriotism.
ca-today.why: Canada has a vast land, an ageing population and low birth rates, so leaders of every party have looked to immigrants to fill jobs and pay for pensions, and Canadian policy chooses many by skill. Most Canadians live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, and over two-thirds of exports go to the United States, so American decisions shape Canada's economy and politics.
ca-today.after: Canada is one of the world's most diverse countries: Toronto and Vancouver are among the most multicultural cities anywhere. Growth slowed to about 0.5% in the year to July 2026, when the population reached about 41.8 million. Canada faces pressing questions: how to house newcomers, how to depend less on the US, how to profit from oil while fighting climate change, as record 2023 wildfires burned about 15 million hectares, and how to make reconciliation with Indigenous peoples real.

dd-hinduism.what: Hinduism has no single founder. It grew from the Vedic religion of north-west India, whose oldest text, the Rigveda, was composed around 1500–1200 BC. Over the next thousand years the Upanishads explored the self and ultimate reality, and the great epics, the Mahabharata and Ramayana, took shape. From about AD 300 temple worship of gods such as Vishnu, Shiva and the goddess Devi flourished, and devotional bhakti movements spread from south India. Hindu kings carried the faith to Southeast Asia. Under Muslim and then British rule most Indians stayed Hindu, and in the 1800s reformers reshaped the tradition. Today it is the world's third-largest religion.
dd-hinduism.why: Hinduism grew by absorbing rather than replacing: Vedic ritual, local gods, philosophy and devotion were woven together over centuries. Brahmin priests preserved the sacred texts, while temples, pilgrimages and festivals bound together a vast land with many languages. Because it had no single church or creed, it could adapt to new rulers and ideas, which helped it outlast empires and survive centuries of rule by Muslim dynasties and Britain.
dd-hinduism.after: Hindu ideas such as karma, rebirth, yoga and meditation, which shaped Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, have spread worldwide. In 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 1.2 billion people were Hindu, about 95% of them in India. Caste, though outlawed as a basis for discrimination by India's constitution, still shapes many lives, and the rise of Hindu nationalism has made the faith central to Indian politics.

sections.t: The word 'Hindu' comes from the Persian name for the Indus river, and many Hindus call their faith Sanatana Dharma, the eternal order. It holds many gods: Vishnu the preserver, who descends to earth in forms such as Rama and Krishna; Shiva, destroyer and renewer; and the goddess in forms like Durga and Lakshmi, beside the elephant-headed Ganesha.
