Indonesia became the world's third-largest democracy, East Timor became independent, and a peace deal ended war in Aceh after the 2004 tsunami killed about 170,000 people there.

items: Alongside Christian, Hindu and Buddhist minorities.
Earthquakes and eruptions are part of life.
Nickel, palm oil, a new capital

units.title: From the Indus to the Guptas

cards.p: India is a subcontinent, walled off by the Himalayas to the north. The great river plains of the Indus and the Ganges fed huge populations, and the monsoon rains, arriving each summer, decide whether harvests succeed. Today about 1.4 billion people live here, speaking hundreds of languages.

The Indus civilisation built planned cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro around 2600–1900 BC. Later, Indo-Aryan peoples composed the Vedas, sacred hymns, from about 1500 BC, the roots of Hinduism and of the caste (varna) system that ranked society into priests, warriors, merchants and labourers.

items: End suffering by ending craving: the Eightfold Path.
Absolute non-violence to every living being.
One God, equality, service; centred on Punjab.
cards.p: About 80% of Indians are Hindu and 14% Muslim; India also has large Christian, Sikh, Buddhist and Jain communities.

The Maurya Empire (from 322 BC) united most of India; Ashoka, after a bloody war, embraced Buddhism and non-violence. Under the Guptas (about 320–550) India had a golden age: mathematicians developed the decimal system and zero.

cards.q: Which number concept came from ancient India?
a: Zero as a number, with decimal place value
Roman numerals
Negative numbers on an abacus
The metric system
cards.why: It spread to the world through Arab scholars.

cards.p:
From the 1000s Muslim armies raided from Afghanistan; the Delhi Sultanate ruled the north from 1206. In 1526 Babur, from Central Asia, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire.

Akbar (1556–1605) won over Hindus with tolerance and debate. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for his wife. Aurangzeb (1658–1707) expanded the empire to its widest but ruled as a strict Muslim, and it broke up after him.

cards.q: Who built the Taj Mahal?
a: Shah Jahan
Akbar
Ashoka
Aurangzeb
cards.why: As a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

cards.p: The English East India Company came to trade cotton, spices and tea. As the Mughals weakened it used its private army: it won Bengal at Plassey in 1757 and over a century took most of India. After a great rebellion in 1857, the British government took over: the Raj.

Britain built railways, universities and a civil service, and made English the elite language. But it drained wealth, destroyed India's cotton industry to favour Lancashire's, and famines killed millions. Indians were second-class in their own country.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, demanded self-rule. Mohandas Gandhi led mass non-violent resistance: boycotts, strikes and the 1930 Salt March. After World War II a weakened Britain agreed to go.

But the Muslim League feared Hindu rule and demanded Pakistan. In August 1947 British India was partitioned; about a million died in the violence and some 15 million fled across the new borders. Gandhi was murdered by a Hindu extremist in 1948.

cards.q: What happened at Partition in 1947?
a: British India split into India and Pakistan amid mass violence
India became a British colony
The Mughals took power
India joined the Soviet Union

cards.p:
Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, built a secular democratic republic with a constitution (1950) that outlawed caste discrimination. India stayed non-aligned in the Cold War. It fought wars with Pakistan, largely over Kashmir, and with China in 1962.

Indira Gandhi suspended democracy in an emergency in 1975–77 and was assassinated in 1984.

After reforms in 1991 opened the economy, India grew fast, with an IT industry centred on Bengaluru. Hindu nationalism rose: Narendra Modi's BJP has governed since 2014. In 2023 India passed China as the most populous country and landed a probe near the Moon's south pole. It is expected to become the third-largest economy.

items: Hundreds of languages and many faiths
Tension over Hindu nationalism and minorities.

cards.s: India is the world’s most populous country.

cards.p: Ireland is an island of green, rain-fed farmland on the western edge of Europe. Newgrange, a great passage tomb older than the pyramids, aligns with the winter sunrise. Celtic languages arrived in the Iron Age; Irish (Gaelic) is still an official language.

Saint Patrick, a Briton, brought Christianity in the 400s. While much of Europe was in turmoil, Irish monasteries preserved learning and produced masterpieces such as the Book of Kells, and Irish monks re-founded monasteries across Europe. Vikings raided from 795 and founded Dublin.

cards.q: Who brought Christianity to Ireland?
a: Saint Patrick
Saint George
Henry VIII
Oliver Cromwell

cards.p: Anglo-Normans invaded in 1169, and English kings claimed Ireland. After the Reformation, Protestant England tightened its grip on Catholic Ireland. In the 1600s land was confiscated and given to English and Scottish Protestant settlers, especially in Ulster: the Plantation. Cromwell's campaign (1649–50) was brutal, and Penal Laws barred Catholics from owning land or voting.

In 1801 Ireland was united with Britain. From 1845 potato blight destroyed the crop most poor families lived on. Food was still exported while about a million people died and another million emigrated. Emigration continued for a century, and today about 70 million people worldwide claim Irish descent, as many as 30 million in the US.
From about 8.5 million to about 4.5 million, through famine and emigration. It still has not fully recovered.

cards.q: What caused the Great Famine?
a: Potato blight, made worse by British policy
A war with Spain
A volcanic eruption
A drought

cards.p: At Easter 1916 Irish republicans seized Dublin; the rising was crushed and its leaders executed, which turned opinion toward independence. A war of independence (1919–21) led to a treaty: 26 counties became the Irish Free State in 1922, while six Protestant-majority counties in the north stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland. A civil war over the treaty followed. Ireland became a republic in 1949.

hl: Northern Ireland stays in the UK

cards.p: In Northern Ireland, Catholic nationalists faced discrimination; from 1968 conflict between republicans, unionists and British forces, 'the Troubles', killed about 3,500 people. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought peace and shared government.

Ireland joined the European Community in 1973 and, with low taxes, attracted tech and pharma giants (Apple, Google, Meta), becoming one of the richest countries in Europe: the 'Celtic Tiger'. Once deeply Catholic, it voted to legalise same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion in 2018.

Iran is a high plateau ringed by mountains, between the Middle East, Central Asia and South Asia. Its people mostly speak Persian (Farsi), an Indo-European language, not Arabic, and its sense of being an ancient, distinct civilisation is very strong.

Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 550s BC, the largest the world had yet seen, from Egypt to India. It was known for tolerating conquered peoples' religions; Cyrus let the exiled Jews return home. Darius I built the ceremonial capital Persepolis. Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

Ancient Persia's religion, Zoroastrianism, taught a cosmic struggle between good and evil, with judgement after death, ideas that may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The Parthians and then the Sasanians (224–651) ruled great empires that rivalled Rome and Byzantium. Nowruz, the Persian new year, comes from this era.

cards.q: What language do most Iranians speak?
a: Persian (Farsi)
Arabic
Turkish
Urdu

units.title: Islamic Iran and the Shia faith

cards.p: Arab armies conquered Persia in 651, and Iranians gradually became Muslim, but kept their language and culture; Persian poetry by Ferdowsi, Rumi, Hafez and Omar Khayyam is still loved and recited.

In 1501 the Safavid dynasty made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, setting Iran apart from its Sunni Ottoman neighbours. Today about 90% of Iranians are Shia, and the mourning for Imam Hussein, killed at Karbala in 680, is central to its religious life. Shah Abbas made Isfahan one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
In the 1800s weak Qajar shahs lost the Caucasus to Russia, and Britain and Russia competed for influence. Oil was found in 1908, and a British company, later BP, controlled it.

cards.q: Which branch of Islam do most Iranians follow?
a: Shia
Sunni
Sufi only
Ibadi
cards.why: Made the state religion by the Safavids in 1501.

units.title: Shahs, revolution and the Islamic Republic

cards.p: Reza Shah Pahlavi modernised Iran from 1925. In 1951 Prime Minister Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry; in 1953 a coup organised by the CIA and Britain overthrew him and strengthened Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who ruled with US backing and a feared secret police. Many Iranians never forgot it.

In 1979 mass protests drove out the shah. Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile and created an Islamic Republic, ruled by Shia clerics under a Supreme Leader. Students seized the US embassy and held 52 hostages for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980; the war lasted eight years and killed hundreds of thousands.

Iran backs allies across the region, such as Hezbollah and the Houthis, and its nuclear programme has brought sanctions. Protests, such as 'Woman, Life, Freedom' in 2022, have been crushed. In February 2026 US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, and war since has disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

pins: A fifth of the world’s oil passes here

items: Nowruz, poetry, a sense of greatness.
Often at odds with its rulers.

cards.p: Iraq is ancient Mesopotamia, 'the land between the rivers', the Tigris and the Euphrates. Here, in Sumer, the first cities, writing and law codes appeared over 5,000 years ago. Today it is a mainly Arab, Shia-majority country with a Kurdish north and huge oil reserves.

Sumer invented writing around 3200 BC. Babylon's King Hammurabi wrote one of the first law codes (c. 1750 BC). The Assyrians built a feared empire from Nineveh, and Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, with its legendary Hanging Gardens, destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.

Arabs brought Islam in the 630s; the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala grew around the shrines of Ali and Husayn. The Abbasid caliphs founded Baghdad in 762, and it became the world's centre of learning, until the Mongols sacked it in 1258.

cards.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?
a: The land between the rivers
The land of kings
The fertile crescent
The desert kingdom

cards.p: After World War I Britain created Iraq from three Ottoman provinces with different peoples, Shia Arabs, Sunni Arabs and Kurds, and installed a king. A 1958 revolution ended the monarchy. In 1979 Saddam Hussein of the Baath party took power.

Saddam attacked Iran in 1980 (an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands), gassed Kurds at Halabja in 1988, and invaded Kuwait in 1990, provoking the Gulf War. In 2003 a US-led invasion toppled him; insurgency and Sunni–Shia civil war followed, and in 2014 the Islamic State seized Mosul before being defeated in 2017.

items: Much damaged by war and looting.

cards.p: Iceland is a volcanic island in the North Atlantic, with glaciers, geysers and hot springs; almost all its electricity and heating come from geothermal and hydro power.

Norse settlers arrived from 874. In 930 they founded the Althing, one of the oldest parliaments in the world, at Þingvellir. Medieval Icelanders wrote the great sagas. Norway and then Denmark ruled from 1262.

cards.q: What did Icelanders found in 930?
a: The Althing, one of the oldest parliaments
A Viking empire
Reykjavík university
A navy

cards.p: Iceland gained home rule in 1918 and became a fully independent republic in 1944. It won 'Cod Wars' against Britain over fishing waters.
Its banks collapsed in 2008, but tourism helped it recover. It has no army, high equality, and elected the world's first woman president, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, in 1980.

cards.s: Iceland elected the world’s first woman president.

units.title: Ancient Israel and the Jewish people

cards.p: Israel is a small country, about the size of New Jersey, on the eastern Mediterranean, between the sea and the Jordan River. Jerusalem is holy to three religions: Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Few places have been fought over so long.

Around 1000 BC, by biblical tradition, King David made Jerusalem his capital, and his son Solomon built the First Temple. The Israelites developed monotheism, the belief in one God, and the Hebrew Bible. Babylon destroyed the Temple in 586 BC and exiled many; they returned and built a Second Temple.

Rome conquered the land. After revolts, the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70 (its Western Wall survives) and in 135 expelled Jews from Jerusalem, renaming the province Palaestina. For almost 2,000 years most Jews lived in the diaspora, scattered across the world, often persecuted, praying 'next year in Jerusalem'.

cards.q: What is the Western Wall?
a: A surviving part of the Second Temple
A Crusader castle
The border with Lebanon
A Roman aqueduct

cards.p: Arab Muslims took the land in 636; the Dome of the Rock was built in Jerusalem in 691, on the site of the Temple. Crusaders held it for a time. From 1517 it was part of the Ottoman Empire, with a mostly Arab Muslim population and Christian and Jewish minorities.

In the late 1800s, amid pogroms in Russia and antisemitism in Europe, Theodor Herzl founded Zionism: a movement for a Jewish homeland in the ancient land. Jewish settlers began arriving. In 1917 Britain's Balfour Declaration supported 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, which Britain ruled from 1920; it had also made promises to the Arabs.

After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew. In 1947 the UN proposed partition; Jewish leaders accepted, Arab leaders rejected it. On 14 May 1948 Israel declared independence, and its Arab neighbours attacked. Israel won. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled: the Nakba, 'catastrophe'. Over the next years about 800,000 Jews left or were driven from Arab countries, many to Israel.

cards.q: What did the Balfour Declaration of 1917 do?
a: Supported a Jewish national home in Palestine
Created the state of Israel
Ended the Ottoman Empire
Divided Jerusalem

cards.p: In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel took the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, the Golan Heights and Sinai. Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973. Egypt made peace in 1979 and got Sinai back; Jordan made peace in 1994. Israeli settlements have grown in the occupied West Bank.

Palestinian uprisings (intifadas) began in 1987 and 2000. The 1993 Oslo Accords created limited Palestinian self-rule but no state. Hamas took over Gaza in 2007. On 7 October 2023 Hamas attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking hostages; Israel's war in Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and devastated the territory.

items: Any Jew can become a citizen.
The unresolved question at the centre.

cards.p: Italy is a long peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean, with the Alps sealing it off in the north and the Apennine mountains running down its spine. That position made it the natural centre of the Mediterranean world, and the heart of an empire.

Rome began as a small town on the Tiber, traditionally founded in 753 BC. It became a republic around 509 BC, conquered Italy, destroyed Carthage, and ruled the whole Mediterranean. After Julius Caesar's murder in 44 BC, Augustus became the first emperor.

At its height under Trajan in AD 117 the empire ran from Britain to Iraq.

Rome left Latin, the root of Italian, French and Spanish; Roman law; roads, aqueducts and the Colosseum; and Christianity, which became the empire's religion in 380. The Pope, bishop of Rome, made the city the centre of Catholic Christianity, as it still is: Vatican City is a tiny independent state inside Rome.

cards.q: What happened to the Western Roman Empire in 476?
a: The last western emperor was deposed
It conquered Persia
It became Christian
It moved its capital to Paris
cards.why: The East, the Byzantine Empire, survived until 1453.

cards.p: After Rome fell, Italy stayed divided for 1,400 years: among Lombards, Byzantines, the Papal States, Normans in the south, and later Spain, France and Austria. Rich trading city-states grew: Venice and Genoa ruled the sea trade with the East; Florence and Milan grew rich on banking and cloth.

From about 1400, Italy led the Renaissance, the 'rebirth' of ancient learning and art. Florence, under the Medici bankers, was its heart: Brunelleschi's dome, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael. Machiavelli wrote The Prince. Galileo later turned a telescope on the heavens.

Italy's cities are still full of this art, the reason millions visit.

Once the Atlantic route to Asia opened, Mediterranean trade declined, and Italy's states became prizes fought over by Spain, France and Austria. Napoleon conquered the peninsula around 1800; afterwards Austria dominated the north.

cards.q: Which city was the heart of the Italian Renaissance?
a: Florence
Rome
Naples
Turin
cards.why: Paid for by the Medici bankers.

cards.p:
In the 1800s the Risorgimento, 'resurgence', sought to unite Italy. The statesman Cavour of Piedmont used diplomacy and war with Austria; the soldier Garibaldi led 1,000 volunteer 'Red Shirts' to conquer Sicily and Naples in 1860. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, and Rome became its capital in 1871.

'We have made Italy; now we must make Italians,' said one politician: most people still spoke local dialects.

Unification left a deep gap between the industrial north and the poor, rural south, the Mezzogiorno. Millions emigrated, mostly from the south, to the Americas: today tens of millions of Americans, Argentines and Brazilians have Italian roots. The Mafia grew in Sicily where the state was weak.

After World War I, Benito Mussolini's Fascists seized power in 1922: the world's first fascist regime. He crushed opposition, invaded Ethiopia, and allied with Hitler. Defeats in World War II brought his overthrow in 1943; partisans shot him in 1945.

In 1946 Italians voted to abolish the monarchy and became a republic.

Postwar Italy was a founding member of the European Community and had an 'economic miracle', becoming famous for design, fashion and cars such as Fiat and Ferrari. Politics were unstable, with dozens of governments, and the 1970s brought terrorism.

In the 1990s corruption scandals swept away the old parties; the billionaire Silvio Berlusconi then dominated politics for two decades.
Italy has the oldest population in Europe after Japan's, slow growth and high debt. Since 2022 Giorgia Meloni, from a party with roots in post-fascism, has led a right-wing government.

items: Loyalty to your town and region, its food and dialect.
Catholic tradition is woven into life, even for the non-religious.
Family ties and businesses run society.

cards.q: What divides Italy's economy?
a: A rich industrial north and a poorer south
An east-west mountain range
Two official languages
Catholics and Protestants
cards.why: The gap dates back to unification.

cards.p: Jamaica is a mountainous Caribbean island south of Cuba, its motto 'Out of many, one people'. Most Jamaicans are of African descent.

The Taíno called it Xaymaca, 'land of wood and water'. Spain took it in 1494, Britain in 1655. It became Britain's richest sugar colony, worked by enslaved Africans who outnumbered whites ten to one. Escaped slaves, the Maroons, fought Britain to a treaty in 1739. Slavery ended in 1838.

cards.q: Who were the Maroons?
a: Escaped enslaved people who won freedom in the mountains
Spanish soldiers
British planters
Taíno chiefs

cards.p: After the 1865 Morant Bay rebellion was brutally suppressed, Britain ruled directly. Labour protests in the 1930s led to self-government, and Jamaica became independent in 1962.

Jamaica gave the world reggae, Bob Marley, ska and dancehall, Rastafari, and the fastest sprinters, such as Usain Bolt. Marcus Garvey inspired Black pride worldwide. Gang violence and debt are challenges.

cards.s: Bob Marley was Jamaican.

cards.p: Jordan is a mostly desert country east of the Jordan River, with the Dead Sea, the lowest point on land, and the red sandstone city of Petra. It has few resources, not even much water, but a key location.

The Nabataeans carved Petra into rock cliffs and grew rich on the incense trade; Rome annexed it in 106. Jesus was baptised in the Jordan River, by tradition at Bethany. Muslim Arabs ruled from the 630s; then the Ottomans.

cards.q: Who carved the city of Petra?
a: The Nabataeans
The Romans
The Ottomans
The Egyptians

cards.p: After World War I Britain created Transjordan for Abdullah, of the Hashemite family that claims descent from the Prophet. Independent in 1946, it took the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 1948 and lost them to Israel in 1967.

Jordan has absorbed waves of refugees, Palestinians (over half of Jordanians have Palestinian roots), Iraqis and Syrians, and stayed stable under King Hussein and, since 1999, King Abdullah II. It made peace with Israel in 1994.

cards.s: Jordan made peace with Israel in 1994.
cards.why: The second Arab state to do so.

units.title: Islands, gods and the first emperors

cards.p:
Japan is a chain of mountainous islands off the coast of Asia: four main ones (Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku) and thousands of smaller ones. Mountains cover about three-quarters of the land, so people crowded onto narrow coastal plains, as they still do: Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya sit on the few big flat areas.

The sea protected Japan. It was invaded seriously only twice before 1945, and both attempts failed. That isolation let it borrow from China and Korea on its own terms.

For over 10,000 years the Jōmon people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, and made some of the world's oldest pottery.

From about 300 BC, newcomers from Korea and China, the Yayoi, brought wet-rice farming, bronze and iron. Rice became the base of Japanese life, wealth and even taxes for 2,000 years.

cards.h: Shinto: the way of the gods
cards.p:
Japan's native religion is Shinto. It has no founder or holy book. Its followers honour kami: spirits found in mountains, rivers, trees, ancestors and great people. Shrines, marked by red torii gates, are places to meet the kami; purity, gratitude and harmony with nature matter more than doctrine.

According to myth, the emperors descend from the sun goddess Amaterasu. Japan's imperial family claims an unbroken line from the 6th century or earlier, the oldest monarchy in the world.

From the 500s Japan's Yamato rulers looked to China, then the most advanced state in the world. Buddhism arrived from Korea around 538 and was championed by Prince Shōtoku. Japan adopted Chinese characters for writing, Confucian ideas about government and Chinese-style law.

In 710 a planned capital was built at Nara, copying the Chinese capital Chang'an.

r: From India via China and Korea
cards.p: Most Japanese mix the two without seeing a conflict: 'born Shinto, die Buddhist', as the saying goes.

cards.q: What are kami in Shinto?
a: Spirits in nature, ancestors and great people
Buddhist monks
Samurai warriors
Chinese emperors

cards.s: Japan's imperial family is the oldest continuing monarchy in the world.
cards.why: It claims an unbroken line going back at least to the 6th century.

cards.p:
In 794 the court moved to Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, which stayed the imperial capital for over a thousand years.

In the Heian period Japan stopped copying China so closely and developed its own culture. A Japanese phonetic script, kana, made writing in Japanese easier.

Around 1000, Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at court, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel. Court life prized poetry, beauty and refined manners.

Real power slipped from the emperors to the Fujiwara family, who ruled as regents by marrying their daughters to emperors. In the provinces, landowners hired armed men to protect their estates: the first samurai.

cards.q: What is The Tale of Genji?
a: A novel of court life written around 1000
A Shinto holy book
A samurai law code
A history of Japan written by Chinese monks
cards.why: Murasaki Shikibu wrote it at the Heian court.

cards.p:
In the 1180s two warrior clans, the Taira and Minamoto, fought for control. The Minamoto won, and in 1192 their leader Minamoto no Yoritomo was named shogun, 'great general', ruling from Kamakura.

For almost 700 years Japan had two rulers: an emperor in Kyoto with great prestige but little power, and a shogun with the army and the real power.

items: Mounted archers, later swordsmen, serving a lord.
Loyalty, courage, self-discipline and honour; idealised later.
Meditation and simplicity appealed to warriors.

cards.p:
In 1274 and 1281 Kublai Khan, who had conquered China, sent huge fleets to invade Japan. Samurai fought them on the beaches of Kyushu, and both times typhoons wrecked the Mongol fleets.

The Japanese called the storms kamikaze, 'divine winds', proof that the gods protected Japan, a word reused in World War II.

From 1467 the shoguns lost control and Japan broke into a century of civil war, the Sengoku period, as local lords called daimyō fought each other. Portuguese traders arrived in 1543 bringing guns, and Jesuit missionaries such as Francis Xavier converted many Japanese to Christianity.

steps: Used massed musketeers to conquer central Japan; killed by a rebel general in 1582.
A peasant-born general who finished uniting Japan and invaded Korea (1592–98), and failed.
Won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and became shogun in 1603.
cards.p: A Japanese saying: Nobunaga mixed the rice cake, Hideyoshi baked it, and Ieyasu ate it.

cards.q: Who held real power in Japan for most of 1192–1867?
a: The shogun
The emperor
The Buddhist monks
The Portuguese
cards.why: The emperor reigned in Kyoto; the shogun ruled.

cards.p:
The Tokugawa shoguns ruled from Edo, today's Tokyo, and kept the peace for over 250 years. Daimyō had to spend every other year in Edo and leave their families there as hostages, which kept them loyal and poor.

Society was ranked: samurai at the top, then farmers, artisans and merchants. Edo grew into perhaps the largest city in the world, with about a million people by 1700.

Fearing that Christian missionaries were preparing the way for European conquest, the shoguns banned Christianity, executed thousands of believers, and in the 1630s closed Japan. Japanese could not leave on pain of death, and only Dutch and Chinese traders could visit, at Nagasaki.

This policy, sakoku, lasted over 200 years.

Peace brought prosperity. In the cities a lively popular culture grew: kabuki theatre, puppet theatre, haiku poetry by Bashō and colourful woodblock prints, such as Hokusai's Great Wave. Many Japanese traditions seen as ancient today, from sushi to the tea ceremony as practised now, took their modern shape in this era.

cards.s: During its closed period, Japan traded with no foreigners at all.
cards.why: Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed at Nagasaki.

units.title: Opening up and racing to modernise

cards.p:
In 1853 US Commodore Perry arrived in Edo Bay with steam-powered warships and demanded that Japan open to trade. Japan, with no navy to match, gave way, and other Western powers followed with unequal treaties.

Many samurai were furious that the shogun had bowed to foreigners. In 1868 they overthrew him and 'restored' power to the teenage Emperor Meiji: the Meiji Restoration.

Japan's new leaders decided the only way to avoid being colonised like China was to copy the West, fast. In a few decades they abolished the samurai class, built railways, factories and a modern army and navy, made schooling compulsory and wrote a constitution (1889) modelled on Germany's.

The capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital'.

Japan then built an empire like the Western powers. It defeated China in 1894–95 and took Taiwan, then shocked the world by defeating Russia in 1904–05, the first time an Asian power beat a European one in modern war. In 1910 it annexed Korea, ruling it harshly until 1945.

cards.q: Why did Meiji Japan modernise so fast?
a: To avoid being colonised by Western powers
Because the emperor had been to Europe
Because China ordered it to
To join the Soviet Union
cards.why: Its slogan was "rich country, strong army".

cards.s: Japan defeated Russia in a war in 1904–05.
cards.why: It was the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European one.

cards.p:
In the 1910s and 1920s Japan moved towards democracy, with political parties and, from 1925, votes for all men. But the Great Depression hit hard, and army officers and nationalists, some of whom assassinated politicians, gained power.

They argued Japan needed an empire in Asia for land and raw materials. In 1931 the army seized Manchuria, and in 1937 Japan invaded China. At Nanjing its troops massacred huge numbers of civilians.

Cut off from American oil in 1941, Japan struck: on 7 December 1941 it attacked Pearl Harbor and swept across South-East Asia. At its height its empire stretched from Burma to the Pacific islands.

After defeat at Midway in 1942 the tide turned. American forces fought island by island towards Japan, and firebombing destroyed much of Tokyo in 1945.

On 6 August 1945 the US dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August on Nagasaki; the Soviet Union also declared war. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito broadcast Japan's surrender, the first time most Japanese had heard his voice.

About 3 million Japanese had died, and the cities lay in ruins.

cards.q: What drew Japan into war with the United States in 1941?
a: The US cut off its oil after its expansion in China and Indochina
The US invaded Korea
Japan wanted to colonise California
Germany ordered it to
cards.why: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor to clear the way to the oil of South-East Asia.

cards.p:
The US occupied Japan from 1945 to 1952 and remade it. A new constitution (1947) made Japan a democracy, gave women the vote and turned the emperor into a symbol with no political power. Hirohito publicly denied he was divine.

Its Article 9 renounces war and, read literally, armed forces. Japan has instead 'Self-Defence Forces' and relies on an alliance with the US, which keeps bases in Japan, especially on Okinawa.

From the 1950s to the 1980s Japan grew faster than almost any country in history, becoming the world's second-largest economy. Companies such as Toyota, Sony and Honda became global names, the bullet train opened for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and lifetime employment and hard work became national ideals.

In 1990 a huge stock and property bubble burst, and decades of slow growth, the 'lost decades', followed.

cards.note: Rounded figures. Nearly 30% of people are now over 65, the highest share of any large country.

cards.p:
Japan sits where four tectonic plates meet, so earthquakes and tsunamis are part of life. In March 2011 a magnitude 9 earthquake and tsunami killed about 18,000 people and caused meltdowns at the Fukushima nuclear plant.

Today Japan's biggest challenge is people: a very low birth rate means the population is shrinking and ageing fast, with labour shortages and growing reliance on foreign workers.

Memories of the war still shape relations. China and both Koreas say Japan has not fully faced its wartime and colonial record; visits by politicians to the Yasukuni Shrine, which honours the war dead including convicted war criminals, cause anger. Japan also disputes islands with Russia, South Korea and China.

In October 2025 Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first woman prime minister, a hawk who wants a stronger military as China's power grows.

items: Politeness, consensus and not standing out.
A deep wariness of war, now being debated.
The old kept alongside the new.
The oldest population of any large country
The defining challenge of the century.

cards.q: What does Article 9 of the 1947 constitution do?
a: Renounces war as a sovereign right
Makes the emperor head of the army
Bans foreign trade
Makes Shinto the state religion
cards.why: Japan keeps Self-Defence Forces and relies on its US alliance.

cards.s: Japan's population is growing quickly.
cards.why: It peaked around 2008 and is shrinking and ageing.

cards.p: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, a vast steppe between Russia and China. Horses may first have been domesticated here around 3500 BC. It is rich in oil, uranium and metals.
Turkic nomads herded across the steppe for millennia; the Silk Road crossed the south. The Kazakh Khanate formed in the 1460s. Russia absorbed it step by step in the 1700s–1800s.

cards.q: What is Kazakhstan the largest of?
a: Landlocked countries
Islands
Deserts
Mountain ranges

cards.p: Under Stalin, forced settlement of the nomads caused a famine (1930–33) that killed about 1.5 million Kazakhs, a third or more. Deported peoples were sent here; the Soviets tested hundreds of nuclear bombs at Semipalatinsk and launched Gagarin from Baikonur.

Kazakhstan became independent in 1991 and gave up its Soviet nuclear arsenal. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled until 2019 and built a new capital, Astana. Oil brought wealth; unrest in 2022 left over 200 dead.

cards.s: Gagarin, the first person in space, was launched from Kazakhstan.

units.title: Cradle of humankind and the coast

cards.p: Kenya straddles the equator, from Indian Ocean beaches to highlands, savannahs and the Great Rift Valley. Some of the oldest fossils of human ancestors were found here, around Lake Turkana. Its savannah wildlife and the great migration draw visitors from around the world.

For a thousand years the coast was part of the Indian Ocean trade. Swahili city-states such as Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu traded with Arabia, Persia, India and China; Swahili, a Bantu language with many Arabic words, became the lingua franca of East Africa. The Portuguese and then Omani Arabs controlled the coast.
Inland lived dozens of peoples: the Kikuyu farmers of the highlands, the Luo by Lake Victoria, the Kalenjin, and the cattle-herding Maasai. Kenya has more than 40 ethnic groups.

cards.q: Which language is the lingua franca of East Africa?
a: Swahili
Arabic
Portuguese
Zulu

cards.p: Britain made Kenya a protectorate in 1895 and built a railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria. White settlers took the best highland land, the 'White Highlands', and Africans were pushed onto reserves and taxed.

In 1952 the Mau Mau uprising, mostly Kikuyu, fought for land and freedom. Britain crushed it brutally, holding tens of thousands in detention camps where many were tortured. Independence came in 1963, with Jomo Kenyatta, a jailed nationalist, as leader.

cards.q: What was the Mau Mau uprising?
a: A rebellion against British colonial rule over land
A Swahili trading league
A 1990s election
A wildlife conservation campaign
cards.why: Britain crushed it brutally in the 1950s.

cards.p: Kenyatta and then Daniel arap Moi ruled a one-party state; Moi allowed multi-party elections in 1991. The disputed 2007 election led to ethnic violence that killed over 1,000. A new 2010 constitution spread power to 47 counties.

Kenya is East Africa's economic hub, a pioneer of mobile money (M-Pesa), famous for tea, flowers and long-distance runners. Wangari Maathai won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 for planting trees. Al-Shabaab attacks from Somalia, debt and protests by young Kenyans in 2024 over taxes are challenges.

items: Elections often split along ethnic lines.

cards.p: Kyrgyzstan is a small, very mountainous country in Central Asia; the Tian Shan range covers most of it. Lake Issyk-Kul is one of the largest mountain lakes. Kyrgyz are traditionally nomadic herders who live in yurts.
The Silk Road passed through. The Kyrgyz celebrate the epic of Manas, one of the longest poems in the world. The Kokand Khanate ruled before Russia took the region in 1876.

cards.q: What is the epic of Manas?
a: A huge Kyrgyz oral epic poem
A mountain
A Soviet law
A Silk Road city
cards.why: One of the longest poems ever.

cards.p: Under Soviet rule nomads were forced onto collective farms; in 1916 a revolt against Russian rule had been brutally crushed.
Independent in 1991, Kyrgyzstan was Central Asia's most open country, and its people toppled presidents in 2005, 2010 and 2020. Sadyr Japarov, in power since 2020, has concentrated control.

cards.s: Protests have toppled several Kyrgyz presidents.

cards.p: Cambodia lies on the Mekong River and the great Tonlé Sap lake in mainland South-East Asia. Most people are Khmer and Theravada Buddhist.

From 802 the Khmer Empire dominated mainland South-East Asia. Its capital Angkor was among the largest cities of the pre-industrial world, and Angkor Wat, built in the 1100s, is the largest religious monument on Earth, now on Cambodia's flag. The empire declined after the 1400s; France made Cambodia a protectorate in 1863.

hl: Khmer Empire at its height, roughly

cards.q: What is Angkor Wat?
a: The largest religious monument on Earth
A royal palace in Phnom Penh
A French fort
A mountain
cards.why: Built by the Khmer Empire in the 1100s.

cards.p: Cambodia became independent in 1953. Dragged into the Vietnam War and heavily bombed by the US, it fell in 1975 to the Khmer Rouge. Pol Pot emptied the cities and forced everyone into labour camps; about 1.7 to 2 million people, a quarter of the population, died from execution, starvation and disease. Vietnam invaded and ended the regime in 1979.
After UN-run elections in 1993, Hun Sen dominated politics for decades; his son Hun Manet became prime minister in 2023. Tourism to Angkor and garment factories drive the economy.

cards.s: About a quarter of Cambodians died under the Khmer Rouge.

cards.p: Kiribati (pronounced 'Kiribass') is 33 atolls spread across 3.5 million km² of Pacific Ocean, straddling the equator and the Date Line; its Line Islands are the first place on Earth to see each new day.
Micronesian people settled the islands. Britain ruled them as the Gilbert Islands; the Battle of Tarawa in 1943 was one of the Pacific war's bloodiest.

cards.q: Which country is first to see each new day?
a: Kiribati
New Zealand
Japan
Fiji

cards.p: Kiribati became independent in 1979; it moved the Date Line in 1995 so all its islands share one day.
Most land is less than 2 m above sea level; Kiribati has bought land in Fiji as insurance against rising seas.

cards.s: Kiribati bought land in Fiji because of rising seas.

cards.p: St Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Americas, two volcanic islands. Alexander Hamilton, a US founding father, was born on Nevis.
In 1623 St Kitts became England's first Caribbean colony, the 'mother colony' of the British West Indies. Sugar made it rich; Brimstone Hill fortress is a World Heritage site.

cards.q: Which US founding father was born on Nevis?
a: Alexander Hamilton
George Washington
Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin

cards.p: Independent in 1983, it was the last British Caribbean island to become a country. Sugar ended in 2005.
Tourism and selling citizenship to investors support it; Nevis has the right to secede by referendum.

cards.s: St Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Americas.

cards.p: Korea is a mountainous peninsula between China, Japan and Russia. Its position has made it a battleground and a bridge: Buddhism, writing and Confucianism reached Japan through Korea. Today it is divided: South Korea, a democracy of 51 million, and communist North Korea.

Three kingdoms, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, ruled Korea until Silla unified most of it in 668. The Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), from which 'Korea' comes, printed books with metal movable type in 1377, before Gutenberg.

The Joseon dynasty (1392–1910) made Korea a deeply Confucian society. In 1443 King Sejong created Hangul, a simple alphabet, so ordinary people could read.

Japan invaded in 1592–98; Admiral Yi Sun-sin's ironclad 'turtle ships' helped drive it out. Later Joseon closed itself off, earning the name 'Hermit Kingdom'. In the 1800s it was caught between China, Japan and Russia, and in 1910 Japan annexed it.

cards.q: Who created the Korean alphabet, Hangul?
a: King Sejong
Admiral Yi
Confucius
Kim Il-sung
cards.why: In 1443, so ordinary people could read.

cards.p: Japan ruled Korea harshly from 1910 to 1945: it tried to erase Korean language and names, conscripted labourers and forced women into military brothels (the 'comfort women'). The memory still strains relations with Japan.

In 1945 Korea was split at the 38th parallel: Soviet troops in the north, Americans in the south. Two states formed in 1948. In 1950 the North invaded; a US-led UN force and then Chinese armies joined in. About 3 million died, and the 1953 armistice left the border near where it began, with a heavily armed demilitarised zone (DMZ). No peace treaty was ever signed.

cards.q: Has the Korean War formally ended?
a: No, only an armistice was signed in 1953
Yes, with a 1953 peace treaty
Yes, in 1991
Yes, when Korea reunified
cards.why: The two Koreas are technically still at war.

cards.p: In 1960 South Korea was poorer than many African countries. Under the dictator Park Chung-hee and big family conglomerates, the chaebol (Samsung, Hyundai, LG), it industrialised at astonishing speed: the 'Miracle on the Han River'. It is now one of the world's richest, most high-tech countries.

Mass protests in 1987 forced the generals to allow free elections. Democracy has been vigorous: two presidents were jailed for corruption, and in December 2024 President Yoon declared martial law, which parliament overturned within hours; he was removed from office in 2025.

items: Fear, hope of reunification, and family separation.
Fast growth, fast internet, fast culture.

cards.p: Kuwait is a small, desert country at the head of the Persian Gulf, holding about 6% of the world's oil reserves.
Kuwait grew as a trading and pearling port; the Al-Sabah family has ruled since 1752. It became a British protectorate in 1899. Oil was found in 1938.

cards.q: Which family has ruled Kuwait since 1752?
a: Al-Sabah
Al-Saud
Al-Thani
Al-Khalifa

cards.p: Kuwait became independent in 1961. In August 1990 Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded and annexed it. A US-led coalition drove Iraq out in February 1991; retreating troops set 600 oil wells on fire.
Kuwait has the Gulf's most powerful elected parliament, though the emir suspended it in 2024. Oil funds generous welfare for citizens, who are a minority of residents.

cards.s: Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.

units.title: The land of a million elephants

cards.p: Laos is the only landlocked country in South-East Asia, mountainous and forested, with the Mekong River along much of its western border. Most Lao are Theravada Buddhists; Luang Prabang's temples are a World Heritage site.
In 1353 Fa Ngum founded Lan Xang, 'land of a million elephants'. It later split into rival kingdoms dominated by Siam and Vietnam. France made Laos part of French Indochina in 1893.

cards.q: What was Lan Xang?
a: A Lao kingdom, 'land of a million elephants'
A French fort
A Mekong dam
A Vietnamese emperor

cards.p: Laos became independent in 1953. During the Vietnam War, the US secretly bombed it to cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail: over 2 million tons of bombs, making Laos the most heavily bombed country per person in history. Unexploded bombs still kill and maim.
The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975 and still rules alone. Laos has opened its economy, with Chinese-built railways and Mekong dams that sell power to neighbours.

cards.s: Laos is the most heavily bombed country per person in history.
cards.why: By the US during the Vietnam War.

cards.p: Lebanon is a small, mountainous country on the eastern Mediterranean, whose cedar tree is on its flag. It has 18 official religious communities: Christians (notably Maronites), Sunni and Shia Muslims, and Druze.

The Phoenician cities of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were great sea traders; they spread the alphabet, ancestor of the Greek and Latin letters, and founded Carthage. Later Romans built the vast temples of Baalbek, and the Ottomans ruled from 1516.

cards.q: Which ancient people, from Lebanon, spread the alphabet?
a: The Phoenicians
The Greeks
The Egyptians
The Romans
cards.why: Sea traders from Tyre, Sidon and Byblos.

cards.p: France created modern Lebanon in 1920; independent in 1943, it shared power by religion: a Maronite president, a Sunni prime minister, a Shia speaker. Beirut became 'the Paris of the Middle East'. A civil war (1975–90) killed about 150,000.

Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Shia militia and party, became the strongest force. Since 2019 a banking collapse wiped out savings, and a huge explosion at Beirut's port in 2020 killed over 200. War between Israel and Hezbollah in 2024 devastated the south.

cards.s: Lebanon shares power among its religious communities.

cards.p: Liberia, on West Africa's Atlantic coast, is Africa's oldest republic. Its name means 'land of the free', its flag resembles the US flag, and its capital Monrovia is named after US President Monroe.

From 1822 the American Colonization Society settled freed African Americans here. Liberia declared independence in 1847. The settlers, Americo-Liberians, about 5% of people, ruled over the indigenous majority for over a century. Liberia was never colonised by Europe.

cards.q: Who founded Liberia?
a: Freed African Americans, with a US society
Britain
France
Portugal

cards.p: In 1980 Samuel Doe, from an indigenous group, killed the president in a coup. Civil wars (1989–2003), led by warlords such as Charles Taylor, later convicted of war crimes, killed about 250,000.

cards.h: Peace and Africa’s first woman president
cards.p: After peace, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected woman head of state in 2006 and won the Nobel Peace Prize. Liberia survived Ebola in 2014–15 and has had peaceful elections since.

cards.s: Liberia elected Africa’s first woman head of state.

cards.p: Libya is a large, mostly desert country on Africa's Mediterranean coast, with Africa's largest proven oil reserves. Most people live along the coast, in the regions of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica.
Greeks founded Cyrene; Rome built Leptis Magna, birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s, and the Ottomans ruled from 1551.

cards.q: What does Libya have the largest of in Africa?
a: Proven oil reserves
Population
Rainforest
Lakes
cards.why: Most of it under the desert.

cards.p: Italy invaded in 1911 and fought a brutal war against resistance led by Omar Mukhtar, killing perhaps tens of thousands in camps. Libya became an independent kingdom in 1951; oil was found in 1959.

Colonel Muammar Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled for 42 years, using oil money for welfare and for sponsoring terrorism, such as the 1988 Lockerbie bombing. In 2011 a NATO-backed uprising overthrew and killed him. Libya has since been split between rival governments in east and west.

cards.s: Gaddafi ruled Libya for over 40 years.

cards.p: Saint Lucia is a volcanic Caribbean island with the twin Piton peaks.
Britain and France fought over it so often, about 14 times, that it was called 'the Helen of the West Indies'. Britain kept it from 1814; French creole is still widely spoken.

cards.q: Why was Saint Lucia called "the Helen of the West Indies"?
a: Britain and France fought over it many times
It was named after a queen
For its beauty contests
For its ships

cards.p: Saint Lucia became independent in 1979.
It has two Nobel laureates, poet Derek Walcott and economist Arthur Lewis, more per person than any country. Tourism drives the economy.

cards.s: Saint Lucia has two Nobel Prize winners.

cards.p: Liechtenstein is a tiny, doubly landlocked principality between Switzerland and Austria, one of only two such countries.
The princely Liechtenstein family bought the land and in 1719 it became a principality of the Holy Roman Empire. It became independent in 1806.

cards.q: Which currency does Liechtenstein use?
a: The Swiss franc
The euro
Its own
The US dollar
cards.why: It is in a customs union with Switzerland.

cards.p: Liechtenstein abolished its army in 1868 and stayed neutral in both world wars. It uses the Swiss franc.
From poverty it became one of the richest countries per person, through banking and industry; it has more registered companies than people. The prince holds real power.

cards.s: Liechtenstein has no army.

cards.p: Sri Lanka is a tropical island off India's southern tip, famous for tea, spices and beaches. About 70% of its people are Sinhalese Buddhists; Tamils, mostly Hindu, live mainly in the north and east.

Buddhism arrived around 250 BC, sent by the Indian emperor Ashoka, and Sri Lanka became its stronghold; Anuradhapura and Sigiriya rock fortress are ancient wonders. The Portuguese, Dutch and then British (from 1796) took the coast; Britain conquered Kandy in 1815, planted tea and brought Tamil workers from India.

cards.q: Which religion do most Sri Lankans follow?
a: Buddhism
Hinduism
Islam
Christianity

cards.p: Ceylon won independence in 1948 and became Sri Lanka in 1972; in 1960 it had the world's first woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike. Policies favouring Sinhalese fuelled Tamil anger, and the Tamil Tigers fought a civil war for a separate state (1983–2009) that killed up to 100,000. It ended in a bloody army offensive.
The 2004 tsunami killed about 35,000. In 2022 economic collapse and mass protests drove out President Rajapaksa. In 2024 voters elected a left-wing outsider, Anura Kumara Dissanayake.

cards.s: Sri Lanka had the world’s first woman prime minister.

cards.p: Lesotho is a small, high mountain kingdom completely surrounded by South Africa; its lowest point is over 1,400 m, the highest of any country.
King Moshoeshoe I united the Basotho in the 1820s from his mountain fortress, Thaba Bosiu, and asked Britain for protection from the Boers; it became the British protectorate of Basutoland.

cards.q: What is unusual about Lesotho’s location?
a: It is completely surrounded by South Africa
It is an island
It is below sea level
It is in the Sahara

cards.p: Lesotho became independent in 1966. Politics have been marked by coups and instability.
It sells water to South Africa from mountain dams and makes clothes for export; HIV rates are among the highest in the world.

cards.s: Lesotho has the highest lowest point of any country.

cards.p: Lithuania is the largest of the three Baltic states, on the Baltic Sea. Lithuanian is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages. Lithuanians were the last people in Europe to become Christian, in 1387.

The Grand Duchy of Lithuania, from the 1200s, became the largest state in Europe in the 1400s, stretching to the Black Sea. In 1569 it united with Poland in the Commonwealth; Russia annexed it in 1795.

hl: Grand Duchy at its height, roughly

cards.q: When did Lithuanians adopt Christianity?
cards.why: The last pagan people in Europe.

cards.p: Lithuania was independent 1918–40. The Soviets occupied it in 1940, then the Nazis, who murdered about 95% of its Jews; Vilnius had been 'the Jerusalem of the North'. Soviet rule returned with mass deportations to Siberia.
In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence; Soviet troops killed 14 at Vilnius TV tower in January 1991. It joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and the euro in 2015.

cards.s: Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

cards.p: Luxembourg is a tiny, wealthy grand duchy between France, Germany and Belgium, the world's last grand duchy. People speak Luxembourgish, French and German.
It began as a castle in 963. Its fortress was so strong it was called 'the Gibraltar of the North'. Ruled by many powers, it became independent in stages in the 1800s.

cards.q: What kind of state is Luxembourg?
a: A grand duchy
A republic
A principality
An empire

cards.p: Germany occupied Luxembourg in both world wars.
A founder of the EU and NATO, it hosts EU institutions and is a major banking centre, with one of the highest incomes per person in the world. Public transport is free.

cards.s: Public transport in Luxembourg is free.

cards.p: Latvia is the middle of the three Baltic states, flat and forested. Riga, founded in 1201, has Europe's finest Art Nouveau architecture. Latvian is a Baltic language.
German crusading knights conquered the region in the 1200s; Riga joined the Hanseatic trade league. Poland, Sweden and then Russia (from 1710) ruled it, while German barons owned the land.

cards.q: Which city was founded in 1201?
a: Riga
Tallinn
Vilnius
Helsinki

cards.p: Latvia was independent 1918–40. The Soviets occupied it in 1940, then the Nazis, who murdered most of its Jews; Soviet rule returned with deportations and Russian settlement.
The Singing Revolution and the 'Baltic Way' human chain of 1989 led to independence in 1991. Latvia joined NATO and the EU in 2004. About a quarter of residents are Russian speakers.

cards.s: Latvia joined the EU in 2004.

cards.p: Morocco sits in the north-west corner of Africa, 14 km from Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar, with Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts, the Atlas mountains and the Sahara. Its people are a mix of Amazigh (Berber) and Arab heritage.

The Amazigh (Berbers) are the original people of North Africa. Phoenicians, Carthage and Rome traded on the coast. Arabs brought Islam around 700, and Moroccan Berber armies led the conquest of Spain in 711.

Berber dynasties, the Almoravids and Almohads, ruled empires stretching into Spain in the 1000s–1200s and built Marrakesh. Fez, home to al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 and often called the oldest university in the world, became a centre of learning. The Alaouite dynasty has ruled since the 1600s, one of the oldest reigning royal families.

cards.q: Who are the Amazigh?
a: The original Berber peoples of North Africa
Arab conquerors
French settlers
Spanish Moors
cards.why: Their language is now official in Morocco.

cards.p: In 1912 France made most of Morocco a protectorate, with Spain holding the north and south. Morocco won independence in 1956 under Sultan, later King, Mohammed V.

King Hassan II (1961–99) ruled with an iron hand in the 'years of lead'. In 1975 the Green March sent 350,000 Moroccans into Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony Morocco claims; a conflict with the Polisario independence movement followed. King Mohammed VI, since 1999, has made limited reforms, especially after the 2011 protests.

items: The king holds religious and political authority.
Plus French as a business language.
Close ties with Spain and France.

cards.p: Monaco is the world's second-smallest country, a city-state on the French Riviera, and the most densely populated.
In 1297 Francesco Grimaldi, disguised as a monk, seized the fortress; his family still rules, one of the oldest dynasties in Europe.

cards.q: Which family has ruled Monaco since 1297?
a: The Grimaldis
The Bourbons
The Habsburgs
The Medici

cards.p: Monaco lost most of its land in 1861 and opened the Monte Carlo casino to make money. Residents pay no income tax.
Prince Rainier married film star Grace Kelly in 1956. The Monaco Grand Prix and wealthy residents make it a symbol of luxury.

cards.s: Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world.

cards.p: Moldova is a small, landlocked country between Romania and Ukraine, of rolling hills and vineyards. Most people speak Romanian. It is one of Europe's poorest countries.
The principality of Moldavia, founded in 1359, had Stephen the Great as its hero. In 1812 Russia took its eastern half, Bessarabia, today's Moldova; western Moldavia became part of Romania.

cards.q: What language do most Moldovans speak?
a: Romanian
Russian
Ukrainian
Hungarian

cards.p: Bessarabia joined Romania in 1918; the Soviets annexed it in 1940 and deported many.
Independent since 1991, Moldova lost control of Transnistria, a Russian-backed breakaway strip, after a 1992 war. It became an EU candidate in 2022 and is trying to escape Russian influence.

cards.s: Transnistria is a Russian-backed breakaway region of Moldova.

cards.p: Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island, split from Africa 160 million years ago; about 90% of its wildlife, such as lemurs, lives nowhere else. Its first settlers came not from Africa but from Borneo, over 6,000 km away, about 1,500 years ago, then Bantu Africans arrived; Malagasy is related to languages of Indonesia.
The Merina kingdom of the highlands unified most of the island in the 1800s. Queen Ranavalona I resisted Europeans and Christianity. France conquered it in 1895–96.

cards.q: Where did Madagascar’s first settlers come from?
a: Borneo, in South-East Asia
Egypt
India
Portugal
cards.why: Malagasy is related to Indonesian languages.

cards.p: France ruled until 1960 and brutally crushed a 1947 uprising, killing tens of thousands.

Independent since 1960, Madagascar has been one of the world's poorest countries, troubled by coups and political crises; youth protests toppled the president in 2025. Deforestation threatens its unique forests.

cards.s: Lemurs live naturally only on Madagascar.
cards.why: About 90% of its wildlife is unique.

cards.p: The Maldives are about 1,200 coral islands in the Indian Ocean, the flattest country on Earth; the average land height is about 1.5 m.

People arrived from South Asia; the islands were Buddhist until 1153, when the king converted to Islam. Sultans ruled for centuries; the Portuguese briefly held Malé, and Britain made it a protectorate in 1887.

cards.q: What is unusual about the Maldives’ geography?
a: It is the flattest country on Earth
It is mostly desert
It has the highest mountains
It is landlocked

cards.p: The Maldives became independent in 1965 and a republic in 1968; Maumoon Gayoom ruled for 30 years.
Luxury resorts made it the richest country in South Asia per person. Rising seas threaten its existence; in 2009 the cabinet held an underwater meeting to raise the alarm.

cards.s: The Maldives was Buddhist before becoming Muslim.

cards.p: Mexico is a land of high plateaus between two mountain ranges, with deserts in the north and jungles in the south. The fertile Valley of Mexico, 2,200 m up, has been the heart of the country for a thousand years. Maize was domesticated here about 9,000 years ago and still feeds the nation.

The Olmecs (from about 1200 BC) carved colossal stone heads. Teotihuacan, near Mexico City, was one of the largest cities in the world around AD 500, with its Pyramid of the Sun. In the south, the Maya built city-states with writing, astronomy and the concept of zero.

In 1325 the Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, today Mexico City. By 1500 it held perhaps 200,000 people, with canals, causeways and floating gardens. The Aztec Empire took tribute from conquered peoples, and its religion demanded human sacrifice to keep the sun moving, which made it many enemies.

The eagle on a cactus eating a snake, the sign that told the Mexica where to build, is on Mexico's flag.

cards.q: Where is Mexico City built?
a: On the site of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan
On a Maya city in the jungle
On the Pacific coast
In the northern desert
cards.why: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco.

cards.p: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed with about 500 men. He won thousands of allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, who hated the Aztecs, and he was helped by La Malinche, a Nahua woman who interpreted for him. Smallpox devastated Tenochtitlan, and it fell in 1521.

For three centuries Mexico was New Spain, the richest Spanish colony, thanks to silver mines at Zacatecas and Guanajuato. Disease killed perhaps 90% of the native population. A mixed, mestizo society grew, ranked by race, with Spanish-born at the top.

In 1531 the Virgin of Guadalupe was said to appear to an indigenous man, Juan Diego; she became the symbol of Mexican Catholicism and identity.

pins: Most visited Catholic shrine in the world

cards.p: On 16 September 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell in Dolores and called for revolt: the 'Grito de Dolores', still celebrated as Independence Day. Hidalgo was executed, but the war went on, and Mexico won independence in 1821.

cards.q: What is celebrated on 16 September in Mexico?
a: Hidalgo's call for independence in 1810
The fall of Tenochtitlan
The 1917 constitution
Cinco de Mayo

cards.p: The young nation was unstable. Texas broke away in 1836, and in the war with the US (1846–48) Mexico lost California and the whole south-west, about half its territory. It still shapes how Mexicans see their northern neighbour.

Benito Juárez, a Zapotec lawyer, led liberal reforms separating Church and state. France invaded and installed an Austrian archduke, Maximilian, as emperor; Mexican forces beat the French at Puebla on 5 May 1862 (Cinco de Mayo), and Juárez had Maximilian shot in 1867.

Porfirio Díaz ruled as dictator for 35 years, building railways while land piled up in a few hands. In 1910 revolution exploded: Emiliano Zapata in the south fought for 'land and liberty', Pancho Villa in the north. About a million died.

The 1917 constitution promised land reform and workers' rights, and in 1938 President Cárdenas nationalised the oil industry, creating Pemex.

From 1929 one party, the PRI, ruled for 71 years, mixing reform, patronage and repression; in 1968 troops killed protesting students at Tlatelolco. In 1994 NAFTA tied Mexico's economy to the US, and a Zapatista uprising in Chiapas demanded indigenous rights.

In 2000 an opposition candidate finally won the presidency.

From 2006 a war on drug cartels, which smuggle drugs north and guns south, has killed hundreds of thousands. In 2024 Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first woman president. Mexico is now the US's largest trading partner, and millions of Mexicans live in the US.

items: Pride in ancient roots, from Aztec symbols to Day of the Dead.
Deeply Catholic, yet with a secular state.
So far from God, so close to the US
The 1910 revolution is the founding story of the modern state.

cards.p: The Marshall Islands are 29 coral atolls in the central Pacific. Marshallese navigators used 'stick charts' of curved sticks to map ocean swells.
Germany and Japan ruled the islands; after World War II the US tested 67 nuclear weapons here, at Bikini and Enewetak atolls (1946–58), displacing islanders and spreading radiation.

cards.q: What happened at Bikini Atoll?
a: The US tested nuclear weapons
A famous naval battle
The first Pacific settlement
A volcanic eruption

cards.p: The Marshall Islands became independent in 1986 in free association with the US, which keeps a missile-test base at Kwajalein.
Rising seas threaten the low atolls; many Marshallese have moved to the US.

cards.s: Marshallese navigators used stick charts.

cards.p: North Macedonia is a landlocked Balkan country with Lake Ohrid, one of Europe's oldest lakes. Most people are Macedonian Slavs; about a quarter are Albanian.
Ancient Macedon (Philip and Alexander) lay largely in today's Greece. The region was Roman and Byzantine; Ohrid was a centre of Slavic Christian learning. The Ottomans ruled for over 500 years.

cards.q: Why did the country change its name in 2019?
a: To settle a dispute with Greece
To join Albania
After a war
To honour Alexander

cards.p: Divided after the Balkan Wars, it became part of Yugoslavia and peacefully independent in 1991.
Greece objected to the name 'Macedonia', claiming Alexander's heritage. In 2019 the country became 'North Macedonia', joined NATO in 2020, and seeks EU entry.

cards.s: North Macedonia joined NATO in 2020.

cards.p: Mali is a large, landlocked country; its north is Sahara and its south the Sahel, crossed by the Niger River, whose inland delta fed great cities.

In 1235 Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire, whose story is still sung by griots. It controlled the gold trade across the Sahara. Its ruler Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that he lowered its price in Cairo; he may have been one of the richest people ever.

Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning, with libraries of manuscripts. Later the Songhai Empire ruled until Morocco invaded in 1591.

cards.q: Who was Mansa Musa?
a: A ruler of Mali famed for his wealth in gold
A Moroccan sultan
A French governor
A Songhai general

cards.p: France conquered the region in the 1890s as French Sudan. It became independent as Mali in 1960, taking the name of the old empire.

In 2012 Tuareg rebels and jihadists seized the north, destroying shrines in Timbuktu; French troops drove them back in 2013. Military coups in 2020 and 2021 brought a junta that expelled French forces and turned to Russia's Wagner group. Violence continues.

cards.s: Mali took its name from a medieval empire.
cards.why: The empire of Sundiata and Mansa Musa.

cards.p: Malta is a small island nation between Sicily and North Africa. Its language is the only Semitic language written in Latin letters, mixing Arabic, Italian and English.

Its megalithic temples are older than Stonehenge and the pyramids. Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans ruled it. In 1530 the Knights of St John took over; they withstood the Great Siege by the Ottomans in 1565 and built the fortress capital Valletta.

cards.q: Who defended Malta in the Great Siege of 1565?
a: The Knights of St John
The British navy
The Romans
The Venetians

cards.p: Britain ruled from 1800. In World War II Malta withstood relentless bombing; King George VI awarded the whole island the George Cross.
Malta became independent in 1964, a republic in 1974, and joined the EU in 2004. It is the EU's smallest member.

cards.s: The whole of Malta was awarded the George Cross.
cards.why: For its bravery in World War II.

cards.p: Myanmar (Burma) lies between India, China and Thailand, around the Irrawaddy River valley. About 90% of people are Theravada Buddhists; golden pagodas such as Shwedagon in Yangon dominate the skyline. Many ethnic minorities, such as the Shan, Karen and Kachin, live in the hills around the Burman heartland.
The kingdom of Pagan (Bagan) unified the valley in the 1000s and built over 10,000 temples, about 2,000 still standing. Later Burmese kingdoms fought Siam, destroying Ayutthaya in 1767.

Britain conquered Burma in three wars (1824–85) and ruled it as part of India, bringing in Indian workers. Nationalists led by Aung San won independence in 1948, but he was assassinated months before.

cards.q: What is the main religion of Myanmar?
a: Theravada Buddhism
Islam
Hinduism
Christianity

cards.p: Ethnic insurgencies began almost at once. In 1962 General Ne Win seized power; decades of military rule and isolation impoverished the country. Aung San's daughter, Aung San Suu Kyi, led the democracy movement and spent 15 years under house arrest; she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.

A partial opening from 2011 brought Suu Kyi to power in 2016. In 2017 the army drove over 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh in a campaign the UN called genocidal. In 2021 the army staged a coup; a civil war with resistance forces and ethnic armies has raged since.
Montenegro, 'black mountain', is a small Balkan country with dramatic peaks and the fjord-like Bay of Kotor on the Adriatic.
Its mountain clans, led by prince-bishops at Cetinje, kept practical independence from the Ottomans for centuries. Montenegro was recognised as independent in 1878 and became a kingdom.

cards.q: What does 'Montenegro' mean?
a: Black mountain
Blue sea
White city
Free land
cards.why: From the dark forests on its peaks.

cards.p: In 1918 Montenegro was absorbed into Yugoslavia.
It voted narrowly (55.5%) to leave its union with Serbia in 2006. It joined NATO in 2017, uses the euro and hopes to join the EU; tourism is booming.

cards.s: Montenegro became independent from Serbia in 2006.

cards.p: Mongolia is a vast, landlocked country of grassland steppe, mountains and the Gobi desert between Russia and China, with the lowest population density of any country. About a third of people are still nomadic herders living in gers (yurts).

Nomadic peoples such as the Xiongnu threatened China for centuries. In 1206 Temüjin united the Mongol tribes as Genghis Khan; his empire became the largest land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary. After it broke up, Mongols adopted Tibetan Buddhism and were later absorbed by the Qing.

cards.q: Who united the Mongols in 1206?
a: Genghis Khan
Kublai Khan
Timur
Attila
cards.why: He built the largest land empire ever.

cards.p: Mongolia broke from the Qing in 1911 and in 1924 became the world's second communist state, a Soviet satellite. Buddhist monasteries were destroyed and thousands of monks killed in the 1930s.
A peaceful revolution in 1990 brought democracy, rare in the region. Copper and coal mining boom, and Genghis Khan is again celebrated as the national hero.

cards.s: Mongolia is a democracy.

cards.p: Mozambique stretches 2,500 km along the Indian Ocean in south-east Africa, with the Zambezi River crossing it. Portuguese is the official language.

Swahili traders ran coastal towns, trading gold from Great Zimbabwe. Vasco da Gama stopped here in 1498, and Portugal ruled the coast, later the interior, for nearly 500 years, using forced labour and shipping slaves.

cards.q: Which European country ruled Mozambique?
a: Portugal
Britain
France
Belgium

cards.p: FRELIMO fought a liberation war from 1964 and won independence in 1975. A brutal civil war (1977–92) against RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and South Africa, killed about a million people.
Peace brought growth, but cyclones, debt scandals and, since 2017, an Islamist insurgency in the gas-rich northern province of Cabo Delgado have hit hard.

cards.s: Mozambique won independence in 1975.

cards.p: Mauritania is a vast, mostly Saharan country in north-west Africa, bridging the Arab Maghreb and Black Africa. Its old caravan towns, such as Chinguetti with its libraries, were centres of Islamic learning.
The Almoravid movement began here in the 1040s among Sanhaja Berbers and conquered Morocco and Muslim Spain. Arab tribes later settled. France colonised the region from 1903.

cards.q: Which movement that conquered Spain began in Mauritania?
a: The Almoravids
The Mamluks
The Ottomans
The Umayyads

cards.p: Mauritania became independent in 1960. Coups were frequent. It was one of the last countries to abolish slavery, in 1981, and made it a crime only in 2007; the practice persists.
Iron ore, fish and gold support the economy. Mauritania saw its first peaceful transfer of power in 2019.

cards.s: Mauritania abolished slavery only in 1981.
cards.why: One of the last countries to do so.

cards.p: Mauritius is an Indian Ocean island east of Madagascar, once home of the dodo, extinct by about 1681 after humans arrived.

Uninhabited until the Dutch (1598), it was then French and from 1810 British. Sugar was grown by enslaved Africans and, after 1835, by Indian indentured workers, whose descendants are now the majority.

cards.q: Which extinct bird lived on Mauritius?
a: The dodo
The moa
The great auk
The passenger pigeon

cards.p: Mauritius became independent in 1968.
It became one of Africa's richest and most democratic countries, moving from sugar to textiles, tourism and finance. Britain agreed in 2025 to return the Chagos Islands.

cards.s: Most Mauritians are of Indian descent.

cards.p: Malawi is a narrow, landlocked country along Lake Malawi, the third-largest lake in Africa, famous for hundreds of species of colourful cichlid fish. It calls itself 'the warm heart of Africa'.

The Maravi kingdom ruled from the 1400s. In the 1800s Arab-Swahili slave traders raided the region; the explorer David Livingstone campaigned against them. Britain made it the protectorate of Nyasaland in 1891.

cards.q: Which lake gives Malawi much of its character?
a: Lake Malawi
Lake Victoria
Lake Chad
Lake Tanganyika
cards.why: Home to hundreds of fish species.

cards.p: Malawi became independent in 1964 under Hastings Banda, who ruled as 'President for Life' until a 1994 referendum brought multi-party democracy.
Malawi is peaceful but one of the world's poorest countries, dependent on tobacco and farming. In 2020 its courts overturned a fraudulent election, a rare event in Africa.

cards.s: Malawi’s courts annulled a presidential election in 2020.
cards.why: And a re-run changed the result.

cards.p: Malaysia has two parts: the Malay Peninsula and Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo, separated by the South China Sea. Its people are Malay (mostly Muslim), Chinese and Indian, plus indigenous groups: a multi-ethnic federation.

Around 1400 a Sumatran prince founded Malacca on the strait that carries trade between India and China. Its rulers became Muslim, and it grew into a great trading port, spreading Islam across the region. Portugal took it in 1511, then the Dutch.

Britain took Penang (1786), Singapore and Malacca, then the Malay states, ruling through their sultans. It brought Chinese workers for tin mines and Indians for rubber plantations, creating today's mix.

cards.q: Why was Malacca so important?
a: It controlled the strait between India and China
It had gold mines
It was the Mughal capital
It grew tea
cards.why: A great trading port from about 1400.

cards.p: After the Japanese occupation and a communist insurgency, Malaya became independent in 1957. Malaysia was formed in 1963 with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore; Singapore left in 1965. Race riots in 1969 led to policies favouring Malays (bumiputera).

Under Mahathir Mohamad (1981–2003) Malaysia industrialised fast; Kuala Lumpur's Petronas Towers became a symbol. The 1MDB scandal, in which billions were looted, ended the long-ruling coalition's rule in 2018. Anwar Ibrahim became prime minister in 2022.

cards.s: Singapore was part of Malaysia for two years.

cards.p: Namibia, in south-western Africa, has the Namib, the oldest desert on Earth, with its giant red dunes, and the Skeleton Coast. It is one of the least densely populated countries.

San rock art here is tens of thousands of years old. Germany colonised the land as South West Africa in 1884. When the Herero and Nama rose up in 1904, German forces killed most of them, driving many into the desert: the first genocide of the 20th century, acknowledged by Germany in 2021.

cards.q: Which colonial power committed genocide in Namibia?
a: Germany
Britain
Portugal
France

cards.p: South Africa took over in 1915 and imposed apartheid. SWAPO fought a long liberation war.
Namibia became independent in 1990 under Sam Nujoma. It is stable and democratic, with diamonds, uranium and tourism; Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first woman president in 2025.

cards.s: Namibia was ruled by South Africa until 1990.

cards.p: Niger is a vast, landlocked country, mostly Sahara, with the Niger River in the south-west where most people live. It has one of the world's youngest and fastest-growing populations and is a major uranium producer.
Tuareg nomads ran caravans across the Sahara; Agadez was a crossroads. In the south, Hausa states and the Songhai and Kanem-Bornu empires ruled. France conquered it by 1922.

cards.q: What mineral is Niger a major producer of?
a: Uranium
Diamonds
Copper
Silver

cards.p: Niger became independent in 1960. Droughts, famines, Tuareg rebellions and several coups followed. It is one of the poorest countries on Earth.
In July 2023 the army overthrew the elected president, expelled French and US troops, and allied with Mali and Burkina Faso and Russia. Jihadist attacks continue in the west.

cards.s: Niger has one of the world's youngest populations.

cards.p: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with over 220 million people and more than 250 ethnic groups. The largest are the Hausa-Fulani in the mostly Muslim north, the Yoruba in the south-west and the Igbo in the Christian south-east. The Niger and Benue rivers meet in the middle. Lagos is one of the biggest cities in Africa.

The Nok culture made terracotta sculptures from about 500 BC. The Yoruba city of Ife and the kingdom of Benin made famous brass and bronze sculptures. In the north, Hausa city-states such as Kano traded across the Sahara, and Islam spread; in 1804 Usman dan Fodio's jihad founded the Sokoto Caliphate.

From the 1500s the coast became a centre of the Atlantic slave trade: the Bights of Benin and Biafra shipped millions of people to the Americas. Yoruba religion and culture survive in Brazil and Cuba.

cards.q: Which kingdom is famous for its bronze sculptures?
a: Benin
Mali
Kongo
Aksum
cards.why: Many were looted by Britain in 1897.

cards.p: Britain took Lagos in 1861 and, after conquering the region (including looting Benin City in 1897), joined north and south into one colony, Nigeria, in 1914. It ruled the north indirectly through emirs and the south more directly, keeping the regions very different.
Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960. Political parties formed along regional and ethnic lines, which made the new federation fragile.

cards.q: When did Nigeria become independent?

cards.p: Two coups in 1966 and massacres of Igbo in the north led the south-east to secede as Biafra in 1967. The civil war (1967–70) and blockade-driven famine killed between half a million and two million people. Nigeria stayed united.

Oil in the Niger Delta made Nigeria Africa's biggest producer, but the money fed corruption and military rulers for most of 1966–1999, while the Delta was polluted and stayed poor. Democracy returned in 1999 and has survived since.

Nigeria is a cultural powerhouse: Nollywood is one of the world's biggest film industries, Afrobeats music is global, and writers like Chinua Achebe and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie are read everywhere. But the jihadist group Boko Haram, kidnappings and poverty remain grave problems.

items: Balancing north, west and east is the key to politics.
Wealth and the curse of corruption.

cards.p: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America, with two huge lakes and a chain of volcanoes. The Pacific side was Spanish; the Caribbean Mosquito Coast was long under British influence.

Spain founded Granada and León in 1524. After independence (1821), rival cities fought for power; in 1856 an American adventurer, William Walker, briefly made himself president. The US eyed a canal route here before choosing Panama.

cards.q: Which country in Central America is the largest?
a: Nicaragua
Honduras
Guatemala
Panama

cards.p: US Marines occupied Nicaragua (1912–33) and fought the guerrilla Augusto Sandino. The Somoza family dictatorship ruled from 1936 until the Sandinista revolution of 1979. The US backed 'Contra' rebels against the Sandinistas in the 1980s.

Voters elected Violeta Chamorro in 1990. Daniel Ortega, a Sandinista leader, returned in 2007 and, with his wife as co-president, has crushed opposition, especially after 2018 protests in which hundreds were killed.

cards.s: The Sandinistas took power in a 1979 revolution.

cards.p: 'Netherlands' means 'low lands': about a quarter of the country lies below sea level. For a thousand years the Dutch built dikes, drained lakes with windmills and created new land, polders. 'God created the world, but the Dutch created the Netherlands,' goes the saying. Working together against the water shaped a culture of consensus.
