Energy supply is a constant worry, and Russian drones from the war next door have crashed on Moldovan soil.
q: Which country lost Transnistria, where Russian troops are still stationed, after a short war in 1992?
Which country restored the Latin alphabet in 1989 after Moscow had insisted its language be written in Cyrillic?
Which country's Mileștii Mici and Cricova wine cellars run for tens of kilometres underground?

TKM.t: Turkmen tribes were nomadic herders and horse breeders, and their oases, such as Merv, were once great Silk Road cities. Russia conquered them in the 1880s, after storming the fortress of Geok Tepe in a bloody battle in 1881. In 1924 the Soviets created the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, forced the nomads onto collective farms and dug the Karakum Canal to carry water from the Amu Darya to cotton fields. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the local Communist Party boss, Saparmurat Niyazov, stayed on as president. Calling himself Turkmenbashi, 'leader of the Turkmens', he built golden statues of himself, renamed months after himself and his mother, and made his book, the Ruhnama, required reading. He declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995. Gas exports, increasingly to China, paid for marble buildings in Ashgabat. After Niyazov died in 2006, his dentist and health minister, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow, took over and built a personality cult of his own.
TKM.c: Most of the country is the Karakum Desert, where the Darvaza gas crater, the 'Door to Hell', has burned since Soviet times. Turkmen carpets, with their deep red patterns, appear on the flag, and the golden Akhal-Teke horse has its own national holiday. Ashgabat is a city of white marble and empty boulevards, and few foreign tourists visit because visas are hard to get.
TKM.p: In 2022 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow handed the presidency to his son Serdar through an election with no real opposition, but he still wields great power as chairman of the People's Council, the top legislative body. Turkmenistan has no free press, opposition parties or independent courts, and is ranked among the least free countries in the world. Its economy rests on huge gas reserves, sold mostly to China. In 2025 it began issuing electronic visas and in 2026 legalised cryptocurrency mining, but food shortages and emigration remain common.
q: Which country's first president called himself Turkmenbashi and renamed months after himself and his mother?
Which country declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995?
Which country's desert holds the burning Darvaza gas crater, the 'Door to Hell'?

JOR.t: For centuries the land east of the Jordan River was a thinly populated corner of the Ottoman Empire, crossed by Bedouin tribes and by pilgrims heading to Mecca. During World War I the Hashemite family of Mecca led the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans with British support, helped by T. E. Lawrence. Afterwards Britain created Transjordan in 1921 and gave it to the Hashemite prince Abdullah, and it became an independent kingdom in 1946. In the 1948 war Jordan took the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and many Palestinian refugees became citizens. Abdullah was assassinated in Jerusalem in 1951, and his grandson Hussein ruled from 1953 to 1999, steering a small, poor country between larger neighbours. Jordan lost the West Bank to Israel in the 1967 war. In 1970 the army fought and expelled Palestinian guerrilla groups in what became known as Black September. Hussein made peace with Israel in 1994, and his son Abdullah II succeeded him in 1999.
JOR.c: Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock by the Nabataeans, is its most famous sight, and the desert of Wadi Rum has stood in for Mars in films. Mansaf, lamb cooked in fermented dried yogurt and served over rice, is the national dish, eaten at weddings and funerals. Many Jordanians have Palestinian roots, and Bedouin hospitality, with endless cups of cardamom coffee, is a point of pride.
JOR.p: King Abdullah II, on the throne since 1999, holds most power, and in 2024 he made Jafar Hassan, his former chief of staff, prime minister. The Islamic Action Front won the most seats of any party in the 2024 election, but in 2025 the government banned the Muslim Brotherhood after arresting members accused of a weapons plot. Anger over the war in Gaza runs high. During the 2026 Iran war its air defences shot down Iranian missiles and drones, and an Iranian strike hit an air base used by US forces. Unemployment and debt are chronic problems.
q: Which kingdom did Britain create in 1921 for the Hashemite prince Abdullah?
Which country fought and expelled Palestinian guerrilla groups in 1970, an event known as Black September?
Which country's most famous sight is Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock?

NPL.t: For centuries the Kathmandu Valley was home to small Newar kingdoms famous for their temples and pagodas. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered them and founded modern Nepal. It was never colonised, but after losing a war with the British East India Company in 1816 it gave up land and began sending Gurkha soldiers to serve Britain, and they fought in both world wars. From 1846 to 1951 the Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers and kept the country sealed off. After their fall Nepal opened to the world, just as Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first ascent of Everest in 1953. Kings ruled with little democracy until protests in 1990. A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 killed about 17,000 people, and in 2001 the crown prince shot dead King Birendra and much of the royal family. After mass protests in 2006 the Maoists made peace, and in 2008 an elected assembly abolished the monarchy.
NPL.c: Nepal holds eight of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres, including Everest, and Sherpa guides lead most expeditions. Most people are Hindu, but Lumbini is the Buddha's birthplace, and Buddhist prayer flags flutter across the hills. Dal bhat, lentils with rice, is eaten twice a day, and momo dumplings are everywhere. Its flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
NPL.p: In September 2025 young people angered by corruption and a ban on social media staged the 'Gen Z' protests. More than 70 people were killed, crowds set fire to parliament and politicians' homes, and Prime Minister K. P. Sharma Oli resigned. Sushila Karki, a former chief justice, led an interim government until elections in March 2026, which the Rastriya Swatantra Party won by a landslide. Balen Shah, a former rapper and mayor of Kathmandu in his mid-thirties, became prime minister, and Oli was arrested over the crackdown. Corruption, jobs and the millions of Nepalis working abroad are the big issues.
q: Which country's crown prince shot dead the king and much of the royal family in 2001?
Which country abolished its monarchy in 2008 after a Maoist insurgency?
Which country has the only national flag that is not a rectangle?

LSO.t: King Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees from the wars of the early 1800s into the Basotho nation, using the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu as a fortress. When Boer settlers seized much of his best farmland, he asked Britain for protection in 1868, and the deal kept his mountain kingdom, then called Basutoland, out of South Africa. Britain ran it cheaply, and generations of Basotho men went to work in South Africa's gold mines. It became independent in 1966, completely surrounded by South Africa. When the ruling party lost the 1970 election, Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan suspended the constitution and ruled until a 1986 military coup backed by apartheid South Africa. Elections returned in 1993, but a disputed 1998 vote led to riots and an intervention by South African and Botswana troops. The whole country lies above 1,400 m, the highest low point of any country. Since 2004 the Lesotho Highlands Water Project has dammed its rivers to sell water to Johannesburg.
LSO.c: Sesotho and English are official, and nearly everyone is Basotho. The Basotho blanket, worn like a cloak against the mountain cold, and the conical mokorotlo hat are national symbols. Herders on sturdy Basotho ponies cross the high passes, and Afriski in the Maluti Mountains is one of Africa's few ski resorts. Lesotho has one of the world's highest HIV rates.
LSO.p: Sam Matekane, a diamond-mining millionaire, became prime minister in 2022 after his new Revolution for Prosperity party won the most seats; King Letsie III has a mostly ceremonial role. Coalition governments in Lesotho often collapse, and efforts to reform the constitution and curb the army's role in politics have dragged on for years. In 2025 the United States announced a 50% tariff on Lesotho's goods, threatening the clothing factories that make jeans for American brands and employ thousands. The government declared a two-year state of disaster over unemployment. Lesotho also depends heavily on water sales and customs payments from South Africa.
q: Which mountain kingdom did Moshoeshoe I build, using the flat-topped Thaba Bosiu as a fortress?
Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
Which country lies entirely above 1,400 m, where people wear blankets like cloaks and the conical mokorotlo hat?

CMR.t: Germany claimed Kamerun in 1884. During World War I, British and French troops took it, and afterwards the League of Nations split it between France, which got most of it, and Britain, which got two strips along Nigeria. In the 1950s France fought a brutal, little-known war against the UPC independence movement, which went on after independence; in 2025 France officially acknowledged it as a war. French Cameroon became independent in 1960, and in 1961 the southern British strip voted to join it while the northern strip joined Nigeria. That is why Cameroon is officially bilingual in French and English. The first president, Ahmadou Ahidjo, turned the federation into a one-party unitary state. In 1982 he handed power to his prime minister, Paul Biya, who allowed multiparty elections from 1992 but kept winning them. Oil, timber and cocoa helped make it one of Central Africa's larger economies, but English-speakers increasingly felt sidelined by the French-speaking majority.
CMR.c: With more than 250 languages, Cameroon is often called 'Africa in miniature': it has rainforest, savanna, beaches and Mount Cameroon, an active volcano. Makossa and bikutsi music are famous across Africa, and so is its football team, the Indomitable Lions, with stars such as Roger Milla and Samuel Eto'o. Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves and peanuts, is a national dish.
CMR.p: Paul Biya, president since 1982 and in his nineties the world's oldest head of state, won an eighth term in October 2025 with 53.7% of the official vote. His former minister Issa Tchiroma claimed he had won; protests followed, several people were killed and Tchiroma fled abroad. In 2026 parliament restored the post of vice president, who would take over if Biya died or left office, and postponed parliamentary elections. The war between the army and English-speaking separatists in the northwest and southwest, which began in 2017, still kills people, and Boko Haram attacks continue in the far north.
q: Which country, once German Kamerun, is officially bilingual because a British strip voted to join the French part in 1961?
Which country has been led by Paul Biya since 1982?
Which country is called 'Africa in miniature', and whose football team is the Indomitable Lions?

GAB.t: Portuguese sailors named the estuary of the Como River 'Gabão' in the 1470s, and the coast became a centre of the slave trade. France founded Libreville in 1849 as a settlement for freed slaves and later made Gabon part of French Equatorial Africa. In 1913 the doctor Albert Schweitzer founded his famous jungle hospital at Lambaréné. Gabon became independent in 1960 under Léon M'ba, and when soldiers overthrew him in 1964, French paratroopers flew in and put him back. His successor Omar Bongo ruled from 1967 until his death in 2009, becoming the symbol of 'Françafrique', the web of personal, business and military ties between France and its former colonies. Oil, manganese and timber made Gabon one of the richest countries in Africa per person, and French troops stayed in Libreville. His son Ali Bongo, president from 2009 to 2023, won disputed elections in 2009 and 2016, and suffered a stroke in 2018. When he was declared the winner of another election in August 2023, army officers seized power within hours.
GAB.c: French is the official language, alongside Fang, Myene and other Bantu languages. About 85% of the country is rainforest, with a network of national parks that are home to forest elephants, gorillas and surfing hippos at Loango. Bwiti, a spiritual tradition using the iboga plant, is part of national identity. Libreville's seafront and nightlife are among the liveliest in Central Africa.
GAB.p: General Brice Oligui Nguema, who led the 2023 coup that ended the Bongo family's 56 years in power, was elected president in April 2025 with about 90% of the vote under a new constitution that abolished the post of prime minister. Ali Bongo's wife and son were released and left the country, then were sentenced in absentia to 20 years for embezzlement. Supporters praise Oligui for building projects; critics say he has kept old networks and is concentrating power. In 2026 the government blocked social media nationwide and asked the IMF for help with its debts.
q: Which country did Omar Bongo rule from 1967 to 2009 as a symbol of 'Françafrique'?
Which country's army seized power within hours of Ali Bongo being declared the winner of the August 2023 election?
Which country is about 85% rainforest, with surfing hippos at Loango?

NER.t: The Niger River crosses only the southwest corner of this huge, mostly desert country. Before colonial rule the area held Hausa city-states, part of the Kanem-Bornu empire and the Tuareg sultanate of Agadez, a hub for caravans crossing the Sahara. France conquered it around 1900 and made it part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960 under Hamani Diori, who kept close ties with France. Uranium found near Arlit in the north was mined by French-led companies from the early 1970s and fuelled French nuclear power stations. Niger then lived through coups in 1974, 1996, 1999 and 2010, and Tuareg rebellions in the 1990s and 2000s. Droughts in the 1970s and 1980s brought famine. Since the 2010s jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have attacked from Mali and Burkina Faso in the west, and Boko Haram from around Lake Chad in the southeast. Western countries made Niger a key partner against them, until the army turned on that alliance.
NER.c: Hausa is the most widely spoken language, and most people are Muslim. Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so the population is very young. Tuareg nomads are known for silver jewellery, the Agadez cross and the indigo veils worn by men. Each year Wodaabe herders gather for the Gerewol, where young men paint their faces and dance to be chosen by women. Agadez's mud-brick minaret is a landmark.
NER.p: General Abdourahamane Tiani, head of the presidential guard, seized power in July 2023 and detained the elected president, Mohamed Bazoum. In March 2025 Tiani was sworn in as president for a five-year transition, and political parties were dissolved. Ali Lamine Zeine is prime minister. The junta expelled French and US troops, turned to Russia and, with Mali and Burkina Faso, left ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States. In 2025 it nationalised the main uranium mine run by France's Orano. Jihadist attacks have grown worse, including two raids on Niamey's airport in 2026, and the junta said it defeated a coup attempt in August 2026.
q: Which country's uranium, mined near Arlit from the 1970s, fuelled French nuclear power stations?
Which country had coups in 1974, 1996, 1999 and 2010, and saw Tuareg rebellions in the 1990s and 2000s?
Which country, with one of the world's highest birth rates, holds the Gerewol, where Wodaabe men dance to be chosen?

BFA.t: The Mossi kingdoms around Ouagadougou were among West Africa's most durable states, resisting Mali and Songhai for centuries before France conquered them in the 1890s. France drew this landlocked colony as Upper Volta, after the Volta rivers, and used it mainly as a reservoir of labour for plantations in Côte d'Ivoire and soldiers for its armies in both world wars. It became independent in 1960 and had its first coup in 1966. In 1983 a 33-year-old captain, Thomas Sankara, took power and the next year renamed it Burkina Faso, 'land of upright people'. He vaccinated children, planted millions of trees, banned forced marriage and rejected foreign aid that came with conditions. In 1987 he was killed in a coup led by his friend Blaise Compaoré, who ruled for 27 years until a popular uprising drove him out in 2014. From 2015 jihadist groups spreading from Mali began attacking the north, and by the 2020s armed groups controlled large parts of the countryside.
BFA.c: Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival, every two years, as well as a major crafts fair. French is official, alongside Mooré and dozens of other languages. Faso Dan Fani, a handwoven cotton cloth Sankara made a symbol of self-reliance, is still worn proudly, and Sankara is remembered across Africa as a model of honest leadership.
BFA.p: Captain Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since a September 2022 coup, the country's second that year, and in 2024 extended military rule to 2029. With Mali and Niger he formed the Alliance of Sahel States, expelled French troops, turned to Russia and left the West African bloc ECOWAS in January 2025. Popular online across Africa for his anti-Western message, at home he has dissolved all political parties, shut down hundreds of civic groups, and drafted critics into the army. The jihadist group JNIM still kills soldiers and civilians in large attacks, and the government cut diplomatic ties with France in June 2026.
q: Which country was called Upper Volta under French rule?
Which country's young leader Thomas Sankara planted millions of trees before he was killed in a 1987 coup?
Which country's capital hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival?

TGO.t: Germany claimed Togoland in 1884 and called it a 'model colony', built on cotton and palm oil plantations and forced labour. In World War I British and French troops seized it within weeks, and afterwards the League of Nations split it: France got the larger eastern part and Britain the west. In 1956 the British part voted to join the Gold Coast, soon to be Ghana, which divided the Ewe people between two countries. French Togo became independent in 1960 under Sylvanus Olympio. In 1963 he was shot dead in one of Africa's first post-independence coups, and in 1967 an army officer, Gnassingbé Eyadéma, took power. He ruled a one-party state for 38 years as a close ally of France during the Cold War, and crushed pro-democracy protests in the early 1990s. When he died in 2005 the army installed his son Faure Gnassingbé, who then won a disputed election marred by violence that killed hundreds. The same family has ruled ever since 1967.
TGO.c: French is official, and Ewe in the south and Kabiyè in the north are widely spoken. Christianity, Islam and Vodun beliefs often mix. Lomé's Akodessewa market sells items for traditional healing, and the Batammariba people in the north build fortress-like clay tower houses, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Fufu, pounded yam, is eaten with spicy sauces, and the footballer Emmanuel Adebayor is a national hero.
TGO.p: Faure Gnassingbé has led Togo since 2005, and in 2025 he kept power under a new constitution that turned the country into a parliamentary system. The presidency became largely ceremonial, now held by Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, chosen by parliament in 2025, while Gnassingbé took the powerful new post of President of the Council of Ministers, which has no term limits. Critics called it a constitutional coup, and protests in June 2025 were put down, leaving several people dead. Jihadist groups from Burkina Faso have attacked the far north since 2021. The port of Lomé, a regional trade hub, drives the economy.
q: Which country's first president, Sylvanus Olympio, was shot dead in a 1963 coup?
Which country has been ruled by the Gnassingbé family since 1967?
Which country's Batammariba people build fortress-like clay tower houses, a UNESCO site?

GHA.t: The Asante kingdom, based in Kumasi, grew rich on gold and trade and fought the British in a series of wars before Britain annexed it in 1902. On the coast, the British Gold Coast took its name from its gold, and forts such as Cape Coast and Elmina were centres of the slave trade. In the 20th century cocoa farming made it one of Britain's wealthiest African colonies. After World War II, riots in 1948 fuelled demands for self-rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah. In 1957 it became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence, taking the name of a medieval West African empire, and inspired the wave that swept Africa in 1960. Nkrumah became a leading voice for African unity, but he built a one-party state and was overthrown in 1966 while visiting China. Coups and economic decline followed. Jerry Rawlings, who seized power in 1979 and again in 1981, later oversaw a return to multiparty elections in 1992, and power has since changed hands peacefully several times.
GHA.c: English is official, with Akan (Twi) widely spoken. Kente cloth, highlife music and jollof rice (which Ghana and Nigeria endlessly argue over) are cultural exports, and Afrobeats stars fill stadiums. Funerals are big, colourful events, sometimes with coffins shaped like fish, cars or shoes. Many African Americans visit or settle here, drawn by the history of the slave forts.
GHA.p: John Mahama, president from 2012 to 2017, returned to power in January 2025 after his National Democratic Congress defeated the party of Nana Akufo-Addo, president from 2017 to 2025, in a landslide. He inherited the aftermath of a 2022 debt default and high inflation; with an IMF rescue the economy recovered, and Ghana left the IMF programme in 2026. Illegal gold mining, called galamsey, which poisons rivers and destroys forests, is a major issue. In August 2025 a military helicopter crash killed the defence and environment ministers. In 2026 parliament passed a strict anti-LGBT bill, criticised by human rights groups.
q: Which country, once the Gold Coast, was the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence, in 1957?
Which country's leader Kwame Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966 while visiting China?
Which country is known for kente cloth, highlife music and coffins shaped like fish, cars or shoes?

GNB.t: Portuguese traders arrived in the 1440s, and the coast became a source of captives for the Atlantic slave trade, run from trading posts such as Cacheu. Portugal took full control of the interior only in the early 20th century and invested very little. In 1956 Amílcar Cabral, an agronomist, founded the PAIGC to free Guinea and Cape Verde, and from 1963 it fought one of Africa's most effective guerrilla wars, eventually controlling much of the countryside. Cabral was assassinated in 1973, but the rebels declared independence that year, and Portugal recognised it in 1974 after its own Carnation Revolution. Cabral's half-brother Luís Cabral became president, until a 1980 coup by João Bernardo 'Nino' Vieira ended plans to unite with Cape Verde. A civil war in 1998–99 drove Vieira out; he later returned, and in 2009 he was killed by soldiers. Coups and attempted coups have been frequent since independence, and in the 2000s South American cartels used the country's islands and creeks as a transit point for cocaine heading to Europe.
GNB.c: Portuguese is official, but most people speak Guinea-Bissau Creole. Cashew nuts are the main export and income for many families. Gumbe music and the Bijagós Islands, a World Heritage Site where saltwater hippos and sea turtles live and some islands are run by women, are distinctive. Carnival in Bissau, with huge masks, is the biggest festival.
GNB.p: In November 2025, the day before results of a presidential election were due, the army seized power and removed Umaro Sissoco Embaló, president from 2020 to 2025; both he and his rival Fernando Dias had claimed victory, and armed men destroyed most of the tally sheets. General Horta Inta-A Na Man leads a military transition, with Ilídio Vieira Té as prime minister. West African and African Union bodies suspended the country. Opposition leader Domingos Simões Pereira was jailed. In August 2026 voters approved a new constitution that strengthens the presidency, and new elections were called for December 2026.
q: Which country's PAIGC, founded by Amílcar Cabral, fought one of Africa's most effective guerrilla wars against Portugal?
Which country's president 'Nino' Vieira was killed by soldiers in 2009?
Which country's Bijagós Islands are home to saltwater hippos, and cashew nuts are the main export?

USA.t: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776 and, in the 1800s, pushed west to the Pacific, taking land from Native nations and Mexico. A civil war from 1861 to 1865 ended slavery but not racial segregation in the South. By 1900 the United States had the world's largest economy. It joined World War I late, in 1917, then turned inward until Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 brought it into World War II. It ended that war by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and emerged as a superpower, rebuilding Western Europe and Japan and founding NATO. In the Cold War against the Soviet Union it fought in Korea and Vietnam and landed on the Moon in 1969. At home, the civil rights movement led by Martin Luther King Jr won laws in the 1960s that ended legal segregation. After the Soviet Union fell in 1991 it was the only superpower, but the attacks of 11 September 2001 drew it into long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
USA.c: American films, music, fast food, sport and technology companies shape culture around the world. People come from every part of the world, and English and Spanish are the most widely spoken languages. Americans are more religious than people in most rich countries, follow American football, baseball and basketball, and gather for Thanksgiving turkey and Fourth of July fireworks. In 2026 the country marked 250 years of independence.
USA.p: Donald Trump, who was president from 2017 to 2021, won back the White House in November 2024, and Republicans control both houses of Congress. His second term has brought sweeping tariffs, partly struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2026, and mass deportation drives that led to deadly shootings by immigration agents. Abroad, US forces captured Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, Trump pressed Denmark to hand over Greenland, and in February the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, pushing up fuel prices.
q: Which country was formed by 13 colonies that declared independence in 1776?
Which country dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and landed on the Moon in 1969?
Which country marked 250 years of independence in 2026?

CAN.t: Canada was formed in 1867 when Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined in Confederation, partly from fear of the United States after its Civil War. Railways tied it together, and by 1871 it reached the Pacific, pushing aside First Nations and Métis peoples on the prairies. In World War I about 60,000 Canadians died, and the capture of Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a founding national story. In World War II Canadian troops landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, and the country came out of the war as an industrial power and a founding member of NATO in 1949. Independence from Britain came step by step, from the Statute of Westminster in 1931 to its own constitution and Charter of Rights in 1982. Quebec's Quiet Revolution in the 1960s fed a movement for independence, which lost referendums in 1980 and, by a whisker, in 1995. Free trade with the US from 1989, widened to include Mexico in 1994, tied its economy closely to its neighbour.
CAN.c: Canada is officially bilingual, and French dominates in Quebec, where Montreal is one of the world's largest French-speaking cities. Most Canadians live within a few hundred kilometres of the US border, and Toronto and Vancouver draw immigrants from all over the world. Ice hockey is the national obsession, alongside maple syrup, poutine and Tim Hortons coffee. Indigenous peoples, from the Inuit to the Haida, are reclaiming their languages and land.
CAN.p: Mark Carney, a former governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, became Liberal leader and prime minister in March 2025 after Justin Trudeau resigned, and won the April 2025 election. MPs crossing the floor from the Conservatives and the NDP gave the Liberals a majority in April 2026, with Pierre Poilievre's Conservatives in opposition. The dominant issue is the United States: Donald Trump's tariffs and talk of making Canada the 51st state rallied Canadians to buy Canadian and pushed the government to seek other partners, including a trade deal with China in January 2026. In October 2026 Albertans voted against moving towards a separation referendum.
q: Which country was formed by Confederation in 1867, partly from fear of its neighbour after the Civil War?
Which country's capture of Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a founding national story?
Which country is officially bilingual, with ice hockey, maple syrup and poutine?

MEX.t: Spain conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521 and built Mexico City on the ruins of its capital, Tenochtitlan. New Spain's silver made the Spanish crown rich, while Indigenous people died in huge numbers from war and new diseases. Mexico won independence in 1821 after a long war, but by 1848 it had lost about half its territory, from Texas to California, to the United States. Under Porfirio Díaz, who ruled for over 30 years, railways and foreign investment grew while peasants lost their land. The Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, with leaders such as Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata, killed perhaps a million people and produced a constitution promising land reform. In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas nationalised the oil industry. One party, later called the PRI, held power for 71 years until Vicente Fox won in 2000. The NAFTA trade deal of 1994 tied Mexico's economy to the US, and after 2006 a government war on drug cartels unleashed violence that has killed hundreds of thousands.
MEX.c: Mexico has more Spanish speakers than any other country. Its cuisine, from tacos and tamales to mole and pozole, is on UNESCO's heritage list, as is the Day of the Dead, when families build altars to welcome back the dead. Mariachi bands, lucha libre wrestling and football are national passions, and Diego Rivera's murals and Frida Kahlo's paintings are known worldwide. Mexico co-hosted the 2026 World Cup.
MEX.p: Claudia Sheinbaum, a climate scientist and ally of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, president from 2018 to 2024, won the 2024 election by a landslide to become Mexico's first woman president. Her Morena party controls congress and pushed through a reform making judges elected; turnout in the first judicial election in 2025 was only about 13%, and critics say it weakens checks on power. Relations with Donald Trump's US dominate: tariffs, cartels designated as terrorists, and mass handovers of cartel bosses. In February 2026 security forces killed Nemesio Oseguera, 'El Mencho', head of the Jalisco cartel.
q: Which country lost about half its territory, from Texas to California, to the United States by 1848?
Which country's revolution of 1910 to 1920 featured Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata?
Which country has more Spanish speakers than any other and celebrates the Day of the Dead?

BLZ.t: Maya cities such as Caracol and Lamanai flourished here for centuries before Europeans arrived. Spain claimed the coast but never settled it, and from the 1600s British woodcutters, the Baymen, cut logwood and later mahogany with enslaved African labour. In 1798 they beat off a Spanish attack at St George's Caye, and in 1862 Britain made the territory the colony of British Honduras. Guatemala, independent since 1821, insisted it had inherited Spain's claim. That claim delayed independence: after self-government in 1964, George Price and the People's United Party pushed for freedom, but needed British protection. Renamed Belize in 1973, it became independent in 1981, while Cold War civil wars raged in Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua, and British troops stayed on to guard the border. Guatemala recognised Belize in 1991 but kept its territorial claim. In 2018 and 2019 both countries voted in referendums to send the dispute to the International Court of Justice.
BLZ.c: Belize is the only Central American country where English is the official language, though Kriol and Spanish are heard everywhere, along with Maya languages and Garifuna. The Belize Barrier Reef and the Great Blue Hole draw divers, and Maya ruins rise from the jungle. Rice and beans with stewed chicken is the everyday meal, and Garifuna drumming and punta music celebrate a people of mixed African and Indigenous Caribbean roots.
BLZ.p: Johnny Briceño of the People's United Party has been prime minister since 2020. In March 2025 his party won a second landslide, taking 26 of 31 seats against the United Democratic Party. Guatemala's claim to much of Belize's territory is before the International Court of Justice. The government's priorities are debt, the cost of living, crime in Belize City and protecting the reef. In 2025 it agreed to accept some migrants deported from the US and joined a free-movement deal with Barbados, Dominica and St Vincent. Belize is one of the few countries that recognise Taiwan.
q: Which country was the colony of British Honduras?
Which country's independence was delayed by Guatemala's claim that it had inherited Spain's rights to it?
Which is the only Central American country with English as its official language, home to the Great Blue Hole?

PAN.t: Panama's narrow isthmus has always been a crossing point. Spanish treasure from Peru was carried across it to the Caribbean, and after independence from Spain in 1821 it joined Colombia. During the California gold rush an American company built a railway across it, finished in 1855. A French attempt to dig a canal, led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, collapsed in the 1880s after thousands of workers died of yellow fever and malaria. When Colombia rejected US terms for a canal, Theodore Roosevelt backed a Panamanian revolt, and in 1903 the new country handed the US a strip of land, the Canal Zone. The canal opened in 1914, just as World War I began. Anger at US control boiled over in riots in 1964, and in 1977 Omar Torrijos and Jimmy Carter agreed to hand the canal over. In 1989 the US invaded to remove the military ruler Manuel Noriega, a former CIA ally wanted for drug trafficking. Panama took control of the canal in 1999 and later widened it.
PAN.c: Panama uses the US dollar, and the canal, banking and shipping have given Panama City a skyline of glass towers. The Guna people govern their own region along the San Blas islands and are known for colourful mola textiles. Sancocho, a chicken soup, is the national dish. The 'Panama hat' is actually made in Ecuador; it got its name because canal workers wore them.
PAN.p: José Raúl Mulino became president in 2024, standing in for the former president Ricardo Martinelli, who was barred from running after a money-laundering conviction. Donald Trump's threats to take back the canal put Panama under pressure: it left China's Belt and Road Initiative in 2025 and let US troops train near the canal, and in 2026 its Supreme Court cancelled a Hong Kong company's concession to run ports at both ends. A 2025 pension reform set off months of strikes and protests, and a giant copper mine shut after mass protests in 2023 remains a divisive question.
q: Which country broke away from Colombia in 1903 with Theodore Roosevelt's backing?
Which country did the US invade in 1989 to remove Manuel Noriega?
Which country gave its name to a hat that is actually made in Ecuador?

VEN.t: Venezuela, the homeland of Simón Bolívar, declared independence in 1811 and left Gran Colombia in 1830. Through the 1800s and early 1900s it was ruled by caudillos, strongmen such as Juan Vicente Gómez. Oil found around Lake Maracaibo in 1914 made it one of the world's top exporters by the late 1920s, and its oil helped fuel the Allies in World War II. Democracy took root after the dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez fell in 1958, and in 1960 Venezuela helped found OPEC. Oil made it one of Latin America's richest countries, but the wealth was unevenly shared, and when prices fell, riots in Caracas in 1989 were put down with hundreds killed. Hugo Chávez, a paratrooper who had led a failed coup in 1992, was elected president in 1998 and launched a socialist 'Bolivarian revolution', spending oil money on the poor while taking control of institutions. After his death in 2013 Nicolás Maduro took over; oil output collapsed, hyperinflation followed, and about eight million Venezuelans left the country.
VEN.c: Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves and Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall. Arepas, corn cakes stuffed with cheese or meat, are eaten every day, and at Christmas families make hallacas wrapped in banana leaves. Baseball is the most popular sport, and many players reach the US major leagues. El Sistema, a free youth orchestra programme, trained the conductor Gustavo Dudamel.
VEN.p: Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's vice-president, has been interim president since January 2026, when US forces struck Caracas and captured Nicolás Maduro, flying him to New York, where he pleaded not guilty to drug-trafficking charges. Maduro had claimed victory in the 2024 election, though the opposition's tallies showed Edmundo González had won, and the opposition leader María Corina Machado won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize. Rodríguez's government has since restored relations with the United States, released hundreds of political prisoners under an amnesty, and opened the oil industry to private firms, but Chávez's party still holds the main institutions.
q: Which country, the homeland of Simón Bolívar, helped found OPEC in 1960?
Which country did Hugo Chávez lead in a socialist 'Bolivarian revolution' from 1998?
Which country has the world's largest proven oil reserves and Angel Falls?

PNG.t: People have lived in New Guinea for at least 50,000 years, and highlanders were among the world's first farmers. In the 1880s the island was split three ways: the Dutch in the west, Germany in the northeast and Britain in the southeast, which it handed to Australia in 1906. Australia seized German New Guinea in World War I and later ran both parts together. In the 1930s gold prospectors found about a million people in the highland valleys whom no outsider had known existed. In 1942 Japan captured Rabaul and tried to take Port Moresby overland; Australian troops stopped them on the Kokoda Track, helped by Papuan carriers. Papua New Guinea became independent in 1975 under Michael Somare. From 1988 a revolt against the Panguna copper mine on Bougainville grew into a civil war that killed thousands before a 2001 peace deal. In 2019 Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly for independence, which still awaits approval by the national parliament.
PNG.c: With about 840 languages, Papua New Guinea has more than any other country; Tok Pisin, a creole, is the common tongue. Most people live in rural villages and grow their own food, such as sweet potato and taro. Highland sing-sings showcase feathered headdresses and painted faces. Rugby league is a passion, and a national team, the PNG Chiefs, is due to join Australia's NRL in 2028.
PNG.p: James Marape has been prime minister since 2019 and won the 2022 election, surviving several no-confidence attempts since. Deadly riots in Port Moresby in January 2024, set off by a police pay protest, exposed anger over jobs and prices. The country marked 50 years of independence in 2025 and signed a mutual defence treaty with Australia, though it has also courted China, deciding in 2026 to close Taiwan's office. Tribal violence in the highlands, landslides, Bougainville's push for independence and soldiers' protests in 2026 over army recruitment are other pressing issues.
q: Which country saw Australian troops stop Japan's advance on the Kokoda Track in 1942?
Which country's island of Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence in 2019?
Which country has about 840 languages, more than any other, with Tok Pisin as the common tongue?

EGY.t: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, made Egypt vital to Britain as the shortcut to India, and Britain occupied the country in 1882 after Egypt fell deep into debt. Egypt became nominally independent in 1922 as a kingdom, but British troops stayed, and in World War II the Allies stopped Rommel's advance on the canal at El Alamein in 1942. In 1952 army officers overthrew King Farouk, and Gamal Abdel Nasser became the hero of Arab nationalism. When he nationalised the canal in 1956, Britain, France and Israel invaded, and pressure from the US and the Soviet Union forced them out. Nasser turned to the Soviets, who funded the Aswan High Dam, but Egypt's crushing defeat by Israel in 1967 cost it Sinai. His successor Anwar Sadat switched to the American side, made peace with Israel in 1979 and got Sinai back, and was assassinated by Islamists in 1981. Hosni Mubarak ruled for 30 years until the Arab Spring protests of 2011 forced him out.
EGY.c: With more than 100 million people, Egypt is the most populous Arab country, and Cairo was the capital of Arabic film and music for much of the 20th century; the singer Umm Kulthum is still revered. Koshary, a mix of rice, lentils and pasta, is the classic street food. The pyramids of Giza and the new Grand Egyptian Museum draw millions of visitors.
EGY.p: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi took power in 2013 when the army removed the elected Islamist president Mohamed Morsi, and has been president since 2014; in 2026 he said he would step down in 2030. Thousands of political prisoners are held, and dissent is tightly controlled. The economy has lurched through debt crises and currency collapses, rescued by an IMF loan and huge Gulf investment. Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping slashed Suez Canal income, and the 2026 Iran war pushed fuel prices up again. Egypt is a key mediator in the Gaza war and opposes Ethiopia's giant dam on the Nile.
q: Which country's leader Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised a canal in 1956, provoking an invasion by Britain, France and Israel?
Which country's president Anwar Sadat made peace with Israel in 1979 and was assassinated in 1981?
Which is the most populous Arab country, where the singer Umm Kulthum is still revered?

YEM.t: In ancient times the kingdom of Saba grew rich from the frankincense trade, and later the port of Mocha shipped the world's first traded coffee. In modern times the country was split in two. The north was ruled by Zaydi Shia imams, who threw off Ottoman rule after World War I and kept the country isolated until a 1962 revolution sparked a civil war in which Egypt backed the republicans and Saudi Arabia the royalists. The south was centred on Aden, a British port from 1839. After an armed uprising Britain left in 1967, and South Yemen became the Arab world's only Marxist state, backed by the Soviet Union. As Soviet support faded, the two Yemens united in 1990 under the northern president, Ali Abdullah Saleh, and a southern revolt was crushed in 1994. Arab Spring protests forced Saleh out in 2012. In 2014 the Houthis, a Zaydi rebel movement from the far north, seized the capital, Sana'a, and in 2015 a Saudi-led coalition intervened against them.
YEM.c: Sana'a's old city of decorated mud-brick tower houses is a World Heritage Site, as is Shibam, the 'Manhattan of the desert'. Mocha coffee is named after the Yemeni port where the coffee trade began. Many men wear the curved jambiya dagger and chew qat leaves in long afternoon sessions, and the island of Socotra is famous for its strange dragon's blood trees.
YEM.p: Yemen remains divided. The Houthis hold Sana'a and most of the north's people, while the internationally recognised government sits in Aden under a Presidential Leadership Council led by Rashad al-Alimi, with Shaea al-Zindani as prime minister since January 2026. In early 2026 Saudi-backed forces took back the south from the UAE-backed separatist Southern Transitional Council. The Houthis joined Iran's side in the 2026 war, attacking shipping and Saudi cities, and in October 2026 the government launched an offensive to retake the north. Millions of Yemenis depend on food aid.
q: Which country's south was the Arab world's only Marxist state?
Which country's capital, Sana'a, was seized by the Houthis in 2014?
Which country's island of Socotra is famous for dragon's blood trees, and gave its name to mocha coffee?

MRT.t: For centuries the Moors, Arabic-speaking nomads of Arab and Berber descent, ran camel caravans across this part of the Sahara, and towns such as Chinguetti and Ouadane became centres of trade and Islamic scholarship. France took control in the early 1900s and governed it from Saint-Louis in Senegal, since it had no capital of its own. Nouakchott was built almost from scratch just before independence in 1960. Morocco claimed the whole country and recognised it only in 1969. In 1975 Mauritania took the southern part of Western Sahara, but attacks by the Polisario Front were so costly that a 1978 coup toppled its first president, and it withdrew in 1979. A run of military coups followed, the last in 2008. Tension between the Arab-Berber elite and Black African groups exploded in 1989, when tens of thousands of Black Mauritanians were expelled to Senegal and Mali. Slavery was formally abolished in 1981, later than anywhere else, but owning slaves only became a crime in 2007.
MRT.c: Hassaniya Arabic is the main language, alongside Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof in the south, and almost everyone is Muslim. Sweet green tea is poured from a height and served in three rounds, and camel milk and grilled meat are staples. Men often wear the flowing blue robe called a daraa. Chinguetti's family libraries hold medieval manuscripts, and one of the world's longest trains carries iron ore across the desert to the port of Nouadhibou.
MRT.p: Mohamed Ould Ghazouani, a retired general, has been president since 2019, in the country's first handover between elected presidents; his predecessor was later jailed for corruption. Ghazouani won a second term in 2024 and chaired the African Union in 2024 and 2025. Mokhtar Ould Djay has been prime minister since August 2024. Mauritania is calm compared with its Sahel neighbours, though it hosts many refugees from Mali. It is a launch point for migrant boats to Spain's Canary Islands. A big offshore gas project shared with Senegal is a hope for the economy. Two MPs were jailed in 2026 for insulting the president.
q: Which country withdrew from Western Sahara in 1979 after costly attacks by the Polisario Front?
Which country formally abolished slavery in 1981, later than anywhere else?
Which country's family libraries in Chinguetti hold medieval manuscripts, and one of the world's longest trains carries iron ore across its desert?

GNQ.t: Portugal handed this territory to Spain in 1778, and it became Spain's only colony in sub-Saharan Africa: the volcanic island of Bioko, then called Fernando Pó, plus a mainland strip, Río Muni. Spanish planters grew cocoa on Bioko with labourers from Nigeria. Under pressure from the UN, Spain granted independence in 1968. The first president, Francisco Macías Nguema, quickly built one of the most brutal regimes in African history: he banned opposition, persecuted the educated and the Church, and killed or drove into exile perhaps a third of the population. In 1979 his nephew, Teodoro Obiang, overthrew him and had him executed. Obiang kept tight control through his family and his Fang clan. In the 1990s US companies found large oil and gas fields offshore, and for a time the country had one of the highest incomes per person in Africa, but most of the wealth went to the ruling family while most people stayed poor. In 2004 foreign mercenaries were arrested over a plot to overthrow him.
GNQ.c: It is the only African country with Spanish as an official language, and Fang, Bubi and a Portuguese-based creole on Annobón island are also spoken. Most people are Catholic. Bioko's rainforests are home to rare monkeys and nesting sea turtles. In January 2026 Ciudad de la Paz was formally declared the capital in place of Malabo, on Bioko; it is a new city built in the mainland interior.
GNQ.p: Teodoro Obiang, in power since 1979, is the world's longest-serving president except for Cameroon's Paul Biya, and was re-elected in 2022 with about 95% of the official vote. His son Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, famous for supercars and luxury homes, is widely seen as his heir; in 2025 the World Court allowed France to sell a Paris mansion seized from him in a corruption case. Oil output is falling, squeezing the economy, and in June 2026 the government resigned after missing performance targets. In 2025 the World Court backed the country's claim to small islands held by Gabon.
q: Which country was Spain's only colony in sub-Saharan Africa?
Which country did Teodoro Obiang take over in 1979 after overthrowing his uncle, Francisco Macías Nguema?
Which is the only African country with Spanish as an official language?

GMB.t: The Gambia River was one of the main routes into West Africa for European traders, and from the 1600s British merchants used James Island, near its mouth, as a base for buying gold and enslaved people. Britain later held the river and France the land around it; an 1889 agreement drew the border roughly 10 km either side of the water. The result is Africa's smallest mainland country, a thin strip about 300 km long, almost entirely surrounded by Senegal. It became independent in 1965 under Dawda Jawara, who kept a multiparty democracy for nearly 30 years. After a coup attempt in 1981, Senegalese troops restored him, and the two countries formed a short-lived confederation called Senegambia from 1982 to 1989. In 1994 a young army lieutenant, Yahya Jammeh, seized power and ruled for 22 years through fear, with death squads, torture and a bogus herbal cure for AIDS. When he lost the 2016 election and refused to leave, West African troops moved in and he fled into exile.
GMB.c: English is official, while Mandinka, Wolof and Fula are spoken everywhere, as across the border in Senegal. The kora, a 21-string harp-lute, and griots who sing family histories keep oral traditions alive; Alex Haley traced his book 'Roots' to the village of Juffureh. Benachin, a one-pot rice dish, is a favourite, and beaches near Banjul draw winter tourists from Europe.
GMB.p: Adama Barrow, a former property developer, has been president since he defeated Yahya Jammeh in 2016 and was re-elected in 2021; he is a candidate again in the presidential election set for 5 December 2026. Efforts to replace Jammeh's constitution have repeatedly stalled in parliament. Victims of the Jammeh era are pursuing justice, with trials of former officials in Switzerland and the US and plans for a special court with West African backing. Many young Gambians risk the dangerous 'back way' by boat to Europe. Corruption scandals set off protests in 2025.
q: Which country is a thin strip about 300 km long, almost entirely surrounded by Senegal?
Which country's ruler Yahya Jammeh refused to leave after losing the 2016 election, until West African troops moved in?
Which country's village of Juffureh was traced by Alex Haley in his book 'Roots'?

HKG.t: Britain took Hong Kong Island in 1842 after the First Opium War, which it fought to keep selling Indian opium to China. Kowloon followed in 1860, and in 1898 Britain leased the New Territories for 99 years. Japan occupied the colony from Christmas Day 1941 to 1945. After the communist victory in 1949, hundreds of thousands of refugees poured in from the mainland, and their labour and Shanghai capital turned Hong Kong into a factory town making textiles, toys and electronics. As China opened up after 1978, factories moved across the border to Shenzhen and Hong Kong became a financial centre and China's gateway to the world. The 1898 lease forced talks: in the 1984 Joint Declaration Britain agreed to hand over all of Hong Kong in 1997, and China promised it 'one country, two systems', keeping its own laws, courts, currency and freedoms for 50 years. Disputes over that autonomy led to mass protests in 2003, 2014 and, far larger, 2019.
HKG.c: About seven and a half million people live squeezed between steep green hills and the harbour, most in high-rise flats. Cantonese is the everyday language, with English still used in law and business. People eat dim sum at yum cha, milk tea and pineapple buns at cha chaan teng diners, and roast goose. Hong Kong's kung fu and gangster films made Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan famous worldwide.
HKG.p: Beijing imposed a National Security Law in 2020 after the 2019 protests, and Hong Kong passed its own Article 23 security law in 2024. Most opposition figures are jailed or abroad, and the Democratic Party disbanded in 2025. Publisher Jimmy Lai was convicted of collusion and sedition in December 2025 and sentenced to 20 years in 2026; rights groups condemned the case, while the government says the laws restored stability. Chief Executive John Lee, chosen unopposed in 2022, works with a legislature open only to vetted 'patriots'. A November 2025 fire at a Tai Po housing estate killed 168 people.
q: Which region did Britain take after the First Opium War and hand back in 1997 under 'one country, two systems'?
Which region saw huge protests in 2003, 2014 and, far larger, 2019 over its autonomy?
Where do people eat pineapple buns at cha chaan teng diners, in the city whose films made Bruce Lee famous?

VAT.t: For over a thousand years the popes ruled the Papal States, a band of territory across central Italy. Italian unification swallowed them, and in 1870 Italian troops took Rome itself. Pope Pius IX refused to accept this and called himself a 'prisoner in the Vatican', and his successors stayed inside its walls for almost 60 years. In 1929 Mussolini's government and the Church signed the Lateran Treaty, which created Vatican City as an independent state, made Catholicism Italy's state religion and paid compensation. In World War II the Vatican stayed neutral, and Pius XII's public silence on the Holocaust is still debated, though Church buildings in Rome hid many Jews. The Second Vatican Council of 1962–65 modernised the Church, allowing Mass in local languages. John Paul II, the first Polish pope, travelled the world and backed Solidarity, helping bring down communism in Eastern Europe. Benedict XVI resigned in 2013, the first pope to do so in six centuries, and Francis, the first pope from the Americas, followed.
VAT.c: Smaller than half a square kilometre, it is the smallest country in the world, home to a few hundred residents and the centre of a Church of about 1.4 billion Catholics. St Peter's Basilica, Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling and the Vatican Museums draw millions of visitors. The Swiss Guard, in striped Renaissance uniforms, has protected the pope since 1506, and Latin is still used in official documents.
VAT.p: Pope Francis died in April 2025, and the cardinals elected Robert Prevost, born in Chicago and long a missionary in Peru, who took the name Leo XIV. He is the first pope from the United States. His first encyclical, in May 2026, warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence. In October 2026 the Vatican announced that he had lung cancer and that surgeons had removed part of a lung. Sister Raffaella Petrini runs the city state's administration, the first woman in that role. Finances, abuse cases and divisions between traditionalists and reformers remain challenges; in 2026 the traditionalist Society of St Pius X consecrated bishops against the pope's orders.
q: Which country was created by the Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's government in 1929?
Which country's leader called himself a 'prisoner' there after Italian troops took Rome in 1870?
Which is the smallest country in the world, guarded by the Swiss Guard since 1506?

AUS.t: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived here for at least 50,000 years when Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney in 1788. Settlers spread across the continent, taking land and killing or displacing many Aboriginal people, and gold rushes in the 1850s brought a flood of migrants. In 1901 six colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia, with a White Australia policy to keep out Asian immigrants. In World War I its soldiers landed at Gallipoli in 1915, and the defeat became a founding national story, remembered every year on Anzac Day. When Singapore fell in 1942 and Japan bombed Darwin, Britain could not protect Australia, so it turned to the United States, an alliance sealed by the ANZUS treaty in 1951. After World War II it took in millions of European migrants, ended White Australia in the 1970s and opened up to Asia. A 1967 referendum counted Aboriginal people in the census, and in 2008 the government apologised to the Stolen Generations, children taken from their families.
AUS.c: Most Australians live in a handful of big coastal cities, and about one in three was born overseas, with large Chinese, Indian and Vietnamese communities. Cricket, Aussie rules football, rugby league, barbecues and beach life are national passions. Aboriginal art and Dreaming stories are among the oldest living traditions on Earth. Its kangaroos, koalas, Great Barrier Reef and Uluru draw visitors from everywhere.
AUS.p: Anthony Albanese's Labor Party won a landslide in May 2025, and the opposition Liberal–National Coalition has since split, reunited and changed leaders, with Angus Taylor taking over the Liberals in 2026 while the anti-immigration One Nation party surges. In December 2025 gunmen attacked a Hanukkah event at Bondi Beach, killing 15 people; the government responded with tighter gun laws, hate speech laws and a royal commission into antisemitism. That month a ban on social media for under-16s took effect. Australia recognised Palestine in 2025 and is weighing its AUKUS deal with the US and Britain against trade with China.
q: Which country began as a British penal colony at Sydney in 1788?
Which country turned to the United States for protection after Japan bombed Darwin in 1942?
Which country is home to Uluru and the Great Barrier Reef?

GRL.t: Inuit peoples have lived in Greenland for thousands of years, and Norse settlers led by Erik the Red farmed its south from about 985 until the 1400s. Denmark-Norway colonised the island from 1721, and when the two kingdoms split in 1814 Denmark kept it. In World War II, after Germany occupied Denmark in 1940, the United States took over Greenland's defence and built air bases. In the Cold War the giant Thule base in the far north, now Pituffik Space Base, became a key US early-warning post against Soviet missiles, and Inuit families were moved to make room for it. In 1953 Denmark ended Greenland's colonial status and made it part of the Danish state, then pushed a rapid modernisation that moved people into towns. In the 1960s and 1970s Danish doctors fitted thousands of Inuit women and girls with contraceptive coils, often without consent. Greenland won home rule in 1979, left the European Community in 1985 over fishing rights, and gained wider self-government in 2009.
GRL.c: Most of Greenland's roughly 56,000 people are Inuit and live in small towns along the ice-free southwest coast, linked by boat and plane rather than roads. Greenlandic is the official language. Fishing, above all for shrimp and halibut, is the main industry, and hunting seals and whales is still part of life. People wear beaded national costume on National Day, 21 June.
GRL.p: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, which handles defence and foreign affairs and pays a large grant. Since spring 2025 Jens-Frederik Nielsen of the Democrats has led a broad coalition. Most Greenlanders want independence one day but differ on timing. From 2025 US President Donald Trump said the United States should own the island; in January 2026 he threatened allies with tariffs and would not rule out force. Greenland and Denmark said no, European troops deployed, and Trump backed down. In September 2026 a deal expanded the US military presence while reaffirming Greenlanders' right to decide their own future.
q: Which island did Norse settlers led by Erik the Red farm from about 985?
Which territory left the European Community in 1985 over fishing rights?
Which island's roughly 56,000 people, mostly Inuit, live along its ice-free southwest coast?

FJI.t: Fijian chiefs, led by Ratu Seru Cakobau, ceded the islands to Britain in 1874 after years of debt and unrest. To run sugar plantations without disturbing village life, Britain brought about 60,000 Indian indentured labourers between 1879 and 1916. Most stayed, and by 1946 Indo-Fijians outnumbered Indigenous Fijians. Fijian soldiers fought for the Allies in the Solomon Islands in World War II. Fiji became independent in 1970, but land stayed mostly in Indigenous hands while Indo-Fijians dominated business, and politics split along ethnic lines. When a government backed by Indo-Fijians won the 1987 election, army officer Sitiveni Rabuka staged two coups. Another coup followed in 2000, and in 2006 army chief Frank Bainimarama seized power, promising to end race-based politics. He ruled until 2022, introducing a new constitution in 2013 and winning elections in 2014 and 2018. Tens of thousands of Indo-Fijians emigrated over these decades, and they are now about a third of the population.
FJI.c: Rugby is close to a religion, and Fiji's sevens team won Olympic gold in 2016 and 2020. Kava, a drink made from a pepper root, is shared from a wooden bowl at every gathering. Hindu temples and Diwali sit beside Methodist churches, and Fijian, English and Fiji Hindi are all spoken. Tourism to its coral islands and beach resorts is the biggest earner.
FJI.p: Sitiveni Rabuka, the coup leader of 1987, returned as prime minister after the 2022 election at the head of a three-party coalition, and President Naiqama Lalabalavu is head of state. The government is trying to replace the 2013 constitution, including scrapping the immunity it gave past coup leaders, and in October 2026 Rabuka called a referendum on the changes for December. In 2026 former prime minister Bainimarama was charged with inciting mutiny. Fiji faces a fast-growing HIV epidemic linked to drug use, declared a national emergency in 2026, and cocaine trafficking through the Pacific.
q: Which country received about 60,000 Indian indentured labourers to work its sugar plantations?
Which country saw army officer Sitiveni Rabuka stage two coups in 1987?
Which country's rugby sevens team won Olympic gold in 2016 and 2020?

NZL.t: Polynesian voyagers settled the islands around 1300 and became the Māori. In 1840 British officials and over 500 Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, but the English and Māori versions differed on who held sovereignty, and the founding document is still argued over today. Settler hunger for land led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s and the loss of most Māori land. A farming colony that shipped meat, wool and butter to Britain, it became in 1893 the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections, and a dominion in 1907. Heavy losses at Gallipoli in 1915 forged a national identity alongside Australia's, and its troops fought again in World War II. From 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal began hearing Māori claims, leading to large settlements. When Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973, New Zealand lost its main market and turned to Asia. In 1985 it banned nuclear-armed ships, breaking with the US in the ANZUS alliance.
NZL.c: New Zealanders call themselves Kiwis, after the flightless bird. Māori language and culture are part of everyday life, from greetings like kia ora to the haka performed by the All Blacks before rugby matches. People love the outdoors: tramping, sailing and adventure sports such as bungee jumping. The Lord of the Rings was filmed among its mountains, and Auckland has a large Pacific Islander population.
NZL.p: Christopher Luxon's National Party has governed since 2023 in coalition with ACT and New Zealand First, cutting public spending and thousands of public service jobs while unemployment rose. Its policies on the Treaty of Waitangi and Māori programmes sparked a huge hīkoi protest march in 2024, and Parliament voted down ACT's Treaty Principles Bill in 2025. Luxon survived two party confidence votes in 2026 amid poor polling against Chris Hipkins' Labour. The cost of living and fuel prices, pushed up by the 2026 Iran war, dominate debate, and Luxon called a general election for 7 November 2026.
q: Which country was founded on the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi, whose two language versions differed?
Which country became in 1893 the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections?
Which country's rugby team performs the haka before matches?

MDG.t: Seafarers from Borneo crossed the Indian Ocean to settle Madagascar more than a thousand years ago, and Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab traders followed. In the 1800s the Merina kingdom, based in the highlands around Antananarivo, unified most of the island and traded with Britain. France invaded in 1895, made the island a colony in 1896 and exiled the last queen, Ranavalona III. In World War II British forces seized it from Vichy France in 1942. In 1947 a nationalist uprising was crushed, with tens of thousands of deaths. Madagascar became independent in 1960. Under Didier Ratsiraka, from 1975, it turned to socialism and the Soviet bloc, which left the economy in ruins. Since then politics has swung through mass protests and disputed elections. In 2002 a vote ended in a stand-off between two rival presidents, and in 2009 Andry Rajoelina, the young mayor of the capital, took power with army support. These crises kept it one of the poorest countries in the world. The island split from Africa about 160 million years ago.
MDG.c: Malagasy, related to languages of Indonesia, is spoken across the island, and French is widely used. Rice is eaten at almost every meal. In famadihana, the 'turning of the bones', families rewrap the remains of their ancestors in new cloth and dance with them. About 90% of its wildlife, including all lemurs, lives nowhere else, and Madagascar grows most of the world's vanilla.
MDG.p: Andry Rajoelina, president since 2019, was toppled in October 2025. Youth-led 'Gen Z' protests over constant water and power cuts spread across the country, and at least 22 people were killed. When an elite army unit, CAPSAT, sided with the protesters, Rajoelina fled abroad and parliament voted to remove him. CAPSAT's commander, Colonel Michael Randrianirina, was sworn in as president and promised a transition to elections; in March 2026 he made the anti-corruption chief Mamitiana Rajaonarison prime minister. The African Union suspended Madagascar. Poverty, fuel shortages and cyclones such as Gezani, which wrecked Toamasina in 2026, are the big problems.
q: Which island was first settled by seafarers from Borneo more than a thousand years ago?
Which country's last queen, Ranavalona III, was exiled when France made it a colony in 1896?
Which country grows most of the world's vanilla, and where all lemurs live?

PHL.t: Ferdinand Magellan reached the islands in 1521, and from 1565 Spain ruled them from Manila for over 300 years, spreading Catholicism and naming them after King Philip II. Filipino nationalists, inspired by the writer José Rizal, whom Spain executed in 1896, rose in revolt and declared independence in 1898. But the US won the Spanish–American War that year, bought the islands from Spain and crushed the new republic in a brutal war. American rule brought English, public schools and elected assemblies. Japan invaded in December 1941, and the Battle of Manila in 1945 destroyed most of the capital. Independence came on 4 July 1946, though US military bases stayed until 1992. Ferdinand Marcos, elected in 1965, declared martial law in 1972 and ruled as a dictator while his family amassed a fortune. The murder of opposition leader Benigno Aquino in 1983 led to the peaceful People Power revolution of 1986, which made his widow, Corazon Aquino, president.
PHL.c: The Philippines is Asia's largest Christian country, overwhelmingly Catholic, and Christmas celebrations start in September. Filipino and English are official, and more than 100 languages are spoken across over 7,000 islands. Basketball, the boxer Manny Pacquiao, karaoke and adobo are national passions, jeepneys crowd the streets, and millions of Filipinos work abroad as nurses, sailors and carers, sending money home.
PHL.p: Bongbong Marcos, the dictator's son, won the presidency in 2022 allied with Sara Duterte, daughter of his predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte. The alliance collapsed. In March 2025 Rodrigo Duterte was arrested and flown to the International Criminal Court in The Hague over killings in his war on drugs. Sara Duterte, still vice president, was impeached in 2025 and again in 2026, and her second trial is under way in the Senate. A scandal over billions of pesos stolen from flood-control projects brought mass protests and the arrest of former House speaker Martin Romualdez. Clashes with China at sea continue.
q: Which country was named after Spain's King Philip II?
Which country's People Power revolution of 1986 made Corazon Aquino president?
Which is Asia's largest Christian country, where Christmas celebrations start in September?

LKA.t: Sinhalese kingdoms based at Anuradhapura and later Polonnaruwa built great Buddhist cities and irrigation tanks over 2,000 years ago, while Tamils settled the north. The Portuguese arrived in 1505, the Dutch took the coast in the 1600s, and Britain conquered the whole island, which it called Ceylon, by 1815, bringing in Tamil workers from India to pick tea. Independence came peacefully in 1948. In 1956 Sinhala was made the only official language, angering Tamils, and in 1960 Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first woman prime minister. The country became a republic named Sri Lanka in 1972. Tensions over language, jobs and land boiled over in 1983, when anti-Tamil riots in Colombo began a civil war with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, who wanted a separate state in the north and east. The war killed tens of thousands and ended in 2009, when the army crushed the Tigers and many civilians died in the final months.
LKA.c: Most Sri Lankans are Sinhalese Buddhists; Tamils, mostly Hindu, and Muslims make up large minorities. Ceylon tea from the misty hill country is famous worldwide, rice and curry with coconut sambol is the daily meal, and cricket has been a passion since the 1996 World Cup win. Pilgrims visit the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, where the Esala Perahera parade fills the streets with elephants.
LKA.p: Sri Lanka defaulted on its debts in 2022, and protests drove President Gotabaya Rajapaksa from office. In 2024 voters turned against the old political families and elected Anura Kumara Dissanayake, leader of the leftist National People's Power, which then won a two-thirds majority in parliament. Harini Amarasuriya is prime minister. The government has pursued corruption cases, even arresting former president Ranil Wickremesinghe briefly in 2025, while sticking to an IMF rescue plan. Cyclone Ditwah killed more than 600 people in late 2025, and the 2026 Iran war brought fuel rationing.
q: Which country had the world's first woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, in 1960?
Which country's civil war with the Tamil Tigers lasted from 1983 to 2009?
Which country, once called Ceylon, is famous for its tea and the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy?

BHS.t: Lucayan people met Columbus when he made his first landfall in the Americas here in October 1492. Within a generation the Spanish had carried almost all of them off to work in mines and plantations elsewhere, and they died out. Britain claimed the islands in the 1600s, and in the early 1700s pirates such as Blackbeard used Nassau as a base until a governor drove them out. Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution brought enslaved Africans and cotton plantations, which soon failed. The islands made their living from being close to the US: blockade runners in the American Civil War, rum runners during Prohibition in the 1920s, and, after World War II, tourists and offshore banks. Lynden Pindling's Progressive Liberal Party won power in 1967, breaking the grip of the white merchant elite known as the Bay Street Boys, and led the country to independence in 1973. In 2019 Hurricane Dorian devastated Abaco and Grand Bahama.
BHS.c: Junkanoo, a parade of huge crepe-paper costumes, goatskin drums and cowbells on Boxing Day and New Year's Day, grew from the traditions of enslaved Africans. Conch, eaten raw in salad or fried as fritters, is the national food. Tourism and offshore finance drive the economy. Most visitors arrive by cruise ship in Nassau or fly to the resorts of Paradise Island and the Exumas, famous for their swimming pigs.
BHS.p: Philip Davis of the Progressive Liberal Party has been prime minister since 2021. His party won a majority again in the general election of May 2026, and he began a second term. The Free National Movement is the main opposition. The economy depends on American tourists, so US policy matters a great deal: in July 2026 the US put a 12.5% tariff on Bahamian goods, citing alleged forced labour in supply chains. Other big issues are the cost of living, violent crime in Nassau, migration from Haiti, and the threat that stronger hurricanes and rising seas pose to low-lying islands.
q: Where did Columbus make his first landfall in the Americas, in October 1492?
Which country's capital was a base for pirates such as Blackbeard in the early 1700s?
Which country celebrates Junkanoo, and whose Exumas are famous for swimming pigs?

TWN.t: Austronesian peoples lived on Taiwan for thousands of years before Dutch traders arrived in the 1620s. Chinese settlers followed, and the Qing dynasty ruled the island from 1683 until it lost a war to Japan and handed Taiwan over in 1895. Japan ruled for 50 years, building railways, schools and sugar mills. After World War II the Republic of China, led by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, took control, and in 1947 its troops killed thousands in the 228 Incident, a crackdown on protests. Losing China's civil war to Mao's communists, Chiang retreated to Taiwan in 1949 with around a million soldiers and officials, still claiming to be China's rightful government. Martial law lasted until 1987. Protected by the US during the Cold War, Taiwan grew rich making electronics. In 1971 China's UN seat passed to Beijing, and in 1979 the US switched its formal recognition too. Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996, and in 2000 the opposition won power peacefully.
TWN.c: Taiwan's TSMC makes most of the world's most advanced computer chips. Night markets sell stinky tofu, beef noodle soup and bubble tea, which was invented here. Mandarin is official and Taiwanese Hokkien is widely spoken, temples to Mazu, the sea goddess, are busy with worshippers, and in 2019 Taiwan became the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage.
TWN.p: Lai Ching-te of the Democratic Progressive Party, which stresses Taiwan's separate identity, won the presidency in 2024, but the Kuomintang and the Taiwan People's Party control the legislature, and Cho Jung-tai's government often clashes with it. A mass recall campaign against Kuomintang lawmakers failed in 2025, and an attempt to impeach Lai fell short in May 2026. Ko Wen-je, the TPP's founder, was jailed for 17 years for bribery. China, which claims Taiwan, staged large military drills around it, and only about a dozen countries recognise Taiwan officially. A 2026 trade deal with the US lowered tariffs.
q: To which island did Chiang Kai-shek retreat in 1949 after losing China's civil war?
Which country's 228 Incident of 1947 saw troops kill thousands of protesters?
Where was bubble tea invented, and where does TSMC make most of the world's most advanced chips?

JPN.t: For more than 200 years Japan's shoguns kept the country largely closed to foreigners, until US warships under Commodore Perry forced it open in 1853. In 1868 the Meiji Restoration put the emperor back at the centre and launched a crash programme of modernisation, copying Western railways, factories, schools and armies. Japan defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, the first modern Asian victory over a European power, and took Taiwan and Korea as colonies. In the 1930s militarists took control, seized Manchuria and in 1937 invaded China. The attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the US into World War II, and Japan briefly conquered much of Southeast Asia. It surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Under US occupation it adopted a pacifist constitution, and in the Cold War it became a close US ally. Rapid growth made it the world's second-largest economy by 1968, but a bubble burst around 1990, leaving decades of slow growth.
JPN.c: Japan mixes old custom with high technology: Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples stand among neon-lit cities and bullet trains. Sushi, ramen and cherry-blossom picnics in spring are part of life, and bowing, punctuality and quiet on trains are expected. Anime, manga, video games, Toyota and Sony are known worldwide, and baseball is the most popular team sport. The population is old and shrinking.
JPN.p: Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first woman prime minister in October 2025 after winning the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party, which has governed for almost all of the time since 1955. She called a snap election and in February 2026 won a two-thirds majority in the lower house, the first party to do so since the war. A hawk on defence, she said in November 2025 that Japan could intervene militarily if China attacked Taiwan, setting off a diplomatic crisis in which China restricted exports to Japan. Rising prices, an ageing population, labour shortages, immigration and plans to revise the pacifist constitution are other big issues.
q: Which country did US warships under Commodore Perry force open in 1853?
Which country's Meiji Restoration of 1868 launched a crash programme of modernisation?
Which country gave the world anime, manga, Toyota and Sony?

ISL.t: Norse settlers, many from Norway, arrived around 874, and in 930 they founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland came under Norway in 1262 and later Denmark, and for centuries it was poor, isolated and battered by volcanic eruptions and famine. A 19th-century national movement won home rule in 1904 and sovereignty in a union with the Danish king in 1918. When Germany occupied Denmark in 1940, British troops occupied Iceland to keep it from the Nazis, and American forces replaced them in 1941.
