US-GA.t: Founded in 1733 as a buffer between British South Carolina and Spanish Florida, Georgia was the last of the 13 colonies and joined the Union in 1788. Cotton and slavery spread across the state, and in the 1830s the Cherokee were forced out on the Trail of Tears after gold was found on their land. In 1864 General Sherman burned Atlanta and marched to the sea. After the Civil War, Atlanta rebuilt as the railway hub of the 'New South', but Jim Crow laws and lynching drove many Black Georgians north in the Great Migration. Atlanta was the home of Martin Luther King Jr., and its Black colleges and churches made it a centre of the civil rights movement. Jimmy Carter, a peanut farmer from Plains, became president in 1977. Its airport, Coca-Cola, Delta and CNN made Atlanta a global city, and it hosted the 1996 Olympics. Since 2000, fast growth, immigration and a large Black middle class have turned a solidly Republican state into a fierce battleground.
US-GA.c: Atlanta is home to Coca-Cola, Delta and one of the world's busiest airports, and its hip-hop and trap artists lead the American charts. Peaches, peanuts, Vidalia onions, sweet tea and Sunday church suppers mark the countryside. Savannah's oak-shaded squares draw tourists, the Masters golf tournament is played at Augusta, and film studios have made the state a rival to Hollywood.
US-GA.p: Georgia is a top swing state: Joe Biden won it in 2020 and Trump in 2024, while both its US senators are Democrats. Republicans run state government, and Governor Brian Kemp, in office since 2019, is serving his final term. He signed a six-week abortion ban and courted electric-vehicle and battery plants, including Hyundai's factory near Savannah, where a 2025 immigration raid detained hundreds of workers, most of them South Korean. The Fulton County criminal case against Trump over the 2020 election was dropped in 2025. Hurricane Helene ravaged farms in 2024, and voting rules remain fiercely contested.
q: Which was the last of the 13 colonies, founded in 1733 as a buffer against Spanish Florida?
Which state's capital was burned by General Sherman in 1864 before his march to the sea?
Which state is home to Coca-Cola and Delta, and hosts the Masters at Augusta?

US-SC.t: English planters from Barbados founded Charles Town, now Charleston, in 1670. Rice, indigo and later cotton plantations were worked by enslaved Africans, who made up most of the population, and Charleston was the main port where captives arrived. Fearing that Abraham Lincoln's election threatened slavery, South Carolina was the first state to secede, in December 1860, and the Civil War began when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour in April 1861. Defeat left it poor for generations, and Jim Crow laws kept Black citizens from voting until the civil rights era; a case from Clarendon County was one of those decided in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Fort Jackson and Parris Island trained soldiers and marines for both world wars, and the Savannah River Site made material for nuclear weapons in the Cold War. Since the 1990s, foreign carmakers such as BMW and a booming coast have transformed its economy.
US-SC.c: Gullah Geechee culture, kept alive by descendants of enslaved West Africans on the Sea Islands, shapes its food, crafts such as sweetgrass baskets, and speech. Charleston's pastel houses and church steeples, shrimp and grits, Lowcountry boils and mustard-based barbecue define the coast. Myrtle Beach draws huge summer crowds, and football at Clemson and the University of South Carolina divides families.
US-SC.p: Republicans dominate South Carolina. Henry McMaster, governor since 2017, is serving his last term. Republicans hold large majorities in the legislature, and in 2023 the state supreme court upheld a ban on most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Rapid growth along the coast and around Greenville and Charleston has strained roads, schools and housing, while hurricanes and rising seas threaten the Lowcountry. The state has drawn big car and battery factories, from BMW and Volvo to Scout Motors, and power supply for new industry and data centres is a growing debate.
q: Which was the first state to secede, in December 1860?
In which state's harbour did the Civil War begin, at Fort Sumter?
Which state's Sea Islands keep Gullah Geechee culture alive?

US-NC.t: North Carolina was one of the 13 colonies and ratified the Constitution in 1789, once a Bill of Rights was promised. Tobacco, cotton and the labour of enslaved people built its economy, and it joined the Confederacy in 1861. After the Civil War, tobacco and textile mills, from Durham's cigarettes to the mill towns of the Piedmont, became its industry. On 17 December 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flights at Kitty Hawk on the Outer Banks. The world wars brought huge army and marine bases, Fort Bragg and Camp Lejeune, that still shape the state. In 1960 four Black students sat at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro; their sit-in spread across the South and pushed the civil rights movement forward. From the 1950s Research Triangle Park, between Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill, helped turn a farm state into a centre for universities and technology, while Charlotte grew into a major banking city.
US-NC.c: College basketball rivalries between Duke, UNC and NC State are close to a religion, and Charlotte is the heart of NASCAR racing. Barbecue divides the state: vinegar-based in the east, tomato-tinged in the west. The Blue Ridge Mountains and Outer Banks beaches draw visitors, and fast-growing Charlotte and Raleigh attract newcomers from across the country.
US-NC.p: North Carolina is a swing state that leans Republican in presidential races. Democrat Josh Stein became governor in January 2025, succeeding fellow Democrat Roy Cooper, but Republicans control the legislature and often override his vetoes. Just before he took office, they moved some of the governor's powers to other officials. A 2024 state supreme court race was disputed for six months before the Democrat was confirmed as the winner, and in 2025 Republicans redrew the congressional map to gain a seat. Rebuilding western mountain towns devastated by Hurricane Helene in September 2024, fast population growth and housing costs are major issues.
q: Where did the Wright brothers make the first powered flights, at Kitty Hawk in 1903?
Which state's Greensboro lunch-counter sit-in of 1960 spread across the South?
Which state has Research Triangle Park and the Duke–UNC basketball rivalry?

US-VA.t: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in the Americas, and in 1619 the first enslaved Africans recorded in the English colonies arrived there. Tobacco plantations built on slavery made Virginia the richest and most populous colony. Virginians such as George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison led the American Revolution, which ended with the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781. In the Civil War Richmond was the Confederate capital, Virginia was the main battlefield, its western counties broke away, and the war ended at Appomattox in 1865. Segregation was strict, and in the late 1950s some counties closed their public schools rather than admit Black students. World War II and the Cold War transformed the state: the Pentagon was built in Arlington in 1943, the Norfolk naval base became the world's largest, and the CIA settled at Langley. Northern Virginia's suburbs grew rapidly on defence contracts and technology firms.
US-VA.c: Eight presidents were born in Virginia, more than any other state. Colonial Williamsburg, Monticello and Civil War battlefields draw history lovers, while the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and Virginia Beach draw everyone else. Smithfield ham, Chesapeake Bay oysters and a fast-growing wine industry feed it, and Northern Virginia holds the world's largest cluster of data centres.
US-VA.p: Democrat Abigail Spanberger, a former CIA officer and congresswoman, became Virginia's first woman governor in January 2026 after winning by a wide margin in November 2025, succeeding Republican Glenn Youngkin. Democrats also won the other statewide offices and expanded their majority in the House of Delegates, helped by anger at Trump's cuts to the federal workforce, which hit Northern Virginia hard. In April 2026 voters narrowly approved a Democratic plan to redraw congressional districts, but the state supreme court struck it down in May. Electricity demand from data centres, the cost of living and housing are central issues.
q: Which state was home to Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in the Americas?
Which state's capital was the Confederate capital, and where did the war end at Appomattox?
Which state was the birthplace of eight presidents and has the Pentagon?

US-DC.t: In 1790 Congress chose a site on the Potomac River for a capital that belonged to no state, on land given by Maryland and Virginia. Pierre L'Enfant laid out its wide avenues. British troops burned the White House and the Capitol in 1814. Slavery was abolished here in 1862, and freed people made the city a centre of Black American life, with Howard University founded in 1867. The New Deal and World War II swelled the federal workforce, and during the Cold War Washington became the command centre of the Western alliance. It was also the nation's stage for protest: in 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the Lincoln Memorial. Residents won a vote for president in 1961 and an elected mayor and council in 1973, but Congress can still overrule local laws. Riots in 1968 and the crack epidemic of the 1980s left deep scars; since the 2000s the city has grown richer and gentrified.
US-DC.c: Washington is not a state, and its licence plates protest 'Taxation Without Representation'. The Smithsonian museums on the National Mall are free. Its long Black majority gave it go-go music, the half-smoke sausage and a strong civil rights tradition, and today those neighbourhoods mix with young professionals, students and diplomats from embassies around the world. Cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin draw crowds every spring.
US-DC.p: Washington votes overwhelmingly Democratic and elects a mayor and council, but Congress has the final say over its laws and budget, and its residents have only a non-voting delegate in Congress. Muriel Bowser, mayor since 2015, decided not to seek a fourth term in 2026. In August 2025 President Trump took temporary control of the city's police and sent the National Guard onto the streets, citing crime, over local objections. In November 2025 two Guard soldiers were shot near the White House, and one died. Federal job cuts in 2025 hit the local economy and housing market.
q: Which capital was burned by British troops in 1814?
Where did Martin Luther King Jr. give his 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
Which place's licence plates protest 'Taxation Without Representation'?

US-MD.t: Maryland was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics, and its 1649 Toleration Act was an early law protecting freedom of worship. Tobacco plantations relied on enslaved Africans. Maryland joined the Union in 1788 and gave land for Washington, D.C. In 1814 the defence of Fort McHenry in Baltimore inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner'. A slave state that stayed in the Union during the Civil War, it saw the war's bloodiest single day at Antietam in 1862, and both Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman escaped slavery from here. Baltimore's port, railways and the huge Sparrows Point steelworks made it an industrial city, which built Liberty ships in World War II. In the Cold War the federal government spread into the suburbs: the NSA settled at Fort Meade, and NASA's Goddard centre and the National Institutes of Health grew nearby. Baltimore lost factories and people after the 1968 riots, while the suburbs grew rich. In 2015 the death of Freddie Gray in police custody led to protests in Baltimore.
US-MD.c: Blue crabs from Chesapeake Bay, steamed and dusted with Old Bay seasoning, are the signature meal, cracked with mallets on newspaper-covered tables. The US Naval Academy is in Annapolis, sailing fills the bay and lacrosse is unusually popular. Baltimore offers Ravens football, row houses with marble steps, Edgar Allan Poe's grave and the setting of the TV series 'The Wire'.
US-MD.p: Maryland is firmly Democratic. Wes Moore, an Army veteran and author, became governor in 2023 as the state's first Black governor. A large budget gap led to tax rises in 2025, and federal job cuts under Trump hit Maryland harder than most states because so many residents work for the government. In March 2024 a container ship knocked down Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge, killing six road workers, and rebuilding will take years. In 2025 Moore vetoed a bill to study reparations for slavery, and he has backed redrawing congressional maps in answer to Republican states.
q: Which colony was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics?
Which state's Fort McHenry inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner' in 1814?
Which state is famous for blue crabs with Old Bay, and is the setting of 'The Wire'?

US-DE.t: Swedish and Dutch settlers came first, before England took over. On 7 December 1787 Delaware became the first state to ratify the US Constitution, so it calls itself 'the First State'. It was a slave state that stayed in the Union during the Civil War. In 1802 the French immigrant É. I. du Pont built a gunpowder mill on the Brandywine River, and DuPont grew into one of the world's biggest chemical companies. It supplied explosives in World War I, and in the 1930s its labs invented nylon, later used for parachutes in World War II. In 1899 the state passed a flexible corporation law, and its Court of Chancery, where expert judges decide business disputes without juries, made it the favourite legal home of American companies. In the 1980s loose limits on interest rates drew credit card banks to Wilmington. Joe Biden represented Delaware in the US Senate for 36 years before becoming vice president in 2009.
US-DE.c: Most big American companies are legally registered here, many at a single office address in Wilmington, though few have staff in the state. With no sales tax, shoppers from nearby states flock to its outlet malls. Beach towns such as Rehoboth fill up in summer, scrapple is a breakfast staple, and Joe Biden, president from 2021 to 2025, still lives near Wilmington.
US-DE.p: Delaware is solidly Democratic. Matt Meyer, a former county executive, became governor in January 2025. The state's biggest worry is its business franchise, which pays a large share of the budget. After a Delaware judge struck down Elon Musk's huge Tesla pay package in 2024, Tesla and other firms moved their legal homes to Texas or Nevada, and in 2025 lawmakers rushed through changes to make corporate law friendlier to controlling shareholders. Rising electricity bills, property taxes and school funding are also big issues.
q: Which state was first to ratify the US Constitution, on 7 December 1787?
Which state's DuPont labs invented nylon in the 1930s?
Which state is the legal home of most big American companies, and has no sales tax?

US-NJ.t: New Jersey saw some of the hardest fighting of the American Revolution: George Washington crossed the Delaware to win at Trenton on Christmas night 1776 and again at Princeton days later. It was the third state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787. Wedged between New York and Philadelphia, it industrialised early. Paterson's mills, Newark's factories and Thomas Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park, where he developed the phonograph and the electric light bulb, made it an engine of invention. Millions of immigrants from Italy, Ireland, Poland and elsewhere arrived to work there. In both world wars its shipyards and chemical works ran flat out, and in 1937 the airship Hindenburg burst into flames at Lakehurst. Albert Einstein, a refugee from Nazi Germany, lived and worked in Princeton from 1933. After 1945 highways like the Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway made it a model of American suburbia, and old industries gave way to pharmaceuticals and offices.
US-NJ.c: It is the most densely populated state, and its diners, boardwalks and the Jersey Shore are part of American pop culture. Bruce Springsteen and Frank Sinatra are its musical heroes. Pizza and bagels rival New York's, pork roll sandwiches start the day, and a large share of residents were born abroad, from India, the Dominican Republic and many other countries.
US-NJ.p: Democrat Mikie Sherrill, a former Navy helicopter pilot and congresswoman, became governor in January 2026 after a clear win in November 2025, succeeding fellow Democrat Phil Murphy. Democrats control the legislature, but the state had swung towards Donald Trump in 2024, so her result was watched as a test of his popularity. She campaigned mainly on the cost of living, promising to freeze electricity bills, which soared in 2025 as demand from data centres pushed up power prices. Property taxes, among the highest in the US, housing costs and New Jersey Transit's troubled trains are other big issues.
q: In which state did Washington win at Trenton after crossing the Delaware in 1776?
In which state did Thomas Edison develop the light bulb, and did the Hindenburg burn in 1937?
Which is the most densely populated state, home of Bruce Springsteen and the Jersey Shore?

US-CT.t: Puritans from Massachusetts settled the Connecticut River valley in the 1630s, and the 1639 Fundamental Orders are often called one of the first written constitutions, hence 'the Constitution State'. Connecticut joined the Union in 1788. In the 1800s its inventors and factories in Hartford, New Haven and Waterbury made clocks, brass, rubber goods and Colt revolvers, and immigrants from Ireland, Italy and Poland filled the mills. In both world wars its factories made guns, aircraft engines and submarines, earning it the name 'Arsenal of the Nation'. During the Cold War the Electric Boat yard in Groton built the Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine, launched in 1954, and Pratt & Whitney built jet engines. Hartford became known as the insurance capital of the world. Wealthy New York commuters settled in Fairfield County, while old factory cities such as Bridgeport lost jobs and people. In 2012 a gunman killed 20 children and six adults at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown.
US-CT.c: Yale University dominates New Haven, where coal-fired 'apizza' from old pizzerias draws long queues. Mark Twain wrote Tom Sawyer while living in Hartford. The state mixes wealthy suburbs with yacht clubs, quiet colonial villages with white churches, the UConn basketball teams that fans follow fiercely, and two huge casinos run by Native nations, Foxwoods and Mohegan Sun.
US-CT.p: Connecticut is firmly Democratic. Ned Lamont, a businessman who has been governor since 2019, has kept a tight budget, built large reserves and paid down pension debt. Housing costs and the shortage of new homes in wealthy suburbs dominate debate: in 2025 Lamont vetoed a major housing bill, saying it went too far, then signed a revised version passed in a special session. Electricity bills are among the highest in the country. Federal cuts to Medicaid and research worry hospitals and universities, while Electric Boat is hiring thousands of workers to build submarines.
q: Which state is called 'the Constitution State' after its 1639 Fundamental Orders?
Which state's Groton shipyard built the Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine?
Which state is home to Yale, and whose capital is known as the insurance capital of the world?

US-RI.t: Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts for his religious views, founded Providence in 1636 as a refuge where church and state were kept apart. Rhode Island's merchants later grew rich from shipping, including a large part of the American slave trade. It was the first colony to renounce allegiance to Britain, in May 1776, but it feared a strong central government and was the last of the 13 to ratify the Constitution, in 1790. Around the same time Samuel Slater's mills in Pawtucket started America's industrial revolution, and textile and jewellery factories drew immigrants from Ireland, Italy, Portugal and French Canada. In the Gilded Age the richest families built summer mansions in Newport. Both world wars made Narragansett Bay a naval hub: the Newport torpedo station turned out torpedoes for the fleet, and the Naval War College still trains officers there. After World War II the mills closed, and Providence became known for political corruption before reviving its downtown from the 1990s.
US-RI.c: It is the smallest state, and nowhere is far from the sea. Rhode Islanders drink coffee milk, eat clam chowder, stuffed quahogs and 'hot wieners', and many have Italian, Portuguese or Irish roots. Newport hosts famous jazz and folk festivals and sailing races, and Providence's WaterFire lights bonfires on its rivers on summer evenings.
US-RI.p: Rhode Island is solidly Democratic, and politics is personal. Democrat Dan McKee became governor in 2021 when Gina Raimondo left to join President Biden's cabinet, and won a full term in 2022. His approval ratings have been low, partly because of the Washington Bridge, a main route into Providence that was suddenly closed to westbound traffic in December 2023 because of structural failures and had to be rebuilt. In September 2026 he lost the Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes. Housing costs, among the fastest rising in New England, offshore wind projects that the Trump administration tried to halt in 2025, and the state's finances are key issues.
q: Which colony did Roger Williams found at Providence in 1636, keeping church and state apart?
Which was the last of the 13 colonies to ratify the Constitution, in 1790?
Which is the smallest state, where people drink coffee milk?

US-MA.t: The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in 1620 with help from the Wampanoag people, and Puritans founded Boston in 1630 and Harvard in 1636. Boston led the resistance to Britain: the Boston Tea Party of 1773 and the first battles at Lexington and Concord in 1775 began the Revolution. Massachusetts joined the Union in 1788 and became a centre of the movement to abolish slavery. In the 1800s textile mills at Lowell and Lawrence drew Irish, Italian and French-Canadian workers, and Irish Americans came to dominate Boston politics. In World War II and the Cold War, radar and computer labs at MIT and military contracts built a high-tech industry along Route 128. In 1960 John F. Kennedy of Massachusetts became the first Catholic president. Boston's fights over school busing in the 1970s exposed deep racial divisions. Since then universities, hospitals and biotechnology have made Greater Boston one of the world's great research centres, and in 2004 Massachusetts became the first state to allow same-sex marriage.
US-MA.c: Harvard and MIT draw students and scientists from around the world. Bostonians are known for their accent, the Red Sox and Fenway Park, and the Boston Marathon every April. Clam chowder, lobster rolls and Dunkin' coffee are local staples. Cape Cod's beaches, Plymouth's Pilgrim story and the autumn leaves of the Berkshires draw visitors.
US-MA.p: Massachusetts is among the most Democratic states. Maura Healey, governor since 2023, is the first woman elected to the job. Housing costs, among the highest in the country, are the main issue, and Healey has pushed laws to build more homes. In 2023 and 2024 a surge of migrant families overwhelmed the emergency shelter system, leading to limits on stays. In 2025 Harvard took the Trump administration to court after it froze billions of dollars in research grants, and federal cuts threaten the state's universities and hospitals. High energy costs are another worry.
q: Which state saw the Boston Tea Party and the first battles of the Revolution?
Which became in 2004 the first state to allow same-sex marriage?
Which state is home to Harvard, MIT and the Red Sox?

CN-ZJ.t: Zhejiang has been one of China's richest regions for a thousand years. Hangzhou was the capital of the Southern Song dynasty in the 1100s and 1200s, and Marco Polo called it the finest city in the world. The Grand Canal carried its rice and silk north. After the First Opium War, Ningbo became a treaty port, and Ningbo merchants went on to dominate business in nearby Shanghai. Chiang Kai-shek was born in Fenghua in Zhejiang, and many of his Nationalist leaders were from the province. Japan occupied much of it from 1937, and in 1942 its troops used germ weapons in Zhejiang. After 1978 Zhejiang pioneered private business: Wenzhou's family workshops making shoes, lighters and buttons became the model of bottom-up capitalism, and Yiwu grew into the world's largest market for small goods. In 1999 Jack Ma founded Alibaba in Hangzhou. Xi Jinping was the province's party secretary from 2002 to 2007, and several of his trusted officials came from his time there.
CN-ZJ.c: Hangzhou's West Lake, ringed by willows, pagodas and tea hills, is one of China's classic views, and its Longjing green tea is prized. Shaoxing makes yellow rice wine, and canal towns like Wuzhen draw crowds. The local Wu dialects are very different from Mandarin. Food is light and slightly sweet: Dongpo pork, West Lake fish in vinegar sauce and Ningbo rice cakes. Hangzhou hosted the 2023 Asian Games.
CN-ZJ.p: The party secretary, Wang Hao, outranks the governor, Liu Jie. Zhejiang is China's private-sector heartland, and Beijing named it a demonstration zone for Xi Jinping's 'common prosperity' drive to narrow wealth gaps. Hangzhou became the symbol of China's tech revival in 2025, when local start-up DeepSeek released a low-cost AI model that shook global markets, and robot makers like Unitree drew attention. Alibaba recovered after a government crackdown on tech giants from 2020. Exporters in Yiwu and Ningbo, one of the world's busiest ports, face the strain of US tariffs.
q: Which province's capital was the Southern Song capital, called by Marco Polo the finest city in the world?
Which province's Wenzhou and Yiwu became models of bottom-up capitalism after 1978?
Which province's capital has the West Lake and Longjing tea, and is the home of Alibaba?

CN-SH.t: Shanghai was a modest county town until the First Opium War. In 1842 the Treaty of Nanking opened it to foreign trade, and the British, French and Americans carved out settlements that they ran themselves, outside Chinese law. By the 1920s it was Asia's most cosmopolitan city, with banks along the riverfront Bund, factories, gangsters and jazz. The Chinese Communist Party held its first congress here in 1921. In 1927 Chiang Kai-shek massacred communists and unionists in the city. Japan fought a brutal battle for Shanghai in 1937 and occupied it, and some 20,000 Jewish refugees from Europe found shelter in the Hongkou district. After 1949 foreigners left and Shanghai became a state-run industrial city; it was also the base of the radical 'Gang of Four' during the Cultural Revolution. In 1990 Beijing opened Pudong, the farmland across the river, as a new financial zone, and its skyline of skyscrapers now faces the Bund. Shanghai hosted the 2010 World Expo.
CN-SH.c: China's biggest city, with about 25 million people, Shanghai is its financial capital and most international place. The Bund, the Pudong skyline and the old alleyway lilong houses sit side by side. People speak Shanghainese at home and Mandarin at work. Xiaolongbao soup dumplings, shengjian fried buns and sweet braised pork are local classics. Tesla's first factory outside the United States opened here in 2019.
CN-SH.p: The party secretary, Chen Jining, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Zhu Zhongming. Shanghai's party chief is usually a rising national figure: Li Qiang, its party secretary during the harsh two-month Covid lockdown of 2022, became China's premier in 2023. The city is a centre of carmaking, chips, finance and biotech, and it is building up its stock exchange's tech board. Its challenges are a fast-ageing population, falling house prices and foreign firms scaling back as tensions with the United States grow.
q: Where did the Chinese Communist Party hold its first congress, in 1921?
Which city sheltered some 20,000 Jewish refugees from Europe in its Hongkou district?
Which is China's biggest city, with the Bund and the Pudong skyline?

CN-JS.t: Jiangsu, on the lower Yangtze, has been rich since the Grand Canal connected it to Beijing. Suzhou's silk and gardens and Yangzhou's salt merchants made the region famous. Nanjing, 'southern capital', was the capital of the early Ming dynasty and later of the Taiping rebels, whose defeat in 1864 left the city wrecked. In 1842 the treaty that ended the First Opium War was signed at Nanjing. Sun Yat-sen was sworn in there as first president of the Republic of China in 1912, and Chiang Kai-shek made it his capital from 1927. In December 1937 Japanese troops captured Nanjing and murdered and raped on a huge scale in the Nanjing Massacre; China puts the death toll at 300,000. After 1949 Jiangsu was split in two, then reunited in 1952. From the 1980s rural township enterprises boomed, and Suzhou's industrial parks, built with Singapore, drew foreign factories, making Jiangsu one of the richest provinces.
CN-JS.c: Suzhou's classical gardens and canals and Nanjing's city walls and Purple Mountain are top sights. Jiangsu's Huaiyang cuisine is delicate and slightly sweet: lion's head meatballs, salted duck from Nanjing and Yangzhou fried rice. People here speak Wu dialects in the south and Mandarin in the north. In 2025 an amateur football league between Jiangsu's cities, the 'Su Super League', became a national craze with packed stadiums and fierce banter.
CN-JS.p: The party secretary, Xin Changxing, outranks the governor, Liu Xiaotao. Jiangsu has the second-largest economy among China's provinces, with industries from solar panels and chemicals to chips and biomedicine. It is a manufacturing base for foreign companies, which makes it exposed to US tariffs and supply chains moving elsewhere. Like other provinces it faces a property slump, local-government debts and a rapidly ageing population. Pollution in Lake Tai and the Yangtze has improved after closures of chemical plants.
q: Which province's capital was the scene of a massacre by Japanese troops in December 1937?
In which province was the treaty ending the First Opium War signed, in 1842?
Which province has Suzhou's classical gardens and gave its name to Yangzhou fried rice?

US-OR.t: Chinook, Klamath, Nez Perce and many other peoples lived in what is now Oregon before fur traders came. In the 1840s thousands of American families followed the Oregon Trail to the Willamette Valley, and the 1846 Oregon Treaty with Britain set the border at the 49th parallel. Oregon became a state in 1859, with a constitution that banned Black people from settling there, wording not removed until 1926. Timber, salmon and wheat built its economy, and the Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River brought cheap hydropower in the 1930s. In World War II Portland's Kaiser shipyards built hundreds of cargo ships, drawing thousands of workers, and in 1942 a Japanese floatplane dropped firebombs on its forests. Japanese balloon bombs killed six people near Bly in 1945, the only deaths from enemy action on the US mainland. From the 1970s Oregon led on environmental laws such as a bottle deposit, and the timber industry declined as old forests were protected.
US-OR.c: Portland is known for coffee, craft beer, food carts and the slogan 'Keep Portland Weird'. Nike was founded in Oregon and is still based near Portland. The whole coast is open to the public by law, Crater Lake is the deepest lake in the US, and the dry east of the state is cattle and wheat country with very different politics.
US-OR.p: Oregon is firmly Democratic in Portland, Eugene and Salem, and strongly Republican in the rural east. Democrat Tina Kotek has been governor since 2023. Homelessness, drug addiction and housing costs dominate politics: in 2024 the state reversed its first-in-the-nation decriminalisation of hard drugs. In 2025 Kotek pushed through a petrol tax rise to fund roads, which opponents then challenged by referendum. When President Trump tried to send National Guard troops to Portland in late 2025, saying federal immigration offices needed protection, the state sued, and a federal judge blocked the deployment. Wildfires and the timber economy remain long-running concerns.
q: Which state was the goal of thousands of families on a famous trail in the 1840s?
In which state did Japanese balloon bombs kill six people in 1945, the only enemy-caused deaths on the US mainland?
Which state is Nike's home, with Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the US?

CA-NU.t: Inuit have lived across the Arctic for about a thousand years, hunting seal, whale and caribou. For centuries outsiders came mainly for whales, furs and the search for the Northwest Passage. Change came quickly during the Cold War. The United States and Canada built radar stations of the DEW Line across the Arctic in the 1950s, and Ottawa moved Inuit from nomadic camps into permanent settlements with schools and nursing stations. Many children were sent away to residential schools, and in 1953 some Inuit families were moved to the High Arctic, partly to assert Canada's sovereignty there, where they suffered great hardship. From the 1970s Inuit leaders campaigned for a territory of their own. After decades of negotiation, the largest Indigenous land claim in Canadian history created Nunavut in 1999 by splitting the Northwest Territories. Its name means 'our land' in Inuktitut, and most of its government is meant to reflect Inuit values.
CA-NU.c: About 85% of people are Inuit, and Inuktitut is spoken in homes, schools and the legislature. Throat singing, Inuit sculpture and prints from Cape Dorset, and games like the one-foot high kick are known around the world. Country food such as seal, caribou and Arctic char is shared widely. No roads link its communities to the rest of Canada, so everything arrives by plane or summer sealift.
CA-NU.p: Nunavut has no political parties. After the October 2025 territorial election, which had the lowest turnout in its history, members chose John Main as premier. Housing is the most urgent problem: many homes are badly overcrowded, which worsens health problems such as tuberculosis. Food costs in stores are among the highest in North America. Climate change and growing interest in the Northwest Passage from the United States, Russia and China have made Arctic sovereignty and defence national priorities, and in January 2024 Ottawa and the territory signed a deal giving Nunavut control over its land and resources.
q: Which territory was created in 1999 by the largest Indigenous land claim in Canadian history?
Which territory's name means 'our land' in Inuktitut?
Which territory is about 85% Inuit, with no roads linking its communities to the rest of Canada?

CA-NL.t: Vikings landed at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000 AD, the first Europeans known to reach the Americas. Five centuries later the rich cod fishery of the Grand Banks drew fishermen from England, France, Spain and Portugal, and Newfoundland became one of England's oldest colonies. It stayed apart from Canada in 1867. In World War I its regiment was almost wiped out at Beaumont-Hamel on the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916. War debts and the Great Depression bankrupted it, and in 1934 it gave up self-rule to be run by a British commission. In World War II American and British bases brought jobs. In 1948 a campaign led by Joey Smallwood won two referendums, the second narrowly, and it joined Canada in 1949. The cod fishery collapsed from overfishing, and Ottawa closed it in 1992, putting tens of thousands of people out of work. Offshore oil later brought a new boom.
CA-NL.c: Newfoundlanders have their own dialects, folk music, jokes and a half-hour time zone. Visitors notice the brightly painted houses of St. John's, icebergs drifting past in spring and the tradition of 'screech-in' ceremonies with rum. On 11 September 2001, the town of Gander hosted thousands of stranded air passengers, the story told in the musical 'Come From Away'.
CA-NL.p: Tony Wakeham's Progressive Conservatives won the October 2025 election, ending a decade of Liberal government. A big issue was a proposed deal with Hydro-Québec to rework the Churchill Falls hydroelectric contract, which many Newfoundlanders felt had cheated them for decades. Wakeham ordered an independent review, dropped a promised referendum, and in September 2026 the legislature narrowly approved a revised agreement. The province carries heavy debt from the Muskrat Falls dam, which ran billions over budget. An ageing, shrinking rural population, offshore oil and health care staffing are other big issues.
q: Where did Vikings land at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000 AD?
Which province stayed apart from Canada until 1949, joining after two referendums led by Joey Smallwood?
Which province has its own half-hour time zone, and whose town of Gander inspired 'Come From Away'?

CA-NS.t: Nova Scotia, 'New Scotland', was fought over by France and Britain for a century. Britain expelled most of the French-speaking Acadians in 1755, and Loyalists, Black Loyalists who had escaped slavery, and Scottish Highlanders later settled the land. It was a founding province of Confederation in 1867, though many Nova Scotians resented it, fearing that trade would shift inland to Ontario. Halifax's deep harbour made it the main port for convoys crossing the Atlantic in both world wars. In December 1917 a French munitions ship collided with another vessel and exploded in the harbour. The Halifax Explosion killed about 2,000 people and was the largest man-made blast of its time. Boston, which sent help, still receives a Christmas tree from Nova Scotia every year in thanks. After World War II the coal mines and steel mills of Cape Breton slowly closed, and the cod fishery collapsed in the 1990s, pushing many young people to move west for work.
CA-NS.c: Scottish Gaelic, fiddle music and Celtic festivals live on, especially on Cape Breton Island, and Halifax has one of Canada's oldest Black communities. Lobster, scallops and wild blueberries are its signature foods. The Bluenose schooner on the Canadian dime, the lighthouse at Peggy's Cove and the graves of Titanic victims in Halifax draw visitors from all over the world.
CA-NS.p: Tim Houston's Progressive Conservatives took power in 2021 and won a much bigger majority in a snap election in November 2024, with the NDP becoming the official opposition. Houston has pushed to lower barriers to trade between provinces, and after US tariffs hit in 2025 he argued for opening up offshore wind, mining and possibly natural gas development, which worries environmental groups. Housing shortages in Halifax, crowded emergency rooms and the cost of living are top concerns, and wildfires in 2023 burned homes near Halifax.
q: Which province's capital was devastated in 1917 by the largest man-made explosion of its time?
Which province sends Boston a Christmas tree every year to thank it for help after a 1917 disaster?
Which province has the lighthouse at Peggy's Cove and keeps Gaelic alive on Cape Breton Island?

CN-SD.t: Shandong was the home of Confucius, born in Qufu around 551 BC, whose ideas about family duty, order and learning shaped China for two thousand years. The Yellow River crosses the province to the sea and has changed course here many times with devastating floods. In the scramble for China, Germany seized Qingdao in 1897 after two German missionaries were killed, and Britain leased Weihaiwei. Anger at foreigners and missionaries helped spark the Boxer Rebellion, which began in Shandong in 1899. Japan captured Qingdao from Germany in 1914, and when the Paris Peace Conference let Japan keep Germany's rights in Shandong, students in Beijing protested on 4 May 1919, launching the May Fourth Movement that shaped modern Chinese nationalism. Japan occupied the province again from 1937. After 1949 Shandong's farmers and oil workers at the Shengli field fed and fuelled the country, and after 1978 its coastal cities such as Qingdao and Yantai became export hubs.
CN-SD.c: Qingdao's red-roofed German buildings and the Tsingtao brewery, founded by German settlers in 1903, are its signatures, along with a summer beer festival. Pilgrims climb Mount Tai, the most sacred of China's five holy mountains, and visit the Confucius temple at Qufu. Lu cuisine, one of China's great culinary traditions, is known for seafood, braised dishes and scallions. Shandong people have a reputation for being tall, blunt and loyal.
CN-SD.p: The party secretary, Lin Wu, outranks the governor, Zhou Naixiang. With about 100 million people, Shandong is one of China's most populous provinces and its third-largest economy, but it relies on heavy industry such as steel, chemicals and oil refining. Its many small independent 'teapot' refineries buy much of the sanctioned oil from Iran and Russia, which has drawn US sanctions. Leaders are trying to shift toward greener industry and high-tech manufacturing. Shandong's young people have long competed fiercely in exams for civil service jobs.
q: Which province was the home of Confucius?
Which province's port did Germany seize in 1897, and where did the Boxer Rebellion begin?
Which province has the Tsingtao brewery and Mount Tai, the most sacred of China's five holy mountains?

CN-HE.t: Hebei wraps around Beijing and Tianjin, and its history is tied to guarding the capital. The Great Wall runs across its north, meeting the sea at Shanhaiguan, and Qing emperors built a summer retreat at Chengde beyond the wall. The province was a battlefield again and again: the Boxers fought foreign troops here in 1900, and in July 1937 a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge, just outside Beijing, started full-scale war between China and Japan. In the war, Japanese 'kill all, burn all, loot all' campaigns devastated Hebei villages that supported communist guerrillas. The communist leaders ran the civil war from Xibaipo in Hebei before entering Beijing in 1949. Under the People's Republic, Hebei became a centre of steel and heavy industry. In 1976 the Tangshan earthquake destroyed the city and killed over 240,000 people by the official count, one of the deadliest earthquakes of the century. In 2017 Xi Jinping announced Xiong'an, a new city in Hebei meant to take offices and people out of crowded Beijing.
CN-HE.c: Visitors walk the Great Wall at sections such as Jinshanling and Shanhaiguan and see the Qing resort palaces of Chengde. Hebei's food is simple northern fare: donkey meat burgers, called lurou huoshao, from Baoding, and noodles and dumplings. Wuqiao county is the home of Chinese acrobatics. The seaside resort of Beidaihe is where top Communist Party leaders traditionally gather each summer for informal meetings.
CN-HE.p: The party secretary, Luo Wen, outranks the governor, Wang Zhengpu. Hebei's main job is to serve the capital region: it absorbs offices, universities and factories moved out of Beijing, and it is building Xiong'an, which has filled more slowly than planned. Its steel industry, the largest of any province, has been cut back to fight the smog that once choked Beijing, and air quality has improved. In 2023 floodwater was diverted into low-lying parts of Hebei to protect Beijing and Tianjin, forcing hundreds of thousands to leave their homes.
q: Which province wraps around Beijing, and saw the Marco Polo Bridge clash start war with Japan in 1937?
Which province's city of Tangshan was destroyed by an earthquake in 1976?
Which province has the Qing summer retreat at Chengde and the seaside resort of Beidaihe?

CN-TJ.t: Tianjin grew up as the port for Beijing, where the Grand Canal met the Hai River near the sea. British and French forces took the city during the Second Opium War, and the Treaties of Tianjin in 1858 and the Convention of Peking in 1860 opened it to foreigners. Eventually nine foreign powers, from Britain and Japan to Austria-Hungary and Italy, held concessions here, each building in its own style. In 1900 the Boxers besieged the foreign quarters until an eight-nation army stormed the city. After the Qing fell, retired warlords and the last emperor Puyi lived in Tianjin's concessions. Japan occupied the city from 1937 to 1945. Under the People's Republic it became a heavy industrial port. It was folded into Hebei province in 1958 and made a municipality again in 1967. The 1976 Tangshan earthquake badly damaged it. In the 2000s Beijing poured money into the Binhai New Area. In 2015 explosions at a chemical warehouse in its port killed 173 people.
CN-TJ.c: Tianjin's 'Five Avenues' are lined with European villas from the concession era, and the Italian quarter has piazzas and cafes. Locals are known for crosstalk comedy, xiangsheng, performed in teahouses. Breakfast is jianbing, a crepe with egg and crisp cracker, and the city is famous for Goubuli steamed buns and fried twisted dough sticks called mahua. A giant Ferris wheel sits on a bridge over the river.
CN-TJ.p: The party secretary, Chen Min'er, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Zhang Gong. Tianjin is one of China's most indebted local governments. Its Binhai New Area, once promoted as the next Pudong, fell short, and the city admitted in 2018 that it had inflated its economic figures. Leaders are trying to tie it closer to Beijing and Hebei, and the high-speed train to Beijing takes about half an hour. The port, aerospace and car industries remain important. Tianjin hosted a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2025.
q: Which city had concessions held by nine foreign powers, including Austria-Hungary and Italy?
Which port city did the Boxers besiege in 1900 until an eight-nation army stormed it?
Which city is known for crosstalk comedy and a giant Ferris wheel on a bridge?

CA-NT.t: Dene, Métis and Inuvialuit peoples lived here long before the fur trade. Canada bought this vast area, Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory, from the Hudson's Bay Company in 1870, and for decades it was run from Ottawa with little say for the people who lived there. Provinces and territories were carved out of it until 1999, leaving a much smaller territory. Treaties 8 and 11 were signed with the Dene in 1899 and 1921, largely to open the land to mining and oil. Gold at Yellowknife in the 1930s and oil at Norman Wells brought newcomers. During the Cold War the DEW Line of radar stations was built across the Arctic in the 1950s to warn of Soviet bombers. From the 1970s Indigenous groups fought proposed pipelines and won modern land-claim deals that give them a strong voice in how the land is used. Diamonds were found in 1991, and mines opened later that decade.
CA-NT.c: About half the people are Indigenous, and there are 11 official languages, including nine Indigenous ones. Yellowknife is one of the best places in the world to see the northern lights, and in winter ice roads link remote communities. Hunting, fishing and caribou remain central to life. Diamond mines have driven the economy, though the oldest mines are closing.
CA-NT.p: The territory has no political parties: elected members choose the premier by consensus. They chose R.J. Simpson in December 2023, months after wildfires forced almost all of Yellowknife and Hay River to evacuate. Climate change is the defining issue, bringing fires, low rivers that cut off barge supplies and melting permafrost. The coming closure of diamond mines threatens jobs and revenue, so the government seeks new critical-mineral projects and federal money for roads and Arctic defence. Housing shortages, high costs and addiction weigh on smaller communities.
q: Which territory's capital grew around gold found in the 1930s, with diamonds found in 1991?
Which territory was split in 1999, leaving it much smaller?
Which territory has 11 official languages, nine of them Indigenous?

US-HI.t: Polynesian voyagers reached Hawaii by canoe about a thousand years ago or more. By 1810 Kamehameha I had united the islands into one kingdom. American missionaries and planters arrived in the 1800s, and sugar plantations brought workers from China, Japan, Portugal and the Philippines. In 1893 American businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, and the US annexed the islands in 1898. Pearl Harbor became the main base of the US Pacific Fleet. On 7 December 1941 Japanese planes attacked it, killing about 2,400 Americans and bringing the US into World War II. Martial law ruled the islands until 1944, and Japanese American soldiers from Hawaii fought with great distinction in Europe. Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959, just as jet travel made it a mass tourist destination. From the 1970s a Hawaiian Renaissance revived the language, hula and voyaging canoes, and in 1993 Congress apologised for the overthrow of the kingdom. Barack Obama was born in Honolulu in 1961.
US-HI.c: No ethnic group is a majority: people of Asian, Native Hawaiian, white and mixed descent share a 'local' culture and Hawaiian Pidgin. Lunch might be a plate lunch, poke or Spam musubi. Surfing, hula, outrigger canoeing and the word 'aloha' are part of daily life, and Hawaiian is an official language alongside English.
US-HI.p: Hawaii is one of the most Democratic states. Josh Green, a doctor, has been governor since December 2022. In August 2023 a wildfire destroyed the historic town of Lahaina on Maui and killed about 100 people, the deadliest US wildfire in a century. Rebuilding has been slow, and a settlement of about $4 billion was agreed for victims. Housing is the central issue: many locals are priced out by tourists, holiday rentals and wealthy buyers, and more Native Hawaiians now live on the mainland than in Hawaii. A 2025 'green fee' on hotel stays funds climate protection.
q: Which kingdom's Queen Liliʻuokalani was overthrown by American businessmen in 1893?
Which state was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941, bringing the US into World War II?
Which state has no ethnic majority, and an official language besides English?

CA-PE.t: For a century most of the island was owned by absentee landlords in Britain, and tenant farmers fought a long struggle, the Land Question, to own the land they worked. In 1864 Charlottetown hosted the conference that led to Confederation, but the island held out at first, worried it would lose its voice in a big country. Bankruptcy changed its mind. Its railway had run up huge debts, and in 1873 Canada agreed to take them over and buy out the landlords, so the island joined as the seventh province. Farming and fishing kept it rural for the next century. During World War II it hosted air-training bases where pilots from across the Commonwealth learned to fly. Ferries were the only link to the mainland until 1997, when the 13 km Confederation Bridge opened across the Northumberland Strait. The bridge brought more tourists and commuters, though some islanders worried it would change their quiet way of life.
CA-PE.c: It is Canada's smallest province, famous for potatoes, mussels, oysters and red sand beaches. 'Anne of Green Gables', written by Lucy Maud Montgomery and set in Cavendish, draws visitors from around the world, especially Japan. Summer brings lobster suppers, ceilidhs with fiddle music and the Charlottetown Festival, and many families have Scottish, Irish or Acadian roots.
CA-PE.p: The Progressive Conservatives have governed since 2019. Premier Dennis King resigned in early 2025, and Rob Lantz took over as interim premier. He stepped aside to run for the party leadership and won it in February 2026, returning as premier. The island's population has grown fast through immigration, putting pressure on housing, doctors and schools, and in 2024 the province cut the number of immigrants it nominates. Health care waits, the cost of living and US tariffs on seafood and potatoes are the main concerns.
q: Which province's capital hosted the 1864 conference that led to Confederation, though it held out until 1873?
Which province was linked to the mainland by the 13 km Confederation Bridge in 1997?
Which is Canada's smallest province, famous for potatoes and 'Anne of Green Gables'?

US-UT.t: Ute, Shoshone, Paiute and Navajo peoples lived here before 1847, when Brigham Young led members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, fleeing persecution in the Midwest, into the Salt Lake Valley. A year later the land passed from Mexico to the US. The Mormon settlers irrigated the desert and founded hundreds of towns. In 1869 the golden spike at Promontory Summit joined the first transcontinental railroad. Washington refused statehood while the church allowed polygamy, so Utah only became a state in 1896, after the church gave it up. Copper from Bingham Canyon, one of the world's largest open-pit mines, fed both world wars, and during World War II the government confined Japanese Americans at the Topaz camp. In the Cold War its deserts hosted weapons testing and uranium mining, and fallout from Nevada's nuclear tests drifted over towns such as St George. Salt Lake City hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics, a sign of its new place in the world.
US-UT.c: About four in ten Utahns belong to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and many young members serve missions abroad, so foreign languages are common. It has the youngest population of any state, large families and a love of 'fry sauce' and Jell-O. Its five national parks, from Zion to Arches, and its powder-snow ski resorts draw millions, and 'Silicon Slopes' tech firms fill the valleys.
US-UT.p: Republicans dominate, but in a more moderate style. Spencer Cox, governor since 2021 and re-elected in 2024, is known for his call to 'disagree better'. That message was tested in September 2025, when the conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead while speaking at Utah Valley University. In 2025 a state court threw out the legislature's congressional map for ignoring a voter-approved ban on gerrymandering and adopted one with a Democratic-leaning seat around Salt Lake City. Salt Lake City will host the 2034 Winter Olympics. The shrinking Great Salt Lake, whose dust threatens health, along with drought and housing prices, are top issues.
q: Which state did Brigham Young's followers settle in 1847, gaining statehood only after giving up polygamy?
Where was the golden spike driven at Promontory Summit in 1869?
Which state has the youngest population, five national parks including Zion and Arches?

US-WY.t: Shoshone, Crow, Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota peoples hunted bison on Wyoming's plains. The land came to the US through the Louisiana Purchase and other acquisitions, and the Oregon, Mormon and California trails all crossed it through South Pass. The Union Pacific railroad built Cheyenne and other towns in 1867 and 1868. In 1869 the territory became the first place in the US to give women the vote, partly to attract settlers, and it became a state in 1890, insisting on keeping women's suffrage. In 1872 Yellowstone became the world's first national park. Cattle barons fought small ranchers in the 1892 Johnson County War. In 1925 Nellie Tayloe Ross became the first woman governor in the US. Oil, then huge open-pit coal mines in the Powder River Basin from the 1970s, became the base of its economy. In the Cold War, Minuteman missile silos were dug across the plains around F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Cheyenne.
US-WY.c: Wyoming has the fewest people of any state, and long empty roads separate its small towns. Yellowstone's geysers and the jagged Grand Tetons draw millions. Cowboy culture is real here: ranching, rodeo and Cheyenne Frontier Days, one of the biggest outdoor rodeos, are part of life, and a bucking horse and rider appears on every car number plate.
US-WY.p: Wyoming gave Donald Trump his biggest share of the vote of any state in 2024. Republican Mark Gordon, governor since 2019, cannot run for a third term. The real fight is inside his party, between establishment conservatives like Gordon and the hard-right Freedom Caucus, which gained control of the state House in 2024. Rising home values led to fierce arguments over property tax cuts and how to pay for schools and services. Coal and oil still fund much of the state, which is also betting on new energy, such as a nuclear plant being built at Kemmerer by Bill Gates's TerraPower. Wildfires and drought are growing concerns.
q: Which was the first place in the US to give women the vote, in 1869?
Which state has the world's first national park, created in 1872?
Which state has the fewest people, and a bucking horse on every number plate?

US-NV.t: Nevada was taken from Mexico in 1848 along with the rest of the Southwest. The silver of the Comstock Lode, found in 1859, made Virginia City a boomtown and helped pay for the Union side of the Civil War. President Lincoln rushed Nevada into statehood in 1864, so it calls itself 'Battle Born'. When mining faded, the state found other ways to make money: it legalised gambling in 1931 and offered quick divorces. The Hoover Dam, finished in the 1930s, brought water and power, and after World War II mobsters and then corporations built the casino resorts of the Las Vegas Strip. In the Cold War the government tested about 900 nuclear weapons at the Nevada Test Site, first in the open air, when mushroom clouds could be seen from Las Vegas, and later underground until 1992. Las Vegas became one of America's fastest-growing cities, and its housing boom crashed hard in 2008.
US-NV.c: Las Vegas is the gambling and entertainment capital of the US, with casino resorts, residency shows, huge conventions and now major league sports teams. Reno is the smaller casino city in the north. Most of the state is desert and federal land, home to the secretive Area 51, and every summer the Burning Man festival builds a temporary city in the Black Rock Desert.
US-NV.p: Nevada is one of the closest swing states. Republican Joe Lombardo, a former Las Vegas sheriff, became governor in 2023, while Democrats control the legislature, and he has vetoed bills in record numbers. Donald Trump won the state in 2024, the first Republican to do so since 2004, partly by winning over Latino and working-class voters. The economy depends heavily on Las Vegas tourism, which slumped in 2025 as fewer visitors, including Canadians, came. Housing costs, water from the shrinking Colorado River and Lake Mead, and land for new homes on federal property are long-running issues.
q: Which 'Battle Born' state was rushed into the Union by Lincoln in 1864?
Which state saw about 900 nuclear tests, some with mushroom clouds visible from its biggest city?
Which state has Las Vegas, Area 51 and the Burning Man festival?

US-CO.t: Ute, Cheyenne and Arapaho peoples hunted here before the US gained the east through the 1803 Louisiana Purchase and the west from Mexico in 1848. The 1858 Pike's Peak gold rush brought settlers, and in 1864 militia killed more than 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and old people, at Sand Creek. Colorado joined in 1876, a century after independence, so it is the Centennial State. Silver mining boomed and crashed in the 1890s, and a coal strike ended in the 1914 Ludlow massacre, when troops attacked a tent camp of miners' families. In World War II, Japanese Americans were held at the Amache camp. The Cold War made the state a defence hub: NORAD, which watched North American skies for Soviet missiles and bombers, moved into a bunker inside Cheyenne Mountain in the 1960s, the Air Force Academy opened in Colorado Springs, and the Rocky Flats plant near Denver made plutonium parts for nuclear weapons. Ski resorts and tech firms later made it one of the fastest-growing states.
US-CO.c: Denver is the 'Mile High City', and on weekends its drivers head up Interstate 70 to ski resorts such as Vail or to climb 'fourteeners', peaks over 14,000 feet. Craft breweries, green chile, outdoor gear shops and legal cannabis, sold since 2014, are part of the scene. The Denver Broncos are a statewide obsession.
US-CO.p: Colorado has moved from swing state to reliably Democratic, with Democrats running the legislature and Governor Jared Polis, in office since 2019, serving his final term. Voters wrote abortion rights into the state constitution in 2024. A constitutional tax cap squeezes the budget. In 2025 Trump announced that US Space Command headquarters would move from Colorado Springs to Alabama, and he pressed for the release of Tina Peters, a former county clerk jailed for tampering with voting equipment, whose sentence Polis commuted in 2026. Drought on the Colorado River and wildfires are lasting risks.
q: Which is the Centennial State, which joined the Union a century after independence?
Which state's Cheyenne Mountain bunker housed NORAD during the Cold War?
Which state's capital is the 'Mile High City', with peaks called 'fourteeners'?

US-SD.t: The Lakota, Dakota and Nakota peoples, often called the Sioux, dominated these plains when the US acquired them in the Louisiana Purchase. The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty promised the Lakota the Black Hills, but when Custer's expedition found gold there in 1874, miners flooded in and the US seized the land. South Dakota became a state in 1889. In December 1890 the army killed about 250 Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee, ending the era of the Plains wars. Mount Rushmore was carved in the same Black Hills from 1927 to 1941. In the Cold War Ellsworth Air Force Base hosted bombers and Minuteman missiles. In 1973 American Indian Movement activists occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days to protest broken treaties and poverty on Pine Ridge. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the Black Hills had been taken illegally and awarded compensation; the Lakota refused it, wanting the land back. From 1981 the removal of interest rate caps drew credit-card banks to Sioux Falls.
US-SD.c: Mount Rushmore and the unfinished Crazy Horse Memorial stand in the Black Hills, land sacred to the Lakota. Each August the Sturgis motorcycle rally brings hundreds of thousands of bikers. Pheasant hunting is a passion, the Corn Palace in Mitchell is decorated with murals made of corn, and powwows on the reservations keep Lakota music and dance alive.
US-SD.p: Republicans hold nearly every office. Larry Rhoden became governor in January 2025 when Kristi Noem left to join President Trump's cabinet, and he is serving out the rest of her term. Divisions are mostly within the Republican Party, where a hard-right faction gained ground in the 2024 primaries. In 2025 the legislature banned the use of eminent domain for carbon dioxide pipelines, a blow to a large pipeline planned to carry emissions from ethanol plants. Voters rejected an abortion rights amendment in 2024, leaving a near-total ban in place. Prisons, property taxes and poverty on reservations such as Pine Ridge are key issues.
q: Which state saw the army kill about 250 Lakota at Wounded Knee in 1890?
Which state's Black Hills were promised to the Lakota, then seized after gold was found in 1874?
Which state has Mount Rushmore and the Sturgis motorcycle rally?

US-NE.t: Nebraska's plains were home to the Pawnee, Omaha, Ponca and Lakota before the US bought the land in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Oregon and Mormon trails crossed it along the Platte River. Statehood came in 1867, just after the Civil War, and the Homestead Act of 1862 and the Union Pacific railroad, which started west from Omaha, filled it with farmers, many from Germany, Bohemia and Scandinavia. Droughts and falling crop prices in the 1890s and 1930s drove many off the land. During World War II Omaha's Martin bomber plant built the B-29s that dropped the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. From 1948 Offutt Air Force Base near Omaha was the headquarters of Strategic Air Command, the force of bombers and missiles at the heart of America's Cold War nuclear deterrence. Centre-pivot irrigation, drawing on the vast Ogallala Aquifer, later turned dry land into corn country.
US-NE.c: Nebraska is cattle and corn country, with more cattle than people. Its legislature, the Unicameral, has one house and its members run without party labels, a reform from 1934. Saturdays in autumn belong to Cornhuskers football, Warren Buffett runs Berkshire Hathaway from Omaha, and Arbor Day, now a national tree-planting day, began here in 1872. Runzas, bread pockets filled with beef and cabbage, are a local staple.
US-NE.p: Republican Jim Pillen, a hog farmer and veterinarian, has been governor since 2023. Republicans dominate, though Omaha is competitive: Nebraska splits its electoral votes by district, and the Omaha seat went to the Democrats in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. Republicans have tried to switch to winner-take-all but have lacked the votes in the officially non-partisan legislature. In 2024 voters approved a constitutional amendment allowing a ban on most abortions after the first trimester. Property taxes, worker shortages, farm prices hit by trade wars and water from the Ogallala Aquifer are the main issues.
q: Which state hosted the headquarters of Strategic Air Command from 1948?
Which state's legislature has only one house and members elected without party labels?
Where did Arbor Day begin in 1872, and does Warren Buffett run Berkshire Hathaway?

US-KS.t: Kansa, Osage, Pawnee and other peoples lived on these plains before the US acquired most of them in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. In the 1850s Congress let settlers vote on whether to allow slavery, and pro- and anti-slavery groups fought a small war known as 'Bleeding Kansas', a prelude to the Civil War. Kansas joined as a free state in January 1861. Railways brought cattle drives from Texas to cow towns like Abilene and Dodge City. In the 1930s the Dust Bowl, caused by drought and over-ploughing, blew away topsoil and drove families west. Dwight Eisenhower, who grew up in Abilene, commanded the Allied invasion of Europe in World War II and then became president. Wichita built thousands of bombers and later became the 'Air Capital of the World', home to Cessna, Beechcraft and Boeing plants. The 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling, which ended legal school segregation, began with a case from Topeka, and Cold War missile silos dotted the wheat fields.
US-KS.c: Kansas is famous for wheat fields, huge skies, tornadoes and 'The Wizard of Oz'. Kansas City barbecue and burnt ends are local favourites, and Wichita still builds aircraft. College basketball is a passion, above all at the University of Kansas, where the game's inventor James Naismith coached. Small towns still gather around grain elevators, churches and Friday-night football.
US-KS.p: Kansas leans Republican, but its voters are less predictable than its neighbours'. Democrat Laura Kelly, governor since 2019, works with a Republican legislature that often overrides her vetoes. In 2022 Kansans voted clearly to keep abortion rights in the state constitution, and the issue still shapes politics. Kelly and lawmakers have clashed over tax cuts and Medicaid expansion, which Kansas has not adopted. In late 2025 the Kansas City Chiefs agreed to build a new stadium on the Kansas side of the metro area, backed by state bonds. The shrinking Ogallala Aquifer threatens farming in the west.
q: Which state's fighting over slavery in the 1850s became known as 'Bleeding' before the Civil War?
Which state's capital gave its case to Brown v. Board of Education, which ended legal school segregation?
Which state is the setting of 'The Wizard of Oz', and whose biggest city is the 'Air Capital of the World'?

US-OK.t: Oklahoma's history is tied to Native removal. In the 1830s the US forced the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations from the Southeast to what was called Indian Territory, on journeys such as the Trail of Tears, where thousands died. Promises that the land was theirs forever did not last. From 1889 the government opened land to white settlers in a series of land runs, and tribal governments were broken up before statehood in 1907. Oil booms made Tulsa rich, and in 1921 white mobs destroyed the prosperous Black district of Greenwood, killing dozens and possibly hundreds of people in the Tulsa race massacre. In the 1930s drought and poor farming created the Dust Bowl, sending many 'Okies' to California, as told in The Grapes of Wrath. In 1995 a bomb planted by a far-right extremist killed 168 people at a federal building in Oklahoma City. In 2020 the Supreme Court ruled that much of eastern Oklahoma is still legally a reservation.
US-OK.c: About 39 tribal nations are based in Oklahoma, and Cherokee, Choctaw and other languages are being taught again. Cowboy and rodeo culture is strong, Tulsa's Route 66 and art deco buildings recall its oil boom, and the Oklahoma City Thunder, NBA champions in 2025, unite the state. Fried okra, chicken-fried steak and Sooners football are local staples.
US-OK.p: Republicans control every statewide office and the legislature. Kevin Stitt, governor since 2019, is limited to two terms. His years have brought repeated clashes with tribal nations over gambling deals, taxes and policing since the 2020 Supreme Court ruling. Ryan Walters, the state's elected schools chief, ordered Bibles into classrooms before resigning in 2025, and the US Supreme Court split evenly in 2025 over Oklahoma's attempt to fund a religious charter school, blocking it. The state has one of the strictest abortion bans. Education results, prisons, rural hospitals and severe storms and tornadoes are big issues.
q: Which state was once Indian Territory, the destination of the Trail of Tears?
Which state's city of Tulsa saw the Greenwood race massacre of 1921?
Which state is home to about 39 tribal nations, and whose Thunder won the NBA title in 2025?

US-IA.t: Meskwaki, Sauk, Ioway and other peoples farmed and hunted here before the land became part of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. After the Black Hawk War of 1832, Native nations were forced to give up their land, and Iowa became a state in 1846. Settlers broke the tallgrass prairie with steel ploughs and found some of the richest soil on Earth. German, Scandinavian, Dutch and Czech immigrants built farm towns, while the Meskwaki bought back land to form their own settlement. In the 20th century tractors, hybrid corn and fertiliser made Iowa the centre of American corn and hog farming, and farms grew larger as families left the land. In 1959 Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev toured a farm at Coon Rapids, a famous friendly moment in the Cold War. In the 1980s farm crisis, crop prices crashed and debts soared, driving thousands of farmers into bankruptcy. From 1972 the Iowa caucuses opened the presidential race, making a rural state a stage for national politics.
US-IA.c: Corn and soybean fields stretch to the horizon, and Iowa raises more pigs than any other state, several for every person. The Iowa State Fair, with its butter cow and food on a stick, is a summer ritual. Wind turbines now make more than half the state's electricity, and 'Field of Dreams' and small-town friendliness are part of its image.
US-IA.p: Once a swing state, Iowa has become solidly Republican. Kim Reynolds, governor since 2017, chose not to run again in 2026. She has cut income taxes to a flat rate, created vouchers for private schools and signed a six-week abortion ban, which took effect in 2024. In 2025 Iowa removed gender identity from its civil rights law. Farmers have been hurt by low crop prices and by trade wars, including China's months-long halt to buying US soybeans in 2025. Farm runoff polluting rivers is a lasting issue.
q: Which state's farm at Coon Rapids was toured by Soviet leader Khrushchev in 1959?
Which state's caucuses opened the presidential race from 1972?
Which state raises more pigs than any other, and has a state fair with a butter cow?

US-MO.t: French traders founded St. Louis in 1764, and the area passed to the US in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Missouri's admission as a slave state in 1821 required the Missouri Compromise, which made Maine a free state and banned slavery north of latitude 36°30'. St. Louis and Kansas City became gateways to the West for wagon trains and railways. In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled against Dred Scott, an enslaved man in St. Louis who had sued for his freedom, a decision that pushed the country toward civil war. Missouri stayed in the Union, but guerrilla fighting tore it apart. Kansas City's jazz clubs flourished in the 1930s. Harry Truman, a Missouri farmer and senator, became president in 1945, ordered the atomic bombs dropped on Japan and began the Cold War policy of containing the Soviet Union. In 1946 Winston Churchill gave his 'Iron Curtain' speech at Fulton. In 2014 the police killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson sparked national protests.
US-MO.c: St. Louis's Gateway Arch marks the start of westward expansion, and the city is known for toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake and Budweiser beer. Kansas City argues over the best barbecue and cheers for the Chiefs. Mark Twain's boyhood town of Hannibal, the Ozark lakes and the country music theatres of Branson draw visitors.
US-MO.p: Missouri, once a bellwether, is now solidly Republican. Mike Kehoe became governor in January 2025. In 2024 voters approved a constitutional amendment restoring abortion rights, but courts and lawmakers have fought over it, and in 2025 the legislature voted to ask voters to repeal it. In September 2025, under pressure from Trump, Missouri redrew its congressional map to take a Kansas City seat from Democrats, and opponents launched a petition for a referendum. A tornado tore through north St. Louis in May 2025, and the Chiefs' choice of a new stadium in Kansas was a blow.
q: Which state's admission as a slave state in 1821 required a famous compromise?
Where did Winston Churchill give his 'Iron Curtain' speech in 1946?
Which state has the Gateway Arch and Mark Twain's boyhood town of Hannibal?

CN-BJ.t: Beijing became China's capital under Kublai Khan in the 1200s, and the Ming dynasty built the Forbidden City in the early 1400s. Foreign troops sacked the Summer Palace in 1860 and ended the Boxer siege of the legations in 1900, humiliations taught in every Chinese school. On 4 May 1919, students protested in Beijing against the Paris Peace Conference, sparking a nationalist movement. The capital moved to Nanjing in 1928 and Japan occupied the city from 1937 to 1945. On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen gate, and Beijing became capital again. Old walls were torn down for ring roads, and Tiananmen Square was enlarged for parades. The Cultural Revolution began with Red Guard rallies here in 1966. In the spring of 1989 students occupied Tiananmen Square calling for reform, and on 3 and 4 June the army cleared them, killing several hundred to a few thousand people by most estimates; the event is censored in China. The 2008 Olympics showed off a modern Beijing.
CN-BJ.c: The Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Great Wall at Badaling and Mutianyu, and the old hutong alleys of courtyard houses draw millions of visitors. Peking duck, carved at the table and wrapped in thin pancakes, is the signature dish, along with zhajiangmian noodles. Beijing people speak Mandarin with a distinctive rolled 'r'. The city has hosted both the Summer Olympics in 2008 and the Winter Olympics in 2022.
CN-BJ.p: The party secretary, Yin Li, a member of the Politburo, outranks the mayor, Yin Yong. As the seat of the Communist Party and of Xi Jinping's government, Beijing is the most tightly policed city in China. A September 2025 military parade for the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II was attended by the leaders of Russia and North Korea. The city has cut its population and moved offices to Hebei, while the smog of the 2010s has eased. Tech firms in the Zhongguancun district are at the heart of China's AI race with the United States.
q: Where did Mao proclaim the People's Republic on 1 October 1949?
Which city's central square was cleared by the army on 3 and 4 June 1989?
Which city has hosted both the Summer and Winter Olympics, and is famous for its roast duck?

CN-SC.t: Ringed by mountains, the fertile Sichuan Basin has often been a kingdom of its own. The Dujiangyan irrigation system, built around 256 BC, still waters the Chengdu plain, and the state of Shu here was one of the Three Kingdoms of the 200s. In 1911 protests against a foreign-funded railway scheme in Sichuan helped trigger the revolution that toppled the Qing. Rival warlords then fought over the province for two decades. The Long March crossed western Sichuan in 1935. During World War II the Nationalist government retreated here, and Sichuan supplied many of the soldiers and much of the grain for the war. In the Great Leap Forward famine, Sichuan probably lost more people than any other province. Deng Xiaoping was born in Sichuan, and reforms there in the late 1970s by Zhao Ziyang were a model for the rest of China. Chongqing was split off in 1997. On 12 May 2008 an earthquake at Wenchuan killed about 70,000 people, many children in badly built schools.
CN-SC.c: Sichuan food is famous for mala, the numbing heat of Sichuan pepper with chilli: mapo tofu, kung pao chicken, dan dan noodles and hotpot. Chengdu is a laid-back city of teahouses and mahjong, home to a giant panda breeding centre. Western Sichuan is largely Tibetan, with grasslands and monasteries. Sichuan opera's face-changing performers swap masks in a split second, and the Leshan Giant Buddha is carved into a cliff.
CN-SC.p: The party secretary, Wang Xiaohui, outranks the governor, Shi Xiaolin. Sichuan, with over 80 million people, is a growing inland hub: Chengdu is home to electronics plants, video game studios and China's military aircraft maker. Its hydropower supplies much of eastern China, but droughts, as in 2022, have forced power cuts. Tibetan areas of western Sichuan, especially Aba, saw many of the more than 150 self-immolations by Tibetans protesting Chinese rule since 2009, and controls remain tight. Like many provinces, Sichuan faces local-government debts and an ageing countryside.
q: Which province's Dujiangyan irrigation system, built around 256 BC, still waters its plain?
Which province's Wenchuan earthquake of 2008 killed about 70,000 people?
Which province is famous for mala pepper heat, giant pandas and face-changing opera?

CN-CQ.t: Chongqing grew where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze, a steep river port that became a treaty port open to foreign trade in 1891. Its moment in history came in World War II. After Japan captured Nanjing and Wuhan, Chiang Kai-shek made Chongqing China's wartime capital from 1938 to 1946. Japanese bombers attacked it hundreds of times, killing thousands, and people sheltered in tunnels dug into the hills. The communist leader Zhou Enlai lived here as liaison, and in 1945 Mao Zedong flew in for failed peace talks with Chiang. In the 1960s Mao's 'Third Front' moved weapons and heavy industry to the inland mountains to hide them from attack, and Chongqing gained factories. In 1997 it was split from Sichuan and made a municipality, partly to manage the people displaced by the Three Gorges Dam, whose reservoir floods the valley downriver.
