Its leader from 2007, Bo Xilai, ran a 'red' populist campaign until his fall in a 2012 murder scandal.
CN-CQ.c: Chongqing is a mountain city of fog, river bends, cable cars and monorails that run through apartment blocks, which makes it popular on social media. Hotpot is the signature dish: offal and beef boiled in a broth of chilli and Sichuan pepper. People speak a Sichuanese dialect and are known for being fiery and direct. River cruises leave here for the Three Gorges.
CN-CQ.p: The party secretary, Yuan Jiajun, a Politburo member and former aerospace engineer, outranks the mayor, Chen Xinwu. Chongqing is a manufacturing hub for cars and laptops, and Changan Automobile is shifting to electric cars. The city is a starting point for freight trains to Europe and for a land-sea corridor to Southeast Asia, part of the Belt and Road. Its large administrative area includes poor rural counties. Like many cities it carries heavy debt from building projects, and the property slump has hit hard.
q: Which city was China's wartime capital from 1938 to 1946, bombed hundreds of times by Japan?
Which city was split from Sichuan in 1997, partly to manage people displaced by the Three Gorges Dam?
Which foggy mountain city has monorails running through apartment blocks and is famous for hotpot?

CN-GZ.t: A Chinese saying described Guizhou as a place with 'no three days of clear sky, no three li of flat land and no family with three coins'. Its steep limestone mountains were home to the Miao, Dong, Bouyei and other peoples, and the Ming dynasty only made it a province in 1413, planting military colonies to hold the roads to Yunnan. Qing efforts to replace local chiefs with Chinese officials caused repeated wars, and a great Miao uprising from 1854 to 1873 left much of the province in ruins. In January 1935, during the Long March, the communists held a meeting at Zunyi in Guizhou where Mao Zedong won a leading role in the party. During World War II the province was a refuge behind the front. In the 1960s Mao's 'Third Front' moved military factories into its remote valleys. Guizhou stayed among China's poorest provinces until the 2000s, when Beijing poured money into motorways, high bridges and high-speed railways to connect it.
CN-GZ.c: Guizhou's green karst hills hide the Huangguoshu waterfall, terraced rice fields and Miao and Dong villages with wooden drum towers and silver headdresses. Food is sour and spicy: sour fish soup and chilli dipping sauces. Kweichow Moutai, the fiery sorghum liquor drunk at state banquets, comes from the town of Maotai. In 2023 a village football league in Rongjiang, the 'Village Super League', became a national hit.
CN-GZ.p: The party secretary, Xu Lin, outranks the governor, Li Bingjun. Guizhou's building boom left it with some of the heaviest local-government debts in China, and in 2023 a report published by a provincial think tank said it could not solve them alone; Beijing has since helped refinance. The province has bet on big data centres, drawn by cool weather and cheap hydropower, and on the FAST radio telescope, the world's largest single-dish telescope. Many of its people still work as migrants in the coastal provinces, leaving older people and children behind in villages.
q: In which province did Mao win a leading role in the party at the Zunyi meeting in 1935?
Which province was described as having 'no three days of clear sky, no three li of flat land'?
Which province makes Moutai liquor and has the Huangguoshu waterfall?

CN-HN.t: Hunan, south of Lake Dongting, is known as the cradle of revolutionaries. In the 1850s and 1860s Zeng Guofan raised the Hunan Army that defeated the Taiping rebels and saved the Qing dynasty. Later Hunan produced reformers and radicals, and above all Mao Zedong, born in 1893 to a farming family in Shaoshan. As a young man Mao studied in Changsha, and in 1927 he wrote about the peasant movement in Hunan and led the failed Autumn Harvest Uprising there before retreating to the mountains. Other communist leaders, including Liu Shaoqi and Peng Dehuai, were also from Hunan. During World War II Changsha was fought over four times, and in 1938 the Nationalists burned the city to keep it from the Japanese. Under Mao the province was a showcase of collective farming, and it suffered in the Great Leap famine. Since 1978 it has remained a rice-growing and inland manufacturing province, sending migrants to neighbouring Guangdong.
CN-HN.c: Hunanese food is even hotter than Sichuan's, with fresh and pickled chillies in everything: steamed fish head with chopped chilli, smoked pork and stinky tofu. Mao's red-braised pork is on many menus. Changsha is known for nightlife and Hunan Satellite TV's entertainment shows. The sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie, which inspired the floating mountains in the film Avatar, draw crowds, as does the old town of Fenghuang.
CN-HN.p: The party secretary, Shen Xiaoming, outranks the governor, Mao Weiming. Hunan is a mid-sized inland economy that is trying to move from farming and old industry to heavy machinery, with firms such as Sany and Zoomlion, and to electronics plants that have moved inland from the coast. Its local governments carry large debts, and the property slump has squeezed land sales that once paid their bills. The province is also promoting trade with Africa through a regular China-Africa trade expo in Changsha.
q: Which province was Mao Zedong's birthplace, at Shaoshan?
Which province's capital was burned by the Nationalists in 1938 to keep it from the Japanese?
Which province's Zhangjiajie pillars inspired the floating mountains in 'Avatar'?

CN-NX.t: The Yellow River makes a great loop through Ningxia, and its irrigated plain has been farmed for two thousand years in an otherwise dry land. From the 1030s the Tangut people ruled the Western Xia kingdom from here, controlling Silk Road trade until Genghis Khan destroyed it in 1227; their royal tombs still stand near Yinchuan. Over the following centuries many Hui, Chinese-speaking Muslims descended partly from Silk Road traders, settled in the region. A Muslim revolt across the northwest in the 1860s and 1870s ended in massacres and forced resettlement. After 1911 the Hui warlord Ma Hongkui ruled Ningxia. The communists absorbed it into Gansu in 1954, then in 1958 created the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region as a homeland for the Hui. During the Cultural Revolution mosques were closed and religious leaders persecuted until the late 1970s. Since then Ningxia has been one of China's poorer regions, relying on coal, farming and moving villagers off barren hills.
CN-NX.c: About a third of Ningxia's people are Hui Muslims, and mosques, halal lamb dishes and hand-pulled noodles are part of daily life. Ningxia goji berries are famous across China, and vineyards on the slopes of the Helan Mountains make some of the country's best-known wines. Tourists visit the Western Xia tombs, the Shapotou sand dunes on the Yellow River and film sets built in the desert.
CN-NX.p: The party secretary, Li Yifei, outranks the chairman, Zhang Yupu. Under a campaign to 'sinicise' religion, authorities have removed Arabic-style domes and minarets from many mosques in Ningxia and restricted religious teaching; officials say they are making Islam fit Chinese culture, while Hui and rights groups see it as erasing their identity. Economically, Ningxia is building data centres, solar farms and a coal chemical industry, and it promotes its wine. A gas explosion at a Yinchuan barbecue restaurant killed 31 people in 2023, prompting a national safety campaign.
q: Which region was the base of the Western Xia kingdom, destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1227?
Which autonomous region was created in 1958 as a homeland for the Hui Muslims?
Which region is famous for goji berries and wines from the Helan Mountains?

CN-SN.t: Shaanxi is where China began as an empire. The First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, united China in 221 BC from his base here and was buried near Xi'an with an army of thousands of terracotta soldiers. Xi'an, then called Chang'an, was capital of the Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern end of the Silk Road, among the world's largest cities in the 700s. In 1556 an earthquake in Shaanxi killed some 800,000 people, the deadliest on record. In 1935 the Long March ended in northern Shaanxi, and from 1937 to 1947 the communists ran their base from Yan'an, living in caves cut into the yellow loess hills. In December 1936, in the Xi'an Incident, a Nationalist general kidnapped Chiang Kai-shek and forced him to join the communists against Japan. During the Cultural Revolution, the teenage Xi Jinping was sent to work in a Shaanxi village, Liangjiahe, for seven years. Mao's 'Third Front' later built aircraft and defence plants around Xi'an.
CN-SN.c: The Terracotta Army is one of the world's great archaeological sites. Xi'an's Muslim Quarter fills at night with Hui stalls selling roujiamo, a meat-stuffed flatbread called China's hamburger, and paomo, crumbled bread soaked in mutton soup. Biangbiang noodles, wide as belts, have a character so complex it is famous in itself. Yan'an's caves are a pilgrimage site for the Communist Party's 'red tourism'.
CN-SN.p: The party secretary, Zhao Yide, outranks the governor, Zhao Gang. Xi'an has grown into a hub for aerospace, chips and car batteries, and electric car maker BYD has big factories there. Northern Shaanxi produces coal, oil and gas. As the start of the ancient Silk Road, Xi'an hosted the first China-Central Asia summit in 2023 and runs freight trains toward Europe under the Belt and Road. Because of Xi Jinping's family links, the province is politically sensitive, and it faces debt and a property slump like the rest of China.
q: From which province did the First Emperor unite China in 221 BC?
Which province's Yan'an was the communists' cave base from 1937 to 1947?
Which province has the Terracotta Army and biangbiang noodles?

CN-QH.t: Qinghai, named after the great salt Qinghai Lake, sits on the northeastern Tibetan plateau, where the Yangtze, Yellow and Mekong rivers all begin. Most of it was the Tibetan region of Amdo, and the 14th Dalai Lama was born here in 1935, as was the founder of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, whose Kumbum Monastery still stands. The Qing dynasty took control from the Mongols in the 1720s. After 1911 Qinghai was ruled by the Hui Muslim Ma family of warlords, who fought both Tibetans and the Japanese, and it became a province of the Republic in 1928. The People's Liberation Army arrived in 1949. In the 1950s Tibetan nomads resisted collectivisation and were crushed, and Qinghai became a place of labour camps for prisoners from across China. China's nuclear weapons were designed at a secret base near Qinghai Lake. A railway reached Golmud in 1984 and was extended to Lhasa in 2006. In 2010 an earthquake at Yushu killed about 2,700 people.
CN-QH.c: Qinghai is high, cold and thinly populated, with grasslands where Tibetan herders keep yaks, and huge salt flats such as Chaka that mirror the sky. The capital, Xining, is home to Han Chinese, Hui, Tibetans, Tu and Salar. Lamb, yoghurt, highland barley and yak butter tea are staples. The Tour of Qinghai Lake cycle race and Tibetan horse festivals draw visitors in summer.
CN-QH.p: The party secretary is Luo Dongchuan. Qinghai's salt lakes are among China's main sources of lithium and potash, which matters for electric car batteries and fertiliser. It also has vast solar and wind farms and hydro dams on the upper Yellow River, sending power east. Beijing has created the Sanjiangyuan national park to protect the sources of the great rivers, which has meant moving some herders. Tibetan areas face the same restrictions on religion, language and monasteries as Tibet itself.
q: In which province, named after a great salt lake, was the 14th Dalai Lama born?
Which province's railway reached Golmud in 1984 before being extended to Lhasa?
Where do the Yangtze, Yellow and Mekong rivers all begin?

CN-SX.t: Shanxi, 'west of the mountains', is a high plateau of yellow loess and coal. Its walled towns grew rich on trade with the Mongol steppe, and in the 1800s Shanxi bankers in Pingyao ran China's first nationwide money transfer houses. Buddhist cave carvings at Yungang and the monasteries of Mount Wutai date back over 1,500 years. From 1911 the warlord Yan Xishan ruled Shanxi for almost four decades as a 'model province', building railways and arsenals. When Japan invaded in 1937, communist forces won their first big victory over the Japanese at Pingxingguan and built guerrilla bases in the mountains. In 1949 Taiyuan fell after one of the longest sieges of the civil war. Under Mao, the village of Dazhai was held up as a national model of collective farming. After 1978 Shanxi became China's coal mine, feeding power stations nationwide, with booming 'coal bosses', frequent mine disasters and some of the world's worst air pollution in the 2000s.
CN-SX.c: Shanxi is China's noodle capital, with knife-cut noodles sliced straight into boiling water and dark aged vinegar on almost everything. Pingyao, a walled Ming and Qing town, is a World Heritage Site, as are the Yungang Grottoes and Mount Wutai. Shanxi keeps many of China's oldest wooden temples, which drew new fans after the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong featured them.
CN-SX.p: The party secretary, Tang Dengjie, outranks the governor, Lu Dongliang. Shanxi still mines more than a quarter of China's coal, which keeps the power grid running but ties the province to an industry China wants to shrink. Corruption around coal has brought down many senior officials over the past decade. Leaders want to diversify into new energy, hydrogen and tourism, helped by the success of Black Myth: Wukong. Mine safety remains a concern, and the province is losing young people.
q: Which province's bankers in Pingyao ran China's first nationwide money transfer houses?
Which province's village of Dazhai was held up by Mao as a model of collective farming?
Which province is China's noodle capital and coal mine, with temples featured in 'Black Myth: Wukong'?

CN-JX.t: For a thousand years the kilns of Jingdezhen in Jiangxi made the porcelain that the world simply called 'china', shipped to Persia, Europe and beyond. The province's rice, tea and position on the route between the Yangtze and Guangzhou made it prosperous until the Taiping war of the 1850s and 1860s wrecked it. Jiangxi is central to the Communist Party's founding story. On 1 August 1927 communist troops rose up in Nanchang, the date now celebrated as the birth of the People's Liberation Army. Mao Zedong then set up a base in the Jinggang Mountains, and in 1931 the communists declared a Chinese Soviet Republic with its capital at Ruijin. Chiang Kai-shek's armies encircled it five times, and in October 1934 the communists broke out and began the Long March. Jiangxi then suffered Japanese invasion and the Great Leap famine. After 1978 it lagged behind its coastal neighbours, sending many workers to Guangdong and Zhejiang, and growing by making cars, aircraft and electronics.
CN-JX.c: Jingdezhen is still a porcelain town, full of workshops, kilns and young artists. The misty peaks of Mount Lushan and Sanqingshan, and Wuyuan's white-walled villages among yellow rapeseed fields in spring, attract visitors. Jiangxi food is salty and very spicy, and Nanchang's rice noodles are a breakfast favourite. 'Red tourism' brings party groups to Jinggangshan and Ruijin to retrace the revolution.
CN-JX.p: Yin Hong is the province's party secretary. Jiangxi has become a key source of materials for electric car batteries: Yichun is known as a lithium capital, and Ganzhou mines heavy rare earths, which China restricted for export in 2025 in its trade fight with the United States. Copper smelting and solar panels are also big industries. Like other inland provinces, Jiangxi wrestles with local-government debt and a falling birth rate, and many young people leave for jobs on the coast.
q: Which province's Nanchang uprising of 1 August 1927 is celebrated as the birth of the PLA?
Which province's Ruijin was the capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic, which the communists left on the Long March?
Which province's town of Jingdezhen made the porcelain the world called 'china'?

CN-HA.t: Henan, on the middle Yellow River, is where Chinese civilisation took shape. The Shang dynasty left the first Chinese writing on oracle bones at Anyang around 1200 BC, and Luoyang and Kaifeng served as imperial capitals for centuries. Kaifeng was perhaps the world's largest city under the Northern Song in the 1000s. Floods of the Yellow River have shaped Henan's history. In 1938, to slow the Japanese advance, Chiang Kai-shek's army breached the river's dikes, drowning hundreds of thousands of villagers. In 1942 and 1943 drought, war and government grain requisitions caused a famine that killed perhaps two million or more. The Great Leap Forward hit Henan brutally: in Xinyang prefecture alone, perhaps a million people died in the famine of 1959 to 1960. In 1975 the Banqiao dam collapsed in a typhoon, one of the deadliest dam failures in history. After 1978 Henan, with around 100 million people, sent tens of millions of migrant workers to China's coastal factories.
CN-HA.c: The Shaolin Temple on Mount Song is the legendary home of kung fu, and its monks and martial arts schools draw students from around the world. The Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang hold thousands of Buddhist carvings, and Luoyang holds a peony festival each spring. Food is wheat-based: hui mian stewed noodles, hot and spicy hu la soup for breakfast, and Kaifeng's soup dumplings. Henan opera is popular across northern China.
CN-HA.p: The party secretary, Zhou Zuyi, outranks the governor, Wang Lujin. Zhengzhou is home to Foxconn's 'iPhone City', where a Covid lockdown in 2022 led to worker protests. In 2021 floods in Zhengzhou drowned hundreds of people, including passengers trapped in a subway tunnel. In 2022 depositors protested after rural banks froze their savings, and the province's property market has been one of the weakest in China, with many unfinished flats. Henan is a major grain producer and is trying to keep electronics and car factories, including BYD's, growing.
q: Which province's Anyang has the first Chinese writing, on Shang dynasty oracle bones?
In which province did the Banqiao dam collapse in 1975, one of the deadliest dam failures in history?
Which province has the Shaolin Temple, the legendary home of kung fu?

CN-HB.t: Hubei, 'north of the lake', sits on the middle Yangtze, and its capital Wuhan grew from three river towns into a trade hub after Hankou became a treaty port in 1861. In the 1890s the reforming governor Zhang Zhidong built arsenals, ironworks and schools there. On 10 October 1911 an army mutiny in Wuchang, part of Wuhan, sparked the revolution that ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule, which is why 10 October, 'Double Ten', is still the national day in Taiwan. In 1927 Wuhan was briefly the seat of the left-wing Nationalist government. After Nanjing fell to Japan in 1937, Wuhan served as China's temporary capital until it too fell in 1938. Under the People's Republic, Wuhan built China's first bridge across the Yangtze in 1957 and Wuhan Iron and Steel. Mao famously swam in the Yangtze at Wuhan in 1966. Upriver, the Three Gorges Dam, begun in 1994 and fully working by 2012, is the world's largest hydroelectric plant.
CN-HB.c: Wuhan's breakfast culture is famous, especially hot dry noodles, reganmian, coated in sesame paste. Hubei cooking uses lots of freshwater fish and lotus root from its many lakes. Wuhan is one of China's biggest university cities, with over a million students. Sights include the Yellow Crane Tower, the Three Gorges, and the Wudang Mountains, home of Taoist temples and tai chi.
CN-HB.p: The party secretary, Guan Zhi'ou, outranks the governor, Li Dianxun. Covid-19 was first identified in Wuhan at the end of 2019, and the city was sealed off in a 76-day lockdown in 2020. The virus's origin is still disputed: China rejects suggestions that it came from a Wuhan laboratory. Since then Hubei has invested in cars, chips and optical fibre, with Wuhan becoming a test city for robotaxis. Like other provinces it carries large local-government debts, and the property slump has hit hard.
q: Which province's Wuchang mutiny of 10 October 1911 sparked the revolution that ended imperial rule?
Which province's capital built China's first bridge across the Yangtze in 1957?
Which province has the Three Gorges Dam and is famous for hot dry noodles?

CN-AH.t: Anhui straddles the Huai River and the Yangtze. The north is flat wheat country prone to floods, the south hilly and rich with tea. The founder of the Ming dynasty, Zhu Yuanzhang, was a poor peasant from northern Anhui, and Li Hongzhang, the Qing statesman who negotiated with Western powers in the late 1800s, raised his Huai Army here. In 1938 the breaching of the Yellow River's dikes in neighbouring Henan sent floods across northern Anhui. The decisive Huaihai campaign of the civil war, in 1948 and 1949, was fought partly in northern Anhui. In the Great Leap Forward famine Anhui suffered one of the highest death rates of any province. In 1978, in the village of Xiaogang, 18 farmers secretly signed a pact to divide collective land into family plots. Harvests soared, Deng Xiaoping's government spread the 'household responsibility system' across China, and Xiaogang is now celebrated as the birthplace of reform.
CN-AH.c: Huangshan, the Yellow Mountain, with granite peaks, twisted pines and seas of cloud, has inspired Chinese painters for centuries. Nearby, the white-walled villages of Xidi and Hongcun show the old Huizhou style. Southern Anhui grows famous teas such as Keemun black and Huangshan Maofeng. Hui cuisine favours braised dishes and stinky mandarin fish. Anhui also produced China's Huangmei opera.
CN-AH.p: The party secretary, Li Lecheng, outranks the governor, Wang Dongwei. Anhui has become a star of China's electric car boom. Its capital, Hefei, rescued the start-up NIO with a government investment in 2020 and drew Volkswagen and BYD factories, and Wuhu is home to Chery, one of China's biggest car exporters. Hefei is also a centre of research in quantum computing and fusion, around the University of Science and Technology of China. Its strategy of investing public money directly in companies has been widely copied, though not always successfully.
q: In which province's village of Xiaogang did 18 farmers secretly divide collective land in 1978, starting reform?
Which province was the home of the Ming founder Zhu Yuanzhang?
Which province has Huangshan, the Yellow Mountain, and Keemun black tea?

US-WI.t: Ho-Chunk, Menominee and Ojibwe people lived around the lakes when French fur traders arrived in the 1600s. The land passed to the US with the Northwest Territory, and Wisconsin became a state in 1848. German, Norwegian and Polish immigrants built its dairy farms, breweries and factories, and Milwaukee became a major industrial city. In the early 1900s Governor Robert La Follette led the Progressive movement, which pioneered workers' compensation, primary elections and the use of university experts in government, the 'Wisconsin Idea'. Milwaukee's factories built engines, motorcycles and machinery for both world wars. In the early 1950s Wisconsin senator Joseph McCarthy led a hunt for supposed communists in government that wrecked careers until the Senate condemned him in 1954. From the 1970s many factory jobs disappeared. In 2011 then-governor Scott Walker's law curbing public-sector unions brought huge protests to the capitol in Madison and made Wisconsin a battleground of national politics.
US-WI.c: Wisconsin is 'America's Dairyland', famous for cheese, cheese curds and supper clubs serving Friday fish fry and brandy old fashioneds. Fans of the Green Bay Packers, which they own, wear foam 'cheesehead' hats. Milwaukee is known for beer, bratwurst and Harley-Davidson, and thousands of lakes make summer cabins and winter ice fishing a way of life.
US-WI.p: Wisconsin is one of the most evenly divided swing states, and Donald Trump carried it narrowly in 2024. Democrat Tony Evers, governor since 2019, faces a Republican legislature and has used his veto often; in 2025 he said he would not seek a third term. Its supreme court is a battleground: liberal Susan Crawford won a 2025 race that became the most expensive judicial election in US history, keeping a liberal majority. The court threw out Republican-drawn legislative maps in 2023 and struck down an 1849 abortion ban in 2025. Farm incomes, trade, school funding and Great Lakes water are big issues.
q: Which state's senator Joseph McCarthy led a hunt for supposed communists in the 1950s?
Which state's Governor La Follette pioneered the Progressive movement and the 'Idea' named after it?
Which state is 'America's Dairyland', where Packers fans wear cheesehead hats?

US-IL.t: French explorers and traders came down the Mississippi in the 1670s, and Illinois passed to Britain in 1763 and to the US after the Revolution. It became a state in 1818. Abraham Lincoln built his law career in Springfield before becoming president in 1861. Chicago exploded into America's railway hub, grain market and meatpacking centre, and after the Great Fire of 1871 it rebuilt in steel, giving the world the first skyscrapers. Immigrants from Germany, Ireland, Poland and Italy, and hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners in the Great Migration, filled its factories and neighbourhoods. In the 1920s Prohibition made Al Capone's gangsters notorious. In 1942 Enrico Fermi's team at the University of Chicago built the first nuclear reactor, a key step toward the atomic bomb. After World War II steel mills and factories closed, and Chicago became one of America's most segregated cities. Barack Obama began his political career on the South Side.
US-IL.c: Chicago gave the world electric blues, house music, deep-dish pizza and the skyscraper, and boat tours show off its riverside architecture. Fans split between the Cubs and the White Sox, and Italian beef sandwiches and hot dogs without ketchup are local rules. Outside Chicago, Illinois is mostly flat farmland growing corn and soybeans, with the feel of the rural Midwest.
US-IL.p: Illinois is solidly Democratic, though rural areas vote heavily Republican. JB Pritzker, a billionaire who has been governor since 2019, has become one of the loudest critics of President Trump. In 2025 federal agents launched a large immigration crackdown around Chicago, and Trump tried to send the National Guard into the city over Pritzker's objections, but the courts blocked the deployment. The state also faces old problems: huge pension debts, high property taxes, people moving to cheaper states and a funding crisis for public transport in the Chicago area.
q: Which state's biggest city rebuilt in steel after a great fire in 1871, creating the first skyscrapers?
Which state's university built the first nuclear reactor, under Enrico Fermi, in 1942?
Which state's biggest city gave the world electric blues, house music and deep-dish pizza?

US-KY.t: Daniel Boone led settlers through the Cumberland Gap in the 1770s onto hunting grounds used by Shawnee and Cherokee peoples. Kentucky split from Virginia and became the 15th state in 1792, and both Abraham Lincoln and the Confederate president Jefferson Davis were born here. It was a slave state but stayed with the Union in the Civil War, though thousands of its men fought on each side. Afterwards tobacco, bourbon and horse farms in the Bluegrass region shaped the economy. In the east, coal mining in Appalachia grew from the 1900s, and battles between miners and mine owners, as in 'Bloody Harlan' in the 1930s, made unions a fierce cause. The Fort Knox gold vault opened in 1937, and during World War II it also sheltered the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution. As coal declined from the 1980s, eastern Kentucky became one of the poorest parts of the country, while car factories such as Toyota's plant at Georgetown and the UPS air hub in Louisville created new jobs.
US-KY.c: Most of the world's bourbon is made in Kentucky, and distilleries along the Bourbon Trail draw tourists. The Kentucky Derby, run each May at Churchill Downs, comes with mint juleps and big hats. Bluegrass music, KFC, hot brown sandwiches, Appalachian crafts and the fierce college basketball rivalry between Kentucky and Louisville mark the state.
US-KY.p: Kentucky votes heavily Republican in national races, but Democrat Andy Beshear, governor since 2019, won re-election in 2023 by stressing jobs and disaster recovery, and is talked about as a presidential candidate. The Republican legislature overrides many of his vetoes. Floods in eastern Kentucky in 2022 and 2025 and a deadly tornado in London in May 2025 kept rebuilding at the centre of politics. In November 2025 a UPS cargo plane crashed on take-off in Louisville, killing 15 people. Mitch McConnell, the state's long-serving US senator, chose not to seek re-election in 2026.
q: Which state was the birthplace of both Abraham Lincoln and Jefferson Davis?
Which state's gold vault at Fort Knox sheltered the Declaration of Independence in World War II?
Which state makes most of the world's bourbon and holds a famous Derby every May?

US-AR.t: Quapaw, Caddo and Osage peoples lived here before France claimed the land, which passed to the US in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Arkansas became a slave state in 1836, and cotton plantations spread across its Delta lowlands. It joined the Confederacy in 1861. After the war, sharecropping and Jim Crow laws kept many Black and poor white farmers in poverty, and in 1919 white mobs killed many Black people in the Elaine massacre after sharecroppers tried to form a union. The great Mississippi flood of 1927 and the Great Depression drove thousands away. In 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students, the 'Little Rock Nine', out of Central High School. President Eisenhower sent paratroopers to escort them in, a turning point for desegregation. Later, big business grew from small towns: Sam Walton opened his first Walmart in Rogers in 1962, and Tyson Foods and J.B. Hunt also grew in the northwest. Bill Clinton, governor for 12 years, became president in 1993.
US-AR.c: Walmart is still based in Bentonville, where the Walton family built the Crystal Bridges art museum and miles of mountain-bike trails. Fans call 'Woo Pig Sooie' at University of Arkansas Razorbacks games. Johnny Cash grew up in the Delta, the Ozarks draw canoeists and hikers, and Crater of Diamonds is a public park where visitors dig for diamonds and keep what they find.
US-AR.p: Arkansas is solidly Republican. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Trump's former press secretary and daughter of former governor Mike Huckabee, became governor in 2023. In her first months she signed the LEARNS Act, which raised teacher pay and created vouchers for private schooling, and she has cut the income tax several times. Her plans for a large new state prison and a costly official lectern drew criticism. The northwest, around Walmart's home, is booming, while the Delta keeps losing people. Rural poverty, struggling hospitals and some of the country's worst health outcomes remain central issues.
q: Which state's governor used the National Guard to keep the 'Little Rock Nine' out of Central High in 1957?
Which state was governed for 12 years by Bill Clinton before he became president?
Which state is Walmart's home, with a park where visitors dig for diamonds and keep what they find?

US-TN.t: Tennessee was carved from lands claimed by North Carolina and became the 16th state in 1796. Andrew Jackson of Nashville became president and drove the Cherokee from their lands on the Trail of Tears. Tennessee was the last state to leave the Union in 1861 and the first to rejoin in 1866. In 1920 its legislature cast the deciding vote that gave American women the right to vote, when a young lawmaker switched sides after a letter from his mother. From 1933 the Tennessee Valley Authority, a New Deal agency, built dams that tamed floods and brought electricity to one of the poorest regions in the country. That power drew the Manhattan Project to the secret city of Oak Ridge in World War II, where uranium for the Hiroshima bomb was enriched. Memphis was a centre of the civil rights movement, and in 1968 Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated there. Since the 1980s car plants and Nashville's boom have made it one of the fastest-growing states.
US-TN.c: Nashville is the capital of country music, with the Grand Ole Opry and honky-tonks on Broadway, and Memphis is the home of the blues on Beale Street, soul at Stax and Elvis Presley's Graceland. Hot chicken, Memphis barbecue and Jack Daniel's whiskey from Lynchburg are famous. The Great Smoky Mountains, the most visited national park in the US, straddle its eastern border.
US-TN.p: Republicans hold supermajorities in the legislature, and Bill Lee has been governor since 2019 and cannot run again. After a school shooting in Nashville killed six people in 2023, two young Black Democrats were expelled from the state House for leading a gun-control protest on its floor; both were soon reinstated. In 2025 the state created a statewide school voucher programme. In late 2025 federal agents and the National Guard were sent to Memphis to fight crime, with the governor's support. Rapid growth around Nashville, housing costs and rebuilding after Hurricane Helene's floods in East Tennessee are key issues.
q: Which state cast the deciding vote for women's suffrage in 1920 after a lawmaker heeded his mother?
Which state's secret city of Oak Ridge enriched uranium for the Hiroshima bomb?
Which state has the Grand Ole Opry, Graceland and Jack Daniel's?

US-WV.t: West Virginia was born from the Civil War. When Virginia seceded in 1861, its mountainous western counties, with few slaves and old grievances against the eastern planters, refused to follow, and in 1863 they joined the Union as a new state, the only one formed by breaking away from a Confederate state. Coal made the state. Railways opened the mountains, and coal companies built company towns, paid miners in scrip and fought unions. Tensions exploded in the Mine Wars, ending in 1921 at the Battle of Blair Mountain, where about 10,000 armed miners fought company guards and deputies until the army arrived. West Virginia's coal and chemical plants fuelled both world wars. In the Cold War a secret bunker under the Greenbrier resort was built to shelter Congress in a nuclear war. Mechanisation and later cheap natural gas cut mining jobs, and many people left for the factories of Ohio and Michigan. Since 2000 it has been hit hard by the opioid crisis.
US-WV.c: Mountains cover the whole state, and narrow valleys hold small towns, churches and coal camps. Appalachian fiddle and banjo music, pepperoni rolls, invented as a miner's lunch, and spring festivals for ramps, a wild onion, are local traditions. John Denver's 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' is sung at Mountaineers football games, and the New River Gorge, a national park since 2020, draws rafters and climbers.
US-WV.p: Once a Democratic union stronghold, West Virginia is now one of the most Republican states. Republican Patrick Morrisey, the former attorney general, became governor in January 2025, succeeding Jim Justice, who moved to the US Senate. Morrisey has clashed with the legislature and school boards over his order allowing religious exemptions from school vaccinations, a fight that ended up in the courts. In 2025 he sent National Guard troops to Washington DC to support Trump's crime crackdown. The state's population is shrinking and ageing, and coal's decline, opioid addiction, poverty and flood recovery remain central issues.
q: Which is the only state formed by breaking away from a Confederate state, in 1863?
Which state's Battle of Blair Mountain in 1921 pitted about 10,000 armed miners against company guards?
Which state's football fans sing 'Take Me Home, Country Roads'?

US-IN.t: Miami, Shawnee and other nations lived here; in 1811 US troops under William Henry Harrison defeated Tecumseh's alliance at Tippecanoe, and most Native people were later pushed west. Indiana came from the Northwest Territory and became a state in 1816, and Abraham Lincoln spent his boyhood on a farm in the south. Railways made Indianapolis a crossroads, and steel built industrial cities such as Gary, founded by US Steel in 1906. The Indianapolis 500 car race began in 1911. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan briefly controlled much of the state government before a scandal broke it. In both world wars Indiana's factories made steel, engines and vehicles, and Eli Lilly, which had been the first to mass-produce insulin in the 1920s, made Indianapolis a centre of medicine. From the 1970s, closures of steel mills and car plants hit Gary, Anderson and Muncie, while Indianapolis kept growing. Indiana has voted Republican for president in every election since 1940 except 1964 and 2008.
US-IN.c: Basketball is a passion, from high school gyms to the Pacers, and the film 'Hoosiers' captured it. The Indianapolis 500 draws huge crowds each May. People from Indiana are called Hoosiers, a word whose origin nobody knows for sure. Breaded pork tenderloin sandwiches, sugar cream pie, county fairs and Notre Dame football are part of life.
US-IN.p: Indiana is firmly Republican. Mike Braun, a former US senator, became governor in January 2025 and has focused on cutting property taxes and health care costs. In late 2025 Trump pressed the state to redraw its congressional map to win more Republican seats; the state House passed a new map, but in December the state Senate rejected it, despite threats from the president's allies against the senators who voted no. New data centres and factories bring investment but raise worries about electricity bills and water. Abortion has been almost completely banned since 2023.
q: Which state's Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811 defeated Tecumseh's alliance?
Which state's Eli Lilly was first to mass-produce insulin?
Which state's people are called Hoosiers, and whose capital hosts a famous 500-mile race?

cradles.text: Farming began in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East about 11,500 years ago, and in time it fed the first cities. From about 3500 BC kings, temples and writing appeared along the Tigris and Euphrates in [Iraq](IRQ) and the Nile in [Egypt](EGY). The Indus civilisation of [Pakistan](PAK) and north-west [India](IND) flourished from about 2600 BC, and the Shang kingdom on the Yellow River in [China](CHN) from about 1600 BC.

notes.IRQ: Southern Iraq was Sumer, where cities such as Uruk and Ur grew from about 3500 BC. Its people invented cuneiform, wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay, at first to keep temple accounts.
notes.SYR: Northern Syria lay on the upper Euphrates and shared in Mesopotamian civilisation. Ebla, near Aleppo, left a royal archive of thousands of cuneiform tablets and fragments from around 2400 BC.
notes.TUR: The Tigris and Euphrates rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey. Nearby, at Göbekli Tepe, people built stone monuments around 9500 BC, as farming began.
notes.EGY: Egypt was united into one kingdom around 3100 BC. Almost everyone lived in the narrow, fertile Nile valley and delta, and scribes wrote in hieroglyphs from about 3200 BC.
notes.PAK: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were the largest Indus cities. Indus seals carry a script that has never been deciphered, so we do not know what language these people spoke.
notes.IND: Indus towns spread into today's north-west India, including Dholavira in Gujarat and Rakhigarhi in Haryana. The civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia.
notes.CHN: The Shang kings ruled the middle Yellow River valley. They asked their ancestors questions by cracking bones and shells with heat, and carved the questions, and often the answers, on them in early Chinese characters.
notes.PSE: Jericho, in the West Bank, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth, settled by early farmers around 9500 BC.
notes.IRN: Elam, around Susa in south-west Iran, was a close neighbour and rival of Sumer, with its own early script from about 3100 BC.

pn: c. 9500–8000 BC: one of the earliest farming villages, which by about 8000 BC had a stone wall and tower.
c. 3200 BC: some of the earliest writing appeared here, and by 3000 BC Uruk was probably the largest city in the world.
c. 2560 BC: the Great Pyramid was built for King Khufu, near the capital Memphis. It stayed the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years.
c. 2500 BC: a planned city of baked-brick houses on a street grid, with wells, bathrooms and covered drains.
The last Shang capital, from about 1300 BC. Its oracle bones, from about 1250 BC, carry the oldest known Chinese writing.

cradles.text: Civilisation began again, entirely on its own, in the Americas, where people had domesticated maize, beans and squash. On the desert coast of [Peru](PER), the Norte Chico people built Caral and other towns with stone pyramids and sunken plazas from about 2600 BC, around the time of Egypt's pyramids. In [Mexico](MEX), the Olmecs of the Gulf Coast raised ceremonial centres and carved colossal stone heads from about 1200 BC.

notes.PER: Caral and its neighbours in the Norte Chico valleys grew rich on fish from the Pacific and irrigated cotton. They built monumental towns without pottery or any known writing.
notes.MEX: Maize was first domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. The Olmecs built the first great ceremonial centres of Mesoamerica, on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz and Tabasco.

pn: c. 2600 BC: a town of pyramids and sunken plazas in the Supe valley, often called the oldest city in the Americas.
c. 1200–900 BC: the first great Olmec centre, where ten of the colossal stone heads have been found.
c. 900–400 BC: the later Olmec capital, with an earthen pyramid over 30 metres high.

religions.text: Most of the world's believers follow faiths born in two regions. In northern [India](IND), Hinduism grew out of the Vedic religion from about 1500 BC, and the Buddha taught around 500 BC. In the Middle East, Judaism took shape in the land of today's [Israel](ISR) and [Palestine](PSE), Christianity grew from it after Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30, and Muhammad founded Islam in Mecca and Medina, in [Saudi Arabia](SAU), between 610 and 632.

notes.IND: Hinduism grew from the Vedic religion of north-west India, whose oldest text, the Rigveda, dates from about 1500–1200 BC. India was also the birthplace of Buddhism and Jainism, and of Sikhism, which began in the Punjab around 1500.
notes.PAK: The Rigveda was composed largely in the Punjab, now split between Pakistan and India. Guru Nanak, who founded Sikhism around 1500, was born in 1469 at today's Nankana Sahib, near Lahore.
notes.NPL: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini, in today's southern Nepal, around 500 BC. Scholars' dates for his life vary by up to a century.
notes.ISR: Judaism grew from the religion of the ancient Israelites, whose kingdoms of Israel and Judah stood here from about 900 BC. Exile in Babylon after 586 BC helped shape the faith of the Hebrew Bible.
notes.PSE: Bethlehem, in the West Bank, is where Christian tradition places the birth of Jesus. Christianity began here as a movement among Jews in the Roman province of Judaea.
notes.SAU: Muhammad received his first revelations near Mecca around 610. Driven out, he moved to Medina in 622, returned to take Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam.
notes.IRQ: Jewish tradition says Abraham came from Ur, in southern Iraq. After 586 BC many Jews were exiled to Babylon, which stayed a great centre of Jewish learning for over a thousand years.
notes.IRN: Zoroastrianism, taught by the prophet Zoroaster at a date scholars still debate, was the faith of the Persian kings. It is one of the oldest religions still practised.
notes.CHN: China's own traditions grew separately: Confucius (551–479 BC) taught ethics and duty, and Daoism grew around the book credited to Laozi. Buddhism reached China from India in the first century AD.
notes.LKA: Buddhism arrived around 250 BC, by tradition brought by Mahinda, a son of the Indian emperor Ashoka. Sri Lanka kept alive the oldest surviving school, Theravada.
notes.TUR: Paul, the first great Christian missionary, came from Tarsus. In the AD 40s and 50s he spread the faith through the Greek cities of Anatolia and Greece.
notes.ITA: Rome crucified Jesus and at times persecuted Christians, but the emperor Constantine backed the faith from 312, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion.

pn: One of Hinduism's holiest cities, on the Ganges. Hinduism has no single founder or birthplace: it grew over many centuries across northern India.
Birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, around 500 BC. The emperor Ashoka marked the spot with a pillar around 250 BC.
Where the Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment under a fig tree. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
Site of the Jewish Temple, destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC and by Rome in AD 70. Jesus was crucified here around AD 30.
Muhammad was born here around 570 and received his first revelation nearby around 610. It is Islam's holiest city, home to the Kaaba.
Muhammad moved here in 622, the hijra that begins the Islamic calendar, and died here in 632.

religions.text: In 2020 about 2.3 billion people were Christian, 2 billion Muslim and 1.2 billion Hindu, and 1.9 billion followed no religion, according to the Pew Research Center. Christians are the majority in most of Europe, the Americas and Oceania and much of Africa south of the Sahara, and Muslims from Morocco to [Indonesia](IDN). Nearly all Hindus live in [India](IND) and Nepal, and [Israel](ISR) is the only Jewish-majority country. Muslims were the fastest-growing group.

notes.USA: The US has more Christians than any other country, about 217 million. But their share fell from 78% to 64% between 2010 and 2020, while those with no religion rose to 30%.
notes.BRA: Brazil has the world's second-largest Christian population, about 168 million, and more Catholics than any other country, though Evangelical Protestants have grown fast.
notes.PHL: The Philippines is over 90% Christian, mostly Catholic, a legacy of more than 300 years of Spanish rule. Most of its Muslims live in the south, on Mindanao.
notes.RUS: About 70% of Russians are Christian, mostly Orthodox, and about 8% Muslim, mainly in the North Caucasus and the Volga region.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia's kings adopted Christianity in the 300s, one of the first states to do so. Today about 62% of Ethiopians are Christian, mostly Orthodox, and 36% Muslim.
notes.IDN: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country, about 240 million, 87% of its people. Islam arrived mainly through traders from the 1200s onwards, not by conquest.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created in 1947 as a homeland for the Muslims of British India. It has the world's second-largest Muslim population, about 227 million.
notes.BGD: Bangladesh is about nine-tenths Muslim and has the world's fourth-largest Muslim population.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia holds Islam's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina.
notes.EGY: Egypt is the most populous Arab country, about 95% Muslim. Cairo's al-Azhar, founded in the 970s, is one of the oldest centres of Islamic learning. Most of its Christians are Coptic Orthodox.
notes.IRN: Iran is the largest Shia-majority country. Shia Islam became its state religion under the Safavids, from 1501.
notes.AZE: Azerbaijan is about 95% Muslim and, like Iran, Iraq and Bahrain, mostly Shia. Most Muslims elsewhere are Sunni.
notes.IRQ: Most Iraqis are Shia Muslims, and its cities of Najaf and Karbala hold Shia Islam's holiest shrines after Mecca and Medina.
notes.TUR: Turkey is officially a secular state, though about 97% of Turks are Muslim.
notes.NGA: Nigeria is about 56% Muslim, mostly in the north, and 43% Christian, mostly in the south.
notes.BIH: Bosnia's Muslims, the Bosniaks, are mainly descended from Slavs who converted under Ottoman rule. They make up a little over half the population.
notes.ALB: Albania is about three-quarters Muslim, a legacy of Ottoman rule, with Orthodox and Catholic minorities. Its communist rulers banned all religion from 1967 to 1990.
notes.LBN: Lebanon is about two-thirds Muslim, split between Sunni and Shia, and over a quarter Christian. Its top political offices are shared out among religious communities.
notes.MYS: Islam is Malaysia's official religion, and about 64% of Malaysians are Muslim. Most Chinese Malaysians are Buddhist, and most Indian Malaysians Hindu.
notes.IND: India is home to about 95% of the world's Hindus, some 1.1 billion people, 79% of Indians. Its 213 million Muslims are the world's third-largest Muslim population, and it has most of the world's Sikhs and Jains.
notes.NPL: Nepal is about 81% Hindu. It was the world's last Hindu kingdom until it declared itself secular in 2006 and abolished the monarchy in 2008. About 8% of Nepalis are Buddhist.
notes.THA: Thailand has more Buddhists than any other country, about 68 million, 94% of its people. Like Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, it follows the Theravada school.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka is about 70% Buddhist, mostly Sinhalese. Most Tamils are Hindu, and Hindus make up about 15% of the population.
notes.MNG: Mongolia is just over half Buddhist, in the Tibetan tradition, and about 41% follow no religion, a legacy of nearly seventy years of communist rule.
notes.ISR: Israel is the only Jewish-majority country. About 77% of its people were Jewish in 2020 and 15% Muslim, and it is home to 46% of the world's Jews; the US has most of the rest.
notes.CHN: China has about 1.3 billion people with no religion, two-thirds of the world's total. Many still keep folk customs or visit Buddhist and Daoist temples without belonging to a religion.
notes.JPN: About 57% of Japanese say they have no religion and 37% are Buddhist. Many still visit Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples for festivals and family rites.
notes.CZE: Czechia is one of the least religious countries in the world: about 73% of Czechs say they have no religion.
notes.URY: Uruguay, long Latin America's most secular country, became majority unaffiliated between 2010 and 2020, as did the Netherlands and New Zealand.
notes.GBR: No group is a majority in the UK. Christians fell from a majority in 2010 to 49% in 2020, while 40% had no religion and 6% were Muslim.
notes.FRA: No group is a majority in France: in 2020 about 47% were Christian, 43% had no religion and 9% were Muslim, one of the largest Muslim shares in western Europe.
notes.AUS: Australia fell below a Christian majority between 2010 and 2020: about 47% Christian and 42% with no religion.
notes.KOR: South Korea has no majority religion: 48% have none, 32% are Christian and 19% Buddhist. Christianity grew fast there in the 20th century.
notes.CIV: Côte d'Ivoire is almost evenly split, about 46% Muslim, mainly in the north, and 45% Christian, mainly in the south, so no group is a majority.
notes.SGP: Singapore has no majority religion. Buddhists are the largest group, 31%, followed by people with no religion, Christians and Muslims, at 16–20% each.
notes.MUS: Mauritius is 48% Hindu, mostly descendants of labourers brought from India in the 1800s, with Christian and Muslim minorities, so no group is quite a majority.
notes.TWN: Taiwan is the only place where most people, 52%, follow other religions, mainly Chinese folk religion and Daoism, so it is unlit here.

ancient.text: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 550s BC, and under Darius I it stretched from [Egypt](EGY) and [Turkey](TUR) to the Indus in [Pakistan](PAK), the largest empire the world had yet seen. Its kings ruled through provinces called satrapies, linked by the Royal Road. When Persia invaded [Greece](GRC), the Greek city-states beat it at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis in 480 BC.

notes.IRN: The Persians came from Fars, in south-west Iran. Cyrus the Great was buried at Pasargadae, and Darius I built Persepolis nearby.
notes.IRQ: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. With Susa and Persepolis, it became one of the empire's capitals.
notes.EGY: Cyrus's son Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BC, and the Persian kings ruled it as pharaohs.
notes.TUR: Anatolia's Greek cities rose in the Ionian Revolt of 499–494 BC. Athens had sent them help, which gave Darius a reason to attack Greece.
notes.PAK: Darius I took the Indus valley around 518 BC. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, this Indian province paid more tribute than any other.
notes.AFG: Bactria, in the north, and Arachosia, around Kandahar, were rich eastern provinces of the empire.
notes.ISR: After taking Babylon, Cyrus let the exiled Jews return to Judah, and they rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, completed around 515 BC.
notes.PSE: After taking Babylon, Cyrus let the exiled Jews return to Judah, and they rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, completed around 515 BC.
notes.UZB: Sogdiana, around Samarkand, and Chorasmia, around Khiva, were the empire's far north-eastern provinces.
notes.ARM: Armenia was a Persian province. Its name first appears in writing in Darius I's great rock inscription at Behistun, in Iran.
notes.BGR: Darius crossed into Europe around 513 BC. Thrace, now shared by Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey, was a Persian province until after the Greek victories of 479 BC.
notes.LBY: Cyrenaica, in the east of Libya, was settled by Greeks and submitted to Persia in 525 BC.
notes.GRC: Greece was a patchwork of independent city-states. Led by Athens and Sparta, they defeated Persia at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea in 490–479 BC. Macedonia, in the north, was a Persian vassal.

pn: Begun by Darius I around 518 BC as the empire's ceremonial capital. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BC.
Former capital of Lydia, taken by Cyrus around 546 BC, and the western end of the Royal Road.
508–507 BC: Cleisthenes' reforms began the world's first democracy, in which citizen men voted on laws in an assembly.
490 BC: the Athenians and their allies from Plataea defeated a Persian landing force.

ancient.text: In 334 BC Alexander, the young king of Macedon in northern [Greece](GRC), invaded the Persian Empire. He won every major battle, from Issus to Gaugamela, and marched as far as the Punjab, in today's [Pakistan](PAK) and [India](IND), before his army refused to go further. He died in Babylon, in [Iraq](IRQ), in 323 BC, aged 32. His generals split his empire, but Greek cities, language and art spread from [Egypt](EGY) to Afghanistan.

notes.GRC: Alexander's father, Philip II of Macedon, had made himself master of Greece by 338 BC. Alexander crushed a revolt by Thebes in 335 BC before leaving for Asia. Sparta never joined his league.
notes.MKD: Much of North Macedonia was Paeonia, a kingdom subject to Macedon, whose heartland lay in today's northern Greece.
notes.TUR: Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BC and beat a Persian army at the Granicus river. At Gordium, says the legend, he cut the Gordian knot. Parts of the north stayed outside his rule.
notes.LBN: Tyre, an island city, held out against Alexander for seven months in 332 BC. He built a causeway to reach it, which still joins it to the mainland.
notes.EGY: Egypt welcomed Alexander in 332 BC. He founded Alexandria and visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa. His general Ptolemy later ruled Egypt, and Ptolemy's dynasty lasted until Cleopatra in 30 BC.
notes.IRQ: Alexander won at Gaugamela, near today's Mosul, in 331 BC, and entered Babylon. He planned to make it his capital and died there in 323 BC.
notes.IRN: Alexander took the Persian capitals and burned Persepolis in 330 BC. Darius III was murdered by his own men the same year.
notes.AFG: Bactria and Sogdiana resisted for three years, 329–327 BC, the hardest fighting of the campaign. Alexander married Roxana, a Bactrian noble's daughter, and Greek kings ruled Bactria for two centuries after.
notes.UZB: Samarkand, then called Maracanda, was the chief city of Sogdiana, where Alexander fought a long guerrilla war in 329–327 BC.
notes.TJK: Alexander founded Alexandria Eschate, 'the Furthest', in 329 BC near today's Khujand, on the empire's northern frontier.
notes.PAK: In 326 BC Alexander defeated King Porus and his war elephants at the Hydaspes, today's Jhelum river, then sailed down the Indus to the sea.
notes.IND: Alexander reached the Beas river, in today's Indian Punjab. His exhausted army refused to go further, and he turned back.
notes.CYP: The Greek kings of Cyprus switched to Alexander's side in 332 BC and sent ships to help him besiege Tyre.

pn: Capital of Macedon, where Alexander was born in 356 BC. He became king at 20, in 336 BC.
333 BC: Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III, who fled, leaving his family behind.
Founded by Alexander in 331 BC. It became the greatest city of the Greek world, with its famous Library and lighthouse.
331 BC: Alexander's decisive victory over Darius III. The Persian Empire fell with it.
326 BC: after eight years of marching, Alexander's soldiers refused to go further east, and he turned back.
June 323 BC: Alexander died here after a fever, aged 32. He named no adult heir.

ancient.text: The king of Qin united [China](CHN) in 221 BC as its First Emperor, and standardised its writing, coins and weights. The Han dynasty that followed ruled from 202 BC to AD 220, so long that most Chinese still call themselves Han. Around AD 100 its rule ran from [North Korea](PRK) to [Vietnam](VNM), and a census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people, roughly as many as lived in the Roman Empire.

notes.CHN: Han China covered the heartland of today's China but not Tibet, most of Inner Mongolia or the far north-east. In the far west, Han generals controlled the oasis states of today's Xinjiang on and off.
notes.VNM: The Han conquered the kingdom of Nanyue in 111 BC. Northern Vietnam then stayed under Chinese rule, with breaks, until 938. The Trưng sisters led a famous revolt in AD 40–43.
notes.PRK: In 108 BC the Han destroyed the Korean kingdom of Gojoseon and set up commanderies. One, Lelang, around today's Pyongyang, lasted until AD 313.
notes.KOR: Southern Korea lay outside Han rule, though its peoples traded with the Han commandery at Lelang.
notes.MNG: The steppe was home to the Xiongnu, nomad horsemen who were Han China's great rival. Han armies broke the northern Xiongnu in AD 89.
notes.JPN: Japan was not ruled by the Han, but in AD 57 the Han emperor sent a gold seal to the king of Na, in Kyushu. A seal found in 1784 is thought to be that one.
notes.UZB: In 104–101 BC Han armies marched to the Fergana valley, now shared by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, to win its famous 'heavenly horses'.

pn: Capital of the Western Han, 202 BC–AD 9, and the eastern end of the Silk Road.
Capital of the Eastern Han from AD 25. Here in 105 the court official Cai Lun presented an improved paper to the emperor.
c. 210 BC: thousands of life-size clay soldiers were buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.
The western end of the Han wall and the gateway from China to the Silk Road.

silk.text: In 138 BC the Han emperor sent the envoy Zhang Qian west from [China](CHN), and caravan routes soon linked China with Central Asia, [Iran](IRN) and the Mediterranean. They split around the Taklamakan Desert, following oases along its northern and southern edges, and met again at Kashgar. Silk travelled west; horses, glass, silver and Buddhism, from India, travelled east. The name 'Silk Road' was coined only in 1877.

notes.CHN: Han China pushed west along the Gansu Corridor to control the trade, and silk was its most famous export. Paper and, later, porcelain also went west.
notes.KGZ: Routes crossed the Tian Shan here. In 751, in the Talas valley on today's Kyrgyz–Kazakh border, an Arab army defeated a Tang Chinese army.
notes.UZB: Samarkand and Bukhara were the busiest trading cities of Central Asia, and Sogdian merchants carried goods as far as China.
notes.TKM: Merv was one of the great cities of the Persian and later the Islamic world, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1221.
notes.IRN: Parthian and then Sasanian Persia controlled the middle of the route and profited as the go-between for China and Rome.
notes.IRQ: Ctesiphon, the Parthian and Sasanian capital, and later Baghdad, founded in 762, stood where the caravan routes met the Tigris.
notes.SYR: Caravan cities such as Palmyra grew rich passing Eastern goods on to the Mediterranean ports.
notes.TUR: Antioch and Constantinople were western ends of the routes. In the 550s monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople, so the Byzantines could make their own silk.

pn: Capital of the Han and Tang dynasties and the eastern start of the routes. Under the Tang (618–907) it was among the largest cities in the world.
Oasis gateway to the desert. Its Mogao Caves hold Buddhist art and manuscripts from the 300s to the 1300s.
Where the northern and southern routes met before crossing the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains.
Home of the Sogdians, the great middlemen of Silk Road trade from about the 300s to the 700s.
A huge oasis city on the road into Persia. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221.
Capital of Roman Syria and a western end of the routes, close to the Mediterranean ports.

silk.text: Ships could carry far more than camels. Sailors used the monsoon winds, which blow from the south-west in summer and the north-east in winter, to cross the Indian Ocean. Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay and Chinese ships linked [China](CHN) with [India](IND), [Sri Lanka](LKA), the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, carrying spices, porcelain, cotton and silk. From 1405 to 1433 China's admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets along these routes.

notes.CHN: Under the Song and Yuan dynasties (960–1368), southern ports such as Guangzhou and Quanzhou led China's sea trade, and porcelain became a major export.
notes.VNM: Champa, a kingdom on Vietnam's central coast, was a regular stop for ships sailing between China and the Strait of Malacca.
notes.IDN: Srivijaya, a Buddhist kingdom based on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca and its trade from the 600s to the 1000s.
notes.MYS: The Sultanate of Malacca, founded around 1400, became the main port of the strait. The Portuguese captured it in 1511.
notes.SGP: In the 1300s the island at the strait's southern end was a trading port called Temasek.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka sat midway across the Indian Ocean, a meeting place for ships from China, Persia and Arabia and a source of gems and cinnamon.
notes.IND: Ports on the Malabar coast exported pepper, the most prized spice. Hoards of Roman coins in southern India show trade with Rome from the 1st century AD.
notes.OMN: Sohar and Muscat were home ports of Arab sailors, who crossed to India and beyond with the monsoon.
notes.IRN: Siraf and later Hormuz were Persia's great ports on the Gulf.
notes.IRQ: From 762 Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, drew Indian Ocean trade up the Gulf through Basra.
notes.YEM: Aden, at the mouth of the Red Sea, handled much of the trade between India and Egypt in the Middle Ages.
notes.EGY: Under Rome, ships sailed from Egypt's Red Sea ports to India. In the Middle Ages Cairo and Alexandria controlled the spice trade to Europe.

pn: Zaitun to foreign traders. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, in the 1200s and 1300s, both rated it one of the world's greatest ports.
Founded around 1400, the Sultanate of Malacca controlled the strait and grew rich where Chinese, Indian and Arab traders met.
The great pepper port of India's Malabar coast. Zheng He's fleets called here, and Vasco da Gama landed in 1498.
An island port guarding the mouth of the Persian Gulf, a great market for Indian Ocean goods from the 1300s.
At the mouth of the Red Sea, the main stop on the medieval trade between India and Egypt.
Where Eastern goods reached the Mediterranean, after crossing the desert from the Red Sea and sailing down the Nile.

rome.text: When the emperor Trajan died in AD 117, Rome ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, which Romans called 'our sea'. Its provinces ran from northern Britain to Egypt and, very briefly, to the Persian Gulf, tied together by roads, trade, Roman law and the Latin and Greek languages. Today's [Italy](ITA), [Spain](ESP), [France](FRA), [Turkey](TUR) and [Egypt](EGY) all lay inside it.

notes.ITA: Italy was the empire's heartland. Rome had united it by the 200s BC, and its free people were Roman citizens long before most provincials.
notes.ESP: Rome conquered Hispania over two centuries, from 218 to 19 BC. Trajan, born at Italica near Seville, was the first emperor from outside Italy.
notes.PRT: Most of Portugal lay in the province of Lusitania, whose capital was Emerita Augusta, today's Mérida in Spain.
notes.FRA: Southern France was Roman from the 120s BC, and Julius Caesar conquered the rest of Gaul in 58–50 BC. The Latin spoken there later grew into French.
notes.GBR: Rome invaded Britain in AD 43 and held England and Wales, but never held Scotland for long. In 122 Hadrian began a wall across the north.
notes.NLD: The Rhine was the frontier, so only the south of today's Netherlands was Roman.
notes.DEU: Rome held Germany west of the Rhine and south of the Danube, and the corner between them. After losing three legions in AD 9 it never conquered the rest.
notes.ROU: Trajan conquered Dacia in 101–106 for its gold mines. Rome gave it up around 271, but Romanian is still a Latin-based language.
notes.TUR: Anatolia was one of the richest parts of the empire, full of Greek-speaking cities such as Ephesus.
notes.EGY: Egypt became Roman in 30 BC, after the death of Cleopatra. Its Nile grain helped feed the city of Rome.
notes.TUN: Rome destroyed its old rival Carthage in 146 BC. Rebuilt as a Roman city, Carthage became one of the largest in the empire.
notes.ISR: Judaea rebelled in AD 66 and Rome destroyed Jerusalem's Temple in 70. After another revolt in the 130s the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.
notes.PSE: Judaea rebelled in AD 66 and Rome destroyed Jerusalem's Temple in 70. After another revolt in the 130s the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.
notes.JOR: Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom, with its rock-cut city of Petra, in 106 as the province of Arabia.
notes.SAU: The province of Arabia reached into north-west Arabia, as far as the Nabataean town of Hegra (Mada'in Salih).
notes.LBY: Only the coast was Roman: Tripolitania in the west, with the great city of Leptis Magna, and Cyrenaica in the east.
notes.MAR: Northern Morocco was the province of Mauretania Tingitana, named after Tingis, today's Tangier.
notes.ARM: Trajan made Armenia a province in 114. Hadrian, who succeeded him in 117, soon gave it up, and it went back to being a kingdom under Roman influence.
notes.IRQ: Trajan took the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in 116 and reached the Persian Gulf. Revolts followed, and Hadrian pulled back to the Euphrates.

pn: The capital, with perhaps a million people in the 100s AD, fed by grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa.
In 117 still the Greek city of Byzantium. Constantine refounded it as his new capital in 330; today it is Istanbul.
The empire's second city and the port that shipped Egypt's grain to Rome.

rome.text: When the emperor Theodosius I died in 395, the empire was split for good between his two sons. The Western Empire, ruled from [Italy](ITA), was overrun by Germanic peoples and ended in 476. The Eastern Empire, ruled from Constantinople in today's [Turkey](TUR) and later called Byzantine, spoke mainly Greek and outlived the West by almost 1,000 years, until the Ottomans took the city in 1453.

notes.ITA: Italy was the Western Empire's heart. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, the date usually given for the fall of Rome.
notes.GBR: Rome withdrew its army from Britain around 410, and Anglo-Saxons settled much of England over the next two centuries.
notes.FRA: Visigoths, Burgundians and Franks took over Gaul in the 400s. The Franks gave France its name.
notes.ESP: The Visigoths ruled Spain from the 400s until the Arab conquest of 711.
notes.TUN: The Vandals took Roman Africa and its capital Carthage in 439, cutting the West off from some of its richest lands.
notes.DEU: The Rhine frontier gave way after Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed it in 406, and Franks and Alamanni settled west of the river.
notes.BIH: The line between East and West ran roughly along the Drina, today's border between Bosnia and Serbia. It later also roughly divided Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
notes.SRB: Most of Serbia was Eastern, but the north around Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) belonged to the West.
notes.LBY: The line crossed the Gulf of Sirte: Tripolitania in the west went to the Western Empire and Cyrenaica in the east to the Eastern.
notes.ROU: Rome had abandoned Dacia around 271. Only Dobruja, between the lower Danube and the Black Sea, was still Roman, and it went to the East.
notes.TUR: Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 on the site of Byzantium. It stayed the Eastern capital until the Ottomans took it in 1453. The far east, around Kars and Van, was Persian.
notes.GRC: Greece was the Eastern Empire's Greek-speaking core. Greek replaced Latin as the language of government in the 600s.
notes.EGY: Egypt was the East's richest province until the Arabs conquered it in 639–642.
notes.SYR: Syria stayed Eastern Roman until the Arab conquests of the 630s.
notes.MNE: Most of Montenegro lay in the province of Praevalitana, which went to the East; the far north belonged to Dalmatia in the West.

pn: 410: sacked by the Visigoths under Alaric, the first time in 800 years an enemy had taken the city.
Western capital from 402. Here in 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
Capital of the East from its founding in 330 until the Ottoman conquest on 29 May 1453.

americas.text: Long before Europeans arrived, the Americas had great cities and states. The Maya of [Guatemala](GTM), [Belize](BLZ) and southern [Mexico](MEX) built stone cities and a full writing system, flourishing about 250–900. The Aztecs ruled central Mexico from their island city Tenochtitlan, and the Inca, from Cusco in [Peru](PER), built the largest empire in the Americas along the Andes.

notes.GTM: Guatemala's Petén lowlands held great Classic Maya cities such as Tikal. Many of them were abandoned in the 800s, but Maya people and languages live on there today.
notes.BLZ: Belize lay in the Maya heartland, with cities such as Caracol, which fought wars against Tikal.
notes.HND: Western Honduras held Copán, one of the finest Classic Maya cities, famous for its carved stelae and hieroglyphic stairway.
notes.SLV: Western El Salvador lay on the southern edge of the Maya world.
notes.MEX: The Aztecs ruled much of central and southern Mexico through tribute, but not the far north or west. Maya lands in the south-east, outside their empire, had held cities such as Palenque and Chichén Itzá.
notes.PER: Peru was the heart of the Inca Empire. Under Pachacuti, from about 1438, the Inca spread out from Cusco along the Andes and the Pacific coast.
notes.ECU: The Inca conquered the Ecuadorian highlands late in the 1400s, and Quito became the empire's northern capital.
notes.BOL: The Inca held the high Altiplano around Lake Titicaca, which their legends made the birthplace of their people.
notes.CHL: The Inca ruled northern and central Chile as far as the Maule River. The Mapuche further south stopped them.
notes.ARG: The Inca held the Andean northwest of Argentina, as far south as Mendoza.
notes.COL: The Inca Empire reached only the far south of Colombia, near Pasto.
notes.USA: North America had no empire, but it had towns: Cahokia, near today's St Louis, was a great mound-building centre around 1050–1200.

pn: One of the greatest Classic Maya cities, at its height about 600–800 and abandoned during the 900s.
Founded about 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, the Aztec capital had perhaps 200,000 people. Mexico City stands on its ruins.
The Inca capital. From here roads ran out to the four quarters of the empire.
A royal estate built in the mid-1400s high in the Andes. It escaped Spanish destruction and became world-famous in 1911.

americas.text: Small Spanish forces toppled both great empires with the help of native allies, steel weapons, horses and epidemic disease. Hernán Cortés reached Tenochtitlan in 1519 and destroyed it in 1521, and the city became Mexico City. Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler at Cajamarca in [Peru](PER) in 1532. Within a century epidemics, war and forced labour had killed most of the Americas' native people.

notes.MEX: Cortés landed in 1519 with a few hundred men and won tens of thousands of native allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Aztecs. Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 and Mexico City was built on it.
notes.PER: Pizarro's men captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532, took Cusco in 1533, and founded Lima as their capital in 1535. Inca resistance went on until 1572.
notes.ECU: An epidemic, possibly smallpox, killed the Inca ruler Huayna Capac about 1527. His sons Atahualpa, based in Quito, and Huáscar, based in Cusco, then fought a civil war just before the Spanish came.
notes.BOL: The Spanish found a mountain of silver at Potosí in 1545, which became one of the richest mines in the world.
notes.CHL: Spain founded Santiago in 1541, but the Mapuche in the south resisted Spanish rule for centuries.
notes.DOM: Hispaniola, today's Dominican Republic and Haiti, was Spain's first colony. Its Taíno people were almost wiped out within decades by disease, war and forced labour.
notes.HTI: Hispaniola, today's Haiti and Dominican Republic, was Spain's first colony. Its Taíno people were almost wiped out within decades by disease, war and forced labour.
notes.CUB: Spain conquered Cuba from 1511, and Cortés sailed from there to Mexico in 1519.
notes.GTM: Pedro de Alvarado, one of Cortés's captains, invaded the Maya highlands in 1524. The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén, held out until 1697.
notes.PAN: Panama was the base from which Pizarro sailed south to Peru, and Spain later shipped Peru's silver across the isthmus.
notes.ESP: Spain gained an empire of silver mines and native labour. Historians estimate that within a century of 1492 the native population of the Americas fell by perhaps 80–90%, mostly from disease.

pn: 1519: Cortés lands on the Gulf coast and founds Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz before marching inland.
August 1521: the city falls after a long siege, weakened by smallpox that had swept it the year before.
November 1532: Pizarro's men ambush the Inca ruler Atahualpa and hold him for a vast ransom, then execute him in 1533.
November 1533: the Spanish enter the Inca capital.

islam.text: In 622 Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar. By his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted his rule. Within 30 years the first caliphs took [Syria](SYR) and [Egypt](EGY) from the Byzantines and overthrew the Persian Empire in [Iran](IRN). The Umayyad dynasty, ruling from Damascus, then pushed on to [Spain](ESP) and [Pakistan](PAK), until the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.

notes.SAU: Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610. By his death in 632 most Arabian tribes had accepted his rule, and Arabia became the base for the conquests.
notes.YEM: Yemen's leaders accepted Islam in Muhammad's lifetime, and Yemeni tribesmen fought in the conquests that followed.
notes.SYR: Arab armies beat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk river in 636. Damascus became the Umayyad capital in 661.
notes.ISR: Jerusalem surrendered to the caliph Umar around 637. The Dome of the Rock was completed there in 691–692.
notes.PSE: Jerusalem surrendered to the caliph Umar around 637. The Dome of the Rock was completed there in 691–692.
notes.EGY: Egypt was taken from the Byzantines in 639–642. The Arabs founded a new capital, Fustat, which later grew into Cairo.
notes.IRQ: The Arabs defeated the Persian army at al-Qadisiyya around 636 and took the Persian capital Ctesiphon. They founded garrison cities at Kufa and Basra.
notes.IRN: The Persian Sasanian Empire fell by 651. Iran became mainly Muslim over the following centuries but kept its Persian language.
notes.TUN: The Umayyads founded Kairouan in 670 as their base for the conquest of North Africa.
notes.MAR: Arab armies reached Morocco's Atlantic coast by about 700, and many Berbers joined them. A great Berber revolt from 740 ended the caliphs' rule here.
notes.ESP: In 711 an army of Berbers and Arabs under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Africa and conquered most of Visigothic Spain within a few years. Only the far north held out.
notes.PRT: Most of Portugal became part of al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled part of the Iberian peninsula.
notes.FRA: Umayyad forces held Narbonne and the coast of Languedoc, then called Septimania, from about 719 until 759.
notes.PAK: In 711–712 the young general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, in today's southern Pakistan.
notes.UZB: Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Bukhara and Samarkand between 706 and 712.
notes.AFG: Arab armies took Herat and Balkh in the west and north, but Kabul and the east held out for two more centuries.
notes.ARM: Armenia became a province of the caliphate, governed through its own princes, who paid tribute.

pn: Muhammad's birthplace, around 570, and Islam's holiest city. He returned and took it, largely without fighting, in 630.
622: Muhammad and his followers moved here from Mecca, the Hijra. It was the caliphs' first capital.
Capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. Its Great Mosque was built in about 705–715.
Capital of Muslim Spain, al-Andalus. In 756 an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids founded an emirate here.
732: the Frankish leader Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad raiding army between Tours and Poitiers.

crusades.text: In 1095 Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to take Jerusalem from Muslim rule. Armies marched to Constantinople, fought across Anatolia in today's [Turkey](TUR), took Antioch and in 1099 Jerusalem, and set up four crusader states, mostly along the coast of today's [Israel](ISR), [Lebanon](LBN) and [Syria](SYR). Muslim rulers slowly won them back: Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187, and the last major stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.

notes.ISR: Today's Israel was the heart of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin destroyed its army at Hattin in 1187, and the kingdom survived mainly on the coast, ruled from Acre, until 1291.
notes.PSE: The Kingdom of Jerusalem held the West Bank and Gaza, where it built a castle in 1149. Jerusalem, holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, was the goal of the crusades.
notes.JOR: The kingdom built castles east of the Jordan at Shobak (1115) and Kerak (1142) to control the routes between Syria and Egypt. Saladin took them in 1188–89.
notes.LBN: The County of Tripoli held the north of today's Lebanon, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem held Beirut, Sidon and Tyre in the south.
notes.SYR: Antioch and Tripoli held Syria's coast, but the great inland cities of Aleppo and Damascus stayed under Muslim rule throughout.
notes.TUR: The County of Edessa, around today's Şanlıurfa, was the first crusader state. Its fall to Zengi in 1144 set off the Second Crusade.
