1565: Spain founds the oldest lasting European town in what is now the US.
About 1610: Spain founds the capital of New Mexico.
1608: France founds Quebec, the heart of New France.
1718: France founds New Orleans near the mouth of the Mississippi.

us-colonies.text: The thirteen colonies grew into three regions. [New England](US-MA) had small farms, fishing, trade and strict Puritan towns. The Middle Colonies such as [Pennsylvania](US-PA) and [New York](US-NY) were the most mixed in religion and origin. In the South, [Virginia](US-VA) and [South Carolina](US-SC) grew tobacco and rice on plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who had first been brought to Virginia in 1619.

notes.US-MA: Puritans settled Boston from 1630 to build a godly community. Massachusetts also ran Maine until 1820.
notes.US-RI: Roger Williams founded Rhode Island in 1636 after being expelled from Massachusetts, and it allowed freedom of religion.
notes.US-NY: New York began as the Dutch colony of New Netherland, taken by England in 1664. It was already a diverse trading port.
notes.US-PA: The Quaker William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 with religious freedom, and it drew many German and Scots-Irish settlers.
notes.US-DE: Delaware was settled first by Swedes in 1638, then taken by the Dutch and, in 1664, the English.
notes.US-MD: Maryland was founded in 1634 as a refuge for English Catholics, and like Virginia it grew tobacco with enslaved labour.
notes.US-VA: Virginia's House of Burgesses met in 1619, the first elected assembly in the colonies. By 1750 at least 40% of Virginians were enslaved.
notes.US-SC: South Carolina's rice plantations relied on enslaved Africans, who were a majority of its people from about 1708.
notes.US-GA: Georgia was founded in 1732 as a buffer against Spanish Florida. It banned slavery at first, but allowed it from 1751.
notes.US-VT: Vermont was not one of the colonies. New Hampshire and New York both claimed it, and it was barely settled before the 1760s.

pn: 1607: the first lasting English settlement in North America.
1620: the Pilgrims of the Mayflower land and found Plymouth Colony.
Dutch New Amsterdam from the 1620s; England takes it in 1664 and renames it New York.
1682: William Penn founds the Quaker capital, which becomes the largest colonial city.
1670: English settlers found Charles Town, the rich port of the rice colony.

us-independence.text: Protests against British taxes turned to war at Lexington and Concord in [Massachusetts](US-MA) in April 1775. On 4 July 1776 Congress declared independence in [Philadelphia](US-PA). Victory at Saratoga in 1777 brought [France](FRA) in as an ally, and in 1781 a French and American army trapped the British at Yorktown. The 1783 Treaty of Paris drew the new country's border at the Mississippi, with [Spain](ESP) holding [Florida](US-FL) and Louisiana.

notes.US-MA: Boston was the centre of resistance, from the Boston Tea Party of 1773 to the first shots at Lexington and Concord in 1775.
notes.US-PA: Philadelphia was the rebel capital. Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence there in 1776, and the Constitution was written there in 1787.
notes.US-NY: The victory at Saratoga in 1777 persuaded France to join the war. The British held New York City until the end of 1783.
notes.US-VA: Virginia gave the new nation George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. The British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 ended the main fighting.
notes.US-SC: The British took Charleston in 1780, and much of the later war was a bitter fight in the Carolinas.
notes.US-VT: Vermont declared itself an independent republic in 1777. It joined the Union in 1791 as the 14th state.
notes.US-OH: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 planned new states north of the Ohio River and banned slavery there, making the river a line between free and slave land.
notes.US-KY: Kentucky was part of Virginia until it became a state in 1792.
notes.US-TN: Tennessee was claimed by North Carolina, which handed it to the federal government in 1790. It became a state in 1796.
notes.US-FL: Britain had held Florida since 1763 but returned it to Spain in 1783.
notes.US-LA: France had given Louisiana, the land west of the Mississippi, to Spain in 1762. Spain controlled the river's mouth at New Orleans.
notes.FRA: France sent money, troops and a fleet from 1778, partly for revenge on Britain. The cost helped bring on the French Revolution.
notes.ESP: Spain joined the war against Britain in 1779 and won back Florida in the peace.
notes.CAN: Canada stayed British. Tens of thousands of Loyalists, colonists who had sided with Britain, moved there after the war.

pn: 19 April 1775: the first shots of the war, between British troops and colonial militia.
4 July 1776: the Declaration of Independence. The Constitution is written here in 1787.
October 1777: a British army surrenders, and France joins the war on the American side.
October 1781: General Cornwallis surrenders, effectively ending the fighting.

us-expansion.text: In 1803 [France](FRA) sold Louisiana, the western half of the Mississippi basin, for $15 million, nearly doubling the country. President Thomas Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark up the Missouri River, and they reached the Pacific in 1805. In 1819 [Spain](ESP) handed over [Florida](US-FL) and agreed a border in the West that left [Texas](US-TX) Spanish.

notes.FRA: Napoleon sold Louisiana in 1803 after his army failed to retake Haiti, and he needed money for war with Britain.
notes.US-LA: New Orleans controlled the trade of the whole Mississippi. The district east of the river around Baton Rouge was Spanish West Florida until the US took it in 1810.
notes.US-MO: Lewis and Clark set off from near St. Louis in May 1804, and the city became the gateway to the West.
notes.US-MN: Minnesota came in three pieces: land east of the Mississippi in 1783, Louisiana land west of it, and the Red River valley from Britain in 1818.
notes.US-ND: Most of North Dakota came with Louisiana. The Red River valley in the east came from Britain by a treaty in 1818.
notes.US-MT: Montana east of the Rocky Mountains was Louisiana land. The west came with Oregon in 1846.
notes.US-WY: Most of Wyoming, east of the continental divide, was Louisiana land. The southwest came from Mexico and the far west with Oregon in the 1840s.
notes.US-CO: Eastern Colorado north of the Arkansas River was Louisiana land. The rest came with Texas and from Mexico in the 1840s.
notes.US-AL: The Gulf coast around Mobile was Spanish West Florida until US troops took it in 1813.
notes.US-FL: Spain gave up Florida in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, after Andrew Jackson's troops invaded it in 1818 while fighting the Seminole.
notes.US-TX: The 1819 treaty set the border on the Sabine and Red rivers, leaving Texas to Spain. Mexico, independent from 1821, inherited it.
notes.ESP: Spain, losing its American empire to revolts, ceded Florida in 1819. The US agreed to pay up to $5 million of its citizens' claims against Spain.

pn: 1803: Jefferson tries to buy this port, and Napoleon offers all of Louisiana instead.
Winter 1805–06: Lewis and Clark camp on the Pacific coast before heading home.

us-expansion.text: [Texas](US-TX) broke away from [Mexico](MEX) in 1836 and joined the US in 1845. A treaty with [Britain](GBR) in 1846 split the Oregon Country at the 49th parallel. The war with Mexico in 1846–48 ended with Mexico giving up [California](US-CA) and the Southwest, and the Gadsden Purchase of 1853 added southern [Arizona](US-AZ). Gold found in California in 1848 brought a rush of settlers west.

notes.US-TX: American settlers in Mexican Texas rebelled in 1836. After nine years as a republic, Texas joined the US as a slave state in December 1845, which helped start war with Mexico.
notes.MEX: Counting Texas, Mexico lost about half its territory. In the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo the US paid it $15 million.
notes.US-CA: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill days before the peace treaty was signed. The rush that followed made California a state by 1850.
notes.US-UT: Mormon settlers led by Brigham Young founded Salt Lake City in 1847, on what was still Mexican land.
notes.US-NV: Nevada came from Mexico in 1848. A silver rush from 1859 brought statehood in 1864.
notes.US-NM: Western New Mexico came from Mexico in 1848. Texas claimed the east until 1850, and the southwest corner came with the Gadsden Purchase in 1853.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona north of the Gila River came in 1848. The south, including Tucson, was bought in 1853 for a southern railroad route.
notes.US-CO: Western Colorado came from Mexico in 1848, and a central strip had been claimed by Texas. The east was Louisiana land.
notes.US-WY: Southwestern Wyoming came from Mexico and the far west with Oregon. Most of the rest was Louisiana land.
notes.US-OR: Thousands of settlers took the Oregon Trail from Missouri in the 1840s, strengthening the US claim against Britain.
notes.US-WA: The 1846 treaty set the border at the 49th parallel, and Britain kept all of Vancouver Island.
notes.US-MT: Western Montana, beyond the Rocky Mountains, was part of the Oregon Country.
notes.GBR: Britain and the US had shared the Oregon Country since 1818. Britain's share became British Columbia, now part of Canada.

pn: March 1836: Mexican troops overrun the Texan defenders; Texas wins independence weeks later.
January 1848: gold is found, setting off the California gold rush of 1849.
September 1847: US troops capture the Mexican capital.
1853: the Gadsden Purchase, $10 million for land south of the Gila River.

us-civilwar.text: The Northern states had ended slavery or set it on the way out by 1804, while the Southern economy rested on about 3 million enslaved people, many growing cotton. Every new state reopened the question. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 banned slavery in the Louisiana lands north of 36°30′, but in 1854 Congress let settlers in [Kansas](US-KS) decide, and the territory erupted in violence.

notes.US-MO: Missouri entered as a slave state in 1821 under the Missouri Compromise, balanced by free Maine.
notes.US-ME: Maine split from Massachusetts and joined as a free state in 1820, to balance Missouri.
notes.US-KS: The 1854 Kansas–Nebraska Act let settlers vote on slavery. Pro- and anti-slavery settlers fought for control, and Kansas joined as a free state in January 1861.
notes.US-CA: California joined as a free state in 1850 under a compromise that also passed a harsh law forcing the return of people who escaped slavery.
notes.US-SC: More than half of South Carolina's people were enslaved, the highest share of any state.
notes.US-MS: Mississippi was at the heart of the cotton boom, and over half its people were enslaved.
notes.US-VA: Virginia held more enslaved people than any other state, about 470,000 in 1850.
notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania began abolishing slavery in 1780. Its southern border, the Mason–Dixon line, became the symbolic line between North and South.
notes.US-MA: Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the 1780s, and Boston became a centre of the movement to abolish it everywhere.
notes.US-OH: The Ohio River divided free states from slave states. Many people escaping slavery crossed it on the Underground Railroad.
notes.US-IL: In 1858 Abraham Lincoln of Illinois became nationally known in debates with Stephen Douglas over the spread of slavery.

pn: 1857: in the Dred Scott case, begun here, the Supreme Court rules that Black people cannot be citizens and Congress cannot ban slavery in the territories.
1856: pro-slavery raiders sack this anti-slavery town in "Bleeding Kansas".
October 1859: the abolitionist John Brown raids the federal armoury to start a slave uprising, and is hanged.

us-civilwar.text: After [Abraham Lincoln](US-IL), who opposed the spread of slavery, won the 1860 election, seven Deep South states left the Union, led by [South Carolina](US-SC). Four more followed when war began in April 1861. Four slave states stayed loyal. The North had more people, factories and railroads, and after four years and an estimated 620,000–750,000 soldiers' deaths, the main Confederate army surrendered in April 1865.

notes.US-SC: South Carolina seceded first, on 20 December 1860. The war began when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour.
notes.US-VA: Virginia joined the Confederacy after Fort Sumter, and Richmond became its capital. Most of the fighting in the east was on Virginia soil.
notes.US-WV: Virginia's northwestern counties refused to secede and became the state of West Virginia in 1863.
notes.US-KY: Kentucky, where Lincoln was born, stayed in the Union, though many Kentuckians fought for the South.
notes.US-MD: Maryland surrounded Washington, D.C. on three sides, so Lincoln moved fast, with troops and arrests, to keep it in the Union.
notes.US-MO: Missouri stayed in the Union but suffered vicious guerrilla warfare between Union and Confederate supporters.
notes.US-PA: Gettysburg, in July 1863, was the largest battle of the war. Lincoln's short speech there redefined the war as one for freedom and equality.
notes.US-MS: The fall of Vicksburg on 4 July 1863 gave the Union the whole Mississippi River and cut the Confederacy in two.
notes.US-GA: Sherman took Atlanta in September 1864, then marched to Savannah, wrecking railroads and farms on the way.
notes.US-TX: Word that slavery had ended reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas, on 19 June 1865, a day now marked as Juneteenth.
notes.US-TN: Tennessee was the last state to secede, in June 1861, and much of it was under Union control by 1863.
notes.US-IL: Lincoln, a lawyer from Springfield, Illinois, issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. He was assassinated in April 1865, days after Lee's surrender.
notes.US-NV: Silver-rich Nevada was rushed into statehood in 1864.
notes.US-OK: The nations of Indian Territory were divided by the war, and several, including the Cherokee and Choctaw, signed treaties with the Confederacy.

pn: 12 April 1861: Confederate guns fire on this Union fort in Charleston harbour, starting the war.
September 1862: the bloodiest single day of the war. Lincoln follows it with the Emancipation Proclamation.
July 1863: the largest battle of the war ends Robert E. Lee's invasion of the North.
4 July 1863: the city falls, giving the Union the Mississippi and splitting the Confederacy.
September 1864: General Sherman takes Atlanta, then marches to the sea.
9 April 1865: Lee surrenders his army to Ulysses S. Grant.

us-west.text: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 let President Andrew Jackson exchange land in the West for Native homelands in the East. Over the next two decades about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people were forced from the Southeast to [Indian Territory](US-OK). On the Cherokee Trail of Tears in 1838–39, about 4,000 of some 16,000 people died.

notes.US-GA: Georgia pressed hardest for removal, especially after gold was found on Cherokee land in 1829. It ignored the Supreme Court's 1832 ruling that its laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation.
notes.US-TN: In 1838 the army rounded up most Cherokee into camps in southeastern Tennessee, where the march west began.
notes.US-NC: Several hundred Cherokee stayed in the North Carolina mountains. Their descendants form today's Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
notes.US-AL: Most of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation was forced out of Alabama in 1836–37.
notes.US-MS: The Choctaw of Mississippi were the first nation removed, starting in 1831. The Chickasaw followed from 1837.
notes.US-FL: Many Seminole fought removal in the Second Seminole War, 1835–42. A few hundred were never removed.
notes.US-OK: In Indian Territory the five nations rebuilt their governments, schools and newspapers. Most of it became the state of Oklahoma in 1907.
notes.US-KS: Nations from the north, such as the Shawnee, Delaware and Potawatomi, were sent to reservations in Kansas, then pushed on to Oklahoma after Kansas opened to settlers in 1854.
notes.US-IN: In 1838 the Potawatomi were marched at gunpoint from Indiana to Kansas, a journey they call the Trail of Death.
notes.US-IL: The Sauk leader Black Hawk tried to return to his people's Illinois homeland in 1832 and was crushed in the Black Hawk War.
notes.US-OH: The Wyandot, the last nation with a reservation in Ohio, were removed to Kansas in 1843.

pn: 1835: a small Cherokee faction signs away the nation's land here, against the will of its government.
1839: the Cherokee rebuild their nation and make Tahlequah its capital.

us-west.text: After the Civil War, free farms under the Homestead Act and the first transcontinental railroad, finished in 1869, drew settlers west. Plains nations such as the Lakota and Cheyenne fought for their land, but the army, the settlers and the slaughter of the bison forced them onto reservations. New states followed, [Arizona](US-AZ) completed the 48 contiguous states in 1912, and [Alaska](US-AK) and [Hawaii](US-HI) joined in 1959.

notes.US-DE: Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution, on 7 December 1787.
notes.US-RI: Rhode Island was the last of the 13 to ratify, in May 1790.
notes.US-VT: Vermont, admitted in 1791, was the first state added to the original 13.
notes.US-CA: The gold rush took California straight to statehood in 1850, without its ever being a territory.
notes.US-TX: Texas joined in 1845 directly from being an independent republic.
notes.US-WV: West Virginia split from Virginia during the Civil War and joined in 1863.
notes.US-MN: After the Dakota War of 1862, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato, the largest mass execution in US history.
notes.US-CO: At Sand Creek in 1864 Colorado troops attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp that believed it was under army protection.
notes.US-MT: At the Little Bighorn in 1876 the Lakota and their allies won their greatest victory, but within a year most had been forced onto reservations.
notes.US-SD: Gold found in the Black Hills in 1874 drew miners onto land promised to the Lakota by treaty. The massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890 ended armed resistance.
notes.US-UT: Utah had to wait until 1896, after the Mormon church gave up polygamy in 1890.
notes.US-OK: The government opened Native land in Indian Territory to settlers in land runs from 1889, and Oklahoma became a state in 1907.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona became the 48th state on 14 February 1912, weeks after New Mexico.
notes.US-AK: Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959.
notes.US-HI: Hawaii became the 50th state in August 1959.

pn: 10 May 1869: a golden spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads.
November 1864: Colorado troops kill at least 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and elders.
June 1876: Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors kill George Custer and every soldier in his immediate command.
December 1890: US troops kill at least 250 Lakota, many of them women and children.

us-reconstruction.text: Three amendments remade the Constitution: the 13th ended slavery (1865), the 14th made everyone born in the US a citizen (1868), and the 15th banned denying the vote on grounds of race (1870). With federal troops in the South, Black men voted and won office across the former Confederacy. White terror groups such as the Ku Klux Klan fought back, and in 1877 the last troops left [South Carolina](US-SC) and [Louisiana](US-LA).

notes.US-TN: Tennessee accepted the 14th Amendment and was readmitted in 1866, so it escaped the military rule imposed on the rest of the South in 1867.
notes.US-MS: Mississippi sent the first two Black US senators: Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche K. Bruce in 1875.
notes.US-SC: Black members were a majority of the lower house of South Carolina's legislature during Reconstruction.
notes.US-LA: Louisiana's disputed vote in the 1876 election was part of the deal that made Rutherford Hayes president and ended Reconstruction.
notes.US-FL: Florida was one of three Southern states whose disputed votes decided the 1876 presidential election.
notes.US-GA: Georgia was readmitted in 1868, then put back under military rule after its legislature expelled its Black members. It returned in 1870.
notes.US-KY: Slavery stayed legal in Kentucky until the 13th Amendment took effect in December 1865, since the Emancipation Proclamation applied only to Confederate land.
notes.US-DE: Slavery stayed legal in Delaware until the 13th Amendment took effect in December 1865.
notes.US-TX: Texas was among the last states readmitted, in 1870.

pn: 1865: Confederate veterans found the Ku Klux Klan here.
1870: Hiram Revels of Natchez, Mississippi, becomes the first Black member of the US Congress, as a senator.

us-reconstruction.text: After 1877, 'Jim Crow' laws segregated the South and took away Black votes. Segregation, lynching and poor farm work drove about 6 million Black Southerners north and west between 1910 and 1970, most to factory jobs in big cities: from [Mississippi](US-MS) to Chicago, from [Georgia](US-GA) and the Carolinas to New York, and after 1940 from [Texas](US-TX) to California. In 1910 nine in ten Black Americans lived in the South; by 1970 about half did.

notes.US-MS: Chicago was the main destination for Mississippi's migrants, many of whom rode north on the Illinois Central railroad.
notes.US-IL: Chicago's South Side became one of the largest Black communities in the country, the 'Black Metropolis'.
notes.US-MI: Detroit's car factories drew Black workers from Alabama and across the South.
notes.US-OH: Cleveland's steel mills and factories drew many migrants from Alabama.
notes.US-NY: Migrants from the Carolinas, Georgia and Virginia made Harlem the centre of Black culture, home to the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s.
notes.US-PA: Philadelphia drew many migrants from Virginia and the Carolinas.
notes.US-GA: Many Black Georgians took the trains up the East Coast to Washington, Philadelphia and New York.
notes.US-TX: After 1940 many Black Texans moved west to Los Angeles and Oakland, where war industries were hiring.
notes.US-CA: In the second wave, after 1940, shipyards and factories drew migrants from Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi to Los Angeles and Oakland.
notes.US-LA: Louisiana's 1890 law segregating railway cars led to Plessy v. Ferguson. Its migrants went to Chicago and later to California.

pn: 1896: in Plessy v. Ferguson, a case from New Orleans, the Supreme Court approves "separate but equal" segregation.
1920s: the Harlem Renaissance makes this New York neighbourhood the capital of Black culture.

us-industry.text: Railroads, steel and oil made the US the world's largest industrial producer by about 1900, and more than 20 million immigrants arrived between 1880 and 1920 to work in it. Earlier newcomers had come mainly from [Germany](DEU), [Ireland](IRL) and Britain; now most came from southern and eastern Europe, such as [Italy](ITA) and [Poland](POL). In 1910 about one American in seven was foreign-born. A law of 1882 barred Chinese workers, and one of 1924 sharply cut immigration.

notes.ITA: About 4 million Italians came between 1880 and 1920, mostly poor farmers from the south. Many later went home.
notes.IRL: Irish immigration peaked earlier, after the famine of the 1840s. By 1900 Irish Americans ran the politics of many big cities.
notes.DEU: Germans were the largest immigrant group of the 19th century, and many settled in the Midwest.
notes.POL: Poland did not exist until 1918. Poles came from the German, Russian and Austrian empires, many to work in steel mills and coal mines.
notes.HUN: Austria-Hungary sent over 2 million immigrants in 1901–1910 alone, including Hungarians, Slovaks, Poles and Croats.
notes.UKR: Between 1881 and 1924 about 2 million Jews came from eastern Europe, most fleeing poverty and violent pogroms in the Russian Empire, including today's Ukraine, Belarus and Lithuania.
notes.SWE: Over a million Swedes came, many to farm in Minnesota and the upper Midwest.
notes.CHN: Chinese workers built much of the Central Pacific railroad. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 then barred Chinese labourers, the first US law to ban a nationality.
notes.JPN: Japanese migrants worked on Hawaii's sugar plantations and Western farms until a 1907 agreement limited them.
notes.MEX: The Mexican Revolution from 1910 sent hundreds of thousands north to work on farms and railroads in the Southwest.
notes.US-NY: New York City was the main gateway, and by 1910 about four in ten of its people were foreign-born.
notes.US-MI: Ford's factories near Detroit drew workers from across Europe and, later, Black workers from the South.

pn: 1892–1954: about 12 million immigrants pass through this station in New York harbour.
1910–1940: the station in San Francisco Bay where Chinese and other Asian immigrants were held and questioned.
Steel city: Andrew Carnegie's mills ran on immigrant labour.
Railroad hub and meatpacking centre: 300,000 people in 1870, 2.7 million in 1920.
1913: Henry Ford's moving assembly line makes cars cheap enough for workers to buy.

us-industry.text: The US bought [Alaska](US-AK) from [Russia](RUS) in 1867 for $7.2 million. In 1898 it annexed [Hawaii](US-HI), five years after American businessmen overthrew its queen, and a short war with [Spain](ESP) won [Puerto Rico](PRI), [Guam](GUM) and the [Philippines](PHL). Filipinos fighting for independence then fought US forces until 1902. In 1914 the US opened the Panama Canal.

notes.US-AK: Critics mocked the purchase as 'Seward's Folly', but gold rushes from the 1890s and later oil proved its worth.
notes.RUS: Russia sold Alaska, which it feared it could not defend, after its defeat in the Crimean War.
notes.US-HI: In 1893 American sugar planters and businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani. Congress formally apologised for it in 1993.
notes.PRI: Puerto Ricans were made US citizens in 1917, and the island remains a US territory.
notes.GUM: Guam, taken in 1898, is still a US territory and a major military base.
notes.PHL: The US paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines, then fought Filipino independence fighters in 1899–1902. The Philippines became independent in 1946.
notes.CUB: The US went to war in 1898 in the name of Cuban independence. Cuba became independent in 1902 but under US oversight, and the US kept a base at Guantánamo Bay.
notes.PAN: The US backed Panama's break from Colombia in 1903 and controlled a zone along the canal until 1979. The canal passed to Panama in 1999.
notes.VIR: The US bought the Danish West Indies from Denmark for $25 million in 1917.
notes.ASM: The US took the eastern Samoan islands under an 1899 deal with Germany and Britain.
notes.ESP: The 1898 war cost Spain Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, the last large pieces of its overseas empire.

pn: January 1893: Queen Liliʻuokalani is overthrown at ʻIolani Palace.
February 1898: the US battleship Maine explodes in the harbour, a trigger for war with Spain.
1 May 1898: a US fleet destroys the Spanish squadron in a morning.
15 August 1914: the canal opens, linking the Atlantic and Pacific.

us-depression.text: The 1920s boomed, but the stock market crash of October 1929 began the worst depression in American history: by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job. Drought and over-ploughed soil turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl, and hundreds of thousands of migrants from [Oklahoma](US-OK) and nearby states headed for [California](US-CA). President Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal brought public works, Social Security and the [Tennessee](US-TN) Valley Authority.

notes.US-OK: The Dust Bowl hit the Oklahoma panhandle hardest, but drought and failing farms pushed families out across the state, and 'Okie' became a name for all Plains migrants.
notes.US-KS: Southwestern Kansas was in the heart of the Dust Bowl, where storms stripped the topsoil from millions of acres.
notes.US-TX: The Texas panhandle suffered some of the worst storms. On 'Black Sunday', 14 April 1935, a wall of dust swept across it from Oklahoma.
notes.US-CO: Southeastern Colorado was part of the Dust Bowl, and many of its farm families left.
notes.US-NM: Northeastern New Mexico lay on the Dust Bowl's southwestern edge.
notes.US-CA: Migrants crowded into farm-workers' camps in the Central Valley, as told in John Steinbeck's 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath.
notes.US-TN: The TVA, created in May 1933, built dams that controlled floods and brought electricity to one of the poorest regions in the country.
notes.US-NY: The crash began on Wall Street in October 1929. About 9,000 banks failed across the country between 1930 and 1933.
notes.US-NV: Hoover Dam, on the Nevada–Arizona border, employed thousands of men during the Depression.

pn: October 1929: share prices collapse, beginning the Great Depression.
Finished in 1936: a giant public work that tamed the Colorado River.
1936: the Tennessee Valley Authority's first dam is completed.

us-superpower.text: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in [Hawaii](US-HI) on 7 December 1941 killed about 2,400 Americans and brought the US into the war. Its factories outproduced every other country, and about 16 million Americans served. Out of fear and prejudice the government imprisoned about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, in inland camps. Secret atomic plants in [Tennessee](US-TN), [Washington](US-WA) and [New Mexico](US-NM) built the bombs dropped on [Japan](JPN) in August 1945.

notes.US-HI: The attack sank or damaged eight battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans. Hawaii was a US territory and spent the war under martial law.
notes.US-CA: An order of February 1942 removed everyone of Japanese descent from the West Coast. California had two camps, Manzanar and Tule Lake.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona had two camps. Poston, on the Colorado River Indian Reservation, was the largest of all in area.
notes.US-AR: Two camps, Rohwer and Jerome, held Japanese Americans in the Arkansas Delta.
notes.US-WY: Heart Mountain camp briefly became the third-largest town in Wyoming.
notes.US-ID: Minidoka camp held Japanese Americans mainly from Washington and Oregon.
notes.US-UT: Topaz camp, in the Utah desert, held Japanese Americans mainly from the San Francisco Bay Area.
notes.US-CO: Amache camp, near Granada, held Japanese Americans mainly from California.
notes.US-TN: Oak Ridge, built from nothing in 1942–43, enriched the uranium for the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
notes.US-WA: Hanford made the plutonium for the first atomic test and for the bomb dropped on Nagasaki.
notes.US-NM: Scientists at Los Alamos designed the bombs and tested the first one on 16 July 1945.
notes.US-MI: Detroit's car plants switched to tanks, aircraft engines and bombers, and the city became the 'arsenal of democracy'.
notes.JPN: Atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Japan surrendered days later.

pn: 7 December 1941: Japanese planes strike the US Pacific Fleet.
1942–45: one of ten camps where Japanese Americans were held behind barbed wire.
16 July 1945: the first atomic bomb explodes in the New Mexico desert.
Ford's giant plant near Detroit builds thousands of B-24 bombers.

us-superpower.text: Unlike after 1918, the US stayed engaged with the world after 1945. It helped rebuild Western Europe and in 1949 formed NATO to deter the [Soviet Union](RUS). Treaties with [Japan](JPN), [South Korea](KOR), [Australia](AUS) and others reached across the Pacific. [Alaska](US-AK) and [Hawaii](US-HI) became the 49th and 50th states in 1959. The Cold War brought wars in Korea and [Vietnam](VNM) and ended with the Soviet collapse in 1991.

notes.US-AK: Alaska became the 49th state on 3 January 1959. Facing the Soviet Union across the Bering Strait, it was a front line of air defence.
notes.US-HI: Hawaii became the 50th state on 21 August 1959, and Pearl Harbor remained the base of the US Pacific Fleet.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, starting an arms race with the US. It broke up in 1991.
notes.DEU: West Germany joined NATO in 1955. Divided Berlin was the Cold War's flashpoint, and the Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989.
notes.GBR: Britain, a founding member of NATO, was the closest US ally.
notes.CAN: Canada was a founding member of NATO, and in 1957–58 the two countries set up a joint air-defence command, NORAD.
notes.TUR: Turkey and Greece joined NATO in 1952.
notes.JPN: Occupied by the US until 1952, Japan became an ally under a 1951 security treaty and still hosts US bases.
notes.KOR: The US led the UN side in the Korean War of 1950–53, and has kept troops in South Korea ever since.
notes.AUS: Australia and New Zealand allied with the US in the ANZUS treaty of 1951.
notes.PHL: The Philippines, independent since 1946, signed a defence treaty with the US in 1951.
notes.VNM: The US fought in Vietnam from the mid-1960s to 1973 to stop a communist takeover of the South. About 58,000 Americans died, and the South fell in 1975.

us-civilrights.text: In 1954, in [Brown v. Board of Education](US-KS), the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional; 17 states and Washington, D.C. required it. Southern leaders resisted, and the movement answered with boycotts, sit-ins and marches, from [Montgomery](US-AL) to [Little Rock](US-AR). After the 1963 March on Washington, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in [Memphis](US-TN) in 1968.

notes.US-KS: Kansas let cities segregate elementary schools. Oliver Brown sued Topeka's school board after his daughter Linda was refused a place at a nearby white school.
notes.US-AL: Rosa Parks' arrest in Montgomery in 1955 began the bus boycott that made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Birmingham (1963) and Selma (1965) followed.
notes.US-AR: In 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock's Central High. President Eisenhower sent army troops to escort them in.
notes.US-MS: Before 1965 only about 7% of Black adults in Mississippi were registered to vote. After the Voting Rights Act, about 60% were by 1967.
notes.US-NC: The Greensboro sit-in of February 1960 spread to dozens of Southern cities within weeks.
notes.US-VA: Prince Edward County closed its public schools from 1959 to 1964 rather than integrate them.
notes.US-SC: Briggs v. Elliott, from Clarendon County, was one of the cases the Supreme Court decided together as Brown v. Board.
notes.US-DE: A Delaware case was also one of those decided together as Brown v. Board.
notes.US-TN: Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis on 4 April 1968, where he had come to support striking Black sanitation workers.
notes.US-GA: King was born in Atlanta in 1929, and the city was the base of his Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
notes.US-LA: In 1960 six-year-old Ruby Bridges integrated a New Orleans elementary school, escorted by federal marshals.
notes.US-MD: Thurgood Marshall of Baltimore argued Brown before the Supreme Court and in 1967 became its first Black justice.

pn: 17 May 1954: the Supreme Court rules unanimously that separate schools are "inherently unequal".
1955–56: after Rosa Parks' arrest, a 381-day bus boycott ends segregated buses.
September 1957: army troops escort nine Black students into Central High School.
1 February 1960: four students sit at a whites-only lunch counter, starting a wave of sit-ins.
1963: police turn dogs and fire hoses on young marchers; in September a church bombing kills four girls.
7 March 1965: state troopers beat voting-rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge, 'Bloody Sunday'.

us-today.text: Presidents are chosen state by state in the Electoral College. In 2024 Republican Donald Trump won 31 states and 312 electoral votes, including all seven closely fought swing states. Democrat Kamala Harris won 19 states and Washington, D.C., with 226 votes. Trump also won the national popular vote, 49.8% to 48.3%. Democrats did best in big cities and on the coasts, Republicans in rural areas and the interior.

notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania, with 19 electoral votes, was the biggest swing state. Trump won it, as he had in 2016.
notes.US-MI: Michigan, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-WI: Wisconsin, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-GA: Georgia, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-AZ: Arizona, a swing state, voted for Trump after backing Joe Biden in 2020.
notes.US-NV: Nevada voted Republican for the first time since 2004.
notes.US-NC: North Carolina, a swing state, voted for Trump, as it had in 2016 and 2020.
notes.US-CA: California, the biggest prize with 54 electoral votes, voted for Harris.
notes.US-TX: Texas, with 40 electoral votes, voted for Trump. It has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1980.
notes.US-ME: Maine splits its electoral votes. Harris won the state, but Trump won its rural 2nd district and one electoral vote.
notes.US-NE: Nebraska splits its electoral votes. Trump won the state, but Harris won the Omaha-based 2nd district and one electoral vote.
notes.US-VA: Virginia, once reliably Republican, has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 2008.
notes.US-MN: Minnesota has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 1976, the longest streak of any state.
notes.US-WY: Wyoming gave Trump his highest share of any state, about 72%.

us-today.text: Every ten years the census reshares the 435 seats in the House of Representatives, and electoral votes with them. People have long been moving to the South and West: after 2020 [Texas](US-TX) gained two seats and [Florida](US-FL), North Carolina and three Western states one each. Seven states lost one, among them [New York](US-NY), Pennsylvania and, for the first time, [California](US-CA). The centre of population has moved from Maryland in 1790 to Missouri.

notes.US-TX: Texas, with 29 million people in 2020, gained two seats, more than any other state.
notes.US-FL: Florida, with 21.5 million people, passed New York as the third-largest state in the 2010s.
notes.US-CA: California, with 39.5 million people, is still the largest state, but it lost a seat for the first time in its 170 years of statehood.
notes.US-NY: New York lost a seat. Census officials said it would have kept it with 89 more residents.
notes.US-MT: Montana regained the second House seat it had lost after the 1990 census.
notes.US-WV: West Virginia's population shrank in the 2010s, and it dropped from three seats to two.
notes.US-NC: North Carolina gained a 14th seat, part of the long boom of the Southeast.
notes.US-CO: Colorado gained an eighth seat as the Mountain West kept growing.
notes.US-OR: Oregon gained its sixth seat, its first gain since 1980.
notes.US-PA: Pennsylvania lost a seat, leaving it 17, down from a peak of 36 in the early 20th century.
notes.US-MO: The centre of population in 2020 was in Wright County, Missouri, near the town of Hartville.

pn: 1790: the centre lies in Kent County, Maryland, east of Baltimore.
2020: the centre lies in Wright County, Missouri, almost 900 miles west of where it began.

cn-origins.text: Chinese civilisation grew up on the loess plateau and the flat, flood-prone plain of the lower Yellow River. Around 1200 BC the Shang kings ruled from Anyang in today's [Henan](CN-HA), carving questions to their ancestors on oracle bones. In about 1046 BC the Zhou, from the Wei valley in [Shaanxi](CN-SN), overthrew them. Later Zhou kings lost real power, and the Warring States fought on until 221 BC.

notes.CN-HA: Henan, on the middle Yellow River, was the Shang heartland, with capitals near Zhengzhou and Anyang. Later dynasties often ruled from Luoyang and Kaifeng, also in Henan.
notes.CN-SN: The Wei valley in Shaanxi was the Zhou homeland. Its capital region, around today's Xi'an, later served the Qin, Han and Tang.
notes.CN-SD: Western Shandong lay inside the Shang world. Under the Zhou it held the states of Qi and Lu; Lu was the home of Confucius.
notes.CN-HE: Southern Hebei, on the North China Plain, was part of the Shang heartland around Anyang.
notes.CN-SX: Southern Shanxi, inside the great bend of the Yellow River, lay in the Shang orbit. Under the Zhou it became the powerful state of Jin.
notes.CN-HB: The middle Yangtze was home to Chu, a large southern state that joined the Zhou world but kept its own culture.
notes.CN-SC: At Sanxingdui, near Chengdu, a Bronze Age culture of the Shang era made strikingly different bronze masks and figures.
notes.CN-ZJ: Villages in Zhejiang were growing rice about 7,000 years ago, at sites such as Hemudu. The Yangtze was a second cradle of Chinese farming.

pn: c. 1250–1046 BC: Yin, the last Shang capital. Oracle bones found here carry the earliest known Chinese writing.
c. 1046–771 BC: capital of the Western Zhou, near today's Xi'an.
770 BC: the Zhou court moved east to Luoyang after its western capital was sacked in 771.
551–479 BC: home of Confucius, whose teachings on duty, ritual and good government shaped China for 2,000 years.

cn-qin.text: Between 230 and 221 BC the state of Qin, based in [Shaanxi](CN-SN), conquered its six rivals. Its king became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He divided the land into commanderies run by appointed officials, standardised the script, coins, weights and axle widths, and joined older walls along the northern frontier. In the far south his armies reached the coast around today's Guangzhou, but held it only through scattered garrisons.

notes.CN-SN: Qin grew from the Wei valley in Shaanxi, a fertile basin guarded by mountain passes. Its capital, Xianyang, lay near today's Xi'an.
notes.CN-SC: Qin conquered the Sichuan basin in 316 BC. The Dujiangyan irrigation works it built there still water the Chengdu plain; the western mountains stayed outside its rule.
notes.CN-HA: Han, a state in today's Henan, was the first of the six rivals to fall, in 230 BC.
notes.CN-HB: Chu, the largest rival, ruled the middle Yangtze. Qin crushed it in 223 BC.
notes.CN-SD: Qi, in Shandong, was the last rival standing. It surrendered in 221 BC, completing the unification.
notes.CN-HE: Zhao and Yan, the northern rivals, fell in 228–222 BC. Yan's land around Beijing guarded the north-east frontier.
notes.CN-NM: In 215 BC General Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu nomads out of the Ordos, inside the great loop of the Yellow River, now in Inner Mongolia.
notes.CN-LN: Qin inherited Liaodong, in southern Liaoning, from the conquered state of Yan.
notes.CN-GS: Only eastern Gansu, around Longxi commandery, was Qin. The long Hexi corridor further west belonged to nomads.
notes.CN-GD: Qin armies crossed the southern mountains in the 210s BC and set up Nanhai commandery around Guangzhou. A Qin general later made it the kingdom of Nanyue.
notes.CN-GX: Guilin commandery covered part of Guangxi, reached by the new Lingqu canal.
notes.CN-FJ: Qin named Fujian a commandery, Minzhong, but local Yue chiefs kept real control.

pn: The Qin capital, near today's Xi'an.
Buried with the First Emperor, who died in 210 BC: an army of about 8,000 clay soldiers, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
c. 214 BC: dug to supply the southern campaign, it linked the Yangtze and Pearl river systems.
214 BC: seat of Nanhai commandery, Qin's foothold on the southern coast.

cn-hantang.text: The Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220) kept the Qin system but staffed it with Confucian-trained officials. Emperor Wu (141–87 BC) pushed into [Korea](PRK), northern [Vietnam](VNM) and the Hexi corridor of [Gansu](CN-GS), opening the overland Silk Road to Central Asia. A census in AD 2 counted about 58 million people. Most Chinese still call themselves Han people.

notes.CN-SN: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was the capital of the Western Han. The Eastern Han (AD 25–220) moved the capital to Luoyang.
notes.CN-GS: Han armies drove the Xiongnu out of the Hexi corridor in 121 BC. Four commanderies, from Wuwei to Dunhuang, then guarded the road west.
notes.CN-XJ: From 60 BC a Han Protector-General oversaw the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin. Han control there came and went with its armies.
notes.MNG: The Xiongnu, a nomad confederation based in Mongolia, were the Han's great rival. Early Han emperors bought peace with silk and royal brides.
notes.PRK: Han conquered the Korean kingdom of Gojoseon in 108 BC. Lelang commandery, near Pyongyang, lasted until AD 313.
notes.VNM: Han conquered Nanyue in 111 BC. Northern Vietnam stayed under Chinese rule, with breaks, for over a thousand years, until 939.
notes.CN-GD: Guangdong was the core of Nanyue, a kingdom founded by a former Qin general, until Han conquered it in 111 BC.
notes.CN-YN: Han conquered the Dian kingdom around Kunming in 109 BC. The hills and the far south stayed in local hands.
notes.CN-SC: The Sichuan basin was among the richest Han regions. The mountains of the west were outside Han rule.
notes.CN-HA: Luoyang, in Henan, was the Eastern Han capital and one of the largest cities in the world.

pn: The Western Han capital, today's Xi'an, and the eastern end of the Silk Road.
The westernmost of four Han frontier commanderies in the Hexi corridor, guarding the road west.
104–101 BC: Han armies marched this far west to win the prized 'heavenly horses' of Ferghana.
108 BC: Han conquered the Korean kingdom of Gojoseon and set up Lelang commandery near Pyongyang.
111 BC: Han conquered the kingdom of Nanyue and ruled northern Vietnam as Jiaozhi.

cn-hantang.text: After nearly four centuries of division, the Sui reunited China in 589 and dug the Grand Canal to carry rice from the Yangtze to the north. The Tang (618–907) built on this. From Chang'an they ruled out into [Xinjiang](CN-XJ) and northern [Vietnam](VNM), while Buddhism, merchants and envoys flowed in along the Silk Road. Defeat at the Talas River in 751 and the An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 ended the expansion.

notes.CN-SN: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was again the capital, the eastern end of the Silk Road.
notes.CN-HA: Luoyang, the Tang eastern capital, was the hub of the Sui canal network, which ran south-east to the Yangtze and north-east to the Beijing area.
notes.CN-ZJ: The canal's southern end at Hangzhou tied the rich Yangtze delta, China's growing rice bowl, to the northern capitals.
notes.CN-XJ: The Tang ruled the Tarim oases through the Anxi Protectorate, based at Kucha, and Beiting in the north. Tibet took most of the region after 790.
notes.CN-XZ: The Tibetan Empire, united in the 600s, was the Tang's main rival. In 641 the Tang princess Wencheng married its king, Songtsen Gampo.
notes.CN-QH: Tibet conquered the Tuyuhun kingdom of Qinghai in 663. The Tang held only the Xining area in the east.
notes.CN-YN: Nanzhao united the Erhai region of western Yunnan in 737–38 with Tang support, then took the east and turned on the Tang and defeated its armies in 751 and 754.
notes.VNM: The Tang ruled northern Vietnam as the Protectorate of Annam, the 'Pacified South', from a seat at today's Hanoi.
notes.CN-JL: Manchuria was ruled by Balhae (698–926), a kingdom that sent tribute to the Tang.
notes.CN-GS: The Hexi corridor through Gansu carried the Silk Road traffic. Tibet seized it in the decades after the An Lushan rebellion.

pn: The Tang capital, a planned city of walled wards with Buddhist temples and foreign merchants, one of the largest in the world.
Where the Grand Canal met the Yangtze; a booming trade city under the Tang.
751: an Abbasid Arab army defeated a Tang force near the Talas River, at the western edge of Tang power.
Capital of the Tibetan Empire, which fought the Tang for the Silk Road oases.

cn-songming.text: The Song (960–1279) never ruled the whole Tang realm, but under them farming, trade and cities boomed: they printed books and paper money, used gunpowder weapons and steered ships by compass. In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took the capital, Kaifeng, and the Song moved south to Hangzhou. The peace of 1142 split China along the Huai River. The Mongols later conquered both, finishing the Song in 1279.

notes.CN-HA: Kaifeng, in Henan, was the Northern Song capital until 1127, when the Jin captured the city and two Song emperors.
notes.CN-ZJ: Hangzhou, on the Yangtze delta, became the Song capital. The delta's rice made the south China's economic centre from then on.
notes.CN-HL: The Jurchens, ancestors of the Manchus, came from the forests of Manchuria. They founded the Jin in 1115 and destroyed the Liao in 1125.
notes.CN-JS: The border ran along the Huai River, cutting Jiangsu and Anhui in two.
notes.CN-AH: The border ran along the Huai River, cutting Anhui and Jiangsu in two.
notes.CN-NX: The Tangut Western Xia, ruling from today's Yinchuan, held the Hexi corridor trade route until the Mongols destroyed it in 1227.
notes.CN-YN: The kingdom of Dali ruled Yunnan until a Mongol army under Kublai conquered it in 1253–54.
notes.CN-FJ: Fujian's port of Quanzhou was one of the busiest in the world, trading across the Indian Ocean.
notes.MNG: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206. The Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234 and the Southern Song by 1279.
notes.CN-XZ: Tibet was divided among local rulers and Buddhist monasteries. It came under Mongol overlordship in the mid-1200s.

pn: The Northern Song capital, one of the world's great cities, until the Jin captured it in 1127.
Lin'an, the Southern Song capital. Marco Polo later called it the finest and noblest city in the world.
The Jin capital, Zhongdu, from 1153. From 1267 Kublai Khan built Dadu here, and it has been China's capital most of the time since.
1279: the last Song fleet was destroyed here, and the Mongol Yuan dynasty ruled all of China.

cn-songming.text: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant rebel, drove out the Mongols in 1368 and founded the Ming. The Yongle emperor moved the capital to Beijing in 1421 and rebuilt the Grand Canal to feed it, and Zheng He's fleets sailed as far as East Africa in 1405–33. Then the voyages stopped. Facing Mongol raids, the Ming built most of the brick Great Wall seen today.

notes.CN-BJ: Beijing, close to the steppe frontier, became the capital in 1421 so the emperor could watch the Mongols. Grain came from the south by canal.
notes.CN-JS: Nanjing was the first Ming capital. Zheng He's fleets, carrying about 28,000 men on the first voyage, set out from the Yangtze mouth.
notes.CN-ZJ: The Grand Canal ran about 1,800 km from Hangzhou to Beijing, carrying southern rice to the capital.
notes.CN-SD: In 1411–15 the canal through Shandong's hills was rebuilt with new channels and locks.
notes.CN-YN: Ming armies took Yunnan from the last Mongol loyalists in 1381–82, and Han settlers followed.
notes.CN-GS: The Great Wall's western end, Jiayuguan, guarded the Hexi corridor. Dunhuang lay outside Ming control.
notes.MNG: The Mongols regrouped on the steppe after 1368. In 1449 they captured a Ming emperor at Tumu, and the Ming answered with walls.
notes.CN-HL: Jurchen tribes in Manchuria were nominal Ming vassals. From the 1580s Nurhaci united them, and his heirs named their people Manchus.
notes.CN-XZ: Ming emperors gave titles and gifts to Tibetan lamas. Historians disagree over whether this amounted to rule; most Western scholars say the Ming did not govern Tibet.
notes.TWN: Taiwan was outside Ming rule. The Dutch held its south-west from 1624.
notes.KEN: Zheng He's later voyages reached the Swahili coast of today's Kenya and Somalia.

pn: 1421: the Yongle emperor made Beijing the capital; his Forbidden City was finished in 1420.
The first Ming capital. Zheng He's treasure ships were built in its shipyards.
Zheng He's main port of call in India. He may have died here in 1433.
1415: envoys from Malindi brought a giraffe to the Ming court. Zheng He's fifth voyage (1417–19) reached the town.
Where the Great Wall meets the sea. In 1644 its gate was opened to the Manchus.

cn-qing.text: The Manchus took Beijing in 1644, after rebels had toppled the Ming. Their armies went on to take [Taiwan](TWN) (1683), [Mongolia](MNG), [Tibet](CN-XZ) (1720) and [Xinjiang](CN-XJ) (1755–59), roughly doubling the empire. Qing emperors ruled the old provinces through Confucian officials, and the Inner Asian lands through local nobles, lamas and military governors. Today's China inherits most of these borders.

notes.CN-LN: Mukden, today's Shenyang, was the Manchu capital before 1644. The Qing long restricted Han settlement in Manchuria.
notes.TWN: Ming loyalist Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) expelled the Dutch in 1662. The Qing took the island in 1683, but until the 1870s ruled mainly the western plains, and made it a province in 1885.
notes.MNG: The princes of Outer Mongolia submitted to the Kangxi emperor in 1691. Mongolia declared independence when the Qing fell in 1911.
notes.CN-NM: The southern Mongols allied with the Manchus before 1644, and Inner Mongolia was ruled through their own princes and banners.
notes.CN-XJ: The Qing conquered the Dzungar Khanate and the Tarim Basin in 1755–59; many Dzungars were killed. 'Xinjiang' means 'new frontier'; it became a province in 1884.
notes.CN-XZ: Qing armies entered Lhasa in 1720, and from 1727 Qing residents were posted there. The Dalai Lamas' government ran daily affairs, and Qing influence weakened in the 1800s.
notes.CN-QH: Qinghai, called Amdo by Tibetans, came under a Qing official at Xining from 1724.
notes.RUS: The Qing lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, Outer Manchuria, went to Russia in 1858 and 1860.
notes.KAZ: Qing Xinjiang stretched into today's eastern Kazakhstan. China ceded that land to Russia in 1864.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing stayed the capital. The Qing emperors also ruled as khans to the Mongols and patrons of Tibetan Buddhism.

pn: 1644: Manchu armies entered Beijing after the Ming general Wu Sangui let them through the Shanhai Pass.
1689: China's first treaty with a European power set the border with Russia north of the Amur.
1720: Qing troops drove out Dzungar invaders. From 1727 Qing residents, the ambans, were posted here.
1762: after destroying the Dzungar Khanate, the Qing placed a military governor, the General of Ili, in the Ili valley to rule Xinjiang.
1683: Qing forces took Taiwan from the Zheng family's Ming loyalist regime.

cn-humiliation.text: British merchants sold Indian opium in China. When the Qing seized and destroyed their stocks in 1839, Britain went to war. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Britain [Hong Kong](HKG) and opened five ports to foreign trade. A second war (1856–60) ended with British and French troops burning the emperor's Summer Palace near Beijing. Meanwhile the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) cost an estimated 20–30 million lives.

notes.HKG: Britain took Hong Kong Island in 1842 and Kowloon in 1860, and in 1898 leased the New Territories for 99 years.
notes.CN-GD: In 1839 Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed over 1,000 tonnes of British opium at Humen, near Guangzhou, which set off the war.
notes.CN-JS: The Taipings held Nanjing as their capital from 1853 until Qing forces stormed it in 1864.
notes.CN-GX: The rebellion began in Guangxi, where Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, rose in revolt in 1850–51.
notes.CN-HN: Zeng Guofan raised the Xiang Army in Hunan, the provincial force that did most to defeat the Taipings.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai held out against the Taipings, defended by Qing, Western and Western-officered troops.
notes.CN-FJ: Fuzhou and Xiamen (Amoy) in Fujian were two of the five treaty ports opened in 1842.
notes.CN-BJ: In 1860 British and French troops occupied Beijing and burned the Old Summer Palace.
notes.RUS: By treaties in 1858 and 1860 Russia took the land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, where it founded Vladivostok.

pn: Guangzhou: the only port open to Western trade before 1842. British forces attacked it in both wars.
Xiamen: one of the five treaty ports opened in 1842.
One of the five treaty ports opened in 1842.
One of the five treaty ports opened in 1842.
Opened in 1843, it grew into China's busiest port, with self-governing foreign settlements.
1842: the treaty ending the first war was signed on a British warship here. 1853–64: the Taiping 'Heavenly Capital'.

cn-humiliation.text: Japan defeated China in 1894–95 and took [Taiwan](TWN). Then the powers scrambled for leased ports and 'spheres of influence', zones where each claimed first rights to railways and mines. In 1900 the anti-foreign Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing, and an eight-nation army crushed them. China stayed formally independent, but in 1911 a revolution ended the Qing.

notes.TWN: The Treaty of Shimonoseki gave Taiwan to Japan in 1895. It stayed a Japanese colony for 50 years.
notes.KOR: The 1894–95 war was fought over Korea, which China had to recognise as independent. Japan annexed it in 1910.
notes.CN-SD: Germany used the murder of two missionaries as a pretext to seize Jiaozhou Bay in 1897, then claimed rights across Shandong.
notes.CN-LN: Russia leased Port Arthur and Dalian in 1898 and built railways across Manchuria. Japan won southern Manchuria from Russia in 1905.
notes.CN-YN: France claimed Yunnan from neighbouring Indochina and built a railway from Haiphong, via Hanoi, to Kunming, opened in 1910.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai, at the mouth of the Yangtze, was the commercial capital of Britain's sphere.
notes.CN-GD: France claimed most of Guangdong and Guangxi, but Britain also had strong interests around Hong Kong and Guangzhou.
notes.HKG: In 1898 Britain leased the New Territories for 99 years. That deadline later set the date of Hong Kong's return, 1997.
notes.MAC: Portuguese traders had lived in Macao since 1557, and an 1887 treaty recognised Portuguese rule.
notes.CN-BJ: After the Boxer War the Boxer Protocol of 1901 made China pay a huge indemnity and let foreign troops guard Beijing.

pn: 1898: Germany leased Jiaozhou Bay and built the port of Qingdao.
1898: leased by Russia. Japan took it in the war of 1904–05.
1898: leased by Britain as a naval base.
1898–99: leased by France, next to its colony of Indochina.
1900: Boxers besieged the foreign legations for 55 days until an eight-nation force relieved them.

cn-republic.text: An uprising at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 spread across the provinces, and the last emperor abdicated in 1912. Warlords soon carved up the republic until Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists reunified most of it in 1926–28 and turned on their Communist allies. Encircled in [Jiangxi](CN-JX), about 86,000 Communists broke out in October 1934. A year later perhaps 8,000 reached northern [Shaanxi](CN-SN), led by Mao Zedong.

notes.CN-HB: The Wuchang uprising, in today's Wuhan, set off the 1911 revolution. Within weeks most provinces had broken with the Qing.
notes.CN-JX: The Communists built a soviet state in the hills of southern Jiangxi. Nationalist encirclement campaigns forced them out in 1934.
notes.CN-SN: The marchers reached northern Shaanxi in October 1935. Their base there became the core of Communist power for the next decade.
notes.CN-GZ: At Zunyi in Guizhou, in January 1935, party leaders blamed the defeat in Jiangxi on their military chiefs, and Mao gained influence.
notes.CN-SC: The marchers crossed the Dadu River at Luding, then the snowy passes and marshy grasslands of western Sichuan, where many died.
notes.CN-GD: Sun Yat-sen, the republic's first provisional president, rebuilt his Nationalist party in Guangzhou. The Northern Expedition set out from there in 1926.
notes.CN-JS: Chiang made Nanjing the Nationalist capital in 1927.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing was the capital of the warlord-run republic until 1928, when the Nationalists renamed it Beiping.
notes.MNG: Outer Mongolia declared independence in 1911 and, with Soviet backing, became a people's republic in 1924.
notes.CN-XZ: The 13th Dalai Lama declared Tibet's independence in 1913. His government ran Tibet until 1950; no major state recognised it, and the Republic of China claimed it.

pn: 10 October 1911: an army mutiny here began the revolution. Taiwan still marks the date as its National Day.
July 1921: the Chinese Communist Party held its first congress here. In April 1927 Chiang's forces massacred Communists in the city.
1931–34: capital of the Communists' Chinese Soviet Republic, and the start of the Long March.
January 1935: a party meeting here began Mao's rise to the leadership.
May 1935: Red Army troops seized this chain bridge over the Dadu River.
1937–47: the Communists' headquarters, where their party and armies grew.

cn-republic.text: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and made it the puppet state of Manchukuo. In July 1937 it invaded China proper, taking Beijing, Shanghai and the capital, Nanjing, where its troops massacred civilians. Chiang retreated to [Chongqing](CN-CQ). Japan held the eastern cities and railways while Nationalist and Communist forces fought on. Historians' estimates of China's dead range from about 14 to 20 million. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the civil war resumed.

notes.CN-CQ: Chongqing, behind the Yangtze gorges, was the Nationalist capital from 1938. Japanese air raids hit it repeatedly.
notes.CN-HL: Japan made Puyi, the last Qing emperor, head of Manchukuo in 1932. Manchuria became a base for Japanese heavy industry.
notes.CN-SH: The battle of Shanghai, from August to November 1937, was one of the largest of the war.
notes.CN-HB: Wuhan fell in October 1938 after months of fighting. Japan held the Yangtze up to Yichang.
notes.CN-HA: In 1938 Nationalist troops broke the Yellow River dykes to slow the Japanese advance. The floods killed hundreds of thousands in Henan and beyond.
notes.CN-SX: Japan held Shanxi's cities and railways; Communist guerrillas controlled much of the countryside.
notes.CN-SN: The Communist base around Yan'an, in northern Shaanxi, grew during the war into a state within a state.
notes.CN-YN: The Burma Road from Kunming carried Allied supplies to Free China until Japan took Burma in 1942.
notes.TWN: Taiwan had been a Japanese colony since 1895. In 1945 it passed to the Republic of China, whose government moved there in 1949.
notes.JPN: Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945, after the atomic bombs and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria.
notes.HKG: Japan took British Hong Kong in December 1941 and held it until 1945.
notes.CN-GD: Japan took Guangzhou and the Pearl River Delta in 1938, but much of inland Guangdong stayed in Chinese hands.

pn: 18 September 1931: Japanese officers blew up a railway line and used it as a pretext to seize Manchuria.
7 July 1937: a clash here began the full-scale war.
December 1937: Japanese troops killed civilians and prisoners for weeks. A postwar tribunal put the dead at over 200,000; China's official figure is 300,000.
1938–45: the wartime capital, bombed by Japan for years.
The Communist headquarters. Its guerrilla armies grew behind Japanese lines.

cn-mao.text: On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Chiang's Republic of China moved its government to [Taiwan](TWN), and each claimed to be the only legitimate China. The People's Liberation Army took [Hainan](CN-HI) in 1950 and entered [Tibet](CN-XZ) the same year; a 1951 agreement placed Tibet under Chinese rule. In October 1950 Chinese troops entered the war in [Korea](PRK).

notes.CN-XZ: The PLA defeated Tibet's army at Chamdo in October 1950. The Seventeen Point Agreement of May 1951, signed under military pressure, accepted Chinese rule; the Dalai Lama repudiated it after fleeing in 1959.
notes.TWN: The Republic of China has ruled from Taipei since 1949, governing Taiwan and Penghu (held since 1945), Kinmen and Matsu. The PRC claims Taiwan as a province. The ROC held China's UN seat until 1971.
notes.CN-HI: The PLA crossed the Qiongzhou Strait and took Hainan from the Nationalists in April–May 1950.
notes.CN-XJ: Xinjiang's provincial leaders went over to the Communists in September 1949, and PLA troops arrived that autumn.
notes.CN-NM: Inner Mongolia became an autonomous region in 1947, two years before the People's Republic itself.
notes.PRK: China fought for North Korea from October 1950 until the 1953 armistice. Its official toll is about 180,000 dead; other estimates are higher.
notes.HKG: Britain kept Hong Kong, and Beijing left it alone. Refugees from the mainland swelled its population.
notes.MAC: Portugal kept Macao, which stayed a small trading and gambling port until 1999.
notes.CN-BJ: Beijing became the capital again in 1949, replacing the Nationalist capital, Nanjing.

pn: 1 October 1949: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the Gate of Heavenly Peace.
December 1949: the Republic of China's government moved here.
Islands a few kilometres off Xiamen, still held by Taipei. PRC shelling in 1954–55 and 1958 set off international crises.
October 1950: the People's Liberation Army defeated Tibet's army here.
1959: a Tibetan uprising was crushed and the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile.
October 1950: Chinese troops crossed into Korea as UN forces neared the border.

cn-mao.text: In the Great Leap Forward (1958–62) Mao herded peasants into giant communes and pushed them to make steel in backyard furnaces. Officials reported inflated harvests, the state took grain anyway, and people starved. Scholars' estimates of the dead range from about 15 million to over 40 million. The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) brought a decade of purges and Red Guard violence; estimates of its dead run from hundreds of thousands to millions.

notes.CN-AH: Anhui had the highest death rate, about 18% of its people by Cao Shuji's estimate, under a fiercely Maoist provincial leader.
notes.CN-CQ: Chongqing, then part of Sichuan, lost an estimated 15% of its people.
notes.CN-SC: Sichuan kept sending grain to other provinces as its own people starved. Cao Shuji estimates that 13% of its people died.
notes.CN-GZ: Guizhou lost an estimated 11% of its people.
notes.CN-HN: Hunan, Mao's home province, lost an estimated 8% of its people.
notes.CN-HA: Henan's Xinyang prefecture saw some of the worst local death rates of the famine.
notes.CN-JX: By Cao Shuji's estimate, Jiangxi's death rate was far lower than neighbouring Anhui's.
notes.CN-BJ: From Beijing, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966. Schools closed, and millions of young people were later sent to the countryside.

pn: 1959–60: about a million people died in this Henan prefecture, while state granaries held grain.
July–August 1959: Marshal Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap at a party meeting here. Mao purged him, and the policies continued.
August 1966: Mao greeted about a million Red Guards here, the first of eight mass rallies.

cn-reform.text: Deng Xiaoping's reforms began on the farm: from about 1978 families could work their own plots and sell what they grew beyond a quota. In 1980 four special economic zones opened to foreign investment in [Guangdong](CN-GD) and [Fujian](CN-FJ), facing Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan. Fourteen coastal cities followed in 1984, and all of [Hainan](CN-HI) in 1988. [Hong Kong](HKG) returned to China in 1997 and [Macao](MAC) in 1999.

notes.CN-GD: Guangdong got three of the first four zones. Using Hong Kong's money and know-how, the Pearl River Delta became a vast workshop for the world.
notes.CN-FJ: Xiamen's zone faced Taiwan, and Taiwanese firms later invested heavily on the mainland.
notes.CN-HI: Hainan was split from Guangdong in 1988 and made a province and China's largest special economic zone.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai was one of the 14 open cities of 1984. Its Pudong district opened in 1990.
notes.CN-AH: In 1978 farmers in Xiaogang village, Anhui, secretly divided their commune's land into family plots, a model for the national reform.
notes.HKG: Under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong returned on 1 July 1997 as a special administrative region, promised its own system for 50 years.
notes.MAC: Portugal returned Macao on 20 December 1999, on terms like Hong Kong's.
notes.TWN: Taiwan, governed by the Republic of China, became a multiparty democracy in the late 1980s and 1990s and held its first direct presidential election in 1996.
notes.CN-BJ: Protests for reform filled Tiananmen Square in spring 1989 before the army crushed them on 3–4 June.

pn: 1980: zone set up beside Hong Kong. A county of about 300,000 people in 1979, it had 17.6 million in 2020.
1980: zone set up beside Macao.
1980: zone set up in a region with many relatives overseas.
1980: zone set up facing Taiwan.
1990: Shanghai's Pudong New Area opened. Its farmland became the city's financial district.
4 June 1989: troops cleared protesters from central Beijing. The government put the dead at about 240, including soldiers; other estimates range from several hundred to the low thousands.

cn-today.text: In 1935 the geographer Hu Huanyong drew a line from Heihe to Tengchong. East of it lie the wetter lowlands of farms and cities; west of it, desert, steppe and the Tibetan plateau. At the 2020 census about 94% of people still lived east of the line, on less than half the land. In 2020 [Guangdong](CN-GD) had 126 million people, and [Tibet](CN-XZ) 3.6 million.

notes.CN-GD: China's most populous province: 126 million people in 2020, many of them migrants drawn by the factories of the Pearl River Delta.
notes.CN-HA: Henan, the ancient heartland on the Yellow River, had 99.4 million people in 2020.
notes.CN-JS: Jiangsu had 84.7 million people in 2020, packed into one of China's richest and flattest provinces.
notes.CN-SC: Sichuan had 83.7 million people in 2020, most of them in its eastern basin.
notes.CN-XZ: Tibet had 3.6 million people in 2020, most of them Tibetans, on about an eighth of China's land.
notes.CN-QH: Qinghai, on the high Tibetan plateau, had 5.9 million people in 2020.
notes.CN-NX: Ningxia, home to many Hui Muslims, had 7.2 million people in 2020.
notes.CN-XJ: Xinjiang had 25.9 million people in 2020. By the census, about 45% were Uyghur and 42% Han.
notes.CN-NM: Inner Mongolia had 24 million people in 2020. About four in five are Han; Mongols are under a fifth.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai, China's biggest city, had 24.9 million people in 2020.

pn: Northern end of the Hu line, on the Amur River facing Russia.
Southern end of the Hu line, near the border with Myanmar.

cn-today.text: Four decades of growth made China the world's second-largest economy, but wealth is uneven. In 2025 output per person in [Beijing](CN-BJ) and [Shanghai](CN-SH) was more than twice the national average of about 100,000 yuan, and over four times that of [Gansu](CN-GS). The richest provinces are on the coast; the poorest are inland and in the old industrial north-east. [Hong Kong](HKG) and [Macao](MAC) keep their own economies and laws.

notes.CN-BJ: Beijing had the highest output per person of any province-level region in 2025, about 239,000 yuan.
notes.CN-SH: Shanghai, China's financial and shipping hub, was second, at about 228,000 yuan per person.
notes.CN-JS: Jiangsu, on the Yangtze delta, had the highest output per person of any full province in 2025.
notes.CN-ZJ: Zhejiang is a heartland of private business; the e-commerce giant Alibaba is based in Hangzhou.
notes.CN-GD: Guangdong has the largest economy of any province, but its many migrant workers keep output per person below the richest regions.
notes.CN-NM: Coal and other mining make Inner Mongolia richer per person than most inland provinces.
notes.CN-GS: Gansu, dry and inland, and Heilongjiang had the lowest output per person of any province in 2025, about 56,000 yuan each.
notes.CN-HL: Heilongjiang and Jilin were centres of heavy industry under Mao. Since the 1990s many state factories have closed and people have moved away.
notes.CN-JL: Jilin, like Heilongjiang, is part of the old industrial north-east, which has lagged since the 1990s.
notes.HKG: Hong Kong keeps its own currency, laws and courts. After mass protests in 2019, Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020; critics say it ended many freedoms, while the government says it restored stability.
notes.MAC: Macao, the world's largest gambling centre by revenue, has the highest output per person of any part of China.
notes.TWN: Taiwan has been governed by the Republic of China since 1945, from Taipei since 1949 and is a democracy. The PRC claims it and has not ruled out force; most countries recognise Beijing but keep unofficial ties with Taipei.
notes.CN-XJ: Since 2017 large numbers of Uyghurs and other Muslims have been held in camps that China calls vocational training centres. A 2022 UN human rights report said abuses there may amount to crimes against humanity; China rejected the report.
notes.CN-XZ: The 14th Dalai Lama has lived in exile in India since 1959. China says it has developed and modernised Tibet; exile groups and critics say religion and culture there are tightly controlled.

ca-first.text: People have lived in what is now Canada for at least 12,000 years. By 1500 hundreds of nations had ways of life shaped by the land: [Inuit](CA-NU) hunters across the Arctic, Iroquoian farmers and Anishinaabe peoples around the Great Lakes in [Ontario](CA-ON), bison hunters on the plains of [Alberta](CA-AB), and fishing peoples with great cedar villages on the coast of [British Columbia](CA-BC).

notes.CA-NU: The ancestors of the Inuit, called the Thule, spread east from Alaska about 800 years ago. They hunted seal, whale and caribou with kayaks, harpoons and dog sleds.
notes.CA-NT: Dene peoples hunted and fished in the forests of the Mackenzie valley. On the Arctic coast lived the Inuvialuit, the Inuit of the western Arctic.
notes.CA-YT: Dene First Nations such as the Gwich'in and the Tutchone lived from caribou, moose and salmon, moving with the seasons.
notes.CA-QC: Cree and Innu hunted across the northern forests, and Inuit lived in the far north. In the St Lawrence valley, Iroquoian farmers met Jacques Cartier in 1535.
notes.CA-NL: The Beothuk lived on the island of Newfoundland, the Innu in the forests of Labrador and the Inuit on its northern coast.
notes.CA-ON: Iroquoian farmers such as the Wendat (Huron) grew corn, beans and squash in the south. Anishinaabe peoples such as the Ojibwe lived around the upper Great Lakes, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy lay just south of Lake Ontario.
notes.CA-MB: Bison hunters lived on the southern grasslands, and Cree in the forests of the north.
notes.CA-SK: For thousands of years Plains peoples hunted bison on the southern grasslands. Cree and Dene lived in the northern forests.
notes.CA-AB: The Blackfoot Confederacy lived on the plains of southern Alberta, following the bison on foot. Horses only reached them in the 1700s.
notes.CA-BC: Rich salmon runs supported the Haida, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth, Coast Salish and other coastal nations, known for cedar plank houses, totem poles and potlatch feasts. Plateau peoples lived in the southern interior, and Dene peoples in the northern forests.
notes.CA-NS: The Mi'kmaq lived across today's Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and eastern New Brunswick, fishing on the coast in summer and hunting inland in winter.
notes.CA-NB: The Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet) lived along the Saint John River and the Peskotomuhkati (Passamaquoddy) near the Bay of Fundy, with the Mi'kmaq in the east.
notes.CA-PE: The Mi'kmaq call the island Epekwitk. They had fished and hunted there for thousands of years.

pn: About 1000: Norse from Greenland built a short-lived camp here, the first known Europeans in the Americas. Wood they cut has been dated to 1021.
For nearly 6,000 years Plains peoples drove bison over this cliff to their deaths.
A Haida village on Haida Gwaii, whose standing totem poles are now a World Heritage Site.

ca-newfrance.text: [France](FRA) built its colony on the fur trade, with First Nations as trading partners and allies. Canadiens farmed along the St Lawrence, and Acadians around the Bay of Fundy, while traders paddled west to the Great Lakes and beyond. In 1670 England chartered the Hudson's Bay Company and gave it Rupert's Land, all the lands draining into Hudson Bay. [Britain](GBR) and France fought four wars for the continent.

notes.CA-QC: The heart of New France. About 60,000–70,000 Canadiens lived along the St Lawrence by 1760, most of them farmers. The north, draining into Hudson Bay, was claimed by the Hudson's Bay Company.
notes.CA-ON: French forts and missions dotted the Great Lakes, but few colonists settled. The north of Ontario, draining into Hudson Bay, was claimed by the Hudson's Bay Company.
notes.CA-NB: Acadians and French forts held this land, which Britain also claimed as part of Nova Scotia. The two empires fought over it until 1755.
notes.CA-PE: Île Saint-Jean was French, and many Acadians moved there after Britain took mainland Nova Scotia in 1713.
notes.CA-NS: France gave the Acadian peninsula to Britain in 1713 but kept Cape Breton Island, Île Royale, where it built Louisbourg.
notes.CA-NL: England and France both fished for cod off Newfoundland. France gave up its claim to the island in 1713 but kept fishing rights on part of the shore.
notes.CA-MB: Rupert's Land covered all of today's Manitoba, though French traders built posts here from the 1730s. Cree and Assiniboine traders took furs to the company's posts on Hudson Bay.
notes.CA-SK: The Saskatchewan River drains into Hudson Bay, so most of today's Saskatchewan fell inside Rupert's Land.
notes.CA-NU: The southern mainland of Nunavut, along Hudson Bay, lay inside Rupert's Land, though this was the land of the Inuit.
notes.FRA: France claimed a vast arc from the St Lawrence to Louisiana, but by 1750 it had fewer than 100,000 colonists in North America.
notes.GBR: Britain gained Acadia, Newfoundland and the Hudson Bay coast from France in the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

pn: 24 July 1534: Jacques Cartier planted a cross here and claimed the land for France.
1605: Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain built a settlement here, the heart of early Acadia.
3 July 1608: Champlain founded a trading post that became the capital of New France.
17 May 1642: Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve founded Ville-Marie, later the hub of the fur trade.
From 1719 France built a fortress town here to guard the Gulf of St Lawrence. Britain captured it in 1745 and again in 1758.
From 1684 the Hudson's Bay Company's main post, where Cree and other traders brought furs down to the bay.

ca-british.text: In the Seven Years' War Britain took Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760, and the 1763 Treaty of Paris handed New France to [Britain](GBR). In 1774 Britain let the Canadiens keep their Catholic faith and French civil law. After the American Revolution about 40,000 Loyalists moved north, and in 1791 Britain split the colony into Upper Canada, today's [Ontario](CA-ON), and mostly French-speaking Lower Canada, today's [Quebec](CA-QC).

notes.CA-QC: Most of British North America's people still lived here, French-speaking Catholic Canadiens. The 1774 Quebec Act kept French civil law, which Quebec still uses.
notes.CA-ON: Loyalists settled along Lake Ontario and the upper St Lawrence. In 1791 the area became Upper Canada, with English law and an elected assembly.
notes.CA-NS: Britain deported about 10,000 Acadians from 1755 to 1763. Loyalists, including Black Loyalists, arrived in 1783.
notes.CA-NB: Thousands of Loyalists arrived in 1783, and in 1784 Britain split New Brunswick from Nova Scotia for them. Acadians returning from exile settled its north and east.
notes.CA-PE: Taken from France in 1758, the island became a separate colony, St John's Island, in 1769. It was renamed Prince Edward Island in 1799.
