notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland was valued for its cod fishery. From 1774 to 1809 the Labrador coast belonged to Quebec, then Lower Canada. France kept fishing rights on part of its shore and the nearby islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, which are still French.
notes.CA-MB: The Hudson's Bay Company still held Rupert's Land. Rival traders from Montreal pushed west past it, and Métis communities grew from the fur trade.
notes.GBR: Britain's Royal Proclamation of 1763 said Indigenous land could only be bought by the Crown, by agreement. It became the basis for later treaties.
notes.FRA: France gave up Canada in 1763 but kept Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and its far richer sugar islands in the Caribbean.
notes.USA: American forces invaded Upper and Lower Canada several times in the War of 1812 and were driven back. The 1814 peace left the border unchanged.

pn: 13 September 1759: in a battle of about an hour, British troops took Quebec. Both commanders, Wolfe and Montcalm, were killed.
1783: thousands of Loyalists landed here. The next year Britain created New Brunswick for them.
1783: Black Loyalists, promised freedom for fighting for Britain, founded what was then the largest free Black settlement in North America.
1784: Joseph Brant and Haudenosaunee allies of Britain were granted land here. Six Nations of the Grand River is today Canada's most populous reserve.
13 October 1812: British troops, Canadian militia and Haudenosaunee warriors threw back an American invasion. General Isaac Brock was killed.

ca-confed.text: Worried by the United States during its Civil War, and stuck in political deadlock, colonial leaders met at Charlottetown and Quebec City in 1864. On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act joined [Ontario](CA-ON), [Quebec](CA-QC), [Nova Scotia](CA-NS) and [New Brunswick](CA-NB) as the Dominion of Canada, with John A. Macdonald as the first prime minister. Each province had its own legislature for local affairs.

notes.CA-ON: Canada West, the English-speaking half of the Province of Canada, became Ontario. Its fast-growing population wanted seats by population, one push for Confederation.
notes.CA-QC: Canada East became Quebec, with its own legislature to protect its French language, Catholic schools and civil law. George-Étienne Cartier led its case for Confederation.
notes.CA-NS: Many Nova Scotians felt dragged in. In the first federal election, in 1867, anti-Confederation candidates led by Joseph Howe won 18 of its 19 seats.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick voters turned against Confederation in 1865, then backed it in 1866, partly from fear of raids by Irish-American Fenians.
notes.CA-PE: The Charlottetown Conference met here, but the island stayed out until 1873.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland voters rejected Confederation in 1869, and it stayed separate from Canada until 1949.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia, a colony of gold miners and First Nations on the Pacific, joined in 1871 after Canada promised a railway.
notes.CA-MB: Rupert's Land still belonged to the Hudson's Bay Company. Canada bought it for £300,000 and took it over in 1870.
notes.USA: The US Civil War (1861–65), Fenian raids across the border and American talk of expansion pushed the colonies together. The US bought Alaska in 1867.
notes.GBR: The British Parliament passed the British North America Act. Canada governed itself at home, but Britain still ran its foreign policy.

pn: September 1864: a meeting called to discuss uniting the Maritime colonies turned into talks on a union of all British North America.
October 1864: delegates agreed the 72 Quebec Resolutions, the plan for Confederation.
Chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857 as capital of the Province of Canada, it became the capital of the new Dominion.

ca-confed.text: Canada stretched to three oceans in six years: it took over Rupert's Land in 1870, and [British Columbia](CA-BC) and [Prince Edward Island](CA-PE) joined in 1871 and 1873. Britain handed over the Arctic islands in 1880. [Alberta](CA-AB) and [Saskatchewan](CA-SK) were carved out of the North-West Territories in 1905, [Newfoundland](CA-NL) narrowly voted to join in 1948, and [Nunavut](CA-NU) became a territory in 1999.

notes.CA-ON: Ontario began in 1867 as the land around the lower Great Lakes. It grew north to Hudson Bay in 1889 and 1912, taking in former Hudson's Bay Company land.
notes.CA-QC: Quebec began as the St Lawrence valley. It grew north in 1898 and 1912, when it gained the land of the Cree and Inuit up to Hudson Strait.
notes.CA-MB: Manitoba began on 15 July 1870 as a small "postage stamp" province around the Red River. It was enlarged in 1881 and reached Hudson Bay in 1912.
notes.CA-NT: Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory became Canada's North-West Territories in 1870. Most of the West and North was later carved from it.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia joined on 20 July 1871 on Canada's promise to start a railway to the Pacific within two years and finish it within ten.
notes.CA-PE: Prince Edward Island joined on 1 July 1873, after railway debts pushed it to accept Canada's offer, which included money to buy out absentee landlords.
notes.CA-YT: The Klondike gold rush drew tens of thousands north, and Yukon became a separate territory on 13 June 1898.
notes.CA-AB: Alberta became a province on 1 September 1905, as settlers poured onto the Prairies. Ottawa kept control of its land and resources until 1930.
notes.CA-SK: Saskatchewan became a province in September 1905, with wheat farms spreading across its plains. Ottawa kept control of its land and resources until 1930.
notes.CA-NL: After two referendums in 1948, Newfoundland chose union with Canada by 52% over self-government, and became the tenth province on 31 March 1949.
notes.CA-NU: The Arctic islands came to Canada in 1880. Nunavut, "our land" in Inuktitut, was split from the Northwest Territories on 1 April 1999, and most of its people are Inuit.

ca-west.text: To tie the West to Canada before Americans filled it, and to keep its promise to [British Columbia](CA-BC), Canada backed the Canadian Pacific Railway. The last spike was driven on 7 November 1885, and the first train from Montreal reached the Pacific at Port Moody in 1886. Settlers could now pour onto the Prairies, but the West was home to First Nations and the Métis, whose 1885 resistance ended with Louis Riel hanged for treason.

notes.CA-MB: The Métis of Red River resisted Canada's takeover in 1869–70 and won the Manitoba Act, which made their home a province with French and English rights.
notes.CA-SK: Métis led by Louis Riel and Gabriel Dumont, with some Cree, fought government forces in 1885 after Ottawa ignored their grievances over land.
notes.CA-AB: Treaties 6 and 7 (1876–77) were signed as the bison vanished and Plains peoples faced hunger. The railway reached Calgary in 1883 and crossed the Rockies by Kicking Horse Pass.
notes.CA-BC: British Columbia had threatened to leave Canada over railway delays. The line reached Port Moody in 1886 and Vancouver in 1887. The hardest section ran through its mountains, built partly by about 15,000 Chinese workers.
notes.CA-ON: The line across the rock and muskeg north of Lake Superior was the costliest stretch, finished only in 1885.
notes.CA-QC: Montreal, home of the railway's head office and its main backers, was the eastern end of the line.
notes.CHN: Chinese workers did some of the most dangerous work in the mountains, and many died. Once the line was done, Canada charged Chinese immigrants a $50 head tax from 1885.
notes.USA: American railways were already pushing west. A Canadian line north of the border was meant to keep the Prairies' trade, and loyalty, in Canada.

pn: 1869–70: the Métis under Louis Riel set up a provisional government. Its deal with Ottawa created the province of Manitoba.
May 1885: government troops, rushed west by rail, defeated the Métis at their village, ending the North-West Resistance.
16 November 1885: Louis Riel was hanged for treason. Quebec saw it as an attack on French Catholics, Ontario as justice.
7 November 1885: the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway, a plain iron one, was driven here.

ca-wars.text: Canada went to war in 1914 as part of the British Empire. About 61,000 Canadians died, and the capture of Vimy Ridge in April 1917 became a symbol of nationhood. In 1939 Canada made its own declaration of war, a week after [Britain](GBR). Over a million served and more than 45,000 died. Canadians landed on Juno Beach in [France](FRA) on D-Day and freed much of the [Netherlands](NLD).

notes.FRA: Canadians fought in northern France in both wars, at Vimy Ridge in 1917, then on D-Day in 1944 and in the Battle of Normandy that followed.
notes.BEL: Canadians fought around Ypres from 1915 to 1917, and in 1944 helped clear the Scheldt estuary to open the port of Antwerp.
notes.NLD: The First Canadian Army freed much of the Netherlands in 1944–45, and more than 7,600 Canadians died there. The Dutch still send tulips to Ottawa each year.
notes.ITA: Canadians landed in Sicily in July 1943 and fought up the Italian peninsula until early 1945.
notes.DEU: In early 1945 Canadians fought through the Rhineland into north-western Germany.
notes.GBR: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians trained and waited in Britain, and Canadian airmen flew with Bomber Command against Germany.
notes.HKG: Nearly 2,000 Canadians helped defend Hong Kong against Japan in December 1941. More than 550 never came home, many dying in prison camps.
notes.CA-NS: Halifax was the great convoy port of both wars. On 6 December 1917 a munitions ship exploded in its harbour, killing about 2,000 people.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland, not yet part of Canada, fought separately. On 1 July 1916, at Beaumont-Hamel on the Somme, its regiment was almost wiped out in half an hour.

pn: April 1915: in their first major battle, Canadians held the line against the first large chlorine gas attack of the war.
9–12 April 1917: all four Canadian divisions, fighting together for the first time, took the ridge. 3,598 were killed.
October–November 1917: Canadians captured the village in a sea of mud, at a cost of nearly 16,000 casualties.
19 August 1942: a raid by nearly 5,000 Canadians failed. More than 900 were killed and almost 2,000 captured.
20–28 December 1943: Canadians took this Italian town after a week of street fighting.
6 June 1944: about 14,000 Canadians landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, one of five Allied beaches in Normandy.

ca-wars.text: Forcing men to fight overseas split Canada along language lines. Conscription in 1917 met fierce opposition in [Quebec](CA-QC). In 1942 Prime Minister Mackenzie King asked voters to free him from his promise not to send conscripts overseas: about two in three Canadians said yes, but over 70% of Quebec voters said no. His policy was 'not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary', and he sent conscripts overseas only in late 1944.

notes.CA-QC: About 72% voted no. In the 1917 election, fought over conscription, Quebec had voted almost solidly against Robert Borden's pro-conscription Union government.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario voted 84% yes, the strongest of any province.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick voted 70% yes, the lowest outside Quebec.
notes.CA-NT: The Northwest Territories did not vote: it was not yet an electoral district.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland was not part of Canada, and took no part in the vote.

pn: Easter 1918: troops fired on crowds protesting conscription, killing four people.

ca-quebec.text: From 1960 Quebec's Quiet Revolution took schools, hospitals and welfare from the Catholic Church, built a modern state and nationalised electricity under the slogan 'Maîtres chez nous' (masters in our own house). Many Quebecers came to see themselves as a nation. The Parti Québécois held two referendums on sovereignty: in 1980, 60% voted No; in 1995, the No side won by just 50.6% to 49.4%.

notes.CA-QC: French is the first official language of about 8 in 10 Quebecers. The Charter of the French Language (Bill 101, 1977) made French the language of work, signs and, for most immigrants' children, school.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick became officially bilingual in 1969, the year Ottawa passed its Official Languages Act. About 3 in 10 New Brunswickers are French-speaking, mostly Acadians.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario has the largest French-speaking community outside Quebec, mostly in the east and north.
notes.CA-MB: The 1870 Manitoba Act made French and English equal, but in 1890 Manitoba made English its only official language. The courts struck that law down in 1979 and 1985.
notes.FRA: French president Charles de Gaulle's 1967 cry of "Vive le Québec libre!" gave the sovereignty movement world attention.

pn: 24 July 1967: visiting French president Charles de Gaulle cried "Vive le Québec libre!" from city hall, angering Ottawa.
30 October 1995: with a record 93% turnout, Quebec voted to stay in Canada by about 54,000 votes.

ca-quebec.text: Until 1982 Canada's constitution was a British law that only Britain's Parliament could amend. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau 'patriated' it, adding a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a way to amend it in Canada. Nine provinces agreed in November 1981, but [Quebec](CA-QC)'s government refused, and Quebec has never formally endorsed it. Two later deals to win its consent, the Meech Lake (1987) and Charlottetown (1992) accords, failed.

notes.CA-QC: Quebecers call the night the deal was struck without Premier René Lévesque "the night of the long knives". The Supreme Court ruled in 1982 that Quebec had no veto.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario and New Brunswick backed Trudeau's plan from the start, when the other provinces opposed it.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick backed patriation from the start. The Charter made it the only province whose bilingualism is in the Constitution, from 1982.
notes.CA-AB: Western premiers such as Alberta's Peter Lougheed won the "notwithstanding clause", which lets a legislature override some Charter rights for five years at a time.
notes.CA-MB: In 1990 Elijah Harper, an Oji-Cree member of Manitoba's legislature, blocked the Meech Lake Accord there, saying it ignored Indigenous peoples.
notes.CA-NL: Newfoundland withdrew its approval of the Meech Lake Accord, and the accord died in June 1990.
notes.GBR: The British Parliament passed the Canada Act 1982, giving up its last power to make laws for Canada.

pn: 17 April 1982: Queen Elizabeth II signed the proclamation of the Constitution Act on Parliament Hill.

ca-rights.text: For over a century the federal government and churches took First Nations, Inuit and Métis children from their families to residential schools, aiming to erase their languages and cultures. More than 150,000 children attended, and thousands died. The last federally run school closed in 1996. Ottawa apologised in 2008, and in 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called the system cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action.

notes.CA-AB: Alberta had more schools than any other province or territory: 25 were recognised in the 2007 settlement with former students.
notes.CA-SK: Saskatchewan had many schools. The last federally run one, Gordon's, near Punnichy, closed in 1996.
notes.CA-BC: In 2021 the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation reported about 200 potential unmarked graves at the former Kamloops school, found by ground-penetrating radar. Canadians across the country mourned.
notes.CA-ON: Ontario's schools included the Mohawk Institute in Brantford, one of the oldest, which took boarders from 1831 until 1970.
notes.CA-NS: Shubenacadie, which ran from 1930 to 1967, was the only residential school in the Maritimes. Mi'kmaq children from all three Maritime provinces were sent there.
notes.CA-NB: New Brunswick had no residential school, but some of its First Nations children were sent to Shubenacadie in Nova Scotia.
notes.CA-PE: Prince Edward Island had no residential school, but some Mi'kmaq children from the island were sent to Shubenacadie in Nova Scotia.
notes.CA-NU: Inuit children were sent to residential schools and hostels, often far from home, mainly from the 1950s.
notes.CA-NT: Schools and hostels across the North took in Dene, Métis and Inuit children.
notes.CA-NL: Schools in Labrador run by the Moravian Church and the International Grenfell Association were left out of the national settlement. Former students won their own settlement in 2016 and an apology in 2017.

pn: 11 June 2008: Prime Minister Stephen Harper apologised to former students in the House of Commons.

ca-rights.text: Treaties between the Crown and Indigenous nations still shape who has rights to the land. In the Maritimes, 18th-century Peace and Friendship Treaties gave up no land. The eleven numbered treaties of 1871–1921 cover the Prairies and much of the North. Most of [British Columbia](CA-BC) was never ceded. Since 1975, modern treaties have followed court rulings and the 1982 Constitution; the largest created [Nunavut](CA-NU).

notes.CA-NS: The Mi'kmaq made peace with Britain but gave up no land. In 1999 the Supreme Court's Marshall decision upheld their treaty right to fish for a moderate livelihood.
notes.CA-NB: The Peace and Friendship Treaties with the Wolastoqiyik, Mi'kmaq and Peskotomuhkati gave up no land, so their title was never surrendered by treaty.
notes.CA-PE: The island's Mi'kmaq were party to the Peace and Friendship Treaties, which made peace and trade but did not give up land.
notes.CA-MB: Treaty 1, signed at Lower Fort Garry in 1871, was the first numbered treaty. Many First Nations understood the treaties as agreements to share the land, not to sell it.
notes.CA-SK: Treaties 4 and 6 (1874–76) cover most of southern and central Saskatchewan. In them the Crown promised reserves, annual payments, schools and help with farming.
notes.CA-AB: Treaty 6 (1876), Treaty 7 (1877) with the Blackfoot Confederacy, and Treaty 8 (1899) in the north together cover almost all of Alberta.
notes.CA-ON: Northern Ontario is covered by numbered treaties 3, 5 and 9. Most of the south was covered by earlier treaties, from Upper Canada land surrenders to the 1850 Robinson Treaties.
notes.CA-NT: Treaties 8 and 11 (1899–1921) cover most of the territory. Modern agreements since 1984, such as the Inuvialuit and Tłı̨chǫ agreements, add land and self-government.
notes.CA-NU: The 1993 Nunavut Land Claims Agreement, the largest in Canada, gave Inuit ownership of about 350,000 km² and led to the creation of Nunavut in 1999.
notes.CA-QC: The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975, with the Cree and Inuit, was Canada's first modern treaty. It followed Cree and Inuit court action against a huge hydroelectric project.
notes.CA-YT: Yukon's 1993 Umbrella Final Agreement led to land claim and self-government agreements with 11 of its 14 First Nations.
notes.CA-NL: The Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement of 2005 created Nunatsiavut, an Inuit self-governing region on the Labrador coast.
notes.CA-BC: Only 14 small Douglas Treaties (1850–54), made by the colony of Vancouver Island, and Treaty 8 in the northeast were signed here. Modern treaties, beginning with the Nisga'a in 2000, cover only a few nations.

ca-today.text: The 2021 census counted almost 37 million people, and by July 2026 Canada had about 41.8 million. Most live in the south, in a few big cities. [Ontario](CA-ON) and [Quebec](CA-QC) hold over six in ten Canadians, while the three northern territories, almost 40% of the land, have about 120,000 people between them.

notes.CA-ON: About 14.2 million people, almost four in ten Canadians. It has Toronto, the largest city, and Ottawa, the capital.
notes.CA-QC: About 8.5 million people, most of them French-speaking. Montreal is Canada's second-largest city.
notes.CA-BC: About 5.0 million people, over half of them in and around Vancouver.
notes.CA-AB: About 4.3 million people, most in or near Calgary and Edmonton. Oil and gas drive its economy.
notes.CA-MB: About 1.3 million people, more than half of them in Winnipeg.
notes.CA-SK: About 1.1 million people, on a land of wheat, potash and uranium.
notes.CA-NS: About 970,000 people, the most of the Atlantic provinces.
notes.CA-NB: About 780,000 people, about 3 in 10 of them French-speaking.
notes.CA-NL: About 510,000 people, nearly all of them on the island of Newfoundland.
notes.CA-PE: About 150,000 people, the smallest province in both land and population.
notes.CA-YT: About 40,000 people, most of them in the capital, Whitehorse.
notes.CA-NT: About 41,000 people, roughly half of them Indigenous.
notes.CA-NU: About 37,000 people in a territory larger than Mexico, most of them Inuit.

ca-today.text: Canada keeps growing through immigration. In 2021 over 8.3 million people, 23% of the population, were immigrants, the highest share since Confederation and the highest in the G7. Most settle in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal. Newcomers of 2016–2021 came above all from [India](IND), the [Philippines](PHL) and [China](CHN).

notes.CA-ON: 30% of Ontarians were immigrants, the highest share of any province. Ontario has over 4 million immigrants, half of Canada's total.
notes.CA-BC: 29% of British Columbians were immigrants, many from Asia, and most live in greater Vancouver.
notes.CA-AB: 23% of Albertans were immigrants, many drawn by jobs in Calgary and Edmonton.
notes.CA-MB: About 20% of Manitobans were immigrants. The Philippines is one of its biggest sources of newcomers.
notes.CA-QC: 15% of Quebecers were immigrants. Quebec picks its own economic immigrants and favours French speakers.
notes.CA-SK: About 12.5% of people in Saskatchewan were immigrants.
notes.CA-NT: About 10% of people in the Northwest Territories were immigrants.
notes.CA-NS: About 7% of Nova Scotians were immigrants.
notes.CA-NB: About 6% of New Brunswickers were immigrants.
notes.CA-NL: Under 3% of people in Newfoundland and Labrador were immigrants, the lowest share in Canada.
notes.IND: India was the top source of recent immigrants for the first time, 18.6% of those arriving in 2016–2021.
notes.PHL: The Philippines supplied 11.4% of recent immigrants, the second-largest share.
notes.CHN: China supplied 8.9% of recent immigrants, the third-largest share.

dd-hinduism.text: Hinduism grew from the religion of people who called themselves Arya and composed the Sanskrit hymns of the Rigveda around 1500–1200 BC, in the Punjab of today's [Pakistan](PAK) and [India](IND). Their culture spread east along the Ganges. By about 500 BC texts called the Upanishads taught that the inner self, atman, is one with ultimate reality, brahman, and the ideas of karma and rebirth had taken hold.

notes.PAK: Most of the Rigveda was composed in the land of the 'seven rivers', the Punjab, now split between Pakistan and India. Its hymns praise gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna.
notes.AFG: The Rigveda names rivers of eastern Afghanistan, such as the Kubha, the Kabul river. Most linguists think Indo-Aryan speakers came through this region from Central Asia, a view some in India dispute.
notes.IND: Vedic culture spread from the Punjab and Haryana down the Ganges, where kingdoms and cities grew by 600 BC. Priests, the Brahmins, preserved the Vedas by memory for centuries before they were written down.
notes.NPL: Videha, a late Vedic kingdom, stretched into the plains of today's southern Nepal. Its king Janaka appears in the Upanishads and the Ramayana.
notes.IRN: The Rigveda's language and gods are closely related to those of the Avesta, the oldest Zoroastrian scripture of ancient Iran, showing shared roots.

pn: c. 2600–1900 BC: a city of the Indus Valley civilisation, which declined before the Vedic age. How much it shaped later Hinduism is debated.
Setting of the Mahabharata's great battle, where, in the Bhagavad Gita, the god Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna.
Where the Ganges and Yamuna meet, a holy bathing place and site of the Kumbh Mela, one of the world's largest gatherings.
One of the world's oldest living cities and Hinduism's holiest. Many Hindus hope to die or be cremated on its riverbanks.

dd-hinduism.text: From the early centuries AD, Indian traders and priests carried Hindu and Buddhist ideas across the Bay of Bengal. Kings in [Cambodia](KHM), Champa in today's [Vietnam](VNM), and Java in [Indonesia](IDN) adopted Sanskrit, Indian gods and temple building. At home, dynasties like the Cholas of south [India](IND) built vast temples to Shiva, and devotional bhakti poetry spread. Bali remains Hinduism's outpost in Southeast Asia.

notes.IND: Kingdoms such as the Cholas built great temples, and poet-saints sang devotion to Shiva and Vishnu. From the 1200s the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of the north, but Hindu Vijayanagara, founded in 1336, held the south.
notes.NPL: The kingdoms of the Kathmandu valley blended Hindu and Buddhist worship. Pashupatinath, a temple of Shiva, is one of Hinduism's holiest sites.
notes.KHM: From 802 the Khmer kings of Angkor linked their rule to Shiva or Vishnu and built huge temple-mountains. Later kings turned to Buddhism, which most Cambodians follow today.
notes.VNM: The Cham kingdoms of central Vietnam worshipped Shiva for centuries. Vietnamese armies took their capital, Vijaya, in 1471, but a small Hindu Cham community survives.
notes.IDN: Java's kings built Prambanan and Borobudur in the 800s. The last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom, Majapahit, faded around 1500 as Islam spread, and by tradition many of its nobles fled to Bali.
notes.THA: Khmer temples to Shiva, such as Phanom Rung, stand in north-east Thailand. Thai kings still use court rituals performed by Brahmin priests.
notes.LAO: Wat Phou in southern Laos, begun as a Shiva temple, was a holy site of the Khmer kingdoms.
notes.MYS: Archaeologists have found Hindu and Buddhist temple remains in Kedah's Bujang Valley. The Chola navy raided Kedah in 1025.
notes.LKA: Chola armies conquered northern Sri Lanka in the early 1000s, and Hindu Tamils have long lived in the north and east of the mostly Buddhist island.

pn: c. 1010: the Chola king Rajaraja I completes the great Brihadisvara temple to Shiva.
Early 1100s: built by Suryavarman II for Vishnu, later a Buddhist site. It is the largest religious monument in the world.
Champa's kings built temples here, mostly to Shiva, between the 600s and 1200s.
Mid-800s: Java's largest Hindu temple complex, honouring Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, near the Buddhist Borobudur.
Bali's 'mother temple'. Bali stayed Hindu when most of Java became Muslim.

dd-hinduism.text: About 1.2 billion people were Hindu in 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, about 15% of the world. About 95% of them live in [India](IND), and [Nepal](NPL) is the only other Hindu-majority country. From 1834 to 1917 over a million Indians went as indentured labourers to colonies like [Mauritius](MUS), [Fiji](FJI) and [Guyana](GUY). Large communities now also live in the [United States](USA), [Britain](GBR) and the Gulf.

notes.IND: India has about 1.1 billion Hindus, 79% of its people. Hindu nationalism, championed by the Bharatiya Janata Party, which has led India's government since 2014, has become a powerful political force.
notes.NPL: About 81% of Nepalis are Hindu. Nepal was the world's last Hindu kingdom until it declared itself secular in 2006 and abolished the monarchy in 2008.
notes.MUS: Mauritius is about 48% Hindu, the only country besides India and Nepal where Hindus are the largest group. It was the first colony to receive indentured Indian workers, in 1834.
notes.FJI: Indentured workers arrived from 1879 to 1916. About a quarter of Fijians are Hindu, a share that has fallen as many Indo-Fijians emigrated after the coups that began in 1987.
notes.GUY: About a quarter of Guyanese are Hindu, descendants of indentured workers brought from 1838 to cut sugar cane.
notes.SUR: About a fifth of Surinamese are Hindu. Indian workers arrived from 1873 under a Dutch-British agreement.
notes.TTO: About 18% of Trinidadians are Hindu, and Diwali is a national holiday.
notes.ZAF: Indentured workers came to Natal from 1860, and Gandhi lived in South Africa from 1893 to 1914. Hindus are about 1% of South Africans.
notes.BGD: Hindus were about 22% of East Bengal's people in 1951 but about 8% in Bangladesh's 2022 census, some 13 million, after waves of emigration to India.
notes.PAK: About 2% of Pakistanis, some 5 million, were Hindu in the 2023 census, mostly in Sindh. Most Hindus in what became Pakistan left for India at Partition in 1947.
notes.LKA: About 12–13% of Sri Lankans are Hindu, mostly Tamils in the north and east and on the hill-country tea estates.
notes.BTN: Estimates of Bhutan's Hindu share range from about 11% to 23%, mostly Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa in the south. In the 1990s about 100,000 Lhotshampa were expelled or fled to camps in Nepal.
notes.USA: Hindus are about 1% of Americans, mostly immigrants who arrived after 1965, when the US opened its doors to Asian migrants, and their children.
notes.GBR: About a million Hindus lived in England and Wales in 2021, 1.7% of the population, many from families who came via East Africa.
notes.CAN: About 830,000 Canadians, 2.3%, were Hindu in the 2021 census.
notes.ARE: Millions of Indian workers live in the Gulf states. Abu Dhabi's first traditional Hindu stone temple opened in 2024.
notes.MYS: About 6% of Malaysians are Hindu, mostly Tamils whose ancestors came to work on rubber plantations under British rule.
notes.SGP: About 5% of Singaporeans are Hindu, most of them Tamil.
notes.IDN: About 1.7% of Indonesians are Hindu, most of them on Bali, where nearly nine in ten people are Hindu.

dd-judaism.text: According to the Bible, the Israelites escaped slavery in [Egypt](EGY) and settled in Canaan. By about 900 BC there were two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, in today's [Israel](ISR) and [Palestinian territories](PSE). Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BC. In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and took many Judeans into exile in [Iraq](IRQ), until the Persian king Cyrus let them return in 538 BC.

notes.ISR: The northern kingdom, Israel, was the larger and richer of the two. Assyria conquered it in 722 BC and deported many of its people, the origin of the tradition of the 'ten lost tribes'.
notes.PSE: Judah's heartland lay in the hills around Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Hebron. Its kings claimed descent from David, and its name gave us the words 'Jew' and 'Judaism'.
notes.JOR: Israel held land east of the Jordan river at times, and fought the neighbouring kingdoms of Moab, Ammon and Edom. Moab's Mesha Stele, about 840 BC, boasts of a victory over Israel.
notes.IRQ: Babylon deported Judeans in 597 and 586 BC. Many stayed after the return, and Jews lived in Iraq for about 2,500 years, until most left in 1950–52.
notes.IRN: Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home. The rebuilt Second Temple in Jerusalem was finished around 515 BC.
notes.EGY: The story of slavery and the Exodus from Egypt is central to Judaism and retold every Passover, but archaeologists have found no direct evidence for it. An Egyptian stele of about 1208 BC holds the oldest known mention of 'Israel'.

pn: Capital of Judah. The Bible says King Solomon built the First Temple here, about 950 BC; Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC.
Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, until Assyria took it in 722 BC and deported many of its people.
586–538 BC: the exile. Many scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible was gathered and edited by exiles here and after the return.

dd-judaism.text: After Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70, Jews lived as minorities across the Middle East, North Africa and Europe. Medieval Europe expelled them again and again: from England in 1290, France in 1394, [Spain](ESP) in 1492 and [Portugal](PRT) in 1496–97. Sephardi exiles found refuge in the [Ottoman Empire](TUR), while Ashkenazi Jews moved east to [Poland](POL) and Lithuania.

notes.ESP: Medieval Spain had Europe's largest Jewish community, home to thinkers such as Maimonides, born in Córdoba in 1138. After massacres in 1391 many converted; in 1492 the rest were told to convert or leave.
notes.PRT: Many Jews fled from Spain to Portugal in 1492. In 1497 most were forcibly baptised rather than allowed to leave, and many later fled as 'New Christians'.
notes.GBR: Edward I expelled England's Jews in 1290. They were allowed back only in 1656, under Oliver Cromwell.
notes.FRA: The French crown expelled its Jews several times, finally in 1394. Small communities survived in papal Avignon and in Alsace, which was not yet French.
notes.DEU: The German lands were the cradle of Ashkenazi Jews and of Yiddish. Massacres in the crusades and the Black Death, and expulsions from many cities, pushed Jews east.
notes.POL: Polish rulers protected Jews by charter from 1264. By the 1600s Poland-Lithuania had the largest Jewish community in the world, with its own council of self-government.
notes.LTU: Grand Duke Vytautas granted Lithuania's Jews privileges in 1388. Vilnius later became so famous for learning it was called the 'Jerusalem of Lithuania'.
notes.CZE: Prague had one of Europe's oldest Ashkenazi communities. Its Old-New Synagogue, built around 1270, is still in use.
notes.TUR: Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain. Istanbul and other Ottoman cities gained large Sephardi communities speaking Ladino, a form of Spanish.
notes.GRC: Thessaloniki, then Ottoman, became one of the great Sephardi cities, where Jews were the largest group for about 400 years.
notes.MAR: Jews had lived in Morocco since ancient times, and many exiles from Spain settled in Fez and other cities.
notes.ITA: Italian states varied: some took in exiles, others expelled them. In 1516 Venice confined its Jews to the Ghetto, the origin of the word.
notes.IRQ: Babylonia's academies at Sura and Pumbedita produced the Babylonian Talmud, finished around AD 500–600, the main text of Jewish law after the Bible.
notes.IRN: Jews had lived in Iran since the Babylonian exile, under Persian, Arab and Turkic rulers.
notes.YEM: Yemen's Jews had lived there for well over 1,000 years, keeping their own customs and their own pronunciation of Hebrew.
notes.EGY: Cairo's community was one of the oldest. Maimonides lived there from about 1166, and a synagogue storeroom, the Cairo Geniza, kept hundreds of thousands of its documents.
notes.ISR: Small communities survived in the Land of Israel, in Jerusalem and the Galilee. In the 1500s Safed became the centre of Kabbalah.

pn: 31 March 1492: Ferdinand and Isabella order Spain's Jews to convert or leave. Estimates of those who left range from about 40,000 to 200,000.
From the 1500s Sephardi exiles made Jews the largest group in this Ottoman port, which they remained until the early 1900s.
With Worms and Speyer, a cradle of Ashkenazi Jewry. Crusaders massacred Jews in these Rhineland cities in 1096.
In the 1490s the city's Jews were moved to neighbouring Kazimierz, which grew into a great Jewish centre.
1500s: Sephardi scholars made this Galilee town the centre of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism.

dd-judaism.text: About 15.8 million Jews lived worldwide in 2025, by demographer Sergio DellaPergola's estimates, slightly fewer than before the Holocaust. Nearly half live in [Israel](ISR), founded in 1948, and about 6.3 million in the [United States](USA). [France](FRA), [Canada](CAN) and [Britain](GBR) follow. The old heartlands of [Poland](POL) and the Middle East now have very few Jews.

notes.ISR: Israel was declared in 1948 after a UN plan to partition British Palestine. War followed, and by most estimates about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled. Its conflict with the Palestinians remains unresolved.
notes.USA: About 6.3 million Jews, by Jewish Agency estimates. Most descend from about 2 million Jews who arrived from Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1924, fleeing poverty and pogroms.
notes.FRA: France has Europe's largest Jewish community, roughly 440,000. Most French Jews descend from North African Jews who arrived in the 1950s and 60s.
notes.CAN: Canada has about 400,000 Jews, mainly in Toronto and Montreal.
notes.GBR: About 300,000 Jews live in Britain, most in and around London.
notes.ARG: Argentina has Latin America's largest Jewish community, about 170,000, mostly in Buenos Aires. A bomb at its Jewish centre, AMIA, killed 85 people in 1994.
notes.RUS: The Russian Empire once held the world's largest Jewish population. After the Holocaust, Soviet repression and emigration, above all the million or so Soviet and post-Soviet Jews who moved to Israel in the 1990s, Russia has about 120,000.
notes.DEU: About 500,000 Jews lived in Germany in 1933. The Nazis drove out or murdered almost all of them; the community grew again after 1990 with immigrants from the former Soviet Union.
notes.AUS: About 120,000 Jews live in Australia, mainly in Melbourne and Sydney, many of them descendants of Holocaust survivors.
notes.BRA: Brazil has about 90,000 Jews, just under the 100,000 mark. The oldest synagogue in the Americas, Kahal Zur Israel, opened in Recife in the 1630s under Dutch rule.
notes.POL: About 3.3 million Jews lived in Poland in 1939, a tenth of its people. About 90% were murdered in the Holocaust, and most survivors left.
notes.LTU: About 95% of Lithuania's Jews were murdered in 1941–44, one of the highest shares in Europe. Most were shot near their homes.
notes.BLR: Jews were often the largest group in Belarus's towns before the war. Most were murdered in 1941–44, many in mass shootings.
notes.IRQ: Over 120,000 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel in 1950–52, after Iraq let them leave if they gave up their citizenship. Only a handful remain.
notes.YEM: Nearly all of Yemen's roughly 50,000 Jews were airlifted to Israel in 1949–50. Almost none remain.
notes.MAR: Morocco had about 250,000 Jews in 1948, the largest community in the Arab world. Most left for Israel, France and Canada by the 1970s; about 2,000 remain.
notes.EGY: Egypt had about 75,000 Jews in 1948. Most left after the wars of 1948 and 1956, and only a handful remain.
notes.IRN: Iran has the largest Jewish community in the Muslim Middle East, several thousand people, with one seat reserved for them in parliament.

pn: 1940–45: the largest Nazi death camp. About 1.1 million people were murdered here, about 1 million of them Jews.
1897: Theodor Herzl holds the First Zionist Congress, which calls for a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
14 May 1948: David Ben-Gurion declares the State of Israel.
The New York area has more Jews than any other city region outside Israel.

dd-buddhism.text: Siddhartha Gautama was born, according to tradition, at Lumbini in today's [Nepal](NPL), and taught in the Ganges plain of northern [India](IND) in the 5th century BC. Two centuries later the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, ruling from [Afghanistan](AFG) to [Bangladesh](BGD), turned to Buddhism after a bloody war, carved its values on rocks and pillars, and sent monks abroad. Sri Lankan tradition says his son Mahinda brought the teaching to [Sri Lanka](LKA).

notes.IND: The Buddha lived and taught in today's Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Ashoka ruled nearly all of India except the far south, and his edicts survive on rocks and pillars across it.
notes.NPL: Lumbini, in Nepal's southern lowlands, is honoured as the Buddha's birthplace. Ashoka's inscribed pillar there was rediscovered in 1896.
notes.AFG: Ashoka's empire reached Kandahar, where he set up edicts in Greek and Aramaic, so that the Greek and Persian speakers there could read them.
notes.PAK: The north-west, Gandhara, was part of Ashoka's empire. It later became a great centre of Buddhist learning and art.
notes.BGD: Bengal, at the eastern edge of Ashoka's empire, remained a stronghold of Buddhism for over a thousand years.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka claims an unbroken Buddhist tradition from about 250 BC. Its monks wrote down the Pali scriptures in the 1st century BC, among the earliest Buddhist texts put in writing.

pn: The Buddha's birthplace, by tradition. Ashoka visited and set up a pillar recording it, c. 249 BC.
Where, Buddhists believe, Siddhartha gained enlightenment under a fig tree, the Bodhi tree, aged about 35.
In a deer park here the Buddha preached his first sermon, on the Four Noble Truths, according to tradition.
Where the Buddha died, aged about 80, in the 5th or early 4th century BC; scholars disagree on the exact dates.
Today's Patna: Ashoka's capital, one of the largest cities in the world in the 3rd century BC.
c. 250 BC: Sri Lanka's royal capital, where by tradition Mahinda converted King Devanampiya Tissa.

dd-buddhism.text: Monks travelled with merchants. Overland, Buddhism went from Gandhara in [Pakistan](PAK) through Central Asia to [China](CHN) by the 1st century AD, then on to [Korea](KOR) in 372 and [Japan](JPN) in the 6th century. By sea, it reached [Myanmar](MMR), [Thailand](THA), [Cambodia](KHM) and [Indonesia](IDN), often alongside Hindu cults. Tibet adopted it in the 7th–8th centuries. Chinese pilgrims walked the other way to India to collect scriptures.

notes.PAK: Gandhara, around Peshawar and Taxila, blended Greek and Indian art and gave the Buddha one of his first portraits in human form, in the 1st–2nd centuries AD.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan was a crossroads of Buddhist monasteries for centuries, until Islam spread from the 7th century onwards.
notes.CHN: Buddhism reached China around the 1st century AD. Monks translated thousands of texts, and the pilgrim Xuanzang walked to India and back in 629–645.
notes.KOR: The kingdom of Goguryeo, in the north, received Buddhism from China in 372; Baekje followed in 384 and Silla in the early 6th century.
notes.PRK: Goguryeo, centred on today's North Korea, was the first Korean kingdom to adopt Buddhism, in 372.
notes.JPN: A Korean king from Baekje sent a Buddha statue and scriptures to Japan's court in 538 or 552. Prince Shotoku then championed the new faith.
notes.VNM: Buddhism reached northern Vietnam by sea and from China around the 2nd century AD, and flourished under the Ly and Tran kings, who ruled from 1009 to 1400.
notes.MMR: The kingdom of Bagan adopted Theravada Buddhism in the 11th century and covered its plain with thousands of temples.
notes.THA: Buddhism came early through trade, and Theravada became the main faith of the Thai kingdoms from the 13th century.
notes.KHM: The Khmer kings of Angkor mixed Hindu and Buddhist worship; Theravada Buddhism became Cambodia's main faith from the 13th–14th centuries.
notes.IDN: Java and Sumatra had powerful Buddhist and Hindu kingdoms, such as Srivijaya, before Islam spread there from the 13th century.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka became the stronghold of Theravada, the 'teaching of the elders', and later sent monks to renew it in Myanmar and Thailand.
notes.IND: In India Buddhism thrived in great monastic universities such as Nalanda, which drew students from across Asia, until about 1200.

pn: 6th–7th centuries: two giant Buddhas, about 38 and 55 metres tall, were carved here. The Taliban blew them up in 2001.
From the 4th century to the 14th, monks carved nearly 500 decorated cave temples, the Mogao Caves, at this Silk Road oasis.
The White Horse Temple, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, was founded here in the 1st century AD under the Han.
752: the Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze statue about 15 metres tall, was dedicated in Japan's capital.
c. 800: Javanese kings built this vast stepped temple, still the world's largest Buddhist monument.
c. 779: Tibet's first Buddhist monastery was founded here with royal support.

dd-buddhism.text: The Pew Research Center counted about 324 million Buddhists in 2020, about 4% of humanity, almost all in Asia. Buddhists are the majority in seven countries, from [Sri Lanka](LKA) to [Mongolia](MNG); [Thailand](THA) has the most, about 68 million. In [China](CHN) and [Japan](JPN), Buddhist practice mixes with other traditions and many people do not call themselves Buddhist. In [India](IND), its birthplace, Buddhists are under 1% of the population.

notes.THA: Thailand has the world's largest number of Buddhists, about 68 million, or 94% of its people, by Pew's estimate. Many Thai men still spend a short time as monks.
notes.MMR: About 89% of Myanmar's people are Buddhist, by Pew's estimate, and monks have long played a big part in its politics.
notes.KHM: Cambodia is about 97% Buddhist, by Pew's estimate. The Khmer Rouge tried to wipe out religion in 1975–79, but the monasteries were rebuilt.
notes.LKA: About 70% of Sri Lankans are Buddhist, by Pew's estimate. The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy holds what Buddhists revere as a tooth of the Buddha.
notes.MNG: Mongols adopted Tibetan Buddhism from 1578, when Altan Khan gave the title Dalai Lama to a Tibetan teacher. Monasteries revived after communism ended in 1990.
notes.BTN: Bhutan follows the Tibetan-style Vajrayana tradition, and its 2008 constitution calls Buddhism the country's spiritual heritage.
notes.CHN: China has tens of millions of Buddhists, including Tibetans. Pew counted about 53 million self-identified Buddhists in 2020, though far more worship at Buddhist temples.
notes.JPN: Most Japanese have Buddhist funerals and visit Shinto shrines too, but many do not call themselves members of any religion.
notes.IND: India had about 8.4 million Buddhists in its 2011 census, many of them followers of B. R. Ambedkar, who converted with hundreds of thousands of Dalits in 1956.
notes.NPL: Lumbini is a pilgrimage site, but about 8% of Nepal's people are Buddhist; most are Hindu.
notes.AFG: Once a land of monasteries, Afghanistan has been almost entirely Muslim for centuries.
notes.IDN: Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country, yet Borobudur still draws Buddhist pilgrims every year for the Vesak festival.

dd-chinafaiths.text: As the old Zhou kingdom of [China](CHN) broke into warring states, thinkers argued over how to bring back order: the 'Hundred Schools'. Confucius taught that order begins with virtuous rulers and loyal families. Daoists, inspired by the book credited to Laozi, urged people to follow the Dao, the natural 'way', and not to force things. The Qin, who united China in 221 BC, favoured harsh Legalist laws instead, but the Han made Confucianism the state's official learning.

notes.CHN: Confucius, Mencius, Laozi and Zhuangzi all lived in north and central China between about 550 and 280 BC. In 213 BC the Qin burned many books, Confucian classics among them; the Han revived them.

pn: 551 BC: Confucius was born in the small state of Lu. He died here in 479 BC, and his descendants lived beside his temple for over 2,000 years.
The Zhou royal capital. According to legend, Laozi was an archivist here, and Confucius came to consult him.
According to legend, Laozi wrote the Daodejing here for a gatekeeper before riding west, never to be seen again.
136 BC: Emperor Wu of Han made the Confucian classics the basis of official learning, and in 124 BC set up an academy to teach them.
Birthplace of Mencius (c. 372–289 BC), who taught that people are naturally good and may overthrow cruel rulers.

dd-chinafaiths.text: By 1700 Confucian ideas ran the governments of East Asia. [China](CHN) had chosen officials by exams on the Confucian classics since the 600s. [Korea](KOR)'s Joseon kings, from 1392, built one of the most strictly Confucian states ever, and [Vietnam](VNM)'s rulers held similar exams from 1075 to 1919. In [Japan](JPN) the Tokugawa shoguns used Confucian ethics to teach loyalty to samurai, though rank there stayed hereditary rather than won by exams.

notes.CHN: The exams, begun under the Sui around 605, were based from the 1310s on Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian readings of the classics. They were abolished in 1905. Tibet and Xinjiang were not yet under Qing rule.
notes.TWN: The Qing conquered western Taiwan in 1683 and built Confucian schools there; the mountainous east stayed outside their control.
notes.KOR: Korea held state exams on the classics from 958 until 1894. Joseon scholars followed Zhu Xi so strictly that they cut back Buddhist temples and influence.
notes.PRK: The north was part of Joseon Korea, which shaped family rites, ancestor worship and respect for elders across the peninsula.
notes.VNM: Though Vietnam fought hard to stay independent of China, its kings borrowed China's Confucian state model, its exams and classical Chinese writing.
notes.JPN: Japan's samurai studied Confucian texts, but rank stayed hereditary. Confucian ideas of loyalty later shaped the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education.

pn: Every three years, candidates sat the highest exams in the capital; only a few hundred passed each time.
Emperors came to honour Confucius at his temple, and his heir held the hereditary title Duke Yansheng from 1055 to 1935.
From 1398 the Sungkyunkwan academy trained the sons of the elite in the Confucian classics for the state exams.
The Temple of Literature, founded in 1070, holds stone steles carved with the names of those who passed the highest exams.
1690: the shogun Tsunayoshi built a hall to Confucius at Yushima. From 1797 its school was the shogunate's official academy.

dd-chinafaiths.text: Confucianism has no churches or members, but its values of family, education and respect for elders run deep across East Asia. Under Mao, [China](CHN) attacked Confucius as feudal; since the 1980s it has embraced him again. Daoism survives in temples, festivals, tai chi and Chinese medicine, mixed with Buddhism and folk worship of gods and ancestors, from China to [Taiwan](TWN), [Hong Kong](HKG) and [Singapore](SGP).

notes.CHN: Daoism is one of China's five officially recognised religions; Confucianism is not counted as one. From 2004 China opened Confucius Institutes abroad, which critics in some countries saw as tools of state influence.
notes.TWN: Taiwan celebrates Teachers' Day on 28 September, Confucius's traditional birthday, with dawn ceremonies at Confucian temples.
notes.HKG: Many Hong Kong households keep shrines to ancestors and gods, and Daoist and Buddhist temples stand side by side.
notes.SGP: About half of Chinese Singaporeans called themselves Buddhist or Taoist in the 2020 census. In the 1980s schools briefly offered Confucian ethics as a subject.
notes.MYS: Chinese Malaysians, nearly a quarter of the population, keep Daoist and Buddhist temples and festivals such as the Hungry Ghost Festival.
notes.KOR: South Korea's exam-driven schooling, respect for seniority and ancestral rites at Chuseok and Lunar New Year reflect a deep Confucian heritage.
notes.JPN: Few Japanese call themselves Confucian, but ideas of loyalty, hierarchy and duty to family helped shape its schools and companies.
notes.VNM: Vietnamese families honour ancestors at home altars, and students visit Hanoi's Temple of Literature to pray for luck before exams.

pn: 1966: Red Guards smashed statues and dug up graves at the Confucius sites. Restored, they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.
Beijing's main Daoist temple, home of the China Taoist Association, founded in 1957.
One of Hong Kong's busiest temples, mixing Daoist, Buddhist and Confucian worship; crowds gather at Lunar New Year.
Twice a year, Seoul's shrine to Confucius holds the Seokjeon Daeje, a ritual with ancient music and dance.

dd-christianity.text: Jesus, a Jewish teacher, was crucified by the Romans in Jerusalem around AD 30. His followers believed he had risen from the dead, and missionaries such as Paul carried the faith through the cities of the Roman Empire, from [Turkey](TUR) and [Greece](GRC) to [Italy](ITA). After waves of persecution, Constantine backed Christianity from 312, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion. [Armenia](ARM) and [Ethiopia](ETH) adopted it too.

notes.ISR: Jesus preached in Galilee and was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30. The first Christians were Jews who believed he was the Messiah.
notes.PSE: Christian tradition places Jesus's birth in Bethlehem. Constantine had the Church of the Nativity built there in the 330s.
notes.SYR: According to Acts, Paul turned to Christianity on the road to Damascus. Syriac-speaking churches here later carried the faith east into Persia and Asia.
notes.TUR: Paul, born in Tarsus, founded churches across Anatolia. Bishops met at Nicaea in 325, and Constantinople became the empire's Christian capital in 330.
notes.GRC: Paul preached in Philippi, Thessaloniki, Corinth and Athens, and the whole New Testament was written in Greek.
notes.ITA: Constantine won power in Rome in 312 and granted Christians freedom of worship in 313. The bishops of Rome, later called popes, claimed Peter's authority.
notes.EGY: Alexandria was one of the great early churches. Egypt's desert hermits, such as Anthony, began Christian monasticism in the late 200s.
notes.FRA: Christians were martyred at Lyon in 177. By 400 Gaul had bishops in most of its cities.
notes.GBR: Roman Britain had Christian bishops by 314, when some attended a church council at Arles, in Gaul.
notes.ARM: According to tradition, King Tiridates III made Armenia the first Christian state in 301; some historians prefer a date around 314.
notes.GEO: The kingdom of Iberia, in eastern Georgia, adopted Christianity in the 330s, by tradition through a woman missionary, Saint Nino.
notes.ETH: King Ezana of Aksum, whose kingdom covered northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, adopted Christianity around 330–340. Ethiopia's Orthodox Church descends from that conversion.
notes.ERI: Eritrea's highlands and Red Sea port of Adulis were part of the Christian kingdom of Aksum.
notes.IRN: Christians in the Persian Empire formed the Church of the East. They were sometimes persecuted as suspected friends of Rome, Persia's great enemy.

pn: Around AD 30: Jesus is crucified on the orders of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
According to Acts, Jesus's followers were first called 'Christians' here. It was the base for Paul's journeys.
According to tradition, Peter and Paul were executed here under Nero in the 60s AD.
325: Constantine gathers bishops here; they agree the Nicene Creed, still said in many churches.
330: Constantine dedicates his new capital, which became the centre of Eastern Christianity.
c. 330–340: King Ezana adopts Christianity; his later coins carry the cross.

dd-christianity.text: In 1054 the Latin church of Rome and the Greek church of Constantinople excommunicated each other's leaders, a split never healed. From 1517 Martin Luther's protest in [Germany](DEU) launched the Reformation, and by 1600 much of northern Europe was Protestant. Catholic [Spain](ESP) and [Portugal](PRT) carried their faith to the Americas and the [Philippines](PHL), while [Russia](RUS) became the leading Orthodox power.

notes.DEU: Luther's protest split the German lands. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each prince choose Lutheran or Catholic for his territory, roughly north and south.
notes.ESP: Spain was the champion of the Counter-Reformation. Its Inquisition suppressed Protestants, and its empire spread Catholicism across the Americas.
notes.PRT: Portugal took Catholic missions to Brazil, Africa and Asia, from Goa in India to Macau and Japan.
notes.PHL: Spain colonised the Philippines from 1565, and friars converted most of the lowlands. The Muslim south largely resisted.
notes.RUS: After Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, Russia was the only great independent Orthodox state, and from 1589 Moscow had its own patriarch.
notes.ITA: Rome was the seat of the pope, head of the Catholic Church. The Counter-Reformation brought new orders like the Jesuits, founded in 1540, and baroque churches.
notes.FRA: France stayed Catholic, but about a tenth of its people became Protestant Huguenots. After decades of religious wars, the Edict of Nantes granted them toleration in 1598.
notes.GBR: Henry VIII broke with the pope in 1534 to found the Church of England. Scotland's reformation, led by John Knox, was Calvinist.
notes.CHE: Geneva, under John Calvin from 1541, became the centre of Reformed Protestantism, which spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland and Hungary.
notes.NLD: The Dutch revolt against Catholic Spain, from 1568, was partly a religious war. The independent north became mainly Reformed.
notes.SWE: Sweden's kings broke with Rome from the 1520s and made the Lutheran church the state church, as Denmark and Norway also did.
notes.POL: Poland-Lithuania was unusually tolerant, home to Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians and Jews, though the Counter-Reformation made it firmly Catholic.
notes.GRC: Greece's Orthodox Christians lived under Ottoman rule, which allowed them to keep their church under the patriarch in Constantinople.
notes.MEX: Spanish missionaries made New Spain Catholic, often by force and mixed with local traditions. The Virgin of Guadalupe became its great symbol.
notes.PER: Lima became the religious capital of Spanish South America, with an archbishop from 1546 and an Inquisition tribunal from 1570.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia's ancient church survived surrounded by Muslim states. Portuguese soldiers helped it fight off a Muslim invasion in the 1540s.
notes.ARM: The Armenian Church, one of the oldest, held its people together under Ottoman and Persian rule.
notes.EGY: Egypt's Coptic church, once the faith of most Egyptians, had become a minority under centuries of Muslim rule.
notes.IND: The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas, and had been there for well over 1,000 years when the Portuguese arrived.

pn: 1054: papal envoys and the patriarch excommunicate each other. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 the patriarch stayed on under the sultan.
31 October 1517: Martin Luther issues his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences.
1545–63: the Council of Trent reforms the Catholic Church and rejects Protestant teaching.
1589: Moscow gets its own patriarch. Some Russians called it the 'Third Rome' after Constantinople fell.
From the 1520s Spanish friars baptised millions in New Spain, often destroying older temples and images.
Portugal's base in Asia from 1510. The Jesuit Francis Xavier began missions to India and Japan from here in the 1540s.

dd-christianity.text: About 2.3 billion people were Christian in 2020, by Pew Research Center estimates, nearly three in ten people on Earth. The [United States](USA) has the most Christians, mostly Protestant, and [Brazil](BRA) the most Catholics. [Russia](RUS) leads the Orthodox world. As Europe has grown more secular, sub-Saharan Africa, with countries like [Kenya](KEN) and [DR Congo](COD), has become home to more Christians than any other region.

notes.USA: The US has more Christians than any other country, about 217 million in 2020, though their share fell from 78% to 64% in a decade. Most are Protestant, and about a fifth of Americans are Catholic.
notes.BRA: Brazil has more Catholics than any other country, but evangelical Protestants have grown fast, to over a quarter of Brazilians in the 2022 census.
notes.MEX: About three-quarters of Mexicans are Catholic. The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City is one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world.
notes.PHL: About eight in ten Filipinos are Catholic, a legacy of over 300 years of Spanish rule, making it Asia's largest Christian country.
notes.RUS: The Russian Orthodox Church was persecuted under Soviet rule and revived after 1991. It is the largest Orthodox church, closely tied to the state.
notes.UKR: Most Ukrainians are Orthodox. In 2019 the Orthodox Church of Ukraine became independent of Moscow, and Russia's invasion in 2022 pushed many more believers away from the Moscow-linked church.
notes.ITA: Vatican City, inside Rome, is the seat of the pope, head of about 1.4 billion Catholics. Leo XIV, elected in May 2025, is the first pope from the United States.
notes.VAT: The world's smallest state is the seat of the pope and the centre of the Catholic Church.
notes.POL: Poland is one of Europe's most Catholic countries, and Pope John Paul II (1978–2005) was Polish, though church attendance has fallen fast among young Poles.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia's ancient Orthodox church is the country's largest, but Protestants have grown quickly. About a third of Ethiopians are Muslim.
notes.KEN: Kenya is over 80% Christian, mostly Protestant of many kinds, with a large Catholic minority. Most Kenyans became Christian during the 1900s.
notes.COD: DR Congo has one of Africa's largest Christian populations, split between Catholics, Protestants and the home-grown Kimbanguist church.
notes.DEU: Germany is split between Catholics, strongest in the south and west, and Protestants, mainly in the north, a pattern set at the Reformation. Both churches are losing members fast.
notes.GTM: Guatemala, like much of Central America, was solidly Catholic until evangelical and Pentecostal churches grew fast from the 1970s. Protestants are now close to Catholics in number.
notes.NGA: Nigeria has one of the world's largest Christian populations, over 40% of its people, mostly in the south, but is not lit because Muslims are the majority.
notes.GBR: The UK is not lit: in 2020 Christians fell just below half its people, while 40% had no religion.
notes.KOR: About three in ten South Koreans are Christian, mostly Protestant. Christianity grew fast in the 20th century, but South Korea has no majority religion.
notes.CHN: China's Christian population is hard to count; estimates range from about 25 million (Pew Research Center) to over 60 million, many in unregistered churches.

dd-islam.text: Muslims believe that from about 610 God's revelations, later written down as the Quran, came to Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca in today's [Saudi Arabia](SAU), through the angel Gabriel. By his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam. His successors, the caliphs, took [Syria](SYR) and [Egypt](EGY) and overthrew Persia, in today's [Iran](IRN). By 750 their rule ran from [Spain](ESP) to [Pakistan](PAK).

notes.SAU: Muhammad preached in Mecca from around 610, moved to Medina in 622 and returned to take Mecca in 630. By his death in 632 most Arabian tribes had accepted Islam.
notes.YEM: Yemen's leaders accepted Islam in Muhammad's lifetime, and Yemeni tribesmen fought in the conquests that followed.
notes.SYR: Arab armies beat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk river in 636. From 661 Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphs.
notes.EGY: Egypt was taken from the Byzantines in 639–642. Most Egyptians stayed Christian for centuries, becoming mainly Muslim only gradually.
notes.IRN: Persia's Sasanian Empire fell by 651. Iran became mainly Muslim over the following centuries but kept its Persian language.
notes.IRQ: Iraq was the scene of the struggles over who should lead Muslims after Muhammad. Ali, the fourth caliph, ruled from Kufa and was murdered there in 661.
notes.ISR: Jerusalem, holy to Jews and Christians, became Islam's third holiest city. The caliph Umar took it around 637.
notes.PSE: Jerusalem, holy to Jews and Christians, became Islam's third holiest city. The caliph Umar took it around 637.
notes.TUN: The Umayyads founded Kairouan in 670 as their base for conquering North Africa, where many Berbers joined the conquerors.
notes.ESP: In 711 an army of Berbers and Arabs crossed from Africa and conquered most of Spain within a few years. Muslim al-Andalus lasted in part until 1492.
notes.PAK: In 711–712 the young general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, in today's southern Pakistan, bringing Islam to South Asia.
notes.UZB: Arab armies took Bukhara and Samarkand between 706 and 712. Central Asia later produced many of Islam's great scholars.

pn: Muhammad's birthplace, around 570, and home of the Kaaba. He began preaching here around 610 and took the city in 630.
622: Muhammad and his followers move here from Mecca, the Hijra, year one of the Islamic calendar.
Taken around 637. The Dome of the Rock, finished in 691–692, marks the place Muslims link with Muhammad's Night Journey.
661–750: capital of the Umayyad caliphs, who built its Great Mosque in about 705–715.
680: Muhammad's grandson Husayn is killed by Umayyad troops, an event Shia Muslims mourn every year at Ashura.

dd-islam.text: By 1500 Islam had spread far beyond the lands the Arabs conquered. Turkish dynasties carried it into north [India](IND), and the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and much of the Balkans. Merchants, scholars and Sufi mystics carried it along trade routes to West Africa, as in [Mali](MLI), and to [Indonesia](IDN) and [Malaysia](MYS). In the west, Christian Spain took Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in [Spain](ESP), in 1492.

notes.TUR: The Ottomans, a Turkish dynasty from Anatolia, took Constantinople in 1453 and made it their capital; eastern Anatolia was still ruled by rivals. In 1516–17 they conquered the Mamluk lands, including Mecca and Medina.
notes.BIH: The Ottomans took most of Bosnia in 1463, and over the following century many Bosnians converted to Islam.
notes.EGY: The Mamluk sultans ruled Egypt and Syria from Cairo, then one of the world's largest cities, until the Ottomans conquered them in 1516–17.
notes.IRN: In 1501 Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty and made Shia Islam the state religion, turning a mainly Sunni Iran into the centre of the Shia world.
notes.IRQ: The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate. Najaf and Karbala remained the holiest places of Shia Islam after Mecca and Medina.
notes.SAU: Mecca and Medina drew pilgrims from Morocco to Indonesia. The sharifs of Mecca ruled the Hejaz under Mamluk protection.
notes.UZB: Samarkand and Bukhara were great Muslim cities. Timur made Samarkand his capital in the 1370s and filled it with mosques and madrasas.
notes.IND: From 1206 the Delhi Sultanate ruled much of north India, and other sultanates ruled Gujarat, Bengal and the Deccan. Most Indians stayed Hindu, and the south was ruled by Hindu Vijayanagara.
notes.BGD: Bengal had Muslim rulers from about 1204. According to historian Richard Eaton, mass conversion in its eastern delta, today's mainly Muslim Bangladesh, came mostly from the late 1500s, as forests were cleared for rice farming.
notes.MLI: Mali's emperor Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324. By 1500 the Songhay Empire ruled Timbuktu, where rulers and townspeople were Muslim but much of the countryside was not.
notes.NGA: Northern Nigeria's Hausa city-states, such as Kano, had Muslim rulers by the 1400s, alongside older local religions.
notes.SOM: Somalia's coast had been Muslim for centuries. Ibn Battuta described Mogadishu as a rich trading city when he visited in 1331.
notes.TZA: Swahili city-states such as Kilwa, Muslim for centuries, traded gold and ivory across the Indian Ocean. Portugal sacked Kilwa in 1505.
notes.MDV: According to local tradition, the Maldives' king converted to Islam in 1153.
notes.IDN: Islam spread through trading ports from the late 1200s, beginning in northern Sumatra. Java's Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit kingdom was fading, and Muslim coastal sultanates were rising.
notes.MYS: Malacca's sultanate made Islam the faith of the Malay trading world in the 1400s.
notes.PHL: Islam reached the southern Philippines through traders, and the Sulu sultanate was founded around the mid-1400s.
notes.ESP: After Granada fell in 1492, Spain's Muslims were forced to convert from 1499–1502 onwards, and their descendants, the Moriscos, were expelled in 1609–14.

pn: 1453: the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II takes the Byzantine capital and makes it his own.
2 January 1492: the last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrenders to Ferdinand and Isabella.
1258: the Mongols sack the Abbasid capital and kill the last Abbasid caliph.
A desert trading city and centre of Islamic learning, with mosques and libraries of manuscripts.
Capital of the Delhi Sultanate from the early 1200s. In 1526 Babur defeated its last sultan and founded the Mughal Empire.
Its ruler became Muslim in the early 1400s, and its sultanate spread Islam around the Malay world until Portugal took it in 1511.

dd-islam.text: About 2 billion people were Muslim in 2020, a quarter of humanity, by Pew Research Center estimates, and Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group. Most are Sunni. Shia Muslims, about 10–13%, are the majority in [Iran](IRN), [Iraq](IRQ), [Azerbaijan](AZE) and Bahrain. Most Muslims live in Asia: [Indonesia](IDN) has the most, followed by [Pakistan](PAK), [India](IND) and [Bangladesh](BGD).

notes.IDN: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country, about 240 million, nearly nine in ten of its people. Islam arrived mainly through traders, not conquest.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created in 1947 as a homeland for the Muslims of British India. It has the world's second-largest Muslim population, mostly Sunni with a large Shia minority.
notes.IND: India's 213 million Muslims, about 15% of its people, are the world's third-largest Muslim population, though Hindus are the majority.
notes.BGD: Bangladesh, about nine-tenths Muslim, has the world's fourth-largest Muslim population. It split from Pakistan in 1971.
notes.IRN: Iran is the largest Shia-majority country, about nine-tenths Shia. Since the 1979 revolution it has been an Islamic republic led by a senior Shia cleric.
notes.IRQ: Most Iraqis are Shia, though Sunni rulers held power until 2003. Its shrines at Najaf and Karbala draw millions of Shia pilgrims.
notes.AZE: Azerbaijan is mostly Shia, a legacy of Safavid rule, but decades of Soviet rule left it one of the most secular Muslim-majority countries.
notes.BHR: Most of Bahrain's citizens are Shia, while its royal family is Sunni.
notes.LBN: Lebanon's Muslims are split almost evenly between Sunni and Shia, and over a quarter of its people are Christian. Top offices are shared out among religious communities.
notes.OMN: Oman's ruling family follows Ibadi Islam, a third branch older than the Sunni-Shia split. Estimates of the Ibadi and Sunni shares vary, but they are of similar size.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia guards Islam's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina. Its official religious tradition, often called Wahhabism, is a strict Sunni movement of the 1700s.
notes.TUR: Turkey is officially secular, but about 97% of Turks are Muslim, mostly Sunni, with an Alevi minority whose traditions are linked to Shia Islam.
notes.EGY: Egypt is the most populous Arab country and about nine-tenths Muslim, almost all Sunni. Most of its Christians belong to the Coptic Orthodox Church.
notes.NGA: Nigeria is about 56% Muslim, mostly in the north, and 43% Christian, mostly in the south, making it home to one of the world's largest Muslim populations.
notes.YEM: Most Yemenis are Sunni, but about a third or more are Zaydi Shia, the group from which the Houthi movement emerged.
notes.SYR: Most Syrians are Sunni. The Assad family, which ruled from 1970 until it was overthrown in December 2024, came from the Alawite minority, an offshoot of Shia Islam.
notes.ETH: About a third of Ethiopians are Muslim. Islam reached here early: Muslim tradition says some of Muhammad's followers took refuge with Aksum's Christian king around 615.
notes.CIV: Côte d'Ivoire is almost evenly split, about 46% Muslim, mainly in the north, and 45% Christian, mainly in the south.
notes.TZA: About a third of Tanzanians are Muslim, especially on the coast and in Zanzibar, which is almost entirely Muslim.
notes.RUS: Russia has one of Europe's largest Muslim populations, about 8% of its people, mainly Tatars, Bashkirs and peoples of the North Caucasus.

pn: Muslims everywhere pray facing the Kaaba here. In May 2026 about 1.7 million pilgrims made the hajj, by Saudi official count.
Shrine of Ali, whom Shia Muslims see as Muhammad's rightful successor, and a great centre of Shia learning.
Home of al-Azhar, founded in the 970s, one of the most respected centres of Sunni learning.

dd-mesopotamia.text: Southern [Iraq](IRQ) was Sumer, a land of a dozen rival city-states such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash, each with its own god, temple and ruler. Around 2300 BC Sargon of Akkad conquered them all and built the first known empire, reaching into [Syria](SYR) and [Iran](IRN). Ships from [Bahrain](BHR), [Oman](OMN) and the Indus valley in [Pakistan](PAK) brought copper, timber, carnelian and pearls up the Gulf.

notes.IRQ: Sumer filled the far south, among marshes and irrigated fields; Akkad lay just north, near today's Baghdad. Sargon made Akkadian, a Semitic language, the language of power, though Sumerian lived on in temples.
notes.KWT: The head of the Gulf was the gateway for Mesopotamia's sea trade. In the third millennium BC the coastline lay further north than today.
notes.SYR: Sargon and his grandson Naram-Sin campaigned up the Euphrates to Mari and Ebla, and boasted of reaching the 'Cedar Forest' and the 'Silver Mountains' beyond.
notes.TUR: Naram-Sin pushed into south-east Turkey, where a stone stele of an Akkadian king was found near Diyarbakır.
notes.IRN: Elam, around Susa in south-west Iran, was conquered by Sargon but kept its own culture. It was Mesopotamia's great eastern rival for 2,000 years.
notes.BHR: Bahrain was Dilmun, a trading hub the Sumerians also saw as a paradise. Thousands of burial mounds there are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
notes.OMN: Oman was probably Magan, the land of copper and diorite. Naram-Sin claimed to have conquered it and brought back black stone for his statues.
notes.PAK: Meluhha, the Indus civilisation, sent carnelian beads, ivory and timber. Indus seals have been found at Ur and other Mesopotamian cities.
notes.ARE: The coast of today's UAE shared in the copper trade of Magan, with towers and tombs of the Umm an-Nar culture, c. 2600–2000 BC.
notes.IND: Meluhha also reached into north-west India, with Indus cities such as Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat.

pn: c. 3300–3100 BC: the earliest known writing, on clay tablets. Its legendary king Gilgamesh may have ruled here around 2700 BC.
c. 2600 BC: royal tombs filled with gold and dozens of sacrificed attendants. Around 2100 BC King Ur-Nammu built its great ziggurat.
Home of Enlil, chief god of Sumer. Kings sought his temple's blessing, and its ruins have yielded tens of thousands of tablets.
According to the Sumerian King List, kingship came down from heaven here after the Flood. Legend says Sargon began his career as cupbearer to its king.
A city of the state of Lagash. Its ruler Urukagina, around 2350 BC, issued reforms to protect widows and orphans from the powerful.
A rich trading city on the Euphrates. Its palace archive of over 20,000 tablets, from around 1800 BC, records daily royal business.

dd-mesopotamia.text: From Ashur and Nineveh in northern [Iraq](IRQ), Assyrian kings built the largest empire yet seen. They took [Syria](SYR), Phoenicia in [Lebanon](LBN) and the kingdom of Israel, and in 671 BC King Esarhaddon conquered [Egypt](EGY). Assyria ruled by terror and deportation, moving whole peoples across the empire. Yet it fell fast: in 612 BC Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh.

notes.IRQ: Northern Iraq was Assyria's heartland. From about 900 BC its kings campaigned every year, and Babylonia, in the south, was ruled by Assyria or its puppets, though it often rebelled.
notes.SYR: The Aramaean kingdoms of Syria, including Damascus in 732 BC, were turned into provinces. Aramaic, their language, became the shared language of the empire.
notes.LBN: Phoenician ports such as Tyre paid heavy tribute in purple cloth, metals and timber. Sidon rebelled, was destroyed in 677 BC and became a province.
notes.ISR: Assyria took the kingdom of Israel's capital, Samaria, in 722–720 BC, made its land a province and deported many of its people, later called the 'ten lost tribes'. The south belonged to Judah.
notes.PSE: Judah, around Jerusalem, survived as a vassal, while Samaria to the north became a province. According to the Bible and Sennacherib's own annals, he besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC but did not take it.
notes.EGY: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BC. Egypt was ruled through local princes, and one of them, Psamtik I, threw off Assyrian control by about 655 BC.
notes.ARM: Urartu, around Lake Van and the Armenian highlands, was Assyria's toughest rival in the north. Its fortress of Erebuni, built 782 BC, became Yerevan.
notes.IRN: Elam, in south-west Iran, often backed Babylonian revolts. Ashurbanipal's destruction of Susa cleared the way for the Persians, who rose in its old lands.
notes.CYP: An inscription of Esarhaddon lists ten kings of Cyprus who sent him tribute.
notes.TUR: Assyria held south-east Turkey and, at times, Cilicia on the south coast. Urartu held the east around Lake Van, and Phrygia the centre.
notes.JOR: The kingdoms of Ammon, Moab and Edom kept their own kings but paid tribute to Assyria.

pn: Capital from about 700 BC. King Ashurbanipal's library here held thousands of tablets, many now in the British Museum. Destroyed in 612 BC.
The old religious capital, city of the god Ashur, who gave the land and the people their name.
Capital under Ashurnasirpal II from about 879 BC. Islamic State fighters blew up much of its palace in 2015.
701 BC: Sennacherib besieged this city of Judah. Reliefs of the siege lined a room of his palace at Nineveh.
c. 663 BC: Ashurbanipal's army sacked Egypt's great religious capital and carried off its treasures.
c. 647 BC: Ashurbanipal sacked the Elamite capital, and his inscriptions boast of sowing its fields with salt.

dd-mesopotamia.text: After Assyria fell, Babylon in [Iraq](IRQ) took its western lands. Its king Nebuchadnezzar II beat Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, then twice took Jerusalem, destroying it in 587 or 586 BC and deporting many people of Judah to Babylon. He rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale, with the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate. Medes held [Iran](IRN), Lydia ruled western [Turkey](TUR), and [Egypt](EGY) stayed a rival. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon.

notes.IRQ: Babylon was rebuilt with millions of baked bricks, many stamped with Nebuchadnezzar's name. The famous Hanging Gardens appear in no Babylonian text, and some scholars think they were at Nineveh.
notes.ISR: Babylon took the land after Judah's revolts. The exile, from 597 and 586 BC until Cyrus allowed a return after 539 BC, deeply shaped Judaism and the Hebrew Bible.
notes.PSE: Jerusalem was taken in 597 BC and destroyed in 587 or 586 BC. Psalm 137 recalls the exiles weeping 'by the rivers of Babylon'.
notes.SYR: Babylon took Syria from Egypt after Carchemish in 605 BC, and Aramaic remained the everyday language of the region.
notes.LBN: Tyre held out against Nebuchadnezzar for years, then accepted his overlordship. The Phoenician cities kept their trade.
notes.EGY: Egypt under the Saite kings fought Babylon for the Levant, lost at Carchemish, but kept its independence until Persia conquered it in 525 BC.
notes.IRN: The Medes, from western Iran, helped destroy Assyria in 612 BC. Their capital was Ecbatana, today's Hamadan. Cyrus of Persia overthrew them around 550 BC.
notes.TUR: Lydia ruled western Anatolia and, according to Herodotus, made peace with Media at the Halys river in 585 BC after an eclipse stopped a battle. It may also have minted the first coins.
notes.SAU: Nabonidus conquered oases in north-west Arabia, including Tayma, where he lived for about ten years. His absence angered Babylon's priests.
notes.JOR: Babylon absorbed Ammon and Moab, and Edomites moved into southern Judah, later called Idumaea.

pn: Perhaps the largest city in the world under Nebuchadnezzar, with a huge ziggurat often linked to the Tower of Babel.
605 BC: Nebuchadnezzar crushed an Egyptian army here, winning Syria and the Levant for Babylon.
587 or 586 BC: Babylonian troops destroyed the city and Solomon's Temple; many of Judah's people were taken into exile.
According to the historian Josephus, the island city resisted a Babylonian siege for 13 years.
