610–609 BC: the last Assyrian king made his final stand here. Later the moon god's temple was restored by Nabonidus.
From about 552 BC King Nabonidus lived at this Arabian oasis for about ten years, leaving his son Belshazzar in Babylon.

dd-egypt.text: [Egypt](EGY) was a ribbon of green along the Nile, with desert on both sides. Old Kingdom pharaohs ruled from Memphis to the First Cataract at Aswan and built the pyramids of Giza around 2500 BC. Middle Kingdom kings, ruling from Thebes and later near Memphis, pushed south into Nubia in today's [Sudan](SDN) and guarded the Second Cataract with mudbrick forts.

notes.EGY: Nearly all Egyptians lived on the narrow strip watered by the Nile flood, while the deserts were left to miners and caravans. The Old Kingdom lasted c. 2686–2181 BC, the Middle Kingdom c. 2055–1650 BC.
notes.SDN: Nubia, the Nile valley south of Egypt, had gold and trade routes into Africa. The Middle Kingdom conquered Lower Nubia and built a chain of forts against the kingdom of Kerma further south.

pn: c. 2560 BC: the Great Pyramid of Khufu is finished, the largest of Egypt's pyramids.
c. 2650 BC: the step pyramid of Djoser, Egypt's first pyramid, is built near the capital Memphis.
The First Cataract, a stretch of rapids, marked Egypt's traditional southern border.
c. 1860 BC: Senusret III fixes Egypt's frontier here, at the Second Cataract, and forbids Nubians to pass north except to trade.

dd-egypt.text: After driving out the Hyksos around 1550 BC, New Kingdom pharaohs built an empire. Thutmose III campaigned as far as the Euphrates, and Nubia in today's [Sudan](SDN) was ruled as a colony as far as the Fourth Cataract. City-states in today's [Israel](ISR), [Lebanon](LBN) and [Syria](SYR) paid tribute. Ramesses II fought the Hittites of [Turkey](TUR) at Kadesh in 1274 BC, and both sides later made peace.

notes.EGY: Egypt was at its richest and strongest. Pharaohs such as Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II ruled from about 1550 to 1069 BC.
notes.SDN: Egypt conquered the kingdom of Kerma and ruled Nubia to the Fourth Cataract, taking its gold. Boundary inscriptions at Kurgus, further upstream, mark how far its armies went. Later, in the 700s BC, Nubian kings from Napata conquered Egypt.
notes.ISR: Canaanite city-states such as Megiddo, Hazor and Gaza were ruled by local kings under Egyptian governors and garrisons.
notes.PSE: Gaza was the main Egyptian base in Canaan and the starting point for campaigns north.
notes.LBN: Byblos had traded with Egypt for over a thousand years, shipping cedar wood, and its kings were loyal vassals.
notes.SYR: Egypt fought first the Mitanni and then the Hittites for control of Syria. Kadesh, near today's Homs, marked roughly the northern edge of Egyptian rule.
notes.JOR: Egyptian control reached into the Jordan valley, though much of the land east of it lay beyond.
notes.TUR: The Hittites, ruling from Hattusa in central Anatolia, were Egypt's great rival for Syria. A copy of their peace treaty with Ramesses II survives in Istanbul.
notes.IRQ: Mitanni, Egypt's first rival in the north, ruled northern Syria and northern Iraq. Its kings later sent daughters to marry pharaohs.

pn: The New Kingdom's religious capital, with the temples of Karnak and Luxor and the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings.
c. 1264 BC: Ramesses II carves two temples into a cliff in Nubia. They were moved uphill in 1964–68 to escape Lake Nasser.
c. 1346 BC: Akhenaten builds a new capital for the worship of one sun god, the Aten. It was abandoned soon after his death.
c. 1457 BC: Thutmose III defeats a coalition of Canaanite kings, one of the earliest battles recorded in detail.
1274 BC: Ramesses II fights the Hittites in a battle both sides claimed. About 1259 BC they signed one of the oldest known peace treaties.

dd-egypt.text: In 332 BC Alexander the Great took [Egypt](EGY) from the Persians and founded Alexandria. His general Ptolemy made himself king, and his family ruled for almost 300 years, at times holding [Cyprus](CYP), eastern [Libya](LBY) and the southern Levant. The last of them, Cleopatra VII, allied with Rome's Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, but lost to Octavian. In 30 BC [Rome](ITA) took Egypt.

notes.EGY: The Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs, building temples in Egyptian style, but their court in Alexandria spoke Greek. Egypt's grain made them rich.
notes.CYP: Cyprus was a Ptolemaic possession for most of the dynasty. Mark Antony returned it to Cleopatra in the 30s BC.
notes.LBY: Cyrenaica, eastern Libya, was a group of Greek cities ruled by the Ptolemies, apart from a spell of independence under King Magas (c. 276–250 BC). It passed to Rome in 96 BC.
notes.ISR: The Ptolemies ruled the southern Levant until the rival Seleucid kingdom took it in about 200 BC.
notes.SYR: Southern Syria was fought over by the Ptolemies and the Seleucids, the Greek dynasty that ruled from Antioch, in a series of Syrian Wars.
notes.GRC: The Ptolemies were Macedonian Greeks. Egypt's independence ended in Greek waters, at the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC.
notes.ITA: Octavian, soon to be Augustus, made Egypt a Roman province in 30 BC. Its grain fed the city of Rome for centuries.

pn: Founded 331 BC. The Ptolemies' capital had the Great Library and the Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders.
196 BC: a decree is carved in three scripts. French soldiers found the stone here in 1799, and it unlocked hieroglyphs in 1822.
AD 394: the last known hieroglyphic inscription is carved in the temple of Isis here.
31 BC: Octavian's fleet defeats Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece. Both died by their own hand in Alexandria the next year.

dd-greece.text: Ancient [Greece](GRC) was never one country but hundreds of independent city-states, or poleis. From about 750 BC, short of good farmland, they sent out settlers who founded new cities around the Mediterranean and Black Sea: in southern [Italy](ITA) and Sicily, [France](FRA), [Spain](ESP), [Libya](LBY) and [Ukraine](UKR), joining older Greek cities on the Aegean coast of [Turkey](TUR). Plato said the Greeks lived around the sea 'like frogs around a pond'.

notes.GRC: Mountains and sea split Greece into small city-states, each with its own laws, army and gods' festivals. They shared a language, Homer's epics and games such as the Olympics.
notes.TUR: The Aegean coast, called Ionia, held some of the richest Greek cities, such as Miletus and Ephesus. Byzantium guarded the Bosporus.
notes.ITA: So many Greeks settled in southern Italy and Sicily that Romans called it Magna Graecia, 'Great Greece'. Naples began as the Greek Neapolis, 'new city'.
notes.FRA: Massalia traded wine and pottery up the Rhône into Gaul and founded colonies of its own, such as Nikaia, today's Nice, and Antipolis, today's Antibes.
notes.ESP: Phocaean Greeks founded Emporion, today's Empúries in Catalonia, around 575 BC; its name means 'trading post'.
notes.UKR: Greek cities such as Olbia and Panticapaeum, in Crimea, shipped grain to Athens, which came to depend on Black Sea wheat.
notes.LBY: Cyrene, in eastern Libya, became a great Greek city. Its silphium plant was so prized that it appeared on its coins, and was harvested to extinction in Roman times.
notes.EGY: The pharaohs let Greek merchants trade at Naucratis in the Nile delta, and Greek mercenaries served in Egypt's army.
notes.CYP: Cyprus was shared between Greek and Phoenician kingdoms, and was later ruled by Egypt and Persia.
notes.BGR: Greek colonies dotted the Black Sea coast, including Apollonia, today's Sozopol, and Odessos, today's Varna.
notes.RUS: On the Taman peninsula, Greek cities such as Phanagoria traded with the Scythians of the steppe.
notes.ALB: Corinth and Corcyra founded Epidamnus, today's Durrës, and Apollonia on the Adriatic coast.

pn: 776 BC: the traditional date of the first Olympic Games, held every four years in honour of Zeus.
The oracle of Apollo. Cities consulted it before founding colonies, and its priestess, the Pythia, gave often riddling answers.
Founded by Corinth around 733 BC. It grew into one of the largest and richest Greek cities.
c. 600 BC: Greeks from Phocaea, in Ionia, founded the city that is now Marseille, France's oldest city.
Founded by Megara in the 600s BC on the Bosporus; later Constantinople, today Istanbul.
c. 631 BC: settlers from the island of Thera founded Cyrene, which grew rich on grain, horses and a medicinal plant, silphium.

dd-greece.text: After beating Persia, [Greece](GRC) split into two camps: Athens, with its navy and an empire of Aegean allies, and Sparta, with the best army and the Peloponnesian League. Their war lasted 27 years. Athens' great expedition against Syracuse in Sicily, in [Italy](ITA), ended in disaster in 413 BC. Then Persia, ruled from [Iran](IRN), paid for a Spartan fleet, which destroyed Athens' navy in 405 BC.

notes.GRC: Athens led the Delian League, founded in 478 BC to fight Persia, and turned it into an empire paying tribute. Sparta led the Peloponnesian League. Athens surrendered in 404 BC, and Sparta tore down its Long Walls.
notes.ITA: Syracuse, Sicily's greatest Greek city, defeated the Athenian invasion of 415–413 BC. Athens lost tens of thousands of men and about 200 ships.
notes.IRN: Persia's kings had lost the Persian Wars, but by funding Sparta's fleet they won back the Greek cities of Ionia in 387 BC.
notes.TUR: Ionian Greek cities on the coast paid tribute to Athens. When the war turned, many revolted, and they returned to Persian rule after the war.

pn: 430–426 BC: plague struck the crowded city, killing perhaps a quarter of its people, including the leader Pericles in 429 BC.
An unwalled town of a few thousand full citizens, who ruled many times as many unfree helots.
425 BC: Athenians captured about 120 Spartan citizens on Sphacteria island, shocking a Greek world that thought Spartans never surrendered.
413 BC: Athens' invasion force was destroyed; thousands of prisoners were left to die in the city's stone quarries.
405 BC: the Spartan admiral Lysander caught the Athenian fleet on the beach and captured most of it.
Sacred island where the Delian League kept its treasury, until Athens moved it to Athens in 454 BC.

dd-greece.text: Greek thinkers looked for natural explanations of the world. It began in Ionia, on the coast of [Turkey](TUR), where Thales of Miletus asked what everything is made of. Athens, in [Greece](GRC), became the centre of philosophy with Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. In southern [Italy](ITA) Pythagoras' followers studied numbers, and later Alexandria, in [Egypt](EGY), drew mathematicians such as Euclid.

notes.TUR: Ionian thinkers such as Thales, Anaximander and Heraclitus tried to explain nature without myths. Herodotus, the 'father of history', was born at Halicarnassus, today's Bodrum.
notes.GRC: Athens drew thinkers from across the Greek world. Socrates questioned everything, Plato wrote his dialogues, and Aristotle, from Stagira in the north, studied everything from logic to marine life. Democritus of Abdera taught that all things are made of atoms.
notes.ITA: Southern Italy and Sicily were full of thinkers: Pythagoras at Croton, Parmenides at Elea, Empedocles at Acragas, who proposed four elements, and Archimedes at Syracuse.
notes.EGY: After 300 BC Alexandria's Museum and Library made it the scientific capital of the Greek world. Euclid wrote his Elements there, and Eratosthenes measured the Earth.

pn: Thales, active about 585 BC, is often called the first philosopher. According to Herodotus, he predicted a solar eclipse.
Birthplace of Pythagoras, around 570 BC, and of Aristarchus, who argued around 270 BC that the Earth goes around the Sun.
399 BC: Socrates was tried and executed. Plato founded his Academy around 387 BC and Aristotle his Lyceum in 335 BC.
Home of Hippocrates, c. 460–370 BC, who taught that illness had natural causes. Doctors still take an oath named after him.
c. 530 BC: Pythagoras founded a community here whose members believed numbers were the key to the universe.
Home of Archimedes, widely seen as the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He was killed by a Roman soldier when Rome took the city in 212 BC.

dd-persia.text: In 550 BC Cyrus, king of the Persians of south-west [Iran](IRN), overthrew his Median overlords and went on to take Anatolia, [Iraq](IRQ) and Central Asia. His son added [Egypt](EGY), and Darius I reached the Indus in [Pakistan](PAK) and Thrace in [Bulgaria](BGR). About 20 provinces, or satrapies, paid tribute, linked by the Royal Road. Two invasions of [Greece](GRC) failed, at Marathon in 490 BC and Salamis in 480 BC.

notes.IRN: The Persians came from Parsa, today's Fars province. Persian kings called themselves 'King of Kings' and ruled through local elites, not by imposing one religion or language.
notes.IRQ: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, probably with little fighting. Mesopotamia became one of the richest provinces, and Aramaic the common language of government.
notes.ISR: Cyrus let the Jews exiled in Babylon go home and rebuild their Temple in Jerusalem; the Hebrew Bible calls him God's 'anointed'.
notes.EGY: Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC. Darius finished a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, linking Egypt to Persia by ship.
notes.TUR: Cyrus conquered Lydia and the Greek cities of the Aegean coast. Their revolt in 499–494 BC led to the Persian Wars with Greece.
notes.GRC: The Greeks beat Darius at Marathon, then Xerxes at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC. These victories became founding legends of Greek freedom.
notes.PAK: Darius took the Indus valley around 518 BC. According to Herodotus, it paid the largest tribute of any province, in gold dust.
notes.BGR: Darius crossed into Europe around 513 BC and made Thrace a province, and Macedon accepted Persian overlordship for a time.
notes.AFG: Bactria and Arachosia, in today's Afghanistan, were important eastern provinces and suppliers of soldiers.
notes.UZB: Cyrus took Sogdiana, around Samarkand. According to Herodotus he died in 530 BC fighting the Massagetae nomads further north.

pn: Cyrus's capital. His simple stone tomb, built after his death in 530 BC, still stands here.
Begun by Darius I around 518 BC as a ceremonial capital. Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BC.
The main seat of government under Darius I, and the eastern end of the Royal Road.
539 BC: Cyrus took the city, and his clay Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a restorer of local gods and peoples.
c. 546 BC: Cyrus captured the capital of rich King Croesus of Lydia. The Royal Road began here.
490 BC: Athenians defeated a Persian landing force sent by Darius I.

dd-persia.text: After Alexander's conquest and Greek Seleucid rule, the Parthians, horse-riding warriors from the north-east of [Iran](IRN), built a new Persian empire from the 240s BC. By 141 BC they held Mesopotamia, in [Iraq](IRQ). Their mounted archers crushed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC, and for nearly three centuries Rome and Parthia faced each other across the Euphrates, fighting above all over [Armenia](ARM). Parthia grew rich from Silk Road trade passing between China and Rome.

notes.IRN: The Parthians began as the Parni, nomads who settled in Parthia, in north-east Iran. They ruled loosely, through great noble families and vassal kings.
notes.IRQ: Mesopotamia was the economic heart of Parthia, and Ctesiphon its capital. The emperor Trajan conquered it in 116, but Rome gave it up the next year.
notes.ARM: Armenia was the great prize between the two empires. A compromise in AD 63 let a Parthian prince rule Armenia if he was crowned by Rome's emperor.
notes.SYR: The Euphrates, across eastern Syria, was the usual frontier. Rome held the west, governed from Antioch, now in Turkey.
notes.TUR: Eastern Anatolia was the Roman side of the frontier, and Roman legions were based along the upper Euphrates.
notes.TKM: The Parthians' first homeland lay in the south of today's Turkmenistan, around Nisa and the oasis of Merv.
notes.AFG: Parthia held western Afghanistan, around Herat, while the Kushans, patrons of Buddhism, ruled the north and east.

pn: Parthia's winter capital on the Tigris. Roman armies sacked it in 116, 165 and 198.
53 BC: Parthian horse archers destroyed the army of the Roman general Crassus, who was killed in the aftermath.
An early Parthian royal centre near today's Ashgabat; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A frontier city on the Euphrates, held by Parthia until Rome took it in about 165.

dd-persia.text: In 224 Ardashir, a Persian noble from Fars in [Iran](IRN), overthrew the Parthians and founded the Sasanian dynasty, which made Zoroastrianism its state religion. His son Shapur I captured a Roman emperor in 260. From 602 to 628 Persia and the Byzantine Empire, ruled from [Turkey](TUR), fought a ruinous war. Arab Muslim armies then struck both: they took Ctesiphon, in [Iraq](IRQ), in 637 and Iran by 651, and the last Sasanian king was killed at Merv.

notes.IRN: The Sasanians saw themselves as heirs of the Achaemenids and revived Persian kingship, art and Zoroastrian religion. After 651 Iran became Muslim slowly, over centuries.
notes.IRQ: The Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, near today's Baghdad, lay in Iraq. It fell to the Arabs in 637.
notes.TUR: Byzantium, ruled from Constantinople, was Persia's great rival. In 626 Persian and Avar forces besieged Constantinople, but failed.
notes.SYR: Under Khosrow II, Persia overran Byzantine Syria, Palestine and Egypt in 611–619, but Emperor Heraclius won the war by 628 and the lands were handed back.
notes.EGY: Persian armies took Egypt in 619 and held it for about ten years. Arab Muslim forces conquered it from Byzantium in 639–642.
notes.ARM: Armenia was split between the two empires, and in 591 Persia gave Byzantium most of its share as the price of help in a civil war.
notes.YEM: Persia conquered Yemen around 570, and its Persian governor accepted Islam around 628, when Sasanian power was collapsing.
notes.AZE: Caucasian Albania, roughly today's Azerbaijan, was a Sasanian vassal kingdom, guarded by great walls at Derbent, just to the north, against steppe nomads.
notes.TKM: Merv was the Sasanians' north-eastern bastion, and the place where the dynasty ended in 651.

pn: The Sasanian capital. Its great brick arch, the Taq Kasra, still stands; Arab armies took the city in 637.
260: near here Shapur I defeated and captured the Roman emperor Valerian, who died a prisoner.
Beside the tombs of Achaemenid kings, a rock relief shows Shapur I on horseback triumphing over the Roman emperors Valerian and Philip the Arab.
c. 636: Arab Muslim forces defeated the main Sasanian army, opening Mesopotamia to conquest.
642: the Arabs' victory here ended organised Sasanian resistance; Muslims called it the 'victory of victories'.
651: the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv while on the run.

dd-rome.text: By 264 BC Rome ruled peninsular [Italy](ITA), and it then fought three wars with Carthage, a Phoenician sea power based in [Tunisia](TUN). Rome won the first and took Sicily. In 218 BC Carthage's general Hannibal marched from [Spain](ESP) over the Pyrenees and through [France](FRA), then crossed the Alps with war elephants and crushed Roman armies in Italy. Rome refused to give in, and beat him at Zama, in Africa, in 202 BC.

notes.ITA: Rome ruled the peninsula through alliances, and after 241 BC also held Sicily. Celtic Gauls still held the Po valley in the north and joined Hannibal.
notes.TUN: Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, by tradition in 814 BC. It grew rich on trade and ruled the coast of North Africa with a powerful navy.
notes.ESP: Hannibal's family, the Barcids, built a Carthaginian empire in southern and eastern Spain after 237 BC, rich in silver mines. Rome took it in 206 BC.
notes.FRA: Hannibal crossed southern Gaul in 218 BC, fighting his way across the Rhône. It was not yet Roman, though Rome had seized Corsica and Sardinia from Carthage in 238–237 BC.
notes.MLT: Malta was Carthaginian until Rome took it in 218 BC, at the start of the war.
notes.DZA: The coast was dotted with Carthaginian ports, while the interior was ruled by Numidian kings. Numidian cavalry fought for Hannibal and, at Zama, for Rome.
notes.LBY: Carthage held the coast of Tripolitania, with towns such as Leptis. The east, Cyrenaica, was Greek and ruled from Egypt.
notes.GRC: Philip V of Macedon allied with Hannibal in 215 BC. Rome's war with him began its long involvement in Greece.

pn: 219 BC: Hannibal besieged and took this Spanish town, allied to Rome, starting the Second Punic War.
December 218 BC: Hannibal's first great victory in Italy, won in snow and freezing river water.
217 BC: Hannibal ambushed a Roman army in morning fog along the lakeshore and destroyed it.
216 BC: Hannibal surrounded a much larger Roman army. Perhaps 50,000 or more Romans and allies died in a day.
202 BC: the Roman general Scipio, later called Africanus, defeated Hannibal in Africa and won the war. The exact battlefield is uncertain.
146 BC: after a three-year siege Rome destroyed the city, ending the Third Punic War.

dd-rome.text: By the 1st century BC Rome ruled most of the Mediterranean, but rival generals fought for power. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, today's [France](FRA) and [Belgium](BEL), in 58–50 BC, then crossed the Rubicon into [Italy](ITA) with his army in 49 BC, starting a civil war. He won, backed Cleopatra in [Egypt](EGY), and was named dictator for life. On 15 March 44 BC senators stabbed him to death in Rome.

notes.FRA: Southern France had been the Roman province of Narbonensis since the 120s BC. Caesar's war conquered the rest; ancient writers claimed a million Gauls died, a figure that cannot be checked.
notes.BEL: Caesar called the Belgae the bravest of the Gauls. He defeated them in 57 BC and crushed their revolts in 54–53 BC.
notes.ITA: Italy was the heart of the Republic. After the Social War of 91–88 BC, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies.
notes.EGY: Egypt was still independent under the Ptolemies, but its rulers depended on Roman support. Cleopatra had a son, Caesarion, she said was Caesar's.
notes.GBR: Caesar crossed to Britain in 55 and 54 BC, but these were raids, not conquest. Rome invaded for real in AD 43.
notes.DEU: Caesar bridged the Rhine twice, in 55 and 53 BC, to warn off Germanic tribes, but made it the frontier.
notes.TUR: Pompey had reorganised Anatolia in the 60s BC, turning kingdoms into provinces and client states.
notes.IRQ: In 53 BC Parthian horse archers destroyed the army of Crassus, Caesar's ally, at Carrhae. Caesar was planning a war on Parthia when he was killed.
notes.ESP: Spain had been Roman for over a century, but the north-west was not conquered until 19 BC. Caesar fought Pompey's sons here, winning at Munda in 45 BC.
notes.TUN: Caesar beat Pompey's supporters at Thapsus in 46 BC and annexed the Numidian kingdom next door as Africa Nova.
notes.ISR: Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. Judaea kept its own rulers, the high priest Hyrcanus II and his minister Antipater, under Roman supervision, while some coastal cities were attached to the province of Syria.

pn: 52 BC: Caesar besieged the Gallic leader Vercingetorix here, inside a ring of Roman walls, and forced his surrender.
January 49 BC: Caesar led his army across this small river into Italy, breaking the law and starting civil war.
48 BC: Caesar defeated Pompey, who fled to Egypt and was murdered on arrival.
48–47 BC: Caesar, besieged in the city, backed Cleopatra in her civil war against her brother.
47 BC: Caesar beat King Pharnaces of Pontus in a short campaign and reported: 'I came, I saw, I conquered.'
15 March 44 BC: about 60 senators conspired, and Caesar was stabbed 23 times, according to Suetonius.

dd-rome.text: In 376 the Goths, fleeing the Huns, crossed the Danube into the empire, and two years later they killed the emperor Valens at Adrianople. In 410 the Visigoths sacked Rome. Vandals took Carthage, in [Tunisia](TUN), in 439. By 476, when the general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor in [Italy](ITA), Germanic kings ruled [Spain](ESP) and [France](FRA). The Eastern Empire, in [Greece](GRC) and [Turkey](TUR), survived.

notes.ITA: Odoacer, a Germanic officer, deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled as king, keeping the Senate and Roman officials. In 493 Theodoric the Ostrogoth killed him and took Italy.
notes.TUN: The Vandals crossed from Spain in 429 and took Carthage in 439. Losing Africa's grain and taxes was a crippling blow to the Western Empire.
notes.ESP: By 476 the Visigoths ruled most of Spain, while the Suebi held the north-west, around Galicia.
notes.FRA: The Visigoths ruled the south-west from Toulouse, Burgundians the Rhône valley, and Franks the north. A Roman general, Syagrius, held out around Soissons until 486.
notes.BEL: The Franks settled in today's Belgium as Roman allies. Their king Clovis, from Tournai, conquered most of Gaul after 486.
notes.GBR: Rome withdrew its troops around 410. Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northern Germany and Denmark settled much of England over the next two centuries.
notes.GRC: The Greek-speaking East was richer and more populous, and paid or diverted invaders westward. It lasted until 1453.
notes.TUR: Constantinople, founded in 330, was the Eastern capital. Its emperor Zeno received Odoacer's embassy in 476.
notes.DEU: The Rhine frontier collapsed after Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed it, traditionally on 31 December 406. Franks and Alamanni settled west of the river.
notes.HUN: From about 420 the Huns ruled a steppe empire from the Hungarian plain. Attila extorted gold from the East and invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452.
notes.LBY: Tripolitania, in the west, fell to the Vandals. Cyrenaica, in the east, stayed part of the Eastern Empire.

pn: 378: Gothic cavalry and infantry destroyed an eastern Roman army and killed the emperor Valens.
410: the Visigoths under Alaric sacked the city for three days. In 455 the Vandals sacked it again, for two weeks.
439: the Vandal king Gaiseric seized the city, taking Rome's richest African provinces and its fleet base.
451: Romans and Visigoths fought Attila the Hun to a standstill in Gaul. Attila died two years later.
476: Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
Its Theodosian land walls, finished in 413, protected the East's capital and were not broken through until the Ottoman conquest of 1453.

dd-alexander.text: In 334 BC Alexander crossed from Macedon, in northern [Greece](GRC), into Asia. He beat the Persians at the Granicus and at Issus, took [Egypt](EGY) without a fight, and crushed King Darius III at Gaugamela, in [Iraq](IRQ). He then fought for three years in [Afghanistan](AFG) and [Uzbekistan](UZB) and pushed into the Punjab, in [Pakistan](PAK) and [India](IND), where his exhausted army refused to go on. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

notes.GRC: Alexander's father Philip II made Macedon the master of Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BC. Alexander razed rebellious Thebes in 335 BC before leaving for Asia.
notes.MKD: Part of ancient Macedon lay in today's North Macedonia, though its heartland and capital, Pella, lay in today's Greece.
notes.TUR: Alexander freed the Greek cities of the Aegean coast from Persia in 334 BC and, by tradition, cut the Gordian knot at Gordion.
notes.EGY: The Persian governor surrendered Egypt in 332 BC. At the desert oracle of Siwa, priests reportedly greeted Alexander as son of the god Amun.
notes.IRQ: After Gaugamela, Babylon opened its gates. Alexander planned to make it his capital and died there.
notes.IRN: Alexander took Persepolis and burned its palaces in 330 BC. Darius III was murdered by his own nobles that summer.
notes.AFG: Bactria, around Balkh, put up the fiercest resistance. Alexander married Roxana, a Bactrian noblewoman, in 327 BC.
notes.UZB: In Sogdiana, around Samarkand, Alexander fought a hard guerrilla war in 329–327 BC and founded 'Alexandria the Farthest' near Khujand, in Tajikistan.
notes.PAK: Alexander fought down the Indus valley in 326–325 BC, brutally in places, then marched back across the Gedrosian desert, where many of his followers died.
notes.IND: At the Beas river, in today's Indian Punjab, his soldiers, eight years from home, refused to march further east in 326 BC.

pn: May 334 BC: Alexander's first victory over a Persian army, near the Dardanelles; he nearly died in the cavalry fight.
333 BC: Alexander defeated Darius III, who fled, leaving his mother, wife and daughters as captives.
331 BC: Alexander founded the city that became the greatest Greek city of the ancient world, and later his burial place.
1 October 331 BC: Alexander routed Darius's much larger army near today's Erbil, winning the Persian Empire.
326 BC: Alexander defeated the Indian king Porus and his war elephants on the Jhelum river.
June 323 BC: Alexander died here after a short fever, possibly malaria or typhoid; poison was rumoured but is unproven.

dd-alexander.text: Alexander left no adult heir, and his generals fought over his empire for forty years. Three dynasties emerged: the Ptolemies in [Egypt](EGY), the Seleucids in [Syria](SYR), [Iraq](IRQ) and Iran, and the Antigonids in Macedon. Greek settlers in Bactria, in [Afghanistan](AFG), broke away around 250 BC. Seleucus had already handed the far east to India's Mauryan Empire in exchange for 500 war elephants. Greek-speaking kings now ruled millions of Egyptians, Syrians and Persians.

notes.EGY: The Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs and Greek kings at once. Greek was the language of government, and Alexandria drew scholars from across the Mediterranean.
notes.SYR: The Seleucids ruled from Antioch, in today's Turkey near the Syrian border, and fought six wars with the Ptolemies over southern Syria and Palestine.
notes.IRQ: Mesopotamia was the Seleucids' richest region. Babylon's priests kept up their temples and astronomical records under Greek rule.
notes.IRN: The Seleucids held Iran loosely. In the 240s BC the north-eastern province of Parthia broke away, and the Parni nomads soon seized it, the start of a new Persian empire.
notes.AFG: Bactria became an independent Greek kingdom, famous for its silver coins. Southern Afghanistan, around Kandahar, belonged to the Mauryans.
notes.GRC: Macedon dominated Greece, but leagues of cities, the Achaeans and Aetolians, and proud Athens and Sparta kept some independence.
notes.TUR: Western Anatolia was split among the Seleucids, the growing kingdom of Pergamon and smaller states, with Ptolemaic bases on the coast.
notes.PAK: The Mauryan Empire took the Indus lands from Seleucus around 305 BC, and Greek envoys such as Megasthenes visited its court.

pn: Under the Ptolemies: home of the Library, the greatest of the ancient world, and of the Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders.
Founded by Seleucus I in 300 BC, it grew into one of the largest cities of the Greek world.
Seleucus's new Greek capital on the Tigris, which replaced Babylon as Mesopotamia's main city.
A Greek city on the Oxus with a theatre and gymnasium; a stone here carried Greek maxims copied from Delphi.
301 BC: Seleucus and Lysimachus defeated Antigonus, ending hopes of reuniting Alexander's empire.

dd-alexander.text: The Greek kingdoms were swallowed one by one. Rome defeated Macedon in 168 BC and took [Greece](GRC) by 146 BC. Parthia seized Iran and, by 141 BC, [Iraq](IRQ). Pergamon passed to Rome in 133 BC, and Pompey ended the Seleucids in [Syria](SYR) in 64 BC. Last came [Egypt](EGY): after Cleopatra and Mark Antony lost at Actium, Rome took it in 30 BC. Yet the Greek language and culture lived on, in the Roman East for centuries.

notes.GRC: Rome turned Macedon into a province in 148 BC and crushed a Greek revolt in 146 BC. Rome then absorbed Greek art, philosophy and literature.
notes.TUR: Pergamon became the Roman province of Asia, one of Rome's richest. Its Greek cities flourished under Roman rule.
notes.SYR: Weakened by civil wars, the Seleucid kingdom shrank to a rump around Antioch, which Pompey made the Roman province of Syria in 64 BC.
notes.ISR: The Jewish Maccabees revolted against the Seleucids from 167 BC, an event marked by Hanukkah, and won independence; Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC.
notes.EGY: Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemy, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony to keep Egypt independent. Her death in 30 BC ended the Hellenistic age.
notes.IRQ: The Parthian king Mithridates I took Mesopotamia from the Seleucids around 141 BC, and it stayed Persian, apart from brief Roman invasions, until the 7th century.
notes.AFG: The Greco-Bactrian kingdom fell to nomads from the north around 130 BC. Ai-Khanoum was abandoned after about 145 BC.
notes.PAK: Indo-Greek kings ruled parts of the north-west until about AD 10. One of them, Menander, appears in a Buddhist text as King Milinda.

pn: 168 BC: Roman legions destroyed the Macedonian phalanx, ending the Antigonid kingdom.
146 BC: Rome sacked Corinth after a Greek revolt, the same year it destroyed Carthage.
133 BC: its last king, Attalus III, left his kingdom to Rome in his will.
31 BC: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece.
30 BC: Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives here as Octavian arrived, ending Ptolemaic rule.

dd-maya.text: The Maya never formed one empire. Dozens of kingdoms, each with a divine king, shared one culture across [Guatemala](GTM), [Belize](BLZ), southern [Mexico](MEX) and western [Honduras](HND). In the 500s–600s two great powers, Tikal and the Snake kingdom of Calakmul, fought for supremacy through webs of allies. In the 800s most southern lowland cities stopped building, and by about 950 many lay empty.

notes.GTM: The Petén lowlands of northern Guatemala held the densest cluster of Classic cities, including Tikal. A 2018 laser (lidar) survey found over 60,000 structures hidden under the forest there.
notes.MEX: Mexico's Maya lands ran from Chiapas, with Palenque, to the Yucatán Peninsula, with Calakmul in the south and later Chichén Itzá in the north.
notes.BLZ: Belize held Caracol, an ally of Calakmul, and Lamanai, one of the few cities lived in without a break from early times to the Spanish arrival.
notes.HND: Copán, in western Honduras, was the south-eastern edge of the Classic lowlands, famous for its carved stelae and a stairway of over 2,000 glyphs.
notes.SLV: Western El Salvador was on the southern fringe of the Maya world. At Joya de Cerén, ash from an eruption around 600 preserved a whole farming village.

pn: c. 300 BC–AD 150: an early giant city whose La Danta complex is one of the largest ancient structures in the Americas by volume.
378: a Teotihuacan general, Siyaj K'ak', arrived and a new dynasty took power. In 695 Tikal beat Calakmul in battle.
From the 630s: seat of the Snake (Kaan) dynasty, which led a network of allied kingdoms against Tikal.
562: Caracol and its ally, the Snake kingdom, defeated Tikal, and Caracol grew into a large city.
615–683: reign of K'inich Janaab Pakal, whose jade-masked tomb was found inside the Temple of the Inscriptions in 1952.
738: its king Waxaklajuun Ubaah K'awiil, '18 Rabbit', was captured and beheaded by the smaller city of Quiriguá.

dd-maya.text: With no single capital to capture, the Spanish had to conquer the Maya kingdom by kingdom. Pedro de Alvarado invaded the highlands of [Guatemala](GTM) in 1524. In Yucatán, in [Mexico](MEX), the Montejo family needed about twenty years and founded Mérida in 1542. The Itza kingdom in the Petén forest stayed free until March 1697, over 170 years after the fall of the Aztecs.

notes.GTM: Alvarado took the highlands from 1524, helped by thousands of Nahua allies from Mexico. The Itza of the Petén lowlands held out until 1697.
notes.MEX: Yucatán's divided Maya states fought off the Montejos twice before falling by 1546. A great revolt that year in the east was crushed. Chiapas was conquered from 1524.
notes.SLV: Alvarado's forces pushed into Cuscatlán, the land of the Pipil, a Nahua people living beside the Maya, from 1524.
notes.HND: Copán's region, then home to Maya-speaking Ch'orti' people, resisted under a lord recorded as Copan Calel until it was crushed in 1530–31.
notes.BLZ: Belize lay on the remote edge of Spanish Yucatán. Maya towns there, such as Tipu, rebelled in 1638, and Britain later took over the coast.

pn: 1524: Alvarado burned the K'iche' capital and its kings, after a battle near today's Quetzaltenango.
1524: the Kaqchikel capital first allied with the Spanish, then rose against their demands for tribute.
1542: founded by Francisco de Montejo the Younger on the Maya city of T'ho, reusing its stones.
1562: the friar Diego de Landa burned Maya books and idols here; only four Maya codices survive today.
c. 1220–1450: the last great Maya capital of Yucatán, abandoned decades before the Spanish arrived.
March 1697: Spanish forces stormed the island capital of the Itza, the last independent Maya kingdom. Flores stands there today.

dd-maya.text: The Maya did not vanish. Over 6 million people speak about 30 Maya languages, most of them in [Guatemala](GTM), where Maya people are about two-fifths of the population, and in south-eastern [Mexico](MEX). Smaller communities live in [Belize](BLZ) and [Honduras](HND). Maya farmers still grow maize, beans and squash, and some communities keep the old 260-day calendar for rituals.

notes.GTM: In the 2018 census about 42% of Guatemalans identified as Maya. A UN-backed truth commission found that 83% of identified victims of the 1960–96 civil war were Maya, and that state agents committed acts of genocide.
notes.MEX: The 2020 census counted over 2 million speakers of Maya languages in Mexico, above all Yucatec Maya, Tseltal, Tsotsil and Ch'ol, in Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche and Chiapas.
notes.BLZ: About a tenth of Belizeans are Maya, mostly Mopan, Q'eqchi' and Yucatec. In 2015 Belize's top court upheld Maya customary land rights in the south.
notes.HND: A small Ch'orti' Maya community lives around Copán, near the ruins their ancestors' world once included.

pn: Early 1980s: the army destroyed many Ixil Maya villages here, among the worst-hit areas of Guatemala's civil war.
1 January 1994: the Zapatistas, mostly Tsotsil and Tseltal Maya, seized towns in Chiapas demanding land and Indigenous rights.
1847: the Caste War began near here, a Maya rising in Yucatán that lasted in parts until 1901.

dd-africa.text: From highlands in today's [Ethiopia](ETH) and [Eritrea](ERI), Aksum grew rich on Red Sea trade, exporting ivory and gold through its port, Adulis. It minted its own gold coins from about 270. Around 330 King Ezana became a Christian, making Aksum one of the first Christian states. A Persian prophet of the 200s, Mani, listed it among the world's four great powers, with Rome, Persia and China.

notes.ETH: Northern Ethiopia, especially Tigray, was Aksum's heartland. Ethiopia's Orthodox Church traces its roots to Ezana's conversion around 330.
notes.ERI: The Eritrean highlands and coast were part of Aksum, and its port of Adulis lay on the Gulf of Zula.
notes.SDN: Northern Sudan was home to the kingdom of Kush, centred on Meroë. Ezana's inscriptions describe a campaign there in the mid-300s.
notes.YEM: Around 525 Aksum's King Kaleb invaded Himyar in Yemen. Aksumite rule soon gave way to a general, Abraha, who ruled largely on his own.
notes.EGY: Roman Egypt traded with Aksum through Red Sea ports such as Berenice. Christianity reached Aksum through these links.

pn: c. 100–700: the capital, famous for its carved granite stelae; the tallest, now fallen, would have stood about 33 metres high.
c. 200–600: Aksum's main port, where ships from Egypt, Arabia and India traded.
Mid-300s: Ezana's inscriptions record a campaign along the Nile here, as the old kingdom of Kush faded.
c. 1200: long after Aksum, King Lalibela's reign gave its name to a group of churches carved down into solid rock.

dd-africa.text: West Africa's gold paid for an empire three times over. Ghana, in today's [Mauritania](MRT) and [Mali](MLI), ruled the gold trade by the 800s. Mali followed from about 1235 and was at its height around 1350, when camel caravans carried its gold north across the Sahara to [Morocco](MAR) and Egypt in exchange for salt and goods. Songhai, ruling from Gao, became the largest of the three in the 1500s.

notes.MLI: Today's Mali was the heart of all three empires: Ghana in the west, Mali along the upper Niger, and Songhai at Gao and Timbuktu. It took its name from the Mali Empire at independence in 1960.
notes.MRT: Southern Mauritania held Koumbi Saleh, probably Ghana's capital, and the desert-edge trading town of Walata.
notes.SEN: Most of Senegal fell under Mali's rule, including the gold-bearing region of Bambuk on its eastern border.
notes.GMB: The Gambia River valley was Mali's western edge. Portuguese ships sailed up the river in the 1450s, seeking a route to Mali's gold.
notes.GIN: Upper Guinea was Mali's homeland: tradition places Sundiata Keita's origins and the gold fields of Bure here.
notes.GNB: Kaabu, in today's Guinea-Bissau, began as a western province of Mali and later became a kingdom of its own.
notes.MAR: Moroccan merchants ran much of the caravan trade. In 1591 a Moroccan army with firearms crossed the desert and defeated Songhai at Tondibi.
notes.DZA: Oasis towns in the Algerian Sahara, such as those of Tuat, were stops for caravans between the Niger and North Africa.
notes.GHA: Mali's reach extended into northern Ghana. The old Ghana Empire lay hundreds of kilometres north-west and never included today's Ghana, which took the name at independence in 1957.

pn: 1000s: probably the capital of the Ghana Empire, described by the Arab geographer al-Bakri in 1068 as two towns.
From 1324 part of Mali; a great centre of Islamic learning, with mosques such as Djinguereber and Sankore.
A trading city on the inland Niger delta; its Great Mosque, rebuilt in mud brick in 1907, follows the old style.
Capital of Songhai, whose ruler Sonni Ali took Timbuktu from its Tuareg rulers in 1468.
1300s: salt mines in the desert; slabs of salt were carried south and traded for gold.
The main northern end of the caravan route, in today's Morocco, where Saharan gold entered the Mediterranean world.

dd-africa.text: Along the coast of [Kenya](KEN), [Tanzania](TZA) and [Mozambique](MOZ), Muslim city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Mogadishu traded with Arabia, India and China on the monsoon winds. Their language, Swahili, mixed Bantu roots with Arabic words. Inland, the rulers of Great Zimbabwe in [Zimbabwe](ZWE) controlled gold that reached the coast at Sofala. Their stone city, built without mortar, was the largest in southern Africa.

notes.KEN: Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu were among the leading Swahili towns. In 1505 a Portuguese fleet sacked Mombasa.
notes.TZA: Kilwa, on an island off southern Tanzania, controlled the gold trade in the 1300s; Zanzibar and Pemba were Swahili towns too.
notes.MOZ: Sofala, near today's Beira, was the port where Zimbabwe's gold met traders from the north.
notes.SOM: Mogadishu and other Somali ports were part of the same Indian Ocean trade, and Mogadishu was its leading town in the 1200s.
notes.COM: The Comoros were part of the Swahili world, with Muslim towns and trading links to Kilwa and Madagascar.
notes.ZWE: Great Zimbabwe was built from about the 1000s by ancestors of the Shona people. Chinese porcelain and Persian goods found there show its trading reach.
notes.ZAF: Mapungubwe, on today's South Africa's northern border, was an earlier gold-trading kingdom, a forerunner of Great Zimbabwe.

pn: c. 1100–1450: walls up to 11 metres high enclosed the court of a state that grew rich on gold and cattle.
1300s: the richest Swahili town, minting its own coins; Ibn Battuta, visiting in 1331, praised its fine buildings.
1300s: the leading northern port, which once controlled the Sofala gold trade before Kilwa took it.
1498: its ruler gave Vasco da Gama a pilot for the crossing to India.
c. 1220–1300: an earlier kingdom on the Limpopo, known for a small gold-foil rhinoceros found in a royal grave.

dd-byzantium.text: Emperor Justinian (527–565) set out to win back the lost western half of the Roman Empire. His generals took North Africa from the Vandals in 533–534, [Italy](ITA) from the Ostrogoths after a war lasting until 554, and a strip of southern [Spain](ESP) in 552. From Constantinople, today's Istanbul in [Turkey](TUR), the empire again ruled most of the Mediterranean, but plague and war left it exhausted.

notes.TUR: Anatolia and Constantinople were the heart of the empire. Its people called themselves Romans and mostly spoke Greek.
notes.GRC: Greece was an old and largely Greek-speaking part of the eastern empire, with great cities such as Thessaloniki and Corinth.
notes.ITA: The war against the Ostrogoths lasted from 535 to 554 and ruined much of Italy. In 568 the Lombards invaded and took most of the north.
notes.TUN: The Vandal kingdom of North Africa fell in 533–534. Carthage stayed Byzantine until the Arabs took it in 698.
notes.EGY: Egypt's grain fed Constantinople. The plague first reached the empire through the Egyptian port of Pelusium in 541.
notes.SYR: Syria, with Antioch as its great city, faced the Persian Empire. A Persian army sacked Antioch in 540.
notes.ESP: Justinian's troops took a strip of the south-east coast from the Visigoths in 552. Spain was the furthest west the empire reached again.
notes.DZA: Byzantine rule covered the coast and part of the interior of eastern Algeria, the old Roman province of Numidia.
notes.LBY: Cyrenaica, in the east, was already part of the empire. Tripolitania, in the west, was won back from the Vandals in 533.
notes.HRV: The Dalmatian coast, with cities such as Salona near Split, was retaken from the Ostrogoths early in the Gothic War.
notes.ARM: The empire ruled western Armenia, today in eastern Turkey. The lands of today's Armenia were under the Persian Empire until 591.
notes.UKR: The empire held Chersonesus and other towns on the coast of Crimea.
notes.MAR: Morocco lay outside the empire, but the fortress of Septem, today's Spanish city of Ceuta on its coast, guarded the Strait of Gibraltar.
notes.ROU: The empire held Dobruja, the Roman province of Scythia Minor, along the lower Danube and the Black Sea coast.

pn: 537: Hagia Sophia is dedicated, rebuilt in under six years after riots burned the old church in 532.
540: Belisarius takes Ravenna, the Ostrogoths' capital. Its church of San Vitale still shows mosaics of Justinian and Theodora.
533: Belisarius captures the Vandal capital after a lightning campaign.
552: Byzantine troops land in Spain. The province of Spania lasted until the 620s.

dd-byzantium.text: Between 634 and 718 Arab armies took Syria, [Egypt](EGY) and North Africa, and twice besieged Constantinople. The empire held on to Anatolia and Greece, and under Basil II, who conquered [Bulgaria](BGR) by 1018, it recovered much of the Balkans. Then defeat by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to the Turks. Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, and the Ottomans took it in 1453.

notes.EGY: Egypt, the empire's richest province, fell to the Arabs in 639–642. Its loss cost Constantinople its main grain supply.
notes.SYR: After the Battle of Yarmuk in 636 Syria became the heart of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruled from Damascus.
notes.TUN: Carthage fell to the Arabs in 698, ending Byzantine North Africa.
notes.TUR: Anatolia was the core that survived the Arab attacks. After Manzikert in 1071 the Turks settled most of it, and the empire kept only the west and the coasts.
notes.BGR: The Bulgarian state had fought Byzantium for 300 years. Basil II, called the Bulgar-slayer, annexed it by 1018.
notes.GRC: Greece stayed Byzantine. Crete was retaken from the Arabs in 961, and the empire's last foothold, the Morea, fell in 1460.
notes.CYP: Cyprus was shared with the Arabs for three centuries and fully retaken in 965.
notes.ITA: Byzantium lost Ravenna to the Lombards in 751 and Sicily to the Arabs by 902, but held the south of Italy until the Normans took Bari in 1071.
notes.ARM: In 1025 today's Armenia was still ruled by Armenian kings. The empire annexed their kingdom of Ani in 1045, only for the region to fall to the Seljuks after 1064.
notes.GEO: The empire annexed parts of south-west Georgia under Basil II.
notes.SRB: Serbian lands accepted Byzantine overlordship after the fall of Bulgaria in 1018.

pn: 1204: the Fourth Crusade sacks the city. 29 May 1453: the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures it, ending the empire.
1071: the Seljuk Turks defeat and capture Emperor Romanos IV. Turkish groups soon settled much of Anatolia.
1204–1261: capital of the Byzantine state in exile, which won Constantinople back in 1261.
Capital of the Byzantine Morea, a centre of late Byzantine learning. It fell to the Ottomans in 1460.
636: an Arab army defeats the Byzantines, and Syria and Palestine are lost.

dd-byzantium.text: Byzantine missionaries took Christianity, its liturgy and an alphabet to the Slavs. [Bulgaria](BGR) was baptised in 864, and in 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv, in today's [Ukraine](UKR), made Orthodoxy the faith of the Rus. After 1453 [Russia](RUS) saw itself as Byzantium's heir. Today the Orthodox Church is the largest faith from [Greece](GRC) and [Serbia](SRB) to Russia.

notes.GRC: The Church of Greece and the Greek language are Byzantium's most direct heirs. Modern Greeks long called themselves Romioi, 'Romans'.
notes.CYP: Cyprus has its own Orthodox church, independent since the 400s.
notes.BGR: Khan Boris I was baptised in 864. Disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed the Cyrillic alphabet in Bulgaria around 900.
notes.SRB: The Serbs became Christian under Byzantine influence. In 1219 Saint Sava won the Serbian church its independence.
notes.RUS: Ivan III of Moscow married the last emperor's niece and took the double-headed eagle. Moscow came to be called the 'Third Rome'.
notes.UKR: Kyiv's conversion in 988 made it the cradle of Orthodox Christianity among the eastern Slavs.
notes.BLR: Belarus was part of Kyivan Rus when it became Orthodox, and Orthodoxy remains its main faith.
notes.ROU: Romanians are Latin-speaking but took Orthodoxy and, until the 1800s, the Cyrillic alphabet through their Slavic neighbours.
notes.TUR: Hagia Sophia became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020. Few Orthodox Christians remain in Turkey.
notes.GEO: Georgia became Christian in the 300s. It shared Byzantium's Orthodox faith, while keeping its own church and alphabet.

pn: The Ecumenical Patriarch, first among the Orthodox bishops, still has his seat in the city.
Home of the brothers Cyril and Methodius, who in 863 set out to teach the Slavs in their own language.
A community of Orthodox monasteries since the 900s, still self-governing and closed to women.
988: Prince Vladimir is baptised and his people follow, according to the Primary Chronicle in the waters of the Dnieper.

dd-vikings.text: Viking raids began with the sack of Lindisfarne in 793. Danes later settled the north and east of England, the Danelaw, and in 911 a Frankish king granted Normandy in [France](FRA) to the chief Rollo. Norwegians founded Dublin in [Ireland](IRL) and sailed on to [Iceland](ISL) and [Greenland](GRL), and around 1000 they reached Newfoundland in [Canada](CAN), five centuries before Columbus.

notes.NOR: Norwegians raided Scotland and Ireland and settled the Atlantic islands, Iceland and Greenland. Norway became one kingdom under Harald Fairhair and his successors in the late 800s and 900s.
notes.DNK: Danes led the great armies that raided the Frankish lands and conquered much of England. Danish king Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the 1020s.
notes.SWE: Most Swedish Vikings looked east, across the Baltic to the rivers of Russia, though some joined raids in the west.
notes.GBR: Danes conquered half of England after 865. The Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, about 886, left the north and east as the Danelaw. Norse also settled Orkney, Shetland and the Hebrides.
notes.IRL: Norse settlers founded Ireland's first towns, Dublin, Wexford, Waterford and Limerick, but never conquered the Irish kingdoms inland.
notes.FRA: Vikings sacked Paris in 845 and besieged it in 885–86. Normandy, the 'land of the Northmen', grew from the lands granted to Rollo in 911.
notes.ISL: Settlers arrived from about 870, many from Norway and the British Isles. In 930 they founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest assemblies.
notes.FRO: Norse farmers settled the Faroe Islands in the 800s, and their language became today's Faroese.
notes.GRL: Norse colonists farmed the south-west coast of Greenland from about 985. The settlements died out in the 1400s.
notes.CAN: Leif Erikson's voyages reached a land the sagas called Vinland. The base at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, was used only briefly.
notes.IMN: Norse rulers held the Isle of Man for centuries, and its parliament, Tynwald, has a Norse name.

pn: 8 June 793: raiders sack the island monastery, the attack that shocked Christian Europe and opened the Viking Age.
866: the Danish Great Army takes York, which as Jórvík became the Viking capital of northern England.
841: Norse raiders build a fortified base here, which grew into a trading town and Ireland's capital.
911: King Charles the Simple grants Rouen and the lower Seine to Rollo, founding Normandy.
c. 985: Erik the Red founds his farm here, leading the first Norse settlers to Greenland.
c. 1000: the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland. Tree rings show wood was cut there in 1021.

dd-vikings.text: Swedish Vikings, called the Rus, rowed and dragged their boats along the rivers of eastern Europe. On the Dnieper they reached Kyiv and the Black Sea, then Constantinople, the 'great city' they called Miklagard. On the Volga they traded furs and slaves for Arab silver. Their leaders founded Kyivan Rus, a state spanning today's [Ukraine](UKR), [Belarus](BLR) and western [Russia](RUS).

notes.SWE: Tens of thousands of Arab silver coins have been found on the Swedish island of Gotland alone, brought back by trade along the eastern rivers.
notes.RUS: Rus traders founded or joined towns such as Staraya Ladoga and Novgorod. The name Rus, which gave Russia its name, probably came from a word for 'rowers'.
notes.UKR: Kyiv became the Rus capital around 882. The state's princes made treaties with the Byzantine Empire in 911 and 944.
notes.BLR: Polotsk, in today's Belarus, was one of the oldest towns of the Rus, ruled by its own princes.
notes.TUR: Constantinople was the richest city the Rus knew. They raided it and traded with it, and from 988 Norsemen served in the emperor's Varangian Guard.
notes.IRQ: Silver from the Abbasid Caliphate, centred on Baghdad, drew Rus traders down the Volga to the Caspian Sea and caravan routes south.

pn: c. 750: a trading post with Scandinavian settlers, the gateway from the Baltic to the rivers of Russia.
According to the Primary Chronicle, written around 1113, the Varangian Rurik began to rule here in 862.
988: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kyiv is baptised and makes Orthodox Christianity the faith of the Rus.
860: the Rus raid the city's suburbs. Later, Norsemen served the emperors in the Varangian Guard.
921–22: the Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan meets Rus traders on the Volga and describes a ship burial.

dd-russia.text: According to the Primary Chronicle, a Scandinavian named Rurik began to rule at Novgorod in 862, and his successors made Kyiv their capital. Their state, Rus', grew along the river route from the Baltic to the [Byzantine Empire](TUR). In 988 Prince Volodymyr (Vladimir) was baptised, bringing Orthodox Christianity from Constantinople. Today's [Ukraine](UKR), [Belarus](BLR) and [Russia](RUS) all trace their history to this state.

notes.UKR: Kyiv was the capital of Rus' and its greatest city. Ukrainians see Rus' as the foundation of their own history.
notes.BLR: The principalities of Polotsk and Turov, in today's Belarus, were part of Rus'. Belarusians also count it as part of their history.
notes.RUS: Novgorod, Smolensk, Rostov and Vladimir were Rus' towns. Russian historians long treated Rus' as the first Russian state, and Moscow was first mentioned in 1147.
notes.SWE: Scandinavian traders, called Varangians, travelled the rivers to trade furs and slaves for silver; they merged into the local Slavic population within a few generations.
notes.TUR: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, was the great prize of the trade route. A treaty of 911 set rules for Rus' merchants there.
notes.GRC: Greek clergy, icon painters and architects brought Byzantine religion and art to Rus'; its first metropolitans of Kyiv were mostly Greeks.
notes.BGR: Church books reached Rus' in Old Church Slavonic, written in the Cyrillic script that grew up in Bulgaria around 900.

pn: From 882, according to the chronicle, the capital of Rus'. Yaroslav the Wise built its Saint Sophia Cathedral in the 1000s.
862, according to the chronicle: Rurik is invited to rule here. Later a rich trading republic.
The Byzantine capital, which Rus' traders visited and Rus' fleets attacked several times between 860 and 1043.
988: by most accounts Volodymyr was baptised here, in Byzantine Crimea, before marrying the emperor's sister.

dd-russia.text: Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240, and for two centuries the Rus' principalities paid tribute to the Golden Horde. Moscow rose by collecting that tribute. Ivan III ended Mongol overlordship in 1480, and Ivan IV, the Terrible, crowned himself tsar in 1547 and took Kazan and Astrakhan. Cossacks then pushed into Siberia. To the west, [Poland-Lithuania](POL) ruled much of today's [Ukraine](UKR) and [Belarus](BLR), and [Sweden](SWE) contested the Baltic coast.

notes.RUS: Russia doubled in size in the 1500s, taking the Volga khanates and western Siberia. The Time of Troubles followed in 1598–1613, ending with the first Romanov tsar.
notes.POL: Poland-Lithuania was the stronger power around 1600, though western Poland's Silesia and Pomerania lay outside it; its forces even occupied Moscow in 1610–12.
notes.LTU: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania had absorbed most of the old Rus' lands in the west during the 1300s, including Kyiv.
notes.BLR: Belarus was part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania for about four centuries, until the partitions of Poland in 1772–95.
notes.UKR: Most of Ukraine was ruled by Poland-Lithuania; the south was held by the Crimean Khanate, a vassal of the Ottomans. Ukrainian Cossacks lived on the frontier between them.
notes.SWE: Sweden, which then lacked its far south, still Danish, fought Russia for the Baltic coast. In 1617 it shut Russia out of the Baltic until Peter the Great's victory in the Great Northern War, 1700–21.
notes.EST: Northern Estonia came under Swedish rule in 1561, after Ivan IV's Livonian War broke up the old Livonian Order.

pn: 1300s–1400s: Moscow's princes rose as tax collectors for the Golden Horde; the Orthodox metropolitan moved here in 1325.
1478: Ivan III annexed the republic of Novgorod and its vast northern lands.
1480: Moscow's and the Horde's armies faced each other here, and the Horde withdrew, ending its overlordship.
1552: Ivan IV's army stormed the capital of the Kazan Khanate, opening the Volga to Russia.
1582: the Cossack leader Yermak took the capital of the Khanate of Sibir, starting Russia's conquest of Siberia.

dd-russia.text: Peter the Great named Russia an empire in 1721 and moved the capital to St Petersburg. Catherine the Great took Crimea and much of [Ukraine](UKR) and [Poland](POL). In the 1800s Russia added [Finland](FIN), the Caucasus and Central Asia, such as [Kazakhstan](KAZ). By 1914 it covered about 22 million km², a sixth of the world's land, with over 160 million people. Fewer than half spoke Russian as their first language.

notes.RUS: The empire held nearly all of today's Russia, except Kaliningrad, then German, and southern Sakhalin and the Kurils, then Japanese. The 1897 census counted about 44% of its people as native Russian speakers.
notes.UKR: Most of Ukraine was Russian; Galicia and Bukovina in the west belonged to Austria-Hungary. Tsarist officials restricted publishing in Ukrainian from 1863 to 1905.
notes.POL: Central Poland, around Warsaw, was taken in the partitions of 1772–95 and the 1815 settlement. Poles rose against Russian rule in 1830 and 1863.
notes.FIN: Finland was taken from Sweden in 1809 and kept its own parliament and laws; it declared independence in December 1917.
notes.KAZ: The Kazakh steppe came under Russian rule step by step in the 1700s and 1800s, and settlers from European Russia moved onto its farmland.
notes.UZB: Russia conquered Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868; the emirate of Bukhara and khanate of Khiva survived as protectorates.
notes.GEO: Eastern Georgia was annexed in 1801, the west over the following decades. The wider Caucasus took until 1864 to conquer; hundreds of thousands of Circassians, in today's southern Russia, were killed or expelled to the Ottoman Empire.
notes.TUR: The Kars and Ardahan region in north-east Turkey was Russian from 1878 to 1918.
notes.FRA: France was Russia's ally from 1894, and French loans helped pay for Russia's railways and industry.
notes.USA: Alaska was Russian territory until its sale to the United States in 1867.

pn: Founded by Peter the Great in 1703 and capital from 1712. Revolution broke out here in March 1917.
Founded in 1860 on land taken from China, its name means 'ruler of the East'.
Leased from China in 1898 and lost to Japan in 1905, a defeat that helped spark revolution at home.
Capital of Russian America; Russia sold Alaska to the United States for $7.2 million in 1867.
July 1918: the Bolsheviks shot the former tsar Nicholas II and his family here.

dd-mongols.text: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin turned the united tribes of [Mongolia](MNG) on their neighbours. He forced the Western Xia to submit, took the Jin capital, today's Beijing, in 1215, and seized Kara Khitai, in [Kyrgyzstan](KGZ). When the Khwarazmian Empire killed his envoys and merchants in 1218, he destroyed it, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand in [Uzbekistan](UZB). Two of his generals rode on round the Caspian into Russia and back.

notes.MNG: Temüjin, born around 1162, rose from poverty after his father was poisoned. By 1206 he had defeated or absorbed every rival tribe on the Mongolian plateau.
notes.CHN: The Western Xia submitted in 1210 and were wiped out in 1227. The Jin lost Beijing in 1215 and fell in 1234, after Genghis Khan's death.
notes.KGZ: Kara Khitai, a state founded by Khitans fleeing China, was seized by the Naiman prince Kuchlug. Jebe took it in 1218, welcomed by Muslims Kuchlug had persecuted.
notes.KAZ: Otrar, on the Syr Darya in southern Kazakhstan, was a Khwarazmian frontier city. The killing of the Mongol caravan there in 1218 began the war.
notes.UZB: Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench, the great cities of Transoxiana and Khwarazm, fell in 1220–21. Many of their craftsmen were deported to Mongolia.
notes.TKM: Merv fell in 1221. Persian chroniclers claimed over a million people were killed there, a figure historians think exaggerated, but the city never fully recovered.
notes.IRN: The Mongols chased the Khwarazmian shah across Iran, where he died on an island in the Caspian, and sacked Nishapur in 1221.
notes.AFG: Genghis Khan's armies destroyed Balkh, Herat and Bamiyan in 1221 while pursuing the shah's son Jalal al-Din to the Indus.
notes.RUS: Jebe and Subutai's raid reached the steppes of southern Russia and Ukraine in 1223, a first look at lands the Mongols conquered 14 years later.

pn: 1206: a great assembly, or kurultai, on the Onon proclaims Temüjin 'Chinggis Khan', ruler of all the felt-tent peoples.
1215: the Jin capital falls after a long siege and is sacked; the Jin court had already fled south.
1218: the governor kills a Mongol trade caravan of about 450 men. Genghis Khan's revenge destroys the Khwarazmian Empire.
1220: the city surrenders and is plundered and burned, and its people are driven out or killed.
1223: Jebe and Subutai crush an army of Rus princes and Cumans, then ride back east.
1227: Genghis Khan dies during the final campaign against the Western Xia, whose capital, today's Yinchuan, is then destroyed.

dd-mongols.text: In 1236 Batu, Genghis Khan's grandson, and the veteran general Subutai led a great army west. They crushed Volga Bulgaria and the principalities of [Russia](RUS), took Kyiv in [Ukraine](UKR) in 1240, and in April 1241 won two battles in two days, in [Poland](POL) and [Hungary](HUN). In 1242 they suddenly withdrew east. Batu settled on the Volga, and his Golden Horde ruled the Rus princes for over two centuries.

notes.RUS: The Mongols took Ryazan, Vladimir and over a dozen other towns in 1237–38. Novgorod was spared by the spring thaw but paid tribute. Rus princes served the Golden Horde until 1480.
notes.UKR: Kyiv fell in December 1240, and Galicia-Volhynia in the west was devastated and became tributary. The southern steppe became Golden Horde pasture.
notes.MDA: The lands between the Prut and the Dniester, on the western edge of the Cuman steppe, came under the Golden Horde.
notes.POL: Kraków was burned in March 1241, and on 9 April a Polish and German army was beaten at Legnica. The Mongols then turned south to join Batu.
notes.HUN: Hungary suffered worst: after Mohi the Mongols ravaged the country for a year. Estimates of its losses vary widely, often put at 15–25% of the population.
notes.SVK: Upper Hungary, today's Slovakia, was plundered in 1241, though some stone castles held out, a lesson Hungary's king took to heart.
notes.CZE: Part of the northern force rode through Moravia in 1241 on its way to join Batu in Hungary.
notes.HRV: King Béla IV fled to the Dalmatian coast, and a Mongol detachment chased him as far as Trogir in 1242.
notes.BGR: The Mongols withdrew through the Balkans in 1242, and Bulgaria agreed to pay tribute.
notes.AUT: Mongol raiders entered eastern Austria in 1241 and again that winter. One chronicle tells of an attack near Wiener Neustadt, south of Vienna, though the raiders may have been Cumans.

pn: December 1237: the first Rus city to fall, after a siege of about a week; its people were massacred.
February 1238: the capital of the strongest Rus principality is stormed and burned.
December 1240: the old capital of Rus falls after a siege; a papal envoy passing in 1246 saw only about 200 houses left.
9 April 1241: a Mongol force defeats Duke Henry II of Silesia, who is killed in the battle.
11 April 1241: Batu and Subutai destroy the army of King Béla IV of Hungary by the Sajó River.
From the 1240s: Batu's capital on the lower Volga, where Rus princes came to receive their patents to rule.

dd-mongols.text: Mongol armies were not invincible. Egypt's Mamluks beat them at Ain Jalut in 1260 and held [Syria](SYR) and [Egypt](EGY). Kublai Khan's invasions of [Japan](JPN) failed in 1274 and 1281, his invasions of Đại Việt, in northern [Vietnam](VNM), failed three times, and a fleet sent to Java, in [Indonesia](IDN), was driven out in 1293. The Delhi Sultanate in [India](IND) beat back repeated Mongol raids.

notes.EGY: The Mamluks, former slave soldiers mostly from the Cuman steppe, seized power in Egypt in 1250. They fought the Ilkhanate for 60 years and never lost Egypt.
notes.SYR: The Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus in 1260, lost Syria after Ain Jalut, and invaded again in 1281, 1299 and 1303 without holding it.
notes.ISR: Ain Jalut, in the Jezreel Valley, was fought in 1260 after Hülegü had taken most of his army east on news of the Great Khan's death.
notes.JPN: Japan's Kamakura shogunate refused Kublai's demands for submission. The storms credited with wrecking his fleets were later called kamikaze, 'divine winds'.
notes.VNM: Đại Việt was invaded in 1258, 1285 and 1287–88. Each time the Trần court left its capital, waged a war of attrition and struck back.
notes.IDN: Kublai sent a fleet to punish King Kertanegara for insulting his envoy, but Kertanegara was already dead. Majapahit, founded in the turmoil, became Java's great empire.
notes.IND: The Delhi Sultanate fought off Mongol invasions from the 1240s to the 1300s, and its victories at Kili in 1299 and Amroha in 1305 ended the threat.
notes.KOR: Korea's Goryeo kingdom, a Mongol vassal, was made to build ships and supply troops for both invasions of Japan.

pn: 3 September 1260: the Mamluks under Qutuz and Baybars defeat a Mongol army, a defeat the Mongols never avenged.
1274 and 1281: Mongol and Korean forces land, but samurai hold them, behind a new sea wall in 1281. A typhoon wrecks the 1281 fleet; whether a storm struck in 1274 is debated.
1288: Trần Hưng Đạo traps a Mongol fleet on iron-tipped stakes planted in the riverbed and destroys it at low tide.
1293: the Javanese prince Raden Wijaya uses the Mongols to beat his rival, then drives them out and founds Majapahit.
1299 and 1303: Chagatai Mongol armies reach the city, but Sultan Alauddin Khalji holds it and defeats later invasions.

dd-habsburgs.text: The Habsburgs took their name from a castle in [Switzerland](CHE) and won [Austria](AUT) in 1278. Then came a run of lucky marriages: Burgundy's Netherlands in 1477, [Spain](ESP) and its empire through Charles V, king from 1516, and [Bohemia](CZE) and part of [Hungary](HUN) in 1526. By 1550 Charles ruled Spain, the Netherlands, much of Italy and the Americas, while his brother Ferdinand ruled the Austrian lands.

notes.CHE: The family's first lands were in today's Switzerland, but the Swiss Confederation fought them off in the 1300s and took the Aargau, home of Habsburg Castle, in 1415.
notes.AUT: Rudolf I, elected King of the Germans in 1273, took Austria from Bohemia's king in 1278. The family ruled Austria for the next 640 years.
notes.NLD: Maximilian I married Mary, heiress of Burgundy, in 1477. Their grandson Charles V united all 17 provinces of the Netherlands by 1543.
notes.BEL: Brussels was the capital of the Burgundian Netherlands, then the richest region of northern Europe. Charles V grew up nearby, in Mechelen.
notes.FRA: France seized the duchy of Burgundy itself when Mary's father died in 1477, but the Habsburgs won back Franche-Comté and Artois in 1493.
notes.ESP: Philip the Handsome, Maximilian's son, married Joanna of Castile, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, in 1496. Deaths in the family made their son Charles heir to all Spain and its American empire.
notes.ITA: Through Aragon the Habsburgs held Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, and Charles V took Milan in 1535. Imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527.
notes.CZE: Ferdinand, Charles V's brother, had married Anna, sister of the Hungarian and Bohemian king. When the king died at Mohács in 1526, Bohemia's estates elected Ferdinand.
notes.HUN: Ferdinand claimed Hungary in 1526 but held only a strip in the west and north, Royal Hungary. The Ottomans took Buda in 1541 and ruled the centre for 150 years.
notes.SVK: Most of today's Slovakia was in Royal Hungary, and Pressburg, today's Bratislava, served as Hungary's capital while Buda was Ottoman.
notes.HRV: In 1527 Croatia's nobles chose Ferdinand as king. The Habsburgs built the Military Frontier there against the Ottomans.
notes.POL: Silesia, now mostly in Poland, belonged to the Bohemian crown and so passed to the Habsburgs in 1526.
notes.DEU: Charles V was also Holy Roman Emperor, elected in 1519, with authority over the German princes. He failed to stop the Protestant Reformation there.

pn: Built around 1020 in today's Swiss canton of Aargau, the 'Hawk's Castle' gave the family its name.
26 August 1278: Rudolf I defeats King Ottokar II of Bohemia here and wins Austria for his family.
1500: birthplace of Charles V, heir to four grandparents' lands: Austria, Burgundy, Castile and Aragon.
29 August 1526: the Ottomans crush Hungary's army and King Louis II dies, leaving his thrones to his brother-in-law Ferdinand.
1529: the Ottoman sultan Suleiman besieges Vienna but fails to take it.
1557: worn out, Charles V retires to this Spanish monastery after giving up his crowns. He died here in 1558.

dd-habsburgs.text: Charles V split his lands in 1556: [Spain](ESP) went to his son Philip, Austria to Ferdinand. The Spanish line died out in 1700, and after a long war a French Bourbon kept Spain, while Austria took [Belgium](BEL) and Spain's Italian lands. Meanwhile, after the Ottomans' failed siege of Vienna in 1683, Habsburg armies retook all of [Hungary](HUN) and pushed into [Serbia](SRB) and [Romania](ROU). The monarchy now centred on the Danube.

notes.ESP: Charles II's death set off the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–14). His heir Philip V, Louis XIV's grandson, kept Spain and its empire but gave up its European lands.
notes.AUT: Vienna rebuilt in Baroque splendour after 1683. Emperor Charles VI's Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 let a daughter inherit, and Maria Theresa took the throne in 1740.
notes.CZE: After Bohemia's Protestant nobles revolted and lost at the White Mountain in 1620, the Habsburgs ruled it as a Catholic hereditary land.
notes.POL: Silesia, rich and mostly German-speaking, was Habsburg until Prussia seized it in 1740–42, a loss Maria Theresa never accepted.
notes.HUN: The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 gave the Habsburgs almost all of Hungary and Transylvania. A Hungarian revolt led by Ferenc Rákóczi II was put down in 1711.
notes.SRB: The Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 gave Austria Belgrade and northern Serbia, but it lost them to the Ottomans in 1739.
notes.ROU: Transylvania became Habsburg in 1699 and the Banat in 1718. Oltenia, in the south, was held only until the late 1730s.
notes.HRV: Croatia's Slavonia was won back from the Ottomans in 1699, but Dalmatia was still Venetian. The Military Frontier, settled by Serbs and Croats, guarded the border.
notes.BEL: The Spanish Netherlands became the Austrian Netherlands in 1714 and stayed so until French revolutionary armies took them in the 1790s.
notes.ITA: Austria gained Milan, Naples and Sardinia in 1714, then swapped Sardinia for Sicily in 1720. It lost Naples and Sicily to a Spanish Bourbon prince in 1735.

pn: 12 September 1683: a relief army under Poland's King John III Sobieski breaks the Ottoman siege of Vienna.
11 September 1697: Prince Eugene of Savoy routs the Ottoman army, leading to the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.
August 1717: Prince Eugene takes Belgrade. Austria held it until 1739.
1 November 1700: Charles II, last Spanish Habsburg, dies childless, naming a French Bourbon prince as his heir.

dd-habsburgs.text: After defeat by Prussia in 1866, Emperor Franz Joseph made a deal with Hungary in 1867: two states under one monarch, sharing only foreign policy, the army and the budget for them. [Austria](AUT) ruled the west and north, from [Czechia](CZE) to Galicia in [Poland](POL); [Hungary](HUN) ruled the east, including [Croatia](HRV). [Bosnia](BIH), taken from the Ottomans, belonged to both. Its 51 million people spoke about a dozen main languages.

notes.AUT: German-speaking Austrians were about a quarter of the whole empire's people, the largest single group but far from a majority. Franz Joseph reigned for 68 years, from 1848 to 1916.
notes.HUN: The 1867 Compromise gave Hungary its own parliament and government. Hungarian speakers were about half its people, and its leaders pressed others to adopt Hungarian.
notes.CZE: Bohemia and Moravia were the empire's industrial heartland. Czechs and Germans fought bitterly over language in schools and offices.
notes.POL: Galicia, Austria's share of partitioned Poland, gained wide self-rule in the 1860s. Kraków became a centre of Polish culture and politics.
notes.UKR: Eastern Galicia, around Lviv, and northern Bukovina were Austrian. Ukrainians there could organise politically, unlike those in the Russian Empire.
notes.HRV: Croatia-Slavonia had home rule under Hungary, while Dalmatia and Istria, on the coast, were governed by Austria.
notes.SVK: Slovakia was 'Upper Hungary', ruled from Budapest, where Slovak schools were squeezed in favour of Hungarian.
notes.ROU: Transylvania, with its Romanian majority, was part of Hungary. Bukovina, now split between Romania and Ukraine, was Austrian.
notes.SRB: Vojvodina, in today's northern Serbia, was a Hungarian region with Serbs, Hungarians, Germans and others.
notes.BIH: Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908, enraging Serbia. The joint finance ministry ran it.
notes.ITA: Trentino and Trieste, with many Italian speakers, were Austrian. Italy joined the war against Austria-Hungary in 1915 to win them.
notes.MNE: Montenegro was an independent kingdom, but the Bay of Kotor and the coast around Budva belonged to Austria's province of Dalmatia.
notes.SVN: Slovene speakers lived in Carniola and neighbouring Austrian provinces, ruled from Vienna.

pn: By 1910 a capital of over 2 million people, home to Freud, Mahler and Klimt, and also to angry nationalist politics.
1873: Buda, Óbuda and Pest merge. Hungary built its grand Parliament here, finished in 1904.
3 July 1866: Prussia defeats Austria, pushing it out of German affairs and forcing the deal with Hungary.
Austria's great port on the Adriatic, mostly Italian-speaking, now in Italy.
28 June 1914: a Bosnian Serb nationalist shoots the heir, Franz Ferdinand, and the empire goes to war.

dd-ottomans.text: Osman's small state on the Byzantine frontier in north-west [Turkey](TUR) grew fast. His son Orhan took Bursa, and in 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe at Gallipoli. [Bulgaria](BGR), Macedonia and much of northern [Greece](GRC) fell by 1400. Timur crushed them at Ankara in 1402, but they recovered, and Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, then [Serbia](SRB), [Bosnia](BIH) and [Albania](ALB).

notes.TUR: Osman's emirate was one of many Turkish states in Anatolia. The Ottomans absorbed rivals such as Karaman by the 1470s, but the far east stayed outside until the 1500s.
notes.GRC: Thessaly fell in the 1390s, Thessaloniki in 1430 and the Peloponnese in 1460. Venice still held Crete and other islands.
notes.BGR: The Bulgarian capital, Tarnovo, fell in 1393, and the last Bulgarian state was gone by 1396.
notes.SRB: Serbia fought on after Kosovo as an Ottoman vassal, and its last fortress capital, Smederevo, fell in 1459. Belgrade, a Hungarian fortress, held out until 1521.
notes.BIH: Mehmed II conquered Bosnia in 1463 and executed its last king. Over time a large share of Bosnians became Muslim.
notes.ALB: Skanderbeg led an Albanian revolt and held off Ottoman armies for 25 years until his death in 1468. Shkodër fell in 1479.
notes.UNK: Kosovo, scene of the battle of 1389, was fully under Ottoman rule by 1455.
notes.ROU: Wallachia paid tribute from the 1390s but fought back at times, notably under Vlad III, known as Dracula, in 1461–62.
notes.UKR: In 1475 the Ottomans took Genoese Kaffa in Crimea, and the Crimean Khanate became their vassal.

pn: c. 1300: Osman, a Turkish chief, ruled a small emirate around this town on the edge of Byzantine Bithynia.
1326: Orhan took the city after a long blockade and made it his capital; early sultans are buried here.
1354: after an earthquake shattered its walls, Ottoman troops occupied the town, their first firm foothold in Europe.
1389: Ottoman and Serbian-led armies fought on the Field of Blackbirds; both Sultan Murad I and Prince Lazar were killed.
1402: the Central Asian conqueror Timur defeated and captured Bayezid I, plunging the state into a decade of civil war.
29 May 1453: after a 53-day siege with giant cannon, Mehmed II took the city and made it his capital.
