dd-ottomans.text: Selim I beat Safavid Persia at Chaldiran in 1514, then conquered the Mamluk sultanate in 1516–17, taking [Syria](SYR), [Egypt](EGY) and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. His son Suleiman, 'the Magnificent' to Europeans and 'the Lawgiver' to Ottomans, took Belgrade, most of [Hungary](HUN) and Baghdad in [Iraq](IRQ). His navy under Hayreddin Barbarossa dominated the Mediterranean, and North African ports such as Algiers, in [Algeria](DZA), accepted Ottoman rule.

notes.EGY: Egypt was the richest province, sending grain and gold to Istanbul. Its conquest made the sultan protector of Mecca and Medina.
notes.SYR: Selim took Syria in 1516. Damascus became the gathering point for the great annual pilgrim caravan to Mecca.
notes.SAU: The Sharif of Mecca accepted Ottoman rule in 1517, and sultans took the title 'Servant of the Two Holy Sanctuaries'.
notes.HUN: After Mohács in 1526 Hungary fell apart. Suleiman annexed its centre, with Buda, in 1541, while the Habsburgs held the west and north.
notes.IRQ: Suleiman took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534 and Basra in 1546, gaining the shrines of Shia Islam and access to the Persian Gulf.
notes.DZA: The corsair Hayreddin Barbarossa placed Algiers under the sultan around 1519 in return for troops; in 1533 he became admiral of the Ottoman fleet.
notes.LBY: An Ottoman fleet took Tripoli from the Knights of St John in 1551.
notes.YEM: The Ottomans took Aden in 1538 and much of Yemen in the following decades, to block Portuguese ships in the Red Sea.
notes.ROU: Wallachia and Moldavia kept Christian princes under Ottoman overlordship, and Transylvania became a vassal principality after 1541.
notes.AUT: Suleiman besieged Vienna in 1529 but withdrew after less than three weeks, beaten by distance, rain and the approach of winter.

pn: 1514: Selim's guns and Janissaries routed the cavalry of Shah Ismail of Persia, winning eastern Anatolia.
1516: Selim defeated the Mamluk army north of Aleppo; the Mamluk sultan died on the field.
1517: Selim took the Mamluk capital and hanged the last Mamluk sultan at one of its gates.
1538: Barbarossa's fleet beat a Christian alliance led by Venice, Spain and the Pope, securing Ottoman sea power.
1565: a great Ottoman siege of the Knights of St John failed after nearly four months.
1566: Suleiman died in his tent during the siege of this Hungarian fortress, aged about 71.

dd-ottomans.text: In the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 the empire lost almost all its European land, including [Albania](ALB) and Macedonia. In World War I it fought for Germany, deported and killed Armenians in Anatolia, and lost its Arab lands from [Iraq](IRQ) to [Syria](SYR). The 1920 Treaty of Sèvres planned to carve up Anatolia too, but Mustafa Kemal's nationalists fought on, and in 1923 founded the Republic of [Turkey](TUR).

notes.ALB: Albania declared independence in November 1912, as Serbian, Montenegrin and Greek armies overran the Ottoman Balkans.
notes.MKD: Ottoman Macedonia was conquered in 1912 and divided between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria in 1913.
notes.GRC: Greece gained Thessaloniki, Epirus and Crete in 1912–13. Under the 1923 exchange about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece, and about 400,000 Muslims left Greece.
notes.TUR: Kemal's nationalists drove out Greek, French and Armenian forces in 1919–22. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne recognised the republic, declared on 29 October; the caliphate was abolished in 1924.
notes.ARM: In 1915–16 the Ottoman government deported and massacred its Armenian subjects; estimates of the dead range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million. The great majority of historians call it genocide; Turkey rejects the term.
notes.SYR: British and Arab forces took Damascus in October 1918. France then ruled Syria and Lebanon as League of Nations mandates.
notes.IRQ: British troops took Baghdad in 1917 and Mosul after the armistice. Britain ruled Iraq as a mandate.
notes.SAU: Sharif Hussein of Mecca launched the Arab Revolt in 1916 with British support, promised an Arab state that never came as planned.
notes.ISR: British forces took Jerusalem in December 1917, ending 400 years of Ottoman rule in Palestine.
notes.PSE: British forces took Jerusalem in December 1917, ending 400 years of Ottoman rule in Palestine.

pn: 1915–16: endpoint of death marches for deported Armenians; many tens of thousands died in camps and massacres in the desert nearby.
1915: Ottoman forces, with Mustafa Kemal among their commanders, threw back the Allied landings.
January 1919: the Ottoman garrison, besieged since the Arab Revolt of 1916, finally surrendered.
April 1920: the nationalists' Grand National Assembly first met here. Ankara became the republic's capital in 1923.
September 1922: Turkish forces retook the city, ending the Greek army's invasion; a great fire destroyed its Greek and Armenian quarters.
November 1922: the sultanate was abolished, and the last sultan, Mehmed VI, left on a British warship.

dd-aztecinca.text: In 1428 the Mexica of Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan, and this Triple Alliance came to rule much of central and southern [Mexico](MEX), taking tribute from 38 provinces. Some neighbours, such as Tlaxcala and the Purépecha, were never conquered. In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast with about 600 Spaniards, gathered thousands of Tlaxcalan and other native allies, and marched inland to the island capital.

notes.MEX: Aztec rule covered much of central and southern Mexico, from the Gulf coast to the Pacific, but not the north, the Purépecha west or the Maya Yucatán. Mexico City now stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan.
notes.GTM: Highland Maya kingdoms such as the K'iche' and Kaqchikel were independent of the Aztecs. Pedro de Alvarado conquered much of the highlands from 1524.
notes.BLZ: Belize was Maya country beyond Aztec rule. The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén in nearby Guatemala, fell to Spain only in 1697.
notes.ESP: Spain's conquerors were private adventurers licensed by the crown, hoping for gold and land. Cortés acted against the orders of Cuba's governor.

pn: Founded about 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco; by 1519 perhaps 200,000 people lived there. It fell on 13 August 1521.
1519: after fighting the Spaniards, this independent state became their key ally against its old Aztec enemies.
October 1519: Cortés's force and its Tlaxcalan allies killed thousands of people in the city's great plaza.
Capital of the Purépecha (Tarascan) state, which crushed an Aztec invasion in 1479 and stayed independent.
1519: Cortés founded the town of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz near here and scuttled his ships.

dd-aztecinca.text: From Cusco in [Peru](PER), the Inca ruler Pachacuti began a rapid expansion from about 1438. Within a century the empire, Tawantinsuyu or 'the four parts together', ran some 4,000 km along the Andes, from southern [Colombia](COL) to central [Chile](CHL), ruling perhaps 10 million people. A road network tied it together. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and 168 Spaniards captured the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca.

notes.PER: Peru was the empire's heart, from Cusco to the coast. Spain made Lima, founded by Pizarro in 1535, the capital of its South American empire.
notes.ECU: The Incas conquered Ecuador's highlands and coast only in the late 1400s. Huayna Capac died there around 1527, probably of an epidemic, setting off a civil war.
notes.BOL: Western Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca, was a sacred Inca land. After the conquest Spain's silver mine at Potosí, opened in 1545, used forced Indigenous labour.
notes.CHL: Inca rule reached south to about the Maule River, beyond today's Santiago. The Mapuche further south were never conquered.
notes.ARG: North-western Argentina, including Jujuy, Salta and Mendoza, was a southern frontier of the empire, rich in metals.
notes.COL: Only the far south-west of Colombia, near Pasto, came under Inca rule shortly before the Spanish arrived.

pn: The Inca capital, rebuilt by Pachacuti in fitted stone. Spaniards entered it in November 1533.
c. 1450: a royal estate built for Pachacuti, missed by the conquerors and made famous by Hiram Bingham in 1911.
16 November 1532: Pizarro seized Atahualpa here; after a huge ransom of gold and silver was paid, he was executed in 1533.
A major northern centre, conquered in the late 1400s and later the base of Atahualpa's army in the civil war.
1539–1572: refuge of the last independent Inca rulers. Its fall and the execution of Túpac Amaru in 1572 ended Inca rule.

dd-spanish.text: In a century [Spain](ESP) went from finishing the conquest of Granada to ruling the first empire that spanned the globe. Conquistadors took [Mexico](MEX) and [Peru](PER), Manila made the [Philippines](PHL) its Asian outpost, and Habsburg inheritance added Italian lands and the Netherlands. In 1580 Philip II also became king of [Portugal](PRT) and its empire. But the northern Dutch provinces, in today's [Netherlands](NLD), were in open revolt.

notes.ESP: Castile ran the American empire, through the Council of the Indies, while Aragon looked to the Mediterranean. From 1561 the court was based in Madrid.
notes.MEX: New Spain, conquered from 1519, was ruled by a viceroy in Mexico City. Its silver mines at Zacatecas made it rich, but much of the arid north was still beyond Spanish control.
notes.PER: The Viceroyalty of Peru, ruled from Lima, governed almost all of Spanish South America. Its rulers turned Inca roads and labour systems to Spanish use.
notes.PHL: Spain conquered the islands from 1565 and named them after Philip II. The Muslim sultanates of Mindanao and Sulu in the south kept their independence.
notes.PRT: When Portugal's king died without an heir in 1580, his nephew Philip II claimed the throne. Portugal kept its own laws and empire, and broke away again in 1640.
notes.NLD: The Dutch revolt began in 1568 over taxes and the persecution of Protestants. The northern provinces renounced Philip in 1581, and Spain recognised their independence in 1648.
notes.BEL: The southern Netherlands, today's Belgium and Luxembourg, stayed under Spain and Catholic. Antwerp, sacked by unpaid Spanish troops in 1576, later lost much of its trade to Amsterdam.
notes.ITA: Spain ruled Milan, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, about half of Italy. Spanish viceroys governed Naples, then one of Europe's biggest cities.
notes.FRA: Franche-Comté, Artois and Roussillon, now French, were Spanish lands. France took them between 1659 and 1678.
notes.USA: Spain founded St Augustine in Florida in 1565, the oldest continuously settled European city in the US, and began colonising New Mexico in 1598.
notes.CHL: Spain ruled central Chile, but in 1598 a Mapuche uprising began that destroyed the Spanish towns south of the Biobío River.
notes.BRA: Brazil was Portuguese, so it came under Philip's crown in 1580. The Dutch, at war with Spain, attacked and for a time held its sugar-growing north-east.
notes.HTI: All of Hispaniola was Spanish. The western third, today's Haiti, was later settled by French buccaneers and ceded to France in 1697.
notes.JAM: Jamaica was Spanish until England captured it in 1655.

pn: 2 January 1492: the last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrenders to Ferdinand and Isabella, months before Columbus sails.
1521: Cortés and his Indigenous allies take Tenochtitlan. Mexico City, built on its ruins, became the capital of New Spain.
16 November 1532: Pizarro's small force seizes the Inca emperor Atahualpa, who is executed the next year.
1571: Miguel López de Legazpi makes Manila the capital of the Spanish Philippines.
1563–84: Philip II builds this palace-monastery near Madrid, from which he ran his empire on paper.
1580: Spanish troops take Lisbon, and Philip II is accepted as king of Portugal the next year.

dd-spanish.text: Silver from Potosí, in [Bolivia](BOL), and from the mines of [Mexico](MEX) became the empire's lifeblood. Twice a year armed fleets carried it from the Caribbean to Seville in [Spain](ESP), and from 1565 the Manila galleons carried more across the Pacific to the [Philippines](PHL), to buy silk and porcelain from [China](CHN). By some estimates Spanish America produced about 80% of the world's silver between the 1500s and 1800.

notes.BOL: Potosí's silver was mined by Indigenous workers drafted under the mita, a forced labour system adapted from the Incas. Many died from accidents and mercury poisoning.
notes.MEX: Mexico's mines, at Zacatecas and later Guanajuato, overtook Potosí in the 1700s. Silver was refined with mercury, by a process introduced in New Spain in the 1550s.
notes.ESP: The Crown took a fifth of all silver as tax and used it to fight wars across Europe. Even so Philip II defaulted on his debts four times, and much of the silver flowed on to bankers in Genoa and Antwerp.
notes.PHL: Manila lived off the galleon trade. Each year one or two great ships sailed to Acapulco with Chinese goods and returned with silver.
notes.CHN: Ming China had moved to collecting taxes in silver and needed far more than it mined. Historians estimate that much of the world's silver in this era ended up in China.
notes.PER: Silver went down from Potosí by mule and llama to the Pacific, then by ship to Lima's port of Callao and on to Panama.
notes.PAN: Silver was carried across the isthmus by mule train and river to Portobelo, where great trade fairs met the fleet from Spain.
notes.COL: Cartagena was the fortified port where the Tierra Firme fleet loaded silver and gold. It was also a main port of the slave trade.
notes.CUB: Havana grew into the Caribbean's most heavily defended port because the treasure fleets gathered there.

pn: 1545: silver is found in the Cerro Rico, the 'rich hill'. By about 1600 Potosí was one of the largest cities in the Americas.
1546: silver strikes here start a mining boom in northern New Spain.
The fleets from Veracruz and from Portobelo and Cartagena gathered here before crossing the Atlantic together.
From 1503 the Casa de Contratación here controlled all trade with the Americas. The monopoly moved to Cádiz in 1717.
1565–1815: the Mexican end of the Manila galleon route, where Asian silks and spices were unloaded for American silver.
Chinese junks brought silk and porcelain to Manila to trade for silver, making it a hub of the first global trade network.

dd-spanish.text: The empire's deepest legacy is language and faith. Spanish is official and spoken by most people in [Spain](ESP) and 18 American countries plus [Puerto Rico](PRI), and the Instituto Cervantes counted about 519 million native speakers in 2025. [Mexico](MEX) has the most. The [United States](USA) has tens of millions of speakers, while in the [Philippines](PHL), ruled from Madrid for over 300 years, Spanish has almost vanished.

notes.ESP: Spanish, or Castilian, is spoken across Spain, alongside Catalan, Galician and Basque, which are co-official in their regions.
notes.MEX: Mexico has the largest number of Spanish speakers in the world, well over 100 million. Its government also recognises 68 Indigenous languages, such as Nahuatl and Maya.
notes.USA: Spain once held Florida, Texas and the Southwest, and many place names are Spanish. Most of today's speakers come from later migration from Latin America; the Instituto Cervantes counts over 40 million native speakers.
notes.PHL: Spanish was an official language until 1987, but only a small elite ever spoke it. Its legacy is in thousands of loanwords, Spanish surnames, a Spanish-based creole called Chavacano, and the country's Catholic majority.
notes.GNQ: Equatorial Guinea, a Spanish colony until 1968, is the only African country with Spanish as an official language, though most people speak Fang, Bubi and other African languages at home.
notes.PRY: Paraguay is officially bilingual. Most people speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language, and many speak both it and Spanish.
notes.BOL: Bolivia recognises Spanish and over 30 Indigenous languages, and millions speak Quechua or Aymara.
notes.PER: Spanish is the majority language, but Quechua, the Inca language, is spoken by millions, mostly in the Andes.
notes.PRI: Spain ceded Puerto Rico to the United States in 1898. Spanish remains its main language.
notes.CUB: Cuba was one of Spain's last American colonies, and became independent after the war of 1898.
notes.GUM: Spain ruled Guam from 1668 and ceded it to the US in 1898. The Chamorro language keeps many Spanish words.
notes.ARG: Argentina has about 47 million native Spanish speakers. Its Spanish, with Italian-influenced intonation, uses 'vos' instead of 'tú'.

pn: The Real Academia Española, founded here in 1713, works with academies in every Spanish-speaking country to keep one shared standard.

dd-mughals.text: Babur, born in 1483 in the Ferghana Valley of today's [Uzbekistan](UZB), ruled Kabul in [Afghanistan](AFG) before invading India. In 1526 his guns and cavalry beat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat. His son Humayun lost the throne and regained it in 1555 with help from [Persia](IRN). Babur's grandson Akbar, who reigned 1556–1605, conquered northern [India](IND), [Pakistan](PAK) and Bengal, and won over Hindu Rajput princes.

notes.UZB: Babur descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's. Driven out of Ferghana and Samarkand by the Uzbeks, he turned south.
notes.AFG: Kabul was Babur's base and stayed Mughal until 1738. Kandahar changed hands with Persia several times and was lost for good in 1649.
notes.IND: Akbar ruled northern and central India, from Gujarat to Bengal and south into the Deccan. Most of his subjects were Hindu.
notes.PAK: Lahore was one of the Mughal capitals, and Akbar added Kashmir in 1586 and Sindh in 1591.
notes.BGD: Akbar's armies took Bengal from its Afghan rulers in 1576, but local chiefs in the east resisted into the early 1600s.
notes.IRN: Shah Tahmasp of Persia sheltered the exiled Humayun and lent him troops to regain his throne. Persian was the language of the Mughal court.

pn: 21 April 1526: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi. Akbar's army won a second battle here in 1556.
1504: Babur took Kabul, his base for raids into India. He asked to be buried here, and his tomb stands in a garden.
1571–85: Akbar's new red sandstone capital, abandoned after about 15 years.
The main Mughal capital in the 1500s; Akbar rebuilt its great fort from 1565.

dd-mughals.text: Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, Mughal [India](IND) was one of the richest states on earth, with perhaps 150 million people. Its cotton and silk cloth sold from Japan to Europe, and Europeans paid in silver. Trading companies from [England](GBR) and the [Netherlands](NLD) set up posts on the coasts by the emperor's leave, joining the [Portuguese](PRT); [France](FRA) followed in the 1660s. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal and a new walled city at Delhi.

notes.IND: The empire drew most of its revenue from land tax on farmers, much of it assigned to ranked officers called mansabdars, whose rank set how many cavalry they had to keep.
notes.BGD: Bengal was the richest province, famous for fine muslin from Dhaka, which became the provincial capital in 1610. Chittagong, in the south-east, stayed under Arakan until 1666.
notes.PAK: Lahore, Multan and Thatta were major cities, and the Mughal road from Kabul through Lahore to Delhi and Agra carried trade and armies.
notes.AFG: The Mughals held Kabul, but lost Kandahar to Persia in 1649 and failed three times to win it back.
notes.IRN: Safavid Persia was the Mughals' main rival in the west and a model for their court culture, art and language.
notes.GBR: England's East India Company, founded in 1600, sent Sir Thomas Roe to Jahangir's court in 1615 to seek trading rights.
notes.NLD: The Dutch East India Company traded in Bengal and Gujarat, buying cloth to swap for spices in Indonesia.
notes.PRT: Portugal arrived first, in 1498, and held Goa and other coastal forts, but its power was waning by 1650.
notes.FRA: France had no posts in India yet. Its East India Company, founded in 1664, opened one at Surat in 1668 and later made Pondicherry its main base.

pn: c. 1632–1653: Shah Jahan's white marble tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631.
1648: Shah Jahan moved his court to his new city, Shahjahanabad, with its Red Fort.
The empire's chief port and the gateway for pilgrims to Mecca; the English opened a trading post here in 1613.
Portuguese from 1510, outside Mughal rule; Portugal held it until 1961.
A great Mughal city; Aurangzeb's Badshahi Mosque, finished in 1673, was long one of the largest in the world.

dd-mughals.text: After Aurangzeb died in 1707, governors and rivals broke away. In 1739 Nadir Shah of [Persia](IRN) sacked Delhi, and Afghan armies from [Afghanistan](AFG) raided repeatedly. The Marathas came to dominate much of [India](IND). In Bengal, now [Bangladesh](BGD) and eastern India, the British East India Company won at Plassey in 1757 and took over tax collection in 1765. By 1803 the emperor lived under British protection.

notes.IND: The Marathas, rising since Shivaji in the 1600s, became the strongest Indian power; they dominated Delhi and the emperor from the 1770s until the British took the city in 1803.
notes.BGD: The 1765 grant of Bengal's revenues gave the Company the wealth of India's richest province to pay for armies and further conquests.
notes.AFG: Ahmad Shah Durrani, a former officer of Nadir Shah, founded the state that became modern Afghanistan and raided India several times.
notes.PAK: Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh fell under Afghan rule or overlordship after 1747. Punjab later became the core of Ranjit Singh's Sikh kingdom.
notes.IRN: Nadir Shah's loot from Delhi was so vast that he suspended taxes in Persia for three years.
notes.MMR: Rangoon in Burma, under British rule from 1852, became the place of exile and death of the last Mughal emperor.
notes.GBR: After the 1857 uprising, Britain abolished the East India Company's rule and governed India directly from 1858.

pn: 1739: Nadir Shah's troops killed many thousands of residents and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
23 June 1757: Robert Clive's Company army beat the Nawab of Bengal, helped by the defection of the nawab's commander.
1764: the Company defeated the Mughal emperor and his allies; in 1765 he granted it the revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
1761: Ahmad Shah Durrani crushed a Maratha army in one of the bloodiest battles of the century.
10 May 1857: Indian soldiers mutinied here and marched to Delhi, proclaiming the old emperor their leader.
1858: the British exiled the last emperor, Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), to Burma; he died here in 1862.

dd-british.text: From the 1600s English and then British merchants and settlers built an Atlantic empire: colonies in North America, sugar islands such as [Jamaica](JAM) and [Barbados](BRB) worked by enslaved Africans, and forts on the coast of West Africa, such as in [Ghana](GHA). The East India Company traded from ports in [India](IND). Victory over France in the Seven Years' War (1756–63) won [Canada](CAN) and made Britain the leading colonial power.

notes.GBR: England and Scotland united as Great Britain in 1707. Its navy, banks and Atlantic trade made it Europe's leading colonial and commercial power by 1763.
notes.IRL: Ireland was a separate kingdom under the British Crown, with its own parliament, largely run by a Protestant landowning minority. It joined the United Kingdom in 1801.
notes.USA: Thirteen colonies stretched along the Atlantic coast, home to nearly 2 million people by the 1760s. The 1763 treaty also gave Britain the land east of the Mississippi and Florida.
notes.CAN: Britain took New France, with its roughly 70,000 French-speaking Catholics, in the Seven Years' War. Hudson's Bay Company fur traders already worked the far north.
notes.JAM: England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655. Its sugar plantations made planters rich and depended on enslaved Africans, who rose in revolt several times.
notes.BRB: Settled by the English in 1627, Barbados pioneered the sugar plantation system based on enslaved African labour that spread across the Caribbean.
notes.GHA: British forts on the Gold Coast, such as Cape Coast Castle, bought captives from African traders and held them for slave ships.
notes.GMB: Britain held James Island in the Gambia River, a trading post for gold, ivory and enslaved people.
notes.SEN: Britain held French Senegal, including Saint-Louis, from 1758 and lost it again during the American War of Independence.
notes.IND: In 1763 the East India Company held Bombay, Madras and Calcutta. After Plassey it dominated Bengal through Nawabs it installed, and in 1765 it won the right to collect Bengal's taxes.
notes.BGD: Today's Bangladesh was eastern Bengal, rich in textiles and rice, which fell under growing East India Company control after 1757.
notes.GIB: Britain took Gibraltar from Spain in 1704 and kept it under the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht. It still belongs to Britain today.

pn: 1607: the first lasting English colony in North America is founded in Virginia. Tobacco soon makes it pay.
From the 1660s: a British fort on the Gold Coast where captive Africans were held before being shipped across the Atlantic.
Jamaica, taken from Spain in 1655, became Britain's richest sugar colony, with enslaved Africans outnumbering whites about ten to one by the late 1700s.
13 September 1759: British troops take Quebec from the French; in 1763 France gives up Canada.
23 June 1757: Robert Clive's East India Company army defeats the Nawab of Bengal, the start of British rule in India.
Founded as a Company trading post in 1690, it became the capital of British India.

dd-british.text: After the First World War the British Empire was the largest in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land and holding over 400 million people. [India](IND) was its richest possession. Dominions such as [Canada](CAN), [Australia](AUS) and [South Africa](ZAF) governed themselves, while most colonies in Africa and Asia were ruled from London through governors and local chiefs. New League of Nations mandates included [Iraq](IRQ) and Palestine.

notes.GBR: The United Kingdom, with under 50 million people, ruled an empire of over 400 million. The Royal Navy, the world's largest, protected the sea lanes.
notes.IRL: After the War of Independence of 1919–21, 26 counties became the self-governing Irish Free State in 1922; Northern Ireland stayed in the United Kingdom.
notes.IND: British India supplied soldiers, cotton, tea and markets. About 1.3 million Indians served in the First World War. Gandhi's nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920.
notes.CAN: Canada became the first self-governing dominion in 1867. Over 60,000 Canadians died in the First World War, which strengthened demands for full independence.
notes.AUS: Six colonies federated as Australia in 1901. Aboriginal Australians had been dispossessed of most of the continent by British settlement since 1788.
notes.ZAF: Formed in 1910 after Britain defeated the Boer republics, South Africa was ruled by its white minority, which passed laws restricting black land ownership in 1913.
notes.IRQ: Britain ruled Iraq as a mandate after taking it from the Ottomans. A revolt in 1920 was suppressed, partly with air power, and Faisal was made king in 1921.
notes.EGY: A British protectorate from 1914, Egypt rose in revolt in 1919. Britain granted nominal independence in 1922 but kept troops at the Suez Canal.
notes.KEN: Kenya became a crown colony in 1920. White settlers held much of the best highland farmland, and Africans paid taxes that pushed them into wage work.
notes.MYS: British Malaya produced much of the world's tin and rubber, worked largely by migrant labourers from China and India.
notes.ISR: Britain ruled Palestine from 1917–18. In the 1917 Balfour Declaration it had promised to support a Jewish national home there.
notes.PSE: Palestine was ruled by Britain as one mandate. Its Arab majority opposed the Balfour Declaration's promise of a Jewish national home.

pn: The Colonial Office, India Office and the City of London's banks ran an empire whose trade and loans spanned the globe.
Capital of British India from 1911. Around 1,000 British officials of the Indian Civil Service governed over 300 million people.
13 April 1919: troops fire on an unarmed crowd, killing 379 by the official British count and about 1,000 by Indian estimates.
Opened in 1869, it was the empire's lifeline to India. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 largely to protect it.
Founded as a British port in 1819, it guarded the sea route between India and China.

dd-british.text: The Second World War left Britain exhausted. [India](IND) and [Pakistan](PAK) became independent in 1947, then most of Asia followed. In 1957 [Ghana](GHA) led Africa to independence, and by 1968 most African and many Caribbean colonies were free, some after wars such as in [Kenya](KEN). In 1997 [Hong Kong](HKG) was handed to China. Most former colonies joined the Commonwealth, a voluntary association that today has 56 members.

notes.IND: Mass campaigns led by Gandhi and Congress, wartime debts and a navy mutiny in 1946 led Britain to leave in August 1947, splitting India from Pakistan.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was created in 1947 as a homeland for Muslims of British India, in two parts: today's Pakistan and, 1,600 km away, today's Bangladesh.
notes.GHA: The Gold Coast became Ghana in 1957 after a decade of protest and elections led by Kwame Nkrumah, inspiring independence movements across Africa.
notes.KEN: The Mau Mau war killed over 11,000 rebels by official count; some historians estimate far more. In 2013 Britain paid compensation to over 5,000 Kenyans who had been abused in its detention camps.
notes.HKG: A 1984 agreement promised Hong Kong 50 years of its own system under China. After a 2020 security law, Britain said China was breaching it; China rejects this.
notes.IRL: The Irish Free State of 1922 became a fully independent republic in 1949 and left the Commonwealth. Northern Ireland remains in the United Kingdom.
notes.CAN: The 1931 Statute of Westminster recognised Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa as equal, self-governing nations under the Crown.
notes.ZWE: Southern Rhodesia's white minority government declared independence in 1965. After a guerrilla war, majority rule came in 1980 as Zimbabwe.
notes.CYP: Cyprus became independent in 1960 after a Greek Cypriot guerrilla campaign. Britain kept two sovereign military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia.
notes.MYS: Britain fought a communist insurgency, the Malayan Emergency, from 1948, and granted Malaya independence in 1957.
notes.IOT: Britain removed the Chagos Islanders in 1967–73 to make way for a US base on Diego Garcia. A 2025 treaty to hand the islands to Mauritius had not been ratified by Britain as of 2026.
notes.EGY: Egypt became nominally independent in 1922, but British troops stayed at the Suez Canal until 1956.
notes.IRQ: Iraq's mandate ended in 1932, when it joined the League of Nations, though British bases and influence remained.
notes.FLK: Britain has held the Falklands since 1833. Argentina, which calls them the Malvinas, still claims them.

pn: 15 August 1947: India becomes independent, a day after Pakistan, as British India is partitioned amid mass violence.
1956: Britain and France invade after Egypt nationalises the canal, then withdraw under US pressure. It showed Britain was no longer a superpower.
6 March 1957: under Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana becomes the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from Britain.
1952–60: Britain fights the Mau Mau uprising, detaining tens of thousands of Kenyans in camps. Kenya became independent in 1963.
1 July 1997: Britain hands Hong Kong to China, often seen as the end of the empire.
1982: Britain retakes the Falkland Islands after an Argentine invasion. Argentina still claims them.

dd-napoleon.text: Born on Corsica in 1769, Napoleon Bonaparte was 26 when [France](FRA) gave him its army in [Italy](ITA). In 1796–97 he beat the Austrians again and again and dictated the peace. In 1798 he sailed for [Egypt](EGY), taking [Malta](MLT) on the way, to strike at Britain's route to India. He won on land, but Nelson destroyed his fleet, and his march into Ottoman Palestine stalled at Acre, in today's [Israel](ISR). In 1799 he slipped home and seized power.

notes.FRA: Bonaparte returned in October 1799 to a country tired of the Directory. On 9–10 November he led a coup and became First Consul.
notes.ITA: Bonaparte drove the Austrians out of Lombardy, and in 1797 created the Cisalpine Republic around Milan. At Campo Formio he handed the ancient Republic of Venice to Austria.
notes.MLT: The French took Malta from the Knights of St John in June 1798. Britain, helped by Maltese rebels, captured it in 1800 and kept it until 1964.
notes.EGY: Egypt was an Ottoman province run by Mamluk beys. The French were defeated and evacuated in 1801, but over 150 scholars who came with them produced the vast 'Description de l'Égypte', founding modern Egyptology.
notes.ISR: In March 1799 the French stormed Jaffa, and shot thousands of prisoners, at least 2,000 by most estimates. Plague then struck the army, and the siege of Acre failed.
notes.PSE: The army crossed Sinai and took Gaza in February 1799 on its way north.
notes.GBR: Britain saw the Egyptian expedition as a threat to India. Its navy cut the French army off, and a British army forced it to surrender in 1801.
notes.AUT: Austria lost northern Italy and made peace at Campo Formio in October 1797, its first big defeat by the young general.
notes.TUR: The Ottoman sultan declared war on France after the invasion of Egypt and joined the Second Coalition.

pn: November 1796: a three-day battle at a bridge over marshes. Bonaparte's own carefully spread image of himself leading the charge, flag in hand, made him famous.
January 1797: Bonaparte crushes the last Austrian attempt to relieve Mantua, and Austria soon asks for peace.
21 July 1798: French squares break the charges of the Mamluk cavalry near Cairo.
1 August 1798: at the Battle of the Nile, Nelson's fleet destroys the French fleet, trapping the army in Egypt.
July 1799: French soldiers find the Rosetta Stone, later the key to reading hieroglyphs. Britain took it in 1801.
March–May 1799: the Ottoman fortress, helped by British ships, holds out for two months, and Bonaparte turns back.

dd-napoleon.text: In June 1812 about 450,000 men crossed the Neman into the Russian Empire, today's [Lithuania](LTU), and more followed. Only about half were French: [Germans](DEU), [Poles](POL), [Italians](ITA) and [Austrians](AUT) marched too. The Russians fell back, fought at Borodino and abandoned Moscow, which burned. Napoleon waited a month for a peace offer that never came, then retreated in October. Hunger, cold, disease and Cossack raids destroyed his army.

notes.RUS: Tsar Alexander I's general Kutuzov avoided defeat, gave up Moscow and let winter and hunger work. Russians call it the Patriotic War, the subject of Tolstoy's 'War and Peace'.
notes.FRA: Napoleon's quarrel with the tsar, who had left the Continental System blockading Britain, led to the war. He left the army in December and raced back to Paris.
notes.DEU: German states sent more troops than any nation but France. Prussia's corps of about 20,000 changed sides at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812, starting Germany's war of liberation.
notes.POL: About 90,000 Poles and Lithuanians served, hoping Napoleon would restore Poland. Prince Józef Poniatowski commanded the Polish corps.
notes.AUT: Austria, now Napoleon's ally by marriage, sent about 30,000 men under Schwarzenberg on the southern flank. They fought little and lost lightly.
notes.ITA: Napoleon's stepson Eugène led the corps of the Kingdom of Italy, which fought at Borodino and Maloyaroslavets.
notes.CHE: Swiss regiments fought a famous rearguard action at the Berezina in November 1812, and few of them came home.
notes.LTU: Lithuania, ruled by Russia since 1795, welcomed Napoleon in Vilnius, and some Lithuanians joined his army.
notes.BLR: Most of the march and the worst of the retreat, including the Berezina crossing, passed through today's Belarus.

pn: 24 June 1812: the Grande Armée crosses the Neman River on pontoon bridges.
7 September 1812: the bloodiest day of the Napoleonic Wars, with at least 70,000 killed, wounded or captured on both sides.
14 September 1812: Napoleon enters an almost empty city. Fires, probably set on the Russian governor's orders, burn most of it.
24 October 1812: a battle here blocks the road south, forcing the army back along the stripped route it came by.
26–29 November 1812: engineers working in icy water build bridges, and the remnants of the army escape across the river.
December 1812: thousands die here in the cold. A mass grave found in 2001 held the remains of over 3,000 soldiers.

dd-napoleon.text: Beaten by a coalition in 1813–14, Napoleon gave up his throne and was sent to the island of Elba, off [Italy](ITA). In February 1815 he escaped, landed in [France](FRA) and reached Paris without a shot fired. These Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in [Belgium](BEL), where a British-led army and the Prussians beat him. The British shipped him to [Saint Helena](SHN), a remote island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

notes.FRA: Louis XVIII, brother of the guillotined king, fled when Napoleon returned, then came back after Waterloo. In 1840 Napoleon's body was brought home to Les Invalides in Paris.
notes.BEL: Waterloo lies just south of Brussels, then part of the new United Kingdom of the Netherlands. The battlefield's Lion's Mound was raised in the 1820s.
notes.GBR: The Duke of Wellington's army was only about one-third British; the rest were Dutch, Belgian and German. Napoleon surrendered to a British warship in July 1815.
notes.DEU: Field Marshal Blücher's Prussian army was decisive, and Hanover, Brunswick and Nassau sent troops to Wellington.
notes.NLD: Dutch and Belgian troops under the Prince of Orange held the crossroads at Quatre Bras on 16 June, and fought at Waterloo two days later.
notes.ITA: Elba, off the Tuscan coast, was given to Napoleon to rule in April 1814. He left it on 26 February 1815.
notes.SHN: Saint Helena lies nearly 2,000 km from Africa. Most historians think Napoleon died of stomach cancer; theories of arsenic poisoning are disputed.
notes.AUT: At the Congress of Vienna, Europe's powers redrew the map in 1814–15. They declared Napoleon an outlaw when he returned.

pn: May 1814 – February 1815: Napoleon rules tiny Elba as its sovereign, with a guard of about 1,000 men.
7 March 1815: royal troops sent to stop him go over to Napoleon after he walks towards them and dares them to shoot.
16 June 1815: Napoleon's last victory, over the Prussians, who retreat but stay in the fight.
18 June 1815: Wellington holds the ridge all day until Blücher's Prussians arrive, and the French army breaks.
1815–1821: Napoleon lives here under British guard, dictating memoirs, until his death on 5 May 1821.

dd-greatgame.text: Through the 1800s the [Russian Empire](RUS) pushed south into Central Asia, taking [Uzbekistan](UZB) and [Turkmenistan](TKM), while Britain ruled [India](IND) and feared a Russian march on it. Neither side wanted the other on its border, so [Afghanistan](AFG) became the buffer. Britain and the Afghan emir agreed the Durand Line in 1893, the thin Wakhan Corridor kept the two empires apart, and in 1907 they settled their rivalry by treaty.

notes.RUS: Russia conquered the Kazakh steppe and then the khanates of Central Asia between the 1840s and 1880s, bringing its border to Afghanistan.
notes.UZB: Russia took Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868, and made Bukhara and Khiva protectorates.
notes.TKM: Russia defeated the Turkmen at Geok Tepe in 1881 and took Merv in 1884, alarming Britain because it brought Russia close to Herat.
notes.TJK: The Pamir mountains were divided in 1895, with Russia taking the lands north of the Wakhan.
notes.AFG: Britain fought wars here in 1839–42 and 1878–80, then left the emir to rule at home while it controlled his foreign policy. Afghanistan's borders were drawn by the two empires.
notes.PAK: The Durand Line of 1893 split the Pashtun lands between Afghanistan and British India. Afghanistan has never formally accepted it as an international border.
notes.IND: British strategists feared Russia might invade India through Afghanistan, though historians doubt Russia ever seriously planned it.
notes.IRN: The 1907 convention gave Russia a sphere of influence in northern Persia and Britain one in the south-east, without asking the Persians.
notes.CHN: The 1907 convention also covered Tibet: both empires agreed to deal with it only through China. Qing China held Xinjiang, on the corridor's eastern end.
notes.MMR: Britain completed its conquest of Burma in 1885–86, adding it to British India.

pn: Afghanistan's capital, occupied by British-Indian armies in 1839–42 and 1879–80.
1842: the emir executes two British officers, Charles Stoddart and Arthur Conolly; Russia makes Bukhara a protectorate in 1868.
March 1885: Russian troops defeat an Afghan force here, and Britain and Russia come close to war.
1893–95: this narrow strip, in places only about 13 km wide, was left to Afghanistan so that Russian and British territory would not touch.
The main pass between Afghanistan and India, and the route of British invasions.

dd-greatgame.text: Three great powers sent armies into [Afghanistan](AFG). [Britain](GBR) invaded in 1839 and lost almost a whole army retreating from Kabul in 1842. The [Soviet Union](RUS) invaded in 1979 to prop up a communist government and left in 1989. The [United States](USA) and its allies invaded in 2001 after the 9/11 attacks and left in 2021, as the Taliban took back power. Each won the first battles easily and then struggled to hold the country.

notes.AFG: Afghans fought each other as well as the invaders in every war. The Soviet war and the civil wars after it killed perhaps a million or more people and drove millions into exile.
notes.GBR: In January 1842 about 4,500 British and Indian soldiers and some 12,000 camp followers left Kabul in winter; almost all were killed, captured or died of cold. Britain fought again in 1878–80 and 1919.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union sent about 100,000 troops at its peak. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died, and the last troops left on 15 February 1989.
notes.UZB: Soviet columns entered Afghanistan from Termez, in Soviet Uzbekistan, in December 1979 and left the same way in 1989.
notes.USA: The US went in after 9/11 because the Taliban sheltered al-Qaeda. About 2,400 US service members died before the withdrawal agreed with the Taliban in 2020 was completed in 2021.
notes.PAK: Pakistan hosted millions of Afghan refugees and channelled US and Saudi aid to the anti-Soviet mujahideen. After 2001 it was a US ally, while Taliban leaders found refuge on its soil.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia matched US funding for the mujahideen in the 1980s, and Arab volunteers, including Osama bin Laden, joined the fight.
notes.IRN: Iran hosted millions of Afghan refugees and backed Shia and Persian-speaking Afghan groups.

pn: 13 January 1842: the last British soldiers of the retreating army make a stand here and are overwhelmed.
January 1842: Dr William Brydon reaches the British garrison here, famous as the sole survivor, though a few others straggled in later.
15 August 2021: the Taliban enter the city; the last US flight leaves on 30 August.
1994: the Taliban movement rises here, and it remained their spiritual home.
December 2001: Osama bin Laden escapes US-backed forces in these mountain caves.

dd-israel.text: Britain took Palestine from the Ottoman Empire in 1917–18 and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate. In the 1917 Balfour Declaration it had promised to support a 'national home for the Jewish people' there, without prejudicing the 'civil and religious rights' of the Arab majority. Jewish immigration grew, especially after the Nazis came to power in [Germany](DEU), and Arab opposition grew with it. Land east of the Jordan River became [Transjordan](JOR), and [Syria](SYR) and [Lebanon](LBN) went to France.

notes.ISR: The 1922 census counted about 757,000 people, about 11% of them Jewish. By 1947 there were about 1.9 million, roughly a third Jewish.
notes.PSE: Palestinian Arabs, Muslim and Christian, were the large majority. Their leaders rejected the Balfour Declaration and demanded independence and an end to Jewish immigration.
notes.JOR: Transjordan was part of the Palestine mandate but closed to Jewish settlement. It became independent as Jordan in 1946.
notes.SYR: France ruled Syria as a mandate after crushing King Faisal's Arab kingdom in 1920. It became independent in 1946.
notes.LBN: France created Greater Lebanon in 1920 with a Christian majority at the time. It became independent in 1943.
notes.DEU: Nazi persecution from 1933 drove tens of thousands of German and other European Jews to Palestine in the 1930s, before Britain limited immigration in 1939.
notes.GBR: Britain made promises to Arab leaders, to Zionists and, in secret, to France during the First World War. It handed the problem to the UN in 1947.

pn: December 1917: British troops under General Allenby enter the city. In 1946 the Irgun, a Jewish underground group, bombs British offices in the King David Hotel, killing 91 people.
Founded in 1909 beside the Arab port of Jaffa, it grew into the largest Jewish city. Israel's independence was declared here on 14 May 1948.
August 1929: Arab rioters kill 67 Jews during unrest across Palestine; British police kill some of the rioters.
April 1936: a general strike begins the Arab Revolt against British rule and Jewish immigration, crushed by 1939.

dd-israel.text: In 1947 the UN proposed splitting Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Jewish leaders accepted and Arab leaders rejected the plan, and civil war began. [Israel](ISR) declared independence in May 1948 and defeated the armies of its neighbours. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. [Jordan](JOR) took the West Bank and [Egypt](EGY) ran Gaza. In June 1967 Israel captured both, now the Palestinian territories ([Palestine](PSE)), plus Sinai and the Golan Heights from [Syria](SYR).

notes.ISR: Israel calls 1948 its War of Independence. About 6,000 Israelis, around 1% of the Jewish population, were killed. Israel took in Holocaust survivors and, over the next decades, most Jews from Arab countries.
notes.PSE: Palestinians call 1948 the Nakba, the 'catastrophe': hundreds of villages emptied and refugees were not allowed back. After 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and about 300,000 more Palestinians fled.
notes.JOR: Jordan's army held the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 1948 and annexed them in 1950. It lost them in 1967 and gave up its claim in 1988.
notes.EGY: Egypt ran the Gaza Strip from 1948 to 1967 without annexing it. Israel took Sinai in 1967; Egypt won it back through the 1979 peace treaty.
notes.SYR: Israel took the Golan Heights in 1967 and applied its law there in 1981. Most countries regard it as occupied Syrian land; the US recognised Israeli sovereignty in 2019.
notes.IRQ: About 120,000 Iraqi Jews, a community over 2,500 years old, were airlifted to Israel in 1951–52 after facing growing persecution.
notes.YEM: About 49,000 Yemeni Jews were flown to Israel in 1949–50, in an airlift known as Operation Magic Carpet.
notes.MAR: Morocco had the Arab world's largest Jewish community, about 250,000 people. Most left for Israel, France and Canada in the 1950s and 1960s.

pn: 9 April 1948: Irgun and Lehi fighters kill over 100 villagers, including women and children. News of it spread fear and flight among Palestinians.
13 May 1948: Arab forces overrun this Jewish settlement bloc, and about 130 defenders and residents are killed, many after surrendering.
July 1948: Israeli forces take Lydda and Ramle and expel most of their Arab residents, tens of thousands of people.
Divided from 1948: Jordan held the Old City and the east, Israel the west. Israel took East Jerusalem in 1967 and later annexed it, a move most countries do not recognise.
1948: about 200,000 refugees crowd into the Gaza Strip, tripling its population. Most of its people today descend from them.

dd-israel.text: [Egypt](EGY) made peace with [Israel](ISR) in 1979 and [Jordan](JOR) in 1994. The 1993 Oslo Accords set up a Palestinian Authority, but no Palestinian state followed. In 2020 the [United Arab Emirates](ARE), [Bahrain](BHR) and [Morocco](MAR) established ties with Israel. On 7 October 2023 Hamas attacked Israel from [Gaza](PSE), starting a devastating war that spread to Lebanon and, in 2024–2026, to direct fighting with [Iran](IRN). A Gaza ceasefire began in October 2025, but violence continued.

notes.ISR: About 10 million people live in Israel, a fifth of them Arab citizens. Israel says its Gaza war aimed to destroy Hamas and free the hostages, all of whom were returned, alive or dead, by January 2026.
notes.PSE: More than 74,000 people were killed in Gaza by October 2026, by the count of its Hamas-run health ministry, which the UN has found broadly reliable; Israel says many were fighters. Israel still held over half the Strip.
notes.EGY: Egypt became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, at Camp David in 1978–79, and regained Sinai. President Anwar Sadat was assassinated in 1981, partly over the treaty.
notes.JOR: Jordan signed a peace treaty in 1994. Many of its citizens are of Palestinian origin, and it is the custodian of Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem.
notes.ARE: The UAE established full relations with Israel in 2020 under the US-brokered Abraham Accords, and kept them through the Gaza war despite criticism.
notes.BHR: Bahrain joined the Abraham Accords alongside the UAE in September 2020.
notes.MAR: Morocco restored ties with Israel in December 2020, as the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan, which has had diplomatic relations with Israel since 1992, agreed in November 2025 to join the Abraham Accords, the first country to do so since 2021.
notes.SDN: Sudan signed the Abraham Accords declaration in January 2021, but full relations never followed, and it fell into civil war in 2023.
notes.IRN: Iran backs Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis. It exchanged missile strikes with Israel in 2024, and fought wars with Israel, joined by the US, in June 2025 and from February 2026.
notes.LBN: Hezbollah fired on Israel from October 2023. Israel's 2024 offensive killed its leader Hassan Nasrallah. War resumed in March 2026 alongside the Iran war; after truces in April and June, Israeli troops still held part of southern Lebanon.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia was in US-brokered talks on recognising Israel before 7 October 2023. It says it will only do so with a path to a Palestinian state.

pn: 4 November 1995: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who signed the Oslo Accords, is shot dead by an Israeli Jewish extremist opposed to them.
Seat of the Palestinian Authority, which since 2007 has governed parts of the West Bank but not Gaza.
7 October 2023: Hamas-led fighters kill about 1,200 people in southern Israel, most of them civilians, and take 251 hostages. Over 100 died in this kibbutz alone.
2023–25: Israeli bombardment and ground fighting destroy most of the city. In August 2025 UN-backed experts declared famine there; Israel disputed the finding.

Gaza's crossing to Egypt. Israel took it in May 2024. Its reopening, part of the 2025 ceasefire plan, was delayed until all hostages' remains were returned; limited foot crossings began in February 2026, with repeated closures since.

dd-holocaust.text: When Hitler took power in 1933, about 523,000 Jews lived in [Germany](DEU). The Nazis drove them out of jobs, schools and public life, and the 1935 Nuremberg Laws took away their citizenship. After the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938, Jews in Germany and annexed [Austria](AUT) tried desperately to leave. About 400,000 escaped by 1939, many to the [United States](USA), Palestine and [Britain](GBR), but most countries limited how many they would admit.

notes.DEU: In 1933 Jews were less than 1% of Germany's people. By the end of 1939 about 202,000 remained, and in October 1941 the Nazis banned emigration.
notes.AUT: After the Anschluss of March 1938, Vienna's Jews were humiliated in the streets and robbed. About 117,000 left Austria by September 1939.
notes.CZE: Germany took the Sudetenland in 1938 and the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939, bringing over 100,000 more Jews under Nazi rule.
notes.USA: About 95,000 Jewish refugees from the German Reich reached the US by 1939. Strict quotas held numbers down: by June 1939, 309,000 had applied for 27,000 places.
notes.GBR: About 40,000 refugees reached Britain by 1939. After Kristallnacht the Kindertransport brought about 10,000 Jewish children, most of whom never saw their parents again.
notes.ISR: About 60,000 German Jews reached British-ruled Palestine in 1933–39. In 1939 Britain sharply limited Jewish immigration there, amid Arab opposition.
notes.PSE: About 60,000 German Jews reached British-ruled Palestine in 1933–39. In 1939 Britain sharply limited Jewish immigration there, amid Arab opposition.
notes.ARG: About 75,000 refugees went to Central and South America, mainly to Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Bolivia.
notes.CHN: Shanghai, partly under Japanese control, required no entry visa, and more than 18,000 Jews from the German Reich found refuge there.
notes.NLD: Thousands of refugees found shelter in the Netherlands, among them the family of Anne Frank. Germany overran it in May 1940, and most were caught.
notes.FRA: France took in many refugees, but after its defeat in 1940 Vichy police helped round up foreign Jews for deportation.
notes.POL: In October 1938 Germany expelled about 17,000 Polish-born Jews to the Polish border. The son of one family shot a German diplomat in Paris, the pretext for Kristallnacht.
notes.CHE: Switzerland asked Germany in 1938 to stamp Jews' passports with a 'J', making it easier to turn them away at the border.

pn: March 1933: one of the first concentration camps opens, for communists, social democrats and other political opponents.
15 September 1935: the Nuremberg Laws strip Jews of citizenship and ban marriage between Jews and other Germans.
9–10 November 1938: in Kristallnacht, mobs across Germany and Austria burn synagogues and wreck Jewish shops. About 30,000 Jewish men are sent to camps.
July 1938: delegates of 32 countries meet to discuss Jewish refugees. Almost none agree to take more.
1941: one of six killing centres of the Nazi 'euthanasia' programme, where disabled patients were murdered in gas chambers.

dd-holocaust.text: After invading [Poland](POL) in 1939, Germany forced its Jews into sealed ghettos, where hunger and disease killed hundreds of thousands. When Germany invaded the [Soviet Union](RUS) in June 1941, mobile killing units, the Einsatzgruppen, with police battalions and local collaborators, shot Jews town by town across [Lithuania](LTU), [Belarus](BLR) and [Ukraine](UKR). About 2 million Jews were murdered in mass shootings. In January 1942 officials met at Wannsee to coordinate the murder of all Europe's Jews.

notes.POL: Poland had Europe's largest Jewish community, about 3.3 million. In the ghettos people were crammed in, starved and used for forced labour, and about nine in ten Polish Jews were eventually murdered.
notes.LTU: About nine in ten of Lithuania's Jews were murdered, most shot in 1941 by German units and Lithuanian collaborators, many at Ponary outside Vilnius.
notes.LVA: Most of Riga's Jews were shot in the Rumbula forest in late 1941, along with Jews deported there from Germany.
notes.EST: Most of Estonia's small Jewish community fled east; almost all of the roughly 1,000 who stayed were murdered in 1941. Jews deported from elsewhere were later killed in camps there.
notes.BLR: Belarus had hundreds of Jewish towns, most destroyed by shootings in 1941–42. Thousands of Jews escaped to the forests and fought as partisans.
notes.UKR: Most of the Jews murdered in Ukraine were shot near their homes in 1941–42 by German units, often helped by local police. Babi Yar was one of the largest massacres.
notes.MDA: Romanian and German forces killed tens of thousands of Jews in Bessarabia in 1941 and deported survivors to camps in Transnistria, where many more died.
notes.RUS: German units shot Jews, Roma and communist officials in the occupied west of Russia. Soviet prisoners of war were starved to death in their hundreds of thousands in the first winter.
notes.DEU: From October 1941 Jews from Germany, Austria and Prague were deported to ghettos in Łódź, Riga, Minsk and Kaunas. Many were shot soon after arrival.
notes.SRB: German forces in occupied Serbia shot most Jewish men in 1941 as 'hostages' and gassed the women and children in a van in 1942.

pn: Sealed in November 1940 with over 400,000 people. In summer 1942 about 265,000 were deported to Treblinka; the survivors rose up in April 1943.
Sealed in 1940 with about 160,000 Jews, it was the last large ghetto, emptied in August 1944, mostly to Auschwitz.
December 1941: the first death camp begins killing Jews with poison gas, in vans. At least 152,000 were murdered here.
1941–44: in a forest outside Vilnius, about 70,000 Jews were shot, along with thousands of Poles and Soviet prisoners.
29–30 September 1941: German units shoot 33,771 Jews from Kyiv in this ravine in two days.
20 January 1942: Reinhard Heydrich chairs a meeting of 15 senior officials to coordinate the 'Final Solution', the murder of Europe's Jews.

dd-holocaust.text: From 1942 trains carried Jews from across Europe to death camps that Germany built in occupied [Poland](POL). At Treblinka, Sobibor and Bełżec almost everyone was gassed on arrival. At Auschwitz-Birkenau, the largest, SS doctors chose some for forced labour and sent the rest to the gas chambers. Jews were deported from [France](FRA), the [Netherlands](NLD), [Greece](GRC), [Italy](ITA) and, in 1944, [Hungary](HUN). In [Denmark](DNK) and [Bulgaria](BGR), most Jews were saved.

notes.POL: The six death camps, Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau, were all built by Germany in occupied Poland. About 2.7 million Jews were murdered in them.
notes.FRA: About 75,000 Jews were deported from France, many rounded up by French police under the Vichy government. About three in four of France's Jews survived, many helped into hiding.
notes.NLD: About 102,000 Dutch Jews, three in four, were deported from the Westerbork camp and murdered. Anne Frank, whose diary became famous, was one of them.
notes.BEL: Nearly 25,000 Jews were deported from Belgium. Many more survived in hiding, helped by a well-organised resistance.
notes.GRC: Most of Greece's Jews were murdered, including almost all of the old community of Thessaloniki, deported to Auschwitz in 1943.
notes.ITA: Italy passed anti-Jewish laws in 1938, but deportations began only after Germany occupied the north in 1943. Nearly 8,000 Jews in Italy were murdered.
notes.HUN: Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944. From mid-May to early July Hungarian gendarmes helped deport over 420,000 Jews, nearly all of them to Auschwitz.
notes.SVK: In 1942 the Slovak state handed about 58,000 of its Jews to Germany for deportation, and paid for each one.
notes.NOR: Over 700 of Norway's roughly 2,100 Jews were deported in 1942–43, most aboard the ship Donau. About half the community escaped to Sweden.
notes.MKD: Bulgaria, which occupied Macedonia, deported over 7,000 of its Jews to Treblinka in March 1943. Almost none survived.
notes.DNK: In October 1943 Danes ferried about 7,200 Jews across the sea to neutral Sweden, saving almost all of Denmark's Jews.
notes.BGR: Protests in March 1943 stopped the deportation of Bulgaria's own 48,000 Jews, and they survived. Bulgaria did deport over 11,000 Jews from the lands it occupied.
notes.ALB: Albanians, Muslim and Christian, hid Jews under their code of honour, besa. Almost all Jews in Albania survived.
notes.DEU: About 165,000 German Jews were murdered. Many were sent first to the Theresienstadt ghetto, near Prague, or straight to the ghettos and camps of the east.

pn: 1942–1945: the largest death camp. About 1.1 million people were murdered here, about 1 million of them Jews. Soviet troops reached it on 27 January 1945.
1942–1943: about 925,000 Jews were murdered here. Prisoners rose up in August 1943; very few of them survived the war.
1942–1943: at least 167,000 Jews were murdered here. A prisoner revolt on 14 October 1943 led to its closure.
1942: about 435,000 Jews were murdered here in under a year. Only a handful of people are known to have survived.
1941–1944: a concentration and death camp at Lublin. The Majdanek museum estimates 78,000 dead, 59,000 of them Jews. In July 1944 it was the first major camp liberated.
1941–1944: the transit camp outside Paris from which most of the 75,000 Jews deported from France left.

dd-pacific.text: [Japan](JPN) invaded [China](CHN) in 1937. After striking Pearl Harbor in December 1941 it conquered the [Philippines](PHL), [Malaya](MYS), [Indonesia](IDN) and [Burma](MMR) in six months. The tide turned at Midway in June 1942. US forces then fought island by island towards Japan, from Guadalcanal to Okinawa, and the war ended after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

notes.JPN: About 2.5–3 million Japanese died. US firebombing burned most big cities, and a single raid on Tokyo in March 1945 killed perhaps 100,000 people.
notes.CHN: China fought Japan from 1937, losing many millions of soldiers and civilians. Japan held the north-east, the coast and the main cities, but never the whole country.
notes.KOR: A Japanese colony since 1910. Koreans were drafted as labourers and soldiers, and many women were forced into military brothels as so-called 'comfort women'.
notes.TWN: A Japanese colony since 1895 and a base for the 1941–42 invasions to the south.
notes.PHL: A US territory, conquered by Japan by May 1942. MacArthur's forces landed at Leyte in October 1944, and the battle for Manila in 1945 killed about 100,000 civilians.
notes.MYS: British Malaya fell in ten weeks. Singapore surrendered on 15 February 1942, with about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops taken prisoner.
notes.SGP: Singapore's surrender in February 1942 was Britain's worst military defeat. Thousands of Chinese residents were then massacred by the Japanese.
notes.IDN: Japan wanted the Dutch East Indies above all for their oil. It conquered them by March 1942.
notes.MMR: Japan drove the British out of Burma in 1942. Allied prisoners and Asian labourers built the Burma Railway, where many tens of thousands died.
notes.THA: Thailand, the only Southeast Asian country never colonised by Europeans, let Japanese troops pass in December 1941 and then allied with Japan.
notes.USA: The US entered the war after Pearl Harbor and supplied most of the Allied forces in the Pacific.
notes.AUS: Japanese planes bombed Darwin in February 1942, and Australian troops halted the Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track in New Guinea.
notes.SLB: Guadalcanal, August 1942 to February 1943, was the first major Allied land offensive against Japan.
notes.KIR: Tarawa, November 1943: about 1,000 US Marines and nearly all of some 4,700 Japanese troops and Korean labourers died in three days.
notes.MNP: Saipan fell in July 1944, putting Tokyo within range of US B-29 bombers. The Enola Gay flew from neighbouring Tinian.
notes.KHM: French officials kept running Indochina with Japanese troops stationed there from 1941. Thailand annexed western Cambodia and parts of Laos in 1941.
notes.IND: British India raised the largest volunteer army in history, which stopped Japan's invasion at Imphal and Kohima in 1944.

pn: December 1937: Japanese troops take China's capital and massacre civilians and prisoners for weeks. Estimates of the dead vary widely, from about 40,000 to over 300,000; the postwar Tokyo tribunal put it at more than 200,000.
7 December 1941: Japanese carrier planes attack the US Pacific Fleet, killing about 2,400 Americans.
4–7 June 1942: US carrier planes sink four Japanese aircraft carriers, the turning point of the Pacific war.
6 August 1945: the first atomic bomb used in war. By the end of 1945 about 140,000 people had died.
9 August 1945: the second atomic bomb kills about 70,000 people by the end of the year.

dd-pacific.text: Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 and signed on 2 September. The US occupied [Japan](JPN) until 1952. [Korea](KOR) was split at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US zones, and [Taiwan](TWN) came under the Republic of China. In Southeast Asia, nationalists who had seen European rulers beaten declared independence in [Indonesia](IDN) and [Vietnam](VNM), and colonial empires there broke up within a few years.

notes.JPN: Under General MacArthur, Japan got a new constitution in 1947 that kept the emperor as a symbol and renounced war. The occupation ended in 1952.
notes.KOR: US troops took the surrender south of the 38th parallel. Rival states formed in 1948, and the Korean War followed in 1950.
notes.PRK: Soviet troops took the surrender north of the 38th parallel and backed Kim Il Sung, who led North Korea from 1948.
notes.TWN: The Republic of China took control of Taiwan in October 1945. Its government retreated there in 1949 after losing China's civil war to the communists.
notes.CHN: Victory over Japan was followed by renewed civil war, won by Mao Zedong's communists in 1949.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union took southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands. Russia and Japan still dispute the southernmost Kurils.
notes.PHL: The US granted the Philippines independence, as promised before the war, on 4 July 1946.
notes.IDN: The Dutch tried to return, and four years of fighting and talks followed before they recognised Indonesia in 1949.
notes.VNM: France fought to regain Indochina until its defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, when Vietnam was divided.
notes.MMR: Burma won independence from Britain in 1948.
notes.MYS: The British returned to Malaya, which became independent in 1957.

pn: 2 September 1945: Japan signs the surrender on the battleship USS Missouri.
17 August 1945: Sukarno and Hatta declare Indonesia's independence.
2 September 1945: Ho Chi Minh declares Vietnam's independence.
9 August 1945: the Soviet Union attacks Japan's armies in Manchuria.

dd-vietnam.text: France ruled [Vietnam](VNM), [Laos](LAO) and [Cambodia](KHM) as French Indochina from the 1880s. In 1946 Ho Chi Minh's communist-led Viet Minh began a war for independence, and in May 1954 it defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu. The Geneva Accords then split Vietnam at the 17th parallel: a communist North and a Western-backed South. Nationwide elections promised for 1956 never took place.

notes.VNM: Vietnam fought France from 1946 to 1954. The Geneva Accords split it at the 17th parallel, and about 800,000–1 million people, mostly Catholics, moved south.
notes.LAO: Laos became fully independent in 1953–54. Its civil war between royalists and the communist Pathet Lao became bound up with Vietnam's.
notes.KHM: Cambodia won independence from France in 1953 under King Norodom Sihanouk, who tried to keep it neutral.
notes.FRA: France fought to keep Indochina after World War II, with growing US funding. Defeat at Dien Bien Phu brought it to the peace table at Geneva.
notes.CHN: Communist China, after 1949, supplied the Viet Minh with weapons, advisers and artillery used at Dien Bien Phu.

pn: March–May 1954: the Viet Minh besiege a French base for 56 days. Its fall ends French rule in Indochina.
2 September 1945: Ho Chi Minh declares Vietnam's independence. From 1954 Hanoi is the North's capital.
From 1955: capital of the Republic of Vietnam, the South, under Ngo Dinh Diem.

dd-vietnam.text: Communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, fought to topple South [Vietnam](VNM), supplied by North Vietnam down the Ho Chi Minh Trail through [Laos](LAO) and [Cambodia](KHM). From 1965 the [United States](USA) sent combat troops and bombed the North, with over 500,000 soldiers there by 1968. American forces left in 1973, and on 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon.

notes.VNM: About 58,000 Americans died. Estimates of Vietnamese dead, soldiers and civilians, range from under 1 million to over 3 million; Vietnam's government gave about 3 million in 1995.
notes.LAO: The Trail ran mainly through eastern Laos. The US dropped over 2 million tons of bombs on Laos in 1964–73, and unexploded bombs still kill and injure people.
notes.KHM: The US secretly bombed Trail bases in Cambodia from 1969 and invaded briefly in 1970. The war helped the Khmer Rouge take power in April 1975.
notes.USA: The US went from advisers in the 1950s to over 500,000 troops in 1968. It withdrew after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords.

pn: 1968: the old imperial capital is fought over for nearly a month during the Tet Offensive, and much of it is destroyed.
16 March 1968: US soldiers kill between 347 and 504 unarmed villagers, by US Army and Vietnamese counts.
30 April 1975: North Vietnamese forces take the city, renamed Ho Chi Minh City, as the last Americans leave by helicopter.
1965–72: the North's capital is bombed in campaigns such as Rolling Thunder and, at Christmas 1972, Linebacker II.
1954: the French defeat here led to the split of Vietnam and, in time, to the American war.

dd-vietnam.text: The [United States](USA) persuaded allies to send troops: [South Korea](KOR) sent the most, with up to 50,000 at a time, followed by [Thailand](THA), [Australia](AUS), the [Philippines](PHL) and [New Zealand](NZL). North Vietnam fought with weapons, aid and advisers from the [Soviet Union](RUS) and [China](CHN), though the two communist giants were bitter rivals by then.

notes.USA: About 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam and about 58,000 died. At the peak, in 1969, over 540,000 were there at once.
notes.KOR: South Korea sent about 320,000 troops in all, up to 50,000 at a time, and about 5,000 died. The US paid generously, which helped South Korea's economy.
notes.AUS: About 60,000 Australians served, many of them conscripts, and about 520 died. The war divided Australia as it did America.
notes.NZL: New Zealand sent a small force, at most about 550 at once, mostly artillery and infantry serving with the Australians. 37 were killed.
notes.THA: Thailand sent up to about 11,500 troops and let US bombers fly from its air bases against North Vietnam and Laos.
notes.PHL: The Philippines sent about 2,000 engineers, medics and security troops in 1966–69, in a non-combat role.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union supplied most of the North's heavy weapons, including surface-to-air missiles, jets and tanks, and trained its crews.
notes.CHN: China sent food, rifles and, by its own accounts, over 300,000 engineering and anti-aircraft troops to North Vietnam in 1965–68.
notes.VNM: South Vietnam's own army lost an estimated 200,000–250,000 dead. After 1975 the country was reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

dd-berlin.text: After Germany's surrender in May 1945, the [United States](USA), [Britain](GBR), [France](FRA) and the [Soviet Union](RUS) each occupied a zone of [Germany](DEU). Berlin lay about 160 km inside the Soviet zone, but it too was split into four sectors. Germany's lands east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to [Poland](POL). In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone East Germany.

notes.DEU: The four powers ran Germany jointly through the Allied Control Council in Berlin, but they soon split. West Germany was founded in May 1949 and communist East Germany in October.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union held the largest zone in the east and the eastern sector of Berlin. It took heavy reparations, dismantling factories and shipping them east.
notes.USA: The US held the south, including Bavaria, and the south-western sector of Berlin. From 1947 its Marshall Plan aid helped rebuild western Germany.
notes.GBR: Britain held the north-west, including the industrial Ruhr, and the western sector of Berlin around Charlottenburg and Spandau.
notes.FRA: France was given a zone in the south-west, carved from the American and British zones, and a sector in northern Berlin.
notes.POL: Poland was moved west: it gained German lands east of the Oder–Neisse line and lost its own eastern lands to the Soviet Union.
notes.AUT: Austria and Vienna were also divided into four zones, but the occupiers left in 1955 when Austria agreed to stay neutral.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia, like Poland, expelled most of its ethnic Germans after the war. An estimated 12–14 million Germans fled or were expelled from eastern Europe.

pn: May 1945: the Red Army takes the city. In July US, British and later French troops move into the western sectors.
July–August 1945: Truman, Stalin and Churchill, then Attlee, agree how to run occupied Germany and move its eastern border west.
May 1949: the Federal Republic of Germany, West Germany, is founded with this small Rhine city as its provisional capital.

dd-berlin.text: In June 1948, after the western powers launched a new currency, the [Soviet Union](RUS) cut road, rail and canal links to West Berlin, hoping to force them out. Instead the [United States](USA) and [Britain](GBR) supplied the city's two million people by air. Over eleven months planes flew in food, medicine and, above all, coal along three air corridors. In May 1949 Stalin gave up the blockade.

notes.DEU: West Berlin's 2 million people lived on rations. On Easter 1949 crews delivered nearly 13,000 tons in 24 hours, and the Soviets lifted the blockade on 12 May.
notes.USA: The US Air Force flew about three quarters of the cargo. About 278,000 flights in all brought about 2.3 million tons, nearly two thirds of it coal.
notes.GBR: The RAF and British civil airlines flew about a quarter of the cargo, much of it from bases around Hamburg and Hanover.
notes.CAN: Air crews from Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa flew with the RAF.
notes.AUS: Australian crews flew RAF transports into Berlin, and one Australian airman was among those killed in airlift accidents.
notes.FRA: France had few transport planes, but its engineers built Tegel airport in its sector, then blew up a Soviet-controlled radio mast that stood in the way.
notes.RUS: Stalin hoped to force the West out of Berlin or stop a separate West German state. The blockade failed, and it hastened both NATO and West Germany in 1949.

pn: West Berlin's main airport. At the peak, planes landed every few minutes, and the pilot Gail Halvorsen dropped sweets for children on tiny parachutes.
The RAF's airfield in the British sector, which also took flying boats landing on the nearby Havel lakes.
Built in the French sector in under 90 days in 1948, mostly by hand, with thousands of Berliners working on it.
The main US airlift base, at Frankfurt, with Wiesbaden nearby. The 'Air Bridge' memorial here matches one at Tempelhof.

dd-berlin.text: By 1961 over 2.5 million people had fled East [Germany](DEU), most through Berlin. On 13 August its government sealed the border with barbed wire, then a wall. The Wall stood for 28 years. In 1989, with Mikhail Gorbachev's [Soviet Union](RUS) no longer willing to use force, [Hungary](HUN) opened its border to [Austria](AUT), East Germans crowded embassies in [Czechoslovakia](CZE) and mass protests swept East Germany. On 9 November the Wall opened.

notes.DEU: The Wall ran about 155 km around West Berlin. At least 140 people were killed at it or died in connection with it, according to the Berlin Wall Memorial. Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.
notes.HUN: Hungary's reformers began removing the fence on the Austrian border in May 1989 and, on 11 September, let East Germans leave freely. Tens of thousands did.
notes.AUT: Neutral Austria was the gateway west. East Germans who crossed from Hungary travelled on to West Germany, which treated them as its own citizens.
notes.CZE: East Germans climbed into the West German embassy in Prague. Sealed trains took them west through East Germany, a humiliation for its rulers.
notes.POL: Poland's Solidarity movement won semi-free elections in June 1989, and East Germans also sought refuge in the West German embassy in Warsaw.
notes.RUS: Gorbachev's reforms let the Soviet bloc's peoples choose their own path, and Soviet troops stayed in their barracks. In 1990 he accepted a united Germany in NATO.
notes.USA: Presidents Kennedy, in 1963, and Reagan, in 1987, gave famous speeches in West Berlin: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' and 'Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'

pn: 9 November 1989: after a botched announcement, crowds gather, and at about 11.30 pm guards open the Bornholmer Strasse crossing.
9 October 1989: about 70,000 people march peacefully, chanting 'We are the people'. Security forces do not shoot.
September 1989: thousands of East Germans camp in the West German embassy garden. On 30 September they are told they may leave for the West.
19 August 1989: at the Pan-European Picnic, a border gate to Austria opens briefly and about 600 East Germans run through.

dd-partition.text: At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 British India became two countries: Hindu-majority [India](IND) and Muslim-majority [Pakistan](PAK), whose eastern wing is today's [Bangladesh](BGD). The provinces of Punjab and Bengal were cut in two by lines drawn in five weeks by a British lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, and published only after independence. Somewhere between 10 and 20 million people crossed the new borders, and hundreds of thousands were killed.

notes.IND: India received most of British India and about 330 million people, including some 35 million Muslims who stayed. It took over most of the 560-odd princely states, by persuasion or, in Hyderabad in 1948, by force.
notes.PAK: West Pakistan included western Punjab, Sindh, the North-West Frontier and Baluchistan. Millions of Muslim refugees from India arrived, and most Hindus and Sikhs left.
notes.BGD: Eastern Bengal became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by India. It had more people than the west but less power, which led to its breakaway in 1971.
notes.GBR: Britain, exhausted by war, brought forward its exit from June 1948 to August 1947. Lord Mountbatten, the last viceroy, argued speed would limit bloodshed; critics say haste made it worse.

pn: 15 August 1947: Jawaharlal Nehru becomes India's first prime minister. In September Muslims are killed in large numbers in the city, and many flee to Pakistan.
Pakistan's first capital, where Muhammad Ali Jinnah was sworn in as Governor-General on 15 August 1947.
A mixed city with many Hindus and Sikhs, it was awarded to Pakistan. Most of its non-Muslims fled east amid fires and killings.
The Sikhs' holiest city went to India. Trains of refugees reached it and Lahore carrying the dead, killed on the way.
16 August 1946: 'Direct Action Day' riots kill an estimated 4,000 people. In September 1947 Gandhi's fast helps calm the city.
October 1946: Hindus are attacked by Muslim mobs in eastern Bengal, and Gandhi walks from village to village appealing for peace.

dd-partition.text: Kashmir, a Muslim-majority princely state with a Hindu ruler, joined [India](IND) in October 1947 as tribal fighters from [Pakistan](PAK) invaded. The two fought wars over it in 1947–48 and 1965, and the 1971 war created [Bangladesh](BGD). Today India holds about 55% of the old state, Pakistan about 30% and [China](CHN) about 15%. Both India and Pakistan claim all of it, and in 1998 both tested nuclear weapons.
