notes.IND: India sees all of Kashmir as Indian by the 1947 accession. It has fought an insurgency in the valley since 1989, and in 2019 ended the region's special autonomy and split it into two union territories.
notes.PAK: Pakistan argues that Muslim-majority Kashmir should have been Pakistani and calls for the UN-backed plebiscite promised in 1948–49, which has never been held. India accuses it of backing militants.
notes.BGD: In 1971 Pakistan's army cracked down on Bengali nationalists. Death estimates range from 26,000, by a Pakistani inquiry, to 3 million, Bangladesh's official figure; about 10 million fled to India before India intervened.
notes.CHN: China controls Aksai Chin in the east, which India claims and lost in the 1962 war, and the Shaksgam valley, ceded by Pakistan in 1963.

pn: October 1947: Indian troops are flown in to defend the city after the Maharaja signs accession to India.
16 December 1971: Pakistan's forces in the east surrender to Indian and Bangladeshi forces, and about 90,000 soldiers and officials become prisoners. Bangladesh is born.
1999: India drives back Pakistani troops and militants from heights they had occupied, a year after both countries tested nuclear weapons.
Since 1984 Indian and Pakistani troops have faced each other here, at up to about 6,000 m. More have died from cold and avalanches than from fighting.
22 April 2025: gunmen kill 26 people, most of them tourists. India blames Pakistan, which denies it, and four days of military strikes between them follow in May.

dd-rwanda.text: On 6 April 1994 a plane carrying [Rwanda](RWA)'s Hutu president was shot down over Kigali. Within hours Hutu extremist militias and soldiers began killing Tutsi and moderate Hutu, at roadblocks and in churches where victims had sought refuge. In about 100 days some 800,000 people were killed, by UN estimates. The Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front, which had invaded from [Uganda](UGA) in 1990, ended the genocide by taking the country, and some 2 million Hutu fled, mostly into Zaire, now [DR Congo](COD).

notes.RWA: Rwanda's government counted over 1 million victims; the UN estimate is about 800,000, perhaps 70 percent of Rwanda's Tutsi. Between 250,000 and 500,000 women were raped, by UN estimates.
notes.UGA: Paul Kagame and other RPF leaders grew up as refugees in Uganda and fought in Yoweri Museveni's rebel army there before invading Rwanda in October 1990.
notes.COD: The camps around Goma and Bukavu held ordinary civilians but also the soldiers and militiamen who had led the genocide, and they soon rearmed.
notes.TZA: Hundreds of thousands fled east into Tanzania. The UN tribunal for Rwanda sat in Arusha, Tanzania, from 1994 to 2015 and convicted 62 people.
notes.BDI: Burundi's president, Cyprien Ntaryamira, also died in the plane. Burundi, with a similar Hutu–Tutsi divide, was itself in civil war from 1993.
notes.BEL: Belgium, the colonial ruler until 1962, had fixed Hutu and Tutsi as races on identity cards. Ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed on 7 April, and Belgium withdrew its troops.
notes.FRA: France was Habyarimana's close ally and armed his forces. A 2021 French inquiry found 'heavy and overwhelming responsibilities' but no complicity in the genocide. A report commissioned by Rwanda said France bore 'significant responsibility' for enabling it.
notes.USA: The UN, with US and British backing, cut its peacekeeping force from about 2,500 to 270 in April. President Clinton later called the failure to act one of his greatest regrets.

pn: 6 April 1994: President Habyarimana's plane is shot down; who fired is still disputed. The RPF takes the capital on 4 July.
April 1994: thousands of people sheltering in this Catholic church are killed. It is now a genocide memorial.
21 April 1994: tens of thousands of Tutsi lured to an unfinished school are killed in a few days. Bodies preserved in lime are displayed there today.
July 1994: about a million refugees pour into this Zairean town in days, and cholera kills tens of thousands in the camps.

dd-rwanda.text: In 1996 [Rwanda](RWA) and [Uganda](UGA) invaded Zaire to break up the Hutu militia camps and backed Laurent-Désiré Kabila, who toppled the dictator Mobutu in May 1997 and renamed the country [DR Congo](COD). When Kabila turned on his backers in 1998 they invaded again. [Angola](AGO), [Zimbabwe](ZWE) and [Namibia](NAM) sent troops to save him. Nine African countries and dozens of armed groups fought, often over gold, diamonds and coltan.

notes.COD: A 2008 survey by the International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million excess deaths in 1998–2007, mostly from disease and hunger; other researchers think the toll was lower. A transitional government took office in 2003.
notes.RWA: Rwanda said it was hunting the génocidaires. A UN panel in 2001 accused it, and Uganda, of plundering eastern Congo's minerals. Rwanda withdrew its troops after the 2002 Pretoria Accord.
notes.UGA: Uganda backed its own rebel movements in the north-east. In 2005 the International Court of Justice found it had illegally occupied parts of Congo.
notes.BDI: Burundi sent troops to fight Hutu rebels from Burundi who were based in eastern Congo.
notes.AGO: Angola intervened to protect Kinshasa and to deny bases to its own UNITA rebels. Its tanks and planes stopped a rebel advance on the capital in 1998.
notes.ZWE: Zimbabwe sent up to about 11,000 troops. Its generals and businessmen won mining and timber deals in return.
notes.NAM: Namibia sent a smaller force to back Kabila, alongside its allies Angola and Zimbabwe.
notes.TCD: Chad sent about 2,000 troops to support Kabila in 1998–99.

pn: 17 May 1997: Kabila's rebels enter the capital as Mobutu flees after 32 years in power. Kabila is assassinated here in January 2001.
1999–2000: former allies Rwanda and Uganda fight each other three times for this river city, killing hundreds of civilians.
2003: ethnic militias massacre civilians in Ituri; a French-led EU force is sent to restore order.
July 1999: a ceasefire signed here leads to a UN peacekeeping mission, but the fighting goes on.

dd-rwanda.text: The war never fully ended in eastern [DR Congo](COD), home to over 100 armed groups. In January 2025 the M23 rebels, backed by [Rwanda](RWA) according to UN experts and the US, seized Goma, then Bukavu. Rwanda denies directing M23 and cites the threat of Hutu militias. A US-brokered peace deal was signed in Washington in December 2025, and Qatar mediated talks with M23, but in October 2026 the rebels still held both cities.

notes.COD: About 7 million people were displaced inside Congo in 2025, by UN counts. In October 2026 former president Joseph Kabila, sentenced to death in absentia in 2025, launched a new anti-government front with M23 in Goma.
notes.RWA: UN experts reported thousands of Rwandan troops in Congo. In March 2026 the US sanctioned Rwanda's army, which Rwanda called one-sided; Kigali says the Hutu FDLR militia, founded by génocidaires, threatens it.
notes.UGA: Since 2021 Uganda's army has fought the ADF, an Islamic State-linked militia, inside Congo. UN experts have also accused Uganda of tolerating support for M23, which it denies.
notes.BDI: Burundi sent thousands of troops to fight alongside Congo's army against M23, which it sees as backed by its rival, Rwanda.
notes.USA: The US brokered a Congo–Rwanda deal signed in June 2025, and the Washington Accords signed by Presidents Tshisekedi and Kagame in December, linked to US access to Congo's minerals.
notes.QAT: Qatar hosted direct talks between Congo's government and M23, producing a framework agreement in November 2025 and a ceasefire-monitoring deal in February 2026.

pn: January 2025: M23 takes the city of about 2 million; the UN said about 3,000 people were killed in the fighting.
February 2025: M23 takes South Kivu's capital with little resistance.
December 2025: M23 seizes this lake port days after the Washington signing, then withdraws under US pressure.
A coltan mine that produces a large share of the world's supply, controlled by M23 since 2024, according to UN experts.

dd-ukraine.text: [Ukraine](UKR) became independent in 1991 with its Soviet borders, Crimea included. From 1999 NATO took in former Soviet-bloc states, from [Poland](POL) to the Baltic states: [Russia](RUS) called this a threat, the new members called it protection. In 2014, after protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president, Russia seized and annexed Crimea, and Russian-backed separatists took part of the Donbas. About 14,000 people died in that war by 2021.

notes.UKR: Ukraine declared independence in August 1991 and over 90% voted for it that December. Its politics swung between leaders looking to Europe and to Russia, until protests in 2014 toppled President Yanukovych.
notes.RUS: Russia saw NATO's growth as a betrayal and a threat. In 2014 it annexed Crimea after a referendum held under its troops that the UN General Assembly called invalid, and armed separatists in the Donbas, at first denying it.
notes.POL: Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004. Like other former Soviet-bloc states, it sought NATO membership as protection from Russia.
notes.EST: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Soviet republics until 1991, joined NATO in 2004, bringing the alliance to Russia's border.
notes.LVA: Latvia joined NATO and the EU in 2004. About a quarter of its people are ethnic Russians.
notes.LTU: Lithuania, the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in 1990, joined NATO in 2004.
notes.BLR: Belarus stayed Russia's close ally under Alexander Lukashenko, in power since 1994. The Minsk ceasefire deals for the Donbas were signed in its capital in 2014–15.
notes.DEU: Germany and France brokered the Minsk deals of 2014–15 with Russia and Ukraine. They lowered the fighting but were never fully carried out.
notes.FRA: France and Germany mediated between Russia and Ukraine in the 'Normandy format', first held in June 2014.
notes.USA: The US signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum and backed NATO's enlargement. After 2014 it sanctioned Russia and trained and armed Ukraine's army.
notes.GBR: Britain also signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which gave Ukraine assurances but no promise of military defence.
notes.GEO: Georgia fought a five-day war with Russia in August 2008, months after NATO promised it future membership. Russia then recognised two breakaway regions.

pn: December 1994: in the Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the US and Britain promise to respect Ukraine's borders as it gives up its nuclear weapons.
April 2008: a NATO summit declares that Ukraine and Georgia 'will become members', but sets no timetable.
November 2013–February 2014: protests in Kyiv's Independence Square. About 100 protesters are killed before President Yanukovych flees.
Home of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, leased from Ukraine after 1991. In March 2014 Russia annexed Crimea.
17 July 2014: a Malaysia Airlines jet is shot down by a Russian Buk missile, investigators found, killing all 298 on board.

dd-ukraine.text: On 24 February 2022 Russia attacked from the north, east and south, partly from [Belarus](BLR). It failed to take Kyiv and pulled back from the north by early April. Ukrainian counter-offensives freed most of Kharkiv region and the city of Kherson that autumn, but a 2023 offensive stalled. Since then [Russia](RUS) has advanced slowly and at great cost. In October 2026 it held about a fifth of [Ukraine](UKR), and the fighting went on.

notes.UKR: Ukraine's army has an estimated 125,000–150,000 dead (CSIS, mid-2026). The UN had verified over 16,000 civilian deaths by mid-2026 and says the true number is much higher. About 5.8 million Ukrainians lived abroad as refugees.
notes.RUS: Russia called the war a 'special military operation'. CSIS estimated up to 450,000 Russian soldiers dead by mid-2026; Russia publishes no full figures. In September 2022 it claimed to annex four Ukrainian regions it did not fully control.
notes.BLR: Belarus let Russian troops invade from its territory in 2022 and later hosted Russian tactical nuclear weapons, but its own army has not fought in Ukraine.
notes.POL: Poland became the main route for Western weapons into Ukraine and took in millions of refugees, close to a million of whom remained in 2026.
notes.MDA: Moldova, Ukraine's south-western neighbour, has Russian troops in its breakaway region of Transnistria. It became an EU candidate alongside Ukraine in 2022.

pn: February–March 2022: Russian columns from Belarus reach the capital's outskirts but cannot take it, and withdraw by early April.
March 2022: after Russian troops left this suburb, the bodies of hundreds of civilians were found; Russia denied responsibility.
February–May 2022: Russia besieges and takes the port city. The last defenders, in the Azovstal steelworks, surrender in May.
November 2022: Russian forces pull back across the Dnipro, and Ukraine retakes the only regional capital Russia had seized in 2022.
Europe's largest nuclear power plant, held by Russian forces since March 2022 and shut down.
December 2025: Russia claims this road and rail hub after more than a year of fighting. By February 2026 analysts judged it held the whole town.

dd-ukraine.text: Most of Europe, the [United States](USA), [Japan](JPN) and their allies sanctioned [Russia](RUS) and armed or funded [Ukraine](UKR). Russia drew on [Iranian](IRN) drone designs, and in late 2024 [North Korea](PRK) sent thousands of troops to help it fight. Much of the world stayed neutral: [China](CHN), [India](IND) and [Turkey](TUR) became the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which kept its war economy going.

notes.UKR: Ukraine depended on Western weapons and money but built a huge drone industry of its own, striking deep into Russia at refineries and airfields.
notes.RUS: Sanctions cut Russia off from most Western trade and froze about $300 billion of its central bank reserves. It redirected oil exports to Asia and turned its economy towards arms production.
notes.USA: The US was Ukraine's largest single supplier of weapons in 2022–24. From 2025 the Trump administration cut direct aid, sold arms through European buyers and led peace talks.
notes.DEU: Germany became Ukraine's largest European arms supplier and ended its dependence on Russian gas, which had supplied over half its imports before the war.
notes.GBR: Britain trained tens of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers from 2022 and was among the first to send tanks and long-range missiles.
notes.FIN: Finland, neutral for decades, joined NATO in April 2023 because of the invasion, doubling NATO's land border with Russia.
notes.SWE: Sweden ended about two centuries of military non-alignment and joined NATO in March 2024.
notes.HUN: Hungary, though an EU and NATO member, kept close ties with Moscow under Viktor Orbán and often delayed EU aid and sanctions. Orbán lost power after an election in April 2026.
notes.BLR: Belarus served as a launch pad for the 2022 invasion and stayed Russia's closest ally.
notes.IRN: Iran supplied Shahed attack drones from 2022. Russia later built its own version, the Geran-2, in large numbers.
notes.PRK: North Korea sent about 11,000–12,000 troops in late 2024, who fought to push Ukrainian forces out of Russia's Kursk region, and supplied millions of artillery shells.
notes.CHN: China declared a 'no limits' partnership with Russia weeks before the invasion. It did not openly send weapons but supplied machine parts and electronics and bought much of Russia's oil.
notes.IND: India stayed neutral and became one of the largest buyers of discounted Russian oil, which strained its ties with the US.
notes.TUR: Turkey, a NATO member, sold drones to Ukraine but did not sanction Russia. It helped broker the 2022 Black Sea grain deal and hosted early peace talks.

dd-terror.text: On 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people in the [United States](USA). Al-Qaeda's leader, Osama bin Laden, was sheltered by the Taliban in [Afghanistan](AFG). A US-led invasion toppled the Taliban within weeks, and a NATO-led force from about 50 countries later joined. Bin Laden was killed in [Pakistan](PAK) in 2011. In August 2021, as US troops left, the Taliban retook Kabul.

notes.USA: About 2,400 US service members died in Afghanistan, the longest war in US history. The US also spent over $2 trillion there, by the Costs of War project's estimate.
notes.AFG: The Costs of War project estimates about 176,000 people were killed directly in the war, including over 46,000 Afghan civilians. In 2021 the Taliban restored strict rule, barring girls from secondary school.
notes.PAK: Pakistan was a key US ally and supply route, but the Taliban leadership operated from its territory. US drone strikes there killed thousands from 2004, among them hundreds of civilians by independent counts.
notes.GBR: Britain sent the second-largest force, up to about 9,500 troops, mostly in Helmand province. 457 British service personnel died.
notes.CAN: Canada fought in Kandahar province from 2006 to 2011, and 158 Canadian soldiers died.
notes.DEU: Germany led the mission in the quieter north and kept troops there until 2021, its first ground war since 1945.
notes.AUS: Australia sent troops from 2001 to 2021. A 2020 inquiry found credible evidence that some special forces soldiers unlawfully killed 39 Afghans.

pn: 11 September 2001: two hijacked airliners hit the Twin Towers, which collapse within two hours. About 2,750 people die in New York.
11 September 2001: a third plane hits the US Defense Department's headquarters, killing 184 people on board and in the building.
11 September 2001: passengers fight the hijackers of a fourth plane, which crashes in a field, killing all 40 passengers and crew.
December 2001: bin Laden escapes US-backed Afghan forces from these mountain caves into Pakistan.
2 May 2011: US Navy SEALs kill bin Laden in a compound near Pakistan's military academy.
15 August 2021: the Taliban enter Kabul. A suicide bombing at the airport on 26 August kills about 170 Afghans and 13 US troops.

dd-terror.text: In March 2003 the [United States](USA) and [Britain](GBR), with [Australia](AUS) and [Poland](POL), invaded [Iraq](IRQ), saying Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction; none were found. [France](FRA), [Germany](DEU) and [Russia](RUS) opposed the war at the UN. Saddam fell within weeks, but an insurgency, al-Qaeda bombings and a sectarian civil war between Sunni and Shia followed. US troops left at the end of 2011.

notes.USA: About 4,400 US troops died in Iraq. A troop 'surge' in 2007 and a deal with Sunni tribes reduced the violence before the US withdrew in 2011.
notes.IRQ: Iraq Body Count has documented about 190,000 to 210,000 civilian deaths by violence since 2003; other estimates are far higher. Disbanding Saddam's army and party left many angry and jobless men.
notes.GBR: Prime Minister Tony Blair backed the war despite huge protests. The 2016 Chilcot inquiry found that Britain went to war before peaceful options were exhausted, on flawed intelligence.
notes.AUS: Australia sent about 2,000 personnel for the invasion, including special forces, ships and aircraft.
notes.POL: Poland sent special forces for the invasion and later commanded a multinational zone in south-central Iraq.
notes.ESP: Spain withdrew its troops in 2004, after al-Qaeda-inspired bombers killed 193 people on Madrid commuter trains.
notes.FRA: France threatened to veto a UN resolution authorising force, arguing that weapons inspections should continue.
notes.DEU: Germany, which had troops in Afghanistan, refused to join the Iraq war.
notes.RUS: Russia opposed the invasion at the UN, calling it unjustified.

pn: 9 April 2003: US troops reach central Baghdad and a statue of Saddam is pulled down. He was captured in December and executed in 2006.
April 2004: photos of US soldiers abusing Iraqi prisoners at this prison cause outrage around the world.
2004: US forces fight two battles for this Sunni insurgent stronghold, the bloodiest urban fighting of the war for American troops.
22 February 2006: al-Qaeda in Iraq bombs a revered Shia shrine, setting off waves of sectarian killing.
British forces held southern Iraq around Basra from 2003 until 2009. 179 British service personnel died in the war.

dd-terror.text: Al-Qaeda in Iraq survived, and in Syria's civil war it was reborn as the Islamic State, or ISIS. In June 2014 it seized Mosul in [Iraq](IRQ) and declared a 'caliphate' across Iraq and [Syria](SYR), ruling millions of people by terror. Groups in [Libya](LBY), [Egypt](EGY), [Nigeria](NGA) and [Afghanistan](AFG) pledged loyalty. A US-led coalition and local forces destroyed the caliphate by March 2019, but ISIS cells survive.

notes.IRQ: ISIS swept across Sunni areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014, as the Iraqi army collapsed. Iraq declared victory in December 2017.
notes.SYR: ISIS grew in the chaos of Syria's civil war, ruling the east from Raqqa. Kurdish-led forces, with US support, did most of the ground fighting against it.
notes.LBY: ISIS held the coastal city of Sirte in 2015–16, amid Libya's civil war.
notes.EGY: An ISIS affiliate fought Egypt's army in northern Sinai and claimed the 2015 bombing of a Russian airliner that killed 224 people.
notes.NGA: Boko Haram pledged loyalty to ISIS in 2015. Its ISIS-backed faction, Islamic State West Africa Province, still fights around Lake Chad.
notes.AFG: ISIS's Khorasan branch appeared in 2015. It is a rival of the Taliban and carried out the 2021 Kabul airport bombing.
notes.YEM: ISIS gained a small foothold in Yemen's civil war, though al-Qaeda's local branch remained stronger there.

pn: June 2014: ISIS takes Iraq's second city; in July its leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi appears in its great mosque. Iraqi forces retake it in July 2017 after nine months of fighting.
August 2014: ISIS kills thousands of Yazidi men and enslaves thousands of women and children, crimes UN investigators called genocide.
The caliphate's capital in Syria. Kurdish-led forces backed by US air power take it in October 2017.
March 2019: ISIS loses its last village. Al-Baghdadi is killed in a US raid in October 2019.
13 November 2015: ISIS gunmen and suicide bombers kill 130 people at a concert hall, cafes and the national stadium.
2015–16: ISIS holds Gaddafi's home town on Libya's coast until Libyan forces, backed by US air strikes, drive it out.

dd-syria.text: In December 2010 a street vendor in [Tunisia](TUN) set himself on fire after officials confiscated his goods, and protests spread across the Arab world. Within about a year rulers fell in Tunisia, [Egypt](EGY), [Libya](LBY) and [Yemen](YEM). In [Bahrain](BHR) the uprising was crushed with Saudi-led help, and in [Syria](SYR) peaceful protests met gunfire and turned into civil war. Elsewhere kings and presidents offered money or reforms.

notes.TUN: President Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011 after 23 years in power. Tunisia was long the Arab Spring's one democratic success, until President Kais Saied took sweeping powers in 2021.
notes.EGY: Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011. The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 election, but the army removed him in July 2013, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi became president.
notes.LBY: Rebels backed by NATO air strikes overthrew Muammar Gaddafi, who was killed in October 2011. Libya later split between rival governments in Tripoli and the east, still divided in 2026.
notes.YEM: President Ali Abdullah Saleh handed power to his deputy in 2012. In 2014 the Houthi movement took the capital, Sanaa, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015.
notes.SYR: President Bashar al-Assad called the protesters foreign-backed terrorists and sent in the army. By 2012 armed rebellion had become full civil war.
notes.BHR: Mainly Shia protesters demanded reform from the Sunni monarchy. Gulf troops helped crush the movement, and many activists were jailed.
notes.MAR: King Mohammed VI offered a new constitution, approved by referendum in July 2011, that gave parliament and the prime minister more power.
notes.DZA: Algeria lifted a 19-year state of emergency and raised spending. Mass protests came later, in 2019, and forced out President Bouteflika.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia announced well over $100 billion in spending on jobs and housing, and banned protests. It sent troops to Bahrain.

pn: 17 December 2010: Mohamed Bouazizi sets himself on fire here. His death in January sparks nationwide protests.
January–February 2011: hundreds of thousands camp in Cairo's main square for 18 days until Mubarak resigns.
February 2011: Libya's revolt begins here. In March a UN-authorised, NATO-led air campaign stops Gaddafi's forces retaking the city.
March 2011: arrests of teenagers for anti-government graffiti spark protests that spread across Syria.
March 2011: troops from Saudi Arabia and the UAE arrive, and the protest camp at the Pearl Roundabout is cleared.

dd-syria.text: Syria's war drew in the world. [Russia](RUS), [Iran](IRN) and Lebanon's Hezbollah fought for Assad. [Turkey](TUR), the Gulf states and Western countries backed rebel groups, and a [US](USA)-led coalition bombed the Islamic State. Over half of Syria's 22 million people were driven from their homes; more than 6 million fled abroad, many to [Lebanon](LBN), [Jordan](JOR) and Turkey, and about a million reached Europe, mostly [Germany](DEU).

notes.SYR: The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitor, counted over 600,000 dead by 2025. In 2022 the UN estimated about 307,000 civilians killed in 2011–2021.
notes.RUS: Russia began air strikes in September 2015, turning the war in Assad's favour. Its bases at Hmeimim and Tartus gave it a foothold on the Mediterranean.
notes.IRN: Iran sent Revolutionary Guard officers and organised militias from Lebanon, Iraq, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Syria was its land bridge to Hezbollah.
notes.USA: The US armed some rebels, then from 2014 led a coalition of over 80 countries against the Islamic State, partnering with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
notes.TUR: Turkey hosted about 3.7 million Syrian refugees at the peak, more than any other country. From 2016 its army and allied Syrian factions took strips of the north, mainly to push back Kurdish forces it links to the PKK.
notes.LBN: Lebanon took in over a million registered Syrian refugees, about one in five of its residents at the peak. Hezbollah fought for Assad from 2012–13.
notes.JOR: Jordan registered about 650,000 Syrian refugees; its government put the total at about 1.3 million. Za'atari camp became one of the world's largest.
notes.DEU: In 2015 Chancellor Angela Merkel kept Germany's borders open. Germany took in more Syrians than any other EU country, close to a million by 2024.
notes.ISR: Israel stayed out of the ground war but carried out hundreds of air strikes on Iranian and Hezbollah targets in Syria.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia and Qatar funded and armed rival rebel groups, many of them Islamist, especially in 2012–2015.

pn: 21 August 2013: a sarin attack kills hundreds near Damascus; UN investigators later blamed other attacks on the government.
December 2016: after four years of fighting, government forces backed by Russia and Iran retake the rebel-held east of the city.
2014–2017: the Islamic State's de facto capital, taken by Kurdish-led forces with US air support in October 2017.
From 2015: the last big rebel stronghold, dominated by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. A Russian–Turkish ceasefire held there from March 2020.

dd-syria.text: On 27 November 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham swept out of Idlib, and on 8 December Assad fled to [Russia](RUS). The HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa became interim president. [Turkey](TUR), [Saudi Arabia](SAU) and [Qatar](QAT) backed the new government, and the [United States](USA) lifted sanctions in 2025. Sectarian killings shook the coast and Suwayda in 2025. In January 2026 Damascus took Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and the oil fields from the Kurdish-led SDF, while [Israel](ISR) kept troops in the south.

notes.SYR: A March 2025 constitutional declaration set a five-year transition. By mid-2026 UNHCR counted over 1.7 million refugees and nearly 2 million displaced Syrians returned home, but much of the country lay in ruins.
notes.TUR: Turkey was HTS's main outside patron in Idlib and became the new government's closest ally, helping rebuild its army.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia hosted Sharaa's first foreign trip in February 2025, paid off some of Syria's World Bank debt with Qatar, and promised investment.
notes.QAT: Qatar, which never restored ties with Assad, funded salaries and electricity supplies and helped broker deals for the new government.
notes.USA: Sharaa once led al-Qaeda's Syrian branch, but broke with it in 2016. The US dropped its bounty on him, lifted sanctions, repealed the Caesar Act in December 2025, and hosted him at the White House.
notes.ISR: Israel seized the buffer zone after Assad fell, citing security, and bombed much of Syria's old army. It says it protects the Druze; Damascus calls its presence an occupation.
notes.RUS: Russia gave Assad and his family asylum in Moscow. In August 2026 Damascus and Moscow agreed to turn its Hmeimim and Tartus bases into joint training centres; a final deal was still pending in October.
notes.IRN: Assad's fall cut Iran's land route to Hezbollah. In 2026, during Iran's war with Israel and the US, Syria did not join the fighting.

pn: 8 December 2024: rebels enter the capital and Assad's family rule, begun by his father in 1970, ends.
March 2025: after attacks by Assad loyalists, a government inquiry found over 1,400 people, mostly Alawite civilians, were killed.
July 2025: clashes between Druze fighters, Bedouin tribes and government forces kill over 1,700, a UN inquiry found; Israel strikes Damascus.
January 2026: after a short government offensive, the SDF hands over Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and the oil fields.
From December 2024: Israeli troops hold the UN buffer zone on the Golan and positions beyond it. US-mediated security talks had produced no deal by October 2026.

dd-humans.text: Our species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa: the oldest known fossils, about 300,000 years old, come from [Morocco](MAR). We were not alone. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia, from [Spain](ESP) to [Uzbekistan](UZB) and as far as Siberia, and their cousins the Denisovans across eastern Asia, from Siberia in [Russia](RUS) to [China](CHN). On the island of Flores, in [Indonesia](IDN), lived the tiny Homo floresiensis.

notes.MAR: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, dated to about 300,000 years ago, showed in 2017 that Homo sapiens was older, and more widespread in Africa, than once thought.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia has some of the oldest Homo sapiens fossils, from Omo Kibish and Herto, and much older human ancestors, such as 'Lucy', about 3.2 million years old.
notes.ZAF: Caves on South Africa's south coast, such as Blombos and Pinnacle Point, show people collecting shellfish, using ochre and making beads well over 70,000 years ago.
notes.ESP: Neanderthals lived in Iberia until about 40,000 years ago or a little later. Gibraltar, at its southern tip, was one of their last known homes.
notes.FRA: France has many Neanderthal sites, including burials such as La Chapelle-aux-Saints. Whether Neanderthals buried their dead on purpose is still debated, though most experts now think some did.
notes.ISR: Caves on Mount Carmel were home both to early Homo sapiens, from about 180,000 years ago, and later to Neanderthals: a meeting ground of the two.
notes.IRQ: At Shanidar Cave, in Iraqi Kurdistan, Neanderthals cared for a man who lived for years with a withered arm and other injuries.
notes.UZB: A Neanderthal child was found at Teshik-Tash in 1938. DNA later showed Neanderthals ranged even further east, to Siberia's Altai mountains.
notes.RUS: Denisova Cave, in the Altai mountains, held both Neanderthals and Denisovans. One girl from there, 'Denny', had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
notes.CHN: A skull found in Harbin in 1933 was identified in 2025, from ancient proteins and DNA, as Denisovan. A Denisovan jaw was also found high on the Tibetan Plateau.
notes.TWN: A jaw dredged up by fishermen from the seabed off Taiwan's Penghu islands, once dry land, was identified as a Denisovan man's in 2025.
notes.LAO: A child's tooth from Cobra Cave, in northern Laos, between about 164,000 and 131,000 years old, is probably Denisovan.
notes.IDN: Homo floresiensis lived on Flores from at least 100,000 to about 60,000 years ago. Small-bodied humans, probably its ancestors, were on the island 700,000 years ago.
notes.GBR: Neanderthals came and went in Britain as ice sheets advanced and retreated, and Britain was often joined to the continent by land.

pn: Skulls and teeth found here were dated in 2017 to about 300,000 years ago, the oldest known Homo sapiens.
Omo I, found in 1967, is at least 230,000 years old, by a 2022 dating of the volcanic ash above it.
c. 75,000 years ago: people here engraved a piece of ochre with criss-cross lines, among the oldest known designs.
1856: quarrymen found bones in a cave here, near Düsseldorf. The valley gave the Neanderthals their name.
2010: DNA from a finger bone found here revealed a human group no one knew existed, the Denisovans.
2003: the skeleton of a tiny adult human was found in this cave, nicknamed 'the hobbit' by the press.

dd-humans.text: Small groups of Homo sapiens had left Africa before, but the great spread began roughly 60,000–50,000 years ago. People followed coasts across Asia and crossed open sea to reach [Australia](AUS) by at least 50,000 years ago. They entered Europe by about 45,000 years ago. During the last Ice Age, sea levels were lower, and people walked from Siberia into Alaska, then down to [Chile](CHL) by about 14,500 years ago.

notes.AUS: People reached Australia by at least 50,000 years ago, and some researchers argue 65,000, crossing open sea from Indonesia. Aboriginal Australians have one of the longest continuous cultures on Earth.
notes.CHL: Monte Verde, in southern Chile, showed that people had reached the far south of the Americas by about 14,500 years ago, earlier than once thought.
notes.IDN: Islands such as Sulawesi were stepping stones to Australia. A hand stencil on Muna, off Sulawesi, is at least 67,800 years old.
notes.PNG: New Guinea was joined to Australia when seas were low. Papuans carry about 4% Denisovan DNA, among the highest shares of any living people, though the Ayta Magbukon of the Philippines carry more.
notes.FRA: Ice Age artists painted Chauvet Cave about 36,000 years ago, and Lascaux about 17,000 years ago, with horses, lions and bulls.
notes.USA: People crossed from Siberia over Beringia, a land bridge exposed by low seas. Footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, may show people there over 20,000 years ago.
notes.JPN: People crossed to Japan by about 38,000 years ago, possibly by boat, and were making some of the world's earliest pottery by about 16,000 years ago.
notes.RUS: Hunters reached the Arctic coast of Siberia by about 32,000 years ago, at the Yana site, surviving extreme cold with sewn clothing and mammoth hunting.
notes.GBR: Ice sheets drove people out of Britain more than once. It has been lived in continuously only since about 12,000 years ago.
notes.NZL: New Zealand was among the last large lands to be settled, by Polynesian voyagers around AD 1250–1300. Iceland was settled about 870.
notes.IND: Modern humans passed through South Asia on the coastal route. Stone tools from Jwalapuram, buried by a huge eruption 74,000 years ago, may be theirs or another species'.
notes.CAN: At the height of the Ice Age, ice sheets covered almost all of Canada. People probably first moved south along the Pacific coast, or later through an ice-free corridor.
notes.NOR: Ice sheets covered Scandinavia, and people settled Norway, Sweden and Finland only as the ice melted, after about 13,000 years ago.

pn: At least 67,800 years ago: a hand stencil in a cave on this island off Sulawesi, the oldest dated rock art known, reported in 2026.
c. 42,000 years ago: a man was buried here sprinkled with red ochre, the oldest known ritual burial in Australia.
c. 45,000 years ago: bones from this Bulgarian cave are among the oldest Homo sapiens remains in Europe.
Human footprints here were dated to 21,000–23,000 years ago, an early arrival in the Americas that some experts still question.
c. 14,500 years ago: a camp with huts, food remains and a footprint, widely accepted as proof of people in South America by then.

dd-humans.text: As the Ice Age ended, people in several places tamed wild plants and animals, each on their own. Wheat, barley, sheep and goats came first, about 9500 BC, in the Fertile Crescent, from [Turkey](TUR) to [Iraq](IRQ). Rice and millet followed in [China](CHN), taro and bananas in [Papua New Guinea](PNG), maize and squash in [Mexico](MEX), and potatoes and llamas in the Andes of [Peru](PER).

notes.TUR: South-east Turkey was part of the Fertile Crescent. Einkorn wheat was first domesticated near the Karacadağ hills, and cattle and pigs were tamed nearby.
notes.IRQ: Goats were domesticated in the Zagros mountains of Iraq and Iran around 8000 BC. Farming later spread into the dry plains, where irrigation fed the first cities.
notes.ISR: The Natufians, who lived in caves and villages on Mount Carmel and around the Sea of Galilee, gathered wild cereals and settled down even before farming began.
notes.PSE: Jericho, in the Jordan valley, was among the first farming villages, from about 9500 BC. Figs may have been grown at nearby Gilgal even before cereals.
notes.SYR: At Abu Hureyra on the Euphrates, hunter-gatherers became farmers over a few thousand years. Their bones show the strain of grinding grain all day.
notes.CHN: Foxtail and broomcorn millet were domesticated in the Yellow River valley, and rice along the Yangtze, from about 8000 BC. Pigs and later silkworms followed.
notes.PNG: New Guinea's highlanders invented farming on their own, one of the clearest independent centres. Kuk Swamp is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
notes.MEX: Maize was bred from a wild grass, teosinte, in the Balsas valley about 9,000 years ago. Early cobs were barely the size of a thumb.
notes.PER: Andean farmers bred thousands of potato varieties from about 8,000 years ago, and tamed llamas and alpacas for wool, meat and transport.
notes.BOL: The potato was probably first domesticated near Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia.
notes.SDN: Sorghum was domesticated in the Sahel, with early evidence from eastern Sudan about 3000 BC. Africa also gave the world coffee, yams and African rice.
notes.USA: In eastern North America, people domesticated sunflowers, squash and other seed plants on their own, from about 3000–2000 BC.
notes.EGY: Farming reached Egypt from the Fertile Crescent around 5000 BC, with wheat, barley, sheep and goats, and fed the Nile valley's later kingdoms.

pn: c. 7100–5950 BC: a farming town of perhaps several thousand people, whose mud-brick houses were entered through the roof.
Seeds suggest hunter-gatherers here may have grown rye around 11,000 BC, a claim some experts dispute. The site now lies under Lake Assad.
c. 8000 BC: villagers on the lower Yangtze tempered their pottery with rice husks, early evidence of rice cultivation.
By about 5000 BC, and perhaps far earlier, highlanders here dug drains and mounds to grow taro and bananas.
Squash seeds from this cave in Oaxaca, about 10,000 years old, are among the oldest domesticated plants in the Americas.

dd-languages.text: Most scholars think the ancestor of English, Hindi, Persian and Russian was spoken around 4000–3000 BC on the steppes of today's [Ukraine](UKR) and southern [Russia](RUS), by herders who used horses and wagons. Their descendants carried related languages west into Europe and south-east to [Iran](IRN) and [India](IND). By 500 BC they were spoken from [Ireland](IRL) to the Ganges valley. Today almost half the world speaks one.

notes.UKR: The leading theory places the Indo-European homeland on the steppe north of the Black Sea. Herders of the Yamnaya culture, c. 3300–2600 BC, are widely linked to the spread.
notes.RUS: The southern Russian steppe, between the Volga and the Don, is part of the most widely accepted homeland. Ancient DNA shows steppe herders moved west into Europe around 3000–2500 BC.
notes.IRN: Old Persian and Avestan, the language of Zoroastrian scripture, belong to the Iranian branch. Persian, Kurdish and Pashto descend from it.
notes.IND: Sanskrit, the language of the Rigveda, composed around 1500–1200 BC, is Indo-European. Hindi, Bengali and Marathi descend from it, but South India's Dravidian languages, such as Tamil, are a separate family.
notes.IRL: Celtic languages, including Irish, reached Ireland and Britain by the first millennium BC.
notes.GRC: Greek is the European branch with the longest written record, from Linear B tablets of about 1400 BC.
notes.TUR: The Hittites of central Anatolia wrote the first known Indo-European texts. Their branch died out, and Turkish, which arrived much later, belongs to a different family.
notes.CHN: Tocharian was written in Buddhist texts from the Tarim Basin around AD 500–800, thousands of kilometres east of its relatives.
notes.ESP: Celtic and other Indo-European languages spread into Iberia, but non-Indo-European Iberian and the ancestor of Basque survived. Basque is still spoken today.
notes.ITA: Latin was one of several Italic languages. Etruscan, spoken in Tuscany, was not Indo-European and died out under Roman rule.
notes.FIN: Finnish, like Estonian and Hungarian, belongs to the separate Uralic family.
notes.DEU: Germanic languages, ancestors of German, English, Dutch and the Scandinavian tongues, developed in northern Germany and southern Scandinavia.

pn: c. 1650–1200 BC: capital of the Hittites, whose clay tablets are the oldest substantial texts in any Indo-European language.
c. 1400–1200 BC: Mycenaean palace scribes write an early form of Greek in the Linear B script.

dd-languages.text: Conquest, trade and religion spread a few languages across continents. Arabic moved out of [Arabia](SAU) with Islam after 632. From 1492 [Spain](ESP) and [Portugal](PRT) took their languages to the Americas and beyond, and [Britain](GBR) and [France](FRA) planted English and French on every continent. Darker colours show where it became most people's mother tongue, lighter colours where it is an official or main second language.

notes.SAU: Arabic spread from Arabia with the Islamic conquests after 632. It replaced Aramaic, Coptic and Berber languages as the everyday tongue from Iraq to Morocco over several centuries.
notes.EGY: Egyptians gradually switched from Coptic, the last stage of ancient Egyptian, to Arabic. Coptic survives only in church services.
notes.IRN: Iran converted to Islam but kept Persian, which borrowed many Arabic words and adopted the Arabic script.
notes.MAR: Arabic is the main language, but about a quarter or more of Moroccans speak a Berber (Amazigh) language, official since 2011.
notes.ESP: Spanish, or Castilian, spread across Spain during the Reconquista and to the Americas after 1492. Today it has about 500 million native speakers, second only to Mandarin.
notes.MEX: Mexico has the most Spanish speakers of any country, about 130 million, though it still has 68 recognised Indigenous languages, such as Nahuatl and Maya.
notes.PRY: Paraguay is officially bilingual. Most Paraguayans speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language, often alongside Spanish.
notes.BRA: Portuguese colonisers and settlers made Brazil the world's largest Portuguese-speaking country, with over 200 million people.
notes.AGO: Portuguese is Angola's official language and, especially in cities, increasingly the first language of young people.
notes.GBR: English grew from the Germanic dialects of Anglo-Saxon settlers after AD 400, absorbing Norse and Norman French words.
notes.USA: The United States has no official language at federal level in law, though a 2025 executive order designated English. Its economic and cultural power spread English worldwide after 1945.
notes.IND: British rule made English the language of law and higher education. India still uses it, alongside Hindi, as an official language of its central government.
notes.NGA: Nigeria has over 500 languages, and English, the colonial language, is the official language that links them.
notes.FRA: French spread across France itself only gradually: in 1794 Abbé Grégoire reported that only about 3 million of some 28 million people spoke it well.
notes.COD: DR Congo, a former Belgian colony, is the most populous country with French as its official language, though most Congolese speak it as a second language.
notes.HTI: Most Haitians speak Haitian Creole, which grew from French, as their mother tongue. Both are official.
notes.CAN: Most Canadians speak English, but French, brought by settlers from the 1600s, is the main language of Quebec. Both are official.

pn: 632: the Prophet Muhammad dies here. Within a century Arab armies reach Spain and Central Asia, and Arabic, the language of the Quran, spreads with Islam.
1607: the first lasting English settlement in North America. Today over a billion people speak English, mostly as a second language.

dd-languages.text: Ethnologue counts about 7,100–7,200 living languages, but most have few speakers and roughly two in five are endangered. About half are spoken in Asia and the Pacific, with over 800 in [Papua New Guinea](PNG) alone. Mandarin in [China](CHN) has the most native speakers, about a billion. Some languages have been brought back: Hebrew in [Israel](ISR) was revived as an everyday tongue, while most Indigenous languages of [Australia](AUS) are at risk.

notes.PNG: Papua New Guinea has over 800 living languages, more than any other country, for about 10 million people. Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, is the common language.
notes.IDN: Indonesia has about 700 languages. Indonesian, based on Malay, was chosen as the national language in 1928 and now unites the country.
notes.NGA: Nigeria has over 500 languages. Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are the largest, with tens of millions of speakers each.
notes.IND: India has over 400 living languages from four main families. Its constitution lists 22 scheduled languages, and Hindi is the most widely spoken.
notes.CHN: Mandarin has about a billion native speakers, the most of any language. Other Chinese languages, such as Cantonese and Wu, are not mutually intelligible with it, though they share a writing system.
notes.ISR: Hebrew was mainly a written and religious language for nearly 2,000 years. Revived as an everyday tongue from the 1880s, it is now the first language of millions of Israelis.
notes.NZL: By the 1970s few young people spoke Māori. Language 'nests' for preschoolers began in 1982, and Māori became an official language in 1987.
notes.GBR: Welsh is spoken by about one in six people in Wales. Welsh-medium schools and broadcasting helped slow a long decline.
notes.AUS: Over 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken when Europeans arrived in 1788. About 120 are still spoken, but only about 12 are still learned by children as a first language.
notes.USA: Hundreds of Native American languages were spoken before European contact. Most surviving ones are endangered, after generations of boarding schools that punished children for speaking them.
notes.CAN: Canada's 2021 census recorded about 70 Indigenous languages. Cree is the most widely spoken, and many have only elderly speakers.

dd-writing.text: Writing was invented independently at least three times. In [Mesopotamia](IRQ) scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform into clay from about 3300–3000 BC, and [Egypt](EGY) had hieroglyphs almost as early. In [China](CHN) characters appear on oracle bones by about 1250 BC, and in [Mexico](MEX) and [Guatemala](GTM) the Zapotec, Maya and their neighbours created scripts from about 600–300 BC. The script of the Indus valley, in [Pakistan](PAK), is still unread.

notes.IRQ: Sumerian scribes first used pictures for accounts, then wedge-shaped signs for sounds and words. Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years, for laws, letters and the Epic of Gilgamesh.
notes.SYR: Cuneiform was written across Syria. At Ugarit, around 1400 BC, scribes even used a short cuneiform alphabet of 30 signs.
notes.IRN: The Persian kings carved cuneiform at Behistun around 520 BC in three languages. Copying it in the 1830s–40s helped scholars decipher cuneiform.
notes.TUR: The Hittites of Anatolia wrote their language in cuneiform, and Assyrian merchants at Kanesh left thousands of tablets around 1900 BC.
notes.EGY: Egyptian hieroglyphs mixed pictures for words with signs for sounds. Scribes also used faster cursive scripts, hieratic and later demotic, for everyday writing.
notes.SDN: The kingdom of Kush, in today's Sudan, used hieroglyphs and then its own Meroitic script, which can be read aloud but is still largely not understood.
notes.PAK: The Indus civilisation left over 4,000 short inscriptions, mostly on seals. Whether the signs record a language is still debated.
notes.IND: Indus cities such as Dholavira and Lothal lay in today's India. After the Indus script vanished, India seems to have had no writing until Brahmi appeared in the 200s BC.
notes.CHN: The oracle-bone inscriptions are the oldest known Chinese writing. Chinese is the only one of the first scripts still in use, though the characters changed greatly over time.
notes.MEX: In Oaxaca, Zapotec carvings with signs may date to about 600–300 BC, though their dating is debated. Mesoamerican writing grew without any contact with the Old World.
notes.GTM: Maya writing, mixing word signs and syllables, flourished in Classic city-states such as Tikal. Most of it was deciphered only from the 1950s to the 1980s.
notes.BLZ: Maya cities in Belize, such as Caracol, left carved monuments recording kings, wars and dates.
notes.HND: Copán, in western Honduras, has the longest known Maya inscription, the Hieroglyphic Stairway, with over 2,000 glyphs.

pn: c. 3300–3000 BC: some of the earliest known writing, clay tablets recording grain, beer, animals and workers.
c. 3200 BC: small bone and ivory labels from a royal tomb carry some of the earliest Egyptian signs.
c. 2500 BC: a great Indus city where many stamp seals with short inscriptions were found. No one has deciphered them.
c. 1250–1050 BC: Shang kings have questions to their ancestors carved on turtle shells and ox bones. The script is the ancestor of today's Chinese characters.
196 BC: a decree is carved in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Found here in 1799, the stone helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
c. 300–200 BC: a painted column of glyphs in this Maya town is among the earliest known Maya writing.

dd-writing.text: Around 1900–1500 BC, Semitic-speaking workers in [Egypt](EGY) and Sinai borrowed a few hieroglyphs to write single sounds: the first alphabet. Phoenician traders from [Lebanon](LBN) carried their version around the Mediterranean. The [Greeks](GRC) added vowels, the Romans in [Italy](ITA) adapted it, and Aramaic letters gave rise to Hebrew and Arabic. In the late 800s Slavic churchmen in [Bulgaria](BGR) shaped the script now called Cyrillic.

notes.EGY: The first alphabet seems to have grown from Egyptian hieroglyphs: the sign for an ox head, alef in Semitic, came to stand for the sound A, the ancestor of our letter A.
notes.LBN: The Phoenician cities of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon used 22 letters, all consonants. Their trade spread the alphabet from Cyprus to Spain.
notes.ISR: Hebrew was first written in a Phoenician-style script. After about 500 BC Jews adopted the Aramaic 'square' letters still used for Hebrew today.
notes.PSE: Early Hebrew and other local inscriptions from around 1000–600 BC are found across the southern Levant, including today's West Bank.
notes.SYR: Ugarit's scribes wrote an early alphabet in cuneiform signs, and Aramaic began among peoples of Syria. Syriac, a form of Aramaic, became the script of many Middle Eastern Christians.
notes.GRC: The Greeks adapted Phoenician letters around 800 BC and turned some unneeded consonants into vowels, making the first full alphabet. Alpha and beta gave the alphabet its name.
notes.CYP: Cyprus, where Phoenician and Greek settlers lived side by side, was one of the likely places where Greeks learned the alphabet.
notes.TUR: The Greek cities of Ionia, on Turkey's west coast, were leading centres of early Greek writing. Phrygians and Lydians also made alphabets of their own.
notes.ITA: The Etruscans borrowed Greek letters, and the Romans took them from the Etruscans. The Roman Empire then carried the Latin alphabet across western Europe.
notes.IRQ: Aramaic became the common language of the Assyrian and then Persian empires, so its alphabet spread from Egypt to India.
notes.JOR: Nabataean inscriptions from Petra and the desert show the step-by-step change from Aramaic letters towards Arabic ones.
notes.SAU: The Arabic script was used for the Quran in the 600s, and it spread with Islam from Spain to Indonesia.
notes.IRN: The Persian Empire ran on Aramaic scribes. After the Arab conquest Persian came to be written in Arabic letters, with a few added.
notes.BGR: The missionaries Cyril and Methodius created Glagolitic for Slavic around 863. Their disciples in Bulgaria then shaped Cyrillic, mostly from Greek capitals.
notes.MKD: At Ohrid, Saint Clement and Saint Naum ran a school that trained thousands of Slavic priests and writers in the late 800s.
notes.IND: India's Brahmi script, used for Emperor Ashoka's edicts in the 200s BC, may have been inspired by Aramaic. It is the ancestor of most South and Southeast Asian scripts.
notes.TUN: Carthage, near Tunis, was the greatest Phoenician colony. The Romans destroyed it in 146 BC.

pn: c. 1800–1500 BC: at Egyptian turquoise mines in Sinai, Semitic-speaking workers scratch short texts in an early alphabet.
c. 1000 BC: the sarcophagus of King Ahiram carries one of the oldest long texts in the Phoenician alphabet.
Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BC, Carthage kept writing a Phoenician (Punic) script for centuries.
c. 740 BC: a wine jug from Athens carries one of the oldest known Greek alphabet inscriptions, a line of verse.
The Nabataeans of Petra wrote a form of Aramaic. Their script slowly turned into the Arabic letters by about AD 500.
c. 890s: scholars of the Bulgarian capital develop Cyrillic, named after the missionary Cyril.

dd-writing.text: Today the [Latin alphabet](ITA) is the most widely used script, carried abroad by European empires and adopted by countries such as [Turkey](TUR) and [Vietnam](VNM). Cyrillic is used in [Russia](RUS) and its neighbours, Arabic script from Morocco to [Pakistan](PAK), and Chinese characters in [China](CHN) and, with kana, [Japan](JPN). Most scripts of [India](IND) and Southeast Asia descend from Brahmi. [Korea](KOR), [Greece](GRC) and [Israel](ISR) keep scripts of their own.

notes.ITA: The Latin alphabet of ancient Rome is now used, alone or beside other scripts, by most of the world's people, for languages from English to Swahili and Indonesian.
notes.TUR: In 1928 Turkey switched from Arabic to Latin letters in a few months, part of Atatürk's reforms to make the country more secular and Western.
notes.VNM: Vietnamese was once written in Chinese characters. A Latin alphabet devised by Catholic missionaries in the 1600s, quốc ngữ, became the national script in the 20th century.
notes.UZB: Uzbekistan officially moved from Cyrillic to Latin letters in 1993, though Cyrillic is still widely seen. Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan also switched.
notes.SOM: Somali got an official Latin alphabet only in 1972. Before that, Arabic and other scripts had been tried.
notes.RUS: Russia uses a Cyrillic alphabet reformed by Peter the Great in 1708 and again in 1918. The Soviet Union spread Cyrillic to many languages of Central Asia and Siberia.
notes.TCD: Chad's official languages are French, written in Latin letters, and Arabic, written in Arabic script. Djibouti and the Comoros also use both.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan still writes Kazakh mainly in Cyrillic. It has long planned a switch to a Latin alphabet, but the change has been repeatedly delayed.
notes.MNG: Mongolia adopted Cyrillic under Soviet influence in the 1940s. It is reviving its traditional vertical script, now used beside Cyrillic in official documents.
notes.BIH: Both Latin and Cyrillic are official. Bosnian and Croatian are written in Latin letters, while many Serbs in Bosnia use Cyrillic.
notes.SRB: Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters. Cyrillic is the official script, but Latin is common in daily life.
notes.PAK: Urdu, Pakistan's national language, is written in an elegant hanging Arabic style called Nastaliq.
notes.IRN: Persian uses the Arabic script with four added letters for sounds that Arabic lacks.
notes.CHN: China simplified many characters in the 1950s and 1960s to boost literacy, and created pinyin, a Latin spelling used for typing and teaching.
notes.TWN: Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao still use traditional, unsimplified Chinese characters.
notes.JPN: Japanese mixes Chinese characters, kanji, with two syllable scripts, hiragana and katakana, developed from Chinese characters around the 800s–900s.
notes.IND: India's banknotes carry 17 languages. Hindi uses Devanagari, but Bengali, Tamil, Telugu and other languages each have their own Brahmi-derived script.
notes.THA: Thai, Lao, Khmer and Burmese scripts descend from South Indian forms of Brahmi that spread with trade and Buddhism.
notes.KOR: Koreans wrote in Chinese characters until Hangul. Today both Koreas use Hangul almost entirely, and its simple design is admired by linguists.
notes.GRC: Greece still uses the Greek alphabet, little changed for over 2,000 years. Cyprus uses it too.
notes.ISR: Hebrew, revived as an everyday spoken language from the late 1800s, is written in the square Hebrew alphabet, right to left.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia and Eritrea use Ge'ez script, in which each sign stands for a consonant plus a vowel. It is one of the oldest scripts still in everyday use in Africa.

pn: c. 1450–55: Johannes Gutenberg prints with metal movable type, and printing spreads across Europe within 50 years.
1446: King Sejong publishes Hangul, a 28-letter alphabet designed so ordinary people could learn to read quickly.
1928: Turkey replaces Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, and Atatürk tours the country teaching the new letters.

dd-money.text: In [Mesopotamia](IRQ), from about 3000 BC, temples and palaces kept accounts in barley and in silver weighed in shekels. The first coins, stamped lumps of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, appeared in Lydia in western [Turkey](TUR) around 630–600 BC and spread to [Greece](GRC) and Persia. [India](IND) and [China](CHN) developed their own metal coins at about the same time, apparently independently.

notes.IRQ: Mesopotamians used silver, weighed out in shekels of about 8 grams, to value goods and settle debts, and barley to pay wages. Loans with interest were common.
notes.SYR: Northern Syria was part of the same trading world, and hoards of cut silver pieces, valued by weight, have been found across the Levant.
notes.TUR: Lydia's kings, at Sardis, issued the first known coins around 630–600 BC. The earliest found were buried at the temple of Artemis at Ephesus.
notes.GRC: Greek cities took up coins quickly, and by 500 BC there were hundreds of local mints. Coins helped pay soldiers, rowers and public works.
notes.IRN: Persia's King Darius I issued a gold coin, the daric, around 515 BC, after his empire took over Lydia.
notes.IND: Silver 'punch-marked' coins, stamped with symbols such as suns and animals, circulated in the Ganges kingdoms by about the 5th century BC.
notes.CHN: Cowrie shells were used as money in Shang China. Bronze coins shaped like spades and knives followed from about the 7th–5th centuries BC.
notes.EGY: Egypt ran largely without coins until the Persians and Greeks arrived. Values were often reckoned in weights of copper, the deben.

pn: c. 3300–3000 BC: scribes write some of the first clay tablets, mostly accounts of grain, animals and goods.
c. 1754 BC: the laws of King Hammurabi set wages, fees and maximum interest rates in silver and barley.
c. 550 BC: King Croesus of Lydia is credited with the first coins of pure gold and pure silver.
From c. 510 BC: silver 'owls', minted from the mines of Laurion, become the most trusted coins of the Greek world.
221 BC: the First Emperor of Qin makes a round bronze coin with a square hole standard across China. The shape lasted over 2,000 years.

dd-money.text: China's Song dynasty issued the first government paper money in the 1020s. In [Italy](ITA), bankers in Florence, Venice and Genoa spread bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping. From 1545 silver from Potosí, in [Bolivia](BOL), and from [Mexico](MEX) flooded the world as Spanish 'pieces of eight', and much of it ended up in [China](CHN). The [Netherlands](NLD) and [England](GBR) then built public banks, stock markets and national debts.

notes.CHN: Paper money spread under the Song and Mongol Yuan, and Marco Polo marvelled at it. Over-printing caused inflation, and the Ming dynasty largely gave up paper notes by the 1400s, turning to silver.
notes.ITA: Italian merchant bankers moved money across Europe with bills of exchange instead of chests of coins. Luca Pacioli described double-entry bookkeeping in print in 1494.
notes.ESP: Spain minted American silver into the 'piece of eight', or Spanish dollar, which became the first global currency, used from the Americas to China.
notes.BOL: Potosí's silver mountain, the Cerro Rico, produced vast amounts of silver from 1545. The mines were worked largely by Indigenous people forced to serve under the mita labour draft.
notes.MEX: Mexico's mines, such as Zacatecas, became even larger producers than Potosí in the 1700s. The Manila galleons carried Mexican silver across the Pacific to trade for Chinese silk and porcelain.
notes.PER: Peru was the centre of Spanish rule in South America, and its Huancavelica mine supplied the mercury used to refine Potosí's silver.
notes.NLD: Amsterdam was Europe's financial centre in the 1600s. Its bank offered a stable money of account, and Dutch East India Company shares were the first to be traded continuously.
notes.GBR: The Bank of England, founded in 1694, and a national debt backed by Parliament let Britain borrow cheaply, which helped it win wars against richer France.
notes.SWE: Sweden's copper coins were so heavy, some plates weighing over 10 kilograms, that paper notes were a welcome alternative in the 1660s.

pn: 1024: after merchants' paper notes fail, the Song government issues its own jiaozi, the world's first official paper money.
1397–1494: the Medici Bank, with branches from London to Rome, becomes the most famous bank in Europe.
1545: Spaniards begin mining a mountain of silver, worked largely by forced Indigenous labour. Potosí grew into one of the largest cities in the Americas.
1661: Stockholms Banco issues Europe's first banknotes. It printed too many and failed within a few years.
1602–09: the Dutch East India Company sells shares, traded on a new exchange, and the city founds the Bank of Amsterdam.
1694: the Bank of England is founded to lend money to the government for its war with France.

dd-money.text: Most money is now numbers in bank accounts, backed by trust in governments rather than gold. The [US dollar](USA) is the world's main currency, used in most foreign-exchange trades and adopted by countries such as [Ecuador](ECU). Twenty-one EU countries share the euro, [Bulgaria](BGR) the newest in 2026. Phone payments boomed, from [Kenya](KEN)'s M-Pesa to [India](IND)'s UPI and [Brazil](BRA)'s Pix.

notes.USA: The dollar makes up over half of the world's foreign-exchange reserves and is on one side of almost 90% of currency trades. In 1971 President Nixon ended its link to gold.
notes.ECU: Ecuador replaced its sucre with the US dollar in 2000, after a banking crisis and runaway inflation.
notes.SLV: El Salvador adopted the dollar in 2001. In 2021 it became the first country to make bitcoin legal tender, but in 2025, under a deal with the IMF, made accepting it voluntary.
notes.PAN: Panama has used the US dollar since 1904, alongside its own balboa coins.
notes.DEU: Germany gave up the Deutschmark for the euro. Euro notes and coins replaced national money in 12 countries on 1 January 2002.
notes.BGR: Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, becoming the euro area's 21st member.
notes.MNE: Montenegro uses the euro without being in the EU, as does Kosovo. Neither has any say in how it is managed.
notes.GBR: Britain kept the pound sterling, one of the oldest currencies still in use, whose roots go back to Anglo-Saxon silver pennies.
notes.KEN: M-Pesa, launched in 2007, let Kenyans send money by text message on basic phones. It is now used by most adults in the country.
notes.IND: India's UPI, launched in 2016, lets people pay instantly by scanning a QR code. It handled about 24.5 billion payments in August 2026 alone.
notes.BRA: Brazil's central bank launched the free instant-payment system Pix in 2020. By 2024 three in four Brazilians used it, more than used cash, a central bank survey found.
notes.CHN: In Chinese cities most people pay with Alipay or WeChat Pay by scanning QR codes, and the central bank is testing a digital yuan.
notes.SWE: Sweden is one of the most cashless countries: by the mid-2020s only about one in ten shop purchases were paid in cash, according to its central bank.

pn: Home of the European Central Bank, which has set interest rates for the euro since 1999.
Home of the Federal Reserve, founded in 1913, whose decisions on interest rates move markets worldwide.
July 1944: Allied nations peg their currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce. The system ended in 1971.

dd-democracy.text: Around 508 BC the city of Athens in [Greece](GRC) gave its male citizens the power to vote on laws: the first known democracy. [Rome](ITA) ran a republic with elected officials for nearly 500 years. In 930 [Iceland](ISL) founded the Althing, an assembly of free men. In [England](GBR), Magna Carta in 1215 put the king under the law, and in 1689 Parliament won lasting power over the Crown.

notes.GRC: Athens was a democracy for most of the years 508–322 BC. Adult male citizens voted directly, but women, slaves and foreigners, the majority of residents, had no say.
notes.ITA: Rome's Republic elected two consuls each year and had a powerful Senate, but the rich dominated it. It ended when Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.
notes.ISL: Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, made laws and settled disputes for the whole island. It is often called the world's oldest surviving parliament.
notes.GBR: Magna Carta of 1215 said even the king must obey the law. England's Parliament grew from the 1200s, and after 1689 the Crown could not rule without it.
notes.CHE: Swiss communities kept old traditions of open-air assemblies, and two small cantons still vote by a show of hands in the town square.

pn: From about 508 BC: citizens meet on the Pnyx hill to debate and vote on laws, war and peace.
509 BC: by Roman tradition, the last king is expelled and the Republic begins.
AD 930: Icelanders found the Althing, which met here in the open air each summer.
June 1215: King John agrees to Magna Carta in a meadow beside the Thames.
1689: the Bill of Rights bars the monarch from raising taxes or keeping an army in peacetime without Parliament's consent.

dd-democracy.text: The American Revolution of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789 spread the idea that power comes from the people. At first, though, the vote went mostly to men, often only those with property. Women won it first in [New Zealand](NZL) in 1893, then [Australia](AUS), [Finland](FIN) and [Norway](NOR). After World War I a wave followed, including [Britain](GBR), [Germany](DEU) and the [United States](USA).

notes.NZL: In 1893 New Zealand gave women, including Māori women, the vote after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures.
notes.AUS: Australian women won the federal vote in 1902, but most Aboriginal people were shut out of it until 1962.
notes.FIN: Finland, then a self-governing part of the Russian Empire, gave women full voting rights in 1906, and in 1907 elected 19 women to parliament, a world first.
notes.NOR: Norway gave women the vote on equal terms with men in 1913, after granting it to some women in 1907.
notes.USA: The Constitution of 1787 left voting rules to the states, mostly limited to white men. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote in 1920, but many Black Americans were blocked until the 1960s.
notes.GBR: Britain widened the male vote in Reform Acts from 1832. After the suffragettes' long campaign, women over 30 won the vote in 1918, and all women over 21 in 1928.
notes.FRA: France's revolution proclaimed the rights of man in 1789, and all men got the vote in 1848. French women won the vote only in 1944.
notes.DEU: Germany's new republic gave women the vote in November 1918, and they voted in January 1919. The republic fell to Hitler in 1933.
notes.RUS: Russia's Provisional Government gave women the vote in 1917, but the Bolsheviks soon dissolved the elected assembly and ruled as a single party.
notes.CAN: Most Canadian women won the federal vote in 1918, but many people of Asian origin and First Nations people were excluded for decades longer.

pn: 1776: the Declaration of Independence. 1787: the US Constitution, the oldest written national constitution still in use.
August 1789: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen proclaims that sovereignty rests with the nation.
September 1893: New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country where women can vote in national elections.

dd-democracy.text: The V-Dem Institute in Sweden rates every country each year. By its count, at the end of 2025 there were 87 democracies and 92 autocracies, and about three in four people lived under autocratic rule. [India](IND), the world's largest electorate, is rated an electoral autocracy, and the [United States](USA) lost its long-held rating as a liberal democracy. [Taiwan](TWN) and [South Korea](KOR) are rated liberal democracies.

notes.IND: India held the world's largest election in 2024, with about 640 million votes cast. V-Dem first rated it an electoral autocracy in its 2021 report, and its data now class it as one since 2017, citing pressure on the media and opponents; India's government rejects the label.
notes.USA: V-Dem says US democracy declined at a speed unprecedented in modern history in 2025, and downgraded it from liberal to electoral democracy for the first time in over 50 years.
notes.TWN: Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996 and is now rated one of Asia's strongest democracies.
notes.KOR: South Korea moved from military rule to democracy in 1987. In 2024–25 its courts and parliament removed a president who had declared martial law.
notes.CHN: China is ruled by the Communist Party, with no competitive national elections. With over 1.4 billion people, it is the largest closed autocracy.
notes.HUN: V-Dem rated Hungary an electoral autocracy under Viktor Orbán. In April 2026 voters ousted him, and Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a two-thirds majority.
notes.RUS: Russia holds elections, but leading opponents are barred, jailed or exiled. Vladimir Putin has led the country since 2000 as president or prime minister.
notes.BRA: Brazil returned to democracy in 1985 after 21 years of military rule. In 2025 its supreme court convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a coup.
notes.IDN: Indonesia was rated a democracy from 1999, after Suharto's fall. V-Dem downgraded it to an electoral autocracy from 2024.
notes.GBR: V-Dem rates Britain an electoral democracy. Its Parliament grew over centuries, and it has no single written constitution.
notes.DNK: Denmark is regularly rated among the world's strongest democracies, along with its Nordic neighbours.
notes.ZAF: South Africa held its first election open to all races in 1994, ending apartheid, and has kept competitive elections since.
notes.MEX: Mexico ended 71 years of one-party rule in 2000. V-Dem downgraded it to an electoral autocracy from 2024.

dd-medicine.text: Around 400 BC Hippocrates of Kos, in [Greece](GRC), taught that illness had natural causes, and Galen, a Greek doctor in Rome, shaped medicine for over 1,000 years. [India](IND)'s Ayurveda and [China](CHN)'s Inner Classic set out their own systems. From the 800s physicians of the Islamic world, in cities such as Baghdad in [Iraq](IRQ) and Cairo in [Egypt](EGY), ran great hospitals and wrote textbooks studied in Europe for centuries.

notes.GRC: The Hippocratic doctors explained illness as an imbalance of four body fluids, the humours. The Hippocratic Oath, in changed forms, is still taken by some new doctors.
notes.ITA: Galen's many books, based on animal dissection and long practice in Rome, became the unquestioned authority in Europe and the Islamic world until the 1500s.
notes.TUR: Pergamon's healing sanctuary of Asclepius drew the sick from across the Roman world. Byzantine Constantinople later ran hospitals of its own.
notes.IRQ: Abbasid Baghdad translated Greek medical books into Arabic in the 800s. Its hospitals, called bimaristans, trained doctors and treated the sick for free.
notes.IRN: Al-Razi came from Rayy, near Tehran, and led hospitals there and in Baghdad. He tested treatments by comparing groups of patients.
notes.UZB: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), born near Bukhara around 980, wrote the Canon of Medicine. In Latin it was taught in European universities until the 1600s.
notes.SYR: Damascus's Nur al-Din hospital, founded in 1154, was a leading medical school. Ibn al-Nafis, trained there, described how blood passes through the lungs in the 1200s.
notes.EGY: Cairo's Mansuri hospital had separate wards for fevers, eye diseases and mental illness, and its endowment paid for patients' care free of charge.
notes.ESP: Al-Andalus produced the surgeon al-Zahrawi. In the 1100s scholars in Toledo translated Arabic medical books into Latin, passing them to Europe.
notes.IND: The Sushruta Samhita, compiled over centuries, describes surgery including rebuilding noses. Ayurveda, based on balancing three doshas, is still widely practised in India.
notes.CHN: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, compiled around the 100s BC, explained health through qi, yin and yang. Chinese doctors were inoculating against smallpox by the later 1500s.

pn: c. 400 BC: Hippocrates teaches here. The Hippocratic writings, by him and his followers, describe diseases by careful observation.
AD 129: Galen is born here. He trained by treating gladiators, then became doctor to Roman emperors.
c. 900: al-Razi heads a hospital and writes the first clear account telling smallpox apart from measles.
c. 1000: the surgeon al-Zahrawi finishes a medical encyclopedia whose surgery volume illustrates about 200 instruments.
1284–85: Sultan Qalawun founds the Mansuri hospital, with wards for different illnesses, open to rich and poor.
1000s–1100s: the first great medical school of medieval Europe, where Arabic texts were studied in Latin and women such as Trota practised.

dd-medicine.text: In 1796 Edward Jenner in [Britain](GBR) tested the first vaccine, against smallpox. Anaesthesia, first shown in public in the [United States](USA) in 1846, made long operations bearable. In the 1860s–80s Louis Pasteur in [France](FRA) and Robert Koch in [Germany](DEU) proved that germs cause disease. Insulin, first used to treat diabetes in [Canada](CAN) in 1922, and penicillin, found in London in 1928 and mass-produced in the 1940s, saved millions.

notes.GBR: Britain gave the world vaccination, Florence Nightingale's modern nursing and Lister's antiseptic surgery. Alexander Fleming noticed penicillin killing bacteria in London in 1928, and an Oxford team turned it into a medicine in 1940–41.
notes.FRA: Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, invented pasteurisation and made a rabies vaccine in 1885. René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816.
notes.DEU: Robert Koch identified the germs of tuberculosis in 1882 and cholera in 1883. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, and Paul Ehrlich's Salvarsan of 1910 was the first modern drug designed to kill a germ.
notes.USA: Ether anaesthesia was first demonstrated in Boston in 1846. In 1943–44 American firms scaled up penicillin production, and supplies were ready for the D-Day landings.
notes.CAN: Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in John Macleod's Toronto laboratory, isolated insulin in 1921, turning diabetes from a death sentence into a treatable illness.
notes.AUT: In Vienna's General Hospital, Semmelweis noticed that mothers delivered by doctors who came from dissections died far more often than those delivered by midwives.
notes.HUN: Ignaz Semmelweis, born in Buda, was mocked for his handwashing rule and died in an asylum in 1865, before germ theory proved him right.

pn: 14 May 1796: Edward Jenner infects a boy with cowpox, then shows he is protected from smallpox.
16 October 1846: at Massachusetts General Hospital, William Morton puts a patient to sleep with ether for surgery.
1847: Ignaz Semmelweis has doctors wash their hands in chlorine, and deaths of new mothers from childbed fever fall sharply.
1854: John Snow traces a cholera outbreak to one water pump, helping prove the disease spreads through dirty water.
1865–67: Joseph Lister uses carbolic acid to kill germs in wounds, and far fewer of his patients die after surgery.
January 1922: a 14-year-old diabetic boy, Leonard Thompson, is the first person treated with insulin.

dd-medicine.text: Worldwide, a baby born in 2023 could expect to live about 73 years, more than twice as long as in 1900, according to UN and other estimates. Lives are longest in places such as [Japan](JPN), [South Korea](KOR) and [Spain](ESP), and shortest in countries hit by poverty and conflict, such as [Nigeria](NGA) and [Chad](TCD). Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, and wild polio survives only in [Afghanistan](AFG) and [Pakistan](PAK).

notes.HKG: Hong Kong, at about 85.5 years, had one of the world's highest life expectancies in the UN's 2023 estimates, behind only the tiny states of Monaco and San Marino.
notes.JPN: Japan, at about 84.7 years, leads all large countries. Low rates of obesity and heart disease and universal health care are among the reasons usually given.
notes.KOR: South Korea's life expectancy, about 84, rose faster than almost anywhere as the country grew rich after the 1960s.
notes.ESP: Spain and Italy, both near 84 years, are among Europe's longest-lived countries.
notes.AUS: Australia and Switzerland both reached about 84 years in the UN's 2023 estimates.
notes.NGA: The UN estimates life expectancy in Nigeria at about 54. More women die in pregnancy and childbirth there than in any other country.
notes.TCD: Chad has some of the world's highest rates of child and maternal death, and its life expectancy is about 55 years, by UN estimates.
notes.LSO: Lesotho's lifespans fell sharply in the AIDS epidemic of the 1990s–2000s. HIV treatment has helped, but about one adult in six lives with HIV.
notes.SSD: War and weak health services keep South Sudan's life expectancy below 60.
