notes.SOM: Somalia, scene of the last natural smallpox case in 1977, still has some of the lowest life expectancies after decades of conflict.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan reported more wild polio cases than Pakistan in 2026, by WHO counts, after years in which Pakistan had more.
notes.PAK: Pakistan and Afghanistan share one zone of polio spread. Insecurity and distrust of vaccination have slowed eradication.
notes.USA: The United States spends more on health per person than any other country, yet its life expectancy, about 79, is lower than in most rich countries. It left the WHO in January 2026.

pn: October 1977: a hospital cook, Ali Maow Maalin, has the world's last natural case of smallpox. He recovered and later worked against polio.
1948: the World Health Organization is founded here. It led the smallpox campaign, and the United States left it in January 2026.
3 December 1967: Christiaan Barnard performs the first human heart transplant at Groote Schuur Hospital.
2020: BioNTech, with Pfizer, develops one of the first mRNA vaccines against Covid-19 in under a year.

dd-plagues.text: Plague reached the Black Sea port of Caffa, in Crimea in today's [Ukraine](UKR), in 1346. Genoese ships carried it to Constantinople, [Italy](ITA) and [France](FRA) in 1347, and it swept on to [England](GBR) and [Spain](ESP) in 1348, [Norway](NOR) in 1349 and [Russia](RUS) by 1352. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people, and many millions across the Middle East and North Africa.

notes.UKR: The plague probably came west from Central Asia with the trade caravans of the Golden Horde, reaching Crimea in 1346.
notes.TUR: Constantinople was struck in 1347, and the emperor John VI wrote of losing his young son.
notes.ITA: Florence may have lost over half its people in 1348. The writer Boccaccio set his Decameron among young people fleeing the city.
notes.FRA: Pope Clement VI, at Avignon, consecrated the river Rhône so that the dead could be thrown in when the graveyards were full.
notes.GBR: England lost perhaps 40–50% of its people in 1348–49, according to many modern estimates.
notes.EGY: Cairo, the largest city in the Mediterranean world, was hit in 1347–49. Arab chroniclers described thousands dying each day.
notes.ESP: King Alfonso XI of Castile died of plague in 1350 while besieging Gibraltar, the only reigning European king known to have died of it.
notes.DEU: As plague came near, mobs blamed Jews for poisoning wells and destroyed hundreds of Jewish communities in 1348–51.
notes.NOR: Bergen was hit in 1349. With so many dead, Norway's crown weakened and farms were left empty for generations.
notes.SWE: Plague crossed from Norway into Sweden in 1350.
notes.RUS: Plague reached Pskov and Novgorod in 1352 and Moscow in 1353.
notes.POL: Plague did reach Poland, but its losses are poorly recorded. Pollen studies show its farming did not decline, which suggests it was hit far less hard than western Europe.
notes.ISL: Iceland escaped the Black Death, but plague reached it in 1402.

pn: 1346: plague breaks out among the Golden Horde army besieging this Genoese trading port.
October 1347: Genoese galleys bring the plague to Sicily, its first landfall in western Europe.
November 1347: plague arrives in France, then follows the roads to Paris by the summer of 1348.
June 1348: plague lands in England at this Dorset port, today part of Weymouth.
1349: a ship from England carries plague to Norway, which may have lost half its people.
1353: plague kills Grand Prince Simeon of Moscow and his sons, among the last places hit in this wave.

dd-plagues.text: Justinian's plague broke out in [Egypt](EGY) in 541 and returned in waves for 200 years. Smallpox, carried by Europeans, devastated the peoples of [Mexico](MEX) and the Americas from 1520. The 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million worldwide. HIV, traced to Kinshasa in today's [DR Congo](COD), has killed about 44 million. COVID-19, first identified in [China](CHN) in 2019, killed over 7 million by official counts.

notes.EGY: Plague reached the port of Pelusium in 541 and then Alexandria, from where grain ships carried it around the Mediterranean.
notes.TUR: Justinian himself caught the plague in 542 and survived. Historians disagree about how many died, from a modest share to perhaps a quarter of the empire.
notes.MEX: Smallpox, measles and other diseases, with war and forced labour, cut central Mexico's population by perhaps 90% within a century, by many estimates.
notes.PER: Smallpox reached the Inca Empire before the Spanish did, probably killing the emperor Huayna Capac around 1527 and setting off a civil war.
notes.USA: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans, more than died in World War I.
notes.ESP: It was called the 'Spanish flu' because neutral Spain's newspapers reported it freely while warring countries censored the news.
notes.IND: British India suffered more 1918 flu deaths than anywhere else, perhaps 12–17 million.
notes.COD: HIV crossed from chimpanzees to humans in south-east Cameroon and spread from Kinshasa along railways and rivers decades before it was recognised.
notes.ZAF: Southern Africa was hit hardest by HIV. South Africa has more people living with HIV than any other country.
notes.CHN: COVID-19 was first identified in Wuhan in December 2019. Its exact origin is still disputed.
notes.GBR: Like most countries, Britain went into lockdown in March 2020, as the virus spread round the world by air within weeks.

pn: 542: Justinian's plague strikes the capital. The historian Procopius wrote of up to 10,000 deaths a day, a figure modern historians doubt.
1520: smallpox kills many in the Aztec capital, including the new emperor Cuitláhuac, months before the Spanish siege.
March 1918: one of the first well-recorded outbreaks of the flu, at an army camp in Kansas. Its true origin is unknown.
c. 1920: genetic studies trace the spread of HIV's main strain to this city, then called Léopoldville.
December 2019: the first cases of COVID-19 are identified. WHO declared it a pandemic on 11 March 2020.

dd-spices.text: In 1450 the most prized spices grew in only a few places. Cloves came from a handful of islands in the north Moluccas, and nutmeg only from the tiny Banda Islands, both in today's [Indonesia](IDN). Pepper grew on the Malabar coast of [India](IND), and the finest cinnamon in [Sri Lanka](LKA). Asian and Arab merchants shipped them west to [Egypt](EGY), where Venetians from [Italy](ITA) bought them for Europe at large mark-ups.

notes.IDN: Cloves grew only on a few islands such as Ternate and Tidore, and nutmeg only on the Banda Islands. Javanese and Malay traders carried them west.
notes.IND: Black pepper, native to the Malabar coast in today's Kerala, was the bulk spice of the trade. Gujarati merchants were among the leading traders of the Indian Ocean.
notes.LKA: Sri Lanka grew the finest cinnamon, the inner bark of a local tree, and was a stopping point on routes between Asia and Arabia.
notes.MYS: Malacca's sultans, Muslim from the early 1400s, made the port a meeting place for merchants from China, India, Arabia and the islands.
notes.YEM: Aden, at the mouth of the Red Sea, was where Indian Ocean cargoes were taxed and reloaded for Egypt.
notes.EGY: The Mamluk sultans of Cairo taxed every load passing from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, one of their main sources of income.
notes.SYR: Spices also travelled overland or up the Persian Gulf to Aleppo, Damascus and Beirut, where Venetians and other Europeans bought them.
notes.ITA: Venice dominated Europe's spice imports in the 1400s, and its rival Genoa traded through the Black Sea and the eastern Mediterranean.
notes.CHN: Ming China's treasure fleets under Zheng He sailed to Malacca, Calicut and East Africa in 1405–33, but China then turned away from long voyages.
notes.SAU: The Mamluks controlled the Hejaz. From the 1420s its port of Jeddah, rather than Aden, became the main stop for spice ships bound for Egypt.
notes.TUR: The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, but they did not cut off the spice trade, which kept flowing through Egypt and Syria.

pn: Ternate and nearby islands were the world's only source of cloves. Their sultans grew rich selling them to visiting traders.
The Banda Islands, a few small volcanic islands, were the only place nutmeg and mace grew.
c. 1400–1511: the sultanate of Malacca controlled the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the hub of Asian trade.
The great pepper port of the Malabar coast, where Arab, Indian and Chinese merchants traded.
Spices brought up the Red Sea and across Egypt were sold here to European merchants, above all Venetians.
Venice's state-run galleys sailed each year to Alexandria and Beirut, and the city resold spices across Europe.

dd-spices.text: Spices reached Europe through many middlemen, so [Portugal](PRT) sought a sea route of its own. Bartolomeu Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached [India](IND) in 1498. Sailing for [Spain](ESP), Columbus went west in 1492 to find Asia and reached the Americas instead. Portugal seized ports from Goa to Malacca, in [Malaysia](MYS), but after 1600 the [Dutch](NLD) took control of the spice islands of [Indonesia](IDN), often by force.

notes.PRT: Prince Henry's captains crept down Africa's coast from the 1420s. Portugal hoped to bypass Muslim and Venetian middlemen, find Christian allies and grow rich on spices.
notes.IND: Portugal took Goa in 1510 and made it the capital of its Asian empire, the Estado da Índia, which it held until 1961.
notes.MYS: Portugal captured Malacca in 1511 and held it until the Dutch took it in 1641.
notes.LKA: The Portuguese controlled Sri Lanka's coasts and cinnamon in the 1500s, until the Dutch drove them out by 1658.
notes.ESP: Spain backed Columbus's westward plan in 1492. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas split the newly found world between Spain and Portugal.
notes.PHL: Magellan was killed on Mactan in 1521. Spain later colonised the islands, named after King Philip II, and founded Manila in 1571.
notes.NLD: The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, had its own army and fleet. From Batavia, today's Jakarta, it forced spice monopolies on the islands.
notes.IDN: In 1621 the Dutch conquered the Banda Islands. Historians estimate that of about 15,000 Bandanese, only around 1,000 remained; the rest were killed, enslaved or fled.
notes.GBR: English traders held the tiny island of Run, in the Bandas, but lost out to the Dutch. The English company turned instead to India, where it later built an empire.
notes.BHS: Columbus's first landfall, on 12 October 1492, was in the Bahamas. He believed until his death that he had reached the edge of Asia.

pn: 1488: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa, proving the Indian Ocean can be reached by sea.
May 1498: Vasco da Gama arrives with a guide picked up in Malindi. The pepper he brought home sold for a huge profit.
1511: Afonso de Albuquerque captures Malacca, giving Portugal the gateway to the spice islands.
1519–22: Magellan's five ships leave here. One returns three years later with 18 men and a cargo of cloves, the first voyage around the world.
1621: Dutch forces under Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquer the Banda Islands to control nutmeg.

dd-spices.text: Columbus's voyages joined two worlds that had been apart for over 10,000 years. Maize from [Mexico](MEX), potatoes from [Peru](PER) and [Bolivia](BOL), tomatoes, chillies and cassava spread across the globe, feeding growing populations from [Ireland](IRL) to [China](CHN). Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar cane went the other way, and sugar plantations in places like [Brazil](BRA) were worked by enslaved Africans. European diseases such as smallpox killed millions of Indigenous Americans.

notes.MEX: Maize was domesticated in southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago. Mexico also gave the world tomatoes, chillies, beans, avocados, vanilla and turkeys.
notes.PER: Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of southern Peru and northern Bolivia, perhaps 7,000–10,000 years ago, and thousands of varieties are still grown there.
notes.BOL: The Andean highlands bred potatoes and quinoa. Spanish ships carried potatoes to Europe by the 1570s.
notes.ECU: Cacao was first domesticated in the upper Amazon, in today's Ecuador, over 5,000 years ago, and later prized by the Maya and Aztecs as a drink.
notes.IRL: By the 1800s millions of poor Irish lived mainly on potatoes. When blight destroyed the crop in 1845–52, about a million people died and a million emigrated.
notes.ITA: Tomatoes reached Italy by the 1540s but were long treated with suspicion. Tomato sauce became common only in the 1700s–1800s.
notes.HUN: Chillies reached Hungary in the 1500s, probably through Ottoman lands, and became paprika, now the national spice.
notes.IND: The Portuguese brought chillies to India in the 1500s. Within a century they were a basic part of Indian cooking.
notes.CHN: Maize and sweet potatoes, which grow on poor hillside soils, spread through China from the late 1500s and helped its population grow.
notes.KOR: Chillies arrived in Korea around the late 1500s or 1600s, and only later turned kimchi red.
notes.THA: Chillies, brought by Portuguese traders, became central to Thai cooking. So did peanuts, tomatoes and papayas from the Americas.
notes.NGA: Portuguese traders brought cassava to West Africa. Nigeria is now the world's largest grower of this American root.
notes.COD: Portuguese ships brought cassava from Brazil to the Kongo region in the 1500s–1600s, and it became a main food of Central Africa.
notes.GHA: Cacao from the Americas only reached West Africa in the 1800s, but Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire now grow about half of the world's cocoa.
notes.CIV: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, growing a crop first domesticated in South America.
notes.BRA: Portuguese Brazil became the world's leading sugar producer by the late 1500s, using millions of enslaved Africans over three centuries.
notes.HTI: French Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was the world's richest sugar colony by the 1780s, until the slave revolution of 1791 that created Haiti.
notes.DOM: Hispaniola had the first sugar mills of the Americas, in the early 1500s, after its Taíno people had been devastated by disease and forced labour.
notes.JAM: British Jamaica became a giant sugar island in the 1700s, where enslaved Africans far outnumbered Europeans.
notes.BRB: Barbados began large-scale sugar growing with enslaved labour in the 1640s, a model copied across the Caribbean.
notes.PNG: Sugar cane was first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago, then spread through Asia to the Mediterranean and the Americas.

pn: 1493: on his second voyage Columbus brings horses, pigs, cattle, wheat and sugar cane to Hispaniola.
1520: smallpox, brought from Europe, sweeps the Aztec capital, killing thousands, including the emperor Cuitláhuac, before the Spanish siege.
1593: according to Chinese records, a merchant brings sweet potato vines from the Spanish Philippines to Fujian. It later helped China feed a fast-growing population.
1692: one of the first printed recipes for tomato sauce, 'in the Spanish style', appears in Naples.

dd-slavery.text: About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto slave ships, by the estimates of the SlaveVoyages database. Almost half came from West Central Africa, today's [Angola](AGO) and the Congo region. Most of the rest came from the coasts of West Africa, from [Senegal](SEN) to [Nigeria](NGA). Europeans rarely went inland: they bought captives at coastal forts and ports from African rulers and merchants, mostly people taken in wars and raids.

notes.AGO: Portuguese Angola, with its ports of Luanda and Benguela, was the single largest source of captives, most of them sent to Brazil.
notes.COD: The Kingdom of Kongo traded with Portugal from the 1480s. Its Christian king Afonso I complained in 1526 that the trade was taking even his own people.
notes.COG: Ports on the Loango coast, in today's Republic of the Congo, supplied many captives to French, Dutch and British ships in the 1700s.
notes.BEN: The kingdom of Dahomey grew powerful by capturing people in wars and selling them at Ouidah. The Bight of Benin was called the 'Slave Coast'.
notes.NGA: The ports of the Bight of Biafra, such as Bonny and Calabar, shipped many Igbo captives. Inland, the Aro network of traders supplied them.
notes.GHA: The Gold Coast had dozens of European forts, including Elmina and Cape Coast Castle. The Asante kingdom became a major supplier in the 1700s.
notes.SEN: Senegambia was an early source of captives, in the 1500s, and later sent many to French and British colonies.
notes.GMB: James Island, in the Gambia River, was a British trading fort from the 1660s.
notes.SLE: Sierra Leone was a source of captives, and from 1787 a British settlement for freed Africans, centred on Freetown.
notes.MOZ: In the 1800s, as Britain tried to suppress the Atlantic trade, Portuguese and Brazilian traders turned to Mozambique for captives.
notes.GBR: British ships carried about 3.3 million Africans, second only to Portuguese and Brazilian ships, which carried about 5.8 million.

pn: This island's 'House of Slaves', with its 'Door of No Return', is a UNESCO World Heritage symbol of the trade, though historians think relatively few captives left from here.
1482: the Portuguese build this castle to trade for gold. Under the Dutch, from 1637, it held captives awaiting ships.
1700s: the main port of the kingdom of Dahomey, from which about a million people were shipped, the second-largest total of any port.
1700s–1830s: a leading port of the Bight of Biafra, run by local merchant rulers who sold captives to British ships.
Founded by the Portuguese in 1576, it shipped over a million people, more than any other port, mostly to Brazil.

dd-slavery.text: About 10.7 million Africans survived the Middle Passage, the voyage of one to three months across the Atlantic; perhaps 1.8 million died at sea. [Brazil](BRA) received almost half, and the sugar islands of the Caribbean, such as [Jamaica](JAM), [Haiti](HTI) and [Cuba](CUB), most of the rest. Fewer than 4% went to mainland North America, but by 1860 the [United States](USA) had about 4 million enslaved people.

notes.BRA: Brazil imported enslaved Africans for over three centuries to work sugar, gold mines and coffee. Today over half of Brazilians identify as Black or of mixed race.
notes.JAM: Jamaica's sugar estates were so deadly that the enslaved population fell without constant new arrivals. In 1831–32 the Baptist War, a huge revolt, hastened abolition.
notes.HTI: French Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was the world's richest sugar and coffee colony by the 1780s, with about half a million enslaved people.
notes.CUB: Cuba became the world's top sugar producer in the 1800s and kept importing captives illegally until the 1860s.
notes.BRB: Barbados was England's first sugar colony, from the 1640s, and its plantation and slave laws became a model for other English colonies.
notes.USA: The US banned imports in 1808, but its enslaved population grew by natural increase to about 4 million in 1860, mostly growing cotton.
notes.SUR: Dutch Suriname's plantations were notoriously harsh. Many enslaved people escaped into the rainforest, where their descendants, the Maroons, still live.
notes.COL: Cartagena was the main slave port of Spanish South America, from which captives were sent on to Peru and the mines of New Granada.
notes.MEX: In the early colonial period New Spain took in many Africans, perhaps about 200,000. Most later merged into Mexico's mixed population.
notes.PER: Captives arrived via Cartagena and Panama to work in coastal plantations, vineyards and households around Lima.

pn: Brazil's first capital and a centre of sugar slavery. Its Yoruba-rooted culture, such as Candomblé, reflects strong ties to the Bight of Benin.
1800s: the busiest slave port in the Americas. Its Valongo Wharf, where about 900,000 captives landed by UNESCO's estimate, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
1700s: Jamaica, Britain's richest sugar colony, received about a million captives, more than any other British colony.
Perhaps two in five of all captives brought to mainland North America landed at this South Carolina port.

dd-slavery.text: Enslaved people rose in revolt from [Haiti](HTI) to [Jamaica](JAM), and campaigners in [Britain](GBR) built a mass movement against the trade. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and freed the enslaved in its colonies in 1834–38. Most new Spanish American republics ended slavery by the 1850s, the [United States](USA) after its civil war in 1865, [Cuba](CUB) in 1886 and [Brazil](BRA), the last, in 1888.

notes.HTI: France abolished slavery in Saint-Domingue in 1793–94 under pressure from the revolt. Napoleon's attempt to restore it failed, and Haiti became the first state founded by formerly enslaved people, in 1804.
notes.GBR: Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and then used its navy to stop others' slave ships. Its 1833 Act paid £20 million in compensation to slave owners, but nothing to the enslaved.
notes.JAM: Freedom came on 1 August 1834, but most freed people had to serve as unpaid 'apprentices' until 1838.
notes.MEX: Mexico abolished slavery in 1829. Its ban was one cause of conflict with American settlers in Texas, who held slaves.
notes.COL: Colombia, which then included Panama, freed its remaining enslaved people in 1852.
notes.BOL: Bolivia declared slavery abolished soon after independence, but the laws were not enforced, and slavery ended in practice only in 1851.
notes.SUR: The Netherlands abolished slavery in 1863, but freed people in Suriname had to keep working on plantations under state supervision until 1873.
notes.VIR: In the Danish West Indies, today's US Virgin Islands, enslaved people revolted in 1848 and the governor declared them free.
notes.USA: Northern states passed laws to end slavery between 1777 and 1804. In the South it ended only through the Civil War and the 13th Amendment of 1865.
notes.FRA: France abolished slavery in 1794, Napoleon restored it in 1802, and it was abolished for good in 1848.
notes.PRI: Spain abolished slavery in Puerto Rico in 1873, with three years of compulsory labour contracts.
notes.CUB: Spain began gradual abolition in Cuba in 1880 and ended it in 1886. Many enslaved and free Black Cubans had fought for independence in the war of 1868–78.
notes.BRA: Brazil ended the trade in 1850 and freed newborn children in 1871. Abolition in 1888 came after mass escapes from plantations, and the monarchy fell the next year.

pn: August 1791: enslaved people rise up in northern Saint-Domingue. Their revolution led to Haiti's independence in 1804.
1807: Parliament bans the British slave trade. The Slavery Abolition Act follows in 1833.
December 1865: the 13th Amendment abolishes slavery throughout the United States.
13 May 1888: Princess Isabel signs the 'Golden Law', freeing Brazil's last 700,000 or so enslaved people.

dd-science.text: In 1543 the Polish astronomer Copernicus, in [Poland](POL), put the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the universe. Tycho Brahe of [Denmark](DNK) measured the planets, Kepler worked out their orbits, and in [Italy](ITA) Galileo turned a telescope on the sky. Scientific societies sprang up in [Britain](GBR) and [France](FRA), and in 1687 Isaac Newton showed that one law of gravity moves both apples and planets.

notes.POL: Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon at Frombork in Royal Prussia, then part of Poland, argued that the Earth spins and circles the Sun. Few accepted it for decades.
notes.BEL: Andreas Vesalius, born in Brussels, dissected human bodies himself and showed that the ancient authority Galen, who had worked mainly from animals, was often wrong.
notes.DNK: Tycho Brahe, a Danish noble, saw a new star in 1572, proving the heavens could change. His observatory stood on Ven, now part of Sweden.
notes.ITA: Galileo's telescope revealed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus in 1609–10. In 1633 the Inquisition condemned him for defending Copernicus, and he spent his last years under house arrest.
notes.CZE: Prague was the seat of Emperor Rudolf II, who hired Tycho and then Kepler. Kepler's three laws of planetary motion appeared in 1609 and 1619.
notes.GBR: After William Harvey showed in 1628 that the heart pumps blood round the body, the Royal Society (1660), Robert Boyle and Newton made England a leader. Newton's Principia (1687) united heaven and Earth under the same laws.
notes.NLD: The Dutch Republic, with its printers and relative tolerance, was a haven for science. Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656.
notes.FRA: René Descartes urged doubting everything not proven. Louis XIV's minister Colbert founded the Academy of Sciences in 1666, paying scientists to research.
notes.DEU: In the 1650s Otto von Guericke showed the force of a vacuum, with teams of horses failing to pull apart two emptied metal hemispheres. Leibniz published calculus in 1684.

pn: 1543: Copernicus, a church canon here, publishes his Sun-centred system in the year of his death.
1543: Andreas Vesalius, who taught anatomy here, publishes the first accurate atlas of the human body. Galileo later taught here, 1592–1610.
1576–97: Tycho Brahe's observatory on the island of Ven, then Danish, today Swedish, makes the most precise sky measurements before the telescope.
1609: working from Tycho's data, Johannes Kepler shows that Mars moves in an ellipse, not a circle.
1670s: the cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek sees single-celled 'little animals', invisible to the eye, through his home-made microscopes.
1687: Newton's Principia, setting out his laws of motion and gravity, appears under the imprint of the Royal Society, founded in 1660.

dd-science.text: Scientists set out to test theories in the field. French expeditions to [Ecuador](ECU) and Lapland, in 1735–44, proved Newton right that the Earth bulges at the equator. James Cook sailed to [Tahiti](PYF) in 1769 to time Venus crossing the Sun. Alexander von Humboldt explored Spanish America, from [Venezuela](VEN) to [Mexico](MEX). In 1835 a young Charles Darwin reached the Galápagos Islands on HMS Beagle.

notes.ECU: The French Geodesic Mission worked near Quito in 1736–43. Its measurements, with Lapland's, showed the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, as Newton had predicted.
notes.FIN: In 1736–37 Pierre-Louis Maupertuis measured a degree of latitude in the Torne valley, today on the Finnish–Swedish border, near the Arctic Circle.
notes.SWE: Carl Linnaeus of Uppsala published his system for naming and classifying living things in 1735. He sent students, his 'apostles', to collect plants worldwide.
notes.PYF: Cook observed the 1769 transit of Venus at Tahiti. Observations from dozens of places around the world gave a far better estimate of the Earth–Sun distance.
notes.NZL: Cook spent six months in 1769–70 charting New Zealand's coasts, the first detailed European map of the islands.
notes.AUS: Cook charted Australia's east coast in 1770. Banks's reports later helped persuade Britain to found a convict colony at Sydney in 1788.
notes.VEN: Humboldt and the botanist Aimé Bonpland explored the Orinoco in 1800 and confirmed that it is linked by a natural channel to the Amazon basin.
notes.MEX: Humboldt studied Mexico's mines, population and geography in 1803–04. His books made him one of the most famous scientists of his age.
notes.CUB: Humboldt visited Cuba twice and wrote an essay on the island that condemned its slavery.
notes.COL: In Bogotá Humboldt met José Celestino Mutis, who led a long Spanish botanical expedition in New Granada.
notes.PER: Humboldt studied the cold Pacific current off Peru, now named after him, and the seabird guano later exported as fertiliser.
notes.GBR: The Beagle left Plymouth in December 1831 to survey South America's coasts. Darwin, its 22-year-old naturalist, published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

pn: 1736–43: French astronomers measure a degree of latitude near the equator, to compare with one measured in Lapland.
3 June 1769: Cook's crew time the transit of Venus, part of a worldwide effort to measure the distance to the Sun.
April 1770: Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander collect so many new plants that Cook names the bay after them.
June 1802: Humboldt climbs to about 5,900 metres on this volcano, then thought the world's highest mountain, and maps how plants change with altitude.
September–October 1835: Darwin collects finches, mockingbirds and tortoises that later helped shape his theory of evolution.

dd-science.text: By 1900 science had changed daily life. Chemists in [France](FRA) named the elements, physicists in [Britain](GBR) tamed electricity, and Darwin explained evolution. Louis Pasteur in France and Robert Koch in [Germany](DEU) proved that germs cause disease, leading to vaccines and safer surgery. Mendeleev in [Russia](RUS) drew up the periodic table, and laboratories in the [United States](USA) began to invent for profit.

notes.GBR: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the basis of electric generators. James Clerk Maxwell explained light as an electromagnetic wave in the 1860s, and Darwin published his theory of evolution in 1859.
notes.FRA: Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, and made a rabies vaccine in 1885. In 1898 Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, and Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium in Paris.
notes.DEU: German research universities, with laboratories and doctoral training, became the model for the world. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
notes.RUS: Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by atomic weight in 1869 and correctly predicted the properties of missing ones, such as gallium and germanium.
notes.ITA: Alessandro Volta built the first electric battery, a stack of metal discs and brine-soaked card, in 1800.
notes.CZE: Brno, where Mendel worked out the laws of inheritance, was then in the Austrian Empire.
notes.SWE: Alfred Nobel, who made his fortune from dynamite, left money in 1895 for prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace, first awarded in 1901.
notes.USA: Edison's Menlo Park laboratory pioneered organised industrial research. By 1900 American universities and companies were building labs on the German model.
notes.POL: Marie Skłodowska-Curie grew up in Warsaw, then under Russian rule, and moved to Paris to study, as women could not attend university in Russian Poland. She named polonium after her homeland.

pn: 1789: Antoine Lavoisier publishes his textbook of modern chemistry, with the first list of elements. He was guillotined in 1794.
1796: Edward Jenner tests the first vaccine, using cowpox to protect a boy against smallpox.
1866: the monk Gregor Mendel publishes his experiments on pea plants, founding genetics. They were ignored until 1900.
1869: Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table leaves gaps for elements not yet found, which were later discovered.
1882: Robert Koch identifies the bacterium that causes tuberculosis, which, Koch said, caused one in seven of all deaths.
1876–79: Thomas Edison's laboratory, an 'invention factory', produces the phonograph and a practical electric light bulb.

dd-capitalism.text: Modern capitalism grew up in Europe's richest trading nations. In the [Netherlands](NLD), the Dutch East India Company sold shares from 1602, and its trading posts stretched from South Africa to [Indonesia](IDN) and Japan. [Britain](GBR) followed with its own East India Company and the Bank of England. In 1776 the Scot Adam Smith argued that free markets, not monopolies, were the true source of the wealth of nations.

notes.NLD: In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic was Europe's richest trading nation, with the biggest merchant fleet and the first modern stock exchange.
notes.GBR: The East India Company, chartered in 1600, grew from a trading firm into a private army and government ruling much of India.
notes.IDN: The VOC made Batavia, today's Jakarta, its Asian headquarters in 1619 and fought wars to control the trade in nutmeg, cloves and pepper.
notes.ZAF: The VOC founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station for ships sailing between Europe and Asia.
notes.IND: After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 the East India Company took control of Bengal, the start of British rule in India.

pn: 1602: the VOC is founded and its shares trade on the Amsterdam exchange, often called the first modern stock market.
1694: the Bank of England is founded to lend money to the government for its war with France.
Adam Smith's home town in Scotland, where he wrote much of The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776.
1641–1850s: the Dutch are the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan, from this small island in Nagasaki harbour.

dd-capitalism.text: Factories, steam power and railways began in [Britain](GBR) around 1760 and made it the 'workshop of the world'. [Belgium](BEL) was the first to follow on the continent, then [France](FRA), Germany and the [United States](USA), which by 1900 had the world's largest economy. [Japan](JPN) industrialised after 1868 and [Russia](RUS) from the 1890s. Industrial capitalism created vast fortunes, big cities and a new working class, and with it trade unions and socialism.

notes.GBR: Coal, cotton, steam engines and a global empire gave Britain a head start; by 1850 it made about half the world's iron and cotton cloth.
notes.USA: Railways, steel, oil and mass immigration made the United States the world's largest economy, and men like Carnegie and Rockefeller among the richest people in history.
notes.JPN: After 1868 Meiji Japan built railways, shipyards and textile mills, often starting them as state firms and then selling them to private companies.
notes.RUS: Finance minister Sergei Witte drove a rush of railway building and foreign investment in the 1890s, including the Trans-Siberian Railway.

pn: Cotton mills made it the world's first industrial city, nicknamed 'Cottonopolis'.
Krupp's steelworks make the Ruhr Germany's industrial heartland.
Andrew Carnegie's steel mills make it the heart of American heavy industry by the 1890s.

dd-capitalism.text: From the late 1970s, governments across the world turned to markets. [Chile](CHL) began in 1975 and [China](CHN) in 1978. Margaret Thatcher in [Britain](GBR) and Ronald Reagan in the [United States](USA) cut taxes and regulation. [Vietnam](VNM) opened up in 1986 and [India](IND) in 1991. When communism fell, Eastern Europe and [Russia](RUS) switched to markets in a rush known as 'shock therapy'.

notes.CHL: Economists trained in Chicago, the 'Chicago Boys', freed prices and trade under General Pinochet's dictatorship from 1975.
notes.CHN: Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops and opened special economic zones to foreign investors.
notes.GBR: Margaret Thatcher, prime minister from 1979, sold state firms such as British Telecom and British Gas and curbed trade union power.
notes.USA: Ronald Reagan, president from 1981, cut income taxes sharply and reduced regulation.
notes.NZL: From 1984 the Labour government's 'Rogernomics' floated the currency and removed subsidies and controls.
notes.VNM: The Doi Moi ('renovation') reforms of 1986 brought markets to communist Vietnam.
notes.IND: In 1991, facing a currency crisis, finance minister Manmohan Singh scrapped licences and cut tariffs and controls.
notes.POL: Poland's 1990 'shock therapy', designed by Leszek Balcerowicz, freed prices and trade almost overnight.
notes.RUS: Prices were freed in January 1992, and rushed privatisation created a small class of super-rich 'oligarchs'.

pn: 1980: a small border town becomes one of China's first special economic zones, open to foreign investors. It is now a city of about 17 million.

dd-pirates.text: Spain's silver fleets sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana, then home through the Florida Straits, past islands held by rival empires. Pirates used havens in the gaps: buccaneers at Tortuga in French [Haiti](HTI) and Port Royal in English [Jamaica](JAM) in the 1600s, then the 'pirate republic' at Nassau in the [Bahamas](BHS) until 1718. Blackbeard sailed from Nassau and died off North Carolina.

notes.CUB: Havana was where Spain's fleets gathered each year before sailing home with silver from Mexico and Peru.
notes.MEX: Veracruz was the port of New Spain, where the treasure fleet loaded Mexican silver.
notes.COL: Cartagena was the fortified port where the galleons collected South American treasure.
notes.PAN: Portobelo was a treasure fair town, sacked by the buccaneer Henry Morgan in 1668.
notes.JAM: England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655 and at first welcomed buccaneers as a defence. Port Royal later turned to hanging pirates.
notes.HTI: French buccaneers settled western Hispaniola from Tortuga, and Spain recognised it as French Saint-Domingue in 1697.
notes.BHS: The Bahamas were a neglected English colony. After 1713 hundreds of pirates used Nassau's harbour, until the first royal governor arrived in 1718.
notes.DOM: The eastern part of Hispaniola stayed Spanish, while buccaneers hunted wild cattle on the island's coasts.
notes.PRI: Spanish Puerto Rico licensed its own privateers, who raided British shipping.
notes.BRB: Barbados was a rich English sugar colony. The gentleman pirate Stede Bonnet was a planter here before he took to piracy in 1717.
notes.USA: Pirates sold goods in the English mainland colonies and attacked their shipping. Blackbeard was killed off North Carolina and Stede Bonnet was hanged at Charleston in 1718.
notes.CUW: Dutch Curaçao was a busy trading hub, where smuggled and captured goods could be sold.

pn: A buccaneer boom town in English Jamaica, later called 'the wickedest city on earth'. An earthquake sank much of it on 7 June 1692.
1600s: a base for French and other buccaneers off northern Hispaniola.
c. 1713–1718: a lawless pirate base, until governor Woodes Rogers arrived in July 1718 with a royal pardon and warships.
July 1715: a hurricane wrecks a Spanish treasure fleet off Florida. Raids on the salvage camps helped launch the Nassau pirates.
May 1718: Blackbeard blockades the port for about a week and takes hostages, demanding a chest of medicines.
22 November 1718: Blackbeard is killed here by sailors under Lieutenant Robert Maynard of the Royal Navy.

dd-pirates.text: In the 1690s some pirates sailed from the Americas round Africa to the Indian Ocean, a voyage called the Pirate Round. They sheltered at Île Sainte-Marie off [Madagascar](MDG) and hunted rich Indian ships in the Red Sea and Arabian Sea. In 1695 Henry Every captured the Mughal ship Ganj-i-Sawai, and the anger in [Mughal India](IND) put the English East India Company in danger.

notes.MDG: Madagascar had no European colony and lay near the shipping lanes. Pirates settled on its east coast in the 1690s–1720s, some marrying into local families.
notes.IND: The Mughal Empire ruled most of India. When its ships were plundered by English pirates, Emperor Aurangzeb's officials briefly shut down English trade and confined English merchants.
notes.PAK: Most of today's Pakistan lay inside the Mughal Empire, whose merchants traded across the Arabian Sea.
notes.BGD: Bengal was one of the Mughal Empire's richest provinces, famous for its cotton cloth.
notes.YEM: Mocha, in Yemen, was the great coffee port, and Indian pilgrim ships to Mecca called there.
notes.GBR: To calm the Mughals, England offered a large reward for Henry Every, starting one of the first worldwide manhunts, but he was never caught.
notes.USA: Merchants in New York and other colonies financed and fenced for Indian Ocean pirates. Captain William Kidd sailed from New York in 1696 as a pirate hunter and was hanged in London in 1701 as a pirate.

pn: 1690s: Adam Baldridge ran a trading post here, supplying pirates and buying their loot for New York merchants.
The narrow mouth of the Red Sea, where pirates waited for ships returning from Mocha and the pilgrimage to Mecca.
The Mughal Empire's main port. After Every's attack in 1695, its officials held the English East India Company responsible.
Every voyage on the Pirate Round had to round Africa's southern tip.

dd-enlightenment.text: The Enlightenment was a conversation across borders, carried by letters, books and travellers. [Britain](GBR) gave it Newton, Locke, Hume and Adam Smith. [France](FRA) was its heart, with Voltaire, Montesquieu, Diderot and the Paris salons. The [Netherlands](NLD) printed books banned elsewhere. In the German lands Kant asked 'What is Enlightenment?', and in [Italy](ITA) Cesare Beccaria argued against torture and the death penalty.

notes.GBR: Newton's Principia (1687) showed the universe ran by natural laws. Locke, Hume and Adam Smith applied reason to government, knowledge and economics.
notes.FRA: Paris salons hosted by women such as Madame Geoffrin brought writers, scientists and nobles together. Many French books were banned, and their authors risked prison.
notes.NLD: The Dutch Republic's relatively free press made it Europe's publisher. Descartes and Locke both spent years there.
notes.CHE: Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712, and Voltaire settled just outside the city.
notes.ITA: Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments (1764) argued against torture and the death penalty and inspired law reform across Europe.
notes.DEU: Berlin, capital of Prussia, was home to the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn and to Frederick the Great's court of writers and scientists.

pn: 1751–1772: Diderot and d'Alembert publish the Encyclopédie, 28 volumes meant to gather all human knowledge.
David Hume and Adam Smith make the city a hub of the 'Scottish Enlightenment'.
1759–1778: Voltaire lives here, just inside France near Geneva, so he can slip across the border if the authorities come for him.
1784: Immanuel Kant, who spent his life in this Prussian city (now Kaliningrad in Russia), defines Enlightenment as 'Dare to know'.

dd-enlightenment.text: Enlightenment ideas left the salons. Some kings tried reform from above: Catherine the Great in [Russia](RUS), Joseph II in [Austria](AUT) and Frederick the Great in Prussia. Elsewhere people took power themselves. The [United States](USA) declared independence in 1776, [France](FRA) proclaimed the Rights of Man in 1789, and in [Haiti](HTI) enslaved people rose up in 1791 and won independence in 1804.

notes.USA: The Declaration of Independence borrowed Locke's ideas about rights and government by consent, and the 1787 Constitution built in Montesquieu's separation of powers.
notes.FRA: The 1789 Declaration said that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. The revolution later turned to terror and war.
notes.HTI: Saint-Domingue's enslaved people rose up in 1791. Led by Toussaint Louverture and then Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated France and founded Haiti in 1804.
notes.RUS: Catherine the Great corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, but serfdom grew harsher during her reign.
notes.AUT: Joseph II abolished serfdom in his lands and tolerated Protestants and Jews in the 1780s.
notes.DEU: Frederick the Great of Prussia, who ruled from 1740 to 1786, called himself 'the first servant of the state' and abolished most torture.

pn: 4 July 1776: Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.
26 August 1789: the National Assembly adopts the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
1 January 1804: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent, the first country founded by formerly enslaved people.

dd-nationalism.text: In 1815 [Italy](ITA) and [Germany](DEU) were divided into many states, while the Ottoman Empire ruled the Balkans. Over the next 60 years nationalism remade the map. [Greece](GRC) won independence in 1830, and [Belgium](BEL) broke away from the Netherlands the same year. Italy was united by 1870 and Germany in 1871, and in 1878 [Serbia](SRB), [Montenegro](MNE) and [Romania](ROU) were recognised as independent.

notes.ITA: Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's 'Thousand' volunteers united Italy under Victor Emmanuel II, proclaimed King of Italy in 1861.
notes.DEU: Bismarck's wars with Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71) created a German Empire led by Prussia.
notes.GRC: Greece's war of independence began in 1821 and won the backing of Britain, France and Russia, which recognised a small Greek state in 1830.
notes.BEL: French-speaking and Catholic Belgians rose against Dutch rule in 1830 and chose a king of their own.
notes.SRB: Serbs rebelled against Ottoman rule from 1804, won self-government and gained full independence at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

pn: 1824: the English poet Lord Byron dies here while supporting the Greek fight for independence.
1870: Italian troops enter Rome, completing unification. It becomes the capital the next year.
18 January 1871: the German Empire is proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors, after France's defeat.

dd-nationalism.text: World War I destroyed four empires. In their place, nationalists founded new states in the name of self-determination: [Poland](POL), Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, [Finland](FIN), the three Baltic states, an [Irish Free State](IRL) and Atatürk's [Turkey](TUR). But borders never matched peoples neatly, leaving millions of people as minorities on the wrong side and grievances that fed the next war.

notes.POL: Poland reappeared in 1918 after 123 years of being partitioned between Russia, Prussia and Austria.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia joined Czechs and Slovaks, but also included about three million Germans in the Sudetenland.
notes.SRB: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later called Yugoslavia, united South Slavs under the Serbian king.
notes.FIN: Finland declared independence from Russia in December 1917, soon after the Bolshevik revolution.
notes.TUR: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk fought off Greek and Allied forces and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923.
notes.IRL: After a war of independence, 26 Irish counties became the Irish Free State in 1922, while Northern Ireland stayed in the UK.
notes.HUN: Hungary lost about two-thirds of its land in the 1920 Treaty of Trianon, leaving millions of Hungarians in neighbouring states.

pn: 28 June 1914: a Bosnian Serb nationalist, Gavrilo Princip, kills Archduke Franz Ferdinand, helping to trigger World War I.
1919: peacemakers in Paris redraw the map of Europe, and President Wilson argues for self-determination.

dd-nationalism.text: Nationalism still makes and breaks countries. Since 2000, [Timor-Leste](TLS), [Montenegro](MNE), [Kosovo](UNK) and [South Sudan](SSD) have become independent. Other movements have voted and lost, or been blocked: Quebec narrowly voted to stay in [Canada](CAN) in 1995, Scotland chose to stay in the [United Kingdom](GBR) in 2014, and 2017 referendums in Catalonia, in [Spain](ESP), and Iraqi Kurdistan were rejected by their national governments.

notes.TLS: Timor-Leste voted for independence from Indonesia in 1999 and became independent in 2002.
notes.MNE: Montenegro voted to leave its union with Serbia in 2006, with 55.5% in favour.
notes.UNK: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Serbia and many other countries do not recognise it.
notes.SSD: South Sudan voted by nearly 99% to leave Sudan and became the world's newest country in 2011.
notes.CAN: Quebec voted to stay in Canada by just over one percentage point in 1995.
notes.GBR: Scotland voted by 55% to 45% to stay in the United Kingdom in 2014.
notes.ESP: Spain's courts declared Catalonia's 2017 independence referendum illegal, and its leaders were jailed or fled abroad.
notes.IRQ: Iraqi Kurds voted overwhelmingly for independence in 2017, but Iraq rejected the result and retook the city of Kirkuk.

dd-women.text: The demand for equal rights was argued in [Britain](GBR) in 1792 and organised in the [United States](USA) from 1848. [New Zealand](NZL) gave women the national vote first, in 1893. Most of Europe and North America followed around World War I, much of Latin America and Asia by 1950, and newly independent nations often from the start. [Switzerland](CHE) waited until 1971, and [Saudi Arabia](SAU) allowed women to vote in local elections in 2015.

notes.GBR: Mary Wollstonecraft argued for women's equality in 1792. After decades of campaigning by suffragists and suffragettes, women over 30 won the vote in 1918, and on equal terms with men in 1928.
notes.USA: The Seneca Falls convention of 1848 launched an organised movement. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote in 1920, though many Black women in the South were kept from voting until the 1960s.
notes.NZL: In 1893 New Zealand gave women, including Māori women, the vote after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures.
notes.AUS: Australian women won the federal vote and the right to stand for parliament in 1902, but most Aboriginal people were shut out until 1962.
notes.FIN: Finland, then a self-governing part of the Russian Empire, gave women full political rights in 1906 and elected 19 women to parliament in 1907, a world first.
notes.NOR: Norway gave women the vote on equal terms with men in 1913.
notes.DEU: German women won the vote in November 1918, after the fall of the Kaiser, and 37 were elected to the national assembly in January 1919.
notes.CAN: Most Canadian women won the federal vote in 1918, but many Asian Canadians and First Nations people were excluded for decades longer.
notes.FRA: France, home of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man, gave women the vote only in 1944. They first voted in 1945.
notes.JPN: Japanese women won the vote in December 1945, under the US occupation, and 39 women were elected to parliament in April 1946.
notes.IND: India's 1950 constitution gave every adult the vote, women and men alike, from the first general election in 1951–52.
notes.TUR: Turkey gave women the national vote in 1934, as part of Atatürk's modernising reforms, earlier than France or Italy.
notes.CHE: Swiss men rejected women's suffrage in a national referendum in 1959 and approved it in 1971. The last canton, Appenzell Innerrhoden, was ordered by a court to allow it in 1990.
notes.PRT: Some educated Portuguese women could vote under the dictatorship, but equal voting rights for all adults came only after the 1974 revolution and were written into the 1976 constitution.
notes.LIE: Liechtenstein's male voters approved women's suffrage in 1984, making it one of the last countries in Europe to do so.
notes.KWT: Kuwait's parliament gave women the vote and the right to stand for office in 2005. The first four women MPs were elected in 2009.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia has no elected national parliament. Women first voted and stood as candidates in municipal elections in December 2015.

pn: 1792: Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, arguing that girls deserve the same education as boys.
July 1848: the first US women's rights convention adopts a Declaration of Sentiments that demands, among other things, the vote.
1903: Emmeline Pankhurst founds the Women's Social and Political Union, the militant suffragettes, under the slogan 'Deeds, not words'.
September 1893: New Zealand becomes the first self-governing country where women can vote in national elections.

dd-women.text: In 1960 [Sri Lanka](LKA)'s Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first woman elected prime minister. [India](IND) and [Israel](ISR) followed in the 1960s, [Britain](GBR) in 1979, and [Iceland](ISL) elected the first woman president by popular vote in 1980. In 1988 [Pakistan](PAK)'s Benazir Bhutto became the first woman to lead a Muslim-majority democracy. Recent firsts include [Mexico](MEX) in 2024 and [Japan](JPN) in 2025.

notes.LKA: Sirimavo Bandaranaike led her party after her husband, the prime minister, was assassinated, and won the 1960 election. She served three terms as prime minister.
notes.IND: Indira Gandhi became prime minister in 1966 and led India for about 16 years in all. She was assassinated in 1984.
notes.ISR: Golda Meir became Israel's prime minister in 1969 and led it through the 1973 Yom Kippur War.
notes.ARG: Isabel Perón, vice-president, succeeded her husband Juan Perón on his death in 1974, becoming the world's first woman president. She was overthrown by a military coup in 1976.
notes.CAF: Elisabeth Domitien became prime minister of the Central African Republic in 1975, the first woman to head a government in Africa.
notes.GBR: Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in 1979 and won three elections in a row, serving until 1990.
notes.PRT: Maria de Lourdes Pintasilgo led a caretaker government in 1979–80, Portugal's only woman prime minister so far.
notes.ISL: Iceland elected Vigdís Finnbogadóttir president in 1980. It has ranked first in the World Economic Forum's gender gap index every year since 2009.
notes.DMA: Eugenia Charles became prime minister of Dominica in 1980 and served 15 years, the first woman to lead a Caribbean country.
notes.NOR: Gro Harlem Brundtland became prime minister in 1981. Her 1986 cabinet was nearly half women, a world first at the time.
notes.PHL: Corazon Aquino became president in 1986 after the 'People Power' protests ended Ferdinand Marcos's rule.
notes.PAK: Benazir Bhutto became prime minister in 1988, aged 35. She was assassinated while campaigning in 2007.
notes.NIC: Violeta Chamorro won the 1990 election, becoming the first woman elected president in the Americas.
notes.IRL: Mary Robinson was elected Ireland's first woman president in 1990 and later became UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
notes.BGD: Khaleda Zia became Bangladesh's first woman prime minister in 1991. She and Sheikh Hasina then alternated in power for most of the next three decades.
notes.FRA: Édith Cresson became France's first woman prime minister in 1991. France has never had a woman president.
notes.TUR: Tansu Çiller became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993.
notes.CAN: Kim Campbell became Canada's first woman prime minister in June 1993 but lost the election that October.
notes.TZA: Samia Suluhu Hassan, vice-president, became Tanzania's first woman president in 2021 after the death of John Magufuli.
notes.ITA: Giorgia Meloni became Italy's first woman prime minister in October 2022.
notes.MEX: Claudia Sheinbaum, a climate scientist and former mayor of Mexico City, became Mexico's first woman president in October 2024.
notes.NAM: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became Namibia's first woman president in March 2025.
notes.JPN: Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first woman prime minister in October 2025.
notes.USA: The United States has never had a woman president. Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024 won major-party nominations but lost.

pn: July 1960: Sirimavo Bandaranaike becomes prime minister of Ceylon, today's Sri Lanka, the world's first elected woman head of government.
June 1980: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir is elected president of Iceland, the first woman voted head of state in a national election. She served 16 years.

dd-women.text: On 1 January 2026 women held 27.5% of seats in the world's parliaments, the Inter-Parliamentary Union counted. Seven countries, including [Rwanda](RWA), [Mexico](MEX) and [Bolivia](BOL), had at least as many women as men in their lower or single chamber, while [Oman](OMN), [Tuvalu](TUV) and [Yemen](YEM) had none. [Iceland](ISL) tops the World Economic Forum's gender gap index, and [Afghanistan](AFG) bars girls from school after the age of about 12.

notes.RWA: Women hold 51 of 80 seats in Rwanda's Chamber of Deputies, about 64%, the world's highest share. Its 2003 constitution reserves at least 30% of seats for women.
notes.CUB: Women hold over half of the seats in Cuba's National Assembly, though the Communist Party is the only legal party.
notes.NIC: Women hold over half of the seats in Nicaragua's National Assembly, under a law requiring parties to alternate men and women on their lists.
notes.MEX: A 2019 constitutional reform requires 'parity in everything' in public office, and women now fill half of Congress. In 2024 Mexico elected its first woman president.
notes.BOL: Women won about 51% of the seats in Bolivia's Chamber of Deputies at the 2025 election, under a law requiring parties to alternate men and women on their lists.
notes.AND: The small Pyrenean state of Andorra has at least as many women as men in its 28-seat parliament.
notes.ARE: In the United Arab Emirates, a 2018 presidential decision reserved half of the Federal National Council's 40 seats for women. The council advises the government and has no power to pass laws on its own.
notes.ISL: Iceland has topped the gender gap index for 17 years in a row. On 24 October 1975 about 90% of Icelandic women went on strike for a day to show their value to society.
notes.FIN: Finland ranked second in the 2026 index. It was the first country in Europe to give women the vote, in 1906.
notes.NOR: Norway ranked third in the 2026 index. In 2003 it required company boards to be at least 40% women, a world first.
notes.OMN: Omani women can vote and stand for the elected Consultative Assembly, but none won a seat in the 2023 election.
notes.TUV: No woman won a seat in Tuvalu's 16-member parliament at the 2024 election.
notes.YEM: Yemen's parliament was elected in 2003 and has not been renewed because of political crisis and civil war. It has no women members.
notes.AFG: Since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, girls have been banned from secondary school and women from universities, most jobs and many public places. No other country bars girls from school.
notes.SAU: Saudi women won the right to drive in 2018, and male guardianship rules were loosened in 2019, though some still apply, for example to marriage.

pn: September 1995: 189 governments adopt the Beijing Platform for Action, the most wide-ranging global plan for women's rights.

dd-communism.text: In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, both from [Germany](DEU), published The Communist Manifesto, and Marx wrote most of his later work in exile in [Britain](GBR). They expected revolution in industrial countries, but it came first in war-weary [Russia](RUS). In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power, won a brutal civil war and in 1922 founded the Soviet Union. [Mongolia](MNG) became the second communist state in 1924.

notes.DEU: Marx and Engels were born in the German Rhineland. Germany had Europe's biggest socialist party, but its communist uprisings in 1919 failed.
notes.GBR: The Manifesto was first printed in London in February 1848. Marx lived in London from 1849 until his death in 1883 and is buried in Highgate Cemetery.
notes.RUS: World War I broke Russia's monarchy in early 1917. In November Lenin's Bolsheviks took power, and the civil war of 1918–21 left millions dead.
notes.UKR: Most of Ukraine became a Soviet republic, a founder of the Soviet Union in 1922. Its western region belonged to Poland between the wars.
notes.BLR: Eastern Belarus became a founding Soviet republic in 1922, while its western part was ruled by Poland until 1939.
notes.GEO: Georgia was independent from 1918 until the Red Army invaded in 1921. Stalin, born in Georgia, rose to lead the Soviet Union after Lenin.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan's steppe came under Soviet rule after the civil war. Forced collectivisation in the early 1930s caused a famine that killed over a million Kazakhs.
notes.MNG: With Red Army help, Mongolian revolutionaries took power in 1921, and the Mongolian People's Republic was declared in 1924, closely tied to Moscow.
notes.POL: Poland defeated the Red Army at Warsaw in 1920, halting the Bolsheviks' hopes of carrying revolution into Europe.

pn: 1818: Karl Marx is born in this town in the Rhineland, then part of Prussia.
1849–1883: Marx lives in exile here and researches Das Kapital in the British Museum reading room.
7 November 1917 (25 October in Russia's old calendar): the Bolsheviks seize the Winter Palace and take power.
From 1918: capital of Soviet Russia and then of the Soviet Union. Lenin dies just outside the city in January 1924.

dd-communism.text: Communism spread in waves. Lenin's revolution in [Russia](RUS) came first. World War II carried the Red Army into Eastern Europe, where Moscow installed communist governments, while Mao Zedong won [China](CHN) in 1949 and Kim Il Sung ruled [North Korea](PRK). Wars against colonial rule brought communists to power in [Vietnam](VNM), and Castro took [Cuba](CUB) in 1959. A last wave in the 1970s reached [Angola](AGO), [Ethiopia](ETH), [Cambodia](KHM) and [Afghanistan](AFG).

notes.CHN: Mao's army of peasants, not factory workers, won China's revolution. China later broke with Moscow and became a rival centre of communism.
notes.PRK: Soviet troops occupied the north of Korea in 1945 and put Kim Il Sung in charge. His family still rules.
notes.VNM: Ho Chi Minh, a founding member of the French Communist Party, led the fight against French rule. The communist North won the war and reunited Vietnam in 1975–76.
notes.CUB: Fidel Castro took power in 1959 as a nationalist rebel, declared the revolution socialist in 1961 and allied with the Soviet Union.
notes.POL: The Red Army drove out the Nazis in 1944–45, and by 1947 Moscow-backed communists controlled Poland through rigged elections.
notes.SRB: Tito's partisans freed Yugoslavia largely by themselves, which let him break with Stalin in 1948.
notes.KHM: The Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh in April 1975 and emptied the cities. Their rule killed an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people.
notes.ETH: The Derg overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974 and turned to the Soviet Union and Cuba for support.
notes.AFG: A communist coup in 1978 provoked a rebellion, and the Soviet invasion of December 1979 began a ten-year war.

pn: 1937–1947: Mao's communists run their wartime base from caves here, building the army that wins China's civil war.
May 1954: Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh defeat the French. Vietnam is split, with a communist North.
11 November 1975: the Marxist MPLA declares Angola independent, helped by thousands of Cuban troops.
April 1978: communists seize power in a coup. In December 1979 the Soviet Union invades to prop them up.

dd-communism.text: World War II spread communism to Eastern Europe, occupied by the Red Army, and in 1949 Mao Zedong won China's civil war. Revolutions followed in [Vietnam](VNM), [Cuba](CUB) and parts of Africa. By the 1980s communist parties ruled about a third of humanity. They were rivals as often as allies: [China](CHN) split from the [Soviet Union](RUS) around 1960, and [Yugoslavia](SRB) went its own way from 1948.

notes.RUS: The Soviet Union was a superpower with the world's largest territory. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation, famine and purges killed millions, and its Gulag camps held millions more.
notes.DEU: East Germany, about a third of today's Germany, was a communist state from 1949 to 1990, watched over by the Stasi secret police.
notes.POL: Poland's Solidarity trade union, founded in 1980 with about 10 million members, became the first big challenge to communist rule from below.
notes.HUN: In 1956 Soviet tanks crushed Hungary's uprising, killing about 2,500 Hungarians, and about 200,000 people fled abroad.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia's 'Prague Spring' reforms were crushed by a Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968.
notes.SRB: Tito's Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and ran its own looser system, with workers' councils and open borders for travel.
notes.CHN: Mao's Great Leap Forward caused a famine in 1959–61 that killed tens of millions. After his death, Deng Xiaoping began market reforms in 1978.
notes.KHM: The Khmer Rouge, who ruled in 1975–79, emptied the cities, and an estimated 1.5–2 million Cambodians died. Vietnam then installed a new communist government.
notes.VNM: Vietnam's communists defeated France and then the US-backed South, uniting the country in 1975–76.
notes.CUB: Cuba became the first communist state in the Americas and depended heavily on Soviet aid and oil.
notes.PRK: North Korea was founded in 1948 under Kim Il Sung, whose family still rules it.
notes.ETH: In 1974 Marxist officers, the Derg, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie. Their rule brought the 'Red Terror' and civil war.
notes.AFG: Communists seized power in 1978, and the Soviet army invaded in December 1979 to prop them up, beginning a ten-year war.
notes.YEM: South Yemen, around Aden, was the Arab world's only Marxist state, from 1969 until it merged with the North in 1990.
notes.AGO: Angola's Marxist MPLA took power at independence in 1975, backed by Cuban troops, and fought a long civil war.

pn: 1961–1989: a wall divides the city to stop East Germans fleeing west. Its fall in November 1989 ends the Cold War divide.
1 October 1949: Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen Gate.
January 1959: Fidel Castro's rebels take power. In 1961 he declares Cuba socialist, 145 km from the United States.

dd-communism.text: In 1989 revolutions, mostly peaceful, swept away communist rule in Eastern Europe, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union broke into 15 countries. Today only five states are ruled by communist parties: [China](CHN), [Vietnam](VNM), [Laos](LAO), [Cuba](CUB) and [North Korea](PRK). China and Vietnam keep one-party rule but have opened their economies to markets, foreign investment and private business.

notes.CHN: China's Communist Party has ruled since 1949. Market reforms since 1978 made China the world's second-largest economy, while the party keeps firm political control.
notes.VNM: Vietnam's 'Doi Moi' reforms of 1986 opened the economy, and it is now a major exporter of electronics and clothing, still under one-party rule.
notes.LAO: Laos has been ruled by the Lao People's Revolutionary Party since 1975 and has opened up to trade and investment, much of it from China.
notes.CUB: Cuba kept communist rule after losing Soviet aid in 1991. In 2026 it faced deep shortages and blackouts after the US moved to cut off its oil supplies.
notes.PRK: North Korea is the most closed of the five, ruled by the Kim family since 1948. Its constitution has dropped references to communism in favour of its own 'Juche' ideas.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union was dissolved in December 1991. Russia's 1990s shift to capitalism brought a deep economic slump before recovery in the 2000s.
notes.POL: Poland's June 1989 elections, the first partly free ones in the bloc, gave Solidarity a landslide. It joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
notes.DEU: East Germany joined West Germany in October 1990, less than a year after the Wall fell.
notes.ROU: Romania's was the only violent overthrow in 1989: dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife were executed on 25 December.
notes.MNG: Mongolia held its first multiparty elections in 1990 and has remained a democracy between Russia and China.

pn: 9 November 1989: crowds pour through the Berlin Wall after East Germany opens its border.
4 June 1989: China's army crushes pro-democracy protests in and around the square, killing hundreds or possibly thousands.
25 December 1991: Mikhail Gorbachev resigns, and the Soviet flag is lowered over the Kremlin.

dd-climate.text: Burning coal powered the Industrial Revolution, first in [Britain](GBR), then in [Belgium](BEL), [Germany](DEU), [France](FRA) and the [United States](USA). At the same time scientists found that carbon dioxide traps heat. In 1896 [Sweden](SWE)'s Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling it would warm the Earth by several degrees. Few took the warning seriously until 1958, when precise measurements began in Hawaii.

notes.GBR: Britain was the first country to run on coal: by 1850 it mined over half the world's coal. In 1859 John Tyndall showed in London that carbon dioxide absorbs heat.
notes.BEL: Belgium was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, on the coalfields of Wallonia, in the early 1800s.
notes.DEU: The Ruhr valley's coal and steel made Germany Europe's leading industrial power by 1900.
notes.FRA: France industrialised more slowly than Britain, using coal from its northern coalfields and imports for railways and iron.
notes.USA: By 1900 the US was the world's largest coal producer, and it soon led in oil too. In 1856 Eunice Foote, in New York State, first showed that carbon dioxide traps the Sun's heat.
notes.SWE: Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist, published the first estimate of how much burning fossil fuels could warm the planet in 1896. He thought it would take thousands of years and might be welcome.

pn: August 1856: Eunice Foote's experiments, showing that air with carbon dioxide heats up more in sunlight, are presented to a US science meeting.
1859: John Tyndall, at the Royal Institution, measures how carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb heat radiation.
1896: Svante Arrhenius estimates that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the world by about 5–6°C.
March 1958: Charles David Keeling begins measuring carbon dioxide here, at about 315 parts per million. The rising 'Keeling Curve' passed 420 in 2023.

dd-climate.text: Burning fossil fuels released a record 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, by the Global Carbon Project's estimate. [China](CHN) emitted about 32%, the [United States](USA) 13%, [India](IND) 8% and the [European Union](DEU) 6%. Over history the picture differs: the United States has emitted about a quarter of all fossil CO2 since 1850, the most of any country. Per person, Americans emit about seven times as much as Indians.

notes.CHN: China became the largest emitter in about 2006 and now emits more than the US and EU combined, mostly from coal. It also installs more solar and wind power than the rest of the world put together, and aims to peak emissions before 2030.
notes.USA: The US has emitted about a quarter of all fossil CO2 since the industrial age began, more than any other country. Its emissions peaked around 2007 but rose again in 2025.
notes.IND: India's emissions are growing fast as its economy expands, but each Indian emits only about 2 tonnes a year, under half the world average.
notes.DEU: The EU's emissions have fallen by over a third since 1990 while its economy grew. Germany is its largest emitter.
notes.RUS: Russia, a major oil, gas and coal producer, emits about 5% of the world's fossil CO2.
notes.JPN: Japan relies heavily on imported coal, gas and oil, and emits under 3% of the world's CO2. Its emissions have been falling since 2013.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has some of the highest emissions per person, burning oil to generate power and desalinate water.
notes.IDN: Indonesia is the world's largest coal exporter and also loses large areas of forest, which adds to its emissions.
notes.BRA: Brazil's fossil emissions are modest, since most of its power comes from hydropower and other renewables, but clearing of the Amazon rainforest releases large amounts of CO2.
notes.GBR: Britain, the first coal economy, has cut its emissions roughly in half since 1990, the fastest in the G7, mainly by phasing out coal.

dd-climate.text: In 2015 nearly every country signed the Paris Agreement, aiming to hold warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C. Each sets its own target. The [United States](USA) left it in January 2026. Several countries, such as [Britain](GBR) in 2024, have shut their last coal power station, while low-lying islands such as [Tuvalu](TUV) and the [Maldives](MDV) face rising seas. In 2025, renewables overtook coal as the world's largest source of electricity.

notes.USA: The US joined the Paris Agreement under President Obama, left under Trump in 2020, rejoined under Biden in 2021 and left again on 27 January 2026. In January 2026 it also announced it would quit the UN climate convention and the IPCC.
notes.IRN: Iran signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 but its parliament has not ratified it.
notes.LBY: Libya signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 but has not ratified it.
notes.YEM: Yemen signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 but, divided by civil war, has not ratified it.
notes.GBR: Britain, where the coal age began, closed its last coal power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, on 30 September 2024, the first G7 country to do so. Its Climate Change Act of 2008 sets legally binding carbon budgets.
notes.BEL: Belgium closed its last coal power station in 2016.
notes.AUT: Austria closed its last coal power station, at Mellach, in April 2020.
notes.SWE: Sweden closed its last coal power plant, in Stockholm, in April 2020, two years ahead of plan.
notes.PRT: Portugal ended coal power in November 2021, when the Pego plant closed.
notes.SVK: Slovakia stopped burning coal for electricity in 2024.
notes.FIN: Finland closed its last major coal power plant, in Helsinki, in April 2025.
notes.IRL: Ireland's Moneypoint station stopped burning coal in June 2025. Wind already supplied over a third of its electricity.
notes.TUV: Most of Tuvalu is less than 3 metres above sea level. Under a 2023 treaty, Australia offers up to 280 Tuvaluans a year the right to move there.
notes.MDV: The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country, with an average height of about 1.5 metres above sea level.
notes.KIR: Most of Kiribati's people live on low coral atolls threatened by rising seas, storm surges and salt water seeping into drinking water.
notes.MHL: The Marshall Islands, low coral atolls in the Pacific, have been among the loudest voices for the 1.5°C limit.
notes.CHN: China pledged in 2025 to cut its emissions by 7–10% from their peak by 2035, its first absolute target.
notes.BRA: Brazil hosted COP30 in Belém in 2025 and cut Amazon deforestation sharply from 2023.

pn: 1992: the Earth Summit agrees the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the basis for all later climate talks.
1997: the Kyoto Protocol sets binding cuts for rich countries. The US never ratified it.
December 2015: nearly 200 countries agree to hold warming well below 2°C, with each setting its own targets.
November 2025: COP30, at the edge of the Amazon, agrees to triple money for adapting to climate change, but not a plan to move away from fossil fuels.
9–20 November 2026: Türkiye is due to host COP31, with Australia as president of the negotiations, an unusual shared arrangement.

dd-oil.text: In 1859 Edwin Drake struck oil in Pennsylvania, and kerosene for lamps was the first big market. Cars, ships and planes soon made oil vital. The [United States](USA) led the world, with [Baku](AZE) in the Russian Empire its great rival around 1900, and [Mexico](MEX) and [Venezuela](VEN) booming in the 1920s. Britain's companies found oil in [Persia](IRN) in 1908, and Americans struck it in [Saudi Arabia](SAU) in 1938.

notes.USA: Oil began here in 1859. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil came to dominate refining until it was broken up in 1911. In 1945 the US produced about two-thirds of the world's oil.
notes.AZE: Baku, then in the Russian Empire, was producing about half the world's oil around 1900. In 1942 Hitler's armies drove towards it but never reached it.
notes.MEX: Mexico's oil boom began in the 1910s, and by 1921 it was the world's second-largest producer. In 1938 it nationalised the foreign oil companies, creating Pemex.
notes.VEN: Oil was found around Lake Maracaibo in the 1910s. By 1928 Venezuela was the world's biggest oil exporter, and oil soon dominated its economy.
notes.IRN: British prospectors struck oil in 1908, and the Anglo-Persian Oil Company was formed in 1909 to exploit it. In 1914 the British government bought a controlling stake to fuel the Royal Navy's new oil-burning ships.
notes.IRQ: A huge gusher at Baba Gurgur, near Kirkuk, in 1927 opened Iraq's oil industry, run by a consortium of British, Dutch, French and American companies.
notes.BHR: In 1932 Bahrain became the first place on the Arab side of the Gulf to strike oil, which encouraged the search in nearby Saudi Arabia.
notes.SAU: Standard Oil of California found oil at Dhahran in 1938. Its Saudi venture became Aramco, and the kingdom's reserves proved to be among the largest on Earth.
notes.KWT: Kuwait struck oil at Burgan in 1938. Exports took off after World War II, turning a small pearling and trading town into a wealthy state.
notes.ROU: Romania's Ploiești fields were Nazi Germany's main source of crude oil, and the Allies bombed them heavily in 1943–44.
notes.IDN: The oil of the Dutch East Indies drew Japan south after the US cut off its oil in 1941. Japan seized the islands in early 1942.

pn: August 1859: Edwin Drake's well strikes oil at about 21 metres, starting the modern oil industry.
January 1901: a gusher near Beaumont, Texas, sprays oil over 40 metres high and launches the Texas oil boom.
Around 1900: Baku's fields, developed by the Nobel brothers among others, produce about half the world's oil.
May 1908: the first big oil find in the Middle East, soon worked by the new Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later BP.
March 1938: the well Dammam No. 7 strikes oil in commercial quantities, the start of Saudi Arabia's oil wealth.

dd-oil.text: In 1960 five producers founded OPEC in Baghdad to win back control of prices from the big Western oil companies. In October 1973, during the Arab–Israeli war, Arab producers cut output and banned sales to the [United States](USA) and the [Netherlands](NLD) for backing Israel. By early 1974 the oil price had roughly quadrupled. [Iran](IRN)'s revolution in 1979 caused a second shock.

notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia led the 1973 embargo under King Faisal. Its huge output and spare capacity made it OPEC's dominant member, and in 1980 it took full ownership of Aramco.
notes.IRN: Iran nationalised its oil in 1951, which led to a 1953 coup backed by the US and Britain. In 1973 it did not join the Arab embargo, but its 1979 revolution sent prices soaring.
notes.IRQ: Iraq hosted OPEC's founding in 1960 and nationalised its oil industry in 1972. Its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, an oil-rich neighbour, led to the Gulf War.
notes.KWT: Kuwait was a founder of OPEC. In 1990 Iraq invaded it, and retreating Iraqi troops set over 600 of its oil wells on fire in 1991.
notes.VEN: Venezuela's oil minister, Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo, was a co-founder of OPEC. Venezuela nationalised its oil industry in 1976.
notes.LBY: Libya's new leader, Muammar Gaddafi, forced oil companies to pay higher prices in 1970, a first crack in their control.
notes.USA: The embargo hit a country that now imported a third of its oil. Americans queued for petrol, and Congress set a national 55 mph speed limit in 1974.
notes.NLD: Embargoed for its support for Israel, the Netherlands banned Sunday driving on ten Sundays from November 1973 to January 1974, leaving motorways to cyclists and walkers.
notes.ARE: Abu Dhabi joined OPEC in 1967, and its membership passed to the United Arab Emirates, formed in 1971.
notes.NGA: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971. Oil from the Niger Delta soon made up most of its exports and government income.
notes.PRT: Portugal was added to the embargo for letting US planes supplying Israel refuel in the Azores.
notes.ZAF: Apartheid South Africa was also embargoed, and built plants to turn its coal into fuel.

pn: September 1960: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela found OPEC.
From 1965: OPEC's headquarters. In 1975 terrorists led by 'Carlos the Jackal' took its oil ministers hostage here.
The narrow exit from the Gulf, through which about a fifth of the world's oil is shipped.

dd-oil.text: Thanks to shale drilling, the [United States](USA) is now the biggest producer, ahead of [Russia](RUS) and [Saudi Arabia](SAU). OPEC's 11 members and 10 partners, together OPEC+, agree output targets. The [UAE](ARE) quit both on 1 May 2026. From March 2026, war between the US, Israel and [Iran](IRN) choked tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and oil passed $100 a barrel.
