notes.USA: The US produced a record of about 13.6 million barrels of crude a day in 2025, the world's largest output, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia leads OPEC and holds some of the world's largest reserves. Its state company, Saudi Aramco, is one of the most valuable companies in the world.
notes.RUS: Russia is the second- or third-largest producer and co-leads OPEC+ with Saudi Arabia. Western sanctions after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine pushed its exports towards China and India.
notes.ARE: The UAE announced on 28 April 2026 that it would leave OPEC and OPEC+ from 1 May, saying it wanted to use its expanded production capacity.
notes.IRN: Iran holds some of the largest oil and gas reserves but has been under heavy sanctions. Its 2026 war with the US and Israel disrupted Gulf shipping.
notes.VEN: Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but output fell below 1 million barrels a day by the 2020s. US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026.
notes.IRQ: Iraq was OPEC's second-largest producer before the 2026 Hormuz crisis, and oil pays for most of its government budget.
notes.CAN: Canada was the fourth-largest producer in 2025, mostly from Alberta's oil sands, and sends most of its exports to the United States.
notes.CHN: China is a major producer but the world's largest crude importer, buying much of its oil from Russia and the Gulf.
notes.NOR: Norway saves its oil income in a sovereign wealth fund, now worth well over a trillion US dollars, one of the world's largest.
notes.BRA: Brazil pumps oil from deep under the Atlantic seabed. In 2025 it joined OPEC+'s wider cooperation charter, without output targets.
notes.GUY: Guyana had no oil output until offshore production began in 2019. It has since become one of the world's fastest-growing producers.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan's giant Tengiz and Kashagan fields make it a major OPEC+ partner, though it has often pumped above its targets.

pn: From March 2026: Iran blocks or threatens shipping after US and Israeli strikes, and oil passes $100 a barrel.
Saudi Arabia's Ghawar, found in 1948, is the world's largest conventional oilfield.
In the 2010s fracking in this Texas and New Mexico basin made the US the world's top producer again.

dd-fascism.text: Benito Mussolini founded the first Fascist movement in Milan in 1919 and took power in [Italy](ITA) in 1922. He promised to revive the glory of ancient Rome. His regime crushed resistance in [Libya](LBY), conquered [Ethiopia](ETH) in 1935–36 with the help of poison gas, and seized [Albania](ALB) in April 1939. In 1936 he joined Hitler in the Rome–Berlin Axis.

notes.ITA: Mussolini ruled from 1922 to 1943. By 1926 Italy was a one-party state with censorship, a secret police and exile to remote islands for opponents.
notes.LBY: Italy invaded Libya in 1911 but held little beyond the coast. In 1923–32 the Fascists reconquered the interior, herding much of the population of Cyrenaica into camps where tens of thousands died.
notes.ETH: Italy invaded in October 1935, using mustard gas against soldiers and civilians. The League of Nations imposed sanctions but did not stop it. Ethiopia was freed by British and Ethiopian forces in 1941.
notes.ERI: Eritrea had been an Italian colony since 1890. It was the main base for the invasion of Ethiopia.
notes.SOM: Southern Somalia was the colony of Italian Somaliland. In 1936 it was merged with Eritrea and Ethiopia into Italian East Africa.
notes.ALB: Albania had long been under Italian influence. Italy invaded on 7 April 1939 and made it part of the Italian crown.
notes.GRC: Italy had held the Dodecanese islands, including Rhodes, since 1912. They passed to Greece in 1947.
notes.HRV: Italy gained Istria and Zadar after World War I and annexed Fiume, today's Rijeka, in 1924. The Fascists pressed Croats and Slovenes there to give up their languages.
notes.SVN: Western Slovenia, including Postojna, was part of Italy between the wars, and its Slovene schools were closed.
notes.DEU: Hitler admired Mussolini. The Rome–Berlin Axis of 1936 became a full military alliance, the Pact of Steel, in May 1939.
notes.ESP: Mussolini sent tens of thousands of troops, and Hitler sent planes, to help Franco win the Spanish Civil War of 1936–39.

pn: 23 March 1919: Mussolini founds the Fasci di Combattimento, the first Fascist movement, at a meeting on Piazza San Sepolcro.
28 October 1922: the March on Rome. Instead of resisting, King Victor Emmanuel III asked Mussolini to form a government.
5 May 1936: Italian troops enter Ethiopia's capital. Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile and appealed to the League of Nations.
7 April 1939: Italy invades Albania, and King Victor Emmanuel III takes its crown days later.

dd-fascism.text: Hitler became chancellor of [Germany](DEU) in January 1933 and within months had abolished democracy. He rearmed and broke the Treaty of Versailles step by step: troops into the Rhineland in 1936, the annexation of [Austria](AUT) in March 1938, the Czech borderlands that autumn and the rest of [Czechia](CZE) in March 1939. On 1 September 1939 he invaded [Poland](POL), and Britain and France declared war.

notes.DEU: The Nazis won 37% of the vote in July 1932, their best free election. Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933, and by July the Nazis were the only legal party.
notes.AUT: Hitler, Austrian by birth, sent troops in on 12 March 1938 and annexed Austria, the Anschluss. Many Austrians cheered, and a controlled vote claimed 99% approval.
notes.CZE: At Munich in September 1938 Britain and France let Germany take the Sudetenland, the German-speaking borderlands. In March 1939 Hitler occupied the rest of the Czech lands.
notes.SVK: Slovakia declared independence under German pressure on 14 March 1939. Its leader, the priest Jozef Tiso, ran a one-party state allied to Germany.
notes.LTU: Germany forced Lithuania to hand over the port of Memel, today's Klaipėda, in March 1939.
notes.POL: Germany invaded on 1 September 1939 and the Soviet Union on 17 September, under their secret pact. Before the war, today's western and northern Poland had been German.
notes.GBR: Britain followed appeasement, trying to satisfy Hitler, until March 1939. It then guaranteed Poland and declared war on 3 September 1939.
notes.FRA: France, scarred by World War I, did not act alone over the Rhineland or Czechoslovakia. It declared war with Britain on 3 September 1939.
notes.RUS: Stalin signed a non-aggression pact with Hitler on 23 August 1939. A secret protocol divided Poland and the Baltic region between them.

pn: November 1923: Hitler's failed Beer Hall Putsch. September 1938: Britain and France agree here to hand Germany the Sudetenland.
Site of the huge Nazi party rallies, and in 1935 of the Nuremberg Laws, which stripped Jews of German citizenship.
27 February 1933: the Reichstag fire. Hitler used it to suspend civil liberties, and in March the Enabling Act let him rule by decree.
7 March 1936: German troops march into the demilitarised Rhineland. Britain and France protest but do nothing.
1 September 1939: a German warship shells this Polish depot at Danzig, among the first shots of World War II.

dd-fascism.text: Fascism inspired movements across Europe. In wartime, Germany put local fascists in power in [Croatia](HRV), [Norway](NOR) and, in 1944, [Hungary](HUN). Other dictators, such as Franco in [Spain](ESP) and Salazar in [Portugal](PRT), borrowed its style but were mainly conservative nationalists. Fascism lost its two leaders within days in April 1945: partisans shot Mussolini, and Hitler killed himself in Berlin.

notes.DEU: Nazism was Germany's form of fascism, built around race. It aimed to conquer 'living space' in the east and to remove, and then murder, Europe's Jews.
notes.ITA: Mussolini was overthrown by his own Fascist Grand Council and the king in July 1943. The Fascist party was dissolved, and Italy's 1948 constitution bans reviving it.
notes.HRV: The Ustaša, led by Ante Pavelić, ruled the Independent State of Croatia from 1941. It murdered hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma.
notes.BIH: Bosnia was part of the Ustaša-ruled Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945.
notes.SVK: Jozef Tiso's Slovak People's Party ran a one-party state allied to Germany and handed most of Slovakia's Jews over for deportation in 1942.
notes.NOR: Vidkun Quisling, leader of a small fascist party, served Germany's occupation as head of government from 1942. His name became a word for traitor, and he was executed in 1945.
notes.HUN: In October 1944 Germany installed Ferenc Szálasi's Arrow Cross. Its militias murdered thousands of Jews in Budapest, many shot on the banks of the Danube.
notes.ESP: Franco won the civil war with Italian and German help and ruled until 1975 through a single party, the Falange. He kept Spain officially out of World War II, though he sent volunteers, the Blue Division, to fight the Soviet Union.
notes.PRT: António de Oliveira Salazar ruled from 1932 to 1968 through his Estado Novo, a Catholic, authoritarian state with a secret police but no mass fascist movement.
notes.ROU: Romania's fascist Iron Guard shared power with General Ion Antonescu in 1940–41, until he crushed it. He then ruled as dictator and Germany's ally.
notes.FRA: After defeat in 1940, Marshal Pétain's Vichy regime ended the republic and collaborated with Germany, though most historians see it as authoritarian rather than fully fascist.
notes.GBR: Oswald Mosley founded the British Union of Fascists in 1932. It never won a seat in Parliament, and Mosley was interned in 1940.

pn: 26 April 1937: German and Italian planes bomb this Basque town for Franco. Picasso's painting made it a symbol of the war.
4 October 1936: tens of thousands of East Londoners block a march by Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists.
1943–45: after his fall, Mussolini heads a German-backed puppet state in northern Italy, named after this lakeside town.
28 April 1945: Italian partisans shoot Mussolini, caught fleeing towards Switzerland. His body was hung up in Milan.
30 April 1945: with Soviet troops in the city, Hitler kills himself in his bunker. Germany surrenders on 8 May.
1945–46: an international tribunal tries 22 leading Nazis; 12 are sentenced to death.

dd-internet.text: In 1936 the British mathematician Alan Turing described a universal computing machine on paper. In the Second World War, [Germany](DEU)'s Konrad Zuse built a working programmable computer, codebreakers in [Britain](GBR) built the electronic Colossus, and the [United States](USA) built ENIAC to calculate artillery tables. After the war the first stored-program computers ran in Britain and the US, and the [Soviet Union](UKR) built its first computer in Kyiv.

notes.GBR: Alan Turing's 1936 paper defined what a computer can do. In the war he helped break Enigma at Bletchley Park, where Colossus, kept secret until the 1970s, was the first large electronic digital computer.
notes.USA: ENIAC, built for the US Army, could do 5,000 additions a second. American firms such as IBM soon dominated the computer business, and the transistor made machines smaller and more reliable.
notes.DEU: Konrad Zuse built his machines largely on his own in Berlin. His Z3 of 1941 is often called the first working programmable, fully automatic computer.
notes.UKR: MESM, built in Kyiv, was among the first stored-program computers in continental Europe. Soviet computing grew fast but later fell behind the West.
notes.RUS: Lebedev's BESM machines, built in Moscow from the early 1950s, did calculations for Soviet nuclear and space programmes.
notes.POL: Polish mathematicians first broke the German Enigma cipher in 1932 and shared their methods with Britain and France in 1939.

pn: May 1941: Konrad Zuse demonstrates the Z3, an electromechanical machine run by programs on punched film. It was destroyed in a 1943 air raid.
1944: Colossus, built by the engineer Tommy Flowers, helps read the German high command's Lorenz cipher.
February 1946: ENIAC, with about 18,000 vacuum tubes, is unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania.
December 1947: at Bell Labs, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley build the first transistor.
21 June 1948: the Manchester 'Baby' runs the first program stored in a computer's own electronic memory.
1950–51: Sergei Lebedev's team builds MESM, the first electronic computer in the Soviet Union.

dd-internet.text: The internet grew out of ARPANET, a US military-funded network that sent its first message in 1969. In 1989–91 the British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN, on the border of [Switzerland](CHE) and [France](FRA). Personal computers from California and phones from [Finland](FIN)'s Nokia brought the network into homes and pockets, while [Japan](JPN), [South Korea](KOR), [Taiwan](TWN) and [China](CHN) became the workshops of the digital age.

notes.USA: TCP/IP, the common language of the internet, became ARPANET's standard in 1983. Silicon Valley firms, from Intel and Apple to Google (1998) and Facebook (2004), led each new wave.
notes.CHE: CERN, Europe's particle physics laboratory near Geneva, created the web so scientists could share documents. The first website went online in 1991.
notes.FRA: Part of CERN lies in France. France also ran Minitel, a national online service on home terminals, from 1982, years before the web.
notes.GBR: Tim Berners-Lee, born in London, invented the web. In Cambridge, ARM was founded in 1990, and its chip designs now run almost all smartphones.
notes.FIN: Nokia was the world's largest mobile phone maker from 1998 until the smartphone era, and Linux, created in Helsinki, now runs most of the world's servers.
notes.SWE: Ericsson helped build the mobile networks of the world, and the Swede Niklas Zennström co-founded Skype.
notes.EST: Skype was built in 2003 by Estonian programmers. Estonia went on to put almost all its public services online.
notes.JPN: Japanese firms such as Sony, Nintendo and Toshiba led consumer electronics, and NTT Docomo's i-mode put the internet on phones in 1999.
notes.KOR: South Korea built one of the world's fastest broadband networks around 2000, and Samsung became the largest maker of memory chips and phones.
notes.TWN: Taiwan's factories made most of the world's laptops and motherboards, and TSMC became the leading chipmaker for other companies.
notes.CHN: China went online in 1994. Its factories assembled most of the world's computers and phones, and firms such as Alibaba and Tencent grew behind state controls on foreign websites.
notes.IND: From the 1990s Bangalore and other Indian cities became centres for software and outsourced IT services, led by firms such as Infosys and TCS.

pn: 29 October 1969: the first ARPANET message is sent to Stanford Research Institute. The system crashed after two letters, 'lo'.
1989–91: Tim Berners-Lee proposes and builds the World Wide Web. CERN made it free for anyone to use in 1993.
1991: a student, Linus Torvalds, releases Linux, and Finland makes the world's first GSM mobile phone call.
Apple, founded in 1976 and based here, launches the Macintosh in 1984 and the iPhone in 2007.
1987: TSMC is founded here as the first company to make chips designed by others.
From 1980: a fishing area becomes a special economic zone and then the world's electronics workshop.

dd-internet.text: About 6 billion people, three in four humans, were online in 2025, according to the UN's ITU, but fewer than one in five in some of the poorest countries, such as [Chad](TCD) and [Burundi](BDI). Since ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, AI chatbots have spread with record speed. Their chips are designed mostly in the [United States](USA) and made mainly in [Taiwan](TWN), with machines from the [Netherlands](NLD), while [China](CHN) races to build its own.

notes.USA: US companies such as Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and Meta lead in AI. The US restricts exports of its most advanced AI chips to China.
notes.TWN: Taiwan's TSMC makes the large majority of the world's most advanced chips, which makes the island central to the world economy and to US–China rivalry.
notes.NLD: ASML's chipmaking machines, each the size of a bus, are made in the Netherlands from parts sourced worldwide. The Dutch government limits their sale to China.
notes.KOR: South Korea's Samsung and SK Hynix make most of the high-bandwidth memory that AI chips need.
notes.JPN: Japan supplies key chipmaking materials and tools, and is backing a national effort to make the most advanced chips again.
notes.CHN: China had about 1.1 billion internet users at the end of 2025, and over 700 million used generative AI by mid-2026, according to its official internet agency, CNNIC.
notes.TCD: In Chad only about one person in eight used the internet in 2024, by ITU estimates. Cost, electricity and coverage are the main barriers.
notes.BDI: Burundi is among the world's least connected countries, with fewer than one in ten people online in 2024, according to the ITU.
notes.AFG: Afghanistan's Taliban government cut internet and phone services nationwide for about two days in September–October 2025, with no official reason given.
notes.IND: India has the second-largest number of internet users after China, and is one of the largest markets for AI chatbots.
notes.EST: Estonia is one of the most digital states: in its 2023 election, about half of all votes were cast online.

pn: 30 November 2022: OpenAI releases ChatGPT. In September 2026 OpenAI said it had about 1.2 billion weekly users.
TSMC, based here, makes most of the world's most advanced chips, including those that train and run AI.
ASML, based here, is the only company that makes the extreme ultraviolet machines needed for the most advanced chips.
January 2025: the start-up DeepSeek releases a powerful AI model built at low cost, despite US limits on chip exports.

dd-nuclear.text: In December 1938 chemists in Berlin split uranium atoms, and scientists soon realised this could release enormous energy. Fearing a Nazi bomb, the [United States](USA), with [Britain](GBR) and [Canada](CAN), built one in the secret Manhattan Project. The first was tested in New Mexico in July 1945, and in August two bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in [Japan](JPN). The [Soviet Union](RUS) tested its own in 1949.

notes.USA: The Manhattan Project employed about 130,000 people at its peak and cost about $2 billion, at secret sites from Tennessee to Washington state.
notes.GBR: British scientists showed in 1940–41 that a bomb was feasible. Britain merged its project into the American one in 1943 and tested its own bomb in 1952.
notes.CAN: Canada supplied uranium and hosted a joint British–Canadian research laboratory that helped the project.
notes.DEU: Germany discovered fission, but its wartime nuclear programme never came close to a bomb. Many of the scientists who built the American bomb were refugees from Nazi Europe.
notes.JPN: Japan is the only country attacked with nuclear weapons. Survivors, the hibakusha, suffered burns, radiation sickness and higher cancer rates for decades.
notes.RUS: Helped by spies inside the Manhattan Project, such as Klaus Fuchs, the Soviet Union tested its first bomb in August 1949, years earlier than the US expected.
notes.KAZ: The Soviet Union's first test was at Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan, where it went on to set off over 450 nuclear explosions by 1989.

pn: December 1938: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split uranium; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explain it as 'fission'.
2 December 1942: Enrico Fermi's team starts the first nuclear chain reaction under a university stadium.
From 1943: J. Robert Oppenheimer leads the secret laboratory that designs the bombs.
16 July 1945: the first nuclear explosion, in the New Mexico desert.
6 August 1945: a uranium bomb destroys the city. About 140,000 people were dead by the end of 1945.
9 August 1945: a plutonium bomb kills about 70,000 people by the end of the year. Japan surrenders days later.

dd-nuclear.text: By 1962 the superpowers had thousands of nuclear weapons. In October an American spy plane photographed Soviet missile sites being built in [Cuba](CUB), 145 km from Florida. President Kennedy ordered a naval 'quarantine' of the island. After 13 tense days, Soviet leader Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to withdraw US missiles from [Turkey](TUR).

notes.CUB: After a failed US-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, Fidel Castro accepted Soviet missiles. About 40,000 Soviet troops were sent to the island.
notes.USA: The US had far more long-range nuclear weapons than the Soviet Union in 1962. Its Strategic Air Command went to DEFCON 2, the highest alert level ever publicly confirmed.
notes.RUS: Khrushchev sent missiles to Cuba to protect his ally and to offset American missiles near Soviet borders. Backing down hurt his standing, and he was ousted in 1964.
notes.TUR: Fifteen US Jupiter missiles in Turkey could reach Moscow. They were quietly removed in April 1963, as secretly promised.
notes.ITA: Italy also hosted 30 US Jupiter missiles, which were removed in 1963 along with those in Turkey.
notes.GBR: Britain, a nuclear power since 1952, hosted 60 US-built Thor missiles from 1958 to 1963, ready to fire during the crisis.

pn: 14 October 1962: a U-2 spy plane photographs Soviet missile sites under construction here.
22 October 1962: Kennedy tells Americans about the missiles on television and announces the quarantine.
28 October 1962: Khrushchev announces on Radio Moscow that the missiles will be removed.

dd-nuclear.text: Nine countries have nuclear weapons, with about 12,200 warheads in January 2026 by SIPRI's estimate; [Russia](RUS) and the [United States](USA) hold about 85% of them. The 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty recognises five nuclear powers. [India](IND), [Pakistan](PAK) and [North Korea](PRK) built bombs outside it, and [Israel](ISR) is believed to have them. [South Africa](ZAF) and [Ukraine](UKR) gave theirs up. The last US–Russian arms limits expired in February 2026.

notes.USA: SIPRI estimated about 5,000 US warheads in January 2026, including over 1,300 retired and awaiting dismantlement. New START, which capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550, expired in February 2026.
notes.RUS: Russia has the largest arsenal, about 5,400 warheads by SIPRI's estimate. It suspended its participation in New START in 2023 and said it would keep the limits only if the US did.
notes.CHN: China has the fastest-growing arsenal, about 620 warheads in January 2026 by SIPRI's estimate, up from about 600 a year earlier.
notes.FRA: France has about 290 warheads in its stockpile by SIPRI's estimate, carried by submarines and Rafale aircraft.
notes.GBR: Britain has about 225 warheads, all now carried on its four Trident submarines. In 2025 it said it would buy F-35A jets to join NATO's nuclear-sharing mission.
notes.IND: India tested a device in 1974 and weapons in 1998, and has about 190 warheads by SIPRI's estimate. It never joined the NPT.
notes.PAK: Pakistan tested weapons in 1998, weeks after India, and has about 170 warheads by SIPRI's estimate.
notes.PRK: North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003 and tested six times from 2006. SIPRI estimates it has about 60 assembled warheads.
notes.ISR: Israel neither confirms nor denies having nuclear weapons. SIPRI estimates about 90 warheads.
notes.BLR: Belarus gave its Soviet-era weapons to Russia by 1996. Since 2023 Russia says it has stationed tactical nuclear weapons there.
notes.ZAF: South Africa secretly built six bombs, then dismantled them and joined the NPT in 1991, the only country to give up weapons it built itself.
notes.UKR: Ukraine inherited about 1,900 Soviet strategic warheads and handed them to Russia by 1996, in return for security assurances in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan sent its inherited Soviet warheads to Russia by 1995 and closed the Semipalatinsk test site in 1991.
notes.IRN: Iran says its programme is peaceful; the US and Israel accuse it of seeking the bomb. US and Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026 hit its nuclear sites, and its status is now unclear.

pn: 2006–2017: North Korea carries out six nuclear tests here.
1974 and 1998: India's nuclear tests in the Rajasthan desert. Pakistan answered with its own tests in May 1998.

dd-globalization.text: Blaming the trade wars of the 1930s for the Depression and war, the [United States](USA) and [Britain](GBR) led the building of a new system. In 1947, 23 countries signed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) to cut tariffs step by step. In 1957 six countries, including [France](FRA) and [West Germany](DEU), founded a common market. The [Soviet Union](RUS) and its allies traded mostly among themselves.

notes.USA: The US, by far the largest economy after 1945, pushed for open trade and stable currencies, and the dollar became the system's anchor.
notes.GBR: Britain helped design the post-war system at Bretton Woods, where the economist John Maynard Keynes led its delegation.
notes.CHN: The Republic of China was a GATT founder, but its government withdrew in 1950 after retreating to Taiwan. The People's Republic joined the WTO only in 2001.
notes.IND: India was a founding member of GATT, but after independence it protected its industries with high tariffs until reforms in 1991.
notes.ZWE: Southern Rhodesia, today's Zimbabwe, signed the GATT in 1947 as a self-governing British colony.
notes.FRA: France and West Germany joined their coal and steel industries in 1951, then founded the European Economic Community in 1957 with Italy and the Benelux countries.
notes.DEU: Only West Germany was in the common market. Its export-led 'economic miracle' made it Europe's industrial powerhouse.
notes.ITA: Italy joined the GATT in 1950 and was a founder of the EEC in 1957. Its north boomed in the 1950s and 1960s.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union set up Comecon in 1949 to link the planned economies of Eastern Europe, largely cut off from Western trade.
notes.CZE: Czechoslovakia signed the GATT in 1947, just before the Communist takeover in 1948, and then joined Comecon in 1949.
notes.JPN: Japan joined the GATT in 1955, and access to Western markets fed its fast export-led growth.

pn: July 1944: Allied nations create the IMF and World Bank and fix exchange rates to the dollar.
October 1947: 23 countries sign the GATT, agreeing about 45,000 tariff cuts.
April 1956: Malcom McLean's tanker Ideal X carries 58 containers to Houston, the start of container shipping.
March 1957: the Treaty of Rome founds the European Economic Community, with a common external tariff.

dd-globalization.text: First [Japan](JPN), then [South Korea](KOR), [Taiwan](TWN), [Hong Kong](HKG) and [Singapore](SGP) grew rich by exporting to Western markets. From 1978 [China](CHN) opened to foreign investment, starting in special economic zones, and joined the World Trade Organization in 2001. Container ships carried its goods west through Singapore and the Suez Canal, and Southeast Asian countries such as [Vietnam](VNM) built export factories too.

notes.JPN: Japan rebuilt after 1945 and by the 1970s exported cars, ships and electronics worldwide. By 1968 it was the world's second-largest economy.
notes.KOR: South Korea, as poor as many African countries in 1960, built firms such as Samsung and Hyundai and became a rich industrial nation.
notes.TWN: Taiwan moved from textiles to electronics. TSMC, founded in 1987, now makes most of the world's most advanced computer chips.
notes.HKG: Hong Kong, a British colony until 1997, was a manufacturing and trading hub, and later the gateway for investment into mainland China.
notes.SGP: Singapore became independent in 1965 and invited multinational companies in, growing into a port, factory and finance hub.
notes.CHN: Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 opened China to foreign investment. After it joined the WTO in December 2001 its exports grew about sevenfold in a decade.
notes.VNM: Vietnam began its 'Doi Moi' market reforms in 1986 and joined the WTO in 2007. It became a major exporter of phones, clothing and shoes.
notes.MYS: Malaysia moved from rubber and tin to electronics, with foreign chip factories in Penang from the 1970s.
notes.THA: Thailand became a major car and electronics maker. Its currency crash started the Asian financial crisis of 1997.
notes.IDN: Indonesia exported oil, then textiles and shoes. It was the country hit hardest by the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis.
notes.EGY: Before attacks on Red Sea shipping from late 2023, the Suez Canal in Egypt carried about an eighth of world trade, on the shortest sea route between Asia and Europe.
notes.MEX: Mexico built export assembly plants, maquiladoras, on the US border, and joined the US and Canada in the NAFTA free-trade area in 1994.

pn: 1980: a fishing area beside Hong Kong becomes China's first special economic zone. It grew into a city of over 17 million.
Since 2010 Shanghai has been the world's busiest container port.
Singapore, on the main sea lane between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, became one of the world's great trans-shipment ports.
Europe's largest port, where many ships from Asia unload their containers.

dd-globalization.text: In 2025 the [United States](USA) raised tariffs to their highest level since the 1930s, hitting [China](CHN) hardest. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court struck down the main tariffs, and the government replaced them with others. China still ran a record trade surplus of about $1.2 trillion. Elsewhere trade deals grew: Asia's RCEP, the world's largest bloc, and an EU deal with [Brazil](BRA) and its Mercosur partners.

notes.USA: The US imposed tariffs on most countries in 2025. After the Supreme Court ruling it used other laws: a 10% global tariff from February 2026, then, from July, tariffs of 10–12.5% on 60 economies, plus higher duties on steel, aluminium and cars.
notes.CHN: US tariffs on Chinese goods briefly reached 145% in April 2025 before a truce. China's exports still grew in 2025 as it sold more to Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe.
notes.CAN: Canada, the largest market for US exports, was hit by US tariffs from 2025. In July 2026 the US declined to renew the North American agreement, which now faces yearly reviews, and put 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods.
notes.MEX: Mexico overtook China as the largest source of US imports in 2023, as some firms moved factories closer to the US market.
notes.DEU: Germany, Europe's biggest exporter, was hit by US tariffs on cars and machinery. In July 2025 the EU agreed a deal with a 15% US tariff ceiling on most goods.
notes.JPN: Japan agreed a trade deal with the US in 2025, pledging large investments in return for lower tariffs. It is also a member of RCEP and the CPTPP, another Asia-Pacific trade pact.
notes.VNM: Vietnam became one of the biggest winners of the shift of factories out of China, and one of the largest sources of US imports.
notes.BRA: The EU signed a long-delayed trade deal with Mercosur in January 2026, after 25 years of talks; its trade part has applied provisionally since May 2026. French and Polish farmers strongly opposed it.
notes.BOL: Bolivia became a full member of Mercosur in 2024 and is not yet part of the EU deal.
notes.IND: India, outside RCEP, faced a 50% US tariff from August 2025, half of it a penalty for buying Russian oil. In February 2026 the US cut it sharply in an interim deal, saying India had agreed to stop those purchases.
notes.AUS: Australia sells about a third of its exports to China, mostly iron ore, and is a member of both RCEP and the CPTPP.
notes.GBR: Britain left the EU in 2020, joined the CPTPP in 2024 and in 2025 was the first country to agree a tariff deal with the Trump administration.

pn: 2 April 2025: President Trump announces tariffs on almost every country. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court rules, 6–3, that the law he used does not allow tariffs.

30 October 2025: Presidents Trump and Xi agree a one-year truce, cutting US tariffs and pausing China's new limits on rare-earth exports. In September 2026 the US said the truce would run to January 2027.
Home of the World Trade Organization, founded in 1995, which has 166 members.

dd-humanrights.text: Fifty-one countries signed up to the UN Charter in 1945. Most of Africa and much of Asia were still colonies with no seat, so the founders came mostly from Europe and the Americas, along with [India](IND), then still British, and [China](CHN), [Egypt](EGY), [Ethiopia](ETH) and [Liberia](LBR). The [Soviet Union](RUS) won two extra seats, for Ukraine and Belarus. Today the UN has 193 members.

notes.CHN: China's seat was held by the Republic of China, whose government fled to Taiwan in 1949. The People's Republic took over the seat in 1971.
notes.TWN: The Republic of China, now based in Taiwan, held China's UN seat until 1971.
notes.IND: British India signed the Charter in 1945, two years before independence.
notes.UKR: Stalin won separate UN seats for Soviet Ukraine and Belarus, giving Moscow three votes in the General Assembly.
notes.POL: Poland missed the San Francisco conference but signed the Charter in October 1945 and counts as a founding member.
notes.ETH: Ethiopia, invaded by Italy in 1935, had seen the old League of Nations fail to protect it.

pn: 26 June 1945: delegates sign the UN Charter at the end of a two-month conference.
The UN's headquarters on the East River opens in the early 1950s.

dd-humanrights.text: On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly, meeting in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Forty-eight countries voted yes and none voted against. Eight abstained: the [Soviet Union](RUS) and its allies objected to parts of it, [Saudi Arabia](SAU) disliked the freedom to change religion, and [South Africa](ZAF) was building apartheid. Two members, [Honduras](HND) and [Yemen](YEM), did not vote.

notes.USA: Eleanor Roosevelt, the US delegate, chaired the committee that drafted the Declaration.
notes.LBN: Lebanon's Charles Malik was one of the Declaration's main authors and philosophers.
notes.FRA: The French jurist René Cassin wrote much of the first full draft. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1968.
notes.CHN: China's delegate P. C. Chang helped make the text less tied to any one culture or religion.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia objected to the articles on freedom to change religion and on equal rights in marriage.
notes.ZAF: South Africa, whose new government began building apartheid in 1948, abstained.
notes.RUS: The Soviet bloc said the text did not go far enough on economic rights and abstained.

pn: 10 December 1948: the General Assembly adopts the Declaration here. 10 December is now Human Rights Day.

dd-humanrights.text: Europe went furthest in turning rights into law. Members of the Council of Europe, founded in 1949, sign the European Convention on Human Rights, and people in them can take a case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, [France](FRA), once courts at home have ruled. Its 46 members stretch from [Iceland](ISL) to [Azerbaijan](AZE). [Russia](RUS) was expelled in 2022 after invading [Ukraine](UKR), and [Belarus](BLR) has never joined.

notes.GBR: British lawyers helped draft the Convention, and since 2000 the UK's Human Rights Act has let its courts apply it directly.
notes.TUR: Turkey has had more judgments against it at the Strasbourg court than any other country.
notes.RUS: Russia joined in 1996 and was expelled in March 2022, weeks after it invaded Ukraine.

pn: The European Court of Human Rights sits here and has delivered tens of thousands of judgments since 1959.

dd-space.text: The [Soviet Union](RUS) launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in October 1957 and put Yuri Gagarin into orbit in April 1961, both from a secret base in today's [Kazakhstan](KAZ). The [United States](USA) answered with the Apollo programme, and in July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon. In 1975 the rivals met in orbit, when an Apollo and a Soyuz docked.

notes.RUS: Moscow ran the Soviet programme, led in secret by the engineer Sergei Korolev. It won the early firsts: satellite, animal, man, woman and spacewalk in orbit.
notes.KAZ: Baikonur Cosmodrome, in the Kazakh steppe, launched Sputnik, Gagarin and Tereshkova. Russia still leases it, and crews to the International Space Station fly from there.
notes.USA: Shocked by Sputnik, the US founded NASA in 1958. Its Apollo programme landed 12 astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.
notes.UKR: Korolev was born in Zhytomyr, in today's Ukraine. Soviet rockets and missiles were also designed and built in Dnipro.
notes.DEU: Wartime Germany built the V-2, the first long-range ballistic missile. After 1945 its engineers, led by Wernher von Braun, went to work for the US, and others for the Soviets.

pn: 4 October 1957: Sputnik 1 is launched from here, and on 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin. Russia still leases the site from Kazakhstan.
From 1960: the closed town outside Moscow where Soviet cosmonauts, including Gagarin and Tereshkova, trained.
16 July 1969: Apollo 11 lifts off from the Kennedy Space Center, next to the Cape Canaveral launch sites.
From 1965: NASA's Mission Control. 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed,' Armstrong radioed on 20 July 1969.
1944: a German V-2 rocket, the ancestor of both sides' space rockets, becomes the first object to reach space, from here.

dd-space.text: After the [Soviet Union](RUS) and the [United States](USA), countries such as [France](FRA), [Japan](JPN), [China](CHN) and [India](IND) built their own launchers. [North Korea](PRK) and [South Korea](KOR) both made it by 2013. Today private companies are joining: Rocket Lab from [New Zealand](NZL) since 2018, and Germany's Isar Aerospace in 2026. European countries also launch together through the European Space Agency.

notes.RUS: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957. Russia inherited its rockets, including the Soyuz, still flying after more than 50 years.
notes.USA: Explorer 1 reached orbit in January 1958. Today US companies such as SpaceX carry out most of the world's launches.
notes.FRA: France became the third space power in 1965, launching its Diamant rocket from Algeria. It later led Europe's Ariane rockets, launched from French Guiana.
notes.JPN: Japan reached orbit in February 1970 with a small rocket called Lambda, launching the satellite Ohsumi.
notes.CHN: China launched its first satellite in April 1970. In 2003 it became the third country to send a person into orbit on its own rocket.
notes.GBR: Britain's Black Arrow put the satellite Prospero into orbit from Australia in 1971, but the programme had already been cancelled. No British rocket has reached orbit since.
notes.IND: India's SLV reached orbit in 1980. It landed a craft near the Moon's south pole in 2023, and in July 2026 the start-up Skyroot also reached orbit.
notes.ISR: Israel launched its first satellite, Ofeq 1, in 1988. Its rockets fire west over the Mediterranean to avoid flying over its neighbours.
notes.IRN: Iran put a satellite into orbit in 2009 with its Safir rocket. Western governments say the programme also helps its missile work.
notes.PRK: After several failed tries, North Korea reached orbit in December 2012. Its space launches are banned by UN resolutions because they use missile technology.
notes.KOR: South Korea reached orbit in 2013 with a rocket whose first stage was Russian. Its fully home-made Nuri rocket first succeeded in 2022.
notes.NZL: Rocket Lab, a company founded in New Zealand and now based in the US, has launched its Electron rocket from the Māhia Peninsula since 2018.
notes.DEU: In September 2026 the Munich company Isar Aerospace reached orbit on its second try, launching from Andøya in Norway.
notes.KAZ: Kazakhstan hosts Baikonur, the world's first launch site, but has never had a rocket of its own.
notes.UKR: Ukraine built Soviet-designed rockets such as the Zenit and Tsyklon, but they flew from Kazakhstan, Russia or a floating platform at sea, never from Ukraine.
notes.AUS: Australia hosted Britain's 1971 launch at Woomera. An Australian company's Eris rocket failed shortly after liftoff in 2025.

dd-polynesia.text: Polynesians' ancestors spoke Austronesian languages, which spread from [Taiwan](TWN) through the [Philippines](PHL) and Indonesia. By about 1350 BC a seafaring people known for their stamped Lapita pottery lived off [Papua New Guinea](PNG). Within a few centuries they sailed into the empty islands beyond, [Vanuatu](VUT), New Caledonia and [Fiji](FJI), and by about 850 BC reached [Tonga](TON) and then [Samoa](WSM), the cradle of Polynesian culture.

notes.TWN: Most linguists trace the Austronesian languages, spoken from Madagascar to Rapa Nui, back to Taiwan, where Indigenous peoples still speak the oldest branches.
notes.PHL: Austronesian farmers and seafarers moved from Taiwan into the Philippines around 2000 BC, carrying pottery, rice and outrigger canoes.
notes.PNG: The Lapita culture first appears in the Bismarck Archipelago, off northern New Guinea, where newcomers mixed with peoples who had lived there for tens of thousands of years.
notes.VUT: Vanuatu was settled by Lapita voyagers around 1000 BC. Their burials at Teouma show they crossed hundreds of kilometres of open sea.
notes.FJI: Fiji was settled around 1000–900 BC. It became a meeting point between Melanesia and Polynesia, trading with Tonga for centuries.
notes.TON: Tonga was reached by about 850 BC. Much later, around 1200, Tongan chiefs built a sea-linked chiefdom whose influence reached Samoa and beyond.
notes.WSM: Samoa was settled soon after Tonga. Here and in Tonga, over centuries of relative isolation, a distinct Polynesian language and culture took shape.
notes.ASM: At To'aga, on Ofu in American Samoa, archaeologists found traces of settlement from around 800 BC.

pn: c. 1350 BC: some of the oldest Lapita sites, with finely stamped pottery, were found on this island in the Bismarcks.
c. 1000 BC: a Lapita cemetery on Efate, Vanuatu, the oldest in Remote Oceania; ancient DNA from it links the settlers to East Asia.
c. 850 BC: a village on Tongatapu, dated by its coral tools, often called the first settlement in Polynesia.

dd-polynesia.text: After a pause of nearly 2,000 years in Western Polynesia, voyagers pushed east. By radiocarbon dating they reached the Society Islands, in [French Polynesia](PYF), around 1025–1120. Within a few generations they found nearly every habitable island in a vast triangle of ocean: Hawaiʻi in the [United States](USA), Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in [Chile](CHL), and last, around 1250–1300, Aotearoa, [New Zealand](NZL).

notes.PYF: The Society Islands, with Tahiti and Raiatea, were the first part of East Polynesia settled. The Marquesas, Tuamotus and Australs followed soon after.
notes.USA: Hawaiʻi, over 4,000 km from Tahiti, was one of the last major places on Earth settled by humans. It became a US state in 1959.
notes.CHL: Rapa Nui, the most remote inhabited island of all, lies about 3,500 km off the coast of Chile, which annexed it in 1888.
notes.NZL: Aotearoa was settled around 1250–1300, the last large land mass on Earth people reached. Māori tradition names the canoes, waka, of the founding voyagers.
notes.COK: The Cook Islands lay on the route between the Society Islands and New Zealand, and Rarotonga became a hub for voyagers.
notes.PCN: Pitcairn and nearby Henderson were settled, then abandoned, Henderson by about 1500 and Pitcairn later, perhaps when trade links to Mangareva broke down.
notes.TON: Tonga and Samoa had been settled for about 2,000 years when East Polynesia was first reached.
notes.WSM: Samoan tradition calls Savaiʻi, its largest island, the ancestral homeland; many East Polynesians remembered a homeland called Hawaiki or Savaiki.

pn: A great marae, or sacred meeting place, on Raiatea, remembered across East Polynesia as a centre of voyaging. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.
Settled around 1200. Islanders carved nearly 1,000 stone statues, the moai, and Chile annexed the island in 1888.
Settled around 1000–1200; estimates vary. Hawaiian tradition remembers later voyages to and from Kahiki, Tahiti.
Settled by Polynesians, who quarried stone tools here, but empty when the Bounty mutineers arrived in 1790.

dd-polynesia.text: Polynesians live in three independent states, [Tonga](TON), [Samoa](WSM) and [Tuvalu](TUV), in self-governing islands tied to New Zealand, and in French, American and British territories. Others are peoples within larger countries: Māori in [New Zealand](NZL), Native Hawaiians in the [United States](USA) and Rapa Nui in [Chile](CHL). In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments, sparking a revival of wayfinding.

notes.TON: Tonga is the Pacific's only kingdom and was never formally colonised; it was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970.
notes.WSM: Samoa, ruled by New Zealand from 1914, became independent in 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so in the 20th century.
notes.TUV: Tuvalu, once the Ellice Islands, became independent from Britain in 1978. Its low atolls are threatened by rising seas.
notes.NZL: In the 2023 census about 18% of New Zealanders identified as Māori. Te reo Māori became an official language in 1987.
notes.USA: American businessmen overthrew the Hawaiian monarchy in 1893, and the US annexed the islands in 1898. Hawaiian, once suppressed in schools, is being revived.
notes.CHL: Rapa Nui has been part of Chile since 1888. Its people have won more say over their island and its moai in recent decades.
notes.PYF: French Polynesia is a self-governing overseas country of France. It hosted France's nuclear tests from 1966 to 1996.
notes.COK: The Cook Islands have governed themselves in free association with New Zealand since 1965.
notes.NIU: Niue, a single raised coral island, has been self-governing in free association with New Zealand since 1974.
notes.FSM: Mau Piailug, the master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia who guided Hōkūleʻa in 1976, taught traditional wayfinding to Hawaiians.

pn: 1 May 1976: Hōkūleʻa set out from Maui, navigated by stars, swells and birds alone.
4 June 1976: after 34 days at sea Hōkūleʻa reached Tahiti, where thousands of people gathered to greet it.
1966–1996: France carried out 193 nuclear tests in French Polynesia, at Moruroa and Fangataufa.

dd-brazil.text: Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed [Brazil](BRA) for [Portugal](PRT) in 1500. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas gave Portugal only the eastern bulge, but slave raiders, cattle ranchers and gold seekers pushed far west, and in 1750 Spain accepted most of their gains. Sugar plantations and then gold mines were worked by enslaved Africans, shipped largely from [Angola](AGO): nearly 5 million in all, more than to any other country.

notes.BRA: Brazil was Portugal's richest colony. Sugar dominated in the 1500s–1600s and gold in the 1700s. Enslaved Africans and their descendants made up much of the population.
notes.PRT: Portugal, a small kingdom, came to depend on Brazilian sugar and gold, much of which flowed on to Britain to pay for imports.
notes.AGO: Portugal held Luanda from 1576. Angola was the largest single source of the Africans taken to Brazil, and Brazilian merchants ran much of the trade.
notes.PRY: Jesuits built missions for the Guaraní in Spanish Paraguay. In the 1620s–30s slave raiders from São Paulo, the bandeirantes, destroyed those in Guairá, now in Brazil, and enslaved thousands.
notes.URY: Portugal founded Colonia do Sacramento in 1680, across the river from Buenos Aires, and the two crowns fought over it for a century until Spain kept it in 1777.
notes.BOL: Gold finds in Mato Grosso in the 1720s drew Portuguese settlers right up to Spain's lands in today's Bolivia.
notes.NLD: The Dutch West India Company seized Brazil's sugar coast in 1630 and was driven out in 1654, taking its know-how to the Caribbean.

pn: 22 April 1500: Cabral's fleet, bound for India, sights the coast near here and claims the land for Portugal.
1549–1763: capital of Brazil and heart of the sugar and slave economy of the north-east.
1630–1654: centre of Dutch Brazil, until Portuguese settlers drove the Dutch out.
Largest community of escaped slaves, with thousands of people, it held out for most of the 1600s until destroyed in 1694.
1690s: gold is found in Minas Gerais, setting off the biggest gold rush the world had yet seen.
1763: becomes the capital, as the port for the gold mines inland.

dd-brazil.text: In 1808 the Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio, and in 1822 Prince Pedro declared [Brazil](BRA) independent and became its emperor. Unlike Spanish America, it stayed in one piece. It lost [Uruguay](URY) in 1828, and with [Argentina](ARG) and Uruguay crushed [Paraguay](PRY) in the bloodiest war in South American history, 1864–1870. Brazil ended slavery in 1888, became a republic in 1889 and bought Acre from [Bolivia](BOL) in 1903.

notes.BRA: Pedro I and his son Pedro II ruled until 1889. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.
notes.PRT: Portugal recognised Brazil's independence in 1825, after Brazil agreed to pay compensation.
notes.URY: Brazil annexed the land as its Cisplatine Province in 1821. After a war with Argentina, Britain helped broker its independence as Uruguay in 1828.
notes.PRY: Paraguay attacked first, in 1864. Estimates vary widely, but many historians believe it lost around half its people to battle, hunger and disease, and it ceded land to Brazil and Argentina.
notes.ARG: Argentina fought with Brazil against Paraguay and gained land in the north-east, including today's Misiones and Formosa provinces.
notes.BOL: Bolivia ceded Acre, rich in rubber trees, in return for £2 million and a promised railway, built by 1912.
notes.GBR: British banks lent heavily to Brazil, and from 1845 the Royal Navy seized slave ships bound for Brazil. Brazil ended the Atlantic slave trade in 1850.

pn: 7 September 1822: by a stream near São Paulo, Prince Pedro proclaims Brazil's independence from Portugal.
13 May 1888: Princess Isabel signs the Golden Law, freeing the last 700,000 or so enslaved people. A coup ends the monarchy in 1889.
1868: after a long siege, the allies take Paraguay's great river fortress, opening the way to Asunción.
January 1869: Brazilian troops occupy Paraguay's capital. They stay until 1876.
1 March 1870: Paraguay's leader Francisco Solano López is killed here by Brazilian soldiers, ending the war.
1903: after a revolt by Brazilian rubber tappers, Bolivia sells Acre to Brazil under the Treaty of Petrópolis.

dd-brazil.text: [Brazil](BRA) has about 213 million people and covers nearly half of South America. It holds about 60% of the Amazon rainforest, which it shares with seven other countries and French Guiana, and is the world's biggest exporter of soybeans, coffee and beef, much of it to [China](CHN). With [Argentina](ARG), Paraguay and Uruguay it founded the Mercosur trade bloc in 1991. On 25 October 2026 President Lula narrowly beat Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff to win a fourth term.

notes.BRA: Lula, president in 2003–2010 and again since 2023, won a fourth term in the 25 October runoff with about 52% of the vote. Flávio, son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had led the first round and did not formally concede.
notes.CHN: China has been Brazil's largest trading partner since 2009, buying vast amounts of its soybeans, iron ore, oil and beef. Both are founding members of the BRICS group.
notes.ARG: Argentina is Brazil's main partner and old rival in South America, and its third-largest trading partner after China and the US.
notes.PRY: Paraguay and Brazil share the Itaipu dam on the Paraná River, one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants.
notes.BOL: Bolivia became a full member of Mercosur in 2024. Like Brazil, it has large parts of the Amazon basin.
notes.URY: Uruguay was briefly a Brazilian province before independence in 1828. Mercosur signed a trade agreement with the EU in January 2026.
notes.PER: The Amazon River rises in the Peruvian Andes. The Amazon Cooperation Treaty of 1978 links the eight countries that share the basin.
notes.COL: Colombia and Brazil share a long border deep in the rainforest, where illegal mining and drug routes cross.
notes.VEN: Venezuela's economic collapse drove hundreds of thousands of migrants into Brazil from 2017, most of them entering through the northern state of Roraima.

pn: Capital since 1960, built from scratch on the inland plateau to draw people away from the coast.
Brazil's richest city and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere, with over 20 million people in its metro area.
November 2025: host of COP30, the UN climate summit, at the mouth of the Amazon.
A city of over 2 million in the heart of the rainforest, once the capital of the rubber boom.

dd-japan.text: After 1639 the Tokugawa shoguns, ruling from Edo, kept most foreigners out of [Japan](JPN) and banned Japanese from going abroad. Trade did not stop, it was channelled: [Dutch](NLD) merchants were confined to the tiny island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour, [Chinese](CHN) traders lived in a walled quarter of the same city, and [Korea](KOR) traded through the island of Tsushima.

notes.JPN: The shoguns ruled Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. Hokkaido was mostly Ainu land, reached through the Matsumae domain in the far south, and the Ryukyu kingdom (Okinawa) was under Satsuma's control from 1609.
notes.NLD: The Dutch East India Company won the trade because it did not try to spread Christianity. Its men were moved to Dejima in 1641 and rarely allowed to leave.
notes.CHN: Chinese merchants were Japan's biggest trading partners, bringing silk, sugar and books, and from 1689 they had to live in a walled quarter of Nagasaki.
notes.KOR: Joseon Korea traded with Japan through a Tsushima post at Busan and sent a dozen grand embassies to Japan during the Tokugawa period.
notes.PRK: This land was part of Joseon Korea, which dealt with Japan through the island of Tsushima.
notes.PRT: Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries had arrived in the 1540s. After the Shimabara uprising of Christian peasants in 1637–38, the Portuguese were expelled in 1639.
notes.ESP: Spanish ships were banned from Japan in 1624, as the shoguns turned against Christianity.
notes.GBR: The English ran a trading post at Hirado from 1613 but gave it up as unprofitable in 1623.

pn: 1600: Tokugawa Ieyasu wins the battle that leaves him master of Japan; he becomes shogun in 1603.
The shogun's capital. By the 1700s it had about a million people, among the largest cities in the world.
Home of the emperor, who was revered but had no real power under the shoguns.
1641–1859: a small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbour where the Dutch were confined.
The lords of this island ran Japan's trade and diplomacy with Korea.

dd-japan.text: In July 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry steamed into the bay at Uraga with four warships, carrying a letter demanding that [Japan](JPN) open its ports to the [United States](USA). He returned in 1854 with more ships and got a treaty. By 1858 Japan had signed unequal treaties with the US, [Britain](GBR), [France](FRA), [Russia](RUS) and the [Netherlands](NLD), and the shogun's weakness in giving way set off his fall.

notes.JPN: Japan's leaders had watched Britain defeat China in the Opium War (1839–42). Facing modern warships with no modern navy of their own, they chose to sign rather than fight.
notes.USA: The US wanted coal and supplies for its ships in the Pacific and safe treatment for shipwrecked sailors. The 1858 Harris Treaty opened more ports and set low tariffs.
notes.GBR: Britain signed a treaty in 1858 on terms like America's: foreigners in Japan were tried in their own consular courts, not Japanese ones.
notes.FRA: France signed in 1858 and later backed the shogun, while Britain grew closer to his rebel opponents.
notes.RUS: Russia sent its own envoy, Putyatin, in 1853, and its 1855 treaty divided the Kuril Islands with Japan.
notes.NLD: The Dutch had warned the shogun in advance that an American fleet was coming, and they too signed a new treaty in 1858.
notes.CHN: Perry sailed from Hong Kong and Shanghai. China's defeat in the Opium War was the warning that made Japan's leaders take him seriously.

pn: 8 July 1853: Perry's steam-powered 'black ships' anchor here and refuse to leave until his letter is accepted.
31 March 1854: the Treaty of Kanagawa opens two ports to American ships and ends two centuries of seclusion.
One of the first two ports opened in 1854, where the first US consul, Townsend Harris, set up in 1856.
The other port named in the 1854 treaty, in the far north on Hokkaido; it opened in 1855.
1853: Perry used the Ryukyu kingdom's port as a base before and after his visits to Japan.

dd-japan.text: In 1868 rebel samurai from Satsuma and Choshu toppled the shogun and restored power to the young Emperor Meiji. The new government copied Western industry, schools and armed forces at great speed. [Japan](JPN) then built an empire: it won [Taiwan](TWN) from China in 1895, beat [Russia](RUS) in 1905 and gained southern Sakhalin, and annexed [Korea](KOR) in 1910.

notes.JPN: The Meiji government abolished the domains in 1871, ended the samurai class, brought in conscription in 1873 and a constitution in 1889. Hokkaido and Okinawa were absorbed as Japanese land.
notes.TWN: China ceded Taiwan after losing the 1894–95 war over Korea. Japan crushed local resistance and ruled the island as a colony until 1945.
notes.KOR: Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in August 1910, ruling it harshly until 1945.
notes.PRK: Part of Korea, annexed by Japan in 1910. Japan later built mines and heavy industry in the north.
notes.RUS: Russia lost the war of 1904–05, the first defeat of a European great power by an Asian one in modern times, and gave southern Sakhalin to Japan.
notes.CHN: China lost the 1894–95 war and Taiwan. After 1905 Japan also took over Russia's leased territory and railway in southern Manchuria.
notes.USA: President Theodore Roosevelt brokered the 1905 peace treaty, signed at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and won the Nobel Peace Prize for it.
notes.GBR: Britain made an alliance with Japan in 1902, the first between a Western power and an Asian one on equal terms.

pn: 1868: Edo is renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital', and the emperor moves there from Kyoto.
April 1895: China signs a treaty here after losing the Sino-Japanese War, giving up Taiwan.
1904–05: Japan besieges and takes this Russian naval base in Manchuria.
May 1905: Admiral Togo's fleet destroys Russia's Baltic Fleet after its voyage halfway round the world.
1905: southern Sakhalin, below 50°N, becomes the Japanese colony of Karafuto until 1945.

dd-australia.text: After losing its American colonies, which had taken about 50,000 of its convicts, [Britain](GBR) needed a new place to send them. In May 1787 eleven ships, the First Fleet, sailed for [Australia](AUS) with about 1,400 people, over 750 of them convicts. On 26 January 1788 they raised the British flag at Sydney Cove, on land where Aboriginal people had lived for at least 50,000 years.

notes.GBR: Britain's prisons and old prison ships were overflowing, and transportation was the usual sentence for many crimes, including theft.
notes.IRL: Tens of thousands of the convicts were Irish, some of them rebels against British rule.
notes.USA: Britain had sent convicts to its American colonies until the War of Independence began in 1775.
notes.AUS: James Cook had claimed the east coast for Britain in 1770. Britain treated the land as terra nullius, belonging to no one, though hundreds of Aboriginal nations lived there.
notes.NZL: Cook charted New Zealand in 1769–70. Māori had arrived from eastern Polynesia around 1250–1300, the last major land mass people settled.

pn: 13 May 1787: the First Fleet sets sail under Captain Arthur Phillip.
August 1787: the fleet spends a month in Portuguese Brazil taking on food, seeds and rum.
October 1787: last port of call, in the Dutch Cape Colony, where the fleet loads livestock and plants.
18–20 January 1788: the ships arrive, but Phillip finds poor soil and little fresh water and moves north.
26 January 1788: the British flag is raised. Australians mark the day as Australia Day; many Aboriginal people call it Invasion Day.

dd-australia.text: Britain founded colonies around [Australia](AUS)'s coast, from Tasmania in 1803 to Western Australia in 1829. Settlers and their sheep pushed inland, and frontier violence and new diseases devastated Aboriginal peoples. In [New Zealand](NZL) the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi led to British rule, then to wars over Māori land. Gold rushes from 1851 brought waves of migrants, and in 1901 the six colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia.

notes.AUS: Historians estimate that frontier violence killed tens of thousands of Aboriginal people, and that disease killed far more. Federation came in 1901, and one of the first laws began the White Australia policy.
notes.NZL: The English and Māori texts of the Treaty of Waitangi differ on what chiefs gave up. Wars from 1845 to 1872 and land confiscations followed. In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote.

pn: 1820s–1832: the Black War in Tasmania. By the 1830s most surviving Aboriginal Tasmanians had been removed to Flinders Island.
10 June 1838: stockmen kill about 28 Wirrayaraay people. Seven of the killers were hanged, a rare punishment for a frontier massacre.
6 February 1840: the first Māori chiefs sign the Treaty of Waitangi with the British Crown.
December 1854: gold miners rebel at the Eureka Stockade against licence fees and lack of a vote.
November 1863: a key battle of the British invasion of the Waikato, after which much Māori land was confiscated.
1901: the first federal parliament meets here. It sits in Melbourne until Canberra opens in 1927.

dd-australia.text: Once overwhelmingly British, [Australia](AUS) opened to Asian migrants after the White Australia policy ended in the 1970s. In the 2021 census over a quarter of Australians had been born overseas, most often in England, [India](IND), [China](CHN), New Zealand and the [Philippines](PHL). [New Zealand](NZL) has close family ties with Pacific islands such as [Samoa](WSM) and the [Cook Islands](COK), and Māori make up about one in six of its people.

notes.AUS: About 27.6% of Australians were born overseas in 2021. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were 3.2% of those counted.
notes.NZL: In the 2023 census about 17.8% of New Zealanders identified as Māori. Te reo Māori has been an official language since 1987.
notes.GBR: England was the top overseas birthplace in Australia's 2021 census, with over 900,000 people. King Charles III is still head of state of both countries.
notes.IND: India passed China and New Zealand to become the second-largest overseas birthplace in Australia in 2021, with about 670,000 people.
notes.CHN: Chinese miners came in the 1850s gold rushes. In 2021 about 550,000 Australians had been born in China.
notes.PHL: The Philippines was the fifth-largest overseas birthplace in Australia in 2021, with about 290,000 people.
notes.VNM: Tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees came after 1975, the first big test of Australia's end to White Australia.
notes.WSM: New Zealand ruled Samoa from 1914 until its independence in 1962. Samoans are the largest Pacific community in New Zealand.
notes.COK: The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens, and far more live in New Zealand than at home.
notes.NIU: Niue, also in free association with New Zealand, has under 2,000 residents; many times more Niueans live in New Zealand.
notes.TON: Tonga, a British protectorate that kept its own monarchy, has a large community in New Zealand and Australia, whose remittances support families at home.

dd-frenchrev.text: In 1789 [France](FRA), western Europe's most populous kingdom with about 28 million people, was bankrupt. Louis XVI called the Estates-General to Versailles, its commoners declared themselves a National Assembly, and Paris crowds stormed the Bastille. By 1793 the king was dead, and the republic was fighting rebels in the west and south. In the richest colony, Saint-Domingue, today's [Haiti](HTI), enslaved people rose in 1791, and France abolished slavery in 1794.

notes.FRA: France was split into three estates: clergy, nobles and everyone else, about 97% of the people. In August 1789 the Assembly abolished noble privileges and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
notes.HTI: Saint-Domingue produced much of the world's sugar and coffee, worked by about half a million enslaved people. Their revolt from 1791 led France's commissioners to free them in 1793, and Paris abolished slavery in all French colonies in 1794.
notes.USA: France's help in the American War of Independence deepened its debts, and officers such as Lafayette came home with ideas of liberty.
notes.GBR: In Britain the revolution split opinion. Edmund Burke warned against it in 1790, and Thomas Paine defended it in 'Rights of Man'.
notes.AUT: Queen Marie Antoinette was the Austrian emperor's sister. Her family ties made Austria an enemy of the revolution, and she was guillotined in October 1793.
notes.CHE: Hundreds of the king's Swiss Guards were killed defending the Tuileries Palace in Paris on 10 August 1792, the day the monarchy fell.

pn: 20 June 1789: locked out of their hall, the deputies of the Third Estate swear the Tennis Court Oath not to part until France has a constitution.
14 July 1789: crowds storm the Bastille fortress for gunpowder. 21 January 1793: Louis XVI is guillotined.
21 June 1791: the royal family, fleeing in disguise towards the border, is recognised and stopped here.
1793: centre of the Vendée uprising, a Catholic and royalist peasant revolt crushed with mass killings.
1793: France's second city rebels against Paris. After a siege, the republic executes nearly 2,000 people there.
1793: royalists hand the naval port to the British. A young artillery captain, Napoleon Bonaparte, helps retake it in December.

dd-frenchrev.text: In April 1792 [France](FRA) declared war on Austria, which held today's [Belgium](BEL), and Prussia joined in. After Louis XVI's execution in 1793, [Britain](GBR), the Dutch Republic, [Spain](ESP) and others joined the First Coalition. Facing invasion and revolt, the republic conscripted all unmarried men aged 18 to 25 and fielded the largest armies Europe had seen. By 1795 it had won Belgium, the Netherlands and the Rhineland.

notes.FRA: The levée en masse of August 1793 put the whole nation on a war footing. France's armies grew to several hundred thousand men, led by officers promoted for talent rather than birth.
notes.AUT: Austria was the main enemy on land. It lost the Austrian Netherlands and, after Napoleon's Italian campaign, made peace at Campo Formio in 1797.
notes.DEU: Prussia invaded France in 1792 but was turned back at Valmy. It made a separate peace in 1795, giving France a free hand west of the Rhine.
notes.BEL: The Austrian Netherlands changed hands twice before France won them in 1794. They were annexed to France in 1795.
notes.NLD: French armies crossed the frozen rivers in the winter of 1794–95. The Dutch Republic became the Batavian Republic, a French ally.
notes.GBR: Britain joined the war in February 1793. Its navy blockaded France and seized French colonies, and it paid allies to fight on land.
notes.ESP: Spain fought France in the Pyrenees in 1793–95, then switched sides and allied with France in 1796.
notes.ITA: Piedmont-Sardinia lost Savoy and Nice to France in 1792 and fought on until 1796. Naples also sent ships and troops.
notes.PRT: Portugal, Britain's old ally, sent troops to help Spain against France in 1793–95.
notes.RUS: Catherine the Great backed the coalition but sent no army, busy partitioning Poland instead.

pn: 20 September 1792: French artillery halts the Prussian invasion. The next day the monarchy was abolished.
6 November 1792: France defeats Austria and overruns the Austrian Netherlands, today's Belgium.
August–December 1793: a British and Spanish fleet holds the port until the republic's army retakes it.
26 June 1794: France wins back Belgium in the first battle watched from a military reconnaissance balloon.

dd-frenchrev.text: Victories let [France](FRA) annex [Belgium](BEL), the Rhineland, Savoy and Nice, and surround itself with 'sister republics' modelled on its own: the Batavian in the [Netherlands](NLD), the Helvetic in [Switzerland](CHE), and several in [Italy](ITA). A Second Coalition, of [Britain](GBR), [Austria](AUT), [Russia](RUS) and the Ottomans, struck back in 1799. That November, General Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup.

notes.FRA: After the Terror ended in 1794, a five-man Directory ruled from 1795. It was weak and corrupt, depended on the army, and was toppled by Bonaparte in 1799.
notes.BEL: Belgium was annexed in 1795 and divided into French departments, with French law, conscription and the closing of monasteries.
notes.DEU: The Rhineland west of the river was occupied from 1794. Austria accepted its loss in 1797, and the Treaty of Lunéville confirmed it as French in 1801.
notes.MCO: France annexed Monaco in 1793. The Grimaldi princes got it back in 1814.
notes.NLD: The Batavian Republic, proclaimed in 1795, abolished the old provinces' privileges and gave the Netherlands its first national constitution in 1798.
notes.CHE: France invaded the old Swiss Confederation in 1798 and set up the centralised Helvetic Republic. Geneva was annexed to France.
notes.ITA: Bonaparte's victories created the Cisalpine Republic around Milan and the Ligurian around Genoa in 1797. Roman and Neapolitan republics followed, but most collapsed in 1799 when Austrian and Russian armies arrived.
notes.AUT: Austria went back to war in 1799 and, with Russian help, drove the French out of most of Italy that year.
notes.RUS: Russian armies under Alexander Suvorov won battles in northern Italy and crossed the Alps into Switzerland in 1799.
notes.GBR: Britain's navy destroyed the French fleet at the Nile in August 1798. In Ireland the United Irishmen rose with French help in 1798, and were crushed.
notes.IRL: The 1798 rising of the United Irishmen, inspired by the French Revolution, was put down with great loss of life. The Act of Union of 1800 then merged Ireland into the United Kingdom.
notes.TUR: The Ottoman Empire joined the coalition after Bonaparte invaded Ottoman Egypt in 1798.

pn: 17 October 1797: Austria gives up Belgium and accepts France's Italian republics, in return for Venice.
February 1798: French troops proclaim a Roman Republic, and Pope Pius VI is taken away. He died a prisoner in France in 1799.
January 1799: the Parthenopean Republic is declared. It fell within five months, and royalists executed many of its leaders.
9–10 November 1799 (18–19 Brumaire): Bonaparte's soldiers clear the legislature, ending the revolutionary decade.

dd-latam.text: In 1800 Spain claimed everything from California to Cape Horn, ruling through great viceroyalties, and Portugal ruled [Brazil](BRA). American-born whites, the creoles, owned land and mines but were kept from top posts, which went to officials from Spain. Below them were Indigenous peoples, people of mixed descent and enslaved Africans. Next door, in French [Haiti](HTI), enslaved people had risen in 1791 and were fighting for freedom.

notes.MEX: New Spain was Spain's richest colony, a major source of the world's silver.
notes.USA: Spain also held Florida and the lands from Texas to California. In 1800 it secretly handed Louisiana back to France, which sold it to the US in 1803.
notes.BRA: Brazil was Portugal's great sugar, gold and coffee colony and imported more enslaved Africans than any other land in the Americas.
notes.HTI: Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was France's richest colony, with about half a million enslaved people. Their revolt began in August 1791.
notes.VEN: Venezuela's cocoa-growing creole elite produced the leader of the north's independence wars, Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas in 1783.
notes.ARG: Buenos Aires grew rich on trade once Spain made it the capital of a new viceroyalty in 1776.
notes.BOL: Upper Peru, today's Bolivia, held the Potosí silver mines and was moved from Peru to the new Río de la Plata viceroyalty in 1776.
notes.PER: Lima was the old heart of Spanish South America, and Peru's elite stayed loyal to Spain longer than any other.
notes.CUB: Cuba was booming as a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans. It stayed Spanish until 1898.

pn: Capital of New Spain and the largest city in the Americas around 1800.
From the 1540s its silver mountain made Spain rich, worked largely by forced Indigenous labour.
1780–81: Túpac Amaru II leads a huge Indigenous revolt against Spanish rule. It is crushed and he is executed.
1808: fleeing Napoleon, the Portuguese royal family moves here, making it the capital of the Portuguese Empire.

dd-latam.text: [Haiti](HTI) won independence in 1804. When Napoleon seized Spain in 1808, its colonies began to govern themselves. Simón Bolívar freed [Venezuela](VEN), [Colombia](COL) and [Ecuador](ECU), while José de San Martín crossed the Andes to free [Chile](CHL) and entered Lima. Their armies finished Spanish rule in [Peru](PER) in 1824. [Mexico](MEX) broke free in 1821, and [Brazil](BRA) became an empire under a Portuguese prince in 1822.

notes.HTI: Haiti's revolution was the only successful uprising of enslaved people to found a state. France made it pay a huge indemnity from 1825 in return for recognition.
notes.VEN: Venezuela declared independence in 1811, but its First Republic fell within a year. Victory at Carabobo in 1821 finally secured it.
notes.COL: Bolívar made Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama one state, Gran Colombia, in 1819–1822.
notes.ECU: Sucre's victory at Pichincha, above Quito, in May 1822 freed Ecuador, which joined Gran Colombia.
notes.BOL: Upper Peru became independent in 1825 and named itself after Bolívar.
notes.ARG: Argentina, then the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, declared independence at Tucumán on 9 July 1816.
notes.CHL: San Martín's army crossed the Andes and won at Chacabuco in 1817. Chile declared independence in 1818.
notes.PER: San Martín declared Peru independent in Lima in 1821, but Spanish armies held the highlands until Ayacucho in 1824.
notes.MEX: Hidalgo's 1810 revolt was crushed, but in 1821 a royalist officer, Agustín de Iturbide, changed sides and Mexico won independence.
notes.BRA: Brazil's break was the least bloody: a Portuguese prince led it, and it kept a monarchy and slavery.
notes.PRY: Paraguay threw off rule from both Spain and Buenos Aires in 1811.
notes.URY: Uruguay, fought over by Brazil and Argentina, became independent in 1828 with British mediation.
notes.CUB: Cuba and Puerto Rico, rich sugar colonies wary of a Haitian-style slave revolt, stayed Spanish.

pn: 1 January 1804: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent after defeating Napoleon's army.
16 September 1810: the priest Miguel Hidalgo calls Mexicans to revolt, the day Mexico celebrates as its independence day.
7 August 1819: after crossing the Andes, Bolívar wins the battle that frees Bogotá.
July 1822: Bolívar and San Martín meet in secret. San Martín soon withdraws, leaving the war to Bolívar.
9 December 1824: Antonio José de Sucre defeats the last big Spanish army in South America.
7 September 1822: Prince Pedro, heir to Portugal's throne, declares Brazil independent and becomes its emperor.

dd-latam.text: Bolívar's Gran Colombia split into [Venezuela](VEN), [Colombia](COL) and [Ecuador](ECU) in 1830–31, and the Central American federation broke into five states. [Mexico](MEX) lost about half its land to the [United States](USA) by 1848. [Paraguay](PRY) was crushed by Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay in 1864–70. Spain kept [Cuba](CUB) and [Puerto Rico](PRI) until the US defeated it in 1898.

notes.VEN: Venezuela left Gran Colombia in 1830 under José Antonio Páez, one of the many military strongmen, or caudillos, who ruled the new nations.
notes.COL: Colombia kept Panama until 1903, when Panama broke away with US backing.
notes.MEX: Mexico lost Texas in 1836 and, after the 1846–48 war, everything from California to New Mexico: about half its land, counting Texas.
notes.USA: The US gained California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico in 1848, after annexing Texas in 1845.
notes.PRY: Paraguay lost land to Brazil and Argentina and a huge share of its people, above all men. Estimates vary widely: the most cited is about half, though some historians put it far lower.
notes.BRA: Brazil was the only lasting monarchy in Latin America. It became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888, and a republic in 1889.
notes.CUB: Cubans fought Spain in 1868–78 and again from 1895. US intervention in 1898 ended Spanish rule, but Cuba came under strong US influence.
notes.PRI: Spain ceded Puerto Rico to the US in 1898, and it remains a US territory.
notes.BOL: In the War of the Pacific, 1879–84, Chile took Bolivia's coast, leaving Bolivia landlocked.

pn: 17 December 1830: Bolívar dies here, ill and disillusioned, as his union falls apart.
September 1847: US troops capture the capital. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo hands over Mexico's north.
February 1898: the USS Maine explodes in the harbour, a spark for the Spanish–American War.

dd-ireland.text: Under the 1801 Act of Union, all of [Ireland](IRL) was ruled from London as part of the [United Kingdom](GBR). Millions of poor Irish people lived almost entirely on potatoes, and from 1845 a blight rotted the crop year after year. About 1 million people died of hunger and disease, and by 1855 about 2 million had left, most for the [United States](USA), [Canada](CAN) and Britain.

notes.IRL: About 8.5 million people lived on the island before the Famine. Death and emigration cut that by a fifth to a quarter, and the island still has fewer people today.
notes.GBR: London's relief was limited by a belief that markets should not be disturbed. Public works and, in 1847, soup kitchens feeding about 3 million people a day came late and were soon cut back.
notes.USA: The US took the most famine emigrants. Irish Catholics met hostility from nativists but became a powerful force in the cities of the north-east.
notes.CAN: About 100,000 people sailed for British North America in 1847 alone, on crowded ships that came to be called 'coffin ships'. Many thousands died at sea or on arrival.
notes.AUS: Fares to Australia were costly, but schemes paid for some, including over 4,000 orphan girls from Irish workhouses sent in 1848–50.

pn: Winter 1846–47: reports and drawings of the starving in this Cork town shocked readers in Britain and beyond.
1847: hundreds of thousands of famine refugees landed here. Many stayed; others sailed on to America.
1847: on this quarantine island near Quebec, over 5,000 people, most of them Irish, died of typhus and were buried.
By 1855 more than one in four New Yorkers had been born in Ireland.

dd-ireland.text: Most Irish Catholics wanted home rule or independence, but most Protestants in the north-east, unionists, wanted to stay in the [United Kingdom](GBR). After the Easter Rising of 1916 and a war of independence from 1919 to 1921, the island was divided.
