Six north-eastern counties became Northern Ireland, inside the UK, and 26 counties became the self-governing Irish Free State, today's [Ireland](IRL), in December 1922.

notes.IRL: The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 split nationalists, and pro- and anti-Treaty forces fought a civil war in 1922–23. The Free State left the Commonwealth and became a republic in 1949.
notes.GBR: Britain created Northern Ireland under the Government of Ireland Act of 1920. Its six counties had a Protestant, unionist majority of about two-thirds, and a large Catholic minority.

pn: 24–29 April 1916: the Easter Rising. Rebels seize the General Post Office and proclaim an Irish Republic; Britain later executes 16 leaders.
21 January 1919: IRA volunteers kill two policemen here on the day the separatist Dáil first meets in Dublin. The war of independence begins.
22 June 1921: King George V opens the new Parliament of Northern Ireland, with a large unionist majority.
22 August 1922: Michael Collins, a leader of the war of independence and head of the new government, is killed in an ambush during the civil war.

dd-ireland.text: In Northern Ireland, unionists, mostly Protestant, ran the government for 50 years, and many Catholics, mostly nationalists, protested discrimination. In 1968–69 civil rights marches led to riots, and British troops arrived. For three decades republican and loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces were caught in a conflict that killed about 3,500 people. The [United Kingdom](GBR), [Ireland](IRL) and the local parties, with help from the [United States](USA), reached the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.

notes.GBR: Britain sent troops in August 1969 and ruled Northern Ireland directly from London from 1972. About 3,500 people died in 1969–2001, over half of them civilians; the IRA's bombs also struck English cities.
notes.IRL: Ireland's 1937 constitution claimed the whole island. In 1998 voters there approved the peace deal by 94% and dropped that claim; in Northern Ireland 71% voted yes.
notes.USA: Irish Americans followed the conflict closely. President Clinton backed the peace process, and Senator George Mitchell chaired the talks that produced the 1998 agreement.

pn: 30 January 1972, Bloody Sunday: British soldiers shoot dead 13 civil rights marchers; another dies later. A 2010 inquiry found that none posed a threat and the killings were unjustified.
10 April 1998: the Good Friday Agreement is reached at Stormont, after talks chaired by US Senator George Mitchell.
17 May 1974: loyalist car bombs in Dublin and Monaghan kill 33 people, the deadliest day of the Troubles.
8 November 1987: an IRA bomb at a Remembrance Day ceremony kills 11 people; a 12th died after years in a coma.
15 August 1998: a car bomb by the Real IRA, a group opposed to the peace deal, kills 29 people, the deadliest single attack of the Troubles.

dd-mexico.text: In 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo launched a revolt against Spanish rule, and in 1821 [Mexico](MEX) won independence, stretching from Oregon's border to Central America. Within a generation it lost about half its land. Texas broke away in 1836 and joined the [United States](USA) in 1845. The US then invaded, took Mexico City in 1847, and in 1848 forced Mexico to cede California and the Southwest.

notes.MEX: Mexico won independence in 1821 under Agustín de Iturbide, who was proclaimed emperor in 1822. It became a republic in 1824, but coups and civil wars followed for decades.
notes.USA: The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the US California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico, and confirmed Texas as American. The US paid $15 million.
notes.GTM: Spain's Central American lands joined Iturbide's empire in 1822 and left in 1823, except Chiapas, which chose to stay with Mexico in 1824.
notes.ESP: Spain tried to reconquer Mexico with a landing at Tampico in 1829, failed, and recognised Mexican independence in 1836.
notes.FRA: France invaded in 1862 and made the Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor of Mexico. Benito Juárez's republicans defeated and executed him in 1867.
notes.CRI: Costa Rica was the southernmost land briefly tied to the Mexican Empire. Central America formed its own federation in 1823.

pn: 16 September 1810: Miguel Hidalgo calls his parishioners to revolt, now celebrated as Independence Day.
6 March 1836: Santa Anna's army storms the mission held by Texan rebels and kills nearly all the defenders.
21 April 1836: Texans rout Santa Anna's army and capture him, securing Texas's independence in practice.
13 September 1847: US troops storm the castle; Mexico honours six young cadets who died defending it.
1853: Mexico sells this strip of desert to the US for $10 million, the Gadsden Purchase, fixing today's border.

dd-mexico.text: In 1910 Francisco Madero rose against Porfirio Díaz, who had ruled [Mexico](MEX) for over 30 years. Díaz fell in 1911, but Madero was murdered in 1913, and rival armies, including Pancho Villa's in the north and Emiliano Zapata's peasants in the south, fought for a decade. The [United States](USA) intervened twice, and [Germany](DEU) tried to lure Mexico into World War I. Hundreds of thousands died.

notes.MEX: Estimates of the revolution's dead range from several hundred thousand to over a million, and many more fled north. The victors' party later ruled Mexico for 71 years.
notes.USA: About 10,000 US troops under General John Pershing hunted Villa in Chihuahua in 1916–17 without catching him. Many Mexicans moved to the US to escape the fighting.
notes.DEU: In the 1917 Zimmermann Telegram, Germany offered to help Mexico regain Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined the war. Mexico declined, but the leak helped bring the US into the war.
notes.GBR: British firms, like American ones, owned much of Mexico's booming oil industry. Mexico nationalised it in 1938.

pn: May 1911: rebels under Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa take the border city, and Díaz resigns and leaves for exile.
February 1913: General Victoriano Huerta seizes power; President Madero is shot days later.
April 1914: US forces seize the port to cut arms supplies to Huerta, and stay seven months.
9 March 1916: Villa's men raid this New Mexico town, killing about 18 Americans. The US sends troops into Mexico.
5 February 1917: the new constitution promises land reform, workers' rights and national ownership of minerals and oil.
10 April 1919: Emiliano Zapata is lured into an ambush here and killed by government troops.

dd-mexico.text: [Mexico](MEX), home to about 133 million people, sends roughly four-fifths of its exports to the [United States](USA), its partner with [Canada](CAN) in the USMCA trade pact, which replaced NAFTA in 2020. At its July 2026 review the US declined to extend the pact unchanged, amid US tariffs on Mexican cars and steel. President Claudia Sheinbaum has stepped up the fight against drug cartels while rejecting any US military action on Mexican soil.

notes.MEX: Morena, the party founded by Andrés Manuel López Obrador, has governed since 2018. Official INEGI figures record well over 400,000 homicides since 2007, and more than 130,000 people listed as missing.
notes.USA: Mexico was the largest US trading partner in 2025. In 2025 the US labelled several Mexican cartels terrorist groups. Over 35 million people of Mexican origin live in the US.
notes.CAN: Canada joined NAFTA with Mexico and the US in 1994. In 2026 both Canada and Mexico sought a long extension of the USMCA, while the US pressed for changes.
notes.GTM: Guatemala shares Mexico's southern border. For years migrants from Central America, and later from much further away, crossed Mexico to reach the US.
notes.HND: Honduras was a major source of migrants in the 2010s, driven by poverty and gang violence. Crossings through Mexico fell sharply in 2025 under tighter US and Mexican controls.
notes.SLV: El Salvador, like Honduras and Guatemala, sent many migrants north, many fleeing gang violence. In 2025 Mexico also sent 10,000 National Guard troops to its US border under a deal with Washington.

pn: 1 October 2024: Claudia Sheinbaum, a climate scientist and former mayor of the city, takes office as Mexico's first woman president.
Industrial capital of the north, where many firms built factories in the 2020s to supply the US market.
Its crossing into San Diego is one of the busiest land border crossings in the world.
From September 2024 rival factions of the Sinaloa cartel fought a bloody war for control of the city.
22 February 2026: Mexican troops fatally wound Nemesio Oseguera, 'El Mencho', leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. Cartel gunmen block roads in some 20 states.

dd-germany.text: Prussia's chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, united Germany through three short wars: against Denmark in 1864, [Austria](AUT) in 1866 and [France](FRA) in 1870–71. On 18 January 1871 the King of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles. The new [German Empire](DEU) left Austria out, took Alsace-Lorraine from France and stretched east across much of today's [Poland](POL).

notes.DEU: The empire joined Prussia with kingdoms such as Bavaria, Saxony and Württemberg. Prussia held about two-thirds of its land, and its king was always emperor.
notes.POL: Today's Poland was then split between Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary. Germany held the largest share, including Silesia, Pomerania, Poznań and much of the Baltic coast.
notes.FRA: France lost the war of 1870–71, paid a large indemnity and gave up Alsace and part of Lorraine. Winning them back became a French national aim.
notes.AUT: Austria had led the German Confederation until Prussia beat it in 1866. Bismarck then built a smaller Germany without it, and the two became allies in 1879.
notes.CZE: Bohemia and Moravia, home to many German speakers, belonged to Austria. The decisive battle of 1866 was fought here, at Königgrätz.
notes.DNK: Prussia and Austria took Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark in 1864. The northern part of Schleswig voted to return to Denmark in 1920.
notes.LTU: Memel (Klaipėda) was the empire's north-eastern tip. Germany lost it after World War I, and it is now Lithuania's main port.
notes.RUS: The Russian Empire bordered Germany in the east. Germany's East Prussia included Königsberg, today Russia's Kaliningrad.
notes.ITA: Italy was unified at the same time. It took Rome in 1870, when French troops left to fight Prussia.

pn: 18 January 1871: Wilhelm I is proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors of the French kings' palace.
2 September 1870: the French emperor Napoleon III surrenders here with his army.
3 July 1866: Prussia beats Austria in today's Czechia, ending Austria's leadership of the German lands.
1871: the city becomes German as capital of the new Reichsland of Alsace-Lorraine. France takes it back in 1918.
Capital of Prussia and of the new empire, which grew into Europe's leading industrial power by 1900.

dd-germany.text: Defeat in World War I cost [Germany](DEU) its colonies and about an eighth of its land in Europe, including Alsace-Lorraine and a corridor to the sea for the new [Poland](POL). Hitler's war to undo this ended in 1945 with a far greater loss: everything east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to Poland and the [Soviet Union](RUS). Some 12 million Germans fled or were expelled westwards.

notes.DEU: Germany lost about a quarter of its 1937 territory in 1945. West Germany accepted the Oder–Neisse border in 1970, and united Germany confirmed it by treaty in 1990.
notes.POL: Poland gained Poznań and a corridor to the Baltic in 1919, then Silesia, Pomerania and southern East Prussia in 1945, while losing its own east to the Soviet Union. Its whole map moved west.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union took northern East Prussia around Königsberg in 1945. As Kaliningrad, it is now a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
notes.FRA: France regained Alsace-Lorraine in 1918. Nazi Germany annexed it in 1940, and it returned to France in 1945.
notes.BEL: Belgium received the small districts of Eupen and Malmedy in 1920. Their German-speaking community still has its own parliament.
notes.DNK: A 1920 vote returned northern Schleswig to Denmark. The border has not changed since, and minorities live on both sides.
notes.LTU: Memel (Klaipėda) was taken from Germany in 1919 and seized by Lithuania in 1923. Hitler took it back in March 1939, and it returned to Lithuania in 1945.
notes.CZE: In 1938 Hitler annexed the German-speaking Sudetenland under the Munich Agreement. After 1945 about 3 million Sudeten Germans were expelled.

pn: 28 June 1919: Germany signs the peace treaty, which also blames it for the war. Most Germans saw it as a humiliation.
1920: made a free city under the League of Nations. Germany's attack on Poland began here on 1 September 1939.
July–August 1945: the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agree to put Germany's eastern lands under Polish and Soviet rule.
Old Prussian capital, taken by the Soviet army in April 1945 and renamed Kaliningrad in 1946.
A German city until 1945. Its people were expelled and replaced by Poles, many themselves uprooted from eastern Poland.

dd-germany.text: In 1949 the zones held by the Western Allies became West Germany, a democracy that joined NATO, and the Soviet zone became East Germany, a communist state in the Warsaw Pact. In 1961 East Germany walled off West Berlin. In 1989 [Hungary](HUN) opened its border, East Germans fled west or protested, and the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November. [Germany](DEU) reunited on 3 October 1990.

notes.DEU: West Germany grew rich in the 'economic miracle' of the 1950s; East Germany became the Eastern bloc's most industrial state but lagged far behind. On 3 October 1990 the East's states joined the Federal Republic.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union kept hundreds of thousands of troops in East Germany. In 1990 Mikhail Gorbachev accepted a united Germany in NATO, and the last Russian troops left in 1994.
notes.USA: The US kept large forces in West Germany and flew in supplies during the Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948–49. Tens of thousands of US troops are still based in Germany, though in May 2026 the US announced it would cut their number.
notes.FRA: France, invaded by Germany three times since 1870, became its closest partner. Their 1963 friendship treaty became the core of European integration.
notes.GBR: Britain held an occupation zone in north-west Germany and a sector of Berlin, and with France, the US and the Soviet Union signed the 1990 treaty ending Allied rights.
notes.HUN: In 1989 Hungary took down its border fence with Austria, and in September let thousands of East Germans cross freely to the West.
notes.POL: Poland's Solidarity movement won partly free elections in June 1989, months before the Wall fell, showing that change in the bloc was possible.
notes.CZE: In autumn 1989 thousands of East Germans crowded into West Germany's embassy in Prague, and were allowed to leave by train for the West.
notes.AUT: Austria, neutral after 1955, was where the first gap in the Iron Curtain opened in 1989, on its border with Hungary.

pn: 13 August 1961 – 9 November 1989: at least 140 people were killed at the Wall or in connection with it, by the Potsdam Centre for Contemporary History's count.
West Germany's capital from 1949. The united parliament voted in 1991 to move back to Berlin.
9 October 1989: about 70,000 people march peacefully for reform, and the security forces do not shoot.
19 August 1989: at the Pan-European Picnic on the Austrian–Hungarian border, about 600 East Germans cross to the West.

dd-iran.text: In 1906 Iranians forced the Qajar shah to accept a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis. A year later [Russia](RUS) and Britain, ruler of [India](IND), split [Persia](IRN) into zones of influence without asking it. Oil struck in 1908 made the south vital to Britain. In 1925 an army officer, Reza Khan, made himself shah, and in 1935 he asked the world to call the country Iran.

notes.IRN: Persia stayed independent, but under the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention Russia claimed the north, Britain the south-east, and a neutral zone lay between. Both powers occupied parts of it in World War I.
notes.RUS: Russia had taken Persia's lands in the Caucasus by 1828. In 1911 its troops helped crush Persia's constitutional government.
notes.IND: Britain wanted Persia's south-east as a buffer for India. From 1914 the Royal Navy ran on oil, much of it from Persia.
notes.GBR: In 1914 the British government bought a controlling stake in the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, which paid Persia only a small share of its profits.
notes.AFG: The 1907 convention also settled Afghanistan and Tibet: Russia accepted Afghanistan as part of Britain's sphere.
notes.AZE: Northern Azerbaijan was Persian until Russia won it in 1813–1828. Many Azerbaijanis still live in Iran, which has more of them than Azerbaijan does.

pn: October 1906: Iran's first parliament, the Majlis, meets. The shah signs a constitution that winter.
1908–09: after the shah shuts down parliament, the city holds out for the constitution through a long siege.
26 May 1908: British prospectors strike oil, the first big find in the Middle East.
1912: the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later BP, opens a refinery here, for decades one of the world's largest.

dd-iran.text: In 1979 a revolution drove out Mohammad Reza Shah, and Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini made [Iran](IRN) an Islamic republic. Students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days. In 1980 [Iraq](IRQ) invaded, hoping to seize oil-rich land from a weakened neighbour. With loans from [Saudi Arabia](SAU) and [Kuwait](KWT), it fought Iran to a standstill until a 1988 ceasefire. Perhaps 500,000 people died.

notes.IRN: Iran lost most of the war's dead. It used volunteers, including teenage Basij fighters, in mass attacks, and accepted a UN ceasefire in 1988, which Khomeini likened to drinking poison.
notes.IRQ: Saddam Hussein expected a quick victory over a country in chaos. Iraq used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and its own Kurds.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia feared Iran's revolution would spread among Gulf Shias and lent Iraq billions of dollars.
notes.KWT: Kuwait lent Iraq billions too. Iraq's demand to have the debts cancelled helped lead to its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
notes.USA: The US leaned towards Iraq, sharing intelligence, but in the Iran–Contra affair it also sold arms secretly to Iran.
notes.ISR: Israel, once a close partner of the Shah, became the Islamic Republic's sworn enemy, though it quietly sold Iran some arms in the 1980s.

pn: 4 November 1979: students seize the US embassy. The 52 remaining hostages are freed on 20 January 1981.
October 1980: Iraqi troops take the port after weeks of street fighting. Iran wins it back in May 1982.
1982–87: Iran launches wave after wave of offensives towards Iraq's second city, at enormous cost.
16 March 1988: Iraqi forces gas this Kurdish town, killing about 5,000 civilians.
3 July 1988: the USS Vincennes shoots down an Iranian airliner by mistake, killing all 290 on board.

dd-iran.text: In June 2025 [Israel](ISR) and the [United States](USA) bombed [Iran](IRN)'s nuclear sites in a twelve-day war. On 28 February 2026 they struck again, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; his son Mojtaba succeeded him. Iran fired missiles at Israel, US bases and Gulf oil sites, and choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. A truce agreed in April broke down in July. In October 2026 the US paused strikes for talks, but attacks on ships went on.

notes.IRN: Iran's government and the rights group HRANA each counted over 3,000 Iranian dead in the 2026 war. Iran calls the strikes illegal aggression.
notes.USA: The US cited Iran's nuclear programme, missiles and killing of protesters. It blockaded Iran's ports, and over 20 US service members had been killed by autumn 2026.
notes.ISR: Israel saw Iran's nuclear programme and armed allies as a threat to its existence. Iran fired hundreds of missiles at it in 2026.
notes.SAU: Saudi Arabia was hit by Iranian strikes and, according to Reuters, struck back quietly. In October 2026 Houthi missiles hit Riyadh's main airport, killing at least 13 people.
notes.ARE: The UAE, home to US forces and a hub for Gulf trade, was struck repeatedly by Iranian missiles and drones.
notes.QAT: Qatar hosts Al Udeid, the largest US base in the region. Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan cut its gas exports, and it expelled Iran's military envoys.
notes.BHR: Bahrain hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet and was struck by Iranian missiles and drones.
notes.KWT: Kuwait hosts US bases and lost soldiers and civilians to Iranian strikes.
notes.OMN: Oman, long a go-between for Iran and the West, was also hit by Iranian drones, though it avoided blaming Iran publicly.
notes.LBN: Hezbollah, Iran's oldest ally, resumed fighting Israel within days of Khamenei's death.
notes.YEM: The Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, attacked shipping in the Red Sea and, in September 2026, seized the Bab al-Mandab coast.
notes.IRQ: Iraq's government stayed out, but Iran-backed militias in Iraq attacked US forces and were struck in return.
notes.PAK: Pakistan helped broker the April 2026 truce and hosted US–Iran talks in Islamabad, which failed.

pn: 28 February 2026: US and Israeli strikes kill Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader since 1989.
22 June 2025: US bombers drop bunker-busting bombs on this uranium enrichment site, dug deep into a mountain.
About a fifth of the world's oil passed through here before the war. Iran's attacks on ships sent oil prices soaring in 2026.
March 2026: Iranian drones and missiles hit Qatar's gas export hub, halting production.
September 2026: the Houthis take Yemen's side of this Red Sea chokepoint, including Perim island in the strait.

dd-koreas.text: [Japan](JPN) annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it for 35 years. It built railways, mines and factories, but for Japan's benefit, and it banned protest and later tried to replace Korean language and names with Japanese ones. Korea, then one country covering today's [North Korea](PRK) and [South Korea](KOR), was freed when Japan surrendered in August 1945.

notes.JPN: Japan won control of Korea by defeating China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, made it a protectorate, and annexed it in August 1910.
notes.KOR: Seoul, renamed Keijō, was the colonial capital. Hundreds of thousands of Koreans were sent to work in Japan, many by force, and many women were forced into military brothels.
notes.PRK: Japan built heavy industry and hydroelectric dams in the north, which left the North more industrialised than the South in 1945.
notes.TWN: Taiwan was Japan's first colony, taken from China in 1895. It passed to the Republic of China in 1945.
notes.CHN: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and ran it as Manchukuo. Korean communist guerrillas, including the young Kim Il Sung, fought the Japanese there.

pn: 1 March 1919: Korean leaders read a declaration of independence, and peaceful protests spread nationwide before Japan crushed them.

dd-koreas.text: In August 1945 the US and the Soviet Union split Korea at the 38th parallel, and in 1948 two rival states were founded. In June 1950 [North Korea](PRK) invaded [South Korea](KOR) and pushed its army back to Pusan. A UN force led by the [United States](USA) counterattacked from Inchon, then [China](CHN) intervened. The 1953 armistice froze the front near where it began, and no peace treaty was ever signed.

notes.PRK: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was founded in September 1948 under Kim Il Sung, who invaded the South in June 1950 with Stalin's approval.
notes.KOR: The Republic of Korea was founded in August 1948 under Syngman Rhee. Seoul changed hands four times during the war.
notes.USA: The US led the UN Command. About 36,000 Americans died, and US troops have stayed in South Korea ever since.
notes.CHN: China entered the war in October 1950 as UN forces neared its border, and pushed them back south of Seoul. Its losses ran to hundreds of thousands.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union armed North Korea and approved the invasion. Its pilots flew combat missions in secret.
notes.JPN: Japan, under US occupation, became the UN forces' supply base, and war orders helped restart its economy.

pn: August–September 1950: US and South Korean troops hold a small corner of the southeast around the port of Pusan (Busan).
15 September 1950: General MacArthur's surprise landing behind North Korean lines; Seoul is retaken within two weeks.
November–December 1950: Chinese armies surround US Marines and others in bitter cold; they fight their way out to the coast.
27 July 1953: the armistice is signed in this village on the front line, now the Joint Security Area on the DMZ.

dd-koreas.text: More than 70 years after the war, the two Koreas could hardly be more different. [South Korea](KOR) is a democracy and a rich exporter, with a treaty alliance with the [United States](USA). [North Korea](PRK) is a one-party dynasty under Kim Jong Un, with nuclear weapons and treaties with [China](CHN) and, since 2024, [Russia](RUS). In 2024 Kim declared the South a hostile state and dropped the goal of reunification.

notes.KOR: South Korea has about 51 million people and has been a democracy since 1987. Its income per person is roughly 28 times the North's, by Bank of Korea estimates.
notes.PRK: North Korea has about 26 million people and has been ruled by the Kim family since 1948. It has carried out six nuclear tests, the last in 2017.
notes.USA: Under a 1953 treaty, about 28,500 US troops are based in South Korea, and the US promises to defend it, including with nuclear weapons.
notes.CHN: China has been North Korea's treaty ally since 1961 and handles the large majority of its trade.
notes.RUS: Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024. North Korea then sent thousands of troops and large amounts of ammunition to help Russia against Ukraine.
notes.JPN: Japan hosts major US bases. North Korean missiles have flown over it, and North Korea abducted Japanese citizens in the 1970s and 1980s.

pn: Capital of South Korea, about 50 km from the DMZ. Around half of South Koreans live in the greater Seoul area.
Capital of North Korea, a showcase city where living is restricted to people trusted by the regime.
The truce village on the DMZ, where Kim Jong Un crossed into the South to meet its president in 2018.

dd-turkey.text: After the Ottoman defeat in 1918, the Allies occupied Istanbul and planned to carve up Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman general, rallied resistance from Ankara. His forces fought [Armenia](ARM) in the east and drove the [Greek](GRC) army out of the west by 1922. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne recognised [Turkey](TUR)'s borders, and the Arab lands stayed under French rule in [Syria](SYR) and Lebanon and British rule in [Iraq](IRQ), Jordan and Palestine.

notes.TUR: The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, replaced the harsher 1920 Treaty of Sèvres. The republic was declared in October, with Mustafa Kemal as president.
notes.GRC: Greece landed at İzmir in 1919 and pushed deep into Anatolia before its defeat in 1922. A 1923 exchange sent about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians to Greece and about 400,000 Muslims to Turkey.
notes.ARM: Turkish nationalist forces defeated the Armenian republic in 1920, and Kars stayed Turkish. Armenia then became Soviet. In 1915–16 most Ottoman Armenians were killed or died in deportations, which the great majority of historians call genocide; Turkey rejects the term.
notes.SYR: France ruled Syria under a League of Nations mandate. Its Alexandretta district, now Hatay, joined Turkey in 1939 after a disputed vote.
notes.IRQ: Turkey claimed oil-rich Mosul, but the League of Nations awarded it to British-ruled Iraq in 1925, and Turkey accepted this in 1926.
notes.LBN: France made Lebanon a separate mandate from Syria in 1920.
notes.JOR: Britain ruled Transjordan and Palestine, former Ottoman provinces, under League of Nations mandates.

pn: 19 May 1919: Mustafa Kemal lands here, the date Turks mark as the start of the War of Independence.
23 April 1920: a Grand National Assembly opens in this small Anatolian town, which becomes the capital in October 1923.
August–September 1921: Turkish forces stop the Greek advance about 80 kilometres from Ankara after three weeks of fighting.
September 1922: Turkish forces retake the city, and a great fire destroys its Greek and Armenian quarters.
November 1922: the Ottoman sultanate is abolished and the last sultan leaves on a British warship. Allied troops leave in 1923.

dd-turkey.text: [Turkey](TUR) joined NATO in 1952, alongside its old rival [Greece](GRC), after Stalin demanded bases on the Turkish Straits. It bordered the Soviet Union in the Caucasus, today's [Georgia](GEO), [Armenia](ARM) and Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan, and US missiles on Turkish soil were traded away in the 1962 Cuban crisis. At home the army, guardian of Atatürk's secular legacy, ousted governments in 1960, 1971 and 1980. In 1974 Turkey invaded [Cyprus](CYP), which remains divided.

notes.TUR: Turkey sent troops to the Korean War, which helped win it NATO membership. It became a multi-party democracy in 1950, but the army intervened about once a decade.
notes.GRC: Greece joined NATO with Turkey in 1952, but the two allies quarrelled bitterly over Cyprus and the Aegean Sea, and came close to war in 1987 and 1996.
notes.CYP: Turkish troops still hold about a third of the island. The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, declared in 1983, is recognised only by Turkey.
notes.GEO: Soviet Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan exclave formed the USSR's border with Turkey, one of only two places where NATO directly bordered the Soviet Union.
notes.ARM: The closed Turkish–Armenian border was a Cold War front line. Turkey closed it again in 1993 over the Karabakh war, and it stayed shut for decades.
notes.BGR: Communist Bulgaria, a Soviet ally, faced Turkey across Thrace. In 1989 about 300,000 Bulgarian Turks fled to Turkey after being forced to adopt Slavic names.
notes.ITA: US Jupiter nuclear missiles were based in Italy and Turkey. Their quiet removal in 1963 was part of the deal that ended the Cuban Missile Crisis.

pn: 1960: officers overthrow Prime Minister Adnan Menderes, who is hanged in 1961. The army forces out governments in 1971 and 1997 and seizes power in 1980.
From 1955: a US air base near Adana, later a hub for operations across the Middle East.
The 1936 Montreux Convention lets Turkey control warships passing through its straits, the Black Sea's only outlet.
July 1974: after a Greek-backed coup on the island, Turkey invades. The capital is still split by a UN buffer zone.

dd-turkey.text: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has led [Turkey](TUR) since 2003, first as prime minister, then as a powerful president. Turkey keeps troops in northern [Syria](SYR) and [Iraq](IRQ), in [Libya](LBY), [Qatar](QAT) and [Somalia](SOM), and helped [Azerbaijan](AZE) win its wars over Karabakh. It hosts millions of Syrians, sells drones widely and has mediated between [Russia](RUS) and [Ukraine](UKR). In 2025 the Kurdish militant PKK announced it would disband, after a war of over 40 years.

notes.TUR: Erdoğan won the 2023 election. In March 2025 his main rival, Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, was jailed on corruption charges he calls political; his trial was still going on in October 2026.
notes.SYR: Turkey backed the rebels who took Damascus in 2024 and is the new government's closest ally. It hosted about 3 million Syrian refugees in 2024, many of whom have since begun to go home.
notes.IRQ: Turkey has dozens of bases in the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, set up to fight the PKK, and good relations with the Kurdish regional government.
notes.LBY: In 2020 Turkish troops and drones helped Tripoli's government repel an attack by eastern commander Khalifa Haftar.
notes.QAT: Turkey opened a base in Qatar in 2015 and stood by it during the 2017–21 Saudi-led blockade.
notes.SOM: Turkey's largest overseas military training base opened in Mogadishu in 2017.
notes.CYP: About a third of Cyprus is held by Turkish forces and the Turkish Cypriot state recognised only by Turkey.
notes.AZE: Turkish drones and support helped Azerbaijan defeat Armenian forces in 2020, and it retook all of Karabakh in 2023.
notes.UKR: Turkey sold Ukraine Bayraktar drones but did not sanction Russia. With the UN it brokered the 2022 Black Sea grain deal and hosted Russian–Ukrainian talks in Istanbul.
notes.IRN: Turkey condemned the 2026 US–Israeli strikes on Iran and stayed out of the war. In March 2026, Turkey said, NATO air defences shot down several Iranian missiles heading into its airspace; Iran denied targeting Turkey.

pn: 15 July 2016: a coup attempt fails as crowds face down tanks; about 250 people are killed. Erdoğan blames the movement of Fethullah Gülen.
6 February 2023: two great earthquakes kill over 53,000 people in Turkey and thousands more in Syria.
PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan has been jailed on this island since 1999. In February 2025 he called on the PKK to lay down its arms.
The PKK's mountain base in Iraq. Its fighters burned weapons in a symbolic ceremony near Sulaymaniyah in July 2025.

dd-japanmodern.text: In August 1945 US atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the [Soviet Union](RUS) attacked, and [Japan](JPN) surrendered. It lost everything it had gained since 1895: [Taiwan](TWN), [Korea](KOR), Manchuria and its other conquests in [China](CHN), and its Pacific islands. American forces under General Douglas MacArthur occupied Japan until 1952, disarmed it and gave it a democratic constitution that renounced war.

notes.JPN: About 3 million Japanese died in the war. The occupation broke up big business groups, gave women the vote and land to tenant farmers, and kept the emperor as a symbol without power.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union declared war on 8 August 1945, overran Manchuria and seized southern Sakhalin and the Kurils. Japan still claims the four southernmost islands as its Northern Territories.
notes.KOR: Korea was freed from Japanese rule in August 1945 but split at the 38th parallel between US and Soviet forces.
notes.PRK: Soviet troops occupied northern Korea, where a communist state was founded in 1948.
notes.TWN: Taiwan passed to the Republic of China in 1945. Its government fled there in 1949 after losing China's civil war.
notes.CHN: China suffered more than any other country from Japan's war, with estimates of 10–20 million or more dead. Japanese troops there surrendered in September 1945.
notes.USA: The US ran the occupation almost alone. MacArthur's staff drafted the new constitution in about a week in February 1946.
notes.MNP: Saipan and the other Northern Marianas were Japanese from 1914. US bombers flew from here to attack Japan, including the planes that dropped the atomic bombs.

pn: 6 August 1945: the first atomic bomb used in war. About 140,000 people had died from it by the end of the year.
9 August 1945: a second atomic bomb kills about 70,000 people by the end of the year.
2 September 1945: Japan formally surrenders aboard the battleship USS Missouri.
3 May 1947: the new constitution takes effect. Its Article 9 renounces war and the maintenance of armed forces.
April–June 1945: the bloodiest battle of the Pacific War. The US ruled Okinawa until 1972.

dd-japanmodern.text: Independent again from 1952, [Japan](JPN) relied on the [United States](USA) for defence and poured its energy into growth. Bullet trains opened for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and by 1968 Japan had the world's second-largest economy. It restored ties with [South Korea](KOR) in 1965 and [China](CHN) in 1972. Toyota, Sony and Honda conquered world markets, and by 1989 a stock and property bubble made Japan seem unstoppable.

notes.JPN: Japan's economy grew about 10% a year in the 1950s and 1960s. One party, the Liberal Democratic Party, governed without a break from 1955 to 1993.
notes.USA: The US kept bases in Japan, opened its market to Japanese goods and bought supplies there for the Korean War. By the 1980s, trade deficits with Japan caused anger in Washington.
notes.KOR: The 1965 treaty restored relations and gave South Korea $800 million in grants and loans, which helped fund its growth. Disputes over colonial-era wrongs continued.
notes.CHN: Japan and China restored relations in September 1972. Japanese aid and investment later helped China's opening-up after 1978.
notes.TWN: Japan ended official relations with Taiwan in 1972 but kept close unofficial trade and cultural ties.
notes.RUS: The Soviet Union and Japan restored relations in 1956 but never signed a peace treaty, because of the dispute over the southern Kurils.

pn: 1 October 1964: the first Shinkansen bullet train opens to Osaka, nine days before Asia's first Olympic Games begin in Tokyo.
1970: Expo 70 draws about 64 million visitors, a showcase of Japan's new wealth and technology.
15 May 1972: the US returns Okinawa to Japan but keeps large bases there.
Home of Toyota, whose 'just-in-time' system made it a model for carmakers worldwide.
1956: officials record a new disease, which the government accepted in 1968 was caused by mercury in factory waste, the worst pollution scandal of the boom years.

dd-japanmodern.text: [Japan](JPN) remains a close ally of the [United States](USA) and the world's fourth-largest economy, but its population is shrinking and ageing. It disputes islands with [Russia](RUS), [China](CHN) and [South Korea](KOR), and North Korean missiles have flown over it. Sanae Takaichi, Japan's first woman prime minister, won a landslide in February 2026, and is raising defence spending amid a deep chill with China.

notes.JPN: Japan had about 122 million people in 2026, with a record 29.6% aged 65 or over and only about 671,000 Japanese births in 2025. In 2025 it raised defence spending to about 2% of GDP, ahead of schedule.
notes.USA: Under the 1960 security treaty the US defends Japan, including, it has said, the Senkaku Islands. Japan hosts more US troops than any other country.
notes.CHN: China is Japan's largest trading partner. After Takaichi said in November 2025 that an attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival, China halted Japanese seafood imports and urged its citizens not to travel there.
notes.KOR: Ties with South Korea improved from 2023, but disputes over Dokdo, which Japan calls Takeshima, and over wartime forced labour still flare.
notes.RUS: Russia holds the four islands Japan claims off Hokkaido. It broke off peace treaty talks in 2022 after Japan backed sanctions over Ukraine.
notes.PRK: North Korea abducted Japanese citizens in the 1970s and 1980s, and has fired missiles over northern Japan, as in 2017 and 2022.
notes.TWN: Taiwan lies about 110 km from Japan's westernmost island, Yonaguni, which is why a war there would directly affect Japan.
notes.AUS: Australia and Japan signed a defence pact in 2022 allowing their forces to train in each other's countries.
notes.PHL: The Philippines, also in disputes with China at sea, signed a similar defence pact with Japan in 2024.

pn: Held by Russia since 1945 and claimed by Japan as its Northern Territories.
Uninhabited islands run by Japan and claimed by China, which calls them Diaoyu, and by Taiwan.
Rocky islets held by South Korea since the 1950s and claimed by Japan.
Less than 1% of Japan's land, but home to about 70% of the land used only by US forces in Japan.
11 March 2011: a tsunami wrecks the nuclear plant, causing three meltdowns. The earthquake and tsunami left about 18,000 people dead or missing.
Capital and economic heart of Japan. About 30% of its people live in the greater Tokyo area.

dd-india.text: Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister from 1947 until his death in 1964, built [India](IND) as a secular democracy with a state-led economy of dams and steel mills. Abroad he refused to join either Cold War bloc and, with leaders of [Yugoslavia](SRB), [Egypt](EGY), [Indonesia](IDN) and [Ghana](GHA), founded the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. That year India took Goa from [Portugal](PRT). In 1962 a border war with [China](CHN) ended in a humiliating defeat.

notes.IND: India's first general election, in 1951–52, had about 173 million voters, most of them unable to read, who chose parties by symbols. Nehru's Congress party won easily.
notes.SRB: Yugoslavia's Tito hosted the first Non-Aligned summit in Belgrade in 1961. He, Nehru and Egypt's Nasser were the movement's leading figures.
notes.EGY: Gamal Abdel Nasser, Nehru's close partner, gave the movement Arab and African weight after the 1956 Suez Crisis.
notes.IDN: Indonesia's Sukarno hosted the 1955 Bandung conference of Asian and African states, a forerunner of the movement, where Nehru was a leading voice.
notes.GHA: Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana to independence in 1957, brought newly free African states into the movement.
notes.CHN: China and India disputed borders in the west and the east. China's 1962 attack shocked India, and the long frontier, the Line of Actual Control, is still not agreed.
notes.PRT: Portugal refused to give up Goa, Daman and Diu peacefully. It recognised India's takeover only in 1974.
notes.RUS: Soviet aid built the Bhilai steel plant, and Moscow backed India's position on Kashmir at the UN, drawing the two countries closer.

pn: 15 August 1947: Nehru raises the flag at the Red Fort. The constitution takes effect on 26 January 1950.
Finished in 1963, one of the great dams Nehru called 'temples of modern India', irrigating Punjab's farms.
December 1961: Indian troops end 451 years of Portuguese rule in two days.
1962: China, which built a road across this high plateau in the 1950s, keeps it after the war. India still claims it.
1962: Chinese troops overrun this Buddhist town in the east, then withdraw. China still claims the region, which it calls South Tibet.

dd-india.text: Indira Gandhi made [India](IND) the dominant power in South Asia. In 1971 Indian troops helped [Bangladesh](BGD) win independence from Pakistan, and in 1974 India tested a nuclear device. Later governments sent peacekeepers to [Sri Lanka](LKA) and foiled a coup in the [Maldives](MDV). Rivalry with [China](CHN) and [Pakistan](PAK), both nuclear powers, remained the great danger: in 2020 Indian and Chinese soldiers fought with clubs and stones in the Himalayas.

notes.IND: India's wars with Pakistan, from 1947 to the clash of May 2025, are covered in the partition deep dive.
notes.BGD: In 1971 Pakistan's army cracked down on East Pakistan, and about 10 million refugees fled to India. India intervened in December, and Pakistan's forces in Dhaka surrendered after 13 days.
notes.LKA: About 1,200 Indian soldiers died fighting the Tamil Tigers in 1987–90. In 1991 a Tamil Tiger suicide bomber killed Rajiv Gandhi, who had sent the troops.
notes.MDV: In 1988 Indian paratroopers flew in overnight to defeat a coup attempt by Sri Lankan Tamil mercenaries against President Gayoom.
notes.CHN: China is India's biggest source of imports and its main strategic rival. After the 2020 clash both sides kept tens of thousands of troops on the border; they agreed on patrolling in 2024.
notes.PAK: Pakistan tested nuclear weapons weeks after India in 1998. The two have fought four wars and many clashes, mostly over Kashmir.
notes.NPL: Nepal's border with India is open, and millions of Nepalis work in India. Border disputes and a 2015 border blockade, which India denied imposing, have strained ties.
notes.BTN: India has guided Bhutan's foreign and defence policy and built its hydropower dams. In 2017 Indian troops faced Chinese road-builders on the Doklam plateau, claimed by Bhutan.

pn: 1974: India's first nuclear test, called a 'peaceful nuclear explosion'. In May 1998 five more tests made India an open nuclear power.
15 June 2020: a clash on the disputed border kills 20 Indian soldiers and, China says, 4 Chinese, the first deaths there since 1975.
1975: the kingdom of Sikkim votes to end its monarchy and becomes an Indian state.
1987: Indian peacekeepers sent to end Sri Lanka's civil war end up fighting the Tamil Tigers; they leave in 1990.

dd-india.text: With over 1.4 billion people, [India](IND) passed [China](CHN) as the most populous country in 2023, and by IMF estimates it is the sixth-largest economy, forecast to pass Britain and [Japan](JPN) in 2027. It works with the [United States](USA), Japan and [Australia](AUS) in the Quad, but also belongs to BRICS with China, [Russia](RUS) and others, and buys Russian oil and arms. Some 35 million people of Indian origin live abroad, many in the Gulf, Britain and North America.

notes.IND: India sent more money home from abroad than any other country, about $130 billion in remittances in 2024. Its income per person was still about a twelfth of Japan's.
notes.USA: About 5 million people of Indian origin live in the US. In 2025 the US raised tariffs on Indian goods to 50%, partly over Russian oil; an interim deal in February 2026 cut them sharply.
notes.CHN: India passed China in population in 2023, by UN estimates. China's economy was still more than four times larger.
notes.JPN: Japan, a Quad partner, has funded India's metro systems and its first high-speed railway, between Mumbai and Ahmedabad.
notes.RUS: India kept buying Russian arms and, after 2022, became one of the largest buyers of Russian oil, declining to join Western sanctions.
notes.ARE: Over 3 million Indians live in the UAE, more than a third of its population, many of them workers who send money home to Kerala and other states.
notes.GBR: About 1.9 million people of Indian origin live in Britain, which ruled India until 1947. Rishi Sunak, of Indian descent, was prime minister in 2022–24.
notes.SAU: About 2.5 million Indians work in Saudi Arabia, many in construction and services.
notes.CAN: Canada has a large Sikh community. Ties froze in 2023 after Canada accused India of a role in killing a Sikh separatist, which India denied; they began to thaw in 2025.

pn: The hub of India's software and outsourcing boom, which took off in the 1990s.
India's financial capital. In November 2008 Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen from Pakistan killed about 166 people here in a three-day attack.
23 August 2023: India's Chandrayaan-3, launched from this spaceport, becomes the first craft to land near the Moon's south pole.

dd-apartheid.text: From 1948 [South Africa](ZAF) classified everyone by race and gave power only to the white minority. It also ruled [Namibia](NAM), in defiance of the UN. Black South Africans were assigned to ten 'homelands', scattered patches inside South Africa too small to show here. Neighbours such as [Zambia](ZMB) and [Mozambique](MOZ), the Frontline States, sheltered exiled resistance movements and suffered South African raids in return.

notes.ZAF: The homelands covered about 13% of the land for about three-quarters of the people. Four were declared 'independent', and about 3.5 million people were forcibly moved under apartheid.
notes.NAM: South Africa took German South West Africa in 1915 and imposed apartheid there. The UN ended its mandate in 1966, but SWAPO fought until independence in 1990.
notes.ZMB: Zambia hosted the ANC's headquarters in exile, in Lusaka, through the 1970s and 1980s.
notes.TZA: Under Julius Nyerere, Tanzania was a founder of the Frontline States and hosted ANC training camps.
notes.MOZ: After independence in 1975 Mozambique sheltered the ANC. South Africa backed the RENAMO rebels against its government, and in 1984 Mozambique signed a non-aggression pact.
notes.AGO: South African troops fought in Angola for years against the government, its Cuban allies and SWAPO bases. The 1988 accords linked Cuba's withdrawal to Namibia's independence.
notes.BWA: Botswana, a multiracial democracy, joined the Frontline States, but depended on South Africa's economy and suffered cross-border raids.
notes.ZWE: White-ruled Rhodesia was an ally of South Africa. As Zimbabwe, under majority rule from 1980, it joined the Frontline States.
notes.LSO: Lesotho, completely surrounded by South Africa, was an independent kingdom from 1966, not a homeland. South African forces raided its capital in 1982.
notes.SWZ: Eswatini, then Swaziland, independent since 1968, was not a homeland, though apartheid planners hoped to merge a homeland into it.

pn: 21 March 1960: police open fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws, killing 69. The ANC and PAC are banned soon after.
16 June 1976: police shoot schoolchildren protesting against lessons in Afrikaans. The uprising spreads; the official toll was 176, other estimates are far higher.
1964–1982: Nelson Mandela is held in the prison on this island off Cape Town for 18 of his 27 years behind bars.
1976: capital of Transkei, the first homeland declared 'independent'. No country except South Africa recognised it.

dd-apartheid.text: Majority rule spread south across Africa. British territories such as [Zambia](ZMB) and [Botswana](BWA) became independent in the 1960s, and Portugal left [Angola](AGO) and [Mozambique](MOZ) in 1975. White-ruled Rhodesia became [Zimbabwe](ZWE) in 1980, and [Namibia](NAM) won independence in 1990. [South Africa](ZAF) came last, with its first election open to all in April 1994.

notes.TZA: Tanganyika became independent from Britain in 1961 and joined Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania.
notes.ZMB: Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia in 1964.
notes.MWI: Nyasaland became independent as Malawi in 1964. Unlike its neighbours, it kept friendly ties with apartheid South Africa.
notes.BWA: Bechuanaland became independent as Botswana in 1966.
notes.AGO: Angola became independent from Portugal in 1975, after a 1974 coup in Lisbon ended the colonial wars. A civil war followed at once.
notes.MOZ: Mozambique became independent from Portugal in June 1975 under FRELIMO, which had fought for independence since 1964.
notes.ZWE: Rhodesia's white minority declared independence from Britain in 1965. After a guerrilla war, elections in 1980 created Zimbabwe.
notes.NAM: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990, about six weeks after Mandela's release. South Africa handed over the port of Walvis Bay in 1994.
notes.ZAF: Apartheid laws were repealed from 1990 to 1991. On 27 April 1994 all adults could vote for the first time, and the ANC won about 62%.

pn: 21 March 1990: Namibia becomes independent, with SWAPO's Sam Nujoma as president.
10 May 1994: Nelson Mandela is sworn in as South Africa's first democratically elected president at the Union Buildings.

dd-eu.text: On 9 May 1950 the French foreign minister, Robert Schuman, proposed putting French and German coal and steel, the stuff of war, under one shared authority. [France](FRA), [West Germany](DEU), [Italy](ITA), [Belgium](BEL), the [Netherlands](NLD) and [Luxembourg](LUX) signed up in 1951, and the 1957 Treaties of Rome created a common market. [Britain](GBR) stayed out and in 1960 set up a looser free trade club instead.

notes.DEU: Only West Germany joined. For its first chancellor, Konrad Adenauer, the community was a way back to equality and trust in Europe. East Germany came in with reunification in 1990.
notes.FRA: France feared a revived Germany. Sharing control of German coal and steel offered security without occupation.
notes.ITA: Italy, a new democracy after Mussolini, saw European integration as a path to recovery and respectability.
notes.BEL: Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg had already formed a customs union, Benelux, in 1944–48.
notes.NLD: The Dutch, great traders, pushed for a wide common market rather than just coal and steel.
notes.LUX: Tiny Luxembourg, a steelmaker, hosted the first European institutions and is still a seat of EU bodies.
notes.GBR: Britain, with its empire and Commonwealth trade, refused to give up sovereignty. It applied to join in 1961, but France's President de Gaulle vetoed it twice.
notes.NOR: Norway helped found the free trade group, and its voters later rejected EU membership twice, in 1972 and 1994.

pn: 9 May 1950: the Schuman Declaration, drafted with Jean Monnet. 9 May is now Europe Day.
Germany's coal and steel heartland, which had armed it for two world wars. Pooling it made a new war between France and Germany impractical.
1952: the High Authority, the first shared European body, starts work here under Jean Monnet.
25 March 1957: the six sign the Treaties of Rome, founding the European Economic Community.

dd-eu.text: [Britain](GBR), [Ireland](IRL) and [Denmark](DNK) joined in 1973. [Greece](GRC), [Spain](ESP) and [Portugal](PRT) followed in the 1980s, after shedding dictatorships. After the Cold War, [Austria](AUT), [Finland](FIN) and [Sweden](SWE) joined in 1995, and in 2004 ten countries came in at once, most of them formerly communist, including [Poland](POL). [Croatia](HRV) was the last to join, in 2013, and in 2020 Britain became the first member to leave.

notes.GBR: The UK joined in 1973 and voted to stay in 1975. In 2016 it voted by 52% to 48% to leave, and it left on 31 January 2020.
notes.IRL: Ireland was one of the poorest members when it joined in 1973. EU funds and the single market helped make it one of the richest.
notes.DNK: Denmark joined with Britain and Ireland, but it keeps its own currency, the krone.
notes.GRC: Greece joined in 1981, seven years after its military dictatorship fell.
notes.ESP: Spain joined in 1986, a decade after the death of the dictator Franco.
notes.PRT: Portugal joined with Spain in 1986, twelve years after its Carnation Revolution ended dictatorship.
notes.AUT: Austria, neutral during the Cold War, joined in 1995.
notes.FIN: Finland, long careful not to provoke the Soviet Union, joined in 1995.
notes.SWE: Sweden joined in 1995, but voted in 2003 not to adopt the euro.
notes.POL: Poland, the largest of the 2004 entrants, has become one of the EU's fastest-growing economies.
notes.HRV: Croatia joined in 2013, the 28th member, eighteen years after its war of independence ended.
notes.CYP: Cyprus joined in 2004 while divided. EU law is suspended in the Turkish Cypriot north.
notes.GRL: Greenland joined in 1973 as part of Denmark, but voted to leave and left in 1985.

pn: 9 November 1989: the Berlin Wall falls, opening the way to German reunification and the EU's eastward growth.
February 1992: the Maastricht Treaty creates the European Union and plans a single currency.
1993: EU leaders set the 'Copenhagen criteria' for new members: democracy, the rule of law and a market economy.
2007: the Lisbon Treaty reforms the EU and, for the first time, sets out how a country can leave.

dd-eu.text: The EU has 27 members and about 450 million people. 21 of them share the euro, most recently [Bulgaria](BGR) from January 2026. [Norway](NOR), [Iceland](ISL) and [Switzerland](CHE) stay outside but trade in its single market. Nine countries are official candidates: [Montenegro](MNE) is closest and could join around 2028, while [Ukraine](UKR) applied days after Russia's 2022 invasion. In August 2026 Icelanders voted against restarting membership talks.

notes.BGR: Bulgaria joined the EU in 2007 and on 1 January 2026 became the 21st country to use the euro.
notes.NOR: Norway voted against joining in 1972 and 1994, but follows most single market rules through the European Economic Area.
notes.ISL: Iceland applied in 2009 and froze talks in 2013. In August 2026 about 53% voted against restarting them, with fishing rights a key worry.
notes.CHE: Switzerland is tied to the EU by over a hundred bilateral treaties and is in the passport-free Schengen area.
notes.MNE: Montenegro has opened every chapter of membership talks, and aims to join around 2028. It already uses the euro, without a formal agreement.
notes.UKR: Ukraine applied in February 2022 and became a candidate that June. Talks formally opened in 2024.
notes.TUR: Turkey has been a candidate since 1999, but its talks have been frozen since 2018.
notes.GEO: Georgia became a candidate in 2023, but the EU says its path is effectively halted after its government paused accession efforts in 2024.
notes.SRB: Serbia has been negotiating since 2014; its refusal to recognise Kosovo and its ties to Russia slow its progress.
notes.UNK: Kosovo applied in 2022 and is a potential candidate. Five EU members do not recognise its independence.
notes.MDA: Moldova became a candidate alongside Ukraine in 2022 and opened talks in 2024.
notes.ALB: Albania has moved quickly through talks and hopes to finish them by 2027.
notes.DNK: Denmark has a legal opt-out from the euro, though it pegs its krone to it.
notes.POL: Poland, like most newer members, is committed to adopting the euro one day but has set no date.

pn: Home of the European Commission and the meetings of national leaders and ministers.
The European Parliament, directly elected since 1979, holds its main sessions here.
The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the euro area from here.
The Court of Justice of the EU, whose rulings national courts must follow on EU law.

cradles.q: What new way of living, begun in the Fertile Crescent, led to the first cities?
a: Hunting herds across the steppe
Farming crops and herding animals
Fishing along the Atlantic coast
Trading silk over long routes
cradles.why: From about 9500 BC people farmed wheat and barley and herded sheep and goats, and in time farming fed villages like Jericho and then cities like Uruk.

cradles.q: Why did farming allow some people to become priests, soldiers, craftsmen and rulers?
a: Kings banned farming in the cities
Farmers were paid in gold coins
It produced surplus food to feed them
Rivers flooded too often to farm
cradles.why: Surplus food meant not everyone had to farm, so some people could specialise as priests, soldiers, craftsmen and rulers.

cradles.q: Why did writing first appear in Mesopotamia?
a: To keep accounts for temples and palaces
To record poems for travelling singers
To send letters to Egypt's kings
To print holy books for everyone
cradles.why: In Sumer writing began as bookkeeping: cuneiform was pressed into clay, at first to keep temple and palace accounts.

cradles.q: What did civilisation look like in the Americas, compared with the Middle East?
a: It was brought by settlers from Egypt
It began only after 1500 AD
It copied Sumerian writing and cities
It began separately, with towns like Caral
cradles.why: Caral in Peru and the Olmecs in Mexico began their own civilisations independently, suggesting such steps followed naturally from farming and dense populations.

cradles.q: Which invention of these early societies is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts?
a: Egyptian hieroglyphs
The Phoenician alphabet
The Indus seal script
Shang oracle-bone writing
cradles.why: After the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BC, the Phoenician alphabet spread and became the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts used today.

religions.q: Which great religions began in northern India?
a: Christianity and Islam
Judaism and Zoroastrianism
Hinduism and Buddhism
Confucianism and Daoism
religions.why: Hinduism grew out of the Vedic religion from about 1500 BC, and the Buddha taught in northern India around 500 BC.

religions.q: What do many historians call the period, about 800–200 BC, of new questions about ethics and salvation?
a: The Axial Age
The Bronze Age
The Middle Ages
The Age of Exploration
religions.why: In the Axial Age, as cities and states grew, thinkers from Greece to India and China, including Confucius, asked new questions about ethics and salvation.

religions.q: How did rulers like Ashoka and Constantine help religions spread?
a: They banned all other faiths at once
They adopted and backed the faiths
They wrote the faiths' holy books
They moved believers to new continents
religions.why: Religions spread when rulers adopted them: Ashoka helped spread Buddhism, and Constantine backed Christianity, which became Rome's state religion in 380.

religions.q: What happened to Buddhism after it began in India?
a: It became India's majority faith today
It vanished everywhere by AD 500
It merged completely with Islam
It faded in India but flourished in East Asia
religions.why: Buddhism faded in India but became central in East and South-East Asia, reaching China from India in the first century AD.

religions.q: What do Judaism, Christianity and Islam share that has also fuelled rivalry?
a: A shared founder in the Buddha
Abraham and the city of Jerusalem
A single holy book for all three
The Vedic hymns of the Rigveda
religions.why: All three honour Abraham and hold Jerusalem sacred, a bond that has also fuelled rivalry and conflict over holy places.

ancient.q: What did Alexander of Macedon achieve between 334 and 323 BC?
a: He united China under one emperor
He conquered Persia and reached India
He founded democracy in Athens
He defeated Persia at Marathon
ancient.why: Alexander invaded the Persian Empire in 334 BC, won every major battle and marched to the Punjab before dying in Babylon, aged 32.

ancient.q: How did the Persian Empire hold together so many conquered peoples?
a: It forced everyone to worship Persian gods
It moved all peoples to Persia
It let them keep their customs, governing through provinces
It ruled every town directly from Athens
ancient.why: Persia used a strong army but a light touch, letting peoples keep their gods and customs and governing through satrapies linked by roads such as the Royal Road.

ancient.q: Why did Qin, rather than another state, manage to unite China in 221 BC?
a: Harsh Legalist laws organised it for war
Persia sent it soldiers and money
Alexander's army helped it conquer
Its rivals agreed to join peacefully
ancient.why: After centuries of war between rival states, Qin, organised for war by harsh Legalist laws, defeated the rest and its king became the First Emperor.

ancient.q: What was one lasting result of Alexander's conquests?
a: Persian replaced Greek across Europe
China adopted Greek writing
Greek language and culture spread from Egypt to Afghanistan
Athens ruled Persia for centuries
ancient.why: Though his generals split his empire, Greek cities, language and art spread from Egypt to Afghanistan, and Rome later inherited this culture.

ancient.q: Why do most Chinese still call themselves Han today?
a: After the dynasty that ruled 202 BC to AD 220
After a river that runs through Beijing
After a Persian word for China
After the first city on the Yellow River
ancient.why: The Han dynasty ruled so long, building on Qin's unification, that it created a lasting idea of one unified China, and most Chinese still call themselves Han.

silk.q: How did goods usually travel along the Silk Road between China and the Mediterranean?
a: One merchant carried them the whole way
Middlemen passed them from city to city
Roman armies escorted them from China
Chinese ships sailed them up the Nile
silk.why: Few merchants made the whole journey; Sogdian, Persian and other middlemen passed goods on through oasis cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand.

silk.q: What was a basic reason for the trade along these routes?
a: Every region made the same goods
Rome forced China to send tribute
Regions made things others wanted but could not produce
Travel was cheaper by land than by sea
silk.why: China long kept the secret of silk, while the Han needed strong Central Asian horses: each region had goods others could not make.

silk.q: What made long sea voyages across the Indian Ocean possible and cheap?
a: Predictable monsoon winds
Steam-powered ships
A canal through Arabia
Roman roads along the coast
silk.why: The monsoon blows from the south-west in summer and the north-east in winter, so ships could cross the Indian Ocean more cheaply than camel caravans.

silk.q: Besides goods, what else did the routes spread?
a: Only coins and precious stones
Nothing; ideas stayed at home
Christianity into China and Japan
Religions, inventions and the Black Death
silk.why: Buddhism reached China, Islam spread into Central Asia, paper, the compass and gunpowder went west, and the routes carried the Black Death to Europe in the 1340s.

silk.q: How did the spice trade help launch the age of European exploration?
a: China invited Europeans to sail east
The Mongols closed every sea route
Portugal sought a sea route to bypass middlemen
Venice wanted a new route to America
silk.why: To bypass the Venetian and Muslim middlemen controlling the spice trade, the Portuguese sought their own route to Asia, leading to Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in 1498.

rome.q: How did Rome change after Augustus took power in 27 BC?
a: It became a republic for the first time
It moved its capital to Carthage
It was split into two empires
It became an empire ruled by emperors
rome.why: After civil wars and Julius Caesar's murder, Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, and two centuries of relative peace followed.

rome.q: Which of these helped Rome conquer and hold its lands?
a: A huge navy of steam ships
Disciplined legions, alliances and roads
Letting each province have its own army
Paying the Huns to fight for it
rome.why: Rome won through disciplined legions, alliances that turned defeated Italians into allies and citizens, and roads that moved troops and trade.

rome.q: Which causes do historians weigh in explaining the fall of the Western Empire?
a: A single defeat by Persia
Civil wars, heavy taxes and Germanic settlement
The Black Death and a famine
An invasion from China
rome.why: Historians weigh many causes differently: repeated civil wars, heavy taxes, a weak economy, a long frontier, and Germanic peoples pushed west by the Huns settling inside the empire.

rome.q: What happened to the Eastern Empire after the West fell in 476?
a: It lasted almost 1,000 years more, until 1453
It fell to the Visigoths the same year
It was ruled from Rome by the Pope
It became part of Persia
rome.why: The richer, better-defended East, ruled from walled Constantinople and later called Byzantine, outlived the West until the Ottomans took the city in 1453.

rome.q: Which is a lasting legacy of Rome in today's world?
a: Arabic as Europe's main language
Chinese characters in Europe
Latin-based languages and Roman law
The Indian caste system
rome.why: Latin grew into Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian, the Latin alphabet is the world's most used, and Roman law underlies much of Europe's and Latin America's law.

americas.q: What happened to the Aztec and Inca empires between 1519 and 1533?
a: They united against Spain and won
Small Spanish forces and native allies toppled both
They were conquered by the Maya
Portugal took them over peacefully
americas.why: Cortés and his allies destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Pizarro seized and executed Atahualpa and took Cusco by 1533.

americas.q: What was the deadliest factor in the swift Spanish conquests?
a: European diseases such as smallpox
Bigger Spanish armies than native ones
Famine caused by Spanish blockades
Volcanic eruptions in the Andes
americas.why: Native peoples had no immunity to smallpox and other European diseases, which killed huge numbers before and during the fighting.

americas.q: Why could a few hundred Spaniards defeat the Aztecs?
a: The Aztecs had no army at all
The Aztecs invited the Spanish to rule
Thousands of native allies like the Tlaxcalans fought beside them
Spanish ships bombarded Tenochtitlan from the sea
americas.why: Peoples who resented Aztec rule, above all the Tlaxcalans, fought in their tens of thousands alongside the Spanish.

americas.q: What happened to the native population within a century of the conquest?
a: It grew quickly with new crops
It stayed about the same
It moved north to escape Spain
Most died from epidemics, war and forced labour
americas.why: Estimates vary widely, but many regions lost over 80 per cent of their people, mostly to disease, along with war and forced labour.

americas.q: Which is a lasting legacy of these American civilisations today?
a: Millions still speak Maya languages and Quechua
Aztec emperors still rule Mexico
Spanish is spoken nowhere in the Americas
Potatoes are grown only in Peru
americas.why: Spanish and Catholicism became dominant, but millions still speak Maya languages and Quechua, and American crops like maize, potatoes and tomatoes spread worldwide.

islam.q: What happened in the century after Muhammad's death in 632?
a: Arabia split into feuding tribes again
Arab armies built an empire from Spain to Central Asia
Byzantium conquered Arabia
Persia converted the Arabs to its faith
islam.why: The caliphs took Syria and Egypt, destroyed Persia's Sasanian Empire, and under the Umayyads reached Spain, Sindh and Central Asia.

islam.q: What did Islam do for Arabia's tribes that helped launch the conquests?
a: It united them under one faith and leader
It made them Byzantine allies
It turned them into settled farmers
It forbade them from leaving Arabia
islam.why: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes, and religious zeal, the hope of booty and the needs of the new state drove them outward.

islam.q: Why did the Byzantine and Persian empires fall so quickly to the Arab armies?
a: They had already converted to Islam
They had no armies in the region
They were exhausted by war with each other and by plague
They were busy fighting the Mongols
islam.why: The two empires had fought a draining war from 602 to 628 and been weakened by plague, and many subjects, tired of taxes and persecution, did not fight hard.

islam.q: What happened to language in the conquered lands from Iraq to Morocco?
a: Greek replaced older languages
Persian became the common language
Latin returned as the main language
Arabic largely replaced older languages
islam.why: Arabic largely replaced older languages from Iraq to Morocco, creating today's Arab world, while Iran kept Persian and people converted only gradually.

islam.q: What lasting division came from the early dispute over who should lead the Muslims?
a: The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims
The split between Catholics and Orthodox
The border between Spain and France
The divide between Arabia and Egypt
islam.why: The quarrel over succession, which turned to civil war before the Umayyads took power in 661, became the lasting split between Sunni and Shia Muslims.

crusades.q: What did the First Crusade achieve in 1099?
a: It took Jerusalem and founded crusader states
It captured Constantinople
It conquered Egypt
It made peace with Saladin
crusades.why: Crusaders took Antioch, then stormed Jerusalem in 1099, killing many of its people, and set up four crusader states mostly along the Levant coast.

crusades.q: What do most historians now think mainly drove the crusaders?
a: A plan to settle in Egypt
Hatred of the Byzantine emperor
Piety and the promise of forgiveness of sins
Orders from the Venetian government
crusades.why: The pope promised forgiveness of sins to those who fought, and Jerusalem was Christianity's holiest place, though land, loot and trade drew some too.

crusades.q: Why did the First Crusade succeed where later ones struggled?
a: The crusaders had guns
The Muslim world was divided between rival rulers
Byzantium sent its whole army
The Mongols attacked the Muslims first
crusades.why: Rival Seljuk princes and the Fatimids of Egypt were divided; later, Saladin united Egypt and Syria and retook Jerusalem in 1187.

crusades.q: How did the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204 change history?
a: It ended the Muslim rule of Jerusalem
It united Eastern and Western Christians
It made Venice part of Byzantium
It crippled Byzantium and eased the later Ottoman advance
crusades.why: The sack of the Christian Byzantine capital crippled the empire, which eased the later Ottoman advance into Europe.

crusades.q: How are the crusades still part of the present?
a: They are invoked in politics and rhetoric on all sides
Crusader states still rule the Levant coast
They are forgotten outside history books
They ended all conflict over Jerusalem
crusades.why: The crusades left relations between Christians, Muslims and Jews more bitter, and they are still remembered and invoked in politics and rhetoric today.

mongol.q: What did Genghis Khan and his heirs build in the 1200s?
a: A sea empire across the Indian Ocean
A small kingdom in northern China
The largest connected land empire in history
A trading league of Silk Road cities
mongol.why: From 1206 the Mongols conquered lands from China to Russia and Iran, and by 1279 they ruled the largest connected land empire in history.

mongol.q: How did Genghis Khan make the Mongol army so effective?
a: Units of ten, hundred and thousand, promoted for loyalty and skill
Hiring European knights as officers
Using only foot soldiers with pikes
Giving command to the oldest noble families
mongol.why: Genghis Khan reorganised the mounted archers into disciplined units, promoting men for loyalty and skill rather than birth.

mongol.q: Why did the Mongol Empire split into four khanates?
a: The Mamluks conquered its centre
Each branch of the family ruled its own lands, then fought over succession
The Black Death killed its rulers
The Ming divided it by treaty
mongol.why: Each branch of Genghis's family ruled its own lands, and a civil war over the succession after 1259 broke their unity.

mongol.q: What did a century of Mongol peace do for travel across Eurasia?
a: It closed the Silk Road for good
It stopped all travel between Europe and China
It ended the spread of disease
It made the Silk Road safer than ever
mongol.why: Goods, ideas and travellers like Marco Polo crossed Eurasia more safely, though the same routes probably helped the Black Death spread west.

mongol.q: How did Mongol rule help shape modern Russia?
a: Moscow rose as the Golden Horde's tax collector
The Mongols founded the city of Kyiv
Russia became part of Yuan China
The Ilkhanate made Russia Muslim
mongol.why: Moscow rose by collecting taxes for the Golden Horde, threw off its rule in 1480, and became the core of the Russian state.

ottoman.q: What did Mehmed II achieve in 1453?
a: He besieged Vienna
He captured Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire
He conquered Egypt and Syria
He founded the Republic of Turkey
ottoman.why: Mehmed II took Constantinople with huge cannon in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and as Istanbul it stayed the Ottoman capital until 1922.

ottoman.q: Which helped the Ottomans hold a vast, mixed empire?
a: A strong state, Janissaries, gunpowder and fairly tolerant rule
Forcing every subject to speak Turkish
Alliances with the Mongol khans
A huge navy in the Atlantic
ottoman.why: A strong central state, a paid standing army of Janissaries, early gunpowder and fairly tolerant rule over Christians and Jews held the empire together.

ottoman.q: Which event marked the start of the empire's long retreat?
a: The fall of Constantinople in 1453
Selim I's conquest of Egypt
The failed second siege of Vienna in 1683
The founding of Bursa in 1326
ottoman.why: After the 1683 siege failed, the empire shrank: Hungary went to the Habsburgs, Crimea to Russia, and Balkan nations broke away in the 1800s.

ottoman.q: What happened after the Ottomans lost World War I?
a: They regained the Balkans
Germany took over the Arab lands
The sultan moved the capital to Cairo
Britain and France divided the Arab lands, and Turkey became a republic
ottoman.why: Britain and France divided the Arab lands, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, abolishing the caliphate in 1924.

ottoman.q: Why does Ottoman history still matter from Bosnia to Iraq?
a: Many borders, conflicts and mixed populations go back to Ottoman rule
The Ottoman sultan still rules there
Every country there speaks Turkish
Ottoman law is still used unchanged
ottoman.why: Many of today's borders, conflicts and mixed populations from Bosnia to Iraq go back to Ottoman rule and its breakup.

old.q: What do San Marino, Andorra, Monaco and Liechtenstein have in common?
a: All were founded after World War II
All are tiny states surviving from before 1800
All were once Ottoman provinces
All were European colonies in Africa
old.why: These microstates are far older than their neighbours: San Marino traces its founding to 301, and Liechtenstein became a principality in 1719.

old.q: Why did Europe's microstates survive while bigger states were swallowed up?
a: They had the strongest armies in Europe
They were hidden on remote islands
Too small to fight over, useful, or protected by treaties
They paid tribute to the Ottomans
old.why: They were too small to be worth a war, useful to bigger neighbours, or protected by treaties and old feudal rights.

old.q: Why did Thailand, Iran and Afghanistan avoid becoming colonies?
a: They were kept as buffers between rival empires
They had no resources anyone wanted
They were allied with Ethiopia
They were too far from Europe to reach
old.why: Rival empires such as Britain, France and Russia preferred to keep them as buffers between their own lands, though most lost territory.

old.q: What did Ethiopia's victory at Adwa in 1896 achieve?
a: It made Ethiopia an Italian colony
It gave Ethiopia control of Italy
It ended the Papal States
It kept Ethiopia independent during the scramble for Africa
old.why: Ethiopia crushed an Italian army with modern rifles and stayed independent, apart from a brief Italian occupation in 1936–41.

a: Italian power in Africa
African independence
The end of the Ottoman Empire
The founding of the Vatican
old.why: Ethiopia's victory at Adwa became a symbol of African independence, and its capital now hosts the African Union.

explore.q: What did the voyages of Columbus, da Gama and Magellan achieve between 1492 and 1522?
a: They proved Asia could not be reached
They joined the world's continents by sea
They mapped the Arctic coast
They found a land route to China
explore.why: Columbus reached the Caribbean, da Gama sailed round Africa to India, and Magellan's fleet went round the world, joining the continents for good.

explore.q: Why did Europeans want new sea routes to Asia?
a: To escape the Black Death
To spread the Reformation
To reach spices and silk without Venetian and Muslim middlemen
To find new land for farmers
explore.why: Europeans wanted direct access to Asia's spices and silk without paying Venetian and Muslim middlemen, and gold to pay for them.

explore.q: What did most to make the conquest of the Americas possible?
a: European diseases such as smallpox
Larger European armies
Better European farming
Treaties with Native rulers
explore.why: Smallpox and other diseases, against which Native peoples had no immunity, did more to make conquest possible than guns or horses.

explore.q: Why were about 12.5 million enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic?
a: To fight in European wars
To settle empty land as free farmers
To crew the ships to Asia
To work sugar plantations and mines
explore.why: Europeans shipped enslaved Africans to work plantations of sugar, coffee, tobacco and cotton, and mines; Brazil took about 4.9 million, more than anywhere else.

explore.q: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese while most of South America speaks Spanish?
a: Brazil was settled before Columbus sailed
The Tordesillas line gave Portugal the east
Spain sold Brazil to Portugal in 1790
Brazil chose Portuguese after independence
explore.why: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas gave Spain lands to the west of its line and Portugal those to the east, and the line crossed South America.

reformation.q: What did Martin Luther begin in 1517?
a: A crusade to retake Jerusalem
A council to unite the churches
An attack on indulgences that split Western Christianity
A war between France and Spain
