reformation.why: Luther's attack on the sale of indulgences started the Reformation, and Western Christianity split into a Protestant north and Catholic south.

reformation.q: How did the printing press help Luther?
a: It let him reach a mass audience quickly
It let the pope censor his writings
It printed money for his army
It replaced the Bible in churches
reformation.why: Printed pamphlets spread Luther's ideas across Germany within weeks, reaching a mass audience the Church could not silence.

reformation.q: Why did many princes and kings back the Reformation?
a: The pope ordered them to
It ended all wars in Europe
It made them richer through the spice trade
It gave them church lands and freed them from pope and emperor
reformation.why: Above all, princes had political reasons: reform gave them control of church lands and freed them from pope and emperor, as Henry VIII's break with Rome showed.

reformation.q: What did the Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia bring?
a: A quick, bloodless victory for Spain
Devastation in Germany, then an end to Europe's religious wars
A reunited Catholic Church
The end of the Holy Roman Empire's princes
reformation.why: The war of 1618–48 killed perhaps 4.5 to 8 million people, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended Europe's wars of religion.

reformation.q: Where can the Reformation's divide still be seen today?
a: In a line through Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands
Only in the Orthodox churches of Russia
In the borders of the Ottoman Empire
Nowhere; Europe reunited in faith
reformation.why: The split left a Protestant north and Catholic south, with a line through Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands that still shows on maps of belief.

asiaemp.q: Which great empires rose in Asia from the 1500s to the 1700s?
a: The Mughals, the Qing and Russia's tsars
The Romans, Persians and Han
The Aztecs, Inca and Maya
The Mongols, Seljuks and Abbasids
asiaemp.why: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, the Manchus founded the Qing in 1644, and Russia expanded across Siberia to the Pacific.

asiaemp.q: What made these empires so powerful?
a: Help from European navies
Control of the Atlantic slave trade
Gunpowder armies and bureaucracies taxing rich farmlands
Gold mines in Siberia
asiaemp.why: They combined cavalry, gunpowder armies and large bureaucracies taxing rich farming populations; India and China each produced around a quarter of world output in 1700.

asiaemp.q: Why did the Qing push into Inner Asia?
a: To reach the Pacific coast
To destroy the rival Dzungar Mongols and secure their frontier
To find furs to sell to Russia
To escape the British East India Company
asiaemp.why: The Qing conquered Mongolia and Xinjiang to destroy the Dzungar Mongols and secure their frontier, completing the conquest in 1759.

asiaemp.q: What happened to the Mughal lands after Aurangzeb died in 1707?
a: The Qing conquered them
They united into one strong state
Russia annexed them
The empire broke up and the East India Company took over
asiaemp.why: The empire broke up, and the British East India Company took over its lands, starting with Bengal after Plassey in 1757.

asiaemp.q: How do Qing frontiers still matter today?
a: They underlie China's claims to Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan
They are the borders of today's Mongolia
They decide India's capital
They divide Russia from Ukraine
asiaemp.why: Today's China rests on the Qing frontiers, the basis of its claims to Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan, though many Tibetans and Uyghurs dispute Chinese rule.

industry.q: What changed in Britain from the 1760s that began the Industrial Revolution?
a: Machines driven by water and then steam transformed production
Farming replaced hunting across the country
Britain banned all trade with its colonies
Factories closed as workers moved to farms
industry.why: Inventors mechanised cotton spinning, Watt's improved steam engine freed factories from rivers, and coal and iron output soared.

industry.q: Why did high wages in Britain help start industrialisation?
a: Workers could buy their own factories
They made labour-saving machines worth buying
They kept people on the farms
They stopped trade unions from forming
industry.why: With labour expensive and coal cheap and close to towns, it paid British owners to buy machines, alongside capital from trade and secure patents.

industry.q: What is the debate called about why Europe, not China or India, industrialised first?
a: The Axial Age
The Scramble for Africa
The Great Divergence
The Columbian Exchange
industry.why: In the Great Divergence debate, some historians stress coal and colonies, others institutions and science.

industry.q: How did industrialisation change the balance of power in the world?
a: It weakened Europe against Asia
It ended empires everywhere
It made all countries equally rich
Industrial nations used steamships, railways and machine guns to dominate others
industry.why: Industrial nations used their new technology to dominate the rest of the world, while cheap machine-made cloth hit India's handloom weavers.

industry.q: Which present-day problem goes back to the Industrial Revolution?
a: The rise in carbon dioxide behind climate change
The split between Sunni and Shia
The Black Death
The Tordesillas line in South America
industry.why: Burning coal and then oil began the rise in carbon dioxide behind today's climate change.

revolutions.q: What happened across the Atlantic world between 1775 and 1824?
a: Spain conquered North America
Revolutions overthrew kings and colonial rule
Britain gained colonies across South America
France restored its old monarchy for good
revolutions.why: The United States, France, Haiti and Spanish America all saw revolutions, and most of the Americas broke free of European rule.

revolutions.q: Which ideas gave many rebels a cause?
a: The divine right of kings
The Napoleonic law code
Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and consent
Mongol laws of conquest
revolutions.why: Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent gave rebels in America, France and beyond a cause.

revolutions.q: How did Napoleon's actions help free Spanish America?
a: He toppled Spain's king, so colonial elites took power
He sold the colonies to Britain
He sent troops to help Bolívar
He banned slavery in Spain's colonies
revolutions.why: When Napoleon forced out Spain's king in 1808, Spanish America had no legitimate ruler, colonial elites took power, and wars of independence followed.

a: It made Haiti a French province
It restored Spanish rule
It united Haiti with the United States
It created the first state born of a slave revolt
revolutions.why: Enslaved people rose in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804, abolishing slavery, though France forced it to pay a huge indemnity in 1825.

revolutions.q: Which ideas from this age still shape politics today?
a: Popular sovereignty, written constitutions and citizens' rights
Rule by divine right of kings
Feudal duties owed to lords
Rule by the Holy Roman Emperor
revolutions.why: The revolutions made popular sovereignty, constitutions and citizens' rights central to politics, and even gave us 'left' and 'right'.

nations.q: What idea kept redrawing the map of Europe and the Americas after 1815?
a: That the pope should rule all Christians
That each people should have its own state
That empires should grow as large as possible
That kings rule by divine right
nations.why: Nationalism, the idea that each people should have its own state, created Italy, Germany and new Balkan states from older empires.

nations.q: What taught people to see themselves as Italians, Germans or Greeks rather than subjects?
a: The French Revolution, newspapers and schools
The Mongol conquests
The crusades
The Black Death
nations.why: The French Revolution, newspapers and schools taught people to think of themselves as members of a nation rather than subjects of a dynasty.

nations.q: How, in the end, were the borders of the new Germany settled?
a: By a vote of all Europeans
By the pope's decision
By a treaty Britain drew up
By Prussia's wars against Denmark, Austria and France
nations.why: Railways and industry made bigger states possible, but armies settled the borders: Bismarck said great questions would be decided by 'iron and blood'.

nations.q: How did the new nation-states help lead to war in 1914?
a: France longed for Alsace-Lorraine, and the Balkans became a powder keg
Italy invaded the United States
Canada declared war on Britain
Bolivia attacked Germany
nations.why: A united Germany became Europe's strongest power, France wanted back Alsace-Lorraine, and rival nationalisms made the Balkans a powder keg; both fed into 1914.

a: It sold its coast to Peru
It never had a coast
Chile took its coast in the War of the Pacific
The Spanish drew its border that way
nations.why: Latin American wars fixed borders that still stand: Chile's victory in the War of the Pacific, 1879–84, took Bolivia's coast and left it landlocked.

scramble.q: What happened to Africa between 1870 and 1914?
a: African kingdoms united against European traders
Europeans gave up their coastal trading posts
European powers came to rule about nine-tenths of it
The Ottoman Empire conquered most of the interior
scramble.why: In 1870 Europeans held about a tenth of Africa, mostly on the coasts; by 1914 they ruled about nine-tenths, leaving only Ethiopia and Liberia independent.

scramble.q: Why did industrial Europe want colonies?
a: To settle surplus farmers on empty land
For raw materials, new markets and safe sea routes
To escape debts owed to African rulers
Because the Berlin Conference ordered every power to expand
scramble.why: Factories needed rubber, cotton and copper, and Britain above all wanted to protect its route to India through the Suez Canal.

scramble.q: What made conquering Africa cheap for Europeans in this period?
a: Most African states invited European rule
African armies had no weapons at all
Diseases had emptied the interior of people
Machine guns, steamships and quinine against malaria
scramble.why: New technology tipped the balance: machine guns won battles, steamships carried troops inland, and quinine let Europeans survive malaria.

scramble.q: How did the scramble for colonies affect relations between the European powers?
a: Imperial rivalry added to the tensions behind World War I
It ended their rivalries by giving each a fair share
It united them in a permanent alliance
It made them abandon their navies
scramble.why: Each power grabbed land to keep the others out, and clashes such as Fashoda in 1898 fed the rivalry that helped lead to war in 1914.

scramble.q: How does the scramble still shape Africa today?
a: European powers handed all land back to precolonial kingdoms
Colonial lines became most borders; many economies still export raw materials
Every African country remains ruled from Europe
Africa's borders were all redrawn by local votes after independence
scramble.why: Straight colonial lines became national borders, often splitting peoples or joining rivals, and economies built to export raw materials are a pattern many still struggle to escape.

ww1.q: What event in June 1914 set off the crisis that became World War I?
a: Germany invaded Belgium
Russia's tsar was overthrown
A Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Britain declared war on Austria-Hungary
ww1.why: The heir to Austria-Hungary was shot in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, declared war on Serbia, and within six weeks the great powers were at war.

ww1.q: Why did a local Balkan crisis turn into a general European war?
a: Rival alliances pulled the great powers in one after another
Serbia invaded Germany
The United States demanded war
Italy attacked France first
ww1.why: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary and declared war on Russia and France, and imperial rivalry, an arms race and nationalism fed the escalation.

ww1.q: What brought Britain into the war in August 1914?
a: The shooting of a British diplomat
Germany's march through neutral Belgium
A Russian attack on India
Austria-Hungary's invasion of Serbia
ww1.why: Germany's plan to defeat France first went through neutral Belgium, and that invasion brought Britain and its whole empire into the war.

ww1.q: Which empires fell as a result of the war?
a: The British, French, Japanese and American
The Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch and Belgian
Only the German Empire
The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman
ww1.why: Four empires fell; new states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared, and Britain and France divided the Arab Middle East between them.

ww1.q: How did the end of World War I help set the stage for later conflict?
a: The harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germany bitter
Germany was given new colonies it could not hold
Britain lost its empire in 1919
The United States took over Europe
ww1.why: Germany resented the Treaty of Versailles, which took land and all its colonies, and that bitterness helped set the stage for World War II.

interwar.q: What happened to much of Europe's politics between the two world wars?
a: Kings everywhere were replaced by elected parliaments
Dictators took power in Russia, Italy, Germany and beyond
Europe united under the League of Nations
Communists won elections across western Europe
interwar.why: Lenin's Bolsheviks took Russia, Mussolini took Italy in 1922 and Hitler Germany in 1933, and by 1938 dictators ruled most of Europe.

interwar.q: How did the Great Depression help Hitler come to power?
a: It made Germany rich enough to rearm
It forced Britain to invite him to rule
Mass unemployment drove voters to extremes
It ended the Treaty of Versailles
interwar.why: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 spread worldwide; with six million Germans out of work, Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and built a dictatorship.

interwar.q: Why did Britain and France choose appeasement towards Hitler?
a: They dreaded another war like the last one
They had secretly allied with Germany
The League of Nations ordered them to
They wanted Germany to fight the United States
interwar.why: Dreading a repeat of World War I, and with a League of Nations that had no army, Britain and France let Hitler take Austria and the Czech lands.

interwar.q: What allowed Hitler to invade Poland in 1939 without fearing a two-front war?
a: A treaty with Britain
The fall of France
Japan's attack on Russia
A pact with Stalin
interwar.why: The Nazi–Soviet Pact of 1939 meant the Soviet Union would not fight Germany, so Hitler could attack Poland.

interwar.q: Which lesson from the 1930s shaped the world after 1945?
a: That trade between countries causes wars
That appeasing aggressors invites war
That democracies should avoid alliances
That governments should never manage the economy
interwar.why: The decade taught leaders that appeasement invites war, and inspired welfare states, economic management and institutions such as the UN and the IMF.

a: The bombing of German cities by the Allies
The Nazi murder of about six million Jews
The Soviet expulsion of Germans from Poland
The siege of Stalingrad
ww2.why: In occupied Europe the Nazis and their collaborators murdered about six million Jews, in mass shootings and in death camps such as Auschwitz.

ww2.q: Why did Japan go to war with the United States in 1941?
a: The US had invaded Japan's home islands
Japan wanted to help Germany take Britain
Japan wanted an Asian empire and oil the US had cut off
The US had attacked China
ww2.why: Japan sought an Asian empire and the oil it lacked; when the US cut off oil in 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and overran South-East Asia.

ww2.q: Where did the tide of the war turn in 1942–43?
a: Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad
Normandy, Hiroshima and Berlin
Warsaw, Paris and London
Pearl Harbor, Singapore and Dunkirk
ww2.why: Victories at Midway in the Pacific, El Alamein in North Africa and Stalingrad in Russia stopped the Axis advance; the Allies then drove towards Germany and Japan.

ww2.q: How did the war change Europe's map and politics?
a: Germany kept its 1939 borders and stayed united
Europe was split between US and Soviet camps
Britain and France gained large new empires
The Soviet Union withdrew from Eastern Europe
ww2.why: Europe was split between US and Soviet camps, Germany and Korea were divided, and Poland was moved west as millions were expelled.

ww2.q: Which lasting institution or law came out of World War II?
a: The League of Nations
The Treaty of Versailles
The Berlin Conference
The United Nations and the Genocide Convention
ww2.why: The United Nations was founded in 1945 to keep the peace, and the Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention.

asia.q: What happened to Europe's Asian empires after 1945?
a: Most colonies became independent within a few decades
Japan took them over permanently
They merged into one Asian federation
Europe expanded them with US support
asia.why: From the Philippines in 1946 and India and Pakistan in 1947 to the Gulf states in 1971, almost all became independent within four decades.

asia.q: How did World War II weaken European rule in Asia?
a: European colonies were untouched by the fighting
Japan's quick conquests shattered the myth of European invincibility
Britain won so easily that it lost interest
Asian nationalists all fought for Japan
asia.why: Japan took Singapore and the Dutch East Indies within three months, showing Europeans could be beaten, and nationalist movements were ready to take over.

asia.q: Why did Britain leave India in 1947 rather than hold it by force?
a: The United States threatened war
India voted to stay British
Britain, nearly bankrupted by the war, could no longer afford to
The Soviet Union invaded India
asia.why: The war left Britain nearly bankrupt, and Gandhi's Indian National Congress, decades old, was ready to take over.

asia.q: What happened when British India was partitioned in 1947?
a: It peacefully became a single federation
It returned to rule by princes
France took over the north-west
Over 10 million people fled across the new borders
asia.why: India and Muslim-majority Pakistan were split amid mass violence; over 10 million fled, and estimates of the dead range from 200,000 to 2 million.

asia.q: Which conflict left by hasty borders still divides India and Pakistan?
a: Tibet
Kashmir
Ceylon
Burma
asia.why: Both claim Kashmir and have fought over it repeatedly, and both now have nuclear weapons.

a: A war fought only in the Arctic
A rivalry between the US and the Soviet Union after 1945
Germany's attempt to rebuild after 1945
A conflict between Britain and France over colonies
coldwar.why: The wartime allies became rivals: an Iron Curtain split Europe, and the superpowers competed through arms races, spies, aid and proxy wars.

coldwar.q: Why did Stalin want communist governments in Eastern Europe?
a: As a friendly buffer after two German invasions
To repay Marshall Plan loans
Because NATO had asked him to
To trade oil with the United States
coldwar.why: After two German invasions, Stalin wanted friendly governments as a buffer; the US, resolved not to repeat 1930s appeasement, set out to contain communism.

coldwar.q: Why did the superpowers never fight each other directly?
a: They had signed a permanent peace treaty
The United Nations had an army between them
Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal
Neither had a large army
coldwar.why: Nuclear weapons made direct war suicidal, so the rivalry ran through proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola and Central America.

coldwar.q: What was the outcome when the Cold War ended in 1989–91?
a: The Soviet Union became the only superpower
Germany stayed divided for good
Communist rule spread to Western Europe
The Soviet Union broke up into 15 countries
coldwar.why: The Berlin Wall opened in 1989 and the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, leaving the United States as the only superpower.

coldwar.q: Which Cold War legacy still shapes the world today?
a: Korea remains divided, and thousands of nuclear warheads still exist
No country is still ruled by a communist party
NATO was dissolved in 1991
Germany is still split in two
coldwar.why: Korea remains divided, communist parties still rule China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, and many warheads built then still exist.

mideast.q: What happened in 1948 as British rule in Palestine ended?
a: A single Arab-Jewish state was created
Israel declared independence and won the war that followed
Egypt annexed all of Palestine
Britain handed Palestine to Jordan peacefully
mideast.why: Israel declared independence and neighbouring Arab states attacked; Israel won, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, and Jordan and Egypt held the West Bank and Gaza.

mideast.q: What is the root of the conflict over Israel and Palestine?
a: A dispute over oil fields in Sinai
A quarrel between Britain and France
Two national movements claiming the same land
Rivalry between Iran and Iraq
mideast.why: Zionism and Palestinian Arab nationalism claimed the same land, and in World War I Britain made promises to both that were hard to reconcile.

mideast.q: Why have outside powers competed for influence in the Middle East?
a: The region holds nearly half the world's proven oil
It is the world's largest grain producer
It controls the Panama Canal
Its population is the world's largest
mideast.why: Nearly half the world's proven oil lies there, which made the Gulf rich and central to US strategy.

a: Egypt and Syria took land from Israel
A Palestinian state was founded
Jordan gained East Jerusalem
Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, Golan and Sinai
mideast.why: In the Six-Day War Israel took those lands; it returned Sinai to Egypt after their 1979 peace and has occupied the West Bank since 1967.

mideast.q: What is the situation of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict today?
a: It was settled by the Oslo Accords
It remains unresolved, with Jerusalem and refugees still disputed
Israel and the US now recognise a State of Palestine
Palestinians have full statehood under UN rule
mideast.why: Oslo brought limited self-rule but no state; settlements grew, Jerusalem and refugees remain disputed, and war came to Gaza again after Hamas's attack of 7 October 2023.

china.q: What did Deng Xiaoping change in China from 1978?
a: He forced peasants into communes
He let farmers sell crops and welcomed foreign investment
He ended Communist Party rule
He closed China to foreign trade
china.why: Deng's 'reform and opening' let farmers sell their crops, opened special economic zones such as Shenzhen, and brought growth near 10% a year for three decades.

china.q: Why did the Communists win China's civil war in 1949?
a: Corruption, inflation and war weakened the Nationalists; Mao won the peasants
Japan helped Mao defeat the Nationalists
The United States backed the Communists
The Nationalists chose to leave for Taiwan without fighting
china.why: Corruption, runaway inflation and eight years of war with Japan weakened the Nationalists, while Mao's party won over the peasants.

china.q: Why did Mao's Great Leap Forward end in disaster?
a: Foreign armies invaded during the harvest
Deng Xiaoping opened markets too early
Utopian plans were forced through with no one able to object
Floods destroyed the new factories
china.why: Peasants were forced into communes and no one could object; the famine of 1958–62 killed tens of millions, with estimates from 15 to over 40 million.

china.q: What was the result of three decades of fast growth after 1978?
a: China became a multi-party democracy
China's population fell by half
China gave up manufacturing for farming
About 800 million people left extreme poverty
china.why: It was the largest fall in poverty in history, and China became the world's biggest manufacturer and goods exporter.

china.q: What shapes China's place in world politics today?
a: Rivalry with the US over trade, technology and Taiwan
A military alliance with the United States
Its membership of the European Union
Its return to Mao-era communes
china.why: Still a one-party state, tightened under Xi Jinping since 2012, China is the second-largest economy and its rivalry with the US now shapes world politics.

europe.q: How did European integration begin in the early 1950s?
a: Britain and France merged their armies
Six countries pooled their coal and steel industries
The Soviet Union proposed a European market
Germany adopted the French franc
europe.why: In 1950 France proposed pooling coal and steel, the industries of war, with West Germany's, and six countries signed up in 1951.

europe.q: What was the main aim of binding France and Germany together?
a: To make another war between them impossible
To rebuild their overseas empires
To compete with Britain for colonies
To leave NATO
europe.why: After two world wars, leaders wanted ties so tight that war between France and Germany would be impossible.

europe.q: Why did former dictatorships and communist states want to join?
a: Membership let them keep their old rulers
The EU paid them to leave NATO
To lock in democracy and catch up economically
They were required to by the United Nations
europe.why: Greece, Spain and Portugal joined after their dictatorships ended, and ten countries, mostly former communist states, joined in 2004.

europe.q: Which country became the first to leave, departing in 2020?
a: Greece
Denmark
Ireland
Britain
europe.why: Britain, a member since 1973, voted to leave in 2016 and departed in 2020, leaving 27 members.

europe.q: What has Western Europe gained from integration since 1945?
a: Its longest peace in centuries and a huge single market
A single army that replaced NATO
One currency used by all 27 members
An end to all arguments over migration and debt
europe.why: The old rivals have not fought each other since 1945, and their single market of about 450 million people sets rules followed far beyond Europe.

africa.q: What was special about 1960 for Africa?
a: Ghana became the first independent state
Portugal freed all its colonies
Seventeen countries became independent, most of them French colonies
Rhodesia became Zimbabwe
africa.why: Ghana led in 1957; in the 'Year of Africa' 17 countries followed, most of them French colonies freed by negotiation.

africa.q: How did the Second World War help bring about African independence?
a: It weakened Britain and France, and returning soldiers demanded rights
It made Britain and France richer than ever
African colonies were given to the United States
Germany granted independence to its colonies
africa.why: The war weakened the colonial powers, Africans who had fought for them came home demanding rights, and the UN and both superpowers opposed old-style empires.

africa.q: Why did independence come through war in places like Algeria and Angola?
a: Their people did not want independence
They had many white settlers or a dictatorship as the colonial power
The UN sent armies to stop independence
They had no nationalist leaders
africa.why: Algeria, Kenya and Rhodesia had many white settlers, and Portugal was a dictatorship; there the end came through war rather than negotiation.

africa.q: What did almost every new African state do about colonial borders?
a: Redrew them along ethnic lines
Merged into one African state
Returned to precolonial kingdoms
Kept them, agreeing in 1964 to respect them
africa.why: Keeping colonial borders meant many countries joined rival peoples and divided others.

africa.q: Which pattern from colonial times still affects many African economies?
a: Dependence on exporting raw materials
Reliance on European factory jobs
Use of a single shared currency
Rule by European governors
africa.why: Economies built to export raw materials stayed dependent on them, even as Africa now has the world's youngest and fastest-growing population.

islands.q: What happened to many small colonies from 1962 to the early 1980s?
a: They were absorbed into larger neighbours
Dozens became independent states, some very small
They all became part of France
They joined the United States
islands.why: From Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago in 1962 to St Kitts and Nevis in 1983, island groups became states, some with fewer than 10,000 people.

islands.q: Why did Britain let its small colonies go?
a: It was cutting overseas costs and turning towards Europe
The islands threatened to join the Soviet Union
It needed their land for military bases
A war with France forced it to
islands.why: Once the big colonies had gone, keeping small ones made little sense to a Britain cutting costs, and a 1960 UN declaration called for a swift end to colonialism.

islands.q: Why did each Caribbean island become a separate country?
a: Britain refused to allow any union
The islands spoke different languages
The West Indies Federation collapsed after Jamaica voted to leave
The UN required each island to stand alone
islands.why: A British-led West Indies Federation collapsed in 1962 after Jamaica voted to leave, so each island went its own way.

islands.q: What power did independence give these microstates?
a: A veto in the UN Security Council
Control of world fishing
Automatic membership of the EU
A UN General Assembly vote equal to China's
islands.why: Each microstate holds a General Assembly vote equal to that of China or the United States.

islands.q: Which issue do low-lying island nations such as Tuvalu and the Maldives press on today?
a: Nuclear disarmament
Climate change and rising seas
Space exploration
Reunion with their former rulers
islands.why: Rising seas threaten low-lying nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives, so many use their UN vote to press on climate change.

collapse.q: What happened to Soviet power between 1989 and 1991?
a: It expanded into Western Europe
Communist rule fell in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union dissolved
It was overthrown by a NATO invasion
Gorbachev became leader of a united Germany
collapse.why: Communist rule fell across Eastern Europe in 1989, Germany reunited in 1990, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries.

collapse.q: Which economic problem helped push the Soviet Union towards reform?
a: A booming economy that needed fewer controls
Debts owed to Eastern European states
A shortage of workers after emigration
Stagnation, heavy arms spending and falling oil income
collapse.why: The economy could not match Western technology, spent heavily on arms and the war in Afghanistan, and lost income when oil prices fell in the 1980s.

collapse.q: What was the key decision that unravelled the Soviet empire?
a: Gorbachev refused to use mass force to hold Eastern Europe
Stalin's death in 1953
The Soviet invasion of Hungary
The building of the Berlin Wall
collapse.why: Unlike in 1956 and 1968, Gorbachev did not send in the tanks in 1989, and openness let nationalism surge in the republics.

collapse.q: What broke central power in the Soviet Union in 1991?
a: A US invasion of Moscow
Gorbachev's re-election
A failed hard-line coup in Moscow in August
The opening of the Berlin Wall
collapse.why: After the August coup failed, most republics declared independence, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned as the Soviet Union dissolved.

collapse.q: How do Russia's leaders now refer to NATO's growth after 1991?
a: As proof that the Cold War never ended
As a grievance cited in their wars with Georgia and Ukraine
As a welcome guarantee of their security
As an idea Russia itself proposed
collapse.why: Former Eastern Bloc and Baltic states joined NATO and the EU, and Russia's leaders came to cite that eastward expansion as a grievance in their wars.

balkans.q: What happened to Yugoslavia in the 1990s?
a: It joined the European Union as one state
It broke apart in a series of wars
It was annexed by the Soviet Union
It peacefully became a federation of equals
balkans.why: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, and wars followed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo; about 140,000 people died.

balkans.q: What had held Yugoslavia's many peoples together until 1980?
a: Tito's one-party rule and 'brotherhood and unity'
NATO peacekeepers
A shared religion
Membership of the European Union
balkans.why: Tito held the six republics together and kept wartime memories of mass killing down; after his death and the failure of communism, the federation weakened.

balkans.q: Why did the breakup turn so violent?
a: Foreign armies invaded to seize land
The republics had no borders at all
Nationalist leaders and large minorities outside home states led to 'ethnic cleansing'
Tito ordered the wars before he died
balkans.why: Leaders such as Milošević and Tuđman turned to nationalism, borders left large Serb and Croat minorities outside their home states, and armed forces tried to redraw the map.

balkans.q: How did the war in Bosnia end in 1995?
a: Serbia conquered the whole country
The UN tribunal ordered a ceasefire
Bosnia joined Croatia
NATO air strikes and the Dayton agreement
balkans.why: After the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre, NATO air strikes and the Dayton agreement ended the war.

balkans.q: Which question from the breakup is still unresolved today?
a: Kosovo's independence, which Serbia does not recognise
Slovenia's membership of the EU
Montenegro's union with Serbia
Whether Croatia exists
balkans.why: Kosovo declared independence in 2008; about half of UN members recognise it and Serbia does not, while Bosnia remains split in two parts.

recent.q: Which became the world's newest country in 2011?
a: Eritrea
Timor-Leste
South Sudan
Namibia
recent.why: South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war, following Namibia, Eritrea and Timor-Leste in the years after the Cold War.

recent.q: What did most of these new countries have in common?
a: They undid arrangements left over from colonial rule
They were all created by the Soviet Union
They all broke away from European states
They were all formed by merging smaller states
recent.why: Borders and rulers had been imposed under colonial rule without the people's consent, and these changes undid them.

recent.q: How did the end of the Cold War help new states emerge?
a: Superpowers began creating new colonies
It removed superpower backing that had kept disputes frozen
It abolished the United Nations
It forced every country to hold a referendum
recent.why: Without superpower backing for the old arrangements, the UN and outside powers became readier to support referendums, as in Eritrea and East Timor.

recent.q: Did independence bring peace to all of these new states?
a: Yes, all became stable democracies
Yes, but only after rejoining their old rulers
No, none of them held elections
No: South Sudan fell into civil war, though Timor-Leste built a democracy
recent.why: South Sudan fell into civil war in 2013 and Eritrea became one of the world's most closed states, while Timor-Leste built a working democracy.

recent.q: Why are new countries rare today?
a: Governments fear secession and international law strongly protects existing borders
The UN has a fixed limit of 193 members
All disputed territories have been settled
No region wants independence any more
recent.why: Existing borders are strongly protected, so cases such as Western Sahara, Kosovo and Somaliland remain unresolved.

today.q: How did the United States respond to the 11 September 2001 attacks?
a: It withdrew its troops from the Middle East
It invaded Afghanistan and, in 2003, Iraq
It declared war on Russia
It left NATO
today.why: After al-Qaeda killed nearly 3,000 people, the US invaded Afghanistan and Iraq; the Taliban retook Kabul in 2021.

today.q: What fed populist politics in many countries after 2001?
a: Falling inequality and less migration
The end of social media
Widening inequality and migration amid globalisation's shocks
A long period of world peace
today.why: Globalisation spread wealth but also shocks such as the 2008 financial crisis, and widening inequality and migration fed populism.

today.q: What happened after the Arab Spring uprisings of 2011?
a: Four rulers fell, but Syria, Libya and Yemen slid into civil war
Every Arab country became a lasting democracy
The uprisings were all crushed within a week
Iran took over the region
today.why: The rulers of Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen fell, but only Tunisia built a lasting democracy, and civil wars followed elsewhere.

today.q: Which event in 2022 marked a turning point for European security?
a: Britain rejoined the European Union
Russia and NATO signed a peace treaty
The Covid-19 pandemic began
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
today.why: Russia, which had annexed Crimea in 2014, launched a full-scale invasion in 2022, and Europe began rearming.

today.q: What has replaced the age of a single dominant power and ever-freer trade?
a: A world government under the UN
Great-power rivalry, higher tariffs and rising military spending
A new era of disarmament
Complete Chinese dominance
today.why: China's rise and a resurgent Russia challenged American leadership; NATO has grown to 32 members, and wars in Ukraine and with Iran continued in October 2026.

now.q: Which country has had the world's largest population since 2023?
a: China
The United States
India
Nigeria
now.why: India passed China in 2023; together they hold over a third of the more than 8.2 billion people on Earth.

now.q: Why are many poorer countries, especially in East Asia, catching up with rich ones?
a: They joined world trade later and grew fast
Rich countries gave them their factories for free
They stopped using coal, oil and gas
Their populations stopped growing first
now.why: Europe, North America and Japan industrialised first and grew rich; countries that later joined world trade, above all in East Asia, are catching up.

now.q: Why do carbon emissions follow industry so closely?
a: Factories are required to emit by law
Only poor countries burn fossil fuels
Emissions come mainly from farming
Cheap coal, oil and gas powered industrial growth
now.why: Fossil fuels powered growth, so China, the biggest manufacturer, emits about a third of the world's CO2, and the US has emitted the most over history.

now.q: What happens to birth rates as countries get richer?
a: They rise sharply
They fall, so populations age
They stay exactly the same
They follow oil prices
now.why: Falling birth rates mean populations age and shrink in the rich world and China, while Africa's grow.

now.q: Where is much of the world's population growth to 2050 expected?
a: Europe
East Asia
North America
Africa
now.why: Africa is expected to hold about a quarter of humanity by 2050, while ageing societies elsewhere struggle to pay for pensions and care.

us-colonies.q: What had happened to the land that became the US by 1763?
a: Native nations, Spain, France and Britain all held parts of it
Spain alone ruled it from Mexico City
Britain had settled it from coast to Pacific
Native nations had kept Europeans out entirely
us-colonies.why: Native nations held most of the land, Spain held Florida and the Southwest, France ran forts down the Mississippi, and Britain's colonies hugged the Atlantic coast.

us-colonies.q: Why did disease make European conquest easier?
a: Settlers brought medicines that Native nations had to buy
Native people had no immunity to diseases such as smallpox
Europeans caught Native diseases and grew stronger
Disease mainly killed the French and Spanish rivals
us-colonies.why: Smallpox and other diseases, to which Native people had no immunity, killed huge numbers, often ahead of the settlers themselves.

us-colonies.q: Why did Britain's colonies outgrow New France?
a: Britain had found far more gold
France banned its people from farming
Britain sent families, not just soldiers and traders
New France was conquered by Spain
us-colonies.why: Britain sent families to farm and settle, so its colonies had about fifteen times as many settlers as New France.

us-colonies.q: How did Britain's victory in the French and Indian War change the colonies?
a: It ended slavery in the Southern colonies
It gave France control of the Ohio Country
It made the colonies rely on Britain more than ever
With France gone, colonists depended less on Britain
us-colonies.why: Driving France from the mainland in 1763 removed the threat that had made the colonists rely on British protection.

us-colonies.q: Which colonial habit later shaped how Americans governed themselves?
a: Rule by appointed military governors
Elected assemblies and self-government
Rule by the Spanish crown
Choosing leaders by Native council
us-colonies.why: From Virginia's first elected assembly in 1619, the colonies built their own assemblies and habits of self-government.

us-independence.q: What did the American Revolution achieve by 1789?
a: An independent republic with a written Constitution
A colony with seats in the British Parliament
A kingdom ruled by George Washington
A union of the colonies with French Canada
us-independence.why: The colonies declared independence in 1776, won the war, and in 1787 wrote a Constitution under which Washington became the first president in 1789.

us-independence.q: Why did British taxes after 1763 anger the colonists so much?
a: They were far higher than taxes in Britain
They were voted by a Parliament where colonists had no seats
They paid for a war against the colonists
They were collected by French officials
us-independence.why: Colonists used to running their own elected assemblies saw taxes from a Parliament where they had no seats as tyranny: 'no taxation without representation'.

us-independence.q: Why was the victory at Saratoga in 1777 a turning point?
a: It captured the British capital
It ended the war at once
It brought France into the war on the American side
It persuaded Spain to give up Florida
us-independence.why: Saratoga persuaded France to join, and French money, troops and ships proved decisive, above all at Yorktown in 1781.

us-independence.q: What did the new nation leave unresolved?
a: Whether to have a president
Whether to stay loyal to Britain
Whether to accept French rule
Slavery, which the Constitution left in place
us-independence.why: The Constitution kept slavery, counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for seats in Congress.

us-independence.q: How does the Revolution still shape the United States today?
a: Its Constitution and Bill of Rights still govern the country
The US still pays taxes to Britain
Its states still answer to France
Its Loyalists still rule Canada
us-independence.why: The Constitution of 1787 and the Bill of Rights still govern the country, and the Declaration's claim of equality inspired revolutions elsewhere.

us-expansion.q: What happened to the United States between 1803 and 1848?
a: It lost its western lands to Mexico
It spread across the continent to the Pacific
It split into Northern and Southern nations
It became a colony of France again
us-expansion.why: The Louisiana Purchase, Florida, Texas, Oregon and the lands taken from Mexico carried the country from the Mississippi to the Pacific.

a: A treaty dividing Oregon with Britain
Napoleon's plan to retake Louisiana
The belief the country was meant to spread across the continent
A law giving free farms to settlers
us-expansion.why: Named in 1845, Manifest Destiny was the belief that the United States was meant to spread across the continent, and it drove demands for new land.

us-expansion.q: Why could the US gain so much land so quickly?
a: Britain gave up all of North America
Native nations sold their land willingly
Mexico asked to join the US
Its rivals were weak, divided or short of money
us-expansion.why: Napoleon needed cash for war with Britain, Spain was losing its empire, and Mexico was newly independent and divided.

us-expansion.q: What did the war with Mexico cost Mexico?
a: About half its territory, counting Texas
Only the city of Tucson
Its independence from Spain
Its Pacific port of Oregon
us-expansion.why: With Texas and the 1848 cession of California and the Southwest, Mexico lost about half its territory, a memory that still shapes relations between the two countries.

us-expansion.q: Which problem did the new western land reopen, leading toward civil war?
a: Whether to keep paying Britain
Whether slavery could spread west
Whether to give Florida back to Spain
Whether gold should be money
us-expansion.why: Each new territory raised whether slavery could spread there, and that fight led directly to the Civil War.

us-civilwar.q: What was the outcome of the Civil War?
a: The Confederacy won independence
The Union survived and slavery was abolished
The North and South agreed to split the West
Britain took back the Southern states
us-civilwar.why: Lee surrendered in 1865, the Union held together, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery, freeing about 4 million people.

us-civilwar.q: What was the central cause of the Civil War?
a: A dispute over tariffs on cotton
Lincoln's plan to abolish the states
Slavery, as seceding states said themselves
Rivalry over the transcontinental railroad
us-civilwar.why: Slavery was the central cause, and the seceding states said so in their own declarations; enslaved people were worth more than all the railroads and factories.

us-civilwar.q: Why did Lincoln's election in 1860 lead Southern states to secede?
a: He promised to raise taxes on the South
He had been born in South Carolina
He planned to sell the South to Mexico
He pledged to stop slavery spreading and won without the South
us-civilwar.why: A party pledged to stop slavery's spread won the White House without a single Southern state, so Southern leaders chose to leave.

us-civilwar.q: How did the war change the federal government?
a: It emerged far stronger, and secession was dead
It was dissolved and rebuilt in Richmond
It lost power to the individual states
It handed the South to military rule forever
us-civilwar.why: The Union's survival ended the idea that a state could leave it, and the federal government came out of the war far stronger.

us-civilwar.q: What struggle did the end of the war begin?
a: Over whether to rejoin Britain
Over what freedom and citizenship would mean for Black Americans
Over whether Texas would become independent
Over who owned the Mississippi River
us-civilwar.why: Slavery was gone, but the struggle over what freedom and equal citizenship would mean for Black Americans was only beginning, and it lasted long after.

us-west.q: What happened to Native nations between 1830 and 1890?
a: They were removed and forced onto reservations
They were given full control of the Plains
They moved east to escape settlers
They joined the Confederacy and won land
us-west.why: Removal forced eastern nations to Indian Territory, and after the Civil War the army, settlers and the bison's slaughter forced the Plains nations onto reservations.

us-west.q: Why did gold strikes matter in this story?
a: They paid for Native schools
They brought sudden waves of intruders onto Native land
They persuaded settlers to go home
They made Native nations rich
us-west.why: Gold in Georgia in 1829 and in the Black Hills in 1874 brought miners onto Native land, often breaking treaties the government had signed.

us-west.q: Why did the slaughter of the bison weaken the Plains nations?
a: The bison were sacred and could not be replaced
Bison hides paid for their rifles
It took away their main source of food
The bison carried their trade goods
us-west.why: The destruction of the bison herds took away the Plains nations' food, helping force them onto reservations.

us-west.q: What did the 1887 Dawes Act do to Native land?
a: It returned the Black Hills to the Lakota
It doubled the size of reservations
It made Indian Territory a separate country
It broke up reservations, shrinking Native land sharply
us-west.why: By breaking up reservations, the Dawes Act helped shrink Native landholdings from about 138 million acres to 48 million by 1934.

us-west.q: What is the position of Native nations today?
a: They have no remaining governments
575 federally recognised tribes have their own governments
They govern the state of Oklahoma alone
They all live in Alaska and Hawaii
us-west.why: Despite removal, war and boarding schools, the nations survived: today there are 575 federally recognised tribes with their own governments.

us-reconstruction.q: What did Reconstruction change for Black Americans at first?
a: Nothing, since slavery continued until 1877
Black men voted and about 2,000 held office
They were all given farms by the government
They moved north at once
us-reconstruction.why: Under federal troops and the new amendments, Black men voted and about 2,000 held office, from sheriffs to US senators.

a: Freed people voted to end it
The Supreme Court abolished the 14th Amendment
White resistance, violence and fraud, plus fading Northern support
Britain pressured the US to withdraw troops
us-reconstruction.why: Most white Southerners used violence, fraud and economic pressure to regain power, while Northern voters tired of occupation and turned elsewhere after the 1873 depression.

us-reconstruction.q: Why did most freed people end up as poor sharecroppers?
a: They preferred city life
The 13th Amendment required it
They chose to farm cotton for profit
They had won rights but little land
us-reconstruction.why: Freed people won legal rights but little land, so most worked as sharecroppers dependent on white landowners.

us-reconstruction.q: What followed when federal troops left the South in 1877?
a: Jim Crow segregation and the loss of Black votes
Full equality for Black Southerners
A second Civil War
The South's return to slavery by law
us-reconstruction.why: Southern states imposed Jim Crow: segregated schools and public places, poll taxes and literacy tests, upheld by the Supreme Court in 1896.

us-reconstruction.q: How did the 14th Amendment matter later on?
a: It was repealed in 1896
It became the legal basis of the civil rights movement
It ended the Great Migration
It gave the vote to women
us-reconstruction.why: Long ignored, the 14th Amendment's promise of citizenship and equal protection later became the legal basis of the civil rights movement.

us-industry.q: What had the United States become by about 1900?
a: A mainly farming nation closed to immigrants
A colony of European investors
The world's largest industrial producer
A country without overseas territories
us-industry.why: Railroads, steel, oil and electricity made the US the world's largest industrial producer by about 1900, a lead it held for over a century.

us-industry.q: Why did American industry grow so fast?
a: Resources, a big market, railroads and cheap immigrant labour
Strict rules on business and low tariffs
Loans from Spain after 1898
A shortage of workers that raised wages
us-industry.why: Huge natural resources, a large market without internal tariffs, linking railroads, immigrant labour and few rules on business all helped companies grow.

us-industry.q: Why did the US take overseas territories in 1898?
a: To stop immigration from Asia
To pay off its war debts
To give Spain new markets
Leaders wanted markets and bases; the Maine's sinking set off war
us-industry.why: Many leaders believed an industrial power needed markets, naval bases and coaling stations, and sympathy for Cuba and the Maine's sinking set off war with Spain.

us-industry.q: How did Americans react to the excesses of the industrial age?
a: They abolished all large companies
The Progressive reforms: antitrust laws, food safety, income tax
They returned to farming in large numbers
They ended immigration completely in 1882
us-industry.why: A Progressive reaction brought antitrust laws, food safety rules, a federal income tax and, in 1920, votes for women.

a: Spain still rules Cuba
The Philippines remains a US territory
Hawaii is an independent kingdom
Puerto Rico and Guam remain US territories
us-industry.why: Puerto Rico and Guam, taken from Spain in 1898, are still US territories, while the Philippines became independent in 1946.

a: A short dip in stock prices in 1929
A collapse where banks failed and a quarter of workers lost jobs
A drought that only hit California
A slump caused by the First World War's losses
us-depression.why: After the 1929 crash, thousands of banks failed, output fell by about a quarter, and by 1933 about a quarter of workers had no job.

a: It rested on borrowed money and stock speculation
It depended on selling alcohol
Women's votes raised taxes
Radio and film cost too much
us-depression.why: The boom rested on borrowed money and speculation, and much of the wealth went to the few.

us-depression.q: Why did a downturn turn into a collapse?
a: Congress banned banks
The Dust Bowl destroyed the factories
Bank panics and a shrinking money supply
Roosevelt raised taxes in 1929
us-depression.why: Panicked savers pulled money from banks and the Federal Reserve let the money supply shrink; tariffs and the gold standard spread the slump worldwide.

us-depression.q: What did the New Deal change about the federal government's role?
a: It handed the economy to the states
It ended all government spending
It made the banks run the government
It became responsible for the economy and a safety net
us-depression.why: The New Deal made the federal government responsible for the economy and for a basic safety net, a role it has kept.

us-depression.q: Which New Deal measures still shape American life?
a: Prohibition and the gold standard
Social Security, insured deposits and the right to join a union
The Dust Bowl farm camps
Tariffs that blocked world trade
us-depression.why: Social Security, insured bank deposits and the right to join a union all came from the New Deal and still shape American life.

us-superpower.q: What role did the US take on after 1945?
a: It retreated into isolation as after 1918
It handed world leadership to Britain
It stayed engaged, leading alliances against the Soviet Union
It joined the Soviet Union in a single bloc
us-superpower.why: Unlike after 1918, the US stayed engaged: it rebuilt Western Europe, formed NATO in 1949 and signed treaties reaching across the Pacific.

us-superpower.q: Why was the US so powerful at the end of the Second World War?
a: Its homeland was untouched and its economy was booming
It had conquered most of Europe
It was the only country with an army
It had taken over Japan's empire before the war
us-superpower.why: The war left the US the only great power with its homeland untouched, producing about half the world's manufactured goods.

us-superpower.q: Why did the US–Soviet rivalry stay a 'cold' war?
a: The two countries were never rivals
The United Nations forbade any fighting
They shared a border in Alaska
Nuclear weapons on both sides deterred direct war
us-superpower.why: Nuclear weapons on both sides kept the rivalry cold, fought instead through arms races and proxy wars such as Korea and Vietnam.

us-superpower.q: How did the Vietnam War affect Americans at home?
a: It united the country behind the government
It divided the country and shook trust in government
It ended the Cold War
It created the suburbs and highways
us-superpower.why: About 58,000 Americans died in Vietnam, and the war divided the country and shook trust in government.

us-superpower.q: What part of the post-war order built by the US still largely stands?
a: The Soviet bloc in Eastern Europe
The camps for Japanese Americans
The UN, NATO and the dollar at the centre of finance
American rule over Japan
us-superpower.why: The United Nations, NATO, the dollar's central role and alliances with Japan and South Korea still largely shape the world order.

us-civilrights.q: What did the civil rights movement achieve by 1965?
a: An end to legal segregation and protection for voting
A separate Black state in the South
Reparations paid to every Black family
The end of the Great Migration
us-civilrights.why: Brown v. Board, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended legal segregation and protected Black voting.

us-civilrights.q: Why did Black veterans of the Second World War push for change?
a: The army promised them land in the South
They wanted to rejoin the army
Having fought fascism abroad, they rejected second-class citizenship
They had been paid less than other soldiers
us-civilrights.why: Black veterans who had fought fascism abroad refused to accept second-class citizenship at home.

us-civilrights.q: How did television help push Congress to act?
a: It ran adverts paid for by the government
It hid the protests from Northern viewers
It let King speak to Congress directly
It brought violence against marchers into living rooms
us-civilrights.why: Televised violence against marchers, from Birmingham to Selma, brought the brutality of segregation's defenders into living rooms and pushed Congress to pass new laws.

us-civilrights.q: What happened to Black voter registration after the Voting Rights Act?
a: It fell as poll taxes rose
It soared, from about 7% to 60% in Mississippi
It stayed the same for decades
It rose only in Northern cities
us-civilrights.why: In Mississippi, Black registration rose from about 7% to about 60% within two years, and thousands of Black officials were elected.

us-civilrights.q: How does the civil rights movement connect to the present?
a: All gaps in wealth and schooling have closed
Its laws were repealed in 2008
Segregation laws returned in the 1970s
It inspired other movements, while debates over race continue
us-civilrights.why: It inspired campaigns for women, Latinos and Native Americans, but gaps in wealth, housing and schooling persist and debates over race, policing and voting continue.

us-today.q: Which event drew the US into long wars in the 2000s?
a: The 2008 financial crisis
The 11 September 2001 attacks
The COVID-19 pandemic
The collapse of the Soviet Union
us-today.why: After al-Qaeda killed nearly 3,000 people on 11 September 2001, the US invaded Afghanistan and later Iraq, staying in both for years.

a: War spending in Iraq
A fall in oil production
Risky mortgage lending and loosely regulated finance
The loss of House seats in New York
us-today.why: Risky mortgage lending and loosely regulated finance caused a housing crash and the worst financial crisis since the 1930s.

us-today.q: Which factors do political scientists link to growing political division?
a: City–rural, education and regional gaps, plus partisan media
A single dispute over the Electoral College
The end of immigration after 2001
The move of the capital to the South
us-today.why: Political scientists link growing division to differences between cities and rural areas, education levels and regions, and to partisan media and the internet.

us-today.q: What does population movement to the South and West change?
a: The number of states in the Union
The size of the Senate
Which party wins every election
How House seats and electoral votes are shared out
us-today.why: The census reshares the 435 House seats every ten years; after 2020 Texas and Florida gained seats while states such as New York and California lost one.

us-today.q: Which describes the United States' position in the world today?
a: The largest economy and strongest military, facing a rising China
A minor power that withdrew from world affairs
The world's second economy after the European Union
A country dependent on imported oil
us-today.why: The US has about a quarter of world output and the strongest military, and shale drilling made it the top oil producer, but it faces a rising China.

cn-origins.q: What do Shang oracle bones from Anyang show?
a: The first Chinese coins
The earliest known Chinese writing
Maps of the Yellow River
Laws of the First Emperor
cn-origins.why: Shang kings carved questions to their ancestors on oracle bones, the earliest known Chinese writing and ancestor of the characters used today.

cn-origins.q: Why did dense populations and strong rulers appear early on the North China Plain?
a: Rice grew there without any rain
Nomads brought farming from the steppe
Soft, fertile loess was easy to farm with simple tools
Bronze tools were found in the soil
cn-origins.why: The soft, fertile loess was easy to farm with simple tools, so dense populations and strong rulers appeared early there.

cn-origins.q: How did the Zhou justify overthrowing the Shang?
a: By claiming descent from the Shang kings
By winning a vote of the great lords
By pointing to their bronze weapons
With the Mandate of Heaven
cn-origins.why: The Mandate of Heaven held that Heaven gave power to a virtuous ruler and took it from a corrupt one.

cn-origins.q: What did the long chaos of the Warring States produce?
a: China's great schools of thought, including Confucianism
A lasting peace under the Zhou kings
The first Silk Road trade with Rome
The Grand Canal
cn-origins.why: Amid the wars, Confucius taught duty and moral example, Daoists sought harmony with nature, and Legalists argued for strict laws, the creed Qin would use.

cn-origins.q: What links Shang writing to China today?
a: It was replaced by an alphabet under the Zhou
It is the direct ancestor of today's Chinese characters
It is used only by Buddhist monks
It survives only in Korea
cn-origins.why: The Shang script is the direct ancestor of today's characters, making Chinese one of the world's oldest continuously written languages.

cn-qin.q: What did the Qin achieve in 221 BC?
a: They overthrew the Shang dynasty
They opened the Silk Road
They unified China under a First Emperor
They founded the Han dynasty
cn-qin.why: Qin destroyed its six rival states one by one, and King Zheng declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.

cn-qin.q: Why could Qin field such huge, disciplined armies?
a: Shang Yang's Legalist reforms rewarded results, not birth
It hired nomad horsemen from the Xiongnu
Its nobles paid for private armies
It bought weapons from the other states
cn-qin.why: From the 350s BC Shang Yang rewarded farmers and soldiers for results, not birth, and imposed harsh laws, creating a disciplined war state.

cn-qin.q: Why did the Qin dynasty fall so quickly after 210 BC?
a: The Xiongnu conquered its capital
The Han dynasty invaded from the south
Its officials refused to use the common script
Severe laws and forced labour turned people against it
cn-qin.why: The same severity, with forced labour on vast projects, turned people against the dynasty once the First Emperor died, and revolts brought it down in 206 BC.

cn-qin.q: Why did Qin's common script matter so much?
a: It let speakers of different languages read the same texts
It replaced Chinese with a new alphabet
It was used only for coins
It was banned by later dynasties
cn-qin.why: A single script let people who spoke very different languages read the same texts, which helped hold China together.

cn-qin.q: What lasting pattern did Qin set for later Chinese states?
a: Rule by hereditary lords in noble domains
An emperor ruling through a salaried bureaucracy
Division into rival kingdoms as the norm
Government by elected assemblies
cn-qin.why: Later dynasties condemned Qin's cruelty but kept its system of one emperor ruling through appointed officials, and unity became the norm.

cn-hantang.q: What did the Han and Tang dynasties have in common?
a: Both ruled only south of the Yangtze
Both ended Confucian learning
Both built large empires reaching into Central Asia
Both ruled from Beijing
cn-hantang.why: Emperor Wu of the Han pushed west and opened the Silk Road, and the Tang ruled from Chang'an out into Central Asia.

cn-hantang.q: How did the Han change the system they inherited from Qin?
a: They kept it but softened it with Confucian ideals
They abolished it and restored noble domains
They replaced officials with army generals
They split China into rival states
cn-hantang.why: The Han kept Qin's centralised machinery but trained officials in the Confucian classics, which gave the state legitimacy and continuity.

cn-hantang.q: Why did both the Han and the Tang break down?
a: Buddhism turned people against the emperors
The Silk Road stopped bringing trade
The Grand Canal flooded the capital
Great families and generals gathered power and peasants rebelled
cn-hantang.why: In both, great families and generals gathered land and armies, peasants rebelled, and the court lost control of the provinces, as in the An Lushan rebellion.

cn-hantang.q: Which system for choosing officials began under the Sui and Tang?
a: Inheritance of office by noble families
Civil service exams that chose officials partly by merit
Election by local assemblies
Appointment by Buddhist monasteries
cn-hantang.why: From the Sui and Tang, civil service exams began choosing officials partly by merit, a system that lasted until 1905.

cn-hantang.q: How does the Han dynasty still shape Chinese identity today?
a: Chinese characters are called Han script only in Japan
The Great Wall is named after it
Most Chinese still call themselves Han people
China's capital is still Chang'an
cn-hantang.why: The Han gave the Chinese majority its name: most Chinese still call themselves Han people.

cn-songming.q: What kind of society did the Song build?
a: A rich, urban society run by exam-chosen scholar-officials
A nomadic empire ruled by cavalry generals
A feudal state of hereditary lords
A small kingdom closed to trade
cn-songming.why: The Song built a rich, urban society run by scholar-officials chosen by exam, with printed books, paper money, gunpowder weapons and the compass.

cn-songming.q: What let the Song population pass 100 million?
a: Grain imported from Mongolia
Fast-ripening rice and draining the Yangtze delta
Conquest of Central Asia
Ending the exam system
cn-songming.why: Fast-ripening rice and the draining of the Yangtze delta fed a population of over 100 million, along with trade and cities.

cn-songming.q: Why did the Ming stop Zheng He's voyages?
a: European fleets had defeated them
The ships could not reach Africa
The real danger, the Mongols, lay on the northern frontier
The emperor had converted to Buddhism
cn-songming.why: The voyages were costly, and the real threat was the Mongols in the north, so the Ming turned to defence, building most of the brick Great Wall.

cn-songming.q: What did Song inventions such as gunpowder and the compass go on to do?
a: They were forgotten after the Mongol conquest
They stayed secret inside China
They were invented again in Japan
They spread west and helped transform Europe
cn-songming.why: Song inventions such as gunpowder and the compass spread west and later helped transform Europe.

cn-songming.q: What question do historians ask about the Ming retreat from the oceans?
a: Why the Mongols never built ships
Why Europe, not China, built global empires
Why Beijing replaced Nanjing as capital
Why the Song lost Kaifeng
cn-songming.why: The Ming left the seas to European ships, a contrast many historians use to ask why Europe, not China, built global empires.

cn-qing.q: How did the Manchu Qing dynasty come to rule China in 1644?
a: They won the throne through a royal marriage
They seized Beijing after rebels had toppled the Ming
The Ming emperor invited them to share power
They arrived by sea and took the southern ports first
cn-qing.why: Rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing and the last Ming emperor died; a Ming general then opened the Shanhai Pass, and the Manchus seized the capital.

cn-qing.q: Why was the Ming dynasty open to conquest by a small Manchu army?
a: A Russian invasion had destroyed its northern armies
Japanese pirates had cut off its trade
Factional politics, bankruptcy, famine and peasant revolts had ruined it
Its emperors had moved the capital to Taiwan
cn-qing.why: The Ming collapsed from within, which let a well-organised Manchu army, allied with Mongols and Han defectors, take power.

cn-qing.q: How did the Qing rule the Inner Asian lands differently from the old provinces?
a: As khans and patrons of Tibetan Buddhism, through local nobles and lamas
Through Chinese officials chosen by the civil exams
By selling them to Russia as trading colonies
By banning all local religion and nobility
cn-qing.why: The old provinces were run by Confucian officials and the exams, while Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang were ruled through nobles, lamas and military governors.

cn-qing.q: What did Qing conquests under Kangxi and Qianlong change?
a: China lost its western provinces to the Dzungars
China became a small coastal trading state
The Ming were restored in the south
The empire roughly doubled, taking in Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang
cn-qing.why: Long wars drew the Qing into Central Asia: they absorbed Mongolia, sent troops to Lhasa in 1720 and conquered Xinjiang in 1755–59.

cn-qing.q: Why do the Qing's borders still matter in China today?
a: They were all given up in the 1911 revolution
Today's China inherits most of them, and Beijing cites this for its claims
They only matter to historians of Russia
They match exactly the borders of the Ming
cn-qing.why: Modern China inherits most Qing borders, including Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan; Tibetan and Uyghur exile groups argue the Qing tie was imperial overlordship, not union.

cn-humiliation.q: What happened to Qing China between the Opium Wars and 1911?
a: It conquered Japan and Korea
It closed itself off and avoided all foreign contact
Foreign powers defeated it repeatedly, and huge rebellions shook it
It became a British colony ruled from Hong Kong
cn-humiliation.why: Wars with Britain, France and Japan forced 'unequal treaties' on China, while the Taiping Rebellion alone cost an estimated 20–30 million lives.

cn-humiliation.q: Why did Britain go to war with China in 1839?
a: The Qing seized and destroyed British opium at Canton
China had invaded British India
China refused to sell Britain any tea
The Boxers had attacked the British legation
cn-humiliation.why: Britain bought vast amounts of tea but had little China wanted, so its merchants smuggled in Indian opium; the Qing ban turned into a war over trade.

cn-humiliation.q: Why did the Self-Strengthening reforms fail to save the Qing?
a: They abolished the army entirely
They handed control of the economy to Japan
They were never attempted
They bought arsenals and ships but left the old system intact
cn-humiliation.why: Modern weapons were bought, but the old system stayed, and conservatives around the Empress Dowager Cixi crushed deeper reform in 1898.

a: British rule in Hong Kong
More than 2,000 years of imperial rule in China
The Taiping Rebellion
Japan's rule over Taiwan
cn-humiliation.why: The Wuchang uprising began a revolution that toppled the Qing in 1911–12, ending China's long line of emperors.

cn-humiliation.q: How does the 'century of humiliation' still matter in China today?
a: It is rarely mentioned by China's leaders
It led China to return Taiwan to Japan
Beijing still invokes it over Taiwan, foreign criticism and national 'rejuvenation'
It ended all disputes over Hong Kong in 1842
cn-humiliation.why: Memories of invasion and lost territory became central to Chinese nationalism, and both Nationalists and Communists promised to end the humiliation.

cn-republic.q: What happened to China between the 1911 revolution and 1949?
a: The Qing were restored and ruled in peace
It split among warlords, was invaded by Japan, and the Communists won a civil war
It became a stable democracy under Sun Yat-sen
It was divided between Britain and France
cn-republic.why: Power passed to Yuan Shikai, then warlords; Chiang's Nationalists reunified much of China, Japan invaded in 1937, and the Communists won in 1949.

cn-republic.q: What sparked the May Fourth protests of 1919?
a: The Versailles treaty gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan
The founding of the Communist Party
Japan's seizure of Manchuria
The Nationalists' move to Taiwan
cn-republic.why: Students were outraged that the Versailles settlement handed Shandong to Japan, and the protests spread nationalist and radical ideas.

cn-republic.q: Why did the Communists, not the Nationalists, win the civil war?
a: The Nationalists refused to fight Japan
The United States backed the Communists
War, corruption and inflation wore down Chiang, while Communists won peasants with land reform
The Communists held all the big cities from 1921
cn-republic.why: Eight years of war exhausted the Nationalists, while the Communists built a disciplined army and won peasant support with land reform where they ruled.

cn-republic.q: What did the war with Japan do to the balance of power in China?
a: It destroyed the Communist forces completely
It made the Nationalists far stronger
It ended the civil war for good
It exhausted the Nationalists while Communist forces grew to around a million
cn-republic.why: The war killed an estimated 14 to 20 million Chinese; Communist forces grew from tens of thousands to around a million.

cn-republic.q: Which present-day division goes back to the Communist victory of 1949?
a: The split between China and Taiwan across the Strait
The border between China and India
The division of Korea
Hong Kong's separate legal system
cn-republic.why: The Republic of China survived only on Taiwan, which it had taken over from Japan in 1945, creating the cross-Strait division that persists today.

cn-mao.q: What did Mao proclaim in Beijing on 1 October 1949?
a: The return of the Qing emperor
A union with the Soviet Union
The People's Republic of China
The Republic of China on Taiwan
cn-mao.why: Mao founded the People's Republic, while Chiang's Republic of China moved to Taiwan; each claimed to be the only legitimate China.

cn-mao.q: Why did the Great Leap Forward cause a famine?
a: A foreign blockade cut off grain imports
Impossible targets led to inflated harvest reports, and the state took grain anyway
Peasants refused to join communes
Floods destroyed every province's crops
cn-mao.why: Officials who doubted the targets were purged, so harvests were overstated and grain was taken from starving villages; estimates of the dead run from 15 to over 40 million.

cn-mao.q: Why did Mao launch the Cultural Revolution in 1966?
a: To end the war in Korea
To prepare China for market reform
To welcome back the Nationalists
He feared the Party was turning bureaucratic and wanted to crush rivals
cn-mao.why: After the Leap's failure, Mao turned Red Guards against teachers, officials and Party rivals he called 'revisionist'.

cn-mao.q: How did China's foreign relations change by the early 1970s?
a: It split from the Soviet Union and turned to the United States
It joined the Soviet Union as a member republic
It cut all ties with the outside world
It handed its UN seat to Taiwan
cn-mao.why: After the split with Moscow around 1960, Beijing took China's UN seat in 1971, and Nixon visited in 1972.

cn-mao.q: Which legacy of the Mao years in Tibet continues today?
a: Tibet's own army still governs Lhasa
Tibet became an independent state in 1959
The Dalai Lama's government in exile in India
The Seventeen Point Agreement is still accepted by both sides
cn-mao.why: After a failed uprising in 1959 the Dalai Lama fled to India, where he set up a government in exile that continues today.

cn-reform.q: What did Deng Xiaoping's reforms change, starting from 1978?
a: They restored collective communes everywhere
They let farmers work their own plots and opened China to foreign investment
They ended Communist Party rule
They closed China's coastal cities to trade
cn-reform.why: Families could sell crops beyond a quota, and special economic zones such as Shenzhen drew foreign capital; output soared.

cn-reform.q: Why was Deng willing to try markets and foreign capital?
a: The Soviet Union demanded it
Taiwan offered to pay for it
Mao's campaigns had left China poor while its neighbours grew rich
China had already become the world's richest country
cn-reform.why: Deng judged that the Party's survival depended on raising living standards, 'crossing the river by feeling for the stones'.

cn-reform.q: What helped fuel the Tiananmen protests of spring 1989?
a: Inflation and corruption brought by reform
A ban on all foreign trade
Japan's invasion of the north
The return of Hong Kong
cn-reform.why: Students and workers called for reform; Party leaders saw a threat to their rule, declared martial law, and the army cleared central Beijing on 3–4 June.

cn-reform.q: What did three decades of reform mean for China's people?
a: A shift to a multiparty democracy
Falling living standards
A return to Maoist campaigns
About 10% growth a year, with hundreds of millions leaving poverty
cn-reform.why: The economy grew roughly 10% a year for three decades and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, while political control stayed firm.

cn-reform.q: On what terms did Hong Kong and Macao return to China?
a: Full integration into the mainland's system at once
'One country, two systems', keeping their own systems for 50 years
As independent states in a loose union
Under joint British and Portuguese rule
cn-reform.why: Hong Kong returned in 1997 and Macao in 1999 as special administrative regions, promised their own systems for 50 years.

cn-today.q: How did China's place in the world change after it joined the WTO in 2001?
a: It became the world's factory and passed Japan as the second-largest economy
It left world trade to focus on farming
It overtook the United States as the largest economy by 2005
It handed its factories to foreign governments
cn-today.why: Cheap labour, infrastructure spending, foreign investment and open markets drove growth; China passed Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.

cn-today.q: Why did Xi Jinping centralise power after 2012?
a: To prepare for multiparty elections
To hand power to the provinces
He argued corruption, factions and Western ideas threatened the Party
To end the Belt and Road Initiative
cn-today.why: Xi said he was restoring the Party's authority and pursuing 'national rejuvenation'; presidential term limits were removed in 2018.

cn-today.q: What is one long-term cause of China's shrinking workforce?
a: Mass emigration to India
Zero-Covid controls lasting into the 2030s
A ban on factory work
Decades of the one-child policy
cn-today.why: The one-child policy, replaced by a two-child limit only in 2016, left fewer young people; China's population began to fall in 2022.

cn-today.q: What did Beijing's 2020 national security law change in Hong Kong?
a: It returned Hong Kong to British rule
Critics say it ended many freedoms; Beijing says it restored stability
It made Hong Kong independent
It abolished Hong Kong's own currency
cn-today.why: After mass protests in 2019, Beijing imposed the law; the two sides describe its effect very differently.

cn-today.q: What rivalry now shapes much of world politics, according to this chapter?
a: China and Japan over the Olympics
China and India over population
China and Russia over Xinjiang
China and the United States over trade, technology and Taiwan
cn-today.why: Beijing treats Taiwan and the South China Sea as matters of sovereignty, while Taiwan, neighbours and the United States see growing military pressure.

ca-first.q: What was the land that became Canada like before Europeans arrived?
a: Almost empty until the Norse settled it
Home to hundreds of distinct nations with different ways of life
Ruled by a single Inuit empire
Settled only along the Pacific coast
ca-first.why: People lived there for at least 12,000 years and built hundreds of nations, from Arctic hunters to Great Lakes farmers and Pacific fishing towns.

ca-first.q: What mainly shaped each nation's way of life?
a: Rules set by European traders
Orders from the Haudenosaunee Confederacy
The land: farming where crops grew, moving with the seasons where they did not
The arrival of horses from Asia
