ca-first.why: Where crops could grow people farmed and settled; elsewhere they followed caribou, bison, fish and seals through the seasons.

ca-first.q: What made large towns of cedar plank houses possible on the Pacific coast?
a: Rich salmon runs
Corn, beans and squash
Bison hunting on horseback
Trade with the Norse
ca-first.why: Salmon fed nations such as the Haida and Coast Salish, known for cedar plank houses, totem poles and potlatch feasts.

ca-first.q: What happened to Indigenous populations after Europeans arrived from the 1500s?
a: They grew rapidly thanks to new crops
They moved to Greenland
They were unaffected for centuries
Diseases brought by newcomers killed many, and numbers fell sharply
ca-first.why: From an estimated 500,000 or more, the population fell sharply, yet these nations endured.

ca-first.q: How do these first nations still shape Canada today?
a: Through treaties and land rights, and names such as Canada and Ottawa
Only through museum collections
Through laws written by the Norse
They do not; their nations disappeared by 1800
ca-first.why: Treaties and land rights still shape Canada, about 1.8 million people identified as Indigenous in 2021, and many place names come from their languages.

ca-newfrance.q: What was New France built on?
a: Gold mines along the St Lawrence
Large slave plantations
The fur trade, with First Nations as partners and allies
Cod fishing alone
ca-newfrance.why: From Champlain's founding of Quebec City in 1608, France's colony depended on furs and on alliances with the Wendat, Algonquin and Innu.

ca-newfrance.q: Why did the fur trade depend on alliances with First Nations?
a: France had banned its colonists from hunting
First Nations controlled the animals, the routes and the know-how
First Nations owned the ships to Europe
The Hudson's Bay Company required it
ca-newfrance.why: Europe's craze for beaver-felt hats made furs valuable, and only First Nations had the animals, the routes and the skills.

ca-newfrance.q: Why did New France stay small compared with the British colonies?
a: France sent few settlers
Disease killed all the filles du roi
Britain banned French ships from the Atlantic
The Great Peace of Montreal forbade new settlers
ca-newfrance.why: By 1760 about 60,000–70,000 Canadiens faced more than a million people in the British colonies to the south.

ca-newfrance.q: What happened to the Acadians from 1755?
a: They won independence from France
They founded Quebec City
They moved north to Hudson Bay
Britain deported about 10,000 of them
ca-newfrance.why: After France lost Acadia in 1713, Britain began deporting the Acadians in 1755, scattering them as far as Louisiana.

ca-newfrance.q: What lasting legacy did New France leave in Canada?
a: English as the language of Quebec
A French-speaking Catholic society that survives as today's Quebec
The end of all First Nations treaties
French rule over Newfoundland
ca-newfrance.why: It also left Acadian communities, the Métis peoples born of the fur trade, and a pattern of alliances and treaties with First Nations.

ca-british.q: What changed for Canada between 1759 and 1763?
a: It became independent
France won back Acadia
Britain conquered New France and France gave up Canada
The United States annexed Quebec
ca-british.why: Wolfe's victory on the Plains of Abraham took Quebec, Montreal fell in 1760, and the 1763 Treaty of Paris handed New France to Britain.

ca-british.q: Why did Britain pass the Quebec Act of 1774?
a: To keep some 70,000 French Catholics loyal as the thirteen colonies grew restless
To force the Canadiens to become Protestant
To punish Quebec for joining the American Revolution
To give Quebec to the Loyalists
ca-british.why: Britain chose tolerance over assimilation, letting the Canadiens keep their Catholic faith and French civil law.

ca-british.q: Why did Britain split the colony into Upper and Lower Canada in 1791?
a: France demanded it in a treaty
To separate fur traders from farmers
To end the War of 1812
Loyalist arrivals created an English-speaking colony that wanted its own laws
ca-british.why: About 40,000 Loyalists fled north after the American Revolution; Upper Canada got English law and an elected assembly.

ca-british.q: What did beating back the American invasions of 1812–14 do for the colonies?
a: It doubled their territory
It gave them a sense of identity apart from the United States
It ended British rule
It won large lands for First Nations allies
ca-british.why: The peace left the border unchanged, but the victory helped the colonies see themselves as distinct; First Nations allies, though, gained little.

ca-british.q: Which British decision of this era still underlies Indigenous treaties today?
a: The 1763 Royal Proclamation: only the Crown could buy Indigenous land, by agreement
The 1791 Constitutional Act
The 1814 peace with the United States
The capture of Quebec in 1759
ca-british.why: The Royal Proclamation became the basis for later treaties, just as the Quebec Act's French civil law still shapes Quebec.

a: Canada won independence after a war with Britain
Four colonies were joined as the Dominion of Canada
Newfoundland joined Canada
Canada bought Rupert's Land
ca-confed.why: The British North America Act joined Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, with John A. Macdonald as prime minister.

ca-confed.q: How did federation offer a way out of the Province of Canada's deadlock?
a: It abolished the French language
It gave Britain direct rule again
Quebec ran its own schools and civil law, while Ontario got seats by population
It merged Ontario and Quebec into one province
ca-confed.why: Each province had its own legislature for local affairs, which let English- and French-speaking halves each get what they most wanted.

ca-confed.q: What outside pressure pushed the colonies to unite?
a: Fear of the United States during and after its Civil War
A French plan to retake Quebec
A Russian claim to British Columbia
Britain's demand for more soldiers in Europe
ca-confed.why: The US Civil War, Fenian raids and American talk of expansion frightened the colonies, and Britain wanted them to pay for their own defence.

ca-confed.q: How did Canada change in the decades after 1867?
a: It shrank as Nova Scotia left
It stayed limited to the St Lawrence valley
It handed the West back to the Hudson's Bay Company
It grew to span three oceans
ca-confed.why: Canada took over Rupert's Land in 1870, gained British Columbia and PEI, the Arctic islands in 1880, and later Newfoundland and Nunavut.

ca-confed.q: Which tension built into Confederation is still argued over today?
a: The balance of power between Ottawa and the provinces, especially Quebec
Whether Canada should rejoin France
Whether Alaska belongs to Canada
The location of the capital
ca-confed.why: Canada became a federation with strong provinces, and the balance between Ottawa and Quebec is still debated.

ca-west.q: What happened when Canada took over the West after buying Rupert's Land?
a: The land was empty and settled peacefully
The Métis resisted twice, and the Crown signed treaties with First Nations
The United States took the Prairies
First Nations were given full control of the railway
ca-west.why: The Red River Resistance created Manitoba in 1870, the numbered treaties followed in 1871–77, and the 1885 North-West Resistance was defeated at Batoche.

ca-west.q: Why did Ottawa push to settle the West and build the railway?
a: To hold the West before Americans moved in, and keep BC's railway promise
To return Rupert's Land to Britain
To create a homeland for the Métis
Because First Nations had asked for settlers
ca-west.why: Canada wanted the Prairies farmed by settlers and loyal to Canada, and it had promised British Columbia a railway to the Pacific.

ca-west.q: Why did starving Plains nations sign the numbered treaties?
a: They wanted to move to the cities
Britain ordered them to
The bison had collapsed and they signed for survival
They had been paid in railway shares
ca-west.why: As the bison vanished, hunger spread; officials withheld rations to push people onto reserves, and many nations saw the treaties as sharing the land, not selling it.

ca-west.q: What did the railway and settlement bring for First Nations?
a: Full voting rights and new hunting grounds
Ownership of the railway's lands
Return of the bison herds
Reserves, the Indian Act, a pass system and residential schools
ca-west.why: The railway opened the Prairies to settlers from about 1896 but tightened federal control over First Nations' lives.

ca-west.q: How is Louis Riel remembered today?
a: As a traitor by all Canadians
As the man who built the railway
Many honour him as a founder of Manitoba
As an American general
ca-west.why: Riel's hanging in 1885 set French Quebec against English Ontario for generations; today many honour him as Manitoba's founder.

ca-wars.q: How did Canada's entry into the two world wars differ?
a: It stayed neutral in both
In 1914 it was at war automatically; in 1939 it declared war on its own
It joined the 1914 war only in 1917
It declared war before Britain both times
ca-wars.why: As part of the British Empire, Canada was at war in 1914; in 1939 it made its own declaration, a week after Britain.

ca-wars.q: Why did many Canadians support going to war in 1914?
a: Germany had invaded Canada
France paid Canada to fight
Quebec demanded it
Many, mostly of British descent, felt loyal to the Empire
ca-wars.why: Canada fought because Britain did, and many Canadians felt strong ties to the Empire.

ca-wars.q: Why did conscription split Canada in both wars?
a: Most English Canadians wanted shared burdens; most French Canadians saw Britain's wars
Western provinces refused to send troops
Only Quebec wanted conscription
The army refused to take conscripts
ca-wars.why: In 1942 over 70% of Quebec voters said no to releasing the government from its promise, while about two in three Canadians said yes.

ca-wars.q: What did Canada gain from its wartime role?
a: New territory in Europe
Control of Hong Kong
Its own signature on the Treaty of Versailles and, in time, full self-government
A seat in the British Parliament
ca-wars.why: Canada signed Versailles separately, and the 1931 Statute of Westminster made it fully self-governing; after 1945 it helped found NATO and the UN.

ca-wars.q: Which wartime episode still shapes Canada's ties with the Netherlands?
a: The Dieppe raid
Canadians freeing much of the Netherlands in 1944–45
The battle of Ypres
The Halifax explosion
ca-wars.why: More than 7,600 Canadians died freeing the Netherlands, and the Dutch still send tulips to Ottawa each year.

ca-quebec.q: What was the Quiet Revolution that began in Quebec in 1960?
a: An armed uprising against Ottawa
A Catholic revival led by the bishops
Quebec's government took over schools, hospitals and welfare and built a modern state
Quebec's vote to leave Canada
ca-quebec.why: Jean Lesage's Liberals took these from the Catholic Church and nationalised electricity under the slogan 'Maîtres chez nous'.

ca-quebec.q: Why did many French-speaking Quebecers want change by 1960?
a: They were a majority at home but often poorer than the English-speaking minority
They were a minority in Quebec
France had cut off trade with Quebec
Ottawa had banned French in schools
ca-quebec.why: An English-speaking minority ran much of business; rising education and a new middle class wanted a modern state that worked in French.

ca-quebec.q: What happened in the two referendums on Quebec sovereignty?
a: Yes won both narrowly
Yes won in 1980 but lost in 1995
No won in 1980 but Yes won in 1995
No won both, about 60% in 1980 and just 50.6% in 1995
ca-quebec.why: The Parti Québécois held both votes; the 1995 result, 50.6% to 49.4%, was extremely close.

a: It made Quebec officially bilingual
It made French the language of work and public life
It ended the Parti Québécois
It brought the constitution home from Britain
ca-quebec.why: The Charter of the French Language made French the common public language, including for signs and, for most immigrants' children, school.

ca-quebec.q: What remains unsettled from the constitutional fights of this era?
a: Whether Canada should have a Charter of Rights
Whether Quebec has a legislature
Quebec has never formally endorsed the 1982 constitution
Whether federal institutions are bilingual
ca-quebec.why: Quebec's government refused to sign in 1982, and the Meech Lake and Charlottetown accords, meant to win its consent, both failed.

ca-rights.q: What changed for Indigenous rights in Canada from 1969 onwards?
a: Ottawa abolished Indian status as planned
Courts, the constitution and new treaties began recognising Aboriginal and treaty rights
All residential schools were opened
Land claims were ended by law
ca-rights.why: The Calder decision of 1973, the first modern treaty in 1975 and the 1982 Constitution all recognised rights that had long been denied.

ca-rights.q: What did residential schools aim to do?
a: Strip Indigenous children of their languages and cultures
Teach Indigenous languages
Train children to run their own nations
Prepare children for the fur trade
ca-rights.why: From the 1880s more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were taken from their families, and thousands died.

ca-rights.q: Why did First Nations leaders reject the federal White Paper of 1969?
a: It gave them too much land
It created Nunavut too early
It came from Quebec's government
They saw abolishing Indian status as assimilation
ca-rights.why: The proposal was withdrawn, and First Nations organisations grew stronger in fighting it.

ca-rights.q: What did the Truth and Reconciliation Commission conclude in 2015?
a: That the schools had mostly helped families
That no further action was needed
That the policy behind the schools was cultural genocide
That the churches had no part in the schools
ca-rights.why: The TRC called the system cultural genocide and issued 94 Calls to Action.

ca-rights.q: Which issue remains unresolved, especially in British Columbia?
a: Land rights, since most of the province was never ceded by treaty
Whether Nunavut should exist
Whether the 1982 Constitution mentions treaty rights
Whether residential schools still operate
ca-rights.why: Only a few historic treaties were signed there, and modern treaties, beginning with the Nisga'a in 2000, cover only a few nations.

ca-today.q: What has driven Canada's fast population growth this century?
a: High birth rates
Immigration, rising steeply
Annexation of new territory
People moving back from the United States
ca-today.why: By 2021 almost one in four Canadians had been born abroad, the highest share in the G7, more and more of them in Asia.

ca-today.q: Why have leaders of every party looked to immigrants?
a: An ageing population and low birth rates leave jobs and pensions to fill
To populate the Arctic territories
Because the United States required it
To replace French speakers in Quebec
ca-today.why: Canada's vast land and ageing population mean it needs workers, and its policy chooses many immigrants by skill.

ca-today.q: Why do American decisions weigh so heavily on Canada?
a: The United States appoints Canada's prime minister
Canada uses the US dollar
Over two-thirds of exports go to the US, and most Canadians live near the border
Canada has no other trading partners
ca-today.why: In 2025 US tariffs and President Trump's talk of annexation set off a wave of Canadian patriotism.

ca-today.q: What did Ottawa do from 2024 as housing costs soared?
a: Banned all new housing
Doubled immigration targets
Moved the capital to Toronto
Cut immigration and temporary residents
ca-today.why: After the population grew by more than a million in 2023, growth slowed to about 0.5% in the year to July 2026.

ca-today.q: Which pressing question does Canada face today, according to this chapter?
a: How to rejoin the British Empire
How to make reconciliation with Indigenous peoples real
How to reverse the 2005 same-sex marriage law
How to leave NATO
ca-today.why: Canada also faces how to house newcomers, depend less on the US, and profit from oil while fighting climate change.

dd-hinduism.q: How did Hinduism come into being?
a: It grew over centuries from Vedic religion, with no single founder
A prophet founded it in a single generation
A king imposed it as a state religion
Missionaries brought it to India from Persia
dd-hinduism.why: Hinduism has no single founder: it grew from the Vedic religion of north-west India, then the Upanishads, the epics and temple worship added to it over centuries.

dd-hinduism.q: Why could Hinduism adapt to so many different rulers and ideas?
a: A single church enforced one creed everywhere
It had no single church or creed and absorbed rather than replaced
Its rulers forbade all other religions
It stayed confined to one small region
dd-hinduism.why: Hinduism wove Vedic ritual, local gods, philosophy and devotion together, and with no single church or creed it could adapt and outlast empires.

dd-hinduism.q: What helped hold together Hindu belief across a vast land of many languages?
a: A single written law code
One shared spoken language
Temples, pilgrimages and festivals, with priests preserving the texts
A permanent all-India empire
dd-hinduism.why: Brahmin priests preserved the sacred texts, while temples, pilgrimages and festivals bound together a vast land with many languages.

dd-hinduism.q: Which ideas, according to the chapter, did Hindu thought help shape in other faiths?
a: Karma, rebirth, yoga and meditation
The Ten Commandments and Shabbat
The Trinity and the sacraments
The Five Pillars and the hajj
dd-hinduism.why: Hindu ideas such as karma, rebirth, yoga and meditation shaped Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism and have since spread worldwide.

dd-hinduism.q: How does caste still matter in India today?
a: It is required by India's constitution
It disappeared completely in 1950
It matters only outside India
It is outlawed as grounds for discrimination but still shapes lives
dd-hinduism.why: India's constitution abolished untouchability in 1950 and reserved places for disadvantaged castes, yet caste still shapes many lives and discrimination persists.

dd-judaism.q: What happened to Judaism after Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70?
a: It died out within a generation
Rabbis rebuilt it around prayer, study and law
It merged with Roman religion
Jews immediately founded a new kingdom
dd-judaism.why: With sacrifice ended, rabbis rebuilt Judaism around the Torah, prayer, study and law kept at home and in the synagogue.

dd-judaism.q: According to many scholars, how did defeat and exile in Babylon affect the Judeans' faith?
a: They abandoned it for Babylonian gods
It sharpened their belief that one God ruled all nations
It made them adopt Persian beliefs
It had no lasting effect
dd-judaism.why: Defeat and exile could have ended the faith; instead, many scholars argue, it sharpened the belief that one God ruled all nations and that history had a purpose.

dd-judaism.q: Why could Judaism survive almost 1,900 years without a state of its own?
a: Roman emperors protected it everywhere
It depended on a single great temple
It centred on a portable book and law kept anywhere
Jews never left the Land of Israel
dd-judaism.why: Centred on the Torah, synagogues that could be built anywhere, and study as worship, Judaism could survive without a temple, a state or a king.

dd-judaism.q: What did the Holocaust do to Europe's Jewish communities?
a: It murdered about two-thirds of Europe's Jews
It moved them peacefully to new homes
It affected only Jews in Germany
It ended antisemitism in Europe
dd-judaism.why: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about 6 million Jews; centuries-old communities in Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine vanished, and Yiddish culture almost disappeared.

dd-judaism.q: Which ideas from Judaism were carried further by Christianity and Islam?
a: Rebirth and karma
Many gods ruling different nations
Worship centred on a living king
A single God who demands justice, and a weekly day of rest
dd-judaism.why: Judaism gave the world the Hebrew Bible, a weekly day of rest and the idea of one God demanding justice; Christianity and Islam both look back to Abraham.

dd-buddhism.q: What do Buddhists believe Siddhartha Gautama achieved at Bodh Gaya?
a: He was crowned emperor of India
He found enlightenment and became the Buddha
He wrote down the Vedas
He founded the city of Pataliputra
dd-buddhism.why: Buddhists believe Siddhartha found enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha, the 'awakened one', then taught for about 45 years.

dd-buddhism.q: Why could the Buddha's teaching appeal to so many people?
a: It was open to anyone, whatever their caste
It was reserved for Brahmin priests
It promised military victory
It required pilgrimage to Mecca
dd-buddhism.why: The Buddha offered a path open to anyone regardless of caste, and his order of monks and nuns, the sangha, spread and preserved the teaching.

dd-buddhism.q: What turning point around 260 BC helped Buddhism spread beyond India?
a: Monks invented printing
Rome adopted Buddhism
The emperor Ashoka turned to it and sent missions abroad
The Silk Road was closed
dd-buddhism.why: After the bloody Kalinga war, Ashoka backed Buddhism, carved its values on rocks and pillars, and sent monks abroad, by tradition his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka.

dd-buddhism.q: Why did Buddhism almost disappear from India after about 1200?
a: Ashoka banned it
Its monks all moved to Japan
Christian missionaries replaced it
Hindu devotion revived, and its royally backed monasteries were sacked
dd-buddhism.why: Buddhism came to depend on royally supported monasteries; as Hindu devotion revived and Turkish armies sacked monasteries around 1200, monks fled to Tibet and Nepal.

dd-buddhism.q: Where is Buddhism mainly practised today?
a: Mostly in Europe
Almost entirely in Asia, though meditation has spread worldwide
Mainly in India, its birthplace
Chiefly in the Middle East
dd-buddhism.why: About 324 million Buddhists live almost all in Asia, from Sri Lanka to Mongolia, while in India Buddhists are under 1%; meditation has spread around the world.

dd-chinafaiths.q: What did Confucius teach would make society orderly?
a: Strict laws and harsh punishments
Virtuous rulers and everyone doing their duty within the family
Withdrawing from society to live in the mountains
Worship of a single creator god
dd-chinafaiths.why: Confucius taught that society would be orderly if rulers were virtuous and everyone did their duty within the family, with filial piety the root of virtue.

dd-chinafaiths.q: What problem were Confucius and the other early Chinese thinkers trying to solve?
a: Invasions from Rome
How to win converts abroad
How to restore peace after the Zhou kingdom collapsed into war
How to end Buddhist influence
dd-chinafaiths.why: These ideas were answers to chaos: the Zhou kingdom had broken into warring states, and the 'Hundred Schools' competed to tell rulers how to restore order.

dd-chinafaiths.q: Why did the Han and later emperors favour Confucianism?
a: It taught loyalty and supplied a trained class of officials
It promised them immortality
It rejected all ritual and hierarchy
It came from a foreign conqueror
dd-chinafaiths.why: Confucianism suited emperors because it taught loyalty and gave them educated officials; from about 605 officials were chosen by exams on the Confucian classics.

dd-chinafaiths.q: How did Confucian ideas shape government beyond China?
a: They were rejected everywhere outside China
They spread only to Europe
They replaced Buddhism in India
Korea and Vietnam copied China's exams on the Confucian classics
dd-chinafaiths.why: Korea's Joseon kings built a strictly Confucian state and Vietnam held similar exams for centuries; Japan used Confucian ethics too, though rank stayed hereditary.

dd-chinafaiths.q: How do these traditions live on in China and East Asia today?
a: They have vanished since the Cultural Revolution
China has revived Confucius, and Daoist ideas like tai chi spread worldwide
Confucianism is now China's only official religion
They survive only in museums
dd-chinafaiths.why: After Mao's attacks, China has revived Confucius as a symbol of national culture since the 1980s, while Daoist ideas from yin and yang to tai chi have spread worldwide.

a: As a Greek philosophy school in Athens
As the official faith of Constantine's army
Among Jewish followers of Jesus, who believed he had risen
As a reform movement within Roman paganism
dd-christianity.why: Christianity began around AD 30 among the Jewish followers of Jesus of Nazareth; believing he had risen, apostles like Paul spread it through Roman cities.

dd-christianity.q: Why did Christianity win converts in crowded Roman cities?
a: It offered forgiveness to anyone, and its churches cared for the needy
It was required by Roman law from the start
It allowed only wealthy citizens to join
It promised military victories over Persia
dd-christianity.why: Christianity offered a personal God, forgiveness and eternal life to anyone, slave or free, and its churches cared for widows, orphans and the sick.

dd-christianity.q: What turned Christianity from a persecuted sect into the faith of rulers?
a: The fall of Jerusalem
The Great Schism of 1054
Luther's 95 Theses
Constantine's backing from 312 and official status in 380
dd-christianity.why: Constantine backed Christianity from 312 and granted freedom of worship in 313; in 380 Theodosius made it Rome's official religion, the faith of rulers and later of empires.

dd-christianity.q: What were Christianity's great splits mainly about, as well as belief?
a: Trade routes and taxes
Authority: the pope's power, and scripture against church tradition
Which language Jesus spoke
Whether to accept non-Jews at all
dd-christianity.why: The 1054 split turned on the pope's authority, and Luther's Reformation on whether scripture outweighed church tradition, dividing Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant.

dd-christianity.q: How has Christianity's centre of gravity shifted in modern times?
a: Back to the Middle East
Towards Western Europe, where attendance is rising
Southwards: sub-Saharan Africa now has more Christians than any other region
It has stayed in Europe as in 1910
dd-christianity.why: In 1910 about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; Europe has grown more secular, while by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had more Christians than any other region.

dd-islam.q: How did Islam begin, according to Muslim belief?
a: Muhammad received revelations from God, recorded in the Quran
A caliph in Baghdad wrote down a new law code
Persian priests reformed their old religion
Ottoman sultans founded it in Constantinople
dd-islam.why: Muslims believe that from about 610 God's revelations came to Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, and were recorded in the Quran.

dd-islam.q: Why could the early Muslim conquests spread so fast?
a: Rome had already converted to Islam
The Byzantine and Persian empires were exhausted by war with each other
Arabia had always been one united kingdom
Europeans invited the caliphs in
dd-islam.why: Islam united Arabia's feuding tribes, and the caliphs' armies struck while the Byzantine and Persian empires were worn out by fighting each other.

dd-islam.q: What first divided Sunni and Shia Muslims?
a: Whether to pray facing Mecca
Whether to keep the five pillars
Different versions of the Quran
A dispute over who should lead Muslims after Muhammad
dd-islam.why: Most accepted Abu Bakr as caliph and became Sunnis; others believed leadership belonged to Muhammad's family through Ali and became the Shia. Both share the Quran and five pillars.

dd-islam.q: How did Islam reach West Africa and Southeast Asia, where most Muslims now live?
a: Mainly through Arab armies conquering them
Through European missionaries
With traders and Sufi mystics along trade routes
Through Mongol invasions
dd-islam.why: Most Muslims live in lands Arab armies never conquered: Islam travelled with merchants across the Sahara and Indian Ocean, and Sufis helped it take root locally.

dd-islam.q: Which legacy of Islamic civilisation still shows in everyday words today?
a: Words like 'algebra' and 'algorithm' from its mathematicians
The Latin alphabet
The seven-day Roman calendar
The Greek Olympic Games
dd-islam.why: Scholars built on Greek, Persian and Indian learning; al-Khwarizmi's book gave us 'algebra' and his name 'algorithm', and Arabic numerals reached Europe through the Islamic world.

dd-mesopotamia.q: What did the Sumerians of southern Iraq first invent writing for?
a: Recording poems and prayers
Keeping temple accounts of goods and rations
Sending letters to Egypt
Carving kings' victories on stone
dd-mesopotamia.why: Writing began at Uruk around 3300 BC as accounting: officials pressed signs into clay to track barley, beer, sheep and workers' rations.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Why did powerful temples and kings grow up in Mesopotamia?
a: Farming needed canals and teamwork, organised labour and stored grain
Mountains protected them from all invaders
The land was rich in stone, timber and metal
Foreign empires appointed them
dd-mesopotamia.why: In a flat, dry land, farming depended on canals and teamwork, so temples and kings that could organise labour, store grain and keep records grew powerful.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Why was Mesopotamia a land of almost constant war?
a: Its people worshipped gods of war only
Rivers made travel impossible
Open plains with no natural borders left cities and empires exposed
Its deserts were full of nomad raiders alone
dd-mesopotamia.why: Open plains with no natural borders meant constant war between cities, and later between empires that tried to control the rivers and trade routes.

dd-mesopotamia.q: What new idea did Hammurabi's code help establish?
a: That all people were equal before the law
That only priests could judge crimes
That laws were secret and unwritten
That a king rules under written law
dd-mesopotamia.why: Hammurabi's laws, carved on a stele around 1750 BC, set punishments, wages and rules for divorce; the idea of a king ruling under written law goes back to Mesopotamia.

dd-mesopotamia.q: Which Mesopotamian legacy do we still use every day?
a: The alphabet we write with
Counting in 60s, giving 60 minutes and 360 degrees
The seven-day weekend
Paper money
dd-mesopotamia.why: Mesopotamians counted in base 60; passed on through Greek astronomers, it still gives us 60 seconds, 60 minutes and 360 degrees in a circle.

dd-egypt.q: What happened in Egypt around 3100 BC?
a: Alexander the Great conquered it
The Great Pyramid was finished
The towns of the Nile valley were united under one king
Rome made it a province
dd-egypt.why: Around 3100 BC the Nile valley's towns were united into one kingdom, beginning about 3,000 years of rule by pharaohs.

dd-egypt.q: Why could Egypt feed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders?
a: The Nile's yearly flood left fertile soil for big grain surpluses
It imported grain from Rome
Rain fell all year in the desert
Its people lived by hunting
dd-egypt.why: The Nile's flood left a strip of black, fertile soil in the desert, so farmers grew large grain surpluses that fed priests, scribes, soldiers and builders.

dd-egypt.q: What helped one king hold the whole country for so long?
a: A huge navy in the Mediterranean
Elected councils in every town
Alliances with the Hittites
The Nile highway, desert barriers, and kings as gods' representatives
dd-egypt.why: The river let one king control the valley, deserts kept most invaders away, and kings ruled as the gods' representatives, keepers of maat, giving the state great authority.

dd-egypt.q: What happened to Egypt's old religion and writing after Roman and Arab rule?
a: They spread across Europe
Christianity and Islam replaced them; hieroglyphs went unread until 1822
They were unchanged until modern times
Romans made hieroglyphs their official script
dd-egypt.why: Christianity, then Islam and Arabic, replaced the old religion and language; the last hieroglyphs were carved in AD 394, and Champollion cracked the script in 1822.

dd-egypt.q: How does ancient Egypt still shape the world today?
a: Its law code is used in modern courts
Its language is spoken across North Africa
Its monuments draw millions of visitors and gave rise to Egyptology
Its calendar is still Egypt's official one
dd-egypt.why: Egypt's monuments still shape how the world imagines the ancient past: its temples and tombs draw millions of visitors and gave rise to the science of Egyptology.

dd-greece.q: What did Athens and Sparta lead the Greek city-states to achieve in 490–479 BC?
a: The conquest of Egypt
Unification into one kingdom
Victory over Rome
Defeat of the Persian invasions
dd-greece.why: The Greeks beat Persia at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 BC, opening Athens' golden age.

dd-greece.q: Why did ancient Greece never form a single kingdom?
a: Mountains and islands split it into many small, independent cities
Persia forbade it
Its people spoke many unrelated languages
Sparta ruled it all directly
dd-greece.why: Greece's mountains and islands divided it into hundreds of fiercely independent city-states that shared a language, Homer's epics and games, but no single ruler.

dd-greece.q: Why did ordinary citizens in Greek cities demand a say in government?
a: Their kings asked them to vote
Egypt taught them democracy
They fought side by side as armoured hoplite infantry
Rome required it
dd-greece.why: Citizens who fought side by side as armoured infantry, the hoplites, demanded a say in government, which helped give rise to Athens' democracy.

dd-greece.q: What did the rivalry between Athens and Sparta finally lead to?
a: A lasting union of all Greeks
War that left the cities weak enough for Macedon and then Rome
Athens conquering Persia
Sparta becoming a democracy
dd-greece.why: Athens lost the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC; weakened by constant wars, the cities fell to Philip II of Macedon in 338 BC and to Rome by 146 BC.

dd-greece.q: Where can Greek influence still be seen today?
a: Only in modern Greece
In democracy, philosophy, theatre, English words and temple-style buildings
Mainly in Chinese government exams
In the Arabic alphabet
dd-greece.why: Greek ideas, from democracy and philosophy to theatre and the Olympics, became a foundation of the West, and buildings like the US Capitol copy Greek temples.

dd-persia.q: What did Cyrus the Great and Darius I build?
a: A Greek alliance of city-states
A Persian empire stretching from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus
The first empire in Mesopotamia
A kingdom confined to southern Iran
dd-persia.why: Cyrus united Medes and Persians in 550 BC and conquered Anatolia, Babylon and Central Asia; under Darius I the empire reached from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus.

dd-persia.q: How did Persian kings hold together such a huge, varied empire?
a: They forced everyone to adopt one religion and language
They deported every conquered people
They left local customs and elites in place in return for tribute
They ruled only from ships
dd-persia.why: Persian kings ruled through local elites, leaving customs and religions largely in place; satrapies paid set tribute and were linked by roads like the Royal Road.

dd-persia.q: Why did Persia fight Greece and Rome for so long?
a: They competed for the same rich borderlands like Anatolia, Syria and Armenia
Rome tried to impose Christianity on Persia
They disagreed about the Olympic Games
Persia wanted to conquer Spain
dd-persia.why: Their rivalry came from competition for the same rich borderlands: Anatolia, Syria, Mesopotamia and Armenia, with Armenia the great prize between Rome and Parthia.

dd-persia.q: What made the Arab Muslim conquest of Persia possible in 633–651?
a: Persia had already converted to Islam
Alexander's heirs invited the Arabs in
A great flood ruined Persia's farms
Persia and Byzantium had exhausted each other in centuries of war
dd-persia.why: Parthians and Sasanians fought Rome and Byzantium for about 700 years; after the ruinous war of 602–628, Arab armies struck both exhausted empires.

dd-persia.q: How did Iran differ from Egypt and Syria after the Arab conquest?
a: It stayed Zoroastrian to this day
It adopted Islam but kept its own Persian language
It became Arabic-speaking within a generation
It was never conquered
dd-persia.why: Most Iranians adopted Islam over centuries, but Iran kept Persian, helped by Ferdowsi's Shahnameh; Iranians still celebrate Nowruz and look back on Cyrus with pride.

dd-rome.q: How did Rome's government change between 509 BC and 27 BC?
a: From a republic of elected magistrates and a Senate to emperors
From a democracy to a monarchy ruled by Carthage
From an empire to a group of city-states
It stayed a kingdom throughout
dd-rome.why: Rome expelled its last king around 509 BC and became a republic; after civil wars between generals, Caesar's heir Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.

dd-rome.q: Why did Rome's manpower seem endless?
a: It hired soldiers from Persia
Every Roman family had ten sons
It turned beaten enemies into allies, and later into citizens
Carthage supplied its armies
dd-rome.why: Rome made defeated enemies into allies who supplied soldiers, and later into citizens; in AD 212 Caracalla made almost all free people Roman citizens.

dd-rome.q: Why did the Roman Republic collapse into civil wars?
a: Its kings returned to power
Hannibal conquered Rome
Germanic tribes destroyed the Senate
City-state institutions could not control generals with private armies
dd-rome.why: The Republic's institutions, built for a city-state, could not control generals with private armies and huge provinces, so rivals like Caesar fought for power.

dd-rome.q: What do most historians now say caused the fall of the Western Empire?
a: A chain of problems: civil wars, invasions, lost rich provinces
Lead poisoning from water pipes alone
A single defeat by Hannibal
The decision to build Constantinople
dd-rome.why: Most historians stress civil wars, the Huns driving Goths into the empire, pressure on a long frontier and the loss of Africa's taxes in 439.

dd-rome.q: Which part of Rome's legacy shapes much of Europe and Latin America today?
a: The worship of Jupiter
Gladiator games
Roman law and the Latin-based Romance languages
The Senate's power to name kings
dd-rome.why: Latin became the Romance languages, and Roman law shaped legal codes across Europe and Latin America; words like senate, republic and citizen come from Rome.

dd-alexander.q: What did Alexander the Great achieve between 334 and 326 BC?
a: He united Greece against Rome
He conquered the Persian Empire and reached India
He founded the Roman Republic
He defended Macedon against Persian invasion
dd-alexander.why: Alexander invaded Persia in 334 BC, won at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, took Egypt and Persepolis, and pushed into India until his army refused to go on.

dd-alexander.q: What had Alexander's father, Philip II, already given him?
a: The best army of its day and a plan to attack Persia
An alliance with Persia
A navy that controlled the Indian Ocean
Rule over Egypt
dd-alexander.why: Philip II built the best army of its day, with long-speared infantry and heavy cavalry, and had already planned the attack on Persia.

dd-alexander.q: Why was the Persian Empire open to conquest?
a: It had no army at all
It had already been conquered by Rome
It was vast but loosely held, and many subjects felt little loyalty
Its king surrendered without fighting
dd-alexander.why: The Persian Empire was vast but loosely held, and many subjects had little loyalty to Darius III; Alexander won others over by keeping local officials and customs.

dd-alexander.q: What happened to Alexander's empire after he died in 323 BC?
a: His son ruled it for fifty years
It became a single Greek republic
Persia immediately took it all back
His generals divided it into rival Greek kingdoms
dd-alexander.why: With no adult heir, his generals fought for forty years; the Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids ruled until Rome and Parthia absorbed them, ending with Egypt in 30 BC.

dd-alexander.q: What lasting legacy did Alexander's conquests leave?
a: Latin became the language of Asia
Greek became a shared language of the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East
Persian replaced Greek in Greece
Buddhism spread to Macedon
dd-alexander.why: The Hellenistic age made Greek a shared language for nearly a thousand years, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek; Greek art even influenced Buddhist sculpture.

dd-maya.q: How was the Classic Maya world organised politically?
a: As one empire ruled from a single capital
As dozens of rival kingdoms, each with a divine king
As a republic of elected councils
As a province of the Aztec Empire
dd-maya.why: The Maya never formed one empire: dozens of kingdoms such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán shared one culture but waged constant wars on one another.

dd-maya.q: What allowed Maya rulers to build temples, palaces and armies?
a: Gold mined in the Andes
Tribute paid by Spain
Maize, beans and squash that fed millions
Trade with China across the Pacific
dd-maya.why: Maize, beans and squash, grown on terraces, raised fields and forest plots, fed millions, and rulers turned that surplus into temples, palaces and armies.

dd-maya.q: What do many scholars think caused the southern lowland cities to empty in the 800s?
a: Severe drought striking a society already strained by war and crowding
A sudden Spanish invasion
A single volcanic eruption
An epidemic brought by Aztec traders
dd-maya.why: Lake sediments show severe droughts; many scholars think they hit a society already strained by warfare, deforestation and dense populations, and kings lost authority when rains failed.

dd-maya.q: Why did the Spanish conquest of the Maya take so long, until 1697?
a: The Maya had firearms
Spain was not interested in the region
Maya cities were all empty
With no single capital, kingdoms had to be conquered one by one
dd-maya.why: With no single capital to capture, Spain conquered kingdom by kingdom; the Itza at Nojpetén stayed free until 1697, over 170 years after the Aztecs fell.

dd-maya.q: What is true of the Maya people today?
a: They vanished when the cities emptied
Over 6 million people still speak Maya languages
They live mainly in South America
They speak only Spanish now
dd-maya.why: The cities emptied but the Maya did not vanish: over 6 million people speak about 30 Maya languages, mostly in Guatemala and south-eastern Mexico.

dd-africa.q: What made Ghana, Mali and Songhai rich and powerful?
a: Silver mines worked by Roman engineers
Control of West African gold traded across the Sahara
Spice plantations on the Atlantic coast
Taxes on Portuguese shipping
dd-africa.why: West Africa had gold and the Sahara had salt; rulers who controlled gold fields and caravan routes could tax them, raise armies and build cities.

dd-africa.q: What made regular trade across the Sahara possible?
a: Railways built by the empires
Rivers flowing through the desert
Camels, from the early centuries AD
Horses bred in Mali
dd-africa.why: From the early centuries AD camels made regular desert crossings possible, linking West African gold to North Africa and the Mediterranean world.

dd-africa.q: What drove the wealth of the Swahili city-states such as Kilwa?
a: Indian Ocean trade carried by the monsoon winds
Camel caravans to Morocco
Conquest of Great Zimbabwe
Tribute from Aksum
dd-africa.why: On the east coast the monsoon winds carried ships to Arabia and India and back each year, and towns like Kilwa grew rich on gold reaching the coast at Sofala.

dd-africa.q: How did Portuguese arrival from the 1400s change these trading states?
a: It made Saharan routes busier than ever
It had no effect on African trade
It led Mali to conquer Portugal
Atlantic trade, including in enslaved people, drew wealth from older routes
dd-africa.why: From the 1400s Atlantic trade, including a vast trade in enslaved people, drew wealth away from the Saharan and Swahili routes.

dd-africa.q: Why did modern Ghana, Mali and Zimbabwe take names from these old states?
a: They were their exact colonial borders
Europeans chose the names for them
To claim a proud African past that colonial writers had denied
They were ruled by the same dynasties
dd-africa.why: Colonial writers denied Africans had built such states, a claim archaeology disproved; at independence Ghana, Mali and Zimbabwe took their names.

a: A Greek kingdom founded by Alexander
An Ottoman province in the Balkans
A crusader state founded in 1204
The eastern Roman Empire, which carried on after the West fell
dd-byzantium.why: The eastern empire, ruled from Constantinople, carried on after 476; its people called themselves Romans, and 'Byzantine' was a later name popularised by Western scholars.

dd-byzantium.q: Why did Constantinople hold out for over a thousand years?
a: Sea on three sides, huge land walls, and skilled diplomacy
It had no enemies nearby
Western Europe always defended it
It paid tribute to Persia
dd-byzantium.why: Its near-impregnable site, a trained bureaucracy, a trusted gold coin and diplomacy that played enemies against each other kept it going; Greek fire helped beat Arab sieges.

dd-byzantium.q: Which event broke the empire into rival states that never fully recovered?
a: The building of Hagia Sophia
The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204
Constantine's move to Byzantium
The baptism of Vladimir of Kyiv
dd-byzantium.why: After losing most of Anatolia at Manzikert in 1071, the empire was broken apart by the Venetian-backed Fourth Crusade of 1204; the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

dd-byzantium.q: How did Byzantium help shape the Renaissance and European law?
a: It invented the printing press
It spread Latin across Asia
Justinian's law code and Greek texts brought to Italy by fleeing scholars
It founded Europe's first universities in Spain
dd-byzantium.why: Justinian's law code became the basis of civil law in much of Europe, and Byzantine scholars fleeing to Italy brought ancient Greek texts that fed the Renaissance.

dd-byzantium.q: Which Byzantine legacy is still alive among many Slavic peoples?
a: Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet
Greek fire
The solidus coin
Rule by Roman emperors
dd-byzantium.why: Missionaries spread Orthodox Christianity and the forerunner of Cyrillic to the Slavs; today over 200 million Orthodox Christians live from Greece and Serbia to Russia.

dd-vikings.q: How did Viking activity change between the sack of Lindisfarne in 793 and about 1000?
a: Raiding grew into conquest and settlement across Europe and the Atlantic
Vikings stopped raiding and turned only to farming at home
Vikings were driven out of every land they had raided
Raids stayed small and never went beyond Britain
dd-vikings.why: Raids grew into conquest: the Danelaw in England, Normandy in France, Dublin, Iceland, Greenland and, briefly, Newfoundland.

dd-vikings.q: What drove ambitious Scandinavian chiefs to go raiding, according to the chapter?
a: They were fleeing a Christian invasion of Scandinavia
They needed silver and land to reward their followers
Their kings ordered them to spread the Norse religion
The Frankish king paid them to attack England
dd-vikings.why: Chiefs needed silver and land to reward followers, and Scandinavia had little good farmland to spare, though historians still debate the causes.

dd-vikings.q: What gave the Vikings their great advantage in reaching so many places?
a: Horse archers who could ride across the steppe
Heavy warships armed with catapults
Light, shallow longships that crossed open sea and rowed up rivers
Maps bought from Arab merchants
dd-vikings.why: Longships drew only about a metre of water, so crews could land on any beach, cross open sea and row far up rivers like the Seine.

dd-vikings.q: What did Rollo's settlers in Normandy go on to do?
a: They founded Dublin and the first Irish towns
They settled Iceland and founded the Althing
They ruled Kyiv and traded with Constantinople
Their Norman descendants conquered England, southern Italy and Sicily
dd-vikings.why: Normandy grew from lands granted to Rollo in 911, and the Normans descended from his settlers conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy and Sicily.

dd-vikings.q: Why does Kyivan Rus still matter to several countries today?
a: It is a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
It was the first kingdom of Sweden
It founded the city of Constantinople
It is where the English language began
dd-vikings.why: Rus princes of Norse origin ruled Kyiv, and after Kyivan Rus became Orthodox in 988 it became a common root of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.

dd-russia.q: What is the broad story of Russia from Kyivan Rus to 1914?
a: A small principality that stayed confined to the area around Moscow
Growth from river princedoms into an empire covering a sixth of the world's land
A Mongol state that ruled China and Europe until 1917
A republic that became a monarchy under Peter the Great
dd-russia.why: From Rus' along the rivers, Moscow rose, expanded across Siberia, the Black Sea and Central Asia, and by 1914 ruled a sixth of the world's land.

dd-russia.q: Why did Russia keep expanding across Eurasia?
a: Mountains and seas forced it to look only eastward
Open plains with few barriers made expansion mean security and new lands to tax
The Ottomans gave it Siberia in exchange for peace
It needed colonies to settle a shrinking population
dd-russia.why: Russia grew across open plains with few natural barriers, where expansion meant security and new lands to tax, and Siberia's furs drew traders east.

dd-russia.q: How did Moscow rise to lead the Rus' lands?
a: It was the capital chosen by Rurik in 862
It defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut
It collected tribute for the Mongols, then threw off their rule in 1480
Byzantium made it the seat of its emperor
dd-russia.why: Moscow's princes rose as the Golden Horde's tax collectors, and Ivan III ended Mongol overlordship in 1480.

dd-russia.q: What finally brought down the tsars in 1917?
a: A Swedish invasion of St Petersburg
The sale of Alaska to the United States
A peaceful vote in the Duma to become a republic
A disastrous world war that exposed autocracy, poverty and late industrialisation
dd-russia.why: The First World War brought huge losses and bread shortages; strikes and mutinies forced Nicholas II to abdicate, and the Bolsheviks then seized power.

dd-russia.q: How does the empire's history still shape the region today?
a: Rival readings of Kyivan Rus' have featured in Russia's war on Ukraine
Russia is now smaller than any of its former republics
Ukraine and Belarus rejoined the Russian Empire in 1991
No country today claims Kyivan Rus' as its history
dd-russia.why: Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all claim Kyivan Rus', and rival readings of that shared past have featured in the full-scale war Russia launched in 2022.

dd-mongols.q: What did Genghis Khan and his heirs achieve in the 1200s?
a: They united the Mongol tribes and conquered lands from China to Russia and Iraq
They built a navy that ruled the Indian Ocean
They conquered Egypt and Japan after long sieges
They founded the Ottoman Empire in Anatolia
dd-mongols.why: Temüjin united the tribes in 1206; he and his heirs took northern China, Central Asia, the Rus principalities and Iraq, and Kublai completed Song China.

dd-mongols.q: What made Mongol armies so effective in the field?
a: Heavy armoured infantry fighting in tight ranks
Fast horse archers, each with several horses, covering huge distances
Gunpowder cannons bought from European traders
Large fleets that landed troops behind enemy lines
dd-mongols.why: Mongol riders were superb horse archers with spare horses, so armies could move scores of kilometres a day and outpace their enemies.

dd-mongols.q: Why did so many cities surrender to the Mongols without a fight?
a: The Mongols promised to make each city independent
The cities were mostly Mongol settlements already
Calculated terror: resisting cities were often massacred, and word spread ahead
Mongol envoys bribed every city governor
dd-mongols.why: Cities that surrendered at once were usually spared, while those that resisted were often massacred, and the news made others give in.

dd-mongols.q: Besides great destruction, what did Mongol rule bring across Eurasia?
a: A single empire that lasted unbroken until 1900
The end of all trade between Europe and China
The spread of Islam to China and Japan
Links that let merchants, envoys and ideas travel from Italy to China
dd-mongols.why: The Pax Mongolica protected merchants and travel, spreading paper money, gunpowder, maps and, probably, the Black Death.

dd-mongols.q: How is Genghis Khan remembered today?
a: Mongolia reveres him as its father; Iran, Iraq and Russia, as a destroyer
Everywhere as a peaceful lawgiver
As a minor chief forgotten outside Mongolia
As the founder of modern China's Communist Party
dd-mongols.why: Memory is divided: Mongolia reveres him as the nation's father, while Iran, Iraq and Russia remember him above all as a destroyer.

dd-habsburgs.q: What did the Habsburg family achieve between 1273 and 1918?
a: They united all of Germany into one nation-state
They rose from minor Swiss counts to rule a vast Central European empire
They conquered the Ottoman Empire and took Constantinople
They ruled France until the Revolution of 1789
dd-habsburgs.why: From Rudolf's election in 1273, the Habsburgs held Austria, the imperial title and, at their height, Spain and its empire, ruling for 640 years.

dd-habsburgs.q: How did the Habsburgs mainly gain their lands?
a: By conquering their neighbours in long wars
By buying territory from bankrupt kings
Through elections, inheritance and well-planned marriages
Through colonies founded by Habsburg merchants
dd-habsburgs.why: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry': marriages brought the Netherlands, Spain, Bohemia and Hungary when other lines died out.

dd-habsburgs.q: What held the Habsburg lands together, and why did that grow weaker?
a: A shared language, until Latin fell out of use
A common nation, until the family moved to Spain
Protestant churches, until the Catholic revival
The dynasty, Church, army and civil service, until nationalism spread
dd-habsburgs.why: The lands had no common language or nation, so dynasty, Church, army and civil service held them; that weakened as nationalism spread in the 1800s.

dd-habsburgs.q: What happened when Austria-Hungary collapsed after defeat in World War I?
a: New or enlarged states such as Czechoslovakia, Poland and Yugoslavia emerged
The empire was absorbed whole into Germany
Spain inherited the Habsburg lands
The Ottomans took back Hungary and Vienna
dd-habsburgs.why: Its collapse in 1918 created or enlarged Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Romania and Italy, with border and minority quarrels for decades.

dd-habsburgs.q: What visible legacy did the Habsburgs leave across Central Europe?
a: A single currency still used from Brussels to Lviv
Baroque palaces, churches and cafés, and Vienna as a capital of music
The German language as the region's only official tongue
A ruling monarchy still governing Austria today
dd-habsburgs.why: The Habsburgs left Baroque palaces, churches and cafés from Brussels to Lviv, and made Vienna a great capital of music.

dd-ottomans.q: What was the arc of Ottoman history from about 1300 to 1923?
a: A frontier state became an empire on three continents, then broke up
A Byzantine province that briefly rebelled and was reconquered
An Arab kingdom that ruled only Egypt and Arabia
A Persian dynasty that moved its capital to Vienna
dd-ottomans.why: Osman's small state took Constantinople in 1453, spread from Hungary to Egypt and Iraq, slowly lost land after 1683 and was dissolved in 1922.

dd-ottomans.q: Why could the early Ottomans expand so quickly?
a: They had the help of a large Venetian fleet
Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided
The Mongols handed them Anatolia
Europe's kings invited them in against the Pope
dd-ottomans.why: They rose on a frontier where Byzantium and the Balkan kingdoms were weak and divided, and built a strong centralised state.

dd-ottomans.q: How did the Ottomans rule their many Christian and Jewish subjects?
a: They forced everyone to convert to Islam at once
They expelled all non-Muslims from their cities
They let them keep their faiths in return for taxes and loyalty
They gave them full equality from the start
dd-ottomans.why: Non-Muslims paid an extra tax and faced limits, but could worship and run their own schools and courts; it was not equality.

dd-ottomans.q: What wore the empire down after the failed siege of Vienna in 1683?
a: A Mongol invasion led by Timur
The loss of Constantinople to Venice
The conversion of the sultans to Christianity
Europe's rising power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism
dd-ottomans.why: Historians stress reform as well as decay, but Europe's economic and military power, Russian expansion, debt and nationalism wore the empire down.

dd-ottomans.q: How does the Ottoman Empire still shape the world today?
a: Over 30 countries were once Ottoman, and many borders trace back to it
Turkey still rules most of the Balkans
The sultanate survives as Turkey's head of state
Ottoman rule left no trace outside Istanbul
dd-ottomans.why: Many borders, conflicts and mixed communities, from Bosnia to Iraq and Israel and Palestine, go back to the empire and its breakup.

dd-aztecinca.q: What happened to the Aztec and Inca empires in the 1500s?
a: They united to drive the Spanish from the Americas
Small Spanish forces, with native allies and disease, conquered both
They traded peacefully with Spain for two centuries
Portugal conquered them both in a single campaign
dd-aztecinca.why: Cortés took Tenochtitlan in 1521 with tens of thousands of native allies, and Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532; Inca resistance lasted until 1572.

dd-aztecinca.q: Why did peoples such as Tlaxcala join the Spaniards against the Aztecs?
a: Spain promised to make them Christian kings of Spain
They mistook the Spaniards for gods
They resented Aztec rule and the tribute they paid
They were Spanish colonists who had settled earlier
dd-aztecinca.why: Both empires were young and built by conquest; many subject peoples resented paying tribute, and Aztec enemies joined the Spaniards in large numbers.

dd-aztecinca.q: What role did European diseases play in the conquests?
a: They had little effect because Americans were immune
They struck only the Spanish soldiers
They arrived a century after the conquests ended
They killed rulers and armies and set off an Inca civil war
dd-aztecinca.why: Smallpox killed many of Tenochtitlan's defenders and its emperor, and in Peru an epidemic set off a civil war between royal brothers before Pizarro arrived.

dd-aztecinca.q: What did Spain build on the ruins of the two empires?
a: A new empire, with Mexico City and Lima as capitals and silver flowing out
A set of independent Indigenous kingdoms under Spanish protection
Nothing, since Spain soon abandoned the Americas
A single Inca-Aztec state ruled from Cusco
dd-aztecinca.why: Mexico City rose over Tenochtitlan, Lima became the capital of Spanish South America, and silver from Potosí and Zacatecas flowed to Europe and China.

dd-aztecinca.q: How do these civilisations live on today?
a: Their languages died out by 1600
Millions still speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag recalls Tenochtitlan
Their cities still stand unchanged as capitals
Spain still governs Mexico and Peru
dd-aztecinca.why: Despite a terrible population collapse, Indigenous peoples endured: millions speak Nahuatl and Quechua, and Mexico's flag shows Tenochtitlan's eagle and cactus.

dd-spanish.q: What did Spain build in the century after 1492?
a: A small trading network of forts on the African coast
The first empire that spanned the globe, from the Americas to the Philippines
A Mediterranean kingdom with no lands outside Europe
A colony limited to the Caribbean islands
dd-spanish.why: From Granada and Columbus in 1492, Spain came to rule Mexico, Peru, the Philippines, much of Italy, the Netherlands and, from 1580, Portugal.

dd-spanish.q: What paid for Spain's global empire and its wars across Europe?
a: Spices grown in the Philippines
Taxes on the Dutch provinces alone
Silver from mines such as Potosí and Zacatecas
Loans from the Aztec and Inca rulers
dd-spanish.why: Silver strikes in the 1540s paid for the empire; the Crown took a fifth as tax and used it to fight wars across Europe.

dd-spanish.q: Why did American silver not make Spain lastingly strong?
a: It was all sunk at sea before reaching Seville
Spain was forbidden from spending it by the Pope
The mines ran dry within ten years
It brought inflation and debt while rivals grew stronger on trade
dd-spanish.why: Silver also brought inflation and debt; Philip II defaulted four times, and the Dutch, English and French grew stronger on trade.

dd-spanish.q: What set off the wars that freed Spanish America?
a: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808
The loss of the Spanish Armada
The discovery of silver at Potosí
The United States' victory in 1898
dd-spanish.why: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 set off the independence wars, and by 1825 Spain had lost the American mainland.

dd-spanish.q: Which is a lasting legacy of the Spanish Empire?
a: Most people in the Philippines speak Spanish at home
Spanish is the native language of about 500 million people
Latin America has few Catholics today
Spain still governs Cuba and Puerto Rico
dd-spanish.why: Spanish is now the native language of about 500 million people, and Latin America is home to roughly 40% of the world's Catholics.

a: A Persian kingdom that never ruled in India
A British trading company based in Bengal
An empire founded by Babur in 1526 that came to rule most of India
A Maratha state founded by Shivaji
dd-mughals.why: Babur, from Central Asia, beat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526; Akbar and his heirs built a vast empire across India.

dd-mughals.q: How did the Mughals hold power over so many people?
a: They brought local elites, such as Hindu Rajput princes, into the system
They forced all subjects to convert to Islam
They ruled only through Persian governors sent from Iran
They relied on British troops to keep order
dd-mughals.why: Rajput princes became generals and in-laws, and nobles held ranked offices paid from land revenue; Akbar also promoted 'peace with all'.

dd-mughals.q: What weakened the empire after Aurangzeb?
a: A sudden Mongol invasion from the north
The loss of the Taj Mahal to Persia
A ban on trade with Europe
Costly Deccan wars, succession struggles and rising Maratha, Sikh and Afghan challengers
dd-mughals.why: Long wars in the Deccan drained the treasury; succession fights, breakaway governors and rival powers followed, and historians debate Aurangzeb's religious policies' role.

dd-mughals.q: Who gained most from the Mughal collapse in the long run?
a: The Ottoman Empire
The British East India Company, using Bengal's wealth
The Portuguese at Goa
The Dutch, who conquered Delhi
dd-mughals.why: The Company won at Plassey in 1757, took Bengal's revenues in 1765 and used them to conquer India; Britain exiled the last emperor in 1858.

dd-mughals.q: How is the Mughal past still present in South Asia?
a: Mughal rulers still govern part of India
Persian is India's national language
Its buildings are national symbols, and Urdu, food and music carry its influence
Its legacy is forgotten and plays no part in politics
dd-mughals.why: The Taj Mahal and Red Fort are national symbols, Urdu grew from the empire's speech, and the Mughal past is argued over in Indian politics.

dd-british.q: What happened to the British Empire between the 1600s and 1997?
a: It grew to about a quarter of the world's land, then unravelled after 1945
It stayed limited to North America and the Caribbean
It was conquered by France in the 1800s
It ended with American independence in 1783
dd-british.why: Despite losing America in 1783, Britain expanded in India, Australia and Africa to a quarter of the world's land, then rapidly decolonised after the Second World War.

dd-british.q: Which strengths helped Britain build such a large empire?
a: A huge population that settled every colony
Alliances with France and Spain
A powerful navy, early industry and banks that could fund wars
Control of the Silk Road trade
dd-british.why: A strong navy, early industry, banks and trading companies, and rivalry with France and Spain drove British expansion.

dd-british.q: How did a few British officials govern hundreds of millions of people?
a: By moving millions of British settlers to India and Africa
By relying on local troops, clerks, princes and chiefs
By banning all local government
By ruling only the coastal ports
dd-british.why: Britain relied on Indian troops and clerks, princely states and, in Africa, indirect rule through chiefs and emirs.

dd-british.q: Why did the empire unravel so quickly after 1945?
a: Parliament voted to abolish the monarchy
Germany took over the colonies
The colonies voted to join the United States
Britain was nearly bankrupt, nationalism was strong and both superpowers opposed empires
dd-british.why: After 1945 Britain was nearly bankrupt, nationalist movements were strong, and both superpowers opposed colonial empires; India left in 1947.

dd-british.q: Which describes how the empire's legacy is seen today?
a: English spread worldwide, but borders and partitions left lasting wounds still debated
Historians agree it brought only benefits
It left no trace in former colonies
Every former colony left the Commonwealth
dd-british.why: English, parliaments and common law spread, but so did wounds such as borders drawn in London and partitions; people still argue how to weigh them.

dd-napoleon.q: What was Napoleon's path from 1799 to 1815?
a: He seized power, became emperor and dominated Europe, then fell after Russia and Waterloo
He served loyally as a general under a restored king
He led France to conquer Britain and Russia permanently
He ruled Italy only and never governed France
dd-napoleon.why: He seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804, crushed Austria, Russia and Prussia, then lost his army in Russia and was beaten at Waterloo.

dd-napoleon.q: Why were the French willing to accept Napoleon's seizure of power?
a: He promised to restore the old nobility
He was the rightful heir of Louis XVI
Worn out by a decade of upheaval, they welcomed order
Britain demanded that France choose him
dd-napoleon.why: The revolution had opened careers to talent and made generals powerful, and a France tired of upheaval welcomed the order he offered.

dd-napoleon.q: What drew Napoleon into his ruinous wars in Spain and Russia?
a: A plan to restore the Holy Roman Empire
His attempt to strangle Britain's trade
A Russian invasion of France
His wish to free Spain's American colonies
dd-napoleon.why: His bid to choke Britain's trade drew him into Spain and Russia; the tsar's leaving the Continental System led to the 1812 invasion.

dd-napoleon.q: Which of Napoleon's changes outlasted his defeat?
a: His family's rule over France and Spain
French control of Russia's Baltic coast
The restored Holy Roman Empire
His Civil Code, which shaped law across Europe and beyond
dd-napoleon.why: Kings were restored in 1815, but his Civil Code shaped the law of much of Europe, Latin America and beyond, and remains French law today.

dd-napoleon.q: How did Napoleon's era help shape modern Europe?
a: By stirring national feeling that helped bring about nation-states
By ending all wars in Europe for a century
By making French the only language of Germany and Italy
By turning Europe into one federal republic
dd-napoleon.why: He ended the Holy Roman Empire, simplified Germany's map and stirred national feeling in Germany, Italy and Spain, feeding the nation-states of the 1800s.

dd-greatgame.q: What was the 'Great Game' of the 1800s?
a: A trade war between Britain and China over tea
The rivalry between Russia and Britain over Central Asia and Afghanistan
A contest between France and Britain for Egypt
Afghanistan's war to conquer British India
dd-greatgame.why: Russia conquered Central Asia while Britain expanded across India, and each feared the other would reach Afghanistan first.

dd-greatgame.q: Why did Britain worry so much about Russia's advance south?
a: It feared a Russian march through the passes on India
Russia threatened to invade Britain itself
Russia controlled the Suez Canal
Afghanistan was Britain's richest colony
dd-greatgame.why: Britain saw India as the jewel of its empire and feared a Russian advance through the mountain passes, though historians doubt Russia seriously planned it.

dd-greatgame.q: How did Afghanistan's place between the two empires shape it?
a: It was split in half between Russia and Britain
It was annexed into British India in 1893
It became a buffer state whose borders the empires drew
It became a Russian protectorate in 1907
dd-greatgame.why: Neither empire wanted the other on its border, so Afghanistan became a buffer, with the Durand Line and Wakhan Corridor drawn between them.

dd-greatgame.q: What has usually defeated invaders of Afghanistan, according to the chapter?
a: Losing the first battles on entering the country
A single united Afghan army
Lack of roads into the country
Holding the country, not entering it
dd-greatgame.why: Each invader won the first battles easily; mountains, local loyalties, cross-border refuges and foreign-backed governments made holding the country the hard part.

dd-greatgame.q: Which Great Game legacy still causes tension today?
a: The Durand Line, which divides the Pashtun people between Afghanistan and Pakistan
Russian rule over northern Afghanistan
British control of Afghan foreign policy
The 1907 partition of Tibet
dd-greatgame.why: The Durand Line of 1893 split the Pashtun lands; Afghanistan has never formally accepted it, and it still strains relations with Pakistan.

dd-israel.q: What happened in 1948 in the former British mandate of Palestine?
a: Britain annexed Palestine into its empire
Israel was founded and won the war; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled
A single Arab-Jewish state was founded under UN rule
Jordan and Egypt divided the whole territory between them
dd-israel.why: Israel declared independence in May 1948 and defeated its neighbours' armies; Israelis call it the War of Independence, Palestinians the Nakba.

dd-israel.q: What lies at the root of the conflict, as the chapter describes it?
a: A dispute between Britain and France over trade routes
Rivalry between Egypt and Jordan
Two national movements claiming the same land
A quarrel over oil fields in the Negev
dd-israel.why: Zionism sought a Jewish homeland in the land of the Bible, while Palestinian Arabs, long rooted there, sought independence and saw Jewish immigration as a threat.

dd-israel.q: Why was the 1967 war a turning point?
a: It ended with a Palestinian state on the 1947 borders
It returned Gaza and the West Bank to Britain
It led Egypt and Jordan to annex Israel
Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, and settlements followed
dd-israel.why: Since 1967 the core disputes have been borders, settlements, security, Jerusalem and the refugees, all tied to the territories Israel captured.

dd-israel.q: What did the 1993 Oslo Accords achieve?
a: Mutual recognition and limited Palestinian self-rule, but no state
A full peace treaty settling Jerusalem
The return of all 1948 refugees
The end of Israeli settlements
dd-israel.why: Israel and the PLO recognised each other and agreed on interim self-rule, leaving borders, Jerusalem, refugees and settlements for talks that never succeeded.

dd-israel.q: Where did the core disputes stand in 2026?
a: They had been settled by a two-state treaty
They remained unresolved, with the West Bank still occupied and doubts about two states
Israel had withdrawn from all the territories it took in 1967
No country recognised a State of Palestine
dd-israel.why: Israel still occupied the West Bank, Gaza lay largely in ruins after the 2023 war, and polls showed many on both sides doubting a two-state solution.

a: The wartime bombing of German cities by the Allies
The forced expulsion of Germans from eastern Europe after 1945
Nazi Germany's murder of about six million Jews, two in every three in Europe
A famine in occupied Poland caused by crop failure
dd-holocaust.why: By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered; Roma, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war and others were also persecuted and killed.

dd-holocaust.q: What role did antisemitism play in Nazi ideology?
a: It was central: Hitler saw Jews as a racial enemy
It was a minor issue the Nazis rarely mentioned
It was introduced only after the war began
It applied only to Jews outside Germany
dd-holocaust.why: Hatred of Jews had deep roots and took a racial form in the 1800s; Nazi ideology made it central, blaming Jews for Germany's defeat and for communism.

dd-holocaust.q: How did persecution in the 1930s become mass murder?
a: It was ordered all at once on the day Hitler took power
It grew step by step, and war and conquest turned it into mass murder
It was carried out by a handful of officials acting alone
It began only after Germany's surrender in 1945
dd-holocaust.why: From laws stripping rights to ghettos, then shootings from 1941 and death camps from 1942; it needed many thousands of officials, soldiers and collaborators.

dd-holocaust.q: How did the world respond legally after the war?
a: It declared that no individual could be held responsible
It handed all cases to German courts alone
It agreed that wartime crimes could not be tried
Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, and genocide was banned by UN convention
dd-holocaust.why: Leading Nazis were tried at Nuremberg, and the word 'genocide' was coined and banned by a UN convention in 1948, though many perpetrators were never punished.

dd-holocaust.q: How is the Holocaust remembered and reflected today?
a: It shaped human rights law and Germany's identity, and is remembered each 27 January
It is remembered only in Israel
It is no longer taught or commemorated
Remembrance is limited to a single museum in Berlin
dd-holocaust.why: It shaped human rights law and Germany's postwar identity, and the UN marks 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated, as Holocaust Remembrance Day.

dd-pacific.q: What was the course of Japan's war in Asia and the Pacific?
a: Japan defended its home islands but never attacked abroad
Japan conquered vast lands by 1942, was driven back, and surrendered in 1945
Japan and the US fought briefly in 1941, then made peace
China invaded and occupied Japan in 1937
dd-pacific.why: After war with China and Pearl Harbor, Japan conquered much of Southeast Asia, but was driven back from Midway on and surrendered in August 1945.

dd-pacific.q: Why did Japan seek an empire in Asia?
a: To spread democracy across the region
To free European colonies at the request of their peoples
To gain raw materials, markets and security for a great power
To protect China from a Soviet invasion
dd-pacific.why: Japan's military-dominated government sought an empire for raw materials, markets and security, and the war in China became a costly stalemate.

dd-pacific.q: What pushed Japan to attack the US in December 1941?
a: An oil embargo after it moved into Indochina, and a refusal to leave China
An American attack on Tokyo
A Soviet alliance with the United States against Japan
Japan's defeat at Midway
dd-pacific.why: The US, Britain and the Netherlands cut off its oil; rather than give up China, Japan gambled on seizing Southeast Asia's oil and crippling the US fleet.

dd-pacific.q: What happened to Japan after its defeat?
a: It kept its empire but lost its emperor
It was divided between the US and the Soviet Union
It became a communist state allied to China
It was occupied by the US and rebuilt as a pacifist democracy
dd-pacific.why: Japan lost its empire, was occupied by the US until 1952 and, under a new constitution renouncing war, became a democracy and US ally.

dd-pacific.q: How did the Pacific War reshape Asia beyond Japan?
a: European colonial rule was restored for good
Korea was divided, and independence movements in Southeast Asia gained pace
China became a Japanese ally
The atomic bomb was never used again or developed further
dd-pacific.why: Korea was split at the 38th parallel, China's civil war resumed, and Japan's defeat of European rulers speeded independence across Southeast Asia.

dd-vietnam.q: How did the Vietnam War end?
a: South Vietnam conquered the North in 1973
The country stayed divided under a UN peace force
US forces left in 1973, and Saigon fell to the North in 1975
France returned to rule Indochina
dd-vietnam.why: After the 1973 Paris Peace Accords US forces left, and in April 1975 Saigon fell; Vietnam was reunited under communist rule in 1976.

dd-vietnam.q: Why did the United States commit troops to Vietnam?
a: It feared communism would spread across Southeast Asia like falling dominoes
It wanted Vietnam's oil fields
France asked it to take over Indochina as a colony
North Vietnam had invaded the United States
dd-vietnam.why: US leaders saw Vietnam as a Cold War front; the 'domino theory' guided four presidents, and each feared being blamed for 'losing' Vietnam.

dd-vietnam.q: Why was the 1968 Tet Offensive a turning point?
a: It won the war for the Viet Cong outright
It led China to send troops to fight the US
It ended the bombing of Laos
Though a military failure, it turned American opinion against the war
dd-vietnam.why: The Viet Cong lost heavily, but leaders had said the war was being won; after Tet, Johnson stood down and moved towards peace talks.

dd-vietnam.q: What happened in the region after 1975?
a: Laos and Cambodia became democracies
Laos and Cambodia also became communist, and many 'boat people' fled Vietnam
Vietnam was split again at the 17th parallel
The US reoccupied Saigon
dd-vietnam.why: Laos and Cambodia became communist in 1975, the Khmer Rouge killed a vast share of Cambodians, and hundreds of thousands fled Vietnam by sea.

dd-vietnam.q: How do Vietnam and the US relate today?
a: They restored relations in 1995 and are now trading partners
They have had no contact since 1975
Vietnam is a US territory
They remain formally at war
dd-vietnam.why: Vietnam opened its economy from 1986, restored relations with the US in 1995, and is now a fast-growing trading partner.

dd-berlin.q: What happened to Berlin on 13 August 1961?
a: The Soviet Union began blockading West Berlin
East Germany sealed the border, and the Wall went up
Germany was divided into four occupation zones
The Western allies flew coal into the city
dd-berlin.why: East Germany sealed West Berlin's border with barbed wire, soon replaced by concrete, and the Wall split the city for 28 years.

dd-berlin.q: Why did East Germany build the Berlin Wall?
a: To keep out Western armies after the airlift
To protect Berlin from a NATO invasion
It was losing young and skilled workers who fled west
The four occupying powers agreed it would end the blockade
dd-berlin.why: Well over 2.5 million East Germans had fled west by 1961, most through Berlin's open border, draining the East of its young and skilled people.

dd-berlin.q: Why did the Wall fall in 1989 rather than earlier?
a: Gorbachev would not use Soviet troops, and East Germans fled and protested
West Germany invaded and forced the border open
