East Germany's leaders voted to reunite with the West
The United States paid the Soviet Union to remove it
dd-berlin.why: Gorbachev's Soviet Union no longer propped up communist rulers by force, and East Germans fleeing through Hungary and protesting at home forced the issue.

dd-berlin.q: What did reunification in 1990 mean for eastern Germany?
a: West Germany adopted the East's economic system
Berlin stayed divided as a free city
Eastern wages and jobs caught up within a year
It joined the West's democracy and economy, at great cost
dd-berlin.why: The East was merged into West Germany's democracy and economy; it cost a great deal, and eastern wages and jobs took decades to catch up.

dd-berlin.q: What marked the milestone Berlin passed in February 2018?
a: The Wall was finally demolished completely
The Wall had been gone longer than it stood
Parliament moved back into the Reichstag
The Stasi files were opened to the public
dd-berlin.why: The Wall stood for 28 years; by February 2018 it had been gone for longer, and only short stretches survive as memorials.

dd-partition.q: What happened to British India in August 1947?
a: It became one united, independent India
It was split into two independent states, India and Pakistan
Britain handed Punjab and Bengal to Pakistan alone
It became independent as three states, including Bangladesh
dd-partition.why: Pakistan became independent on 14 August and India on 15 August, with Punjab and Bengal cut in two by new borders.

dd-partition.q: What did the Muslim League under Jinnah argue?
a: That Britain should stay to protect minorities
That Kashmir should become fully independent
That Muslims were a separate nation, at risk in a Hindu-majority India
That India should be split along its rivers and railways
dd-partition.why: Jinnah's Muslim League argued Muslims were a separate nation and, from 1940, demanded Pakistan; Congress leaders, seeking a united India, rejected this.

dd-partition.q: Why did Britain bring the handover forward to August 1947?
a: Congress and the League had agreed a detailed settlement
Weakened by war, it chose a fast exit over a negotiated settlement
The United Nations ordered it to leave at once
Radcliffe needed more time to finish the border
dd-partition.why: Exhausted by the Second World War, Britain chose speed; Mountbatten argued it would limit bloodshed, while critics say the haste made it worse.

dd-partition.q: What happened to people when the new borders were announced?
a: Most stayed put, as the borders followed old provinces
Only soldiers and officials were moved
Between 10 and 20 million people fled, amid massacres on both sides
Britain organised a peaceful exchange of populations
dd-partition.why: Hindus and Sikhs fled east and Muslims west, in one of history's largest migrations, while mobs and militias on all sides killed hundreds of thousands.

dd-partition.q: How does partition still shape the region today?
a: India and Pakistan remain rivals, both claiming divided Kashmir
Pakistan and India have since reunited as one federation
Kashmir became an independent state after a UN plebiscite
The border is open, so split families visit freely
dd-partition.why: The two nuclear-armed rivals have fought several wars, clashed again in 2025, and both still claim Kashmir, divided along the Line of Control.

dd-rwanda.q: What happened in Rwanda between April and July 1994?
a: A border war with Uganda over refugees
Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in 100 days
Belgium returned to restore colonial rule
A peaceful election ended the Tutsi monarchy
dd-rwanda.why: After the president's plane was shot down, extremist militias and soldiers killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, by UN estimates, until the RPF won the war.

dd-rwanda.q: How did Belgian rule help harden the Hutu–Tutsi divide?
a: It banned the Kinyarwanda language
It moved Tutsi herders out of the country
It fixed Hutu and Tutsi as 'races' on identity cards
It gave the Hutu majority control of the royal court
dd-rwanda.why: Influenced by racial theories, Belgium issued identity cards stating each person's group in 1933; in 1994 those cards decided who lived at roadblocks.

dd-rwanda.q: How did the genocide's organisers turn neighbours against neighbours?
a: Lists of names, militias, and hate radio calling Tutsi 'cockroaches'
Foreign armies forced villagers to fight
The UN peacekeepers handed over Tutsi refugees
Churches called for war against Uganda
dd-rwanda.why: The killing was organised: officials and the Interahamwe used lists, and radio spread hate for months, then broadcast names and hiding places.

dd-rwanda.q: What did Rwanda's war lead to beyond its borders?
a: A lasting peace across the Great Lakes region
Belgium's return as colonial ruler of Congo
Uganda annexing northern Rwanda
Two Congo wars, the second drawing in nine African countries
dd-rwanda.why: About 2 million Hutu fled, mostly to Zaire, among them armed militias; Rwanda's pursuit of them set off the Congo wars of 1996 to 2003.

dd-rwanda.q: Where does the conflict that grew from 1994 stand in 2026?
a: Eastern Congo is at peace after the Washington Accords
Fighting goes on in eastern Congo, where M23 holds Goma and Bukavu
Rwanda has merged with Burundi
The UN now governs eastern Congo directly
dd-rwanda.why: M23, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, took Goma and Bukavu in 2025; despite US- and Qatari-brokered deals, the war went on in October 2026.

a: Protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president
Russia annexed Crimea after a referendum
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union
dd-ukraine.why: Russia attacked from the north, east and south, partly from Belarus; it failed to take Kyiv, and the war became a long grinding struggle.

dd-ukraine.q: How did Russia's leaders see Ukraine and NATO's growth?
a: As part of Russia's historic sphere, with NATO's expansion a threat
As a fellow NATO member to be protected
As a neutral buffer they had no interest in
As a rival nuclear power threatening Moscow
dd-ukraine.why: Russia's leaders called NATO's expansion a threat, and Putin argued Russians and Ukrainians were 'one people'; most historians and international bodies reject Russia's claims about the war.

dd-ukraine.q: What turned Ukraine further away from Russia from 2014?
a: Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons
Russia seized Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas
Ukraine joined NATO and the EU
Belarus invaded Ukraine's north
dd-ukraine.why: After protests toppled a pro-Russian president in 2014, Russia annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas, and most Ukrainians looked increasingly towards Europe.

dd-ukraine.q: Which change in Europe did the war bring about?
a: Europe became more dependent on Russian gas
NATO dissolved its eastern commands
Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and defence spending rose sharply
Germany left the European Union
dd-ukraine.why: Neutral Finland and Sweden joined NATO, Europe sharply cut its reliance on Russian gas, and defence spending rose the most since the Cold War.

dd-ukraine.q: How is this war changing warfare elsewhere?
a: It proved tanks make drones useless
Cheap drones, used at huge scale, are changing how armies fight
It ended the use of trenches and minefields
It showed that air power alone wins wars
dd-ukraine.why: Both sides build millions of drones a year; small FPV drones hunt soldiers and vehicles, and armies everywhere are learning from it.

dd-terror.q: What did the United States do in response to the 11 September attacks?
a: It declared a 'war on terror' and invaded Afghanistan
It invaded Saudi Arabia, home of most hijackers
It withdrew its troops from the Middle East
It asked the UN to try bin Laden in court
dd-terror.why: President Bush declared a 'war on terror', and in October 2001 US-led forces toppled the Taliban, who had sheltered Osama bin Laden.

dd-terror.q: What did al-Qaeda hope its attacks on America would achieve?
a: A peace deal over Afghanistan
Draw the United States into a ruinous war
Win US support against the Soviets
Persuade the US to sell it weapons
dd-terror.why: Al-Qaeda blamed the US for its troops in Saudi Arabia and its support for Israel and Arab rulers, and hoped to draw America into a ruinous war.

dd-terror.q: What reason did the US and Britain give for invading Iraq in 2003?
a: Iraq had sheltered the 9/11 hijackers
Iraq had invaded Kuwait again
Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction
The Islamic State had seized Mosul
dd-terror.why: They cited weapons of mass destruction, but none were found; critics said the war was overreach, and years of insurgency and sectarian war followed.

dd-terror.q: How did the Islamic State come to rise?
a: It grew out of the Taliban government in Kabul
It was founded by Iraq's army after 2003
It began as a branch of Hezbollah
Al-Qaeda in Iraq survived and regrouped in Syria's civil war
dd-terror.why: Weakened by 2010, al-Qaeda in Iraq regrouped amid Syria's chaos and, as ISIS, seized Mosul in 2014 and declared a 'caliphate'.

dd-terror.q: Where did Afghanistan end up after twenty years of war?
a: A NATO-protected democracy
Ruled again by the Taliban, still in power in 2026
Divided between Pakistan and Iran
Governed by al-Qaeda's leaders
dd-terror.why: As US troops left in August 2021, the Afghan army collapsed and the Taliban swept back into Kabul; they still ruled in 2026.

dd-syria.q: How did Syria's 2011 uprising turn into civil war?
a: Assad resigned and rival parties fought over power
Assad met peaceful protests with bullets, and the country slid into war
Israel invaded and the army split
The Islamic State began the protests in Damascus
dd-syria.why: Security forces fired on protesters, starting in Daraa; some soldiers deserted to form the Free Syrian Army, and by 2012 it was full civil war.

dd-syria.q: What drove protests across the Arab world in 2010–2011?
a: Unemployment, corruption, food prices and police brutality under long-ruling leaders
Anger at falling oil prices in Europe
A call from the United Nations for elections
A war between Tunisia and Egypt
dd-syria.why: Young, fast-growing populations faced joblessness and rising prices under rulers in power for decades, and satellite TV and social media spread the protests quickly.

dd-syria.q: Why did Assad's regime fight rather than fall like Egypt's or Tunisia's?
a: It had the support of most Syrian rebels
Western powers protected it from the start
Its army and security chiefs came largely from its Alawite minority
Syria had no army able to remove him
dd-syria.why: Many security chiefs came from the Assad family's Alawite minority, so the regime fought on, and the war became a sectarian and international proxy struggle.

dd-syria.q: What changed the course of the war in Assad's favour from 2015?
a: A UN peace deal
Turkey's invasion of the north
Russia's air campaign
The US arming his army
dd-syria.why: Russian air strikes from September 2015 helped Assad retake Aleppo in 2016 and most of the country by 2018.

dd-syria.q: What was Syria's situation in 2026, after Assad's fall?
a: A settled democracy with all refugees home
Ruled again by Assad's family from Moscow
Divided between Russia and Iran
Al-Sharaa's government won sanctions relief, but the future remained uncertain
dd-syria.why: Ahmed al-Sharaa's government won sanctions relief and took over the north-east, but sectarian killings, Israeli troops in the south and ruined cities left much unsettled.

dd-humans.q: Where did our species, Homo sapiens, evolve?
a: In Europe, alongside the Neanderthals
In Africa, with the oldest fossils in Morocco
In Siberia, near Denisova Cave
In the Fertile Crescent
dd-humans.why: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa; fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are about 300,000 years old, and small bands later spread out across the world.

dd-humans.q: What helped modern humans spread into so many different environments?
a: Farming, which they took with them from Africa
Larger brains than the Neanderthals
Language, planning, trade and flexible tools
Horses that let them travel fast
dd-humans.why: Language, planning, long-distance trade and adaptable tools let small groups cope with deserts, rainforests and Arctic cold.

dd-humans.q: How did Ice Age conditions help people reach the Americas?
a: Low sea levels joined Siberia to Alaska
Warm seas let them sail across the Atlantic
Ice sheets made a bridge from Europe
Glaciers carved a canal through Canada
dd-humans.why: Low Ice Age seas exposed land between Siberia and Alaska, and people moved south, reaching Chile by about 14,500 years ago.

dd-humans.q: What did farming change for human societies?
a: It made early farmers taller and healthier
It ended disease by moving people away from animals
It kept populations small and stable
It fed many more people, leading to towns, cities and kings
dd-humans.why: Fields fed far more people than foraging; stored surplus could be taxed and fought over, opening the way to towns, cities, inequality and states.

dd-humans.q: What link to the Neanderthals do most people outside Africa carry today?
a: None; Neanderthals left no descendants
A little Neanderthal DNA, about 1–2%
Half of their genes come from Neanderthals
Only their stone-tool traditions
dd-humans.why: Modern humans and Neanderthals sometimes had children together, so most people of non-African descent carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA.

dd-languages.q: Who probably spoke the ancestor of the Indo-European languages?
a: Farmers in the Nile valley
Herders on the steppes north of the Black Sea
Traders in the ports of Phoenicia
Canoe voyagers from Taiwan
dd-languages.why: Most scholars, backed by ancient DNA, place its speakers on the steppe around 4000–3000 BC; their descendants carried related languages across Europe and into Iran and India.

dd-languages.q: Why does a language usually spread?
a: Because it is easier to learn than others
Because it has more words
Because its speakers grow in number or power
Because it has an alphabet
dd-languages.why: A language rarely spreads because it is better; farming, conquest, trade and religion spread their speakers' tongues, and people switch to the language of jobs and government.

dd-languages.q: What did nation-states from the 1800s do to languages within their borders?
a: Promoted one standard language, pushing regional ones aside
Gave every regional language official status
Banned the teaching of foreign languages
Replaced national languages with Latin
dd-languages.why: National schools, armies and radio pushed regional and Indigenous languages, from Breton in France to those of the Americas, toward the national standard.

dd-languages.q: What does today's world language map still show?
a: That most countries speak their ancient languages unchanged
That languages spread evenly across continents
That Mandarin is spoken on every continent
Old migrations and empires, such as Spanish in Latin America
dd-languages.why: Spanish and Portuguese in Latin America, English and French across Africa, and Arabic from Morocco to Iraq trace earlier conquests and empires.

dd-languages.q: What do revivals such as Hebrew and Māori show about endangered languages?
a: Only languages with alphabets can survive
Decline can be reversed
Revived languages stay in prayer and study only
Endangered languages always die within a generation
dd-languages.why: About two in five languages are endangered, but Hebrew became an everyday tongue again, and Māori language nests brought new young speakers.

dd-writing.q: What were the first Mesopotamian scribes mostly writing down?
a: Epic poems like Gilgamesh
Accounts of grain, animals and workers
Prayers for the temple gods
Letters between kings
dd-writing.why: Writing began as bookkeeping: most early tablets from Uruk list rations, sheep, beer and workers; literature came much later.

dd-writing.q: Why did early cities and kings need writing?
a: To collect taxes and trade with records that outlasted memory
To teach every child to read
To print holy books for the public
To send messages by sea
dd-writing.why: As cities, temples and kings collected taxes and traded goods, they needed records that would outlast human memory.

dd-writing.q: Why did the alphabet spread so widely?
a: It was invented by the Roman emperors
It used pictures that everyone recognised
A few dozen letters were far easier to learn than hundreds of signs
It was the only script that could be carved
dd-writing.why: One sign per sound meant a few dozen letters; Phoenician traders, then Greeks, Romans, empires and religions carried it far.

dd-writing.q: What did printing and mass schooling change about reading?
a: Reading moved from a small elite to most adults
It made handwriting illegal
It ended the use of the alphabet
It kept reading for scribes and priests
dd-writing.why: For thousands of years reading belonged to scribes and priests; in 1820 one adult in eight could read, and today about 88% can.

dd-writing.q: What do the world's scripts today still trace?
a: The order in which languages were invented
Where paper was first made
The location of ancient libraries
Old empires and faiths
dd-writing.why: Latin letters spread with European empires, Arabic script with Islam and Cyrillic with Slavic churchmen and later the Soviet Union.

dd-money.q: What is today's money mostly, and what gives it value?
a: Gold coins, valued by their weight
Paper notes, each backed by silver
Digital money, valued through trust in governments and central banks
Cryptocurrency, valued by the cost of mining it
dd-money.why: Almost all money is now digital, numbers in bank accounts, and its value rests on trust in the governments and central banks that issue it.

dd-money.q: What practical problem does money solve for ordinary people?
a: It removes the need for any debts
It lets them compare values, store wealth and settle debts with strangers
It guarantees that prices never rise
It replaces the need for trade
dd-money.why: Money lets people compare the value of very different things, store wealth and settle debts with strangers.

dd-money.q: Why did rulers want to issue coins and paper money?
a: To pay soldiers and collect taxes more easily, and for profit and power
To stop merchants from trading abroad
To replace barter, which every society relied on
Because banks refused to lend to them
dd-money.why: Coins and notes made it easier to pay soldiers and collect taxes, and the right to issue money brought rulers profit and power.

dd-money.q: What happened when governments printed far too much paper money?
a: Prices fell and goods became cheaper
Gold became worthless
Banks closed and switched to barter
Trust collapsed, and prices soared, as in Germany in 1923
dd-money.why: A note is worth something only if people trust others will accept it; in 1923 a dollar cost about 4.2 trillion marks.

dd-money.q: What does the dollar's role as the world's main currency give the United States?
a: Unusual financial power
Control of the euro
A link between its money and gold
Freedom from inflation
dd-money.why: The dollar is over half of world reserves and on one side of almost 90% of currency trades, giving the US unusual financial power.

dd-democracy.q: What was new about Athens around 508 BC?
a: Its king shared power with a Senate
Its male citizens voted directly on laws
All its residents, including women and slaves, could vote
It elected representatives to a parliament
dd-democracy.why: Athens became the first known democracy: adult male citizens voted directly in the Assembly, while women, slaves and foreigners had no say.

dd-democracy.q: How did assemblies such as Parliament come to limit kings?
a: Rulers needing taxes and soldiers bargained with those who paid and fought
Kings gave up power after reading Locke
The Pope ordered kings to share power
Foreign armies imposed them
dd-democracy.why: Assemblies grew out of the bargain between rulers needing taxes and soldiers and the people who paid and fought, slowly limiting royal power.

dd-democracy.q: What idea did the American and French revolutions spread?
a: That kings rule by the will of God
That only men of property should rule
That power comes from the people
That the Church should choose governments
dd-democracy.why: The revolutions of 1776 and 1789 declared that power comes from the people, and over the next 150 years the vote widened to all men and women.

dd-democracy.q: How did the vote change between the late 1700s and the mid-1900s?
a: It narrowed to men of property
It passed from parliaments to kings
It was abolished across Europe
It spread from men of property to all men, then women
dd-democracy.why: After campaigns by workers and women, the vote widened; New Zealand let women vote nationally first, in 1893.

dd-democracy.q: What has happened to democracy worldwide since about 2010?
a: It has declined in many countries, and autocracies again outnumber democracies
Every country has become a liberal democracy
Elections have been abolished almost everywhere
It has spread faster than ever before
dd-democracy.why: By V-Dem's count, at the end of 2025 there were 92 autocracies and 87 democracies; yet voters still remove governments peacefully, as in Hungary in 2026.

dd-medicine.q: What was the great medical change that came in a rush after 1796?
a: Doctors first explained illness by natural causes
Vaccines, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and germ theory
The first hospitals opened in Baghdad
Bloodletting became the standard cure
dd-medicine.why: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and Pasteur and Koch's proof that germs cause disease transformed medicine within a century.

dd-medicine.q: Why could doctors rarely cure diseases for most of history?
a: Governments banned medical research
They had no hospitals to work in
They did not know what caused diseases
They refused to study Greek writings
dd-medicine.why: Doctors could describe illnesses, but theories such as the four humours had no idea of germs, so treatments like bloodletting did little good.

dd-medicine.q: What turned medical discoveries into protection for millions?
a: Governments funding clean water, research and public health
Doctors keeping their findings secret
The return to Galen's teachings
Ending the use of microscopes
dd-medicine.why: Growing cities, industrial wealth and governments that paid for clean water, research and public health spread the benefits of new science.

dd-medicine.q: How did medicine and clean water roughly double how long people live?
a: By letting adults live past 120
Mostly by saving babies and children
By ending all infectious diseases
Mostly by curing old age
dd-medicine.why: Low life expectancy in the past was dragged down by child deaths; vaccines, clean water, antibiotics and better food saved children above all.

dd-medicine.q: What challenge to health remains today?
a: Smallpox has returned worldwide
Life expectancy is now equal everywhere
Germ theory has been disproved
Huge gaps between countries, and germs that resist antibiotics
dd-medicine.why: A baby in Japan can expect to live about 30 years longer than one in Nigeria, and resistant germs, pandemics and ageing pose new problems.

dd-plagues.q: What was the Black Death of 1347–1353?
a: A flu pandemic that began in Spain
A smallpox outbreak in the Americas
Bubonic plague that killed perhaps a third to half of Europe
A famine caused by failed harvests
dd-plagues.why: Plague arrived on ships from the Black Sea in 1347 and swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353.

dd-plagues.q: How did the Black Death travel from Asia to Europe?
a: Along trade networks, carried by ships, rats and goods
By birds migrating south for the winter
Through contaminated wells
With Crusaders returning from Jerusalem
dd-plagues.why: Pandemics follow people: the plague came west along trade routes, and ships, rats and trade goods did most to carry it.

dd-plagues.q: Why did smallpox devastate the peoples of the Americas?
a: They had no immunity to diseases long circulating in Eurasia
Their cities had no water supplies
The Spanish spread it deliberately in every city
It was a new disease that also killed most Europeans
dd-plagues.why: Indigenous Americans had never met diseases that had circulated in Eurasia for thousands of years, so smallpox, measles and others spread with terrible force.

dd-plagues.q: What did the Black Death change for Europe's surviving workers?
a: Serfdom was strengthened everywhere
Wages rose and serfdom weakened in the west
Workers lost the right to move
Most farms switched to enslaved labour
dd-plagues.why: With so many dead, workers were scarce; survivors demanded higher pay, England tried to freeze wages, and serfdom slowly faded in the west.

dd-plagues.q: What lasting tools did pandemics help create?
a: Plague-doctor masks still used today
The end of all long-distance trade
Quarantine, public health bodies and vaccines
Laws banning crowded cities
dd-plagues.why: From quarantine in Ragusa and Venice to the WHO in 1948 and vaccines, pandemics built public health; COVID-19 vaccines came in under a year.

dd-spices.q: What did Portugal set out to do in the late 1400s?
a: Conquer Venice and take its trade
Reach the source of spices by sea, around Africa
Find a western route to the Americas
Grow pepper and cloves in Europe
dd-spices.why: Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, opening a sea route to the spice lands.

dd-spices.q: Why were spices so valuable in Europe?
a: They hid the taste of rotten meat
Every merchant was forced to buy them by law
They grew in so few places and passed through many middlemen
They were the only way to preserve grain
dd-spices.why: Spices were luxuries for flavour, medicine and prestige; nutmeg grew only on the Banda Islands, and each merchant along the way added a mark-up.

dd-spices.q: What let Portugal and Spain cross oceans and seize ports?
a: Better ships, navigation and guns
Alliances with the Ottoman sultans
Maps bought from Venetian merchants
Help from Ming China's fleets
dd-spices.why: Better ships, navigation and guns let Atlantic states cross oceans and take ports, while profits from spices, silver and sugar funded more voyages.

a: A treaty dividing the world between Spain and Portugal
A Dutch trade in nutmeg for Manhattan
A market in Venice for American goods
A two-way flow of crops, animals, people and diseases
dd-spices.why: Columbus's voyages joined the Americas and the rest of the world, swapping maize, potatoes and chillies for horses, cattle, wheat and sugar, and spreading deadly diseases.

dd-spices.q: How does the Columbian Exchange still show today?
a: Spices still come only from Indonesia
In what the whole world eats, from Italian tomatoes to Indian chillies
Most of Europe still trades through Venice
Potatoes are grown only in the Andes
dd-spices.why: Before 1492 Italy had no tomatoes, India and Thailand no chillies and Ireland no potatoes; American crops now feed people worldwide.

dd-slavery.q: What was the Atlantic slave trade?
a: The shipping of about 12.5 million enslaved Africans to the Americas
A trade in sugar between Brazil and Portugal
European settlers moving to Africa to farm
The movement of Indigenous Americans to Europe
dd-slavery.why: From the early 1500s European traders shipped about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic, most to grow sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean.

dd-slavery.q: Why did colonists in the Americas turn to enslaved African labour?
a: African workers were paid more than Europeans
They wanted cheap plantation labour, and Indigenous populations had collapsed
European laws required it
Sugar could only be grown by Africans
dd-slavery.why: Profitable sugar needed large gangs of workers, and disease, conquest and forced labour had devastated Indigenous populations.

dd-slavery.q: How did European traders usually obtain captives?
a: By raiding deep inland themselves
By capturing them at sea
By buying them at coastal forts from African rulers and merchants
By taking them from Brazil
dd-slavery.why: Europeans rarely went inland; African states and merchants sold captives, mostly taken in wars and raids, for cloth, guns and other goods.

dd-slavery.q: What populations did the trade create in the Americas?
a: Mainly European communities in the Caribbean
Small groups that disappeared by 1820
Mostly Indigenous communities in Brazil
Large African-descended populations in Brazil, the Caribbean and the US
dd-slavery.why: The trade moved more people across the Atlantic than any migration before 1820, creating the large African-descended populations of Brazil, the Caribbean and the United States.

dd-slavery.q: Which legacy of slavery is still debated today?
a: Whether the trade ever happened
Racism built to defend slavery, and calls for reparations
Whether Brazil should restore the monarchy
How to restart sugar plantations
dd-slavery.why: Ideas of racial inferiority grew to justify slavery and outlived it, and debates over memory and reparations continue today.

dd-science.q: What did Newton's Principia of 1687 achieve?
a: It proved the Earth was flat
It explained the heavens and Earth with the same laws
It discovered the moons of Jupiter
It founded the Royal Society
dd-science.why: Newton showed that one law of gravity moves both falling apples and orbiting planets, uniting heaven and Earth under the same mathematics.

dd-science.q: How did printing help the Scientific Revolution?
a: It let the Church control new ideas
It replaced the need for experiments
It let scholars share results quickly and check each other's work
It made telescopes cheaper to build
dd-science.why: Printed books spread results fast, so others could test and challenge them, and even Galileo's condemnation could not stop the new ideas spreading.

dd-science.q: Why could Galileo and Leeuwenhoek see what no ancient writer had seen?
a: They read lost Greek texts
They used new instruments like the telescope and microscope
They travelled to China
They were paid by the Pope
dd-science.why: Galileo's telescope revealed Jupiter's moons and Leeuwenhoek's microscopes showed single-celled 'little animals', challenging old authorities with direct observation.

dd-science.q: How did science change death rates by 1900?
a: Germ theory, vaccines and clean water began a fall in deaths
Death rates rose because of new factories
Medicine stayed unchanged until 1950
Only the rich benefited from new discoveries
dd-science.why: Pasteur and Koch proved germs cause disease, and vaccines and clean water began the fall in death rates that let the world's population soar.

dd-science.q: What is the lasting legacy of the Scientific Revolution today?
a: Trust in ancient authorities like Galen
A ban on publishing unchecked ideas
Science taught only by the Church
A method of testing ideas by experiment and publishing them
dd-science.why: Testing ideas against observation and publishing so others can check them still drives modern medicine, computing and space flight.

dd-capitalism.q: What made the Dutch East India Company a milestone in capitalism?
a: It was run by the king
It sold shares that investors could buy and resell
It banned foreign trade
It printed the first paper money
dd-capitalism.why: From 1602 the VOC raised money from many investors by selling shares, traded on Amsterdam's exchange, often called the first modern stock market.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Adam Smith argue in The Wealth of Nations?
a: Free markets and competition make nations rich
Governments should own all factories
Countries should hoard gold
Trade between countries is harmful
dd-capitalism.why: Smith argued that self-interest in free markets benefits society 'as if by an invisible hand', and attacked mercantilist tariffs and monopolies.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Keynes say governments should do in an economic slump?
a: Cut all spending
Abolish the banks
Ban imports
Spend to revive demand
dd-capitalism.why: After the Great Depression, Keynes argued that government spending could revive demand and jobs, shaping the mixed economies built after World War II.

dd-capitalism.q: Which country began market reforms under Deng Xiaoping in 1978?
a: Japan
Vietnam
China
India
dd-capitalism.why: Deng's reforms let farmers sell surplus crops and opened China to foreign investment, starting decades of rapid growth.

dd-capitalism.q: What started the 2008 global financial crisis?
a: Risky mortgage lending in the United States
A war in the Middle East
The collapse of the euro
A pandemic
dd-capitalism.why: Banks made and traded huge numbers of risky American home loans; when house prices fell, the losses spread through the global financial system.

dd-pirates.q: What was the 'pirate republic' at Nassau?
a: A Spanish fort guarding silver fleets
A Royal Navy base for hunting pirates
A pirate haven in the Bahamas from about 1715 to 1718
A French colony on Hispaniola
dd-pirates.why: Hundreds of pirates, including Hornigold, Blackbeard and Vane, used Nassau's harbour in the neglected Bahamas until Woodes Rogers arrived as governor in 1718.

dd-pirates.q: Why did so many sailors turn to piracy after 1713?
a: Peace threw thousands of trained privateers out of work
Spain paid them to attack England
The Royal Navy doubled its wages
Pirates were legally licensed by Parliament
dd-pirates.why: Wars had trained thousands as licensed privateers; when peace came in 1713 many lost their work, and harsh merchant life pushed others to join willingly.

dd-pirates.q: Why could pirates find safe harbours in the Americas?
a: The Royal Navy protected them
Weak colonial government and merchants keen on cheap goods
Spain gave them its ports
They were all pardoned each year
dd-pirates.why: Colonies like the Bahamas were neglected, and merchants in places such as New York financed pirates and bought their stolen goods.

dd-pirates.q: How was the golden age of piracy brought to an end?
a: Pirates retired rich on buried treasure
Spain conquered the Bahamas
A great hurricane destroyed their ships
Pardons, naval patrols and colonial courts with mass hangings
dd-pirates.why: The 1717 pardon, Rogers taking Nassau, navy hunts and local trials under a 1700 law broke the havens; by about 1726 the great crews were gone.

dd-pirates.q: What does this history suggest about piracy today?
a: It returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia
It ended for good in the 1720s
It exists only in novels and films
It is now legal under licence
dd-pirates.why: Piracy never vanished; it reappeared off Somalia in the 2000s, while novels and films reshaped the golden age into a romantic legend.

dd-enlightenment.q: What did Enlightenment thinkers believe should guide how society is run?
a: Reason and evidence
The will of the king
Church tradition alone
Ancient custom
dd-enlightenment.why: They argued that reason and evidence, rather than tradition, Church or king, should decide how people live and are governed.

dd-enlightenment.q: What did Montesquieu propose to stop any ruler becoming a tyrant?
a: A state religion
Rule by philosophers
Separate legislative, executive and judicial powers
Abolishing all laws
dd-enlightenment.why: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that dividing power between separate branches protects liberty, an idea built into the US Constitution.

dd-enlightenment.q: Why did Enlightenment ideas spread so quickly in the 1700s?
a: Governments paid for every book
Cheap printing, rising literacy and coffee houses created eager readers
Universities taught nothing else
Kings ordered everyone to read them
dd-enlightenment.why: Rising literacy, cheap printing, salons and coffee houses gave new ideas a wide public, and banned books were often printed abroad.

dd-enlightenment.q: Which revolutions drew directly on Enlightenment ideas?
a: The Russian and Chinese revolutions
The Meiji Restoration and the Glorious Revolution
The Mexican and Iranian revolutions
The American, French and Haitian revolutions
dd-enlightenment.why: The American Declaration of Independence, France's Rights of Man and Haiti's revolt against slavery all used the language of natural rights and equality.

dd-enlightenment.q: What was a major contradiction in the Enlightenment?
a: It rejected all science
Many of its thinkers accepted slavery and excluded women
It banned printing
It defended rule by priests
dd-enlightenment.why: Jefferson owned enslaved people and most thinkers kept women out of politics; critics like Wollstonecraft and Toussaint Louverture used its own ideas against these limits.

dd-nationalism.q: What is the central idea of nationalism?
a: Each nation should govern itself in its own state
Kings rule by the will of God
All countries should merge into one
Trade should always be free
dd-nationalism.why: Nationalists believe that people sharing a language, culture or history form a nation that should rule itself.

a: By a vote of all Germans
Through Bismarck's wars against Denmark, Austria and France
By Napoleon's conquests
Through a treaty with Britain
dd-nationalism.why: Bismarck united Germany by 'blood and iron', and the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles after France's defeat in 1871.

dd-nationalism.q: Why was nationalism dangerous for Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire?
a: They had no armies
Their capitals were too small
They ruled many peoples who wanted their own states
They were too democratic
dd-nationalism.why: These empires ruled Serbs, Poles, Czechs, Arabs and many others. As each people demanded self-rule, the empires broke apart, finally after World War I.

dd-nationalism.q: What did Woodrow Wilson call for in 1918?
a: A return of the monarchies
A world government
German unification
Self-determination for peoples
dd-nationalism.why: Wilson argued that peoples should choose their own governments, encouraging new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.

dd-nationalism.q: Which event shows the dark side of nationalism?
a: The forced population exchange between Greece and Turkey in 1923
The founding of the Red Cross
The first modern Olympic Games
The invention of the printing press
dd-nationalism.why: Building nation-states often meant expelling minorities: about 1.6 million people were forced to move between Greece and Turkey in 1923.

dd-women.q: What did women's movements win over the century after Seneca Falls?
a: Equal seats in every parliament
University entry, control of property and wages, and the vote
An end to all pay gaps
The right to lead the Church
dd-women.why: Movements in dozens of countries won access to universities, rights to their own property and wages, and the vote, first in New Zealand in 1893.

dd-women.q: Why did Enlightenment ideas help women's rights campaigners?
a: They said only the rich should vote
They praised the old monarchies
Ideas of equal rights were hard to limit to men
They called for women to stay at home
dd-women.why: Wollstonecraft argued women were only less educated, not inferior, and claims of equal rights proved hard to restrict to men alone.

dd-women.q: How did the two world wars help win the vote in countries like Britain?
a: Women filling factories and offices made the case harder to refuse
Governments needed women as soldiers
Suffragettes stopped campaigning entirely
The wars ended militant protest by law
dd-women.why: War work by millions of women from 1914 shifted opinion, and in 1918 British women over 30 won the vote.

dd-women.q: After 1945, what changes let women plan careers as well as families?
a: Laws banning women from factories
The end of universities for men
Fewer service-sector jobs
The contraceptive pill, higher education and equal pay laws
dd-women.why: The pill, approved in the US in 1960, more education and equal pay laws such as Britain's in 1970 opened paid careers to women.

dd-women.q: Which describes women's rights around the world today?
a: Full equality has been reached everywhere
Big gains, but gaps in pay and politics remain
Women still cannot vote in most countries
Girls are barred from school in most of Asia
dd-women.why: Women vote almost everywhere, yet hold about 27.5% of parliamentary seats, earn roughly a fifth less, and Afghanistan alone bars girls from secondary school.

dd-communism.q: Where did the first communist revolution actually happen?
a: Industrial Britain in 1848
Germany after World War I
Russia in 1917
China in 1911
dd-communism.why: Marx expected revolution in industrial countries like Britain and Germany, but Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in war-weary Russia in 1917.

dd-communism.q: Why did Marx's ideas inspire millions of people?
a: Industrialisation brought great wealth alongside harsh poverty
They promised a return to monarchy
They were imposed by the Church
They guaranteed free travel abroad
dd-communism.why: Amid the harsh poverty of industrial society, Marx's promise of a classless society of equals drew millions of followers.

dd-communism.q: Where did communists most often win power?
a: In rich, peaceful democracies
Where wars had shattered old regimes or against colonial rule
Only through free elections
Mainly in Western Europe
dd-communism.why: World War I broke Russia's monarchy, war shattered China in the 1940s, and in places like Vietnam communists led struggles against colonial rule.

dd-communism.q: Why did communist rule collapse in Eastern Europe in 1989?
a: NATO invaded the Soviet bloc
China ordered its allies to reform
Mao's death ended Soviet support
Stagnant economies, lack of freedom and Gorbachev's refusal to use force
dd-communism.why: Planned economies stagnated, people resented the lack of freedom, and Gorbachev made clear he would not send tanks, so the regimes fell one after another.

dd-communism.q: Which describes the five communist-ruled states today?
a: They all run strict planned economies
They have all become democracies
China and Vietnam keep one-party rule but run market economies
They are all allied with Russia
dd-communism.why: China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea are still ruled by communist parties, and China and Vietnam have opened their economies to markets.

dd-climate.q: What happened to global emissions after the climate treaties of 1992, 1997 and 2015?
a: They fell to pre-industrial levels
They kept rising, reaching a record in 2025
They stopped completely after Paris
They halved within a decade
dd-climate.why: Despite Rio, Kyoto and Paris, burning fossil fuels released a record 38 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, when the world was about 1.4°C warmer.

dd-climate.q: Why does warming build up as fossil fuels are burned?
a: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries and traps heat
Coal smoke blocks out the Sun
Burning fuel heats the oceans directly
Factories release heat that cannot escape
dd-climate.why: Fossil fuels release long-buried carbon dioxide that traps heat and lingers for centuries, so warming grows as emissions accumulate.

dd-climate.q: Why has cutting emissions proved so hard for governments?
a: Scientists disagree that CO2 traps heat
Renewables have always cost more than coal
Cheap fuels underpin economies, and countries dispute who cuts first and pays
No country has ever signed a climate treaty
dd-climate.why: Fossil fuels were cheap and reliable, the benefits of cutting are global while costs are local, and rich and developing countries disagree over who should act first.

dd-climate.q: What does the IPCC conclude about the effects of warming?
a: Warming is entirely natural
It affects only polar regions
It will bring only milder winters
Human activity has warmed the planet, bringing more extremes and rising seas
dd-climate.why: The IPCC finds human influence has unequivocally warmed the planet, bringing heatwaves, heavier rain, melting ice and rising seas, with the poorest often hit hardest.

dd-climate.q: Which change in 2025 shows how the energy picture is shifting?
a: Renewables overtook coal as the largest source of electricity
Oil replaced coal for power stations
Every country closed its coal plants
The US rejoined the Paris Agreement
dd-climate.why: Solar and wind became the cheapest new electricity in most places, though debates continue over the speed of change, its costs and who pays.

dd-oil.q: How did oil's place in the world change during the 20th century?
a: It was replaced by coal for transport
It became the fuel of cars, ships, aircraft and war
It was used only for lamps
It stayed a minor American industry
dd-oil.why: Kerosene lamps came first, but cars, ships and aircraft made oil the fuel of the 20th century, and world wars were fought partly over access to it.

dd-oil.q: Why did oil beat coal as the fuel for transport?
a: It was found in every country
It produced no carbon dioxide
It packs much energy into an easily moved, stored liquid
Governments banned coal in 1912
dd-oil.why: Oil's energy-rich liquid form made it ideal for vehicles, and it also became the base of plastics and chemicals.

dd-oil.q: Why has oil so often been a source of conflict?
a: The cheapest oil lies in a few places, far from big users
Oil companies refused to sell to anyone
Oil was found only in Europe
OPEC banned all exports after 1960
dd-oil.why: This mismatch made governments fight for supplies and producers fight foreign companies for control, from the 1973 embargo to Kuwait in 1990.

dd-oil.q: What did the 1973 Arab oil embargo do to the West?
a: It lowered petrol prices
It ended US support for Israel
It made Western companies take over Gulf oilfields
It quadrupled prices, caused queues and pushed the West into recession
dd-oil.why: Saudi crude rose from about $3 to almost $12 a barrel, petrol ran short, and the shock spurred searches for new oil in the North Sea and Alaska.

dd-oil.q: Why is oil's future now being reshaped?
a: The world's oil has run out
Burning oil drives climate change, and electric cars are spreading
OPEC has banned new drilling
Plastics no longer use oil
dd-oil.why: Oil produces about a third of fossil-fuel carbon dioxide, so the shift to electric cars and clean energy is reshaping the industry, though demand still rose slowly.

dd-fascism.q: What did fascist regimes do once in power in Italy and Germany?
a: Built one-party states, rearmed and expanded by force
Held regular free elections
Disarmed and joined the League of Nations
Shared power with socialist parties
dd-fascism.why: Italy became a one-party state by 1926 and Hitler crushed opposition within months; both rearmed, seized territory, and Germany's invasion of Poland began World War II.

dd-fascism.q: Why were people drawn to fascism after World War I?
a: They wanted closer ties with Britain
Bitter veterans, ruined economies and fear of communist revolution
They hoped for a return to Roman law
Fascists promised to end all armies
dd-fascism.why: The war left resentment over defeat or broken promises, economic ruin and fear of a Russian-style revolution, and fascists offered order, pride and a strong leader.

dd-fascism.q: How did Mussolini and Hitler actually come to power?
a: By winning outright majorities in free elections
Through successful military coups
Conservative elites appointed them, hoping to use them against the left
Foreign powers installed them
dd-fascism.why: The king made Mussolini prime minister after the March on Rome, and Hindenburg's conservatives made Hitler chancellor, believing they could control him.

dd-fascism.q: What did fascism's wars lead to?
a: A lasting peace in Europe by 1940
The spread of fascism across the Americas
Fascist victory over the Soviet Union
Tens of millions dead and the Holocaust
dd-fascism.why: Fascism's wars killed tens of millions and led to the Holocaust; both leaders died in April 1945 and leading Nazis were tried at Nuremberg.

dd-fascism.q: How do Germany and Italy guard against fascism's return today?
a: Their laws ban reviving the old parties
They have banned all political parties
They remain under foreign occupation
They ban teaching about the war
dd-fascism.why: Both rebuilt as democracies whose laws, such as Italy's 1948 constitution, ban reviving the old parties, though small neo-fascist groups survived.

dd-internet.q: How did the internet grow from its beginnings?
a: From a 1990s shopping network
From ARPANET, a US research network begun in 1969
From Colossus at Bletchley Park
From Nokia's mobile phones
dd-internet.why: ARPANET grew into the internet, the web made it easy to use from 1991, and smartphones put it in billions of pockets after 2007.

dd-internet.q: Who paid for the first computers and networks?
a: Shops and banks
Universities using student fees
War and Cold War governments, for codebreaking and weapons
Telephone companies selling phones
dd-internet.why: Computers were built to break codes, aim artillery and design nuclear weapons, and US defence money funded early networks such as ARPANET.

dd-internet.q: Why did computers keep getting cheaper and more powerful?
a: Chips kept shrinking, roughly doubling in power every two years
Vacuum tubes became cheaper
Governments set fixed prices
Fewer people bought them
dd-internet.why: Moore's law held for half a century, from 2,300 transistors in 1971 to tens of billions on a phone chip today, so each device was cheaper than the last.

dd-internet.q: Which problems has the digital age brought along with its benefits?
a: The end of international trade
Fewer people able to read
The collapse of all tech companies
Surveillance, misinformation, cybercrime and screen time worries
dd-internet.why: Computing transformed work, shopping, news and friendship, but also brought surveillance, online misinformation, cybercrime and concerns about screen time.

dd-internet.q: Why are Taiwan and advanced chips central to world politics today?
a: Taiwan's TSMC makes most of the most advanced chips, including for AI
Taiwan invented the World Wide Web
Taiwan bans the export of computers
All AI is designed in Taiwan
dd-internet.why: AI chips are designed mostly in the US and made mainly in Taiwan, so rivalry over chips and AI between the US and China centres on the island.

dd-nuclear.q: What followed the Soviet Union's first atomic bomb test in 1949?
a: A treaty banning all nuclear weapons
The US gave up its bombs
An arms race reaching about 70,000 warheads by the mid-1980s
Nuclear weapons were used in Korea
dd-nuclear.why: The superpowers raced to build hydrogen bombs and intercontinental missiles, and by the mid-1980s about 70,000 warheads existed worldwide.

dd-nuclear.q: Why did the United States build the first atomic bombs?
a: It feared Nazi Germany would build one first
It wanted cheap electricity
Japan had already tested one
The Soviet Union threatened to attack
dd-nuclear.why: Fission was discovered in Berlin in 1938, and fearing a Nazi bomb, the US, with Britain and Canada, built one in the secret Manhattan Project.

dd-nuclear.q: Why did the Cold War rivals keep building ever larger arsenals?
a: Treaties required them to
Each believed only its own arsenal could deter the other
They planned to test them all in space
They wanted to sell them to allies
dd-nuclear.why: Each side believed its weapons deterred the other, leading to 'mutually assured destruction', with forces ready to strike within minutes.

dd-nuclear.q: What has the 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty achieved?
a: It abolished all nuclear weapons
It ended nuclear power stations
It made Japan a nuclear power
It has kept nuclear-armed states to nine
dd-nuclear.why: Joined by almost every country, the treaty has limited the spread of the bomb, and South Africa and Ukraine even gave up weapons they held.

dd-nuclear.q: Why are nuclear dangers growing again today?
a: Arsenals are growing, led by China, and the last US–Russian limits expired
The Non-Proliferation Treaty was cancelled
Every country now has nuclear weapons
Nuclear weapons were used in 2025
dd-nuclear.why: No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, but China is expanding fast and New START expired in February 2026, leaving no US–Russian limits.

dd-globalization.q: What happened to world trade after World War II?
a: It shrank as countries raised tariffs
Tariffs fell round after round and trade grew hugely
It was run only by the Soviet Union
It stopped until the 1990s
dd-globalization.why: Under the GATT and later the WTO, tariffs fell step by step, and trade grew from about a quarter of world output in 1960 to around 60% by 2008.

dd-globalization.q: Why did the Allies want rules for open trade after 1945?
a: They blamed 1930s tariff wars for the Depression and war
They wanted to stop Japan exporting
They hoped to end the use of the dollar
The Soviet Union demanded it
dd-globalization.why: Believing tariff wars had deepened the Depression and helped cause war, the US and Britain led the building of the IMF, World Bank and GATT.

dd-globalization.q: How did the shipping container change trade?
a: It made ships slower but safer
It was used only for oil
It slashed the cost of moving goods worldwide
It replaced trade by air
dd-globalization.why: Standard boxes lifted straight from ship to truck or train cut loading costs from almost $6 a ton to about 16 cents, making long supply chains cheap.

dd-globalization.q: Who lost out from globalisation, fuelling a backlash?
a: Consumers, who paid more for goods
China's exporters
East Asia's poorest people
Factory towns in rich countries that lost jobs
dd-globalization.why: Gains were uneven: consumers got cheaper goods and hundreds of millions escaped poverty, but factory towns in the US and Europe lost jobs and inequality rose.

dd-globalization.q: Which describes the direction of world trade today?
a: Tariffs are at record lows everywhere
Governments use tariffs and subsidies, and trade is splitting into rival blocs
All countries have left the WTO
China has stopped exporting
dd-globalization.why: After the 2025 US tariffs, the highest since the 1930s, governments protect industries and security, while others sign new deals such as RCEP and EU–Mercosur.

dd-humanrights.q: Why was the United Nations founded in 1945?
a: To keep the peace after World War II
To run a single world government
To replace national armies
Only to manage world trade
dd-humanrights.why: After the devastation of World War II, 51 countries founded the UN to prevent another world war and give countries a forum to settle disputes.

dd-humanrights.q: Who chaired the committee that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: Winston Churchill
Mahatma Gandhi
Eleanor Roosevelt
Nelson Mandela
dd-humanrights.why: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee, working with authors such as Charles Malik, P. C. Chang and René Cassin.

dd-humanrights.q: Which countries hold a veto on the UN Security Council?
a: Germany, Japan, India, Brazil and Italy
The five largest by population
Whichever members pay the most
The US, Russia, Britain, France and China
dd-humanrights.why: Five victors of World War II hold permanent seats and can veto any Security Council resolution.

dd-humanrights.q: Why was the Universal Declaration not enough to protect rights on its own?
a: It was never translated
It was not a binding law
Only Europe adopted it
It was cancelled in 1950
dd-humanrights.why: The Declaration set standards but did not bind states, so later treaties and courts tried to make rights enforceable.

dd-humanrights.q: Where does the International Criminal Court sit?
a: The Hague
Geneva
New York
Strasbourg
dd-humanrights.why: The ICC opened in The Hague in 2002 to try individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

dd-space.q: What was the Space Race's most famous result?
a: A Soviet base on Mars
Apollo 11 landing people on the Moon in 1969
The first satellite launched by Britain
A joint US–Soviet Moon base
dd-space.why: After early Soviet firsts like Sputnik and Gagarin, Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and twelve Americans walked on the Moon by 1972.

dd-space.q: Why were space rockets so closely tied to the Cold War?
a: They were built to carry tourists
They were invented by NASA for science
A rocket that reaches orbit can also carry a nuclear warhead
Both sides wanted to mine the Moon
dd-space.why: Both superpowers were building long-range nuclear missiles; Korolev's R-7, the first intercontinental missile, launched Sputnik and Gagarin.

dd-space.q: Why did each side race to win 'firsts' in space?
a: To show the world its system was more advanced
Because a treaty required it
To find new places to live
To share technology with each other
dd-space.why: Space firsts were propaganda, meant to prove that communism or capitalism was the more advanced system; Sputnik's shock led the US to found NASA.

dd-space.q: How did the Space Race change everyday life?
a: It ended the use of rockets
It made air travel obsolete
It stopped the arms race
Satellites brought weather forecasts, global television and later GPS
dd-space.why: Weather, communication and navigation satellites grew out of the race, and it poured money into science and computing.

dd-space.q: How does the 1975 Apollo–Soyuz docking connect to space today?
a: It led decades later to the International Space Station
It ended all human spaceflight
It gave the Moon to the United Nations
It made China the leading space power
dd-space.why: The handshake in orbit eased the rivalry and led to the International Space Station, built from 1998 by Russia, the US and partners.

dd-polynesia.q: What did the voyages of the Polynesians' ancestors achieve?
a: They conquered the coasts of Asia
They settled a vast triangle of empty islands, ending with New Zealand
They reached Europe before Columbus
They settled Australia for the first time
dd-polynesia.why: From Lapita times to about 1250–1300, voyagers settled islands no one had reached, from Tonga and Samoa to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand.

dd-polynesia.q: How did Polynesian navigators find islands without instruments?
a: They followed European charts
They drifted wherever the currents took them
They used stars, swells, clouds and birds
They sailed only within sight of land
dd-polynesia.why: Trained navigators steered by rising and setting stars and ocean swells, and read clouds, reflected swells and homing birds to sense land beyond sight.

dd-polynesia.q: Why did voyagers often sail against the prevailing easterly winds?
a: So they could ride home if they found nothing
Because their canoes could not sail downwind
To reach South America first
To escape European ships
dd-polynesia.why: Sailing deliberately into the wind meant a safe return was possible, showing these were planned voyages of discovery, not accidental drifts.

dd-polynesia.q: What happened to Polynesian societies after European contact from the 1760s?
a: They were left untouched until 1950
They conquered parts of Europe
They gave up voyaging willingly
Disease, missionaries and colonial rule arrived
dd-polynesia.why: Contact brought disease, missionaries and colonial rule; Hawaiʻi's monarchy was overthrown, and Rapa Nui and other islands came under foreign powers.

dd-polynesia.q: What did Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage to Tahiti help spark?
a: A revival of wayfinding, languages and Polynesian culture
France's nuclear tests in Polynesia
Proof that Polynesia was settled from America
The end of Polynesian independence
dd-polynesia.why: Sailing by stars, swells and birds alone, Hōkūleʻa showed the old skills worked and helped inspire a revival of voyaging and Māori and Hawaiian languages.

dd-brazil.q: How did Brazil become independent from Portugal?
a: After a long war led by enslaved Africans
Prince Pedro declared independence in 1822 and became emperor
Spain conquered it and set it free
A military coup created a republic in 1822
dd-brazil.why: The Portuguese court had fled Napoleon to Rio in 1808, and in 1822 Prince Pedro, the king's heir, declared Brazil independent as an empire.

dd-brazil.q: Why did Brazil stay united while Spanish America split into many republics?
a: Portugal's monarchy, ruling from Rio and then via its heir
It had no regions to divide
Britain ruled it directly
Its people all spoke Spanish
dd-brazil.why: A shared monarchy gave Brazil's regions a single centre of loyalty, so it stayed in one piece as Spanish America broke apart.

dd-brazil.q: What shaped Brazil into a deeply unequal society?
a: Rapid industrialisation in the 1500s
Equal land grants to settlers
Sugar, gold, coffee and slavery, with land held by a small elite
Mass immigration from Asia
dd-brazil.why: Nearly 5 million enslaved Africans worked plantations and mines, and abolition in 1888 brought no land or compensation, leaving power with a small elite.

dd-brazil.q: What helped bring the military coup of 1964?
a: A war with Paraguay
The fall of the monarchy
The building of Brasília
Inequality and Cold War fear of communism
dd-brazil.why: President Goulart's land reform plans alarmed landowners, business and Washington, and the generals then ruled for 21 years until 1985.

a: Sharply split, with Lula narrowly beating Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff
Ruled again by the military
Dominated by a single party
Governed by a restored emperor
dd-brazil.why: Brazil has been a democracy since 1985, but after Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 coup conviction, Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio in an October 2026 runoff.

dd-japan.q: What did the Meiji Restoration of 1868 do?
a: Restored the shogun's power over the emperor
Toppled the shogun and rebuilt Japan rapidly on Western lines
Closed Japan to all foreign trade
Made Japan a colony of the United States
dd-japan.why: Rebel samurai overthrew the shogun in the emperor's name, and the new government modernised so fast that Japan defeated Russia by 1905.

dd-japan.q: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns close Japan to most foreigners?
a: They feared Christianity and European powers could split the country
Japan had nothing to trade
The emperor ordered them to
China demanded it
dd-japan.why: Remembering the civil wars before 1600, the shoguns banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese and confined Dutch traders to Dejima.

dd-japan.q: Why did Japan give way to Perry's black ships in 1853–54?
a: It wanted American missionaries
Perry offered to make the shogun emperor
It had no answer to steam warships and feared China's fate
The Dutch had already invaded
dd-japan.why: Without a modern navy, and having watched Britain defeat China in the Opium War, Japan's leaders chose to sign treaties rather than fight.

dd-japan.q: What did Japan become after the Meiji reforms?
a: A neutral country with no army
A colony of Britain
A closed country once again
The first non-Western industrial nation and an Asian great power
dd-japan.why: Japan industrialised, won Taiwan in 1895, beat Russia in 1905 and annexed Korea in 1910, ruling its colonies harshly.

dd-japan.q: Why does the Meiji model still matter to Asia today?
a: Its state-led catch-up influenced later Asian economies
It ended all empires in Asia
It made Japan Asia's only democracy
It kept Japan out of every later war
dd-japan.why: Meiji Japan showed a state could deliberately drive rapid modernisation, a model of state-led catch-up that influenced later Asian economies.

dd-australia.q: What did the First Fleet found at Sydney Cove in 1788?
a: A Dutch trading post
A British penal colony on Aboriginal land
An independent Australian republic
A missionary settlement for Māori
dd-australia.why: Convicts and marines landed on land Aboriginal peoples had lived on for at least 50,000 years; Britain sent about 160,000 convicts until 1868.

dd-australia.q: Why did Britain send convicts to Australia?
a: It had lost America and needed a new place for them
Aboriginal leaders invited them
Gold had already been found there
France had offered to share the land
dd-australia.why: America had taken about 50,000 British convicts before independence, so overflowing prisons needed a new destination, and Britain also wanted a Pacific foothold.

dd-australia.q: Why was a treaty made in New Zealand but not in Australia?
a: Australia had no Indigenous people
Māori asked to be ruled by Britain
Britain treated Australia as terra nullius, while Māori strength forced a treaty
Australia's colonies banned treaties
dd-australia.why: British law called Australia land belonging to no one, but in New Zealand Māori strength and missionary pressure led to the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi.

dd-australia.q: What did settlers' demand for land bring to Indigenous peoples?
a: Shared ownership of sheep farms
Equal votes from 1901
Protection under the Treaty of Waitangi in Australia
Frontier violence, disease, wars and land confiscations
dd-australia.why: In Australia frontier violence and disease devastated Aboriginal communities, while in New Zealand wars from 1845 to 1872 brought huge confiscations of Māori land.

dd-australia.q: How have both countries tried to reckon with their colonial past?
a: Through land rights, the Waitangi Tribunal and official apologies
By returning all land to Indigenous owners
By ending migration from Asia
By rejoining Britain as colonies
dd-australia.why: The Mabo case, the 2008 apology and the Waitangi Tribunal marked change, though debates continue, as in Australia's 2023 vote against an Indigenous Voice.

dd-frenchrev.q: What did the French Revolution do to France's monarchy between 1789 and 1793?
a: It made the king share power with Austria
It overthrew the monarchy, declared a republic and executed Louis XVI
It restored the king's absolute power after a short revolt
It replaced Louis XVI with his brother
dd-frenchrev.why: Crowds overthrew the monarchy in 1792, a republic was declared, and Louis XVI was guillotined in January 1793.

dd-frenchrev.q: Why did Louis XVI call the Estates-General in 1789?
a: He wanted to declare war on Britain
Paris crowds had already stormed the Bastille
His crown was bankrupt, and nobles and clergy paid little tax
The pope ordered him to reform the Church
dd-frenchrev.why: Wars, including France's help for the American revolutionaries, left the crown deep in debt, while the nobles and clergy were largely exempt from tax.

dd-frenchrev.q: What pushed the revolution towards the Terror after 1792?
a: War, fear of counter-revolution and hunger
A peace treaty with Austria and Prussia
Napoleon's seizure of power
The return of the king from Varennes as a popular hero
dd-frenchrev.why: With France invaded and in revolt, the Law of Suspects of 1793 allowed mass arrests; about 17,000 people were officially executed.

dd-frenchrev.q: How did the revolution's ideas spread beyond France?
a: Through French colonies in Asia
Through the Catholic Church's support for the republic
Through Britain, which adopted the revolution's constitution
Through its wars, continued by Napoleon, and French-style sister republics
dd-frenchrev.why: France's armies conquered Belgium, the Rhineland and more, and set up sister republics such as the Batavian and Helvetic, spreading equal citizenship and written constitutions.

dd-frenchrev.q: Which of these is a lasting legacy of the French Revolution?
a: The ten-day week
Decimal clocks with ten-hour days
The metric system and the political words 'left' and 'right'
Votes for French women from 1792
dd-frenchrev.why: The revolutionary calendar and decimal time did not last, but the metric system is used almost everywhere and 'left' and 'right' still describe politics.

dd-latam.q: What happened to Spain's American empire between about 1808 and 1825?
a: Most of its colonies won independence in years of war
Spain sold its colonies to the United States
It united into one large independent republic
Britain conquered most of it
dd-latam.why: About twenty new countries emerged; by 1824 Ayacucho ended Spanish power in South America, and only Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish until 1898.

dd-latam.q: What was the real trigger for the independence movements in Spanish America?
a: The discovery of silver at Potosí
Napoleon's conquest of Spain, leaving the colonies without a legitimate king
A ban on the Catholic Church in the colonies
Bolívar's election as king of Spain
dd-latam.why: When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808 and deposed its king, the colonies set up their own governing councils, and many soon declared independence.

dd-latam.q: Why did creole elites resent Spanish rule?
a: Spain had freed all enslaved people against their wishes
They were forbidden to own land or mines
Top posts went to Spaniards, and trade limits and taxes hurt them
Spain forced them to speak Portuguese
dd-latam.why: American-born creoles owned land and mines but were kept from top posts, and they disliked trade limits and new taxes from the Bourbon reforms.

dd-latam.q: What happened to Bolívar's dream of a united South America?
a: It came true and lasted until 1898
Brazil joined it in 1822
Spain accepted it as a self-governing dominion
It failed: Gran Colombia split apart by 1831
dd-latam.why: Gran Colombia broke into Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador in 1830 to 1831, and Bolívar died in 1830 as his union fell apart.

dd-latam.q: Which outcome of independence still shapes Latin America today?
a: Spanish and Portuguese remain the region's shared languages
Indigenous majorities have ruled most countries since 1825
Every country kept a monarchy
The region is still governed from Madrid
dd-latam.why: The new states kept the languages of their former rulers, while power stayed mostly with creole elites rather than Indigenous or Black majorities.

dd-ireland.q: How was Ireland divided after its war of independence?
a: Ireland was split between Britain and France
Six north-eastern counties stayed in the UK; 26 became a Free State
The whole island became an independent republic
Dublin stayed British while the rest became free
dd-ireland.why: Partition created Northern Ireland inside the UK and the self-governing Irish Free State, which became a republic in 1949.

dd-ireland.q: Why did the Great Famine leave such lasting bitterness towards British government?
a: Britain had planted the potato blight deliberately
Ireland had no contact with Britain at the time
London's limited relief, shaped by belief in the free market, came late
The Famine was confined to England
dd-ireland.why: Officials believed markets should not be disturbed; relief came late and was cut back, and most historians blame callous policy rather than a plan to kill.

dd-ireland.q: Why could Ireland not simply become one self-governing country in 1921?
a: Unionists in the north-east, mostly Protestant, wanted to stay British
Nationalists wanted to remain in the United Kingdom
The United States opposed Irish independence
Most Catholics lived in Ulster and wanted British rule
dd-ireland.why: Nationalist and unionist identities could not both be satisfied, so the north-east, with a unionist majority, stayed in the UK.

dd-ireland.q: What did the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 change in Northern Ireland?
a: It made Northern Ireland part of the Republic
It ended all contact between North and South
It gave unionists sole control of the government
It set up power sharing and let a majority decide its status
dd-ireland.why: Northern Ireland stays in the UK while a majority there wishes, and its government must include both unionists and nationalists.

dd-ireland.q: Why did Brexit make the Irish border a delicate question again?
a: It forced Ireland to leave the European Union too
The border now separates the EU from a UK outside it
It undid partition and reunited the island
It ended power sharing in Northern Ireland
dd-ireland.why: Ireland and the UK joined the European Community together in 1973; once the UK left, the Irish border became a frontier between the EU and a non-member.

dd-mexico.q: What did the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920 achieve?
a: It won Mexico's independence from Spain
It toppled Porfirio Díaz, and its heirs ruled Mexico for 71 years
It returned Texas and California to Mexico
It installed a French-backed emperor
dd-mexico.why: The revolution ended Díaz's long rule at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives, and the party its victors formed, later the PRI, governed until 2000.

dd-mexico.q: Why did Mexico lose about half its territory in the 1830s and 1840s?
a: It sold the land to pay for independence
Spain reconquered its northern provinces
Its huge, thinly settled north was indefensible against the expanding US
Britain took it in exchange for oil rights
dd-mexico.why: Texas broke away in 1836, and after the US–Mexican War of 1846 to 1848 Mexico ceded California and the Southwest.

dd-mexico.q: What fuelled the revolution against Porfirio Díaz?
a: Growth enriched foreign investors and landowners while villagers lost their land
Díaz had refused all foreign investment
A German invasion in 1910
Díaz had nationalised the oil industry
dd-mexico.why: Díaz's rapid growth benefited a few, and the 1917 constitution later promised land to the villages and national ownership of minerals and oil.

dd-mexico.q: How did the PRI keep power for 71 years?
a: By banning all elections after 1929
With constant US military support
By letting presidents rule for life
By absorbing unions, farmers and rivals and by managing elections
dd-mexico.why: The party traded jobs, land and favours for votes, rigged results when needed and repressed dissent, a system called 'the perfect dictatorship'.

dd-mexico.q: What is Mexico's relationship with the United States like today?
a: Mexico trades mainly with China and little with the US
Deeply tied economically, but strained by trade, migration and cartels
The US has annexed northern Mexico
Mexico has closed its border to US trade
dd-mexico.why: Since NAFTA Mexico has become the largest US trading partner, while tariffs, migration and drugs and guns crossing the border strain relations.

dd-germany.q: How was Germany first united in 1871?
a: Through Prussian-led wars against Denmark, Austria and France
By a popular revolution that overthrew all the German kings
By a vote of all German-speaking peoples, including Austria
By a treaty imposed by Britain
dd-germany.why: Bismarck's 'blood and iron' made Germany through three short wars, and the King of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in 1871.

dd-germany.q: Which conditions helped the Nazis win mass support?
a: A booming economy and a popular peace treaty
The Versailles treaty, economic collapse and fear of communism
A Soviet invasion of Germany in 1930
The return of the Kaiser
dd-germany.why: Hyperinflation in 1923 and the Great Depression, which left about 6 million jobless, discredited the Weimar Republic and made the Nazis the largest party in 1932.

dd-germany.q: Why was Germany split into two states in 1949?
a: Germans voted to divide their country
France insisted on a separate Rhineland state
The Cold War: each side built a Germany in its own image
The Nazi party survived in the east
dd-germany.why: The Western Allies' zones became democratic West Germany, in NATO, and the Soviet zone became communist East Germany, in the Warsaw Pact.

dd-germany.q: What happened to Germany's eastern lands after 1945?
a: They became an independent Prussian state
They were returned to Austria
They were shared between Britain and France
They went to Poland and the USSR; millions of Germans were expelled
dd-germany.why: Everything east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to Poland and the Soviet Union, and some 12 million Germans fled or were expelled westwards.

dd-germany.q: What is united Germany's place in Europe today?
a: It is outside the EU but tied to it by treaty
It is the EU's largest economy, now spending heavily on defence
It still has two separate governments
It depends on Russian gas more than ever
dd-germany.why: Since 1990 Germany has been the EU's largest economy and most populous member, and after 2022 it cut its reliance on Russian gas and raised defence spending.

dd-iran.q: What did the revolution of 1978 to 1979 do to Iran?
a: It restored the shah after a coup
It made Iran a communist state allied to Moscow
It ended the monarchy and made Iran an Islamic republic
It divided Iran into Russian and British zones
dd-iran.why: A mass uprising drove out Mohammad Reza Shah and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power, creating a state ruled under a senior Islamic jurist.

dd-iran.q: Why did many Iranians come to resent foreign powers?
a: Foreign meddling, above all the 1953 coup that removed Mosaddegh
Foreign powers had refused to buy Iranian oil since 1908
Britain had annexed Iran as a colony
The US had invaded Iran in 1980
dd-iran.why: After Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry, a CIA and MI6-backed coup toppled him in 1953, and the shah returned stronger.

dd-iran.q: Why did such different groups unite against the shah in the 1970s?
a: He had given up Iran's oil to the Soviet Union
Rapid Westernisation, secret-police repression and a widening wealth gap
He had declared war on Iraq
He had made Iran an Islamic state
dd-iran.why: Clerics, leftists, liberals and bazaar merchants were united against the shah's rule, enforced by the SAVAK secret police.

dd-iran.q: How did the Islamic Republic define itself after 1979?
a: As a close ally of the United States
As a neutral state with no foreign interests
As a constitutional monarchy
Against the US and Israel, building armed allies abroad
dd-iran.why: Its enmity with the US and Israel, and its allies such as Hezbollah and the Houthis, shaped decades of sanctions and nuclear disputes.

dd-iran.q: What happened in 2026 that has left Iran's future deeply uncertain?
a: US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, and war continued
Iran signed a lasting peace treaty with Israel
The shah's son was restored to the throne
Iran joined the 2015 nuclear deal again
dd-iran.why: Strikes killed Khamenei in February 2026, his son Mojtaba succeeded him, and the war disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

dd-koreas.q: How did the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 end?
a: With a peace treaty reuniting Korea
With an armistice near the old line, but no peace treaty
With North Korea conquering the whole peninsula
With Korea returned to Japanese rule
dd-koreas.why: After the front swung south and north, it settled near the 38th parallel; the 1953 armistice created the Demilitarised Zone, but no peace treaty was ever signed.

a: Koreans voted for two separate states
China and Japan agreed to share the peninsula
The Cold War began as Japan's empire fell; the superpowers split it
The Korean War had split the country
dd-koreas.why: US and Soviet troops split Korea at the 38th parallel, meant as a temporary line, and neither would accept a united Korea run by the other's side.

dd-koreas.q: What turned the Korean War into a long stalemate after late 1950?
a: China's armies entered and pushed UN forces south again
The Soviet Union invaded South Korea
The US withdrew all its troops
Japan joined the war on the North's side
dd-koreas.why: As UN forces neared its border, China intervened with hundreds of thousands of troops, and from mid-1951 the front stuck near the 38th parallel.

dd-koreas.q: How did the two Koreas develop after the war?
a: Both became poor military dictatorships to this day
The North grew rich while the South stayed poor
Both became democracies allied to China
The South became rich and democratic; the North a nuclear-armed dictatorship
dd-koreas.why: Export-led growth and the 1987 protests made the South rich and democratic, while the Kim family built nuclear weapons in an isolated North.

dd-koreas.q: What did North Korea signal about reunification in 2024?
a: It agreed to reunify under the South's government
It called the South a hostile state and dropped reunification
It signed a peace treaty with the South
It withdrew from its alliance with China
